<meta>This page serves as the Table of Contents (Synopsis) for the second part of Volume II of "Oedipus Aegyptiacus," following the title page. It outlines the final six thematic categories (Classes) that Kircher uses to organize his study of Egyptian wisdom and its influence on other ancient traditions.</meta>

# SYNOPSIS OF PART II.
## OF THE SECOND VOLUME.

**CLASS VII.** Hieroglyphic Mathematics. It encompasses the mathematical Quadrivium, that is, Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astrology. <note>The "Quadrivium" was the traditional four-subject curriculum of the liberal arts, focusing on numbers and their relationships to the physical and celestial worlds.</note>

**CLASS VIII.** Mechanics or Architecture. It investigates the construction of the marvelous machines used by the Egyptians.

**CLASS IX.** Iathrics, or Hieroglyphic Medicine. <term>Iathrics: Derived from the Greek word for "healing," this refers to the art and science of medicine.</term> It declares the Egyptians’ reasoning and method in healing; likewise, it treats the natural and supernatural care of individual limbs, where many curious things concerning herbs, stones, animals, medicinal amulets, and the exorcisms of "ensalmos" <note>original: "ensalmorum". These were rhythmic charms or incantations used in folk healing, particularly in the Spanish tradition which Kircher often references.</note> are brought forth from hieroglyphic doctrine.

**CLASS X.** Chemistry. It treats hieroglyphic Alchemy and its mysteries presented hieroglyphically.

**CLASS XI.** Magic, or Hieroglyphic Magic. It explains the origin of oracles, the types of divinations used by the Egyptians, magical sculptures, amulets, phylacteries, and "periapta" <term>Periapta: From the Greek for "hung around," these are charms or amulets worn around the neck for protection.</term>; furthermore, it sets forth at length the "Telesmata" <note>original: "Telesmata". Talismans or consecrated objects intended to draw down celestial influences.</note> and "Camaea" <note>original: "Camæa". Engraved gems or cameos often believed to have magical or medicinal properties.</note> of the Gnostics, together with a refutation of the superstitions encountered, in order to facilitate the understanding of the hieroglyphics.

**CLASS XII.** Metaphysical Theosophy, or Hieroglyphic Theology: In which the theology of the ancients—Zoroaster, Hermes, Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato—is compared with Egyptian theology to reveal the sources of hieroglyphic doctrine. Here, the mystery of the Most Holy Trinity—already accepted even then by the Egyptians through successive tradition from the first Patriarchs of the world—is explained through various hieroglyphic ornaments. <note>Kircher believed that the ancient Egyptians held a distorted but recognizable version of Christian truths, passed down from the time of Noah.</note> The nature of Angels and Demons is described, as well as their guardianship over individual classes of worldly things, and their descent and attraction through various ceremonies and rites performed in sacrifices using fumigations, scents, herbs, and stones. Thus, it is demonstrated in various ways that the Obelisks and other hieroglyphic inscriptions contain nothing other than the presentation of these aforementioned matters.

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’S HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
<meta>catchword: SE-</meta>
<sig>A</sig>

...they grasped [divine things], so that no mystery in sacred *Theosophy* <note>Divine wisdom or the direct knowledge of God.</note> was so hidden that they did not hope to be able to unlock it through the symbolic reasoning of Arithmetic and Geometry. For since sensible things <note>Physical objects perceived by the senses.</note> exist as certain images of those things which are invisible, and thus all things have a certain proportion to one another—though it be hidden and incomprehensible to us—and since these proportions cannot be conceived without likeness; hence it seemed best to the Ancients, in their continuous contemplation of heavenly things, to employ those images and likenesses which, as they were simpler and more abstract, would also more aptly express the principles of sublime things. Of such a kind are mathematical contemplations, which, since they are mostly occupied with numbers and Geometric figures, brought forth such an abundance of speculations that no great man among the Ancients approached the difficult mysteries of divine things by any other way than the aforementioned path.

<margin>The entire search for truth lies in mathematical disciplines.</margin>
Hence, **Boethius** appropriately asserts that no science of divine things can be reached *without geometry* <note>original: "ἀγεωμέτρητον" (ageometreton). This is a reference to the famous inscription at the entrance of Plato's Academy: "Let no one ignorant of geometry enter here."</note>. **Pythagoras**, truly, and **Plato**, and their followers, placed the entire search for truth in numbers and geometric figures; indeed, **St. Augustine** proves from Plato that the number of things to be created was the primary model in the mind of the Creator. **Aristotle** could certainly not hand down the difference between mathematical species to us in any other way than through the cooperation of numbers; for when he wished to hand down the science of how one natural form is present in another, he judged it necessary to flee to mathematical forms, when he said: *Just as a triangle is in a square, and so in all the rest in a hexagon* <note>original: "Καθάπερ τρίγωνον ἐν τῷ τετραγώνῳ, καὶ ἔτι πᾶσι ἐν τῷ ἑξαγώνῳ". This refers to Aristotle's idea in *De Anima* that more complex forms or souls contain the functions of simpler ones, just as a square can be divided into triangles.</note>; that is, just as a triangle is in a quadrangle, so the lower is present in its superior; which will be explained more fully hereafter. And to embrace many things in a few words, the entire doctrine of truth, by the testimony of **Boethius**, is encompassed both by multitude and by magnitude <note>Boethius divided the mathematical arts into "multitude" (discrete quantities like numbers) and "magnitude" (continuous quantities like space and time).</note>. No one should doubt that the Ancient Greeks drew all these things from the Egyptians; for just as they were the first inventors of letters and mathematics, so, relying on their knowledge of these things, they used them to express all the greatest mysteries of the higher Beings, as will appear shortly. Moreover, they divided the entire mathematical object into fourfold faculties, from which the name of the mathematical **Quadrivium** has remained even to this day: they are Arithmetic, Geometry, Music, and Astrology <note>In the 17th century, "Astrologia" often referred to the entire science of the stars, including what we now call Astronomy.</note>.

<margin>The Mathematical Quadrivium.</margin>
<margin>A species of natural magic called Thaumaturgy.</margin>
From these, then—as if from a most rich spring distinguished by four streams—other and further rivulets flowed out and increased the Egyptian school <note>original: "palæstram", literally a gymnasium or wrestling ground, used here metaphorically for a field of rigorous study.</note> in a wonderful way. Most celebrated among these were Mechanics, Architecture, and that more hidden part of natural Magic, which consists in the knowledge of constructing machines of every kind with a certain impenetrable dexterity of genius; which the more recent writers have therefore judged should be called **Thaumaturgy** <note>From the Greek *thauma* (wonder) and *ergon* (work). It refers to "wonder-working," or using mechanical engineering to create effects that appear miraculous.</note>. Each of these will be treated extensively in this and the following Class, as far as the powers of our genius permit. To the work, then.

<summary>Athanasius Kircher argues that the ancient Egyptians used mathematics—specifically the Quadrivium—as a symbolic language to understand divine mysteries, a system later adopted by Greek philosophers like Plato and Aristotle. He introduces the concept of Thaumaturgy (mechanical wonder-working) as a branch of natural magic rooted in these mathematical principles.</summary>

# TO THE MOST EXALTED PRINCE AND LORD OF THE HOLY ROMAN EMPIRE
# L O R D
# FERDINAND JOHANN
## Prince of Liechtenstein and Nikolsburg, Duke
## of Teschen,
->MY MOST GRACIOUS LORD.<-

Almost three lustra <note>A lustrum is a five-year period; Kircher is referring to a period of fifteen years.</note> have passed, Most Exalted Prince, since by some fate of mine, or perhaps by the breath of some favorable star, while you were staying with me in Rome, you took up the study of both the other Arts and Sciences and especially of divine Mathematics <note>original: "Matheseos"</note> with such ardor of soul, and mastered them with such perfection—a rare example—that as much as *the cypress stands above the wayfaring trees* <note>A quote from Virgil’s Eclogues, used here to describe the Prince's intellectual superiority over his peers.</note>, so much did You excel among others (such is the sublimity of Your genius), becoming a participant in all the secrets <note>original: "arcanorum"</note> contained within my works. Therefore, since I have found Your Highness to be delighted more than others by arguments involving more hidden and intricate Arithmetic, I found no one to whom I could more rightfully judge this present Treatise <note>original: "Syntagma"</note>—which is titled "On the Hieroglyphic Arithmetic of the Ancients"—to be consecrated in honor of Your name. Accept, therefore, this perpetual <term>tekmērion (a Greek term for a "sure sign" or "proof")</term> of my affection and respect for You. You will find here the most worthy pastures for Your most capable mind; you will enter the widest fields of new demonstrations, where you may test the strengths of Your supreme intellect. Farewell, Prince most distinguished in every kind of virtue, and as you have always been accustomed, do not cease to love Your friend, whom you have loved.

<header>CHAPTER I. 6 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC EXERCISES</header>

# S E C T I O N I.

<margin>In what Hieroglyphic Arithmetic consists.</margin>
Let no one, when they perceive that we are about to treat Arithmetic, imagine that we are going to hand down that common calculation used by merchants. Rather, we speak of that more recondite science of numbers through which, by a certain hidden analogy, the more mysterious part of Theology is concluded. Just as this science flows from the divine mind and the supreme Monad <note>original: "monade," referring to the ultimate "One" or the Divine Source from which all reality springs.</note> in a perennial emanation, so too it involves all the mysteries of the four Worlds explained above, and everything contained within them. To perform this truthfully <note>original: "ἀψευδῶς"</note>, let us take the starting point of our discussion from Unity.

## C H A P T E R I.

### On Unity and its Manifold Offspring.

<margin>Unity is the principle of all numbers.</margin>
Number is a certain natural, sprouting principle of the rational structure; for those lacking mind, such as brute animals, do not count. But number itself is nothing other than reason unfolded; for this reason, number is proven to be the principle of those things reached by reason, so that if it were removed, it is certain that nothing at all would remain to reason. Furthermore, Unity is the principle of all numbers, inasmuch as every number flows from it; and it is itself the end of all, for every number is resolved back into it. Nor does Unity obtain its origin from any other, nor is it divided into any number; rather, every number depends so essentially on unity that, far from existing without it, it is certain that all things would instead vanish into nothingness.

<margin>Unity is the Essence of God.</margin>
<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>
Moreover, this Unity is the eternal essence of God, the principle and end of all things, the Alpha and the Omega, opening all and closing all. Thus, all the beings of created things are nothing other than the small seals <note>original: "signacula," implying that every creature bears the "stamp" or mark of its creator.</note> of that supreme Unity. So says Hermes Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure, regarded as the author of the Hermetic Corpus, which explores theology, philosophy, and magic.</note> in the *Pimander*: *"The Monad,"* he says, *"that is, Unity, is the principle, root, and origin of all things; without a principle, however, there is nothing. But a beginning is not of the principle itself, but of another. The Monad, therefore, being the principle of all numbers, contains all while being contained by none; it begets every number, while being begotten by no number. Indeed, that which increases, increases by the power of the Monad, but it vanishes through its own weakness when it can no longer contain the Monad."* Nor does it lack the shadow of divine light that Unity is the limit and measure of all numbers, measuring all things and communicating its name to all numbers.

But because we have treated these matters most extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>One of Kircher's earlier works (1650) detailing the hieroglyphs on the Agonale Obelisk in Rome.</note> on page 178, leaving those aside, let us turn our pen to explaining the secrets of the Monad.

<image-desc>A small decorative woodcut tailpiece featuring a central floral bud flanked by symmetrical scrolling acanthus leaves.</image-desc>

->§ I.<-

<summary>Kircher defines Hieroglyphic Arithmetic not as commerce, but as a divine science of numbers representing the emanation of God (the Monad) into the created world. He argues that Unity is the source and end of all existence, citing the Hermetic tradition to support the idea that all things are "seals" of the One.</summary>
<keywords>Monad, Unity, Hieroglyphic Arithmetic, Hermes Trismegistus, Divine Essence, Pythagoreanism, Symbolism of Numbers</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section where Unity was established as the divine principle of all numbers. Kircher now moves from the nature of Unity to the paradox of the Infinite, exploring how the highest possible state (the Absolute Maximum) and the lowest possible state (the Absolute Minimum) meet in the divine nature.</meta>

<header>CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 7 CH. I.</header>

## § I.

->*How the absolute maximum coincides with the absolute minimum.*<-

<margin>
What the Absolute Maximum is.

What the Absolute Minimum is.

The Absolute Maximum and Minimum coincide without any contradiction.
</margin>
Boethius, the author of this striking statement <note>original: "epiphonematis," a rhetorical term for a pithy or concluding exclamation</note>, says clearly in Book 1 of his *Arithmetic*, as does Cardinal Cusanus in his book *On Learned Ignorance* <note>original: "de docta ignor." referring to Nicholas of Cusa’s famous 15th-century work "De Docta Ignorantia"</note>, that the absolute maximum coincides with the absolute minimum—indeed, that they are the same. Let us see how this is to be understood. The "absolute maximum" in this context denotes nothing other than the greatest possible thing, than which nothing greater can be provided; it is infinite truth, incomprehensible to any human or angelic intellect. For since this maximum is not at all of the nature of those things which admit "the exceeding" and "the exceeded" <note>meaning things that can be compared as more or less</note>, it must necessarily be above everything that can be expressed by the concept of our mind. For all things, whatever they may be, that are apprehended by us through reason or intellect differ so much among themselves and from one another that no precise equality can ever be assigned between them. However, that "greatest equality" is that which is neither other than nor different from anything else, nor does it imply any excess or defect. Thus, being placed above all intellect, it deservedly exceeds every concept of the mind, and so is absolutely the same as the maximum. Furthermore, since this absolute maximum is everything that can possibly be, and the "absolute minimum" is that than which a smaller cannot be conceived, it is clear that the absolute maximum coincides with the absolute minimum. Therefore, the oppositions which the apprehension of our weak mind establishes only have a place in those things that allow for "more" and "less." But the maximum and minimum, just as they are above all opposition, so they can contain no excess or defect in their concept, as Cusanus learnedly proves.

<margin>
Boethius’s statement is proved.
</margin>
Since, therefore, the absolute maximum is absolutely all things in actuality <note>original: "actu," a philosophical term meaning fully realized or "in act," as opposed to "in potential"</note> that can possibly exist, it is necessary that it coincide with the minimum without any opposition. And thus, that which exists above every affirmation and negation, and above all that can be conceived, is conceived "to be" no more than "not to be"; and everything that is conceived "not to be" is no more "not to be" than it "is." Truly, this is so, that it is all things; and so all things, that it is none; and so the maximum that it is the minimum; so light, that it is darkness; <note>original: "vti enim tenebræ eius, ita & lux eius"</note> *for as his darkness is, so also is his light* <note>A reference to Psalm 139:12, suggesting that from God's perspective, opposites are identical</note>. Otherwise, God could not be all possible things in actuality if He were not infinite and the boundary of all. This, however, transcends all intellect, which cannot combine contradictories in its own source through the path of reason; for we walk by those things known to us by nature itself, which—falling far short of this infinite power—cannot simultaneously connect the very contradictories that are separated by an infinite distance. Therefore, above every path of reason, we see that incomprehensible absolute or infinite maximum, to which nothing is opposed, coincide with the minimum. Thus, "Maximum" and "Minimum" in this place are transcendent terms of absolute meaning which, in their absolute simplicity, encompass all things above every "contraction" <note>original: "contractionem," a technical term used by Cusanus to describe how the infinite is limited or "contracted" into specific, finite forms</note> to a quantity of bulk or power. And this maximum

<summary>Kircher explores the mystical mathematical concept of the "coincidence of opposites," arguing that in the infinite nature of God, the greatest possible thing and the smallest possible thing are identical. This philosophical foundation uses the works of Boethius and Nicholas of Cusa to show that divine reality exists beyond human logic and the comparison of "more or less."</summary>

<meta>This page continues the logical progression from the previous section, where Kircher introduced the concept of the Absolute Maximum. He now moves to demonstrate that the absolute minimum is identical to the absolute maximum, and that both find their identity in the concept of "Unity" or the Number One, which he links to the nature of God and the Kabbalistic concept of Ein Sof.</meta>

<header>CHAPTER I. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS, THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.</header>

...and it now falls upon us to demonstrate that the minimum is nothing other than one.

### § II.

->How the Maximum and the Minimum are Absolute Unity.<-

<margin>The Maximum Unity equated with the Minimum Unity.</margin>
Since the concepts of "the exceeding" and "the exceeded" <note>This refers to the comparative relationship where one thing is greater than another</note> belong properly to numerical consideration, the soul is so accustomed to numbers that it cannot conceive of anything finite and bounded without them. If number were removed, the very distinction of things, their order, proportion, harmony, and the very multitude of beings—which cannot be conceived without numbers—would necessarily cease to exist. 

But if that number were infinite, then (according to what has been said) the maximum would coincide in actuality with the minimum, and all the aforementioned things would likewise cease. This is because for a number to be infinite is the same as for it to not exist at all <note>Kircher argues that an actual infinity destroys the distinct steps of counting, effectively reducing the number to zero or a non-entity in terms of practical math</note>. In a finite number, one cannot designate one so great that a greater cannot potentially exist; however, to designate the "maximum number in act," than which no greater can be given, is to designate that which has neither beginning nor end to its multitude. Such a thing would be an infinite number, and consequently, it would admit no distinction of things, no order, no plurality, and no comparison of "more" or "less." Indeed, it would not be a number at all. 

Therefore, it is necessary to reach a minimum in numbering, than which nothing less can exist; and this is unity (the number one). Since there can be nothing less than unity, this unity will be the "minimum simply," and thus it will coincide with the "maximum simply." This unity cannot be a "number" in the usual sense, as it lacks all comparison or excess; rather, it is the principle of all number. Nay, the minimum which this unity represents is the end of all number, because it is the maximum with which the minimum coincides. 

It is, therefore, absolute unity, to which nothing is opposed: the Maximum itself simply, who is God the Blessed. Just as this Unity is the greatest, so it is capable of being multiplied and shared <note>Meaning God's essence can be reflected in many created things without losing its own oneness</note>, since it is everything that can be. Therefore, Unity itself cannot become a number. And this is what the Hebrews call **Ein Sof** <note>original: "אין סוף" Ensuph; literally "Without End" or the Infinite</note>, as we have explained in our work on the Cabala—the infinity of the divine essence. The *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish mystical thought</note> calls this unity the great and boundless sea:

> *A unity simple and absolute in its simple and most absolute unity; in every corner, on every side, and in every examination by which you examine it, you will perceive nothing except simple and supremely absolute unity.* <note>original Hebrew: "אחדות פשוט בתכלית אחדות הפשיטות..."</note>

Let us now prove that this unity is so necessary that, if it did not exist, none of the created things could exist.

<meta>catchword: § III.</meta>

# § III.

->*Absolute Unity exists in act, and is thoroughly necessary.*<-

**I** shall demonstrate that if the "simply Maximum" <note>The "simply Maximum" refers to an absolute, unsurpassable greatness that lacks nothing</note> did not exist, nothing could exist. Since everything that is not the Maximum is finite and has a beginning, it must necessarily come from something else; for if it came from itself, it would have existed before it existed. Therefore, to avoid an infinite regress <note>A logical fallacy where one cause requires a previous cause forever without end</note>, we must grant a simply necessary maximum, without which nothing can exist. Furthermore, since no "being" can be understood without "to be," and the Maximum does not admit any opposition, it is necessary that the minimum coincides with the maximum. Thus, "absolute being" is nothing other than "Maximum being"; just as the greatest Truth is the Maximum in an absolute sense. It is therefore most true that the simply Maximum either is, or is not; or it both is and is not; or it neither is nor is not. For in the infinity of the divine essence, all these states can be considered without any opposition. From this, it is clear why Saint Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian known for "negative theology," which describes God by what He is not</note> repeatedly called God "Being and Non-Being"; and the *Zohar* <note>The foundational work of Jewish Kabbalah</note> explains this with the following very subtle words:

<margin>Why God is called Being and Non-Being by St. Dionysius.</margin>

->I have already told you that for the one who brings Being out of non-being, nothing is missing;<-
->Being is in non-being in the manner of non-being, and non-being is in being in the manner of being,<-
->so that you may learn that non-being is Being, and Being is non-being.<-
<note>original: "כבר אמרתי לך כי המוציא יש מאין אינו חסר ובי היש הוא באין בענין אין והאין הוא ביש בענין יש ללמד שהאין הוא היש והיש הוא האין"</note>

*I have already told you that to the producer of Being from non-being, nothing is lost, and that Being is in non-being as a thing of non-being, and non-being is in being as a thing of being, so that you may learn that non-being is Being, and Being is non-being.* <note>original: "Iam dixi tibi, quòd producenti Ens de non ente nihil decedit..."</note> It is therefore clear from what has been said that the simply Maximum necessarily exists—indeed, it is absolute necessity itself—and this is Absolute Unity. This Unity will therefore be the simply maximum, which we hinted at above, and which Saint Dionysius learnedly demonstrates in his book *On Divine Names*.

# § IV.

**T**here was never any nation that did not worship God and believe Him to be the simply Maximum. The Sissenii <note>Likely referring to the Essenes, an ancient Jewish sect</note> greatly adored Unity; Pythagoras asserted a single trinity. To understand this, it must be known that that which precedes all "otherness" <note>In this philosophical context, "otherness" (alteritas) refers to the state of being different, which allows for change and division</note> is eternal. For otherness is the same as mutability; but everything that naturally precedes mutability is immutable, and consequently eternal.

<margin>Unity is by nature prior to otherness.</margin>
Unity is therefore prior to otherness by its very nature, and since it naturally precedes it, it is eternal. Furthermore, all inequality arises from the "equal" and the "exceeding," from which inequality emerges, being posterior to equality by nature; which I show as follows. All inequality is resolved into equality, for the equal stands between the "greater" and the "lesser"; if, therefore, you take away that which is greater, you will have the equal; likewise if you take away the les-

...taken from the greater, you will once again have what is equal. Inequality, therefore, is reduced to equality through subtraction; thus, equality naturally precedes the unequal. Therefore, "otherness" <note>In philosophy, "otherness" or *alteritas* refers to the state of being different or distinct from something else; here, it refers to the beginning of multiplicity</note> and inequality exist together by nature: for where there is otherness, there is also inequality, and vice versa. Between two things, at the very least, there will be otherness, and these two together will create a "doubling" relative to one of them; hence, there will be inequality by the "excess" of the one. Otherness and inequality, therefore, exist together by nature, but from the previous arguments, equality precedes inequality by nature, and therefore it also precedes otherness. Consequently, equality must be eternal. 

Again, if there are two causes, one of which is prior to the other, the effect of the first will be prior by nature to the effect of the second. Now, Unity is either the connection itself, or the cause of the connection, for it is the "uniter" of all things. The "binary" <note>The number two, or the concept of duality</note>, however, is either division itself or the cause of division. If, then, Unity is the cause of connection and the binary is the cause of division—just as Unity is prior to the binary by nature—so too is connection prior to division by nature. But just as otherness and division exist together by nature, so do Unity and connection. 

Since it has been proven that whatever precedes otherness, division, or changeability is eternal (for it is the "simply Maximum"), and since nothing preceding otherness is anything other than Unity—and Unity is the same as equality and connection—it follows necessarily that Unity, Equality, and Connection are eternal. These are not three eternal things, but one eternal thing; for if there were several eternal things, otherness or multitude would exist before Unity, and one would lack the other, so that none of them would be truly eternal. They would be both eternal and not eternal, all of which is absurd and impossible.

<margin>Unity, equality, and connection, just as they have one being, so they have eternal being.</margin>
It remains, therefore, that Unity, Equality, and Connection, just as they are one, so they are also eternal.

And this is that "Triple Unity" which Pythagoras <note>An ancient Greek philosopher who believed that numbers were the fundamental reality of the universe</note> decreed should be adored; and which the Egyptians called *Hemphta* <note>Kircher's version of an Egyptian creator deity, often associated with the spirit or 'intellect' of the world</note>, and secretly expressed under the "serpent-circle-wing-shaped" figure <note>original Greek: ὄφι-κυκλο-πτερομόρφῳ (*ophi-kyklo-pteromorpho*)</note>—that is, through a globe, a serpent, and a wing joined into a single sacred symbol; concerning which, see the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>A famous ancient Egyptian obelisk in Rome which Kircher famously (and often incorrectly) attempted to decipher</note>.

<margin>The saying of Trismegistus is explained.</margin>
From Unity, therefore, is begotten the "equality of unity," and from these two proceeds "connection." For the one God is the very "entity" of things, or the form of being; Equality is the "equity" of beings, in which there is neither more nor less, nothing above and nothing below. Thus, the generation of Unity is nothing other than the repetition of Unity. For if you multiply Unity twice, or thrice, or more, Unity will then procreate something else from itself, such as the binary, the trinity, or any other number that fits created things. Therefore, in divine matters, Unity repeated only once begets the equality of unity—or, what is the same thing, Unity begets Unity—which is the eternal generation of the Father and the Son. From this, it is clear how that saying of Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom many mystical and philosophical texts were attributed</note> is to be understood:

> *The Monad begat the Monad, and reflected its own ardor back upon itself.* <note>original Latin: "Monas genuit Monadem, & in seipsam suum reflexerit ardorem." A "Monad" is a single, indivisible unit representing God</note>

Just as, therefore, the generation of unity from unity is a single repetition of unity, so the "procession" from both is the repetition of the unity of being and the unity of equality—or, what is the same thing, the connection and union of Unity and Equality. Correcty, then, from Unity and the Equality of Unity—that is, from both—proceeds the Connection. For connection does not belong to one alone, but Unity proceeds from Unity into Equality, and from the Equality of Unity into Union. ## CHAPTER II.
### *Concerning the Outpouring of the Monad into the four Worlds, or from the exterior.*

<margin>The fourfold Unity is explained.</margin>
**W**e have decided to set forth the fourfold unity in this place; the first is the most simple, or *Monadic* <note>original: "Μοναδική" — relating to the Monad, or the number one</note>; the second is *decadic* <note>original: "Δεκαδική" — relating to the number ten</note>, or denary; the third is *hecatontadic* <note>original: "Ἑκατονταδική" — relating to the number one hundred</note> or centenary; the fourth is *chiliatic* <note>original: "Χιλιαδική" — relating to the number one thousand</note> or millenary. The first looks upon the most simple and undivided unity, namely 1; the second looks upon the denary unity, which is also called the root of those following, and is 10; the third contemplates the centenary unity, and is the "squaring" of the preceding denary unity, namely 100; <margin>The nature of each Unity is declared.</margin> the fourth looks toward 1000, that is, the millenary unity, and is the "cube" of the preceding denary unity. Just as these four Monads beautifully explain the flow of a point into a line, a line into a surface, and a surface into a body; so the first can be rightly named the *central monad*, the second the *superficial* <note>In the sense of a line or surface level</note>, the third the *squared*, and the fourth the *solid*. And by this reasoning, with the two extremes established—unity and the thousand—the Pythagoreans defined all other numbers by their approach to or retreat from them; and this is that varied and mysterious *tetractys* <note>original: "τετραϰτύς" — a triangular figure consisting of ten points, sacred to the Pythagoreans</note> of Pythagoras. But between these two, they established two means, namely 10 and 100; and they called the denary the "root," the centenary the "square," and the millenary the "cube." Unity is without division, and is like a point; the denary is the root of the millenary with a single division, for it is "even-odd" <note>A term in Pythagorean arithmetic for numbers that can be divided once by two but not twice</note>, and is like a line; the centenary is with a double division, and is like a surface, for it is divided into 50 and 50, and then 50 into 25 and 25; the millenary indeed is with a triple division, and is like a body, for 1000 is first divided into 500 and 500; then 500 into 250 and 250; again 250 into 125 and 125, and there the division stops. Therefore, just as the monad is devoid of all division, so 10, admitting only one division, is aptly applied to the **Intelligences** <note>Angelic or celestial beings</note>; 100, by its twofold division, shows the **Soul**; and 1000, by its threefold division, aptly shows the **Corporeal World**. But let us explain each one.

<margin>The four unities are explained.</margin>
In the monadic unity, we contemplate the most simple **Mind**, the producer of all things, the divine essence; in the second radical unity, the **Angelic intelligence**; in the squared unity, the **soul**; finally, in the cubic, we behold the **body**; so that in these four distinct unities, we find distinct ratios of properties in each. This means nothing other than that the Mind embraces all things either divinely, intellectually, soulfully <note>original: "animaliter" — relating to the anima or soul</note>, or corporeally. Divinely, indeed, insofar as a thing is truth; intellectually, that is, as the thing is not the truth itself, but truly reflects it; soulfully, that is, as the thing is a likeness of truth; and finally corporeally, that is, as it leaves that likeness behind and enters into confusion.

<margin>The prerogative of the First Unity.</margin>
The First Unity is like the model [exemplar] of all things, preceding all multitude and, consequently, all otherness, opposition, inequality, and division. Although this kind of unity is neither the number two, nor three, nor four, it is nevertheless everything that the numbers two, three, and four consist of. If the species of things were distinguished like numbers, this absolute unity would be of no specific species, no name, and no shape, but would be "all in all." For this unity is the measure of every multitude of genera, species, substances, accidents, and all creatures—the one measure of all measures, the one equality of all equal and unequal things, and the connection of all things joined or separated. Just as unity enfolds, unfolds, and connects every number, whether even or odd, through its own simplicity, so too is this an infinite power: an ineffable unity. If you were to separate everything else from it—if you understood that nothing else has ever been, is, or could be; if you cast away all multitude and entered only into this most simple unity, such that you proved it to be not more "simple" than "non-simple," nor more "one" than "not-one"—then you would know that you have penetrated all secrets. For you will see its life is entirely incorruptible in its absolute unity, in which all things exist. The certainty of this absolute unity is so precise that the mind acts for and through it in all things. No question can exist that does not presuppose it, for it is the being of all beings <note>original: "entitas omnium entium"</note>, the essence of all essences <note>original: "quidditas omnium quidditatum" — 'quiddity' refers to the 'what-ness' or defining nature of a thing</note>, the cause of all causes, and the end of all things. We have seen the miracles of the Omnipotent Unity; now let us proceed to the other unities.

<margin>The power and nature of the Second Decadic Unity.</margin>
The second decadic <note>original: "decadica" — relating to the number ten</note> unity regards Angelic intelligence. Since it is the first to recede from that infinite unity, it is necessarily forced to enter into a mixture of intellectual composition. This composition is formed from "one and another"—that is, from opposites—which do not precede the unity but arise simultaneously with it. In its radical simplicity, these opposites are joined indivisibly and irresolubly. For the decadic unity is "without a root," as no unity precedes it except the first, and it does not arise from the multiplication of any other number, since it is the first to emerge. And although it is distant from the first unity by infinite intervals regarding its essence, it is the most simple expression of the divine work, the steward [promus condus] of the divine models. For the Creator Unity, exerting itself into action, first produced the dyad <note>the number two</note>, which is the decadic monad or the Intellectual World, the absolute image of God and the immediate model; it is the ultimate completion of the number ten, which it represents.

...is simply contracted. God is the light of intelligence, because He is its unity; intelligence, however, is the light of the soul, because it is the soul's unity; and the physical form of the soul's unity exists as number. We do not perceive the unity of the soul in itself, but rather we contemplate it through the sensory investigation of its body. In the same way, we do not see intelligence in itself, but in the soul; nor do we see the first, simplest, and most absolute Unity <note>meaning God</note> as it is in itself, but we contemplate it within intelligence as if within a number and a seal. Therefore, God is the form of intelligence, intelligence is the form of the soul, and the soul is the form of the body. Consequently, **Reason** is to be considered not as the root of the cubic <note>three-dimensional</note> body, but as the medium through which the intellectual root descends into the body; for reason is the instrument of the intellect, and thus the principle or instrumental root of physical things. 

The <term>Monad of one hundred</term> <note>original: "centenaria monas" — representing the number 100</note> symbolizes the soul, while the <term>Monad of one thousand</term> <note>original: "millenaria"</note> represents the body. Now, the number one thousand arises from the leading of the <term>denary</term> <note>the number 10, representing the Intellect</note> into the hundred—that is, from the multiplication of intelligence by the soul. For every number is perfected in the number ten; the number of the simplest unity proceeds through the simplest number into the ten. Therefore, those things which in the first Unity are the simplest unity itself, are found to be divided and varied in its numerical "unfolding" <note>original: "explicatione"</note>. Thus, the Intelligences—which are the number of the simplest and most absolute union—participate intellectually in the nature of number in relation to the First; yet intellectual difference, opposition, and otherness (and similar qualities that belong to number) are, in truth, absolute unity itself. Furthermore, "square" otherness and opposition <note>the level of 2D geometry or the soul</note> exist in Reason as intellectual unity. Finally, "cubic" <note>3D</note> oppositions and othernesses, which are sensible and physical, exist as unity within Reason.

<margin>The power and nature of the Fourth, thousand-fold Unity.</margin>

Lastly, the fourth unity—the thousand-fold—is the final and sensible unfolding of these unions. Just as the thousand is composed of many parts, so too is this unity. The **First Unity** therefore behaves in the manner of a **point**; the second in the manner of a **line**; the third in the manner of a **surface**; and the fourth in the manner of a **body** or a **cube**. The unity of the simplest point is everything that is contained within the linear, superficial, and physical unity; and the unity of the surface unfolds everything that is within the physical unity. Indeed, the three prior unities are not perceptible to the senses and are distinguishable only by the mind itself, which alone considers the point, line, and surface in isolation; the senses, however, can only grasp that which is physical. 

Therefore, if anyone tried to measure mental things by sensible things, they would be doing the same as someone who attempted to measure a point, a line, or a surface with a solid block; they would be acting imprudently, not to say stupidly. Every sensible thing must therefore be raised to the level of reason, or to intelligence, or even to absolute unity. If, in this way, we reduce every sensible, rational, or intellectual multitude to an absolute and infinite simplicity, nothing more can be affirmed about it. For at that point, a thing is no more a "stone" than a "non-stone"; rather, it is *all things*—namely, the simplest unity, God, blessed forever. Hence, just as the absolute unity of that sensible and rational stone is God, so its intellectual unity is intelligence. You see from these unities how the senses return into reason, reason into intelligence, and intelligence into God, where there is both the beginning and the completion in a perfect circle, as <term>Cusanus</term> <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a philosopher and mathematician</note> and <term>Franciscus Patricius</term> <note>Francesco Patrizi (1529–1597), a Neoplatonist philosopher</note> beautifully prove from the *Hermetic* writings.

### CHAPTER II. 14 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

->*A schematic explanation of the four aforementioned Monads.*<-

**F**rom what has been said, it is clear that a certain supreme World is established from the <term>theophanic</term> <note>original: "Theophanico" — a visible manifestation of God</note> descent of the first <term>monad</term> <note>original: "monas" — the number one, representing unity or God</note> into the <term>denary</term> <note>the number ten</note>; a second world from the second monad into the third; and a third World indeed through the descent of the third monad into the fourth, through which a return into unity is made. The center of the first is God, of the second intelligence, of the third reason, and of the fourth sensation. The first center possesses an indivisible entity—all things in all things, everywhere central. All things exist in the first World through absolute unity; all in the second through the intellectual; all in the third through the rational; and all in the fourth through the senses. But let us see how this <term>Pythagorean tetractys</term> <note>a triangular figure consisting of ten points arranged in four rows, which the Pythagoreans used to explain the nature of the universe</note> or "four-fold" exists within God, Angel, Soul, and Body, repeating several points from our *Musurgia*, volume 2, pages 448 and 451.

<margin>An example of mystical arithmetic in the numbers 1, 2, 3, 4</margin>
It is well established that one, two, three, and four joined together produce the <term>denary</term> <note>1 + 2 + 3 + 4 = 10</note>, which is the symbol of the entire Universe, the goal and limit of all things, and it explains the natural power of simple unity. From this very denary, which is a kind of second unity, the explanation of the square root is reached by an equal progression of the four-fold; for 10, 20, 30, and 40 joined together constitute 100, the square of the denary root. Likewise, the hundred-fold unity, by an equal movement, brings forth the thousand-fold; for 100, 200, 300, and 400 joined together constitute 1,000—the cube of the second unity, namely the denary root. There are, therefore, by natural influence, no more than 10 numbers, which are bounded by this four-fold progression; nor does any other variation of repetition occur beyond the thousand-fold (the cube) of the denary root, since the four-fold, through its three-fold repetition, then rises in the order of the denary. You have, therefore, the four-fold of unity, containing in its power the explanation of every number. For the general Unity is distinguished by four units, which are arranged here in a fitting order: the first is the simplest; the second is distant from the first by the addition of a <term>cipher</term> <note>original: "Zyphræ" — meaning the addition of a zero to turn 1 into 10</note> and constitutes the denary root; the third, denoting the hundred, constitutes the square; the fourth, denoting the thousand, constitutes the cube. Thus, the mind contemplates its own entire entity divided into these units in a four-fold way: in the simplest unity it considers God as the Creator of all; in the root or denary unity, it considers intelligence; in the square of intelligence, the contraction or soul; and finally, in the cubic number, which unfolds nothing further, it considers the body. All things in God are God; in intelligence, they are intellect; in the Soul, they are soul; in the body, they are body. And in the first unity, you behold all remaining units, though they are enfolded without division, without difference, and without distinction.

<margin>One skilled in mystical arithmetic can penetrate all secrets.</margin>
Certainly, if anyone were to penetrate this simplest unity alone, having cast aside all multiplicity—so that he proves it to be no more simple than non-simple, no more one than non-one—he should know that he has penetrated all secrets. For through this unity, he will see the unity of the mind stripped of all multiplicity, and he will find that its life is not corruptible in its absolute unity, in which it is all things. Moreover, the most perfect certainty of this absolute unity is such that the Mind acts all things in it and through it; for it is the entity of all entities, the <term>quiddity</term> <note>the "whatness" or essential nature of a thing</note> of all quiddities, the cause of all causes, and the end of all ends.

### CHAPTER II. 16 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACI: THE HIEROGLYPHIC ACADEMY

<margin>All numbers are contained within the Ten.</margin>
Therefore, as we showed at length above, and also in our *Musurgia* <note>original: "Musurgia Universalis," Kircher’s famous 1650 work on music theory and universal harmony</note> volume 2, page 451, every number is contained within the <term>denarius; the number ten</term>; but every progression of numbers is completed by the <term>quaternarius; the number four</term>. For four times ten makes 40. Hence, in the cited passage of the *Musurgia*, we distributed the whole harmonic Diagram into 40 circles. In that distribution, we used the numbers 1, 3, 9, 27; this numerical sequence is highly mystical and was established by Plato in the *Timaeus* <note>Plato’s dialogue concerning the nature of the physical world and cosmology</note> as the symbol of the soul, as will be discussed shortly. For these numbers, when collected together, constitute 40, a number most fitting for our purpose.

<margin>Explanation of the mystical numbers.</margin>
For just as 1, 2, 3, 4 is the most orderly progression of all numbers (for if you multiply the <term>binarius; number two</term> by itself, you produce 4; and if you add 1 to 3, the same number four results), so there is no progression more orderly toward the "forty of the four" (that is, 40) than 1, 3, 9, 27. For just as the first simple numbers 1, 2, 3, 4, taken together make 10, and this multiplied by 4 makes 40; so 1, 3, 9, 27 joined together constitute 40.

<margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin>
According to these principles, we shape the preceding Diagram, in which simple Unity (by which we denote God) touches four circles: namely, the greatest circle of all nature, the highest circle of the World, the highest of the Order, and finally the highest of the Choir. From this Unity, they participate in light and being step by step; first the Universe, after this the highest Order, and in the fourth and last place the highest Choir. You see, consequently, that one Choir communicates light to the next Choir all the way to the very last. You also observe how that which is found in the Universe and in any World is also found in the Order. For the ten-fold unity signifying <term>Intelligence; divine or angelic intellect</term>, the hundred-fold signifying the Soul, and the thousand-fold (as has been said) signifying the Body, exists in one way in the highest World—according to that World’s sublime, simple, and noble nature—and in another way in the middle world, and in yet another way in the lowest, shadowed World. For you will perceive that the lowest part of a higher realm coincides in all things with the highest part of the lower realm; for the "sense" <note>the capacity for perception</note> of a higher World is simpler than the "intelligence" of the Middle World, and the "sense" of a higher Order is more perfect than the "intellect" of the one following it.

<margin>All things in all things.</margin>
You see, therefore, how aptly the whole Universe is distributed—with its triple series of Worlds, nine tens, nine hundreds, and as many thousands—with all of them encompassed by the smallest little circles. To these nine-fold triads, if you add the three units indicated by the three larger circles, you will finally find the thousand-fold unity within the simple unity, marked by the greatest circle which surrounds and folds everything together. You will see how in any World, everything else is contained, and how the law and constitution of mathematical progressions are the same in each series of Worlds. For if the first ten-fold of the superior World were as two, the second as three, and the third as four, you will have a perfect progression. The second World, marked by the tens, will observe the same law of progression, as follows: 200, 300, 400; for if you join these correctly, a mixture of the "ten" emerges in each.

<margin>Further explanation of the figure.</margin>
From these things it is clearly evident how the unity of the intelligence of the lower World, even if it is not of the same nature as the superior or middle world (since it is further removed from their simplicity), nevertheless touches their nature in a wonderful way according to a certain analogy, as appears in the degrees of being of the three Worlds. <margin>Thrones.</margin>

For through these same actions, the minds of the first <term>triad; a group of three</term> are also themselves illuminated most closely and continually by God and set on fire by divine flame; they are both aided in these works and impelled by a certain sweet force, becoming the primary ministers of divine providence.

<margin>Dominations.</margin>

<margin>Virtues & Powers.</margin>
**Powers**, <note>original: *Potestates*</note> however, preserve order in these actions, keeping all things far from confusion. The third Order provides most closely for the human race: the 

<margin>Principalities, Archangels, Angels.</margin>
**Principalities** seem to have the care of Princes <note>secular rulers</note>; the **Archangels** care for the leaders of the people; and finally, the **Angels** care for individual humans. Through these, the whole human race is illuminated in its understanding, purged in its will, and perfected in both. For it was not fitting for that Goodness, which stands above all, to procreate all beings and then leave them to chance, or to permit them to remain alienated and discordant from itself; rather, if they were to remain whole, as is Goodness itself, it was necessary that it join the universe together and keep it continually suspended from itself.

### CHAPTER II. OF THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>The Heracleotic Chain.</margin>
...to be connected to Himself, and to return to the first fountain, He brought it about that they were made fit; but this could by no means happen unless the highest, middle, and lowest beings were bound together by certain chains. This was achieved most aptly through the love and ministry of these Minds <note>referring to the Angelic Intelligences</note>. And this is that Heracleotic Chain <note>original: "catena Heracleotica"; a reference to the "Golden Chain" of Homer or Heraclitus, symbolizing the Great Chain of Being that links all levels of existence</note> connecting all things; this is that ten-stringed instrument <term>decachordon</term> <note>a ten-stringed musical instrument used here as a metaphor for the harmony of the universe</note> of the nature of the Universe, adapting all things into one and the same most beautiful harmony. Thus God flows into all things, but most especially into the Angelic World; this in turn flows into the Celestial World, and the Celestial into the Elemental World in an admirable manner. Again, the triple Choir of the Angelic World, the triple Choir of the Celestial World, and the individual Choirs of this lower World each respond to one another; so much so that there is no string of the lower World that does not have corresponding strings in both the Celestial and Angelic Worlds, according to that famous pronouncement of the more secret Cabalists <note>Jewish mystics and scholars of the Kabbalah</note>:

<margin>Harmony of the Angelic Choirs with the World.</margin>
> *There is no herb below, which does not have a planet above saying to it: grow.* <note>original: "Nulla herba est inferiùs, quae non habeat planetam superiùs dicentem sibi, cresce."</note>

Therefore, when a string in any series of the World is struck, the remaining corresponding strings will immediately be animated into harmony by a certain hidden force and consensus. Beneath the perfect knowledge of these things lies the greatest mystery <term>sacramentum</term> of the entire secret of nature: whoever knows how to apply like to like will know how to produce marvelous effects in the nature of things. But you will understand these things better from the Diagram placed above, in which you see that the circle encompassing all things signifies the eternal, immutable, and immobile Unity.

<margin>Explanation of the figure.</margin>
The three circles represent the three Worlds: the Elemental, the Celestial, and the Angelic. Each of these is again seen divided into three other circles, as if into three Choirs; and the individual Choirs of each World are further divided into three small circles, representing the degrees of beings and things in the Universe. The first Worldly circle signifies, through its 9 small circles, the 9 Choirs of Angels. The second signifies the nine orbits of the heavens, which are: the First Mover <term>Primum mobile</term> <note>the outermost sphere in ancient astronomy</note>, the Firmament <note>the sphere of the fixed stars</note>, and the spheres of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, the Sun, Venus, Mercury, and the Moon. The third circle signifies the nine beings of the Elemental World, which are: man, beast, zoophyte <note>organisms like coral that seem to bridge the gap between plants and animals</note>, tree, shrub, herb, minerals, mixed substances, and the elements. And these are the 27 degrees of beings of the three Worlds. If you join the remaining larger circles to these, 40 circles will emerge—exactly as many as the sum of the aforementioned numbers 1, 3, 9, and 27. The first term, 1, constitutes absolute unity; the second, 3, the superficial or radical; the third, 9, namely the square of three; and finally the fourth, 27, constitutes the cube of three. These, as I said, when joined together give 40, by which the Pythagoreans <note>followers of the philosopher Pythagoras who emphasized the spiritual importance of numbers</note> indicated absolute, radical, plane, and solid numbers. The Hebrews, however, as we have said in our discussion of the Kabbalah, differing with wonderful skill concerning the triple World, make their letters correspond to these numbers. You also see how aptly these things agree with what we said previously regarding the 9 decades of the four Worlds.

<margin>Demonstration by the double pyramid, of light and of darkness.</margin>
All these circles are encompassed by a double pyramid. The first, the pyramid of light, has its base at the summit of the Angelic or luminous heaven and its apex at the lowest degree of the World. The other, the pyramid of darkness, has its base at the lowest degree of the World—namely, in prime matter, which is deprived of all light and action—and its apex terminates at the summit of the Angelic heaven. From this, it follows that just as the supreme World abounds in a wealth of light, so too does it abound in...

<margin>Demonstration of the proposition in the pyramids of light and darkness.</margin>
You see, therefore, that the more the pyramid of light is immersed into the material pyramid, the more light it loses and the more matter it acquires; conversely, the more the material pyramid is immersed in the pyramid of light, the more light it acquires and the more matter it loses, such that the number five <note>original: "quinarius"</note>, being placed in the middle position, always possesses an equal measure of light and darkness. Since, indeed, the World is threefold—supercelestial <note>The divine realm of pure spirit and angels</note>, celestial <note>The realm of the stars and planets</note>, and sublunary <note>The earthly realm below the moon, composed of the four elements and subject to decay</note>—the celestial world obtains a certain middle nature between the two extremes: for the supercelestial World is of light, the sublunary is of darkness, and the celestial is tempered by both light and darkness.

Since its power reaches the sublunary World, it is rightly said to be governed by the supercelestial; for in its power and resistance, its action and passion, it stands in the middle. In the sublunary realm, there is the cycle of life and death; in the supercelestial, there is perfect life and the perpetual stability of all functions; but in the celestial, there is a certain middle nature, composed of both stability and change. If, therefore, you compare these pyramids more precisely to one another, you will find an abundance of perfection in the higher World, a lack of it in the sublunary world, and in the middle of both, a mixture of perfect equality. These things are true not only in the Worlds we have mentioned, but in every specific level within those Worlds.

<margin>This is clearly seen in the combination of the Elements.</margin>
For an Element that mediates between two neighbors, being placed between them, obtains a middle character, participating equally from those surrounding it; and thus, it is a kind of middle ground for the whole group. In this way, air, which stands between water and fire, shares heat from fire and moisture from water; therefore, the nature and property of air is to be hot and moist, participating in both elements that flank it. In the same way, water, being intermediate between air and earth, shares moisture from the former and cold from the latter, thus obtaining a moist-cold nature. This is also clearly seen in mixed bodies;

<margin>In mixed bodies.</margin>
for shrubs mediate between herbs and trees; metals between mineral liquids and earthy substances; brute animals between humans and "plant-animals" <note>original: "zoophyta" — organisms like coral or sponges that were thought to bridge the gap between plants and animals</note>; and between human and divine nature stands the mediator, Christ our Savior.

<margin>In the Heavens.</margin>
In the celestial World, Mercury is the intermediate between Venus and the Moon; just like a kind of celestial water, it participates equally in moisture from Venus and cold from the Moon. Between the three "superior" planets—Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, and Mars ♂—and the three "inferior" ones—Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, and the Moon ☽—the Sun stands as the intermediate, giving and receiving from each; between Saturn ♄ and Mars ♂, Jupiter ♃ is the middle, tempering the harshness <note>original: "malignitatem" — in traditional astrology, Saturn and Mars are "malefic" or harsh planets, while Jupiter is "benefic" and balancing</note> of those crowding him on both sides with his own virtue.

Furthermore, in the supercelestial World, it belongs to the first hierarchy to perfect, to illuminate, and to purge; to the lowest hierarchy, on the contrary, it belongs to be perfected, to be illuminated, and to be purged; but to the middle hierarchy, these operations belong both actively and passively, with a certain reciprocity. Therefore, the mystery of the mentioned proposition is clear from what has been said.

CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER III.

## CHAPTER III.

### *On the hieroglyphic expression of numbers especially used by the Egyptians.*

I find that the Egyptians expressed their numbers in a twofold manner: either <term>hierogrammatically</term> <note>sacred writing using hidden or symbolic meanings</note> or <term>kyriologically</term> <note>from the Greek 'kyrios', meaning a literal or standard way of representing things</note>. In the first method, they expressed their sacred mysteries through the hidden symbols of the most profound things. In the second method, they repeated the object they wished to express through a number as many times as there were units in that number. We must deal first with the latter method, and then with the former.

### §. I.

### *On the Kyriological method of representing numbers used by the Egyptians.*

<margin>All these things are taken from Hermes, as can be seen in the Special Treatise on the Hieroglyphic Worlds.</margin>
We say first, therefore, that hieroglyphic <term>Kyriology</term> was nothing other than placing the signified thing that they wished to express numerically as many times as the number contained units. Thus, for example, a globe or circle placed by itself signified the eternal, superior World; two globes or circles signified two superior Worlds; three globes, three superior Worlds; and four globes or circles, four superior Worlds. They used circles for these Worlds to indicate the eternity of the <term>Genii</term> <note>guiding spirits or divine intelligences</note> presiding over them, for the circle is a figure lacking both beginning and end. However, they displayed the <term>hylæic</term> <note>material or physical</note> or elementary worlds sometimes through squares and quadrangles, and sometimes through right-angled triangles. They used squares when they were suggesting the successive propagation of generation in the worlds of mixtures; hence they also called these "genetic triangles." We deal with all these individually and at greater length in our *Hieroglyphic Geometry*. In like manner, by placing one scepter, they expressed one dominion; with two, a double dominion; with three, triple; with four, quadruple. They also expressed the empires and dominions of a certain Genius by the number of knots carved into the scepters. In short, every hieroglyph placed once, twice, thrice, four times, and so on, denoted a multiplication of the thing signified.

<margin>How the Egyptians express numbers by the multitude of things.</margin>
This custom has been accepted by posterity even to this day. For it is well known that the ancients, since they had not yet discovered certain figures for numbers, expressed them with as many small lines as the number signified. Hence, to indicate one, two, three, four, etc., they placed one, two, three, and four lines, up to ten, in this manner: I. II. III. IIII.
<margin>The ancients used small lines for numbers.</margin>
Certain traces of this still seem to exist among the ancient Romans, when they expressed the <term>Duumviri</term>, <term>Triumviri</term>, and <term>Septemviri</term> <note>Roman boards of two, three, or seven officials</note> thus: II-vir, III-vir, VII-vir.
<margin>How the Egyptians expressed five and ten.</margin>
They seem to have expressed five by the inclination of one line toward another, as is evident here: **V**; and ten by a <term>decussis</term> <note>the crossing of lines to form an X</note>, which seems to consist of these two figures: **V** and **A**.

He also links this ancient tally system to the origins of Roman numerals like V and X.</summary>

[...lines], of which one turns upward and the other downward, joined into one, as appears here: **X**. Regarding this, Horus <note>Horus Apollo, author of the *Hieroglyphica*, a 5th-century treatise on Egyptian symbols</note> says in Book 2, Chapter 28: <note>original Greek: Γραμμὴ ὀρθὴ μία, ἅμα γραμμῇ ἐπικεκαμμένῃ (δίκην χιάσματος, ἢ) δέκα γραμμὰς ἐφεστώσας σημαίνουσι.</note> "A single straight line, together with a curved line (after the fashion of a cross-mark, or X) signifies ten upright lines." That is, by a straight line which is similarly crossed by another line in this manner, **X**, they signify 10 (either as a cross-mark, or as) 10 flat lines. Henceforth, this cross-mark, as a symbol of the <term>Denary</term> <note>the number ten</note> or of perfection, found a place everywhere among hieroglyphic inscriptions; about which there is more at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* page 386 and in the following sections in its proper place.

### § II.
## On the hierogrammatic method of counting, and first on Unity, the Dyad, and the Triad.

<margin>The Phoenix represented by Unity.</margin>
The <term>hierogrammatic</term> <note>sacred writing using symbolic or metaphorical images</note> method of counting consisted in this: they signified numbers through hidden metaphors and the inherent qualities of animals. In this way, when they intended to represent **1**, they placed a phoenix, because this bird is said to have no companion of its own species; see Horus Apollo, Book 2, on this.

<margin>How the Egyptians expressed the Binary (the number 2). Λ [Three circles in a triangle] [Inverted triangle of circles] [A rectangle with a central dot]</margin>
When they wished to signify absolute Unity through the center, they painted a circle, because just as the center is the beginning of all lines and of figures composed of lines, so supreme Unity is the cause of all things existing in the World; about which there is more in *Hieroglyphic Geometry*. They indicated binary numbers <note>the number 2</note> first by any angle of a pair, because the supreme unity, diffused from its center, first produces the <term>Dyad</term> <note>the number two, often representing duality or division</note>, that is, the Intellectual World. For the flow of the <term>monad</term> <note>the number one, representing the indivisible source</note> into "otherness" necessarily creates an angle through the extension of two surrounding lines whose vertex is a point, as will be explained more fully later. Furthermore,

<margin>Two Quails <note>The Latin margin says "Coturnices" (quails), but the text says "cornices" (crows). Horus Apollo uses crows to represent duality.</note> signify the Dyad. || |||</margin>
when they wished to signify the Dyad or the principle of generation, they painted two crows <note>original: "cornices"</note>. For, according to the testimony of Horus, animals of this kind are accustomed to always lay two eggs, from which emerge a male and a female—that is, the active and passive principle—from which all things have the beginning of their generation. Thus, in a pyramid, the Dyad is indicated by the flow of any two hidden lines. Since this number is the principle of diversity, inequality, and dissimilarity, and is the distinction of unity and the first fall away from the "one," it is not undeservedly considered the number of "dissection" in every discipline. By this number, the Egyptians appropriately represented the distribution of opposites and the successions of conflicting qualities in nature—which were also indicated by the Persian Magi under the allegory of <term>Arimanius</term> and <term>Orimazes</term> <note>Ahriman and Ahura Mazda, the Zoroastrian spirits of darkness and light</note>, or by the Egyptians under the history of Osiris and Typhon. Hence,

<margin>Different names for Good and Evil.</margin>
the Pythagoreans, according to Plutarch, assign different names to each principle. They designate the "Good" by the name of unity, the finite, the resting, the straight, the odd, the square, the equal, the right-hand, and the bright. But they label the "Evil" by the name of the binary, the infinite, that which is in motion, the curved, the even, the oblong <note>original: "alterâ dimensione longioris" (longer in one dimension than the other)</note>, the unequal, the left-hand, and the dark; and they establish that these are the principles of the origin of things. Hence Osiris is said to be everything that is beneficial, as was mentioned above,

<margin>Synesius</margin>
according to the testimony of Synesius in Book 1 *On Providence*. Typhon, however, [is the source] of all [evils]...

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS
## CHAPTER III.

...to speak of a workshop of evils, which the Egyptians also call Seth, Bebon, and Smy; <margin>Names of Typhon.</margin> by these words they indicate a certain violent inhibition, contrariety, and overthrowing, without which Horus—that is, the sensible World—could by no means be preserved. Consequently, the Egyptians rightly said (as read in Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian from the 3rd century BCE</note> by way of Plutarch) that the bones of Horus were the Magnet, and those of Typhon were iron. <margin>The bones of Horus are the Magnet; of Typhon, iron.</margin> For just as iron experiences various movements of attraction and repulsion within a Magnet, so the healthy, good, and rational motion of the World somehow turns, draws to itself, and renders more mild that hard and Typhonian force, making it obedient to itself. Hence, they fabricate the myth that Mercury—according to Plutarch—cut out the sinews of Typhon and used them as strings for his lyre, thereby arranging the universe and making it harmonious instead of dissonant. In doing so, he did not abolish the force of the World, but fulfilled it. Thus it happens that this Typhonian force, weak and languid, clings to bodies in this world of changes and various affections; it contrives earthquakes and tremors in the earth, heat and unseasonable winds in the air, as well as fiery whirlwinds and lightning. It infects the waters and the breath with the plague of pestilence, and even rushes out as far as the Moon, raising itself up and darkening the bright air. These two principles of things are well denoted in a pyramid by the flow of two lines from a single point; although others twist this binary toward the production of forms. For just as the binary arises from the one, so—by preserving the logic of similarity—form is first led out from the power of matter; for this reason, it was named by Homer not <term>Aisa</term> <note>Fate or destiny</note> but <term>Eidothea</term>, which is to say, the *Goddess of forms*.

<margin>In ancient times, they traced all things from the one back to the one.</margin> This, therefore, was the consideration of the ancients, who derived all things from the One through a certain perpetual and continuous chain through all levels of reality, and by those same steps referred them back to the One. Because matter is the final thing in the process of <term>resolution</term> <note>breaking a thing down to its basic parts</note>, it must necessarily be the first thing in the composition of bodies. This is clearly shown by the apex of the pyramid: while it returns into lines, surfaces, the body, and from these into itself, it beautifully teaches this process. For that reason, in physics, matter is deservedly called <term>Proteus</term> <note>The shape-shifting sea god, representing the ever-changing nature of physical matter</note>, just as the One was called Proteus in the "First Wisdom." And because form is the second-to-last in resolution, it becomes the second in composition, and thus takes on the nature of the binary (the number 2), whose nature is feminine according to the Pythagoreans. Therefore, those ancient ones—whether Sages, Magi, or even Priests—following the order of nature in composing and resolving things, called matter "Protean," <margin>Matter called Protea.</margin> and established God as the second form, and consequently his daughter, just as the duality is of the one; this the Egyptians also hinted at through Oceanus as the Father and Tethys as the Mother. But enough of these things here.

The Triad (the number 3) is the "firstly triple," and according to Boëtius, is the Leader and Prince of odd numbers: perfect, first, whole, consummate, universal, and total. For just as the <term>Monad</term> (Unity) <margin>The excellence of the Triad.</margin> is simple without an extremity, and the <term>Dyad</term> (the Binary) is a divided and gaping extremity without the unity of a middle; so the Triad, with a wondrous embrace, seizes both that came before it. It surrounds and walls in the Monad by the aid of the Dyad, and it joins and knits the extremes of the Dyad with unity. And just as an act implanted in a divided power is by its nature odd, it forges and fulfills the substance of the whole; so also the Monad, having progressed into the Dyad and being received by its boundaries...

# CHAPTER III. 
## THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...completes the Triad and perfects the number; hence, this number is not undeservedly called the "Prince," a likeness of divine emanation, and the foundation of all contemplation and wisdom. If the primary existence of things occurs in the Monad (the point), and the knowledge and appearance of existing things occurs in the Dyad (the line), then the Triad represents the supreme love and festive pursuit of known and celestial substances. It is no wonder, then, that the ancient philosophers applied themselves with such zeal to the mysteries of the Triad. But let us return to our purpose.

<margin>The equilateral triangle is the hieroglyphic image of the Triad.</margin>
The hieroglyphic Triad is the equilateral triangle. For the Egyptians, it denotes the diffusion of the "three-formed God" <note>original: *τρίμορφους* (trimorphous)</note> into the World, as explained in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's previous work on the Roman obelisk in the Piazza Navona</note>. For Plato reports that Horus flowed forth from the archetypal triangle. By "Horus," he indicates this sensible World; by the "Triangle," he indicates the three-formed Divinity <note>original: *Numen τρίμορφον* (Numen trimorphon)</note>, which, having been stirred from the Monad into the Dyad, and from there into the Triad, established the World. Hence, the contemplation of this matter is quite beautifully conceived 

<margin>What the hieroglyphic diagram of the Bembine Table denotes.</margin>
-> SYMBOLA <-

in that hieroglyphic diagram, which is found twice in the Bembine Table <note>A famous bronze tablet of Egyptian-style figures, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note>: A boy wearing a headband, wrapped in a netted garment, behind whose back is a triangle to which a globe is attached. Furthermore, he is equipped with a bird-headed staff <term>cucuphomorphon: a staff topped with the head of a hoopoe bird, symbolizing the sky or royal power</term>, joined with a *lituus* <term>lituus: a curved wand used for religious divination</term> and a *gnomon* <term>gnomon: an L-shaped tool used by builders or to measure shadows</term>. The boy with the headband signifies nothing other than Horus—that is, the World, which is furnished with an innumerable variety of things and proceeds from the archetypal triangle. Both the triangle and the globe attached to Horus's neck beautifully indicate this. The netted garment represents the unknown and entangled operations and effects of the World; the bird-headed scepter represents the variety, order, and succession of things; the *lituus* represents harmony; and the *gnomon* represents the exact order of distribution and measurement of every individual thing. The triangle truly represents the Three-formed Divinity, who is Hemphta <note>An Egyptian deity name Kircher associated with the supreme spirit</note>, or the supra-mundane Osiris; Isis, who is his Wisdom; and Amun, the "all-formed Spirit" <note>original: *Spiritus παντόμορφος* (Spiritus pantomorphos)</note> who animates all things by his power. Although these are distinguished by three divine names, they are in truth one. For by these three powers, as the Egyptians say, the World is created, animated, and sustained. Therefore, it is not incorrectly said to have flowed forth from the archetypal triangle. See more on these matters in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 212.

<margin>The origin of the Ternary number.</margin>
Just as the Dyad is born from the Monad by the addition of unity, so the Triad is born by the addition of the Monad to the Dyad: a "three-in-one" number reduced from one into one. Because just as unity is the principle of numbers, so the triangle is the first of all straight-lined figures. It is born from the binary and the unity, and in hieroglyphic pyramids it is signified by the letter Delta (Δ). This figure takes its beginning from the point or Monad of the pyramid and is extended through any two sides into the base, by which the Delta is established—that sacred figure celebrated in so many writings of the ancients...
