CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 67 CH. V.

<margin><unclear>Description of the Seal of the Moon</unclear></margin>
The construction of the **Seal of the Moon** <note>original: "Sigilli Lunæ". In Western esotericism, the Moon is associated with the number 9, and its magic square is a 9x9 grid containing the numbers 1 through 81.</note> is made from 9 multiplied by 9, the sum of which is 81; this provides the square whose structure we seek for the Seal of the Moon. Proceed, therefore, in this way: Let a diagram of a <term>Rhomboid</term> <note>A diamond-shaped grid used as a transitional step in arranging numbers before they are collapsed into a final square.</note> figure be made, in which you arrange 9 <term>enneads</term> <note>groups of nine</note> in rows through cells arranged <term>diagonally</term> <note>original: "πλαγίως" (plagios). A Greek term meaning oblique or slanting.</note>, as is apparent from what was said before. Once this is finished, nothing will be easier than to insert the individual numbers written in the four corners into their corresponding empty spaces. Since the method presents absolutely no difficulty, I will describe it in only a few words. 

Since each corner has seven numbers, which are the heads of columns—partly vertical and partly horizontal—the numbers of the highest and lowest corners occupy the same columns, of which the upper ones occupy the head of the columns and the lower ones occupy their base; thus, column **DH** displays 1 at its head and 81 at its base. However, the numbers in the right and left corners occupy the same horizontal columns: whence the <margin><unclear>Transfer of numbers into the square</unclear></margin> transfer of the numbers into the square **abcd** must be established horizontally. Once these things are declared, you will insert the numbers of the highest corner **aDb** into the square without any trouble if you count ten cells downward from the first cell of each column; for the tenth cell will necessarily be that empty one into which the number displayed at the front of the column must be relocated. For example: if you count ten cells downward from 1 within column **DH**, the tenth will be that cell within which 1 must be placed; you proceed in the same manner with the rest of the numbers. 

The numbers of the lower corner, by counting upward, will likewise have every tenth cell within their appropriate columns ready for the number which the base of the appropriate column displays. In the same way, the numbers in the left corner **aGc** in their appropriate horizontal columns will always find the tenth cell capable of receiving the relocated number which any part of the left column displays. Also, each of the numbers in the right corner **bEd** within their horizontal columns will find the tenth cell prepared for receiving the number which the right part of the column displays. For example: 73 will be placed in the tenth cell of the horizontal column **GE**, and they will find 9 within the same column to the left where it may be placed. And in this way, you will have the entire square filled with its numbers with absolutely no effort, in which the numbers of the individual columns—whether vertical, horizontal, or diagonal—when added will always produce 369; these, multiplied by 9 (the side of the square), give the sum of all the numbers: 3321.

## § VIII.
### Concerning cubic squares.

<margin>The power hidden in numbers.</margin>
How great a power lies hidden beneath numbers is something I think can remain hidden only from one who lacks skill in Arithmetic. We have spoken in the preceding sections about the Seals of the seven planets, which come from the seven squares 9, 16, 25, 36, 49, 64, 81, whose roots follow.

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>
It now remains to speak of cubic squares <note>Kircher uses "cubic square" to refer to what we now call a multiplicative magic square.</note>, especially since neither the Ancients nor the Moderns have (as far as I know) sensed the secret method of this progression. If they had known it, they would undoubtedly have dedicated these cubic squares to the seven classes of the elementary World and their presiding Spirits, just as they dedicated the seven [additive] squares to the seven bodies of the sidereal World and their Spirits. But let us perform the duty of Oedipus <note>A reference to the title of the work; Kircher casts himself as Oedipus solving the riddles of ancient wisdom.</note> in unearthing this artifice, which has perhaps remained unknown until now.

<margin>What a cubic square is.</margin>
A cubic square is nothing other than a series of numbers in a geometric progression starting from unity <note>The number 1</note> and continued in a double proportion <note>A doubling sequence: 1, 2, 4, 8...</note>, containing as many terms as there are units in any given square number. For example: if someone wishes to construct a cubic square corresponding to the square of 9 (produced by 3 multiplied by itself), let him proceed as follows. Let 9 terms be placed in a geometric progression starting from unity, as follows:

<margin>Arrangement of the numbers.</margin>
->T 1 2 4 8 16 32 64 128 256 V<-

<margin>Example with an odd number.</margin>
You will insert these terms into the square *a b c d* in exactly the same manner as we taught above in the first paragraph regarding the square of nine for Saturn. But let us give an example. Let a rhomboid diagram be drawn, as you see.

<image-desc>A mathematical diagram titled "diagramma Rhomboidis" used to construct a 3x3 multiplicative magic square. It shows a central grid with corners marked 'a', 'b', 'c', and 'd'. Inside the grid: the middle row contains numbers 64, 16, and 4; the top row has the number 8 in the center; the bottom row has the number 2 in the center. Surrounding this 3x3 grid are four external numbers arranged in a diamond shape: 1 at the top, 256 at the bottom, 128 at the left, and 32 at the right. Dotted lines and arrows indicate how these external numbers are to be transposed into the empty cells of the central grid.</image-desc>

In this diagram, you will place the given geometric progression *T V* in order, as the figure indicates. Then, you will transpose these numbers into the empty cells of the square *a b c d* by the same law used in the square of 9: namely, you will transpose 1 into the opposite cell (the fourth from the first), 256 upwards into the opposite fourth cell, 4 into the fourth cell to the left, and 64 into the fourth cell to the right. By proceeding thus, as you see, you will have a cubic square in which the individual rows—transverse, vertical, and diagonal—will yield the same number. However, there is this difference: whereas the numbers in the preceding squares produced the same sum when added, here they are not to be added, but multiplied by one another to obtain the same total. In this way, the numbers of the individual rows multiplied together will give 4096, as follows—

CHAPTER VI. 70 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

...to have opened the doors of this labor, and to have shown the way to others so that the rest and innumerable other similar things might be discovered with equal daring and skill.

## CHAPTER VI.

->*Concerning the use, effects, and mysteries—or rather, the superstitions—which the Ancients believed to lie hidden under the said Seals, together with their refutation.*<-

---

<margin>The opinion of the Ancients, who thought that all things in the World were produced according to the numbers latent in the mind of God.</margin>
The common sentiment of the Ancient Philosophers was that the species of things behave like numbers, and that the World, and all things that are in the World, were produced according to the numbers latent in the mind of the Creator <note>original: "Opificis," referring to God as the Divine Architect or Craftsman.</note>. For just as certain wonderful properties and powers lie hidden under fixed limits of numbers, however confused and indefinite they may seem, so it is certain that they have a wonderful and incredible connection to one another, which only he knows who has thoroughly mastered the nature of numbers; and who, through the skillful arrangement, shifting, digestion, and combination of them, has obtained a singular expertise in connecting them. In the same way, in the nature of things, innumerable species of things occur, which although they may seem confused and indefinite, nevertheless all breathe together in one harmony through a certain wonderful concatenation; this only he will discover who knows how to fitly and skillfully arrange the species of things according to the ideal arrangement of the aforementioned [numbers], and how to adapt these to those and others through analogous combinations. That the Egyptians were endowed with a certain wonderful industry in correctly arranging these worldly things above all others is shown throughout this work, since they knew how to associate the individual grades of natural things so aptly both to the grades of the Celestial and the Spiritual <note>original: "Genialis," likely referring to the world of the "Genii" or spirits.</note> World, so that once any species of the sublunary World was given, they immediately assigned both a star and a corresponding Intelligence <note>term: Intelligence — in Renaissance philosophy, an "Intelligence" was a spiritual being or angel believed to govern a specific celestial body.</note>; having investigated these, they persuaded themselves that it was impossible not to produce wonderful and prodigious effects through the proper application of these things.

<margin>The power of corresponding numbers according to the Egyptians.</margin>
For they thought that individual numbers had corresponding spirits <note>original: "Genios"</note> in the worldly economy; when they beheld these spirits coordinated into ranks by a certain ineffable skill, they studied how to arrange those numbers—which were naturally implanted in the spirits and toward which the spirits inclined with a certain wonderful force—by a similar skill. They persuaded themselves that nothing was more effective or powerful for attracting these spirits than these [numbers], as if they were things naturally suited to them and committed to their guardianship.

<margin>The investigation of the mysteries of nature without the light of faith is mere superstition.</margin>
But since no treatment of the hidden mysteries of nature can be carried out rightly if the light of the true faith be missing, without the blemish and admixture of demonic commerce...

SECTION VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER VI.

<margin>The Arabs transmitted the superstitions of the Egyptians to their descendants.</margin>

...as it can; hence it happened that they were led down into the precipices of enormous superstitions. The happiness of soul and body, which they sought so solicitously and pursued so studiously, they lost—miserably mocked and cast down by the enemy of the human race <note>A standard reference to the Devil.</note>. Into this same abyss fell all their descendants who, following in their footsteps, used such things unlawfully. This was especially true of the Arabs, who, above all others, strove to propagate this art inherited from the Egyptians—which they placed among their greatest mysteries—to the other nations of the world. But let us see what they promise themselves through superstitious machinations of this kind. And although we have already described all these things extensively in the *Saracenic Kabbalah* <note>original: "Cabala Saracenica." This refers to Kircher’s earlier writings or sections regarding Islamic mystical and occult traditions.</note>; nevertheless, because we omitted many things there, it seemed appropriate to explain them here anew.

Having spoken of the "arithmagic" <note>A portmanteau of "arithmetic" and "magic" used to describe the mystical properties of numbers.</note> Seals of the seven planets, they prepare seven plates of metals appropriated to the said planets. They foolishly persuade themselves that if they carve the said figures upon these at the proper time and hour, they can achieve all things by this aid. But let us look at these fanatical ravings.

## The Seal of Saturn

<margin>The ravings of the Arabs concerning the Seal of Saturn.</margin>

The Arabs cited in the *Saracenic Kabbalah* say that if anyone carves this Seal of Saturn on a lead plate while Saturn is dominant, it brings aid to those in labor, renders a man powerful and safe from enemies, and makes him so favored that when asking something of Princes, he will never suffer a refusal. If, however, the carving is made while Saturn is weak, they believe it brings hindrance to the buildings of mortals, the planting of trees, and all machines; it drags one down from the highest rank of dignity to a dejected fortune; and it prepares and nourishes quarrels and disturbances at will, so that it can even split and put to flight unconquered armies. <margin>Abenpharagi.</margin> These are the words of Abenpharagi <note>Likely referring to Bar Hebraeus (Ibn al-Faraj), a 13th-century scholar whose works were often cited in Latin translations of Eastern occultism.</note>. Behold how nothing is accomplished in these trifles without Astrological vanity and insanity.

<margin>Abenmorgun.</margin>

Abenmorgun <note>Possibly Ibn al-Murgan, another Arabic source on planetary magic.</note> the Arab describes its use in other words in his *Treatise on the Seals of the Seven Planets*, where he has these words, translated from the Arabic idiom into Latin: *“If this figure is written on virgin parchment <note>Parchment made from the skin of a stillborn or very young animal, considered ritually pure.</note> on the day and hour of Saturn, with Saturn situated in the houses of Libra or Aquarius, and it is smoked with alum and asafoetida <note>A pungent resin with a strong, often unpleasant odor, used here in a "suffumigation" or incense ritual.</note>, and tied to the neck of a woman in labor, then she will give birth most happily. If, however, it is carved on a leaden plate while Saturn is retrograde and the Moon is waning, and one places that figure in a newly begun building, then that building will never be finished; and wherever this figure is placed on the day and hour of Saturn, there the most unhappy Spirits of Saturn will stir up all quarrels and perturbations. Saturn has 45 in numbers, and they are placed three by three, then in all places 15 will result; it is necessary, however, that all things be performed with the right hand, and one must add the name of the day and the hour, and the character of the true Angel and the planet.”* But what so many observances and so many foolish machinations contribute to the matter, I cannot perceive. It is manifest, therefore, that a hidden pact lies here with him who, since he is the Author of all wickedness, is accustomed to grant the things sought to these mock-machinists in order to make them slaves to his will. The figure follows.

Once this is done, you shall fumigate it with aloe wood, and ambergris <note>original: ambra</note>, and mastic <note>A resin from the Pistacia lentiscus tree.</note>, and wrap it in a white silk cloth, and carry it with you.

These characters are common to both the Eastern and Western traditions, secretly formed from segments of circles and the drawing of lines; they emerged partly from the hieroglyphics of the Egyptians and partly from the School of the Gymnosophists <note>Ancient Indian philosophers; Kircher believed Egyptian wisdom spread to India</note>, as we shall show more extensively in its proper time and place. <margin>How much astrologers, along with Paracelsus, value the seven Seals.</margin>
And these are the things I thought should be said regarding the **Seals of the seven Planets**, on the occasion of the seven numerical squares; these undoubtedly smell of the dogmas of the Egyptians, and the Arabs, being neighbors to Egypt, received them into their <term>study houses</term> <note>original: "phrontisteria", a Greek-derived term for a place of meditation or schools</note> as if they were most sacred. From these, Europeans took them, such that there are hardly any among those who profess **"characteristic astrology"** <note>a branch of astrology using specific symbols or "characters" to harness planetary power</note> who do not follow them. Among others, these were revived from the underworld and cultivated with the greatest zeal by the impostor **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous physician and occultist whose work Kircher often viewed with deep suspicion despite their shared interests</note>, who describes them at length in his *Archidoxes* <note>original: "archidoxis", a foundational work by Paracelsus on alchemy and the mysteries of nature</note>. Consequently, I stand astonished as to how it could eventually happen that a man of learning could and would devote his mind to such insane, unworthy, foolish fictions that have no foundation in nature. But this is what happens when, having left the path of the right faith, people follow foreign and destructive teachings; once these are soaked in, nothing is easier than to fall into the open snares of the Devil with the loss of one's soul. Hence, I would wish all who are eager for more "curious" learning to be cautious in employing such things.

<margin>In which there is always an intervening pact with a Demon.</margin>
For since they involve an open pact with the demon, as I have said, let people by no means persuade themselves that these things are lawful; rather, let them know that they have long since been outlawed and eliminated by Holy Mother Church, as if having proceeded from a **workshop of Demons**. For no natural cause or physical efficiency can be assigned for such great powers as we have reported these amulets to obtain. Therefore, if indeed some effects do follow from their application, let them believe without doubt that these do not come from anywhere else except from an attraction through a pact entered into with the **Demon**.

<margin>For God does not cooperate in those things which specifically involve evil.</margin>
Nor should you think the cause of these effects is supernatural <note>here meaning "divine"</note>, since God the Best and Greatest, as well as the Angels, do not cooperate in those things which specifically involve evil—such as perverse passions, ambitious striving in acquiring honors and riches, or in winning over the love of women... <note>The sentence continues onto the next page</note>

### SECTION VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER VI.

...anxious care for procuring the itching of the heart, and similar provocations of luxury and lust; in short, all things which are taken up for the sake of disturbing tranquility and public peace, and for inflicting innumerable evils upon one's neighbor, can in no way be reconciled [with reason]. Hence I cannot wonder enough that some, who wish to be held as Christians in both name and religion, so anxiously follow, so studiously inquire into, and finally value so highly this most stupid <term>Mohammedan characterolatry</term> <note>original: "Mahumedanorum characterolatriam". Kircher uses this term to describe the superstitious veneration of symbols or talismans, which he attributes to Islamic traditions.</note>, which is supported by Diabolical foundations and exposed to innumerable superstitions, that they do not blush to prefer it by many leagues <note>original: "parasangis". A parasang was an ancient Persian unit of distance; Kircher uses it here to mean "by a great distance."</note> to the sacred amulets of Christians. On this account, the holy Mother Church is rightfully accustomed to punish those who use such things with fire, as if they were **Idolaters**, **Sorcerers**, and impious men, unworthy of enjoying the common air.

Nor is it enough to thrust forward here some hidden power of nature under I know not what pretext, since no Magical operation, however horrendous and impious, can be assigned that does not clothe its poison with the sacred veil of a more hidden nature—all the more dangerous, certainly, as it displays a greater apparatus of crosses and sacred names. Since, therefore, many **Seals** <note>original: "Sigilla". In this context, these are the planetary characters or talismans discussed on the previous page.</note> of this sort are sent to me from everywhere at all times as if to an interpreter, it seemed right to expose them to public light in this place, having been examined with a peculiar investigation, so that those who might stumble upon such impious machinations might know from whose workshop they proceeded, and might flee with oars and sails as if from an open Scylla and Charybdis <note>Two legendary sea monsters from Greek mythology representing a peril where avoiding one danger risks falling into another.</note> of imminent shipwreck for soul and body.

Indeed, I do not deny that wonderful properties lie hidden beneath the reviewed arrangements of numbers; these, however, were adopted by the ancients not so much to effect anything, as to show that wonderful order, progress, and disposition of natural things through a certain hidden analogy and similarity which the said numbers exhibit. The <term>combinatorial art</term> <note>original: "ars combinativa". A philosophical system, famously championed by Ramon Llull, which sought to understand all knowledge by combining fundamental concepts.</note> of things is a great secret in the nature of the Universe, and whoever reaches it should rightly be considered blessed, as a partaker of the **Angelic mind**. For since Angelic substances have a most perfect knowledge of this combinatorial art, it is better known than it need be said that they also perform wonderful effects by its aid: for while they apply active things to passive things through a continuous combination of things and qualities of this kind dispersed in various beings, what else do they do but distribute confused numbers into a certain wonderful and harmonious order, from whose compositions wonderful effects are then produced?

The frailty of the human intellect cannot reach this perfection, except through certain hidden shadows of similarities known by long experience of things; and to put it better, by a singular gift of divine influence. Moreover, this science consists in the perfect cognition of all natural things, and the knowledge of individual qualities and properties, insofar as the Angels intrinsically, certainly, and infallibly know what the proportion, connection, and sympathy of individual things toward each other might be, and what might be their disagreement, enmity, flight, and **antipathy** <note>original Greek: αντιπάθεια (antipatheia). A natural or chemical opposition between two substances.</note>; who does not see that when these are aptly associated into one according to the laws of formal numbers, wonderful effects—nay, even prodigies—are born? ## THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>CHAPTER VI.</margin>

...we exclude Demons from this science, since they possess all things pertaining to the natural operation of the intellect entirely and most perfectly. Hence, higher Intelligences, relying on the help of this science, perform many things which seem merely **paradoxical** <note>original: παράδοξα (*paradoxa*). Things that seem self-contradictory or impossible according to common sense.</note> to our intellect, although they are by no means situated outside the limits of nature. Just as one unskilled in more secret Arithmetic, while seeing the marvelous properties of numbers proposed here, can by no means be persuaded of such unusual effects. Only he, whom God has willed to be blessed with this gift, clearly foresees all things, demonstrates them, and joins scattered numbers into one with wondrous dexterity; and according to their pattern, as if by a certain **thread of Ariadne** <note>A reference to the Greek myth of the Labyrinth; Kircher uses it to mean a guiding clue that leads one through a complex or "labyrinthine" problem.</note>, he is introduced into the hidden recesses of nature's secrets through the shadows of latent similarities. But since I have decided to treat this marvelous secret professionally in our **Combinatorial Art** <note>Kircher refers here to his *Ars Magna Sciendi sive Combinatoria*, a project to create a universal system of knowledge categorization.</note>, if God grants me life, I have thought it superfluous to dwell longer on these things in this place.

<image-desc>A large, ornate symmetrical woodcut ornament or tailpiece. It features a central grotesque mask or face from which floral and foliate scrolls emerge. On either side, bird-like figures (possibly sirens or harpies) are perched within the scrolling acanthus leaves. ## SECTION II.

### P R E F A C E.

->**Let no one ignorant of Geometry enter**<-
->This was inscribed on the gates of Plato’s Gymnasium;<-
->let us explain what Plato intended by this inscription.<-

---

<margin>The science of Geometry leads to the recognition of invisible things.</margin>
The philosophers of ancient centuries, led by the light of nature, observed certain wonderful properties within geometric quantity and glimpsed an order of nature in the production of things. They seem to have striven for this single goal: that, relying on the knowledge of these shapes, they might arrive at a comprehension of sublime matters. Since they saw that all things exposed to the senses consist of their own points, lines, surfaces, and bodies, they persuaded themselves that it could not be otherwise: the Maker of all things must have used these as an idea and exemplar in the first founding of the World. A line arises from the motion of a point; a surface from a line moved in width; a body from a surface moved in height. 
<margin>The triple dimension signifies the unfolding of the supreme Monad into this world.</margin>
What else do these denote, if not the unfolding of the first and supramundane <term>Monad</term> <note>The "Monad" refers to the ultimate, indivisible unit or "The One," representing God in Neoplatonic and Pythagorean philosophy.</note> into this sensible world? The great Plato saw this when he cried out, <term>God always geometrizes</term> <note>original: "Ὁ Θεὸς ἀεὶ γεωμετρεῖ" (Ho Theos aei geometrei). A famous maxim attributed to Plato.</note>; Hermes Trismegistus marveled at it when he pronounced God to be a Circle whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere; Pythagoras looked up to it when he asserted God was now an Arithmetician, now a Musician, now a Geometer. 
<margin>The passion of ancient philosophers for learning mathematics.</margin>
All later philosophers followed these teachings as followers of their doctrine, constantly asserting that the entire doctrine of truth is contained in nothing other than magnitude and multitude. Hence that supreme passion of the aforementioned philosophers for embracing mathematics and their intense study of it; they thought that no one would ever be great in philosophy who had approached the investigation of difficult things by any way other than the mathematical path. And indeed it is so: for since all things, as Paul the Apostle testifies, are seen as invisible through those things which are made, it must necessarily be confessed that all those things presented to the senses are like certain images, sketches, and <term>catoptric reflections</term> <note>Catoptrics is the study of mirrors. Kircher means that physical objects are reflections of divine truths, like images in a mirror.</note> of invisible things, which place before our eyes and explain the likeness of the primordial light from which all things come. Since we take the first foundations of our investigation from the sensible phantoms of the mind, and the way to the uncertain can only be through that which is already certain and established, then the images from whose metaphorical proportion we investigate unknown and abstract things should be doubtful to no one. Yet most sensible things are agitated in a continuous inconstancy and mutability because of the potential mixture of matter abundant within them. For this reason, the ancients adhered with singular zeal to those sensible things which both abstract from matter and are firm by their nature, having the most evident certainty—such as Geometrical things. At these, as if at a <term>Lydian stone</term> <note>A Lydian stone, or touchstone, was used to test the purity of gold and silver; here it means a standard for testing truth.</note>, they tried to explore the power of their contemplations. That the Egyptians were such people will be demonstrated more than enough by the <term>hierogrammatisms</term> <note>Sacred symbols or characters, specifically those incorporating geometric shapes.</note> composed of geometric figures which we shall bring forward here and there. For just as they were the first inventors of letters and mathematics, so too, relying on the knowledge of them, did they indicate the greatest mysteries and sacraments of higher beings, as will be seen shortly.

CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

# CHAPTER I.

->*Concerning the Circle, or the Hieroglyphic Sphere, as the Image of God unfolding Himself from the Monad into the circuit of all things.*<-

<margin>The wonders of the Circle according to Aristotle in his Mechanical Questions.</margin>
When Aristotle was searching more deeply for the cause of the wonderful and prodigious effects which occur everywhere in mechanics—concerning the lever and the scale, which evoke great admiration in all—he finally found no other cause than that most astounding of all astounding things: the circle. And not without reason: for it is entirely consistent with reason that wonderful effects proceed from a wonderful cause. <margin>Definition of the Circle.</margin> Now, a circle is a plane figure contained by only one line, which is called the circumference, to which all straight lines proceeding from a single point, which they call the center, are equal. In this figure, therefore, the existence of extreme opposites occurs in a wonderful way. For every circle is made from that which moves and that which remains still—one leg of the compass standing fixed, while the other is driven around into a periphery. <margin>The marvelous property of the circle.</margin> Furthermore, it is most remarkable that the line which encompasses the orb of the circle, called the *periphery* <note>original: "περιφέρειαν" (peripherian)</note> by the Greeks, while being entirely devoid of width, also admits a certain agreement of opposites: namely, the concave and the convex <note>The original uses *curuum* (curved) here, but later clarifies it as the opposite of concave.</note>; which are contrary in the same way as "great" and "small." For the midpoint between these latter is the "equal," while for the former it is the "straight." Indeed, for everything that is great, in order to become small, or for that which is small to become great, it must necessarily arrive at the equal before it reaches either extreme. In the same way, a convex line, before it becomes concave, must become as if straight; and a concave line, to pass over to the convex and circular, must similarly first be, in a certain manner, straight.

---

->**§ I.**<-

->*The Circle was held in great admiration and honor among the Egyptians.*<-

<margin>The ancients believed something divine was present in the Circle.</margin>
The Egyptians seem to have been by no means ignorant of these wonderful qualities and powers of the circle. For when they observed certain cyclic, as it were, ever-flowing <note>original: "εὐνάους" (eunaous), likely meaning perennial or eternal cycles.</note> patterns shining forth in all things contained within the circuit of this world; and when they contemplated with the greatest admiration the "spiral ideas" affected by that supreme Architect—something spherical both in Himself and in His works, which, according to Plutarch, were made only according to the pattern of a circle—they judged that something divine resided in the circle. So much so, indeed, that whenever they wished to indicate something great, wonderful, or excellent, in which some traces of divinity might appear, they would demonstrate it by applying a circle or a sphere. <margin>Trismegistus.</margin> From this, that truly Thrice-Greatest Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom and alchemy.</note>, when defining the divine nature, took the circle as his medium. For when asked, "What is God?" he replied: "God is a circle, or an intelligible sphere, whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere." Since God...

# THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS

<margin>CHAPTER I.</margin>
God is not a body, nor can He even be one, because He is supremely simple; for everything that is most perfect must be most simple. He is devoid of all composition, because every composite thing exists after the parts that compose it; therefore, to distinguish Him from a physical sphere, he [Hermes Trismegistus] calls God an **intelligible sphere** <note>The term "intelligible" here refers to something that can only be grasped by the intellect or mind, rather than the physical senses.</note>. Thus, through the center—which is the smallest and simplest part when compared to the circumference—you should understand the divine simplicity; but through the circumference, which is the largest, you should understand the divine immensity. Therefore, the meaning of the aforementioned description is this: God is a circle, or sphere—that is, lacking beginning and end—much more so than a material circle or sphere, so that His eternity may be noted. He is "intelligible" so that His immateriality may be noted. His center—that is, His indivisible essence—is whole everywhere; but His circumference—that is, His immensity—is nowhere, because it cannot be encompassed by any place. We also compare God to the center of a circle, around which all things exist, and from which the universe proceeds in a fixed order into an Orb, until the entire totality of things is completed. For just as the center is neither a magnitude, nor a circle, nor an orb, but the principle <note>In this context, "principle" means the source or origin.</note> of all circles and orbs, by equal measure God is none of those things which are in the World, nor is He the World itself, but He is the principle of the whole World. To this center, therefore, the highest point of every creature is directed, just as in a circle all portions are finished from the circumference into the center through the shape of a pyramid. And from this doctrine of Trismegistus, our **Pythagoras** received that ceremony which he later handed down: namely, that God is to be worshipped by a turning of the body, *revolving in a godly manner* <note>original Greek: "θεοσεβῶς περιφερόμενον" (theosebōs peripheromenon)</note>. **Pierius Valerianus** (in Book 39) is the authority that this was also an institution of Numa Pompilius; for he commanded that before anyone worshipped God, he should turn himself in a circle, and having made the circuit, offer worship to God, because they venerated Him who was to be signified by the circle, the perfect figure. **Pliny**, cited in **Pierius**, says: *In adoring, we carry the right hand to the mouth, and we turn the whole body in a circle.*

But let us return to the place from which we digressed. The Egyptians, therefore, always held the Circle in the greatest veneration among other geometric figures, both for the reasons mentioned and because they saw this mass of the Universe marked by a circular shape. It escapes no one that this shape, of all others, is most suited to the heavens; because, just as it was necessary for the heavens to be the most capacious, simplest, and most perfect, so the most wise Architect chose the most capacious, simplest, and most perfect figure in its construction. For it is most perfect when it possesses all its parts, and it is impossible for it to suffer even the slightest loss. It is most simple because, as the **Platonists** <note>Followers of the philosophy of Plato, who emphasized the mathematical and ideal forms of the universe.</note> feel, there is nothing from which it is made, or into which it may be resolved; otherwise, it would incur birth and decay. It is most capacious because it leaves nothing outside itself, but embraces the whole universe within. That a sphere is of this kind is indicated by the fact that it has the same relationship to other solids that a circle has to its own planes. First, indeed, the figure of a circle is the most capacious of all figures with equal perimeters <note>original: "Isoperimetrarum"</note>; furthermore, it is the most perfect because it undergoes no increase or decrease; and indeed, it is the simplest because it is contained by only one line. So also the sphere is a solid figure, [contained by] one... <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "super-", indicating the sentence continues on the next page.</note>

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>
Another reason why the Circle was held in honor among the Egyptians.
</margin>
...contained by a surface to which all straight lines drawn from a single central point are equal. Therefore, the sphere is also the most capacious shape, because it has a circle as its boundary; it is most perfect, since it does not, like an angular body, increase or decrease anywhere; and indeed it is most simple, for it is enclosed by a single surface. To this cause is added another reason for such great veneration: that through the straight line and the circle, the first and simplest production and representation of things was made—both of those not yet existing and those lying hidden in the coverings of nature. But a circle can be made neither correctly nor skillfully without a point; therefore, by the reasoning of the point and the monad <note>The "monad" refers to a single, indivisible unit or the mathematical principle of "one," often associated with the divine source in Neoplatonic philosophy.</note>, things both began to exist first, and those things defined by a periphery, however large they may be, can in no way lack the service of the central point. 

Now that these things have been demonstrated, it remains for us to say why the Egyptians placed a circle and a sphere upon the heads of their statues, as can be seen from many of the figures on the Obelisks. For one hardly encounters a hieroglyphic figure where something spherical or circular does not occur; yet these have different meanings depending on the nature of what is added to them. A globe, or circle, placed on the heads of statues always represents something divine, eternal, and infinite; but when placed separately, it indicates either God, the World, or the Heavens, as was shown extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Referring to Kircher's own work, *Obeliscus Pamphilius* (1650), which analyzed the hieroglyphs on the Agonal Obelisk in Rome.</note>, in the *Hierogrammatism <note>A term used by Kircher for sacred symbolic writing or diagrams.</note> of the Sphere or Circle*, and as will be copiously shown in Volume III. But so that all these things may be made more clear, it seemed best to begin a little further back by repeating some points from the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

<margin>
Why the Egyptians placed circular crowns or orbs on the heads of the Gods.
</margin>
Antiquity was accustomed to zealously venerate things that were, in the opinion of men, religious and August. Among these, the most noble is a certain circle or orb sometimes circumscribed around the head—an index of veneration and of a Majesty that exceeds the human. This is noted everywhere as being placed around Emperors (whom the Ancients looked up to as raised above the summit of mortality), the Provinces of the Roman World, primary Cities, and even the animals of the Gods. And regarding what pertains to the August [Emperors], there exist bronze coins of Antoninus Pius and Constantius, which are mentioned by Lorenzo Pignoria <note>Lorenzo Pignoria (1571–1631) was an Italian antiquarian famous for his study of the "Isiac Tablet."</note>, a man most skilled in antiquity, in his *Explanation of the Isiac Tablet*. 

<margin>
Lorenzo Pignoria.
</margin>
> *The Egyptians*, he says, *placed this orb on the very top of the heads of their statues; which may be noted both here and elsewhere. One may suspect that the Romans took this from them and varied the habit for the sake of decorum, so that a crown might be fitted in that position to a head in which they thought something divine resided. However, this ornament, through the moderation of subsequent Princes and the silent consensus of all, passed entirely (as most things did) to God and His Saints, and it has retained the ancient name of "diadem" to this day.*

Thus far Pignoria, who is supported by the things that Pierius <note>Pierio Valeriano (1477–1558), author of a massive Renaissance encyclopedia of hieroglyphics and symbols.</note> says on folio 4, book 29.

The Persians also, according to the testimony of Brissonius <note>Barnabé Brisson (1531–1591), a French jurist and scholar who wrote on Persian customs.</note>, when they called Jupiter the "Lord of Heaven," were thought to perform sacrifices to him by ascending the highest lookout point and calling Jupiter the "circle of heaven." This same custom passed to the Turks: hence those morning proclamations from a certain high tower; *La Alla elle Alla* <note>original: "La Alla elle Alla"; this is a transliteration of the Shahada: "La ilaha illa Allah" (There is no god but God).</note> etc., the sense of which is, that God is always, and will always be: nor do they add anything else, except that they also salute their own Muhammad. The Saracens <note>A medieval term for Muslims.</note> also, and many other nations, called God a circle, and from this they concluded that eternity was expressed. The Mughals <note>original: "Mogores"</note> also depict their King, whom they venerate as if with divine honors, shining with a radiant head.

<margin>Fulvius Ursinus.</margin>
<margin>Paruta.</margin>
From this Egyptian custom, the practice of the Greeks and Romans seems to have flowed, of adorning their Gods with a radiant circle. All these things are shown by infinite medals and coins, which you may see in the works of Fulvius Ursinus, Paruta, and other Antiquarians. For it was sometimes customary to paint a crown of rays, or a certain shining light, upon all the Gods, as has been said at length by me in the *Hieroglyphic Apparatus*; and they called this by a specific name, a **Nimbus** <note>In art, a nimbus or halo is a glowing ring or disc surrounding the head of a holy person.</note>, as Servius <note>A 4th-century grammarian known for his commentaries on Virgil.</note> testifies in many places. Indeed, let no one think that while a solid and, as it were, continuous light was customarily attached to the other Divinities, it was divided into rays only for the Sun: for rays in the manner of a circle were also given to those men to whom divinity was attributed. Lucian, in *The Syrian Goddess*, says: <greek>Ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ ἀκτῖνας φορέει</greek> <note>original Greek: "She wears rays upon her head."</note>. And in the *Misanthrope* <note>Referring to Lucian’s dialogue *Timon, or the Misanthrope*.</note> he describes Jupiter: <greek>Κεραυνὸν ἐν τῇ δεξιᾷ ἔχοντα, καὶ ἀκτῖνας ἐπὶ τῇ κεφαλῇ</greek> <note>original Greek: "Holding a thunderbolt in his right hand, and rays upon his head."</note>. Heliodorus testifies that the Ethiopians also had this custom, who in Book 9 of the *Ethiopian Story* elegantly describes these arrangements of rays:
<margin>Servius.</margin>
<margin>Lucian.</margin>
<margin>Heliodorus.</margin>
<greek>πλέγμα, inquit, ᾧ τι κυκλοτερὲς τῇ κεφαλῇ περιθέντες, καὶ τῦτο βέλεσι κτ̅ τὸν κύκλον περιπείραντες (τὰ μὲν ἐπὶ περιφερῶν τὰ βέλεα πρὸς τῇ κεφαλῇ περιτιθέντες), τὰς δὲ ἀκίδας οἷον ἀκτῖνας, εἰς τὸ ἔκτος προβέβληνται</greek> <note>original Greek: "A woven thing, he says, which they place around the head in a circle, and pierce it with arrows around the circle (placing the feathered ends of the arrows against the head), while the points, like rays, project outward."</note>. Surrounding the head with a certain circular wrapping, and piercing it with arrows in a ring, they turn the winged parts toward the head, but the points project outward in the likeness of rays. By these things they wished to indicate nothing other than, according to the Egyptian mind, the signs of a latent divinity. 
<margin>A diadem composed of arrows.</margin>
Hence you will find hardly any image of a man, bird, quadruped, or insect, or a composite of these, among the hieroglyphic inscriptions, to which this circle is not attached; a manifest sign of latent divinity: and therefore a proper invention of the Egyptians, as will be said in the course of the Work. These things having now been proposed, let us look more closely at the secrets of the hieroglyphic circle.

CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 89 CHAPTER I.

<margin>The Egyptians noted that all things tend toward circles.</margin> ...the circuits of movements, whether they considered the orbits of the Heavens and the stars, or finally the Soul of the World and the Supreme <term>Deity</term><note>original: Numen; referring to a divine power or presiding spirit.</note>, they always found that their operations were measured by circular motions. However, because it is necessary that the supreme Deity, who moves all things, is himself necessarily immobile, infinite, and eternal, let us show how, little by little, they suggested through the properties of the Circle that all things are one in God, and God is in all things. For Pherecydes <note>Pherecydes of Syros (c. 580–520 BCE), an early Greek thinker often cited in the Renaissance as a bridge between Egyptian wisdom and Greek philosophy.</note>, a disciple of the Egyptians, suggested this when he sang of God in a hymn to Jove:

> <margin>Pherecydes calls God a Circle, a line, a triangle, a square, a center, and all things.</margin>God is a circle, a square, and even a triangle,
> and in this a line, a center, and all before all. <note>original Greek: Ὁ Θεός ἐστὶ κύκλος, τετράγωνος, καὶ δὲ τρίγωνος, κἀν τῇ δ’ ἡ γραμμή, κέντρον, καὶ πάντα πρὸ πάντων.</note>
> *For God is both a circle, and a square, and a triangle,*
> *And a line, and a center, and the all of all.*

<margin>In what sense it is true that God is both a Circle, a square, a triangle, a point, and a line.</margin>It is asked, therefore, how God can be both a circle, and a square, and a triangle; how He can be a line and a point; and how things so disparate and contrary can be one in God, or can fall within any comprehension of the human intellect regarding the simplicity of the divine nature? I answer that the Ancients learned all these things from the nature of the circle considered abstractly. For we must not think that they considered the circle under its physical properties, but according to a certain analogy of the <term>Mathematical Circle</term> <note>A geometric ideal rather than a physical object.</note> to that circle <margin>A circle considered abstractly, and elevated to the status of the infinite, is both a line, a triangle, a square, and a point.</margin> whose center is everywhere and whose circumference is nowhere. <note>This famous paradox, often called the "Infinite Sphere," suggests that God is present at every point (center) but is unbounded (no circumference).</note> For since all things affected by quantity in any way consist of boundaries, it is necessary that we conceive of them as finite. But if we wish to raise them to the status of an infinite essence, it will not be possible for us to imagine them unless insofar as they are affected by infinite reasons and powers, as <term>Cusanus</term> <note>Nicholas of Cusa (1401–1464), a theologian and mathematician who famously used the "coincidence of opposites" in geometry to explain the nature of God.</note> rightly teaches. To make this clear, I have decided that the following three propositions must be explained.

---

# PROPOSITION I.

**If circles are drawn larger and larger into infinity, each of which touches a straight line at the same point, the greatest and final of these circles, than which none can be larger, will necessarily be infinite, and the same as an infinite straight line.**

<meta>This page continues the geometric and metaphysical exploration of the circle as a divine symbol. CHAPTER I. 90 HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

Having drawn a straight line *ST*, let circles *avo, bun, cum, dul, euk, fut, gu, and hu* be drawn from different centers to its midpoint *V*. It is certain that the smaller the angle the circles form with line *ST* at point *V*, the larger they will be; and the larger the angle, the smaller they will be. This is gathered from the demonstrations by Clavius <note>Christopher Clavius (1538–1612) was a preeminent Jesuit mathematician and astronomer. Kircher cites his commentary on Euclid’s *Elements* to ground this mystical argument in the best science of his day.</note> in Book 3, Proposition 16 of Euclid’s *Elements*. Now, if a circle were described so large that it no longer formed an "angle of contact" <note>An angle of contact (or horn angle) is the infinitesimal angle between a curve and its tangent line.</note> but coincided with the straight line *ST* itself; I say that this circle would necessarily be infinite, and that none greater could be given. For since the centers of the said circles are more remote from point *V* the more obtuse (wider) the circles are and the closer they are to the straight line *ST*, the center must necessarily be infinitely distant from point *V* as soon as the circle coincides with the straight line. Since an infinite <term>radius</term><note>original: semidiameter; the distance from the center to the edge.</note> necessarily implies an infinite circumference, it follows that a circle coinciding with line *ST* will necessarily be infinite; which was to be proven. Nevertheless, no amount of time or human industry could ever actually complete such a task.

->*Corollary.*<-

<margin>God, in the manner just explained, admits contradictory things.</margin>
From this it is clear how not only the Ancients, but also modern theologians, have seemed to posit "contradictories" in God. Following Saint Dionysius <note>Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite (c. 5th–6th century), a theologian famous for "apophatic" or negative theology, which describes God by what He is not, claiming God is beyond all human concepts.</note>, they have described Him as being and non-being, light and darkness, intellect and non-intellect, and so on. For the "greatest circle," beyond which no greater can be given, when considered in this way, is both a circle and not a circle; it is equally curved and straight; it is simultaneously an infinite circumference and an infinite line. Therefore, it necessarily involves what appear to be contradictions; all of which are compatible with God alone. These matters will be declared more fully once we have first explained other things regarding this subject.

---

### PROPOSITION II.

If, in a finite circle, a line attached to the center passes from any point on the circumference to the opposite point, the angle which the said line describes with the diameter at the center will increase continuously toward infinity; thus, the angle of the diameter with which the running line coincides is altogether infinite. In an infinite circle, however, which has no specific size, it is necessary that the circumference, the radius, and the angle be entirely the same.

...to become infinite. For since an infinite angle is that than which no greater can be given, and before a rotating line falls upon the diameter, ever larger and larger angles can be given to infinity through continuous division; it follows that the diameter *a c* truly possesses the power of an infinite angle, since it enfolds all possible angles imaginable within a semicircle; which was the first point. Now, let *a g c e* be an infinite circle, than which no greater can be given. I say that the diameter, the circumference, and the angle coincide as one, and thus all are infinite. For although in our way of conceiving things (by which we are accustomed to conceiving only finite and limited things) a diameter is a straight line, a circumference is a curved line, and an angle is the quantity of two lines inclining toward each other; nevertheless, these distinctions must entirely cease in things that are non-quantitative and infinite. For since the circumference in infinite things is <term>absolute straightness</term> <note>original: "summa rectitudo"; Kircher argues that as a circle becomes infinitely large, the curve of its edge flattens out until it is indistinguishable from a straight line.</note>, it necessarily follows that both the circumference and the diameter are exactly the same. Furthermore, if point *b* remains motionless while point *a* is rotated until it reaches the opposite location *c*, a semicircle will necessarily emerge. And if the diameter *a c* remains motionless while the semicircle is rotated around it, a sphere is born. This sphere is the ultimate state of a line's potential, existing totally <term>in act</term> <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "potency" is the capacity to become something, while "act" (actu) is the full realization of that potential. A sphere is seen here as the "final form" of geometric expansion.</note>, since a sphere is not in potential to any further figure. Therefore, if these figures are finite within the potential of a line, and an infinite line is actually all those things to which a finite line is in potential, it follows that an infinite circle is a triangle, and a sphere, and a diameter, and an angle, and all are equally one; which was the second point. And just as all these things differ in quantities—as they have no proportion to one another—so too the imagination, which does not transcend the realm of the senses, is least able to conceive these things; rather, this is the work of the abstracting intellect alone, as will be clear from what follows.

Let us show, however, how this line and triangle are also at once a circle. Suppose then that triangle *a b c* is infinite; let line *b a* travel from point *b* toward *c* back to point *b*; an infinite <term>great circle</term> <note>The largest possible circle that can be drawn on a sphere, or in this case, an infinite plane.</note> will necessarily be produced from this, of which *b c* is a portion; and since that portion is an arc of an infinite circle, it will necessarily be a straight<gloss>a</gloss> line according to the previous demonstrations, as is *b c*: and because every part of an infinite circumference is infinite; therefore that portion *b c* will be no smaller than the whole infinite circumference, and thus that portion will be equal to the infinite circuit of that circumference. It also necessarily follows that triangle *a b c* is a great or infinite circle: and because its circumference, as was explained in the preceding sections, is a straight line; the arc or portion *b c* of the infinite circle will also be a straight line, and the circumference will not be larger than the infinite line *b c*, since the infinite cannot be greater than the infinite: nor are they two separate lines, because it is impossible for there to be two infinites; therefore the infinite line, which is a triangle, is at the same time a circle. And this is what Pherecydes <note>Pherecydes of Syros (6th century BCE), an early Greek thinker whom Kircher regards as a keeper of ancient Egyptian wisdom.</note> said above, that God is a circle, and a line, and a triangle, and the all of all things; let us now see how this is to be applied to God.

### III.

->How it can be gathered from what has been said that God is all in all,<-

<margin>The simple Maximum is actually all things that exist in potentiality.</margin>

**T**herefore, from this fact—that an infinite line <term>enfolds</term> <note>original: "complicat"; a technical term in Kircher's philosophy meaning to contain many things within a single, unified point or nature.</note> in act everything that a finite line possesses in potential—we gather how the <term>absolute Maximum</term> <note>A name for God, signifying the greatest possible reality in whom all possibilities are already realized.</note> is actually all those things which are in the potentiality of absolute simplicity. For whatever is possible, this very thing is the absolute and simple Maximum—not as it exists as a mere possibility, but as it exists in its highest state; just as a triangle is drawn out from an infinite line, and yet the infinite line is not a triangle insofar as it is made of a finite line, but is actually an infinite triangle, because it is one and the same with the line. This is because absolute possibility in the Maximum is nothing other than the Maximum in act itself, just as the infinite line is actually a circle. But it is different in things that are not the Maximum; for there, potential is not the same as act, just as a finite line is not a triangle. Since, therefore, all things are enfolded in act within that Maximum, contradictories and oppositions necessarily result from it <note>This refers to the "coincidence of opposites," where things that seem like opposites to humans (like a straight line and a curve) are identical in God.</note>, such as that in God

<margin>*Dionysius the Areopagite*</margin>
In God, the maximum and the minimum coincide. For as that great Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher of the late 5th century, whose "Mystical Theology" heavily influenced medieval thought.</note> rightly asserts in his *Mystical Theology*, *God (who is this very "maximum") is not one thing while being not another; nor is He in one place and not in another. For just as He is all things, so He is none of them; for He is the perfect and singular cause of all things above every position, and His excellence is above all negation, by which He is simply absolute from all things and beyond all things.* From this, the Hebrew Theologians—as was explained in our study of the Cabala <note>Kircher refers to Jewish mystical tradition, which he often integrated into his Christian worldview.</note>—call God "Being and non-Being" <note>original: "Ens & non Ens"</note>, agreeing with Dionysius. Hence the Egyptians likewise defined God through both light and darkness or gloom.

Just as, therefore, infinite curvature is infinite straightness; so the essence of God is simultaneously the periphery <note>The outer boundary or circumference.</note> and the straightness, enclosed by no limits. <margin>God is all in all.</margin> Indeed, He is the simplest essence of all essences. And just as all the essences of things—which ever were, will be, or are—are always and from eternity present in that very essence; so all essences are that very essence itself: and just as He is the essence of all, so He is the essence of any one thing as much as all of them. Parmenides undoubtedly alluded to this when he said, "anything is in anything"; although, lacking the light of faith, he was unable to extricate himself from such a deep mystery. <margin>An infinite line is the most adequate figure of all.</margin> Finally, just as an infinite line is the most adequate measure of all things; so the maximum essence of all essences is that in which the maximum and minimum adequately coincide, such that the essence is not larger than the minimum, nor smaller than the maximum. For since one foot <note>A unit of measurement.</note> in an infinite line is not larger than two feet—indeed, since any part of the infinite is infinite—it is necessary that one foot coincides with many. Furthermore, just as a finite line is divisible, an infinite line is indivisible, since the infinite admits no parts into which it could be cut, nor does the maximum fall away from the minimum within it. But since a finite line is infinitely divisible, and no part can be designated so small that a smaller cannot be given, it is impossible for it to be divided into something that is "not a line"; for this property falls only to the infinite line, which is why it is the "reason" <note>In the sense of the underlying principle or logic.</note> of the finite line. In the same way, <margin>Aristotle.</margin> the maximum of all is the reason of all; and reason, according to Aristotle, is a measure. Therefore, just as the infinite line is the perpetual and immutable reason of the finite line; so also the reason of all things, which is God the Blessed, is eternal and subject to no mutation or instability.

<margin>God in all things, and all things in Him.</margin>
And from this it is clear why the Ancients perceived an eternal "reason" of things; for, according to Plato in Chalcidius's commentary on the *Phaedo* <note>A famous Socratic dialogue on the soul; Chalcidius provided the standard Latin translation and commentary in the Middle Ages.</note>, there is one absolute exemplar and Idea of things which, diffused into a multitude, brings forth many exemplars. Since, therefore, the infinite line is the reason of all finite lines, it follows that it is in any one line in such a way that it is in none, and any finite line is in it; just as God is in all things and in nothing, yet all things are in Him.

In this way you shall proceed to the remaining properties of the infinite line, which we say is not so much "one" that it is not equally "three." For we said above that the greatest line is a triangle; and because a line is most simple, that "three-foldness" which is considered within it will also be most simple. And since the whole triangle is a line, every angle in it will also be a line. Therefore, the infinite line is three-fold. However, since it is impossible for there to be multiple "infinites," this trinity...

than trinity; nor is trinity anything other than unity; nor is actuality anything other than unity, trinity, and essence. And from this paradox it is easily clear how the Most Holy Trinity in divine matters is to be conceived. For as St. Augustine <note>St. Augustine of Hippo (354–430 AD), a central figure in Western Christianity whose writings on the Trinity shaped medieval and Renaissance theology.</note> rightly says: *When you begin to count the Trinity in divine matters, you have already departed from the Truth.* <note>original: "Dum incipis numerare in diuinis trinitatem, iam exis Veritatem."</note> Whoever distinguishes the Trinity from essence or unity falls into manifest error. Instead, it must be called the "unitrine" or "triune," whether you call it unity or trinity; and this is the truth. Nor do the numbers four, five, and so on have any place here; for this would be repugnant to the simplicity and perfection of the greatest of all. Since every polygonal figure has the triangle as its simplest element, and since this is the smallest of all polygons (than which no smaller can exist), and since the minimum coincides with the maximum, and so relates to the other figures just as unity relates to numbers; it follows that just as every number

is resolved into unity, so polygons are resolved into the triangle. The greatest triangle, therefore, with which the smallest coincides, encompasses all polygonal figures. A four-sided figure, however, is not the smallest, as is obvious, but exceeds the triangular by one line; hence it implies a contradiction for a quadrangle to be the "maximum." Since it always exceeds triangular figures, a "most-perfectly-equal" figure for them cannot be conceived in any way. If anyone wishes to conceive the measures of all measurable quantities, he must first have the infinite line for length, the greatest triangle for width or surface, and the sphere for depth or the solidity of bodies. Besides these four, no one can reach the multitude of all measurable things with any others. Since, however, there cannot be multiple "maxima" or infinites, the one unique maximum itself is the simplest and most absolute measure of all quantities. And this is that highest, eternal, and unchangeable triangle, the most adequate measure <note>original: "metrum"</note> of all things subsisting in a threefold way <note>Kircher uses "triniter" to describe how things exist in three modes, reflecting the Trinity.</note>, such as operations, and actions in potentiality...

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS.

<note>The text begins mid-sentence, discussing things that exist as a trinity</note> ...essence, object, and act, subsisting as a trinity; similarly visions, understandings, volitions, similarities, dissimilarities, beauties, proportions, correlations, natural appetites, and all other things whose unity of being consists in plurality, just as the being and operation of nature consists in the correlation of the agent and the patient <note>the one acting and the one being acted upon</note>.

## § IV.

*The Circle demonstrates how all things are identified as one in God; and the sphere demonstrates His actual existence in all things.*

<margin>In infinite unity, all the attributes of God are not diverse.</margin>
<margin>What the Hermetic Circle is like.</margin>
<margin>The Greatest is all things.</margin>
Since it is established from what has been said that the triangle is the circle, and the trinity is unity; this unity will undoubtedly be infinite, just as the circle is infinite. Since, however, there cannot be many infinites, the unity in which the triangle and the circle are identified will be more "one" than any unity comprehensible to any intellect in infinity. Its identity will be so great that it precedes even all relative oppositions; for there, "otherness" and "diversity" are not opposed to identity. Therefore, since it is infinite unity, consequently all things that can in any way belong to it are itself, without diversity or alterity <note>otherness</note>; so that His goodness is not one thing and His wisdom another, nor His mercy one thing and His justice another, but in this infinite unity they are altogether one and the same; since all diversity apprehended by us is identity in Him. Thus, in the unity of divine duration, the past and the future are not different from the present, but are one duration and eternity, in which the beginning is the end, and the end the beginning. All these things shine forth beautifully in that infinite circle: for since a circle of this kind is the greatest <note>Latin: *maximus*</note>, its diameter will also be the greatest; and since there cannot be many "greatests," that circle will be "one" to the extent that its diameter is the circumference itself. Since, however, an infinite diameter has an infinite middle, and the middle is the center, it necessarily follows that the diameter, the circumference, and the center are the same. And this is that **Hermetic Circle** <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, about which we have frequently discoursed throughout this entire Work, **whose center is everywhere, and whose circumference is nowhere.** The Greatest, therefore, is most perfectly within every simple and indivisible thing, because the center is infinite and everywhere; likewise, it encompasses all things from without, because the circumference is infinite; equally, it penetrates all things, because the diameter is infinite. It is the beginning of all things, because it is the center; the end of all things, because it is the circumference; the middle of all things, because it is the diameter. It is, furthermore, the efficient cause, because it is the center; the formal cause, because it is the diameter; and the final cause, because it is the circumference. Again, it gives being to all things, because it is the center; it governs all things, because it is the diameter; it preserves all things, because it is the circumference. You see, therefore, how the Greatest is identical with nothing, nor yet diverse; and how all things are in Him, from Him, and through Him; because He is the center, diameter, and circumference. It is also clear how all the attributes of God are identified in God in perfect unity: likewise how God is of all things even...

For those things which He knows, He does not know with a distinction of time, because He does not recognize future things as past, nor past things as present, but as eternal; and He knows mutable things immutably. And this is that fate <note>original: "fatum"</note>, 
<margin>What fate is, and of what kind it is.</margin>which has tormented every single philosopher so greatly. Indeed, all things, when referred back to providence itself, are said to possess necessity; and rightly so, because all things in God are God, who is absolute necessity. For example: tomorrow I am able to travel, or not to travel; whichever I shall do, I will not escape providence, since providence enfolds those contraries within itself. Whence, whatever I shall do, I shall have done according to 
<margin>In the simply maximum, all things are one.</margin>the providence of God. Furthermore, just as in an infinite sphere (from the preceding arguments) the center, the circumference, and the solidity are one; so in the simply maximum <note>The "Maximum" is a term for God as the greatest possible being in whom all opposites coincide.</note> all things are one. For He is the center or beginning, the middle, and the end of all things. And just as the sphere is the actualization of the triangle and the circle, so the Maximum is the actualization of all things. Therefore, every actual existence possesses from Him whatever actuality exists; and every existence exists in act to such an extent as it is from that infinite act itself. And hence the Maximum is the form of forms, and the form of being, or the maximum actual entity; which did not escape the notice of 
Parmenides <note>A pre-Socratic Greek philosopher who argued that reality is a single, unchanging "Being."</note>, who, defining God, says *God is He, for whom to be is anything that is, and to be all that which is*. Then, just as the maximum sphere is the perfection of all figures, so the Maximum is the most perfect of all most perfect things, in which curvature is straightness, composition is simplicity, and diversity is identity, and alterity is unity; in which imperfection is infinite perfection, and possibility is infinite act—the unique and simplest measure of all things existing in the Universe (for in Him the whole is not greater than the part, just as in an infinite sphere, an infinite line is not greater). He is the circulation of all things and of motions; the most absolute reason, measure, and meter of the whole Universe. Whence, not undeservedly, God is defined by 
<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure to whom the Hermetic writings are attributed.</note> as the universality of things. And since He is the entity of the being of all things, and every motion is toward being, therefore the rest of motion is He Himself, who is the end of motion; all things, therefore, tend from Him and toward Him. All these

## CHAPTER II.
Concerning the Circle, the Cross <note>original: "decussi," referring to the X-shaped Roman numeral ten or a decussis cross</note>, and other angular figures; how the Egyptians employed them to indicate the secrets of the sensible World.

<margin>The idea of the Circle, and its analogy to Mathematical circles.</margin>
In the preceding sections, we considered the circle and the triangle as infinite things and as symbols of immense divinity; now let us contemplate these same things as finite, and let us indicate how they expressed the secrets of the sensible World through them. If anyone wishes to depict a circle, he first designates a center, then establishes a line or radius by the opening of a compass, and finally describes a curved line from the straight one, which is the circle. You will find that the same occurs in the "ideal" circle <note>The "ideal" circle refers to the perfect, conceptual form of a circle in the mind or in the divine realm, as opposed to a physical drawing.</note>. For that ineffable circle, which can be named by the names of all things, is such that it contains a center from which a line exists, and from both of these the circumference arises. But since a circle of this kind is infinite, it is necessary—as we said above—that the center, the line, and the circumference itself be equal. Whence, since that infinity is nothing other than eternity and supreme equality, it is certain that the point cannot exist before the line, nor the line before the circumference; rather, from eternity, the center, line, and circumference existed together. Thus, the line, point, and circumference are the unfolding <note>original: "explicatio," a Neoplatonic term meaning the unfolding of a simple unity into a complex form</note> of the point and line. Furthermore, this point in eternity conducts itself in the manner of a generator, or an unfolder, producing from its own "enfolding" <note>original: "complicante," the opposite of unfolding; the state where all things are one</note> power a begotten, consubstantial line. The center and the line together conduct themselves in the manner of an eternally unfolding bond or circumference. Thus, the paternal principle in divine matters acts as the center, the line acts as the principle from a principle (and is called equality), and the circumference acts as the union or bond.

But if you truly understand how a circle, revolved upon an infinite straight line (which is eternity), does not touch it at a single point, you will apprehend how in one *Now* <note>original: "Nunc," the eternal present</note> or instant of eternity, all revolutions of time—whether great or small—subsist. You will see how eternity is the very substance of time, and also the meter and measure of all duration. You will also see that it is false to claim the revolutions of the spheres have existed from eternity, since infinity can by no means be compatible with a number of periodic revolutions. For if we could count ten past revolutions, a hundred, a thousand, or even all of them; and if someone were to say that not all are countable, but that infinite ones preceded us, and then says one more revolution will occur next year, it necessarily follows that those "infinite" ones are the same as one <note>A logical argument against an eternal universe: adding 1 to infinity should be impossible, therefore time must have a beginning</note>; who does not see how absurd that is? Furthermore, the Creator seems to have made two things: namely, "nearly nothing" and the "point"; for there is no medium between a point and nothing. Indeed, a point is so close to nothing that if you add a point to a point, no more results than if you joined nothing to nothing. Then He made "One," and joined the point with the One, so that it is one point; and in this one point lies the enfolding of the entire Universe. The Universe, therefore, is conceived as being led out from that one point, just as one line would be led out from one point, so that from it a triangle or a quadrangle <note>original: "trigonus, aut terragonus" (likely a typo for tetragonus)</note> might be fashioned.

<meta>The text cuts off mid-word "tetragonus" (quadrangle), which is completed on the following page.</meta>
