## CHAPTER II.

The last, and indeed the most perfect, simplest, and most similar to the Creator, is the circle. And while in the triangle, which is made of three angles, unity and trinity coincide in the form of the trigon—namely, the unity of essence and the trinity of angles—in the circle, unity and infinity coincide. This is the unity of essence and the infinity of angles: for a circle is nothing other than a polygon consisting of infinite sides, the actualization of all angles that can be formed from a line. It is clear, therefore, how God, the Creator of all things, produced the entire Universe from a single point which He created, namely through the unfolding of that point into angles, and finally into a circumference.

<margin>Proclus, in the 5th book on Euclid.</margin>
Hence, since the Egyptians had noted a circular property in God as the Archetype <note>The original model or pattern from which all things are copied.</note> of all things, they rightly chose that same circle as the symbol of the sensible World; so that in every way the idea might perfectly correspond to its own Idea. Indeed, beholding the traces and circular actions of all things, they called the World and those things within the World "sensible circles"; but the incorporeal Intelligences <note>Angelic or divine minds that govern the cosmos.</note> they called "invisible circles." Proclus, in the 5th book on Euclid, explains this acutely in his usual manner: *All mathematical things,* he says, *are first in the soul itself; and before numbers, there are numbers that move by themselves; and before visible figures, there are vital figures; and before those things which are harmonized, there are harmonic ratios; and before the bodies which move in orbits, invisible circles were produced.* For when they recognized that the rays of the stars, resting upon the earth as if upon a center, described circles by their rotation, they considered this the proper work of a divine faculty. When they wished to indicate either divinity, or the World, or the Heavens in their symbols, they expressed it by a circle, or a sphere, or some symbol of Isis assumed from inferior things not unlike it. From this I also believe that the shrines, altars, and instruments with which they administered sacred rites were all fashioned with a circular apparatus; and likewise the ceremonies, gestures, and movements were performed in a circle. Since we discuss these matters dispersedly throughout this entire Work and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we wished only to indicate them briefly here.

<margin>What is the Chiasma? And its meanings.</margin>
From the circle, therefore, let us proceed to the remaining angular figures. Since the Ancients noted (as we also said in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*) that from the imaginary flow of a center or point a line is born—one end of which remains unmoved while the other, being led around, describes a curved line which they called a circle—progressing a little deeper from this contemplation, they imagined something angular even within the circle itself. For an angle is established within it: a symbol of pyramidal influence. Then, any other line cutting the diameter at the center forms a decussis <image-desc>cross symbol</image-desc> <note>A cross in the shape of an X.</note>; which, if it were made at right angles, constituted a perfect cross, a symbol of influence into the four quarters of the World; if at acute angles, it specifically produced a *chiasma* <gloss>original Greek: χισδμα</gloss>, or a decussis, a symbol of the pyramidal influence of the Deity. Justin Martyr proves this earlier; he says the World was established by God <gloss>original Greek: "by the power of Christ"</gloss> and <gloss>original Greek: "in the type of the cross"</gloss>; alluding to the mystery of the cross, just as Justin shows in his First Apology before the [Roman] Senate: <gloss>original Greek: "And not only in this way, but also in the type of the cross, which he [Plato] says the heavens also form in their arrangement, as I testify in the words now being declared to you."</gloss> <note>Kircher is referencing a famous passage where Justin Martyr argues that even pagan philosophers like Plato glimpsed the mystery of the Cross in the structure of the universe.</note>

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

### CHAPTER II

<margin>A hieroglyphic of the generation and corruption of things.</margin>
<image-desc>A diagram showing two inverted pyramids connected at their bases. The top pyramid has its apex labeled 'D inverted pyramid.' and its base labeled with points C and E. Points B and F are on the sides. The bottom pyramid has its apex labeled 'A upright pyramid.' and its base labeled with points G and H. Points I and K are on the sides. The overall shape resembles an hourglass or two triangles joined at their vertices.</image-desc>
K represents the <term>denarius</term> <note>The number ten, often considered the number of perfection or completion in Pythagorean thought</note>. For if A is like a seed, D like a tree, and G like another seed, then K is indeed like another tree; thus A progresses into D through B and C, while D progresses into G through E and F, and the <note>original: "septenarius"</note> number seven is closed; then G ascends into K through H and I, and thus the number ten is completed. Therefore, the individual contraction of a species—as the <term>Schools</term> <note>Refers to the Scholastic philosophers of the Middle Ages and Renaissance</note> say—is corruptible in itself within the seed A, but incorruptible within the species; striving to preserve itself by the power of the species contracted within it, and resolving itself into the species, it sheds the individuality of the seed so that it may draw out something like itself through the medium of the species. Thus, by a four-fold progression, it ascends into the tree; for without that medium, it cannot multiply itself in specific likeness. Therefore, A intends to produce G; and because it cannot accomplish this without ascending into D, it ascends into D to reach its goal. But D, being a tree, seeing that it cannot preserve itself except in a similar tree, intends K; however, it cannot reach K without G; therefore it descends into G, so that by its medium, it may reach K. Thus in A a double appetite is joined: the natural, which ends in G, and the accidental, which ends in K. Likewise in D a double appetite is joined: the natural, which finds its end in K, and the accidental, which ends in G. Therefore the number four moves the appetite, with one appetite stimulating the other, so that there is a continuous succession of generation and corruption.

But this discourse, which we have proposed in the Scholastic manner, the <term>Egyptians</term> explain allegorically as follows. <term>Osiris</term> is moisture, <term>Isis</term> is the earth, with whom <term>Osiris</term> is mingled; from these <term>Horus</term> is born from the seed, the spirit that nourishes and makes all things fruitful. <term>Isis</term> raises <term>Horus</term> from the underworld while the seed committed to the earth bursts forth into a plant, a tree, leaves, flowers, and fruits. But with the parching power and dryness of <term>Typhon</term> <note>The Greek name for Set, the god of chaos and storms</note> lying in wait for <term>Horus</term>—which happens in the Autumn season—<term>Horus</term> is meanwhile slain by <term>Typhon</term>; that is, the falling fruit provides a new sowing, which, hidden in the earth, is once again restored by <term>Isis</term> through the industry of <term>Anubis</term>, that is, the <term>Mercurial Farmer</term> <note>Likening the god Anubis/Mercury to the cleverness and labor of the agriculturist</note>.

<margin>What is the rational tree?</margin>
By this likeness, they reasoned symbolically not only concerning the vicissitude of generation and corruption of things exerting itself in the vegetable seed, but also concerning sensible things, and indeed even concerning rational and intellectual things. For from the seed of wonder, the rational tree arises, which bears fruits similar to wonder; through the wonder drawn out, it raises a similar tree of reason. So from the seminal principle of demonstration, the intellectual tree proceeds; exerting seminal principles from itself, through which the intellectual tree rises again. From all these things, narrated perhaps more at length than was proper, it is clear by how subtle a reasoning they indicated the vicissitude of generable things even under this most humble <term>three-lettered character</term> <note>original: "trigramma litera"</note>; and how that <term>world-spirit</term> <note>original: "spiritus mundanus"</note> lurking in the seeds of the things of the Universe gradually ascends and descends, so that it may ascend again, instilling generative principles into each and every thing, so that the <term>World</term> may be preserved in its being; which would by no means happen without this vicissitude.

§ I.

<header>CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS. CHAPTER II.</header>

# § I.

How the *World* is understood *by the Egyptians* to have flowed forth from the archetypal triangle.

<margin>Pallas born from the brain of Jupiter.</margin>
In order for this to be understood, it must be known that by this archetypal triangle, nothing else is understood than the triform Divinity of three, which the *Egyptians* express through three names: *Hemphta* (or *Emeph*), *Phtha*, and *Amun*. These perfectly correspond to the three *Middoth* <note>Hebrew: "measures" or attributes</note> of the *Hebrews* in the *Sephiroth* tree. Therefore, what the *Hebrews* call the *Crown* or *Keter* <note>original: כתר</note>, the *Infinite*, the *Egyptians* call *Hemphta* or *Emeph*: the first craftsman-intellect, whom they also prefigure in the second series of sensible causes through *Osiris* or the *Sun*. Again, just as the *Hebrews* call *Wisdom* <note>original: חכמה, Chokmah</note> the creator of the *World*, so the *Egyptians* call the *Wisdom* of the first intellect *Phtha*. By this name they also call the Counsel of *Isis*, *Mercury*, and even *Isis* herself; she is the full image and pattern of *Osiris*, the first intellect. For this reason, *Orpheus* not inappropriately called her *Pallas*, and for the stated cause the *Ancients* fashioned her as being born from the brain of *Jupiter*. *Amun*, however, responding to the *Hebrews'* *Understanding* <note>original: בינה, Binah</note> or *Intelligence*, is the active power of both from without, by which the *World of Horus* is produced. Hence arises that variety of hieroglyphic objects with which the priests of *Horus* expressed him everywhere: namely the *Staff* or *caduceus* <note>original: κηρύκειον</note>, which is marked with the head of a *Hoopoe*; also the curved staff <note>term: lituus; a curved wand used by Roman augurs for divination</note>, and the *gnomon* <note>term: gnomon; an L-shaped tool used for measuring shadows or as a carpenter's square</note>, and from the back a triangle to which a circle is attached. These indicate nothing other than that the *World*, produced by *God* through his *Wisdom*, shines forth with an admirable variety of things (signified by the *Hoopoe's* head), with the highest harmony (indicated by the curved staff), and finally with a fitting order (indicated by the gnomon).

<margin>Note: the triangle in this figure has a gnomon attached to it.</margin>

<image-desc>A circular diagram depicts a standing human figure, possibly Horus, facing right. The figure has wings on its head and holds two staffs. Text labels "SYMBOLA" are to the left of the figure, and "HOR." is to the right.</image-desc>

Thus, *Plato*, a diligent student of the *Egyptians*, sufficiently demonstrates that *Horus* was produced from *Hemphta* through *Phtha* and *Amun*, while he asserts that this sensible *World* flowed forth from that archetypal triangle. This is clearly indicated by that triangle with the globe attached among the other symbols of *Horus*, and it is expressed quite beautifully and elegantly in the following diagram.

And from these things it appears, and should be manifest to all, that the *Sacrosanct* and thrice-blessed *Trinity*—the greatest and most sublime mystery of the *Christian* faith—has at all times been foreshadowed, even under the obscure fictions of myths.

Furthermore, because *Osiris* is nothing other than the first intellect, that eternal *Sun*...

The eternal and first producer of all things, who through Isis, his consort—namely his **Wisdom**—produced **Horus**, which is to say, the **World**, as the sacred priests <note>original: "Hieromantæ"</note> indicate through various hieroglyphic schemes. <margin>Interpretation of the Symbols of Horus.</margin>
time like a small infant by the Wisdom of God. He is expressed with a horn of plenty to indicate the variety, abundance, and fullness of created things in the World. The Triangle <note>original: "Trigonus"</note> with a globe, inscribed within the cube, signifies that Horus flowed forth from the archetypal triangle. Finally, Horus, pressing his lips and urging silence with his finger, indicates the ineffability of the mysteries. See the figures cited here on pages 151 and 152 of Volume I of the *Oedipus*.

§ II.

### Concerning the Triangle, the Square, and other angular figures exhibited hieroglyphically.

<margin>Clement.</margin>
It must be known that the Egyptian Priests, as has been proven elsewhere, exhibited their secret mysteries not only under the ingenious architecture of sacred animals, but also under various Geometric figures. For they were the inventors of Geometry <note>original: "Germaniæ" - likely a printer's error for "Geometriæ"</note>, and were the most skilled in it above all other mortals, being well aware of its secrets. Hence they were called <unclear>μαρπακεντπιο</unclear> <note>The Greek word is difficult to read, but likely relates to 'mathematics' or 'geometry'. It appears to be 'μαθηματικῶν' or similar, but the letters are very faded/blurry.</note> *Ardenadapta*. Indeed, this kind of science, which among other nations was held in the highest honor and price and possessed few experts, *was almost common in Egypt*, as Clement says in Book 1 of the *Stromata*, which we cited in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 422; see that passage. Therefore, the Egyptian Priests, being duly imbued with Geometric principles, just as they prepared their minds for the higher Sacraments of Philosophy, so too they used Geometric...

They were accustomed to adopt these figures and numerical science for the purpose of philosophizing perfectly, just as we see ingeniously performed in almost all hieroglyphics <note>original: "hierogrammatismis"</note>, partly through numbers and partly through geometric figures. For, weighing the reasons of secret things more deeply, when they discovered that God affects numbers and geometric figures—such as triangles, squares, circles, and harmonic proportions—in His operations, they certainly judged that they could not exhibit these things in a better or more comprehensible way than through the said forms. Following them, <margin>Pythagoras</margin> Pythagoras and Plato—the wise disciples of wise masters—expressed all the greatest mysteries through these same forms of theirs. <margin>Plato.</margin>

<margin>Plato.</margin>

### Just as the Egyptians, therefore, pointed out the origin of things subtly through lines, angles, and figures, so too, according to the origin of figures and bodies resulting from points, lines, and surfaces, they noted the process of the World-Spirit. This Spirit, unfolded into circles from the point or center of its unity, first forms something angular in the lower world; from here, however, returning while it permeates all bodies of the world, it marks out innumerable rectilinear figures below, but above, according to the condition of their natures, it completes its circular revolutions <note>original: "pericyclases," a Greek-derived term for orbital cycles</note>. And that these things are so, Plato beautifully teaches in *Alcinous* <note>Referring to the "Handbook of Platonism" by Alcinous, formerly attributed to Albinus</note> chapters 11 and 12, where he says that the corporeal world is composed of the Elements, in which the process of things occurs through straight lines, and was indicated by the ancients through the square. His commentator explains it thus: In the motion of the Elements, a double position of lines must be considered according to the double position of the Elements. Earth and Water occupy opposite sides in the hieroglyphic square—namely, the base and the side opposite to it; they always obtain a position that is level, or as mathematicians say, parallel to the earth or the Horizon, one above the other. Air and Fire, however, because they tend upward, hence the sides in the hieroglyphic square standing upon the previous lines clearly declare the nature of Air and Fire tending upward; and thus the qualities of the four Elements are aptly expressed through the four sides of the square. Furthermore, when the Sun, traveling through the Zodiac, greatly stirs the mixture of elementary or mixed bodies and disposes them toward the generation of things, they indicated the year not incongruously through three squares. According to Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note>, the year was divided by the Egyptians into three parts: namely, Spring, Summer, and Winter. These parts were denoted by three squares, just as by the four sides, the four months or the four signs of the Zodiac—of which each third of the year consisted—were denoted. For through these twelve signs <note>original: "dodecamoria," the twelve divisions of the Zodiac</note> the Sun—that divine Osiris, the Good Spirit <note>original: "Agathodæmon"</note> of Egypt—passing through, excites the Elements to the production of all things. And to this interpretation of ours, it does not differ—

<margin>How the Infant, etc., signifies the Egyptians.</margin>Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, the author of a famous treatise on hieroglyphs</note> does not differ from these words: *The eye is as the male, the triple eye, etc.* <note>original: "E'τὸ ὦ ὡς ἄρρεν ὀφθαλμὸς, τριαδὲς ὀφθαλμὸς &c."</note> Moreover, they write that an Infant—the most significant of all things—represents a fourth part of a *deia* or a field (a *deia* or field is a measure of land comprising one hundred cubits); and this is because a fourth part of a day is cast between one rising of Sothis <note>The star Sirius</note> and the next. For since the solar year is completed in 365 days, the Egyptians, every fourth year, would intercalate a surplus day which they call *epagomena* <note>intercalary days added to the end of the year</note>, calculating it because four quarters of a day complete a full day. See the very curious details we have handed down regarding this hieroglyphic in the *Prodromus*, and later more extensively in our *Hieroglyphic Astronomy*. You see, therefore, how that super-mundane, triform Agathodæmon <note>The "Good Spirit" or serpent deity</note> moves from that incorruptible, eternal triad of intellectual Worlds (indicated by circles) into the tetradic or fourfold triad of the three elementary Worlds; that is, it is carried from the simple and immutable into the angular, various face of the material mission, subject to corruptions, which the quadrangular figure aptly represents. To clarify these things a little more deeply, *the prologue of the navels* <note>original: "πρόλογος ὀμφαλῶν"</note> etc.

<margin>Bæritius. Malchus the Persian. Meanings of the Triangle.</margin>### It must be known that the Egyptians, to signify the virtues of God, mostly used geometric figures (which Laërtius and Malchus show in their lives of Plato and Pythagoras that those men followed). Among others, however, they especially observed the triangle; and in it, again, three conditions. For either the triangle consisted of three equal sides, and is called *Isopleuron* <note>Equilateral</note>; or only two, and is called *Isosceles*; or three unequal sides, and is called *Scalene*. Through the *Isopleuron*, they denoted the process of the triform divinity into the corporeal World; whence, according to Plato, it was called the "God-like" of the presiding bodies of the World; through the *Isosceles*, its process into the Starry World; through the *Scalene*, of three unequal angles (of which the first is a right angle, the second is double the third), the World of alteration, that is, the elemental world. But through the circle, they aptly denoted the solitary triune nature of God, as will be said later. How they showed this order and series of the generation of all things, Alcinous the Platonist deduces extensively and beautifully in these words: *Since there are two things from which the World is constituted, body and soul, of which the former is visible and tangible, while the latter is neither visible nor tangible, the power and constitution of each is different. For the body itself is joined together from fire, earth, water, and air; since these four, which previously had no order of elements, the Maker of the World formed into the pyramid, the cube, the octahedron, and the icosahedron, and besides all these, the dodecahedron. For matter, insofar as it took the figure of a pyramid, became fire, because this is most suited for cutting and dividing; insofar as it became an octahedron, it simultaneously received the quality of air; just as water, insofar as it was adorned with the form of an icosahedron; but he attributed the figure of the cube to earth, as being the most solid and firm of all. But the dodecahedron he accommodated to the Universe itself. More than all these, however, the nature of planes approaches the principles; since planes are prior to solids. Truly, the two progenitors of the nature of planes are the most beautiful triangles, one Scalene, the other Isosceles. And the Scalene, when it has one right angle, another containing two-thirds of a right angle, and the remaining part a third of the same; this one indeed I call the first...*

## CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS.

Furthermore, the scalene triangle <note>A triangle with three unequal sides.</note> is the element of the pyramid <note>The tetrahedron.</note>, the octahedron, and the icosahedron; for the pyramid is composed of four triangles having all sides equal, each of which is distributed into six scalene triangles of the kind just mentioned. The octahedron, truly, is made of eight, each of which is similarly divided into six scalenes; as is the icosahedron from twenty. *The other truly (I mean the isosceles)* is fit for the construction of the cube, since four triangles of this species joined together produce a square, just as the squares themselves produce the cube. For the dodecahedron, the God of the Universe made use of it; because twelve signs are perceived in the Zodiac in the heavens, each of which is cut into thirty parts; just as in the dodecahedron composed of twelve pentagons, each of these being divided into five triangles, six triangles are contained within <note>The author is describing the internal geometric decomposition of the faces.</note>; and thus in the whole dodecahedron three hundred and sixty triangles are found, as many as there are sections of the Zodiac itself. By these figures, therefore, matter expressed by God was moved: at first indeed by rough traces without order, then by the same God added into order, according to the proportion which all things obtain among themselves in that joining together. Nor yet do these remain discrete in their place, but are in perpetual agitation, and bring about the same matter; since they are driven, constricted by the circuit of the World, and are carried by alternating pulses, and those indeed which are of thinner parts are driven into the region of the thicker. Wherefore nothing at all is left empty or void of body: but even in those, a permanent inequality brings about a shaking, since matter is agitated by them and they by it.

How truly Plato, following the mind of the Egyptians, composed the four regular figures from scalenes—of which one angle is a right angle, the second two-thirds of a right angle, and the remaining truly a third part of the same, that is, of which one angle is 90, the second 60, and the third 30 degrees—since his commentators have worn this subject out even to this point, we have thought it our duty to demonstrate it in this place by geometric reasoning. First, therefore, they described an equilateral triangle A B C, from whose angles A B C they drew as many perpendiculars A D, C F, and B E; and the equilateral triangle was divided into six scalene triangles, all equal and similar, as the numbers show, each of which constitutes one right angle, and the remaining two, partly 60, partly 30 degrees: and those indeed which stand upon the middle point S are 60; those which terminate in points A B C are 30; those finally which consist of the middle sides at points D E F are 90 degrees. And the sides are allotted according to that proportion which the numbers 3, 4, 5 have, the mystery of which will be explained later. Therefore, they called a triangle of this kind sometimes "genetic," sometimes *genesis* <note>original: "γενεσιν" (generation/origin)</note>, or the "nuptial figure," because it was the principle of the generation of all sublunary things, in this manner: By the base B A they denoted the passive principle of things, namely the moist, or Isis; by the normal <note>The perpendicular line.</note> P B standing upon A B they hinted at the active principle of things, namely the hot, or Osiris, the masculine force; truly by A C, the hypotenuse, that composed of both, or Horus:

<header>GYMNASIUM OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS FROM THE OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS</header>

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>How the cube, the symbol of the earth, is composed of triangles.</margin>
From the Scalene triangle <note>original: "Scaleno"; a triangle with three unequal sides</note>, as if from the first principles, the four regular figures—and consequently the four Elements of which they are symbols—are produced. They used to construct the symbol of the Earth, the cube, in this way: they would quadruple the Isosceles triangle <note>original: "Isoscelem"; a triangle with two equal sides</note> *abc*, and a square *abcd* would result; this, multiplied by 6, established the cube *abedifg*. Thus, according to the testimony of Proclus <note>A 5th-century Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote extensively on Euclid's geometry</note>, the Isosceles was the first principle of the earth, while the square was the proximate principle. Furthermore, they constructed the symbol of fire, the pyramid
<margin>How the Tetrahedron, the symbol of fire, is composed of triangles.</margin>
or Tetrahedron, in this manner: Since the Tetrahedron consists of four equilateral triangles, each of which (as was shown a little earlier) is again composed of six Scalenes; 4 multiplied by 6 produced 24 "genetic" Scalenes (for so we shall hereafter call this kind of triangle). Thus, the four-sided pyramid denoted not only fire, but also the whole Universe, into which the fiery power secretly diffused itself; and in this way, they deduced it into a physical body.
<image-desc>A diagram showing a cube with diagonals drawn on its faces, illustrating its construction from triangles.</image-desc>
By subdividing the Equilateral triangle <note>original: "Triangulum Isopleurum"</note> *ACD* into two equal parts, they created two Scalenes *BAC* and *BAD*; by which they indeed noted the procession of the Divine Power <note>original: "Numen"</note> from the archetypal World into the World exposed to alterations and mutations. Cutting these Scalenes in half again, they produced the Isosceles triangles *BFA* and *BEA*, which are indicators of the procession of the Divine Power through the influence of the stars. They cut these Isosceles triangles in half again through the line *FE*, and produced four Equilateral triangles *AFE*, *FEB*, *EBD*, and *FCB*. By folding these together, they formed the Tetrahedron, the first of all solid bodies, with the triad passing into the tetrad <note>The number three becoming four</note>; that is, the figure of the triangle with four planes arose, or the three-sided pyramid. And from three angles, twelve angles were born; so that in this single figure they held the entire sequence of the whole World, both the starry and the elementary.
<image-desc>A diagram showing a tetrahedron (pyramid) subdivided into smaller triangles by internal lines.</image-desc>
<margin>Mystical philosophy in the Tetrahedron.</margin>
For the Triangle <note>original: "Trigonus"</note>, by its triad, expressed the generation of things, as will be shown later; the fourness of the sides expressed the Elements; the three and four joined together gave the sevenfold of the starry World, visible in the circles of the seven planets; the twelve angles denoted the Fixed Stars <note>original: "Aplanes"</note>, or the twelve dimensions of the Zodiac. The figure was sharp and pyramidal, by which they hinted at fire or heat—the active principle of the generation of things—which permeates the elements, the planets, the Fixed Stars, and in a word, everything. Again, since the Octahedron is composed of eight Equilateral
<margin>How the Octahedron, the symbol of air, is made.</margin>
triangles, each of which is again made of six genetic Scalenes; 8 multiplied by 6 gave 48 Scalenes, by which the Octahedron, the symbol of air, is established.
<margin>How the Icosahedron, the symbol of water, is made.</margin>
Finally, since the Icosahedron consists of 20 equilateral triangles, and each of them consists of six Scalenes; these multiplied by 20 will give 120 Scalenes, from which, as if from principles, the Icosahedron is established, and therefore it was adopted as the symbol of water.
<margin>Plato, from the comparison of triangles, came to the knowledge of the proportion of the Elements.</margin>
We have, therefore, 24 genetic Scalenes in the Tetrahedron pyramid, 48 in the Octahedron, and finally 120 in the Icosahedron; from the comparison of which Plato—taught by the Egyptians and Pythagoreans—came to the knowledge of the proportion of the Elements which each one holds toward the other. For because fire, air, and water have the Scalene as their first principle, but the earth has the Isosce-

<header>CHAPTER III.</header>

Furthermore, side AB (3) multiplied by itself makes 9; side BC (4) multiplied by itself constitutes 16; which, joined together, constitute as much as side AC (5) multiplied by itself, namely 25 <note>This is the Pythagorean theorem: $a^2 + b^2 = c^2$.</note>. ### CHAPTER III.
#### On the hieroglyphic mysteries of the pyramid.

<margin>Among the Egyptians, all things are full of mysteries.</margin>
<margin>The mysterious shape of the Obelisk.</margin>
A pyramid is a solid figure whose sides, drawn from one of the planes, converge at a single summit vertex, and it is in solids what the triangle is in planes; both are the primary figures of planes and solids respectively, so that just as all conceivable plane figures are reduced to a single triangle, so solids are reduced to a single pyramid and resolved into it. And although there can be many species of pyramids, such as triangular, quadrangular, pentagonal, etc., the Egyptians seem to have chosen the four-sided pyramid above all to indicate their mysteries. They establish this as twofold: the complete and the truncated. They applied the former to souls bound to bodies, and the latter to the whole Universe, and they called it an Obelisk or the "finger of the Sun" <note>original: "digitum Solis"</note>; nor did it end in a point by a straight path of the sides, but finished in a pyramid just before the apex. What they intended by this mystic construction, we have seen fit to indicate expressly in this place; and first we shall treat of the pyramid properly so called, then of the mysteries of the Obelisk, drawing some points from the Pamphilian Obelisk <note>A reference to the Agonalis Obelisk in Rome, which the author, Athanasius Kircher, helped restore for Pope Innocent X (Pamphili).</note>.

<margin>Tables.</margin>
<margin>Shape of the Obelisk.</margin>
Since, as Clement witnesses in Book 6 of the *Stromata* <note>Clement of Alexandria, a 2nd-century Christian theologian who wrote extensively on Egyptian symbols.</note>, nothing was done among the Egyptians that was not filled with mystery—so much so that even the houses, temples, instruments, and garments which they carried in solemn pomp either in the worship of the Gods or in performing sacrifices, and indeed the very nods and gestures they made, were a certain mystic representation of the highest things signified through riddles <gloss>riddles/enigmas</gloss>—we shall certainly think that they used Obelisks to represent their hieroglyphic wisdom not at all rashly, or without reason, or only for the sake of ornament, as many wrongly believe. Rather, with the greatest zeal and a remarkable investigation of the mind, they wished to acquire for themselves that figure which, being itself full of mysteries, would correspond in every way to the mystic context of the symbols. That the four-sided pyramid is such a figure will be shown copiously in what follows; for whatever the Hierophants <note>Priests or explainers of sacred mysteries.</note> connoted in the description of particular things expressed under symbols, they represented all of this universally on the exterior face of the Obelisk or pyramid, as if in a certain synopsis, or in the outline of a certain stone inscription of riddles <gloss>riddles/enigmas</gloss>; so much so that nothing is so hidden in the inner recesses of nature that it does not seem prefigured here. ### CHAPTER II

...in which Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> explains that within these symbols, as if hidden behind the mask of Silenus, lie the greatest mysteries of Astrology, Geometry, Music, Arithmetic, Theology, and the most recondite Philosophy. We have already shown in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, following Iamblichus, that Pythagoras, Plato, and other Greek philosophers learned their doctrine and true method of philosophizing from these sources. But so that we may demonstrate by the work itself that what we boast of in words is indeed the case:

<margin>Prime matter indicated by the shape of the Obelisk.</margin> We say first that by the pyramid or Obelisk, the Egyptians wished to represent the nature of things and that formless matter <note>The "Materia Prima" or first matter of the universe</note> which has an innate appetite for receiving forms. This is the opinion of Abenephius <note>An Arabic author often cited by Kircher</note>; his words are:
->And the form of the triangles [pyramids] represents their two opposing elements<-
<margin>Abenephius.</margin>
<margin>Artephi.</margin> That is: By the very figure of the pyramids, they signified primordial matter. With this, the Arab Artephi <note>An alchemical author</note> agrees in the chapter where he proves: *All things come from a point*; and after him, a certain author cited in the anonymous works of Pierio <note>Valeriano, author of Hieroglyphica</note> deduces it beautifully. For just as a pyramid, beginning from its highest peak as if from a point, proceeds through lines into surfaces and a body, gradually expanding in all directions; so the nature of all things, proceeding from a single principle and source that cannot be divided—namely, from God the Supreme Architect—subsequently took on various forms and spread into various genera and species, and it joins all things back to that apex and point from which all things flow and emanate. By this, indeed, that first-born origin of the World seems best represented, which, having shaped all parts of the World, produced that appearance which we now see. For formerly the World was formless and muddy, not yet having attained the integrity of its form through the distinct marks of things; for neither had the earth established its center as the foundation of all things, nor did the perpetual motion of the heavens revolve in a fixed seat, but all things lay sluggish, unmoved without the use of the Sun, and weighed down by a dismal silence. Nothing else existed but a formless, diffused sluggishness of matter, before that principle from which all things were produced and constituted, bringing forth the health-giving motion of life, restored the World to the World, and distinguished the heaven from the earth, and the sea from the Continent. At which time the four first Elements of things—from which, as from a root and principle of their kind, everything is begotten—received their own order and proper form, represented by the square base of the pyramid. Another reasoning for the pyramid is given by the Arab Agazael <note>Al-Ghazali</note> in Book 1 of *Judicial Astrology*, namely an Astronomical one, to this effect. For they say, he says, that in that celestial machine there is a circle under which the Sun and the rest of the wandering stars <note>The planets</note> complete their courses and circuits, and in which the life of all living creatures and the birth and death of natural things are placed; so much so that even Aristotle, in his books on *Generation and Corruption*, says that of generation and corruption, and of all mutation...

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS III CHAPTER III

...or that the cause of growth is the approach and retreat of the Sun in that oblique circle, which the Astronomers have called the Zodiac because the life of living creatures depends upon it. Therefore, the Egyptians divide this circle—the only one among the celestial circles to which latitude is attributed—into twelve parts, or <gloss>twelve-signs</gloss> <note>original: δωδεκαμόρια (dodekamoria)</note>, which they call mansions. Over each of these they place individual Angels or Demons, whom they call lesser Gods. They say that all lower things are divided along with them, so much so that whatever is contained under one of them, reaching down even to the center of the earth, is said to be subject to that twelfth-part and its presiding Angel. He intended this sign or twelfth-part to be like a certain pyramid, whose base is in the Zodiac and whose apex is in the center of the earth. Concerning these things, Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> writes thus in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*: "Dividing," he says, "*the heavens into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in whatever other way; they also set authorities over these, whether many or few.*" Again: "*They place one God before these, and thus this Egyptian discourse on principles is like a pyramid which, proceeding from the base—that is, from the multitude—into one, descends from the one into the multitude; governed, clearly, by the one, and by God from every side. An indefinite nature is imperiously contained under a certain defined limit, especially by the sublime unity, the cause of all.*" Indeed, God produced matter through materiality—namely, derived from essentiality—which the Creator, assuming as Unity, fashioned into simple and impassible <gloss>spheres</gloss> <note>original: σφφάρας (sphairas)</note>, but the last part he received for the making of generable and corruptible bodies.

<margin>The distribution of the Zodiac and the Gods presiding over its individual parts.</margin>
<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>

Since, therefore, all things come to be within these pyramids of the Zodiac, and the approach of the Sun causes the birth of things while its retreat causes their destruction, they represented the nature of all things through the pyramid with the least possible incongruity. Indeed, they placed just as many Horoscopes, Decans, and Usiarchs <note><term>Usiarchs</term>: Rulers of "essence" or substance in Hermetic astrology.</note> over each of these twelve pyramids of the twelfth-parts. Mercury <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the god Thoth.</note> is the author of this in chapter 8 *To Aesculapius*, which begins thus: <gloss>And you, the twelve signs</gloss> <note>original: Καὶ σὺ δώδεκα ζώδια</note>, and so on; that is, "*Around it are many companies of Spirits, to be gathered in various forces; and these familiars, existing not far from the immortals, having been allotted this region, act as Overseers of human affairs. They proceed to execute what is commanded by the Gods through whirlwinds, storms, fires, changes, earthquakes, and furthermore through fury and wars, avenging impiety.*" And a little later: "*The Sun is the preserver and nourisher of every kind,*" and the rest that follows. By these words, he insinuates nothing other than the diversity of effects produced from the mixture of different stars existing in different twelfth-parts.

<margin>Trismegistus.</margin>
<margin>Mercury.</margin>

These are indeed nothing other than the twelve signs of the Zodiac, which they called the twelve lesser Gods; and the seven planets, which they called the Usiarchs or greater Gods and Demons. Whence Artephius, in the place cited above, speaks thus:

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS.

<margin>The winged soul.</margin>
...immersed in bodily pleasures and filthy delights, they call heavy, sluggish, and dark; but that soul which, following the guidance of right reason, has raised itself to the contemplation of incorruptible and celestial things, they call lucid, heavenly, and angelic. They were taught, if I am not mistaken, by those who said the heart-soul <note>original: "cordem animam"</note> was winged; that it loses its wings when it yields to bodily desires and vices, and recovers them when, having rejected these, it seeks heavenly things. This is why they fashioned wingless <note>original: "ἀπτεροι" (apteroi)</note> Sphinxes. But they also seem to have wished to sketch the human soul as being of a fiery nature under the form of a pyramid, inasmuch as it adheres to the body no differently than to a base or to the fuel of a fire. This was their intent when they constructed the magnificent tombs of Kings and Heroes under enormous pyramids: to testify that when the body is dissolved and decayed, the soul survives. When it seems fit to the Supreme Maker—that is, in that Hermetic circle of a 36,500-year circuit—the soul would choose another body to enter. This follows the principle by which a pyramid (as is known to Geometers), while the vertex remains unmoved and the base is rotated, describes a circle, and with its whole body a cone; thus the circle signifies that cycle of years, while the cone signifies the body which is perfected in that cycle. For that was the opinion of the Egyptians regarding the restoration of things to the same state in the space of 36,500 years; and Plato testifies that he received this from them when he says in the *Timaeus* that the soul was made thus:
> "It received one portion from the Universe, which is undoubtedly signified by being united to that point which is at the vertex of the pyramid; a second portion double the first; a third, one and a half times the second and triple the first; a fourth, double the second; a fifth, triple the third; a sixth, eight times the first; and finally a seventh, which filled the double and triple intervals with twenty-six parts of the first." <note>This refers to Plato's complex mathematical "World Soul" composition in the Timaeus.</note>
By these numbers, he certainly signifies nothing other than that expansion of lines which, drawn from a point to the base, create an angle; and through the intervals, the very surfaces which are enclosed by the lines. From this it appears that he also received these things from the Egyptians.

Now further, let us see by what reasoning they expressed the said mysteries through the mystical numbers contained in the shape of Obelisks. And first, in the Obelisk, one must consider the apex, then the base, then the sides, and finally the angles (both plane and solid) and the surfaces; all of which are by no means lacking in mysteries. The apex of the Obelisk denoted that supreme summit of things from which all things flow. Furthermore, as to what the dyad <term>dyas: the number two or duality</term> and the triad <term>trias: the number three or trinity</term> denoted in the Obelisk, since we have dealt with all of these extensively both in the preceding sections and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we refer the reader there; therefore, we shall only briefly repeat in this place what has been said scattered here and there. Indeed, they exhibited the dyad through the flow of any two lines of the sides; the triad through the triangle; and the tetrad <term>tetras: the number four</term> or the quaternary number in Obelisks through the four sides. But they did so in a different manner: first, in the pyramidion <note>The small pyramid at the very top of an obelisk.</note> as a triangular quaternary, then in the remaining trunk of the Obelisk as a quadrilateral quaternary. Through the former, they secretly hinted at the Angelic World, insofar as from the center of divinity (which is aptly indicated by the apex of the Obelisk) into the generative nature, the immediate seal of the divine nature [is impressed] as a triangle...

If again you add 3—that is, that Triad, the exemplar of all perfection—to 7, the symbol of worldly perfection, you will again have 10. And since he fills the entire fabric of the Mundane sphere with this love, they aptly expressed this name of love in the sphere itself. For Love not only sends down rays toward the lower things, by which it may unify all, but also by a natural or magical virtue—through the kinship of natures—it attracts them upward, and compels them into mutual embraces with full familiarity. For thus occurs the progress or descent from God, or to speak in the Platonic fashion, from the *Soul of the World* <note>original: "Animâ Mundi"</note> through the universal things of the World, even down to matter; the pyramidal letter **A** aptly represents this process and descent. From here, there is a return again through nature to the presiding governor of nature, namely to that indivisible Monad <note>The "One" or ultimate unity in Neoplatonic thought.</note>, the apex of the mundane pyramid. Similarly, the lower things are directed toward the peripheries of the vastest heavens through the intermediate spaces of the World from the Universal center; this is indicated not absurdly by the radiant letter **V** (an inverted pyramid). What else does this signify but that magical chain of love connecting the higher things to the lower, fixed in a reciprocal 

<margin>What Love properly is according to Dionysius.</margin>

conspiracy <note>In the sense of "breathing together" or harmony.</note> of individual parts? Whence the Areopagite philosopher <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian Neoplatonist.</note> defines supreme love not badly as a certain *Circle perpetually revolved from good into good*. For as it begins from God and allures, it displays the reason of perfect beauty; as it passes into the World, it is chiefly called love; and finally pleasure, insofar as it returns to the Author, converting the beautiful image into the beautiful exemplar by a beautiful revolution. In this circuit, penetrating through all things, it causes the same things to be turned continually upward and downward with itself; not otherwise than a simple ray of the Sun, uniform in itself, creates light in the heaven, splendor in the ether, brightness in the elements, and lucid color in mixed bodies. It is clear, therefore, that the amatory order is the cause of conversion in all things toward divine beauty and the principal form, 

<margin>The amatory order is the cause of things.</margin>

and (to use the words of Proclus <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher.</note>) it leads all following things back to that, joining them, confirming the joined parts, and presently filling the following things from there, it distributes the gifts of divine light springing forth from there through the universe. This was indeed nothing else to the Egyptians than the *Soul of the World*, or the Triform Deity, the cause and origin of all things in the World, which they expressed most aptly in the hieroglyphic Schema placed below: a figure of a winged globe surrounded by serpents leaping forth from both sides, placed above the mundane System. And indeed the globe designates nothing other than first the archetypal Orb, and then the Universe, as has been proven in the preceding pages.
With wings. <note>Catchword for the next page.</note>

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS.

<margin>Macrobius, Martianus, Apuleius.</margin>
By wings, according to the testimony of Macrobius, Martianus, and Apuleius <note>Authors of late antiquity who wrote on Neoplatonism and allegory</note>, a subtle and swift force penetrating all things in the World was denoted; hence it is not surprising that the Egyptians taught the soul was winged, since many Platonists teach this everywhere from the doctrine of Zoroaster and the Egyptians. Porphyry, in Eusebius's *Preparation for the Gospel* (Book 2, Chapter 3), abundantly teaches that the serpent is a symbol of the fertile Spirit; this is shown so clearly by Virgil that he seems to have looked solely to this symbol of the World Soul—which penetrates and vivifies all things—when he sings:
<margin>Porphyry.</margin>

<margin>Virgil, Book 6 of the Aeneid.</margin>
*In the beginning, the Spirit within nourishes the sky and the lands,*
*The liquid plains, the shining orb of the Moon, and the Titan stars;*
*Mind, infused through the limbs, moves the whole mass*
*And mingles itself with the great body.*
<note>original Latin: "Principio Cœlum ac terras... Spiritus intus alit..."</note>

Barachias Abenephi, the Arab, mentions this hieroglyphic in his book *On the Disciplines of the Ancient Egyptians*, which, God willing, we shall soon make public by translating it into Latin. He speaks thus:
<margin>Abenephi.</margin>
->The winged circle is the sign of the breath and spirit of the world.<-
<note>original Arabic: "و الدور محمحين هو علامة نفى وروح العالم"</note>
<margin>On the Obelisks of the Pharaoh.</margin>
He says: "The winged globe, when painted surrounded by serpents, was a symbol of the soul or spirit of the World." And this becomes clear from the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note>, where it is evident from those hieroglyphic schemes—which were considered to contain great mysteries—because it is placed under the Throne of "all-formed nature" in that same Tablet. There, above the winged globe equipped with a scepter-bearing serpent, the sacred characters (a running circle, a hemisphere, and the character placed in the figure of <term>xuar</term> <note>A specific symbolic character or phonetic value in the author's system</note>) produce this meaning: *The lower is joined to that which is above by the power of the World Soul, which gives life to all things, and under whose command all things are subject.* The hieroglyphics follow along with the reading of the same.

<margin>Definition of Love. Hierotheus.</margin>

For he says that Love is a certain power proper to the World Soul and implanted in things, which moves higher things toward the providence of lower things; lower things to be turned toward the sublime; and finally, equals toward a social communion with one another. Whence, in my judgment, you may most correctly establish Love as a certain desire for the good and the beautiful—or for goodness to be conferred or received through beauty itself—namely, a power whose strength is like the emanation of a single magnitude, whose point...

### CHAPTER IV.
The point or apex is the first progression in God through the triple World, distributed in a threefold manner; the end, however, is in matter itself, of which there is a certain infinity around the summit, an infinity of pure power around matter, and an infinite power of connection through all the intermediate grades of nature.

<margin>The force of Love in the Universe. Dionysius the Areopagite.</margin>
Now let us return to love, the first effect of which is the Universe. For Love, according to the testimony of Dionysius <note>Dionysius the Areopagite, a Christian theologian and philosopher</note>, did not permit the King of all to remain without offspring. This same zeal for propagation flowed down from the first Author into all of his images. For through this, the Intelligences move the heavens, and bestow all their gifts upon those that follow. Through this, the stars diffuse their light into the Elements; fire communicates its power to the air, air to the water, water to the earth; the simple elements bestow it upon all mixed or composite things; plants and animals, by the desire of multiplying their own species, bestow it likewise, according to that passage in the *Georgics*, Book 3:
> Thus every race on earth, of men and
> Of the sea-born race, cattle, fish, and birds
> Rush into the fires of madness; love is the same for all. <note>original: "Omnè adeo genus in terris..." from Virgil's Georgics</note>

By the impulse of this same love, the lower things obey the higher ones in turn. Thus the tractable earth is resolved into water, and this then into air, air into fire, and then, digested through imperceptible pores into the ether, small portions of the firmer sublunary substance—partaking of a gradual thickening and coagulation—are snatched higher into the hidden fibers of heaven. There, as is customary in living beings, having been more and more refined, it is first applied, then glued and thoroughly assimilated, and transmuted into a celestial nature. Who then does not see now how aptly that monogram of the word <term>PHYLO</term> <note>Greek: ΦΥΛΟ (Phylo), likely relating to "tribe" or "race," here used as a symbolic root for "Philia" or Love</note> is adapted to the Universe? Certainly, when I scrutinized this a little more deeply, I then recognized that saying of Iamblichus to be true: that the Characters of the Egyptians
<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
are living things. This shines forth most clearly in this instance; in which, under two pyramids entwined in a contrary process within the spherical character <term>Φ</term> <note>The Greek letter Phi, representing the golden ratio or a cosmic sphere in this context</note>, suddenly the colures, meridians, tropics, and equator, the paths of the World's love—that is, the Sun (for in the Sun, worldly love flourishes most)—and finally the entire sphere of love shines forth. Thus, from this it may be understood that Love, diffused through the Universe, is in all things. But since there is a great diversity of things in this World, it is necessary that it is often born from contraries; for no part of the World hates another, except out of love for itself, as Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance Neoplatonist</note> beautifully teaches in his explanation of the *Symposium*; and again, that Love is the most effective cause of contraries;
<margin>Marsilio.</margin>
whence that passage of Plautus is exceedingly elegant:
<margin>Plautus.</margin>
> Divine Astarte, the force, life, and salvation of men and Gods, yet again she is the same Destruction, death, ruin, sea, earth, sky, and stars.
> Whatever temples of Jove we worship, they are led by his nod and obey him.

Hence Orpheus, in the *Argonautica*, not without cause praises this Love as the genius of the World, and as great and most ancient. For since he placed Chaos before the World, and before Saturn, Jupiter, and the other Gods; he surely established Love at the boundaries of Chaos itself, defining it as the principle by which an unformed thing desires ornament, or <term>kosmon</term> <note>Greek: κόσμον, meaning "order" or "the world"</note>, and perfection.

And let these things suffice concerning Geometry.

### CHAPTER I.
## CHAPTER I.
### *On the discovery and etymology of Music.*

<margin>Harmonic proportions were used in the creation of the World.</margin>
The opinion of Pythagoras <note>The ancient Greek philosopher (c. 570–495 BC) who famously linked mathematics, music, and the cosmos.</note> was received by later philosophers with unanimous agreement: that God, about to build the World, made use of harmonic proportions. We know also from the testimony of the Sacred Text <note>A reference to Wisdom of Solomon 11:20: "Thou hast ordered all things in measure and number and weight."</note> that God produced all things in number, weight, and measure. Since, therefore, the "ideas" <note>In the Platonic sense: the eternal forms or blueprints of things.</note> of all things are proven to consist of harmonic numbers, it is necessary that the supreme idea of all things neither can nor should be lacking them. Hence Music, inserted into human breasts by divine power, exerted its vigor immediately from the very cradle of the World; how this happened, I have led myself to explain in this place, repeating several points from my *Musurgia* <note>Kircher refers to his own massive 1650 work, *Musurgia Universalis*, on music theory and acoustics.</note>.

<margin>The first principles and origin of Music.</margin>
In this worldly theater of things, nothing is more easily encountered than sound. Yet, just as it does recently, it gave to the earliest race of mortals various occasions and opportunities for its discovery. And first of all, the whistling of the winds as well as of certain animals—which those first mortals, scattered here and there through the fields, perceived again and again—gave the first occasion for the construction of pipes. These they fashioned in the likeness of nature from oat-stalks, reeds, the shins of cranes, and other hollow stalks of plants. 

<margin>The first rudiments of pipes from reeds.</margin>
Indeed, the sound and din of hollow bodies gave birth to a varied supply of percussion instruments. For since the earliest mortals for the most part devoted their efforts to a rustic and pastoral life, and fixed their dwelling tents there where rich pastures occurred and places watered by streams—and consequently abounded in rushes, reeds, papyrus, and similar offspring of pipe-like growth—it could not be that a people, idle for most of the day, would exist without some relaxation of the mind. It is likely, therefore, that these men first formed various trumpets for themselves from the said pipe-like stalks, and indeed with no less skill than we see shepherds and others who lead a rustic life doing at this time; and perhaps even with greater skill, as they were then of a still more vigorous intellect. Since, moreover, those same first mortals were for the most part skilled in the smith's art (as it is that without which the society of the human race would perish), it certainly could not happen but that they would occasionally excite various sounds and noises from the accidental collision of different bodies while working. From this, it is very probable that they reached the knowledge of various percussion instruments by this occasion, in exactly the same way as happens to us from time to time today.

<margin>The origin of Musical instruments.</margin>
Music, therefore, had the first origin of its discovery not from the Greeks, or Egyptians, or Chaldeans, but from the first men before the Flood; indeed, if all men were removed from the world except for a few boys ignorant of things, I would not doubt that these—driven by necessity, and in time by chance and experience—could fall upon various inventions necessary to the human race. For the inventions of things are innate to man, and not [contained] in books 

<margin>All inventions seem to be accidental.</margin>

alone
<meta>The text continues on the next page with "alone."</meta>

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

...are not only learned, but are brought forth by some remarkable intellect, either by compelling necessity, or by chance, or experience, or by the suggestion of genius. That Music, therefore, existed from the very beginning—besides the fact that the Holy Scriptures clearly testify to it—reason itself dictates, as I have said. Certainly, in the 4th chapter, verse 21 of Genesis, the invention is openly ascribed to <term>Jubal</term> <note>The biblical figure traditionally credited as the ancestor of all who play the harp and flute</note> in these words:

וְשֵׁם אָחִיו יוּבָל הוּא הָיָה אֲבִי כָּל תֹּפֵשׂ כִּנּוֹר וְעוּגָב:
<note>original Hebrew: "And his brother's name was Jubal; he was the father of all those who handle the lyre and pipe."</note>

<margin>Jubal, the Author of Music.</margin> And his brother's name was *Jubal*; he was the father of those who handle, or strike, the Cithara and the Organ. Where the 70 <note>The Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation of the Old Testament</note> have: <gloss>the father of all who handle the lyre and pipe</gloss>, that is, the father, he was the one who demonstrated the Psaltery and the Cithara. What sort of instruments were actually invented by them is contained in our *Musurgia* <note>Kircher's own massive encyclopedia of music, "Musurgia Universalis" (1650)</note> in the chapter on the Music of the Hebrews. But indeed, after the flood, the Egyptians were the first restorers of lost Music. <margin>Music invented in Egypt.</margin> For these people, instructed by Ham and his son Mizraim, illustrated Music to such an extent that even from the Egyptian word *Moy* <note>original: "Moyf"</note> Music took its etymology, because it was discovered and restored at the stagnant marshes of the Nile, on the occasion of the reeds and papyrus offspring (from which they fashioned their pipes) sprouting there in great abundance.

Music, therefore, was without doubt derived from the Egyptian word *Amun* <note>original: "אמון"</note>, which denotes water, and so it seems to openly indicate the first beginnings of the invention of Music. <margin>The etymology of Moses.</margin> Indeed, that Moses drew the etymology of his name from the waters from which he had been extracted needs no other testimony than the Sacred Text; its words are:

וַיִּגְדַּל הַיֶּלֶד וַתְּבִאֵהוּ לְבַת פַּרְעֹה וַיְהִי לָהּ לְבֵן וַתִּקְרָא שְׁמוֹ מֹשֶׁה וַתֹּאמֶר כִּי מִן הַמַּיִם מְשִׁיתִהוּ:
<note>original Hebrew: "And the child grew, and she brought him to Pharaoh's daughter, and he became her son. She named him Moses, saying, 'Because I drew him out of the water.'"</note>

When he was grown, she delivered him to the daughter of Pharaoh; she adopted him in place of a son, and called his name *Moses*, because I drew him out of the waters. From which words it clearly appears that this name *Moses* was not bestowed by his parents, nor by anyone else from the Hebrew Nation, but by the daughter of Pharaoh herself; who, since she had no other familiar language besides the vernacular Egyptian, it is certain that she called the found boy by the Egyptian name *Moses*, as if she were saying, "saved from the waters." Moreover, the most ancient writers, Philo and Flavius Josephus, clearly show this, of whom the former discusses it in the *Life of Moses* as follows:

<margin>Regarding the name of Moses: the Egyptians call water "Mos." And "Moses" means the one saved from the water.</margin>
<note>original Greek: "Και ἀπὸ τῶν παλαιῶν... Μωϋσῆν τὸ ἐκ τοῦ ὕδατος σωθέντα."</note>
And because he had been cast out into the river, he obtained his name from this event. For the Egyptians call water *Mos*, and *Ises* <note>implied by the context of the etymology</note> means "saved." Therefore, the name *Moses* was bestowed as a composite word from both. Rabbi Abraham ibn Ezra agrees with these things, although he records that he was called *Monios* in Egyptian (a word, as I believe, that is corrupted). His words are:

<margin>R. Abenezra.</margin>
וּמִתְחַכְּמֵי מִצְרַיִם מִלְּשׁוֹן מִצְרַיִם מֹשֶׁה מִן הַמַּיִם הַנִּקְרָא מֹשֶׁה...
<note>original Hebrew: "And the wise men of Egypt [say] in the language of Egypt, Moses [is] from the water... as written in the book of service..."</note>

And so it is also read in the books of the Greek Sages; perhaps the daughter of Pharaoh learned our language. Whatever the case may be, this word, *Moses*, is shown clearly in the Vatican Coptic Pentateuch to be an Egyptian word derived from the Coptic term <term>mōou</term> <note>original: "μωου"; the Coptic word for water</note>. This is a word, evidently, that does not differ from <term>mō</term> and <term>ous</term> <note>original: "μω" and "ους"; referring to the components of the name meaning 'water' and 'saved'</note>. <page-num>123</page-num>
<header>CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.</header>

<margin>The invention of the Multi-form Lyre is attributed to Trismegistus.</margin>
By the account of almost all mythologists, the invention of the multi-form lyre is attributed to the same man <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>. And although he was a singular lover of the musical arts, he left behind that common and vulgar music, turning all his labor and industry toward penetrating that most powerful music which consists in the wondrous distribution of the supreme minds and the concord of worldly things, and which regards the order and connection of every individual thing. He used the proportions of harmonic melodies as if they were a magnetic compass <note>original: "pyxis"</note> to guide his journey into the scrutiny of hidden things, about which it is now time for us to discourse.

## CHAPTER II.

*->That Hieroglyphic Music was nothing other than the science of the order of things in the Universe.<-*

<margin>Psellus:</margin>
<margin>The order of the universe is music.</margin>
<margin>Music-Trismegistus.</margin>
Rightly and wisely does Psellus say in his *Music*, "Music is the order of the whole world" <note>original Greek: "Τὴν Μουσιϰὴν εἶναι τὴν τῶν ὅλων ϰόσμου τάξιν"</note>. The Ancients said that Music contains everything. For when they cast their eyes more attentively upon the circuit of the entire Universe, and recognized the order, connection, variety, and diversity of all things, they called it Music itself, in which the consonant corresponds to the dissonant, the lowest to the highest, the highest to the middle, and the middle to the lowest or highest, by a certain wondrous proportion. And Trismegistus speaks of this Music when he says in the *Asclepius*:
> To truly know Music is nothing else than to know the order of all things, and what divine reason has allotted to each.
For the order of individual things, brought together into one by a craftsman’s reason, creates a certain most sweet and true concord of divine melody. Truly, it seemed fitting to discuss in this place what this concord is, and in what it consists.

<margin>Aristotle</margin>
Therefore, just as vocal music or harmony consists in the fit distribution of intervals, by which the highest tones correspond to the lowest and middle tones in exact proportion, so too the intervals of the Tones depend upon one another in such a way that if you scatter their order, you would rightly seem to have confused and disturbed the entire harmony. Dissonances are also so beautifully applied to consonances that if you separate them from one another, you destroy all the sweetness of harmonic symphony. The Egyptians were by no means ignorant of this musical secret; hence, scrutinizing the order of things and their wondrous connection a little more deeply, they said the order of things was nothing other than a Music most perfect in all its numbers, in which the middle things harmonize with the lowest and highest—as if with the bass and treble—not without a certain proportion of intervals. There are *nete* <term>the highest note in a Greek scale</term> or superior sounds in the inferior ones, and inferior or *hypate* <term>the lowest note in a Greek scale</term> in the *nete* or superior ones, and finally the middle ones exist in the extremes. He who sounds the *diapason* <term>an octave</term> or eighth, immediately has the base spread beneath him. For just as the number ten is unity replicated, so also the octave is rightly a replication of the base, since according to the musical proverb: *The judgment concerning octaves is the same*. Again, he who sounds the base soon obtains the *diapente* <term>a perfect fifth</term>, the *diatessaron* <term>a perfect fourth</term>, and the remaining harmonic intervals, and vice versa. So that, by the testimony of Aristotle himself, Music is a thing entirely celestial and divine, [containing] the reason of the entire worldly workmanship...

<margin>All things are in all things</margin>
The heaven above, the heaven below, the stars above, the stars below—all these we receive by the fates. Thus, by the aforementioned philosophical saying, they suggested that admirable harmony of the World, and the connection of the higher things with the lower; for we have said above that a great part of Egyptian philosophy consisted in the scrutiny of this analogy and dependence of the greater World <note>the Macrocosm</note> with the lesser World <note>the Microcosm, or Man</note>. For when they turned themselves quite diligently to exploring the powers of the celestial bodies, their harmony, the established treaty, and the sympathy with the things of nature in the lower world—namely, in what way and by what knot all things thereafter cohere and agree—to this end, they sought how that moving force and nourisher of all things was derived from heaven into the whole circle of the lands, first from the Sun, then from the Moon, and the rest of the Choir of celestial lights; philosophizing a little more deeply, they discovered that all things lie hidden in all things.

<margin>Man is a compendium of the World.</margin>
And to begin with man, they said that he, the most excellent of all creatures, contains within himself all parts of the entire World. For there is nothing in the greater World which is not found in man; the offspring is in all ways similar to the parent, the greatest extracted miracle of nature, and the Kernel of the four Elements, the highest <gloss>masterpiece</gloss> <note>original Greek: "τέχνημα"</note> of God, and the most perfect model of the World. Truly he is every creature, because he is the whole World, and he alone enjoys this honor: that he has a shared symbol with all things, an operation with all things, and a preservation with all things. For the entire machine of the World is collected and reduced into the Microcosm, so that what is above is found below in man as well. The physical body—elementary, visible, and tangible—is from the earth; but the sidereal and astral body is constructed according to the pattern of the archetype.

<margin>Wonders of plants.</margin>
Among plants also, whoever is eager to scrutinize nature may observe miracles on the very day of the Solstice, especially in the leaves of the willow, the white poplar, the elm, the lime tree, and the olive; and from a careful gaze at them, he will notice a tropical harmony <note>referring to the "tropics" or turning points of the sun</note> and a visible sympathy which the leaves of the said trees openly show with the Sun on that very day of the Solstice: for he observed that the upturned parts of the leaves look toward the sky with a different face than they did the day before.

Certainly the Onion, as found in Plutarch, revives and sprouts as the Moon wanes; but as it waxes and grows, the onion withers.
This fact formerly caused the Egyptian Priests not to eat onions, because they alone of all vegetables have powers of diminishing and increasing contrary to the increments and losses of the Lunar star.

### CHAPTER II.

<margin>The origin of natural magic.</margin>
According to Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher whose work heavily influenced Renaissance views on magic and theology.</note>, animals, vegetables, and minerals—by reason of their specific or individual constitution—are imbued with a certain heavenly power. This power is sometimes so familiar and friendly to certain things that it truly joins with them, produces results, and obeys them; yet to other things, it is so contrary and hostile that it halts and binds their operations. And from here, as I judge, arises the origin of **natural magic**. This science was always hidden by the Sages of the Egyptians—as the greatest secret in natural things—under hieroglyphic letters and symbols, lest it be dragged into abuse by the unskilled. We are (alas!) forced to groan in our own century when we behold this most sublime science, the very pinnacle of all philosophical discipline, so miserably corrupted by the writings of ignorant men and filled with old wives' superstitions. However, before we pass from this sublime Egyptian Philosophy to other matters, it seemed fit to add here the words of Proclus, by which the things said above are so confirmed that they alone might suffice as an explanation; for he says thus in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*:

<margin>Proclus on Sacrifice and Magic.</margin>
"Just as lovers progress by reason from the beauty that appears to the senses toward divine beauty little by little; so also the ancient Priests of the Egyptians, when they considered in natural things a certain knowledge and a 'compassion' <note>original: *compassionem*; here meaning a sympathetic resonance or natural connection between objects.</note> of some things for others, and of manifest things for occult powers, and found all things to be in all things, they established a sacred science. For they recognized the highest things in the lowest, and the lowest in the highest; in heaven they saw earthly things according to their cause and in a heavenly manner; and on earth they saw heavenly things, but in an earthly manner. For from where else do we think those plants, which they name **Heliotropes** <note>Sun-turning plants, like the sunflower.</note>, move toward the motion of the Sun, and **Selinotropes** <note>Moon-turning plants.</note> toward the Moon? Truly, all things pray and sing hymns to the Leaders of their Order—some in an intellectual way, others in a natural way, and others in a sensible way. Thus the **Sun-follower** <note>original: *Solisqua*.</note> moves toward the Sun however it can; and if anyone could hear the pulsation sent forth by it into the air as it circles, he would surely perceive by such a sound a certain melody composed for its King, such as a plant can produce. Therefore, on earth one may behold the Sun and Moon, but according to their earthly quality; while in heaven all plants, stones, and animals possess life according to a heavenly nature... an intellectual life. The ancients, contemplating some things of the heavens and others of the earth, drew down divine powers into a lower place through a certain similarity."

<margin>How much similarity is worth.</margin>
"Indeed, similarity itself is a sufficient cause for binding individual things to one another. For if someone heats hemp or papyrus and then brings it near a lamp, even if he does not touch it, he will see the hemp suddenly ignited, and the fire descending from above to the lower parts. We compare the heated hemp or papyrus to a certain kinship of lower things to higher ones; its approach to the lamp to the opportune use of things according to time, place, and matter; the progress of the fire into the hemp to the presence of divine light to that which is capable of receiving it; and finally the ignition of the hemp to a certain participation in the divine seed. What shall I say of the **Lotus**? The Lotus folds its leaves before the rising of the Sun, but as the Sun rises, it unfolds them little by little; and as the Sun ascends to the mid-region of heaven, it expands its leaves; but as it seeks the setting from the midpoint, it gradually contracts its leaves. It seems to honor the Sun by the expansion and contraction of its leaves no less than men do by the gestures of the body and the movement of their labors." And a little later he says: "Not only truly those..."

<margin>Wonders of the Egyptian lotus.</margin>
