# CHAPTER III. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

->Nature delights in nature.<-
->Nature conquers nature.<-
->Nature dominates nature.<-
<note>original Greek: "Ἤ φύσις τὴν φύσιν τέλεῖ. Ἤ φύσις τὴν φύσιν νικᾷ. Ἤ φύσις τὴν φύσιν κρατεῖ." and Latin: "Natura Naturâ delectatur. Natura Naturam vincit. Natura Naturâ dominatur." This is a famous alchemical and philosophical axiom suggesting that the forces of the natural world are self-regulating and can be mastered by understanding their internal relationships.</note>

By these words, which are essentially parallel to those above, they indicated nothing other than the highest mysteries of nature, by whose aid—when wielded by a Wise Man knowledgeable in these things—the miracles of nature and art can be perfected.

### CHAPTER III.

*How, and by which hieroglyphics, the Egyptians expressed the music of the world.*

When the Egyptian <term>Hieromants</term><note>Priests or initiates who interpreted sacred mysteries</note> wished to express the music or harmony of the world, they depicted a boy wrapped in a netted garment. In his hands was a <term>cucuphomorphon</term> scepter (that is, marked with the head of a Hoopoe bird), a curved staff, and a <term>gnomon</term><note>An L-shaped tool used as a square or for measuring shadows</note>. From his back hung a triangle which resolved into a globe, as is made clear in the figure placed here, taken from the <term>Isiac Table</term><note>A famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs, also known as the Bembine Tablet</note>, which we call the Bembine Tablet.

<margin>Note that in this figure, a globe is attached to the triangle.</margin>

<image-desc>A circular diagram depicting a standing human figure, possibly male, in profile facing right. The figure is holding a staff or scepter in its left hand, which has a cross-like top and a serpent coiled around it. A smaller, curved object resembling a hook or a stylized animal head extends from the figure's back. The figure stands on a base. Below the figure, the word "SYMBOL A" is written to the left and "HOR." to the right. The entire image is enclosed within a double circle.</image-desc>

By the boy, the sensible World was indicated, daily flourishing anew through a perpetual succession of generation. He is wrapped in a netted garment because the World, involved in the hidden complexities of the things it contains, is difficult to perceive. By the hoopoe-headed scepter, the great variety of things in this sensible World is shown; by the gnomon, their fit connection and exact rectitude; and finally, by the curved staff, a harmony most perfect in all its measures is expressed. The triangle with the attached circle denoted that this World flowed forth from the <term>archetypal World</term><note>The divine or ideal realm of forms that precedes the physical world</note>, being as similar as possible to its Father and Maker. But since we have treated these matters extensively elsewhere in this book, as well as in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we refer the reader there. Furthermore, the Egyptians used another kind of musical instrument which they called a <term>Sistrum</term><note>A sacred rattle used in ancient Egyptian ritual</note>, and they fashioned it in various forms. Since a more copious occasion for discussing this instrument is given in the third Volume, I did not wish to be longer here. It was, however, for mystical reasons...

But to return to our purpose: several years ago, Michael Schatta the Copt—formerly my secretary for Coptic Manuscripts—sent me from Egypt an inscription from a fallen hieroglyphic column located not far from Memphis. We provide a drawing of it here along with its interpretation. There were two hawks: one lower than the higher one, and the other resting upon the upper pyramid. Each was distinguished by two scepters. In the middle was an instrument, or a seven-stringed Lyre, which was connected by two chains from below and above with the two hawks, as appears in the example placed here.

<image-desc>A vertical column of four distinct hieroglyphic-like images.

<margin>What the symbol signifies.</margin>
<margin>Explanation of the material.</margin>
We say that these symbols signify nothing other than the **Harmony of the World**, by which lower things are connected to higher things as if by a chain. And first, indeed, the hawk with the scepter indicates a celestial nature or force; and by the rock is indicated a double power over lower and higher things. The pyramid upon which it rests signifies a fiery and penetrating nature. The *hydroschema* <note>A term likely referring to a water-symbol or water-vessel shape</note> and the dove signify the two principles of things, air and water, from which the Egyptians believed all things consisted—a point well observed by Athenaeus. For he says it was a religious practice of the Egyptians, as well as the Assyrians, to abstain from fish in veneration of Rhea or Isis; for they thought the nature of things consisted chiefly of water and air. For the former, they venerated fish; for the air, they venerated the dove.

<margin>What the pyramid [signifies].</margin>
The cube signifies the earth, upon which the hawk sits with two scepters, showing the celestial virtue communicated to lower things. By this is caused that wonderful "Concert of the World" indicated by the seven-stringed lyre, by which higher things are united with the lower. Although we approve of this explanation as evident in its substance, it nevertheless seemed appropriate to explain it a little more fully for a better understanding of the Natural Philosophy that flourished among the Egyptians. Thus, those things which were ingeniously devised by the Egyptians may also be explained with ingenuity, and once explained, may be confirmed by the authority of approved writers.

<margin>What the fish and dove [signify].</margin>
<margin>What the cube and symbol [signify].</margin>
Therefore, the Philosophers of the Egyptians, philosophizing more deeply, when they saw that wonderful connection and order of all things, established a certain Spirit or **Soul of the World** <note>original: "Animam Mundi"</note> governing all these things. They compared this to a hawk and signified it through Osiris (the Sun) and Isis (the Moon), as was explained at length above. Thus, the topmost hawk, armed with two scepters, signifies Osiris or the Soul of the World governing higher and lower things with a double power—not poorly [described] by the Poets...

### CHAPTER III.

Indicated by Jupiter and Pluto <note>original: "Iouem & Plutonem"; here referring to the celestial and subterranean aspects of the divine</note>, a circle rising above his head shows his divinity. The Pyramid upon which he rests signifies the fiery nature that penetrates all things. However, the lower hawk resting upon a cube, also shining with a double scepter, indicates the twofold power of the Soul of the World <note>original: "Animæ Mundi"</note>: namely, that which lies hidden in the very bowels of the earth, which is nothing other than Pluto, or a certain subterranean Sun; or Osiris illuminating the subterranean stars, animating them by his power—such as the metals, those seven subterranean planets, along with the remaining army of precious stones filled with various virtues. And the other power is that which lies hidden above the earth in the variety of plants, in the faculties of herbs, trees, and shrubs, which are nothing other than certain terrestrial stars corresponding in substance to the superior stars. <margin>Every planet has a corresponding plant.</margin> (For it was proven above from the ancient Sages that there is no herb on earth that does not have its own star or planet in heaven, animating it, moving it, and making it fruitful by its power.) And this is what Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius Triſmegiſtus"</note> asserts in the book called *The Virgin of the World* <note>original: "Minerua Mundi"; likely referring to the Hermetic text 'Kore Kosmou'</note> in these words: *“It is truly a marvel that all the celestial stars, which are clearly visible in the heavens in their bodies, are also created on earth, lying hidden and enclosed in their spirits. And just as the celestial Sun generates all things in a terrestrial manner by its spiritual heat, so the terrestrial Sun creates and regenerates all things spiritually by its spiritual heat. Through the celestial Sun, His Spirit works all things naturally in nature, but through the terrestrial Sun, that same spirit works all things, but spiritually; for the spirit works through no other medium than the Sun, because it has placed the seat of its habitation in the Sun alone, and nowhere else.”* Thus the four elements lie hidden everywhere: in the heavens in a celestial manner, and in the lower World in its own appropriate and consistent manner, all of which are wonderfully joined together by the power of the divine spirit.

<margin>What the Water-symbol and the Dove signify.</margin> These words are indeed so clear that they seem to reflect our entire hieroglyphic inscription. For what else do the <term>burden</term> <note>onus</note>, the <term>water-symbol</term> <note>hydroſchema</note>, the <term>dove</term>, and the <term>pyramid</term>, placed below and above the Lyre, seem to insinuate, if not the force of the four Elements hidden in all things? For <margin>Pierius.</margin> Pierius learnedly demonstrates that the cube is a symbol of the earth, and a certain anonymous author in the Appendix to Pierius’s Hieroglyphics, book 2, demonstrates in the same place that the Pyramid is a hieroglyphic of fire. We have already taught in various places that the water-symbol is indeed a symbol of water. <margin>Aelianus</margin> Although Aelian and Athenaeus indicated water and air by means of the fish and the dove. <margin>The affinity of the Dove with the air.</margin> For it was said above that the dove and the fish were worshipped by the Assyrians and Egyptians in favor of Rhea, because they considered air and water to be the more powerful parts in which the mistress of nature showed herself. Since every winged animal is an indication of the air, the Ancients honored the dove especially with this name and hieroglyphic, because among domestic birds none flies further from home nor for a longer time, yet mindful of its right path, it returns with the greatest faithfulness and is led to a most gentle habitation with us. Or rather, the cause of this honor might be that there is such great familiarity with the air that it seems to move more safely there than on the ground, and its speed and ease of flight are so great that Maro <note>Virgil</note> says in the 5th book of the *Aeneid*:
->*She skims her liquid path, nor moves her swift wings*<-

<margin>What the seven-stringed instrument and Lyre signify.</margin> Furthermore, in the middle, the Lyre <gloss>from the seven-stringed instrument <note>original Greek: ἀπὸ τοῦ ἑπταχόρδου</note></gloss> presents itself, fastened by chains from above and below; by which nothing else is indicated than that wonderful harmony of the World. In this world, lower things mixed with higher things are accustomed to produce a most pleasant sort of concord, as it were—not only in the bodies of the stars, the intervals of the spheres, and the speeds of their revolutions arranged in a fit order, but also in the harmonious framework of the elements, and even in the successions of the seasons following one another with equal measure. All these things seem to be governed by that celestial and divine Osiris, by the Leader (to speak with Cicero) and Prince and Moderator of the world and the tempering of human religions, as Orpheus well observed in his hymn to the Sun:
<margin>Cicero.</margin>
> Holding a golden lyre, drawing along the harmonious course of the World.

<margin>Macrobius.</margin> Moreover, what the seven strings signify is clear from Macrobius in the *Saturnalia*. <margin>Sidonius. The number seven.</margin> in the *Epithalamium of Polemius and Araneola*, says that the number seven was preserved according to the same model in the Lyre, the Cithara, and the Pipe. Thus in Euripides' 
<margin>Euripides.</margin> *Iphigenia in Tauris*, the Chorus, speaking of Apollo, mentions the <gloss>seven-toned din <note>original Greek: Κέλαδον ἑπτάτονον</note></gloss>. Callimachus follows the myth in his *Hymn to Delos* when he says 
<margin>Callimachus.</margin> this number was chosen by Apollo because, when his mother was giving birth to him, singing swans had circled the island seven times in flight. Truly, because from the equally vibrated succession of the 
<margin>The Myth.</margin> four parts of the year, or the proportioned mixture of the elements, a certain harmony seems to flow, we see a lyre—the indicator of this matter—neatly carved in the middle of the Obelisk by the investigator of the Universe. For just as the power of Music is situated in this: that the various tensions and relaxations of voices, and sounds both high and low, arranged in a congruent measure of time, may come together into a sweet concord; so Osiris, or Apollo, that celestial Cithara-player, striking all parts of the World from the *nete* to the *hypate* <note>The highest and lowest notes in the ancient Greek musical system</note>, and proceeding from these to the *mese* <note>The middle note</note> and the other intermediate strings, produces a most beautiful temperament, having preserved the symmetry (as if according to the number of the seasons), associating the hot with the cold, and the moist with the dry. For as Pliny well says in Book 11, Chapter 49, the nature of the Sun is understood

<margin>Cassiodorus.</margin> "Contrary desires were collected into one assembly, and while the Lyre spoke its faith, all things believed themselves to be adverse no longer." <margin>The seasons of the year.</margin> That is to say, would you judge winter by the lowest notes (the *hypate*), summer by the highest (the *nete*), and spring by the Dorian mode? But as for why he omitted Autumn, the reason is that the ancient Egyptians—as Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> testifies in Book 1, Chapter 2—established only a threefold division of the year. For that reason, they devised three "Hours" <note>The Horae, goddesses of the seasons</note> in number, as Jerome Aleander <note>A 16th-century scholar and cardinal</note> well notes in his explanation of the *Solar Tablet*. Diodorus also writes that Minerva <note>The Roman name for Athena, often identified with the Egyptian Neith</note>, under whom they signified eternity, was called <term>Trismegistos</term> <note>original: Τριςμέγιστος; meaning "Thrice-Greatest"</note> because she changes her nature three times a year: in Spring, Summer, and Winter. The same author also asserts that it was believed by the Egyptians that Osiris and Isis—namely the Sun and the Moon—<term>govern the entire universe through themselves, nourishing and increasing all matter and all principles, which they call gods</term> <note>original: Τὸν συμπαντα κόσμον δι' ἑαυτῶν ἐπιτροπεύειν, καὶ τὰς ἁπάσας ὕλας καὶ τὰς ἀρχὰς ἀνατρέφειν καὶ αὔξειν, ὃ θεοὶν ὀνομάζουσι</note>. They govern the whole world, nourishing and increasing all things, completing the circuit of the three seasons by an invisible motion: namely Spring, Summer, and Winter. The Latin translator who named Autumn here in place of Winter seems to have read <term>chromatismo</term> <note>original: χρωματισμῷ; referring to musical coloration or shading</note> in his copy, unless it was a mistake of negligence. Therefore, in imitation of the ancient three seasons, the Lyre was equipped with three strings. If to this is added the four-stringed instrument (the *tetrachord*) of Terpander and Orpheus—or, as Boethius <note>A 6th-century philosopher</note> would have it, of Mercury—which was harmonized to the four elements of the universe, we shall have the <gloss>Thrice-Greatest</gloss> <note>original: Τριςμέγιστος</note> indicated in our inscription. As we said above, this is a type of the universal and a symbol of the most orderly worldly harmony, by which all members of the World are so in tune with one another that Mercury <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>The legendary sage Hermes Trismegistus</note> <margin>Thrice-Greatest.</margin> contemplating this "dissonant concord" and the "discordant harmony" of all things, dared to say that the whole World with all its parts lies hidden within a single piece of Music. His sayings agree so closely with these two inscriptions which we have explained thus far, that he provides the most abundant and indubitable proof in his books; for he asserts everywhere that whatever things are below are also above, or that which is lower is also higher, and says many other things concerning the Sun and Moon as the parents of all things. <margin>Concerning the comparison of the three worlds to one another.</margin> Elsewhere, however, he transfers these ideas to the Archetypal World when he says: *In the Angelic or "intellectual" World, there are the same beings that are in this visible machine, but spiritually and invisibly*. In the supreme Divine World, <gloss>the intelligible</gloss> <note>original: τῷ νοητῷ</note>, uncreated, infinite, incomprehensible, and <gloss>archetypal</gloss> <note>original: ἀρχετύπῳ</note>, the Angels as well as the World are one, and simultaneously so in a most perfect divine manner.

<margin>This visible world is a shadow and figure of the future state of the Blessed.</margin> And from this long discourse it appears by what reasoning, through this sublime wisdom of the Egyptians, the lowest things show the highest, and corporeal things declare intellectual things. Through the natures and properties of lower and earthly things, they declare those of the superior and celestial; for these lower, external, and visible examples are marks of the superior, and symbols of the invisible internal things, by which we are led by the hand from seductive time to the eternal and spiritual. The whole of creation and this vast machine of the World, in which the invisible Creator exhibits himself to us to be seen and touched, is nothing other than the shadow of God, and a figure of the internal paradise—namely, of that intuition by which creatures are clearly seen and understood, which are the "back parts" <note>A biblical reference to Moses seeing God's back, implying we see God's effects rather than His essence</note> and effects of the Creator...

<margin><unclear>homousios</unclear> <note>Likely "homousios" meaning "of the same substance."</note></margin>Furthermore, each of these Worlds is governed by the one above it and receives the influx of its powers, so that the Archetype itself and the Supreme Artisan—through the angels, heavens, stars, elements, animals, plants, metals, and stones—may then pour the virtues of His omnipotence into us, for whose service He founded all these things. <margin>The 50 Gates of Light.</margin>This is what the Hebrews call <term>Kabbalah <note>original: "מ ק ב ל ה"</note></term> through the 50 gates of understanding; these are the steps or boundaries of all things collected from the first chapter of Genesis, by which, as if by symbols and marks, we are led to the highest knowledge of all things. 

The "Exit" or "Descent," however, occurs where we are rolled down from God to the creatures, from intellectual forms to external forms, and from the center to the circumference. For example, I behold with the physical eye this apple seed; but leaving behind its corporeality, I withdraw from the external form to the inner invisible seed, and with the mental eye, I contemplate the whole tree—with its root, trunk, branches, shoots, leaves, flowers, and fruits—folded within, to be manifested in its own time through separation. That seed does not take those bodily parts from the outside or from elsewhere, but emits each one from itself and from its own inner recesses.

<margin>On the Angelic nature.</margin>Since, indeed, a seed of this kind is an image or shadow of Angelic substance, and folds the entire bodily mass of the tree within its inner recesses without quantity or quality; certainly a single Angel will fold the seeds of all things within himself much more easily, being of a more excellent, higher, and more distinguished nature. For the simpler a thing is (according to Saint Thomas <note>original: "D. Th." referring to Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologica, Part 1, Question 18</note>), the more perfect, absolute, and powerful it is; and whatever a lower power can do, a higher power can do much more perfectly and excellently. Therefore, when an Angel produces wonders, he does not take them from outside himself or from elsewhere, but produces and bestows them from within, from the inner recesses of his virtues (because he is a perfect image of God), when he wills and as often as he wills, without any diminishing of himself. For an Angel carries and possesses all things with him in an Angelic and spiritual manner—indeed, the entire machinery of the World is folded within him, along with all these lower things.

From the abyss of infinity (which the Hebrews call *Ein Sof* <note>original: "אין סוף", meaning "Without End" or the Infinite Godhead in Kabbalistic thought</note>), not out of any necessity of a needy nature, but by His own most free will alone, and out of pure goodness for His own infinite glory, emitting all things from His own bosom as if from the deepest conception and retreat of divinity (Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Hermeticism</note> says, *from the bowels of darkness*), He first produced light through His Word—that is, the Angelic substances. Following that Angelic light were the stars, then these bodies, or the machine of the visible world consisting of seven spheres and four elements. And thus
<margin>How all things are in all things.</margin>
all things are in all things in their own way, and one remains in the other, just as the seed is in the tree, and the tree is in the seed. All visible bodies or elements are in the stars—that is, in the invisible powers or spiritual elements—and the stars or powers are in the bodies. The stars are in the Angels, and the Angels are in the stars. The Angels are in God, and God is in the Angels, so that the higher can always exist without the lower, but not the reverse.
<margin>How all things are in all things.</margin>
Therefore, once God is known, the Angels are known; once these are known, the stars are known—that is, the invisible powers of things; once these are known, all created things, or the visible world, will be known; and once the visible world is known, finally man, the *microcosm* <note>Greek: "μικρόκοσμος", meaning "little world," the idea that man reflects the entire universe</note>, will be known. For the son of the world is such a son as the father is in all things. Thus from visible things we perceive the invisible. Just as, therefore, all things are in God divinely, and in the Angels angelically, so in the world all things are bodily. Whatever exists in the visible world sensibly in the Elements, that same thing exists in the invisible powers of things spiritually; and whatever is in these spiritually, that is in the Angels angelically, and in God divinely. And this is that chain indicated by the Egyptians in the previous inscription—truly a golden one, let down from heaven to our fragility on earth—by whose help we ascend through the order of creatures, from the lowest to the middle, and through these beyond the world to the Maker of things Himself, and we rise up to the One, the first and the highest, toward which, as toward a longed-for goal, all creatures tend with their own effort and voluntary groan. All things, therefore, are in all things; heaven above, heaven below; stars above, stars below; and as Mercury <note>Another name for Hermes Trismegistus</note> well says, the seed is the tree folded up, and the tree is the seed unfolded and explained; unity is number folded up according to Plato; number is unity unfolded; an Angel is the stars folded up, and the stars are an Angel unfolded; God is He in whom, as the Archetype, the world is folded in a divine way, and the world is God (if one may say so) unfolded. So also in the microcosm, the five senses are in the imagination, the imagination in reason, reason in the mind, the mind in God; God is in nothing except in Himself. Thus lower things are seen in their superiors, the last in the penultimate, and again the former in those before them, and always one thing in another, until the highest is reached. This was not poorly suggested by the Egyptians through the seven-stringed Lyre; for from the *hypate* to the *nete* <note>The lowest and highest notes in the ancient Greek musical system</note> through the middle strings, and proceeding in reverse, we see all things contained in all things by a certain wonderful harmony and concord of tones. But enough on these matters, which we have explained more fully so that both the admirable wisdom of the Egyptians and the reasoning of our own philosophy might more easily shine forth. ## CHAPTER IV

*That all the hymns of the Ancients alluded to the music of the world, which they believed that whoever understood it, would perform all kinds of admirable effects by its power.*

<margin>Concerning the music of the gods and the Muse of the gods.</margin>
The Ancients did not only hold the symphony of the world's music <note>The "musica mundana" or music of the spheres—the idea that the universe functions like a giant musical instrument.</note> as a goal for contemplation, but also through practical operation. By its aid, they sought with the greatest zeal the orders, classes, agreements, and disagreements of individual things; they believed they would attain their intent by no easier means than this. Hence, in their sacrifices, they arranged everything according to the pattern of harmonic consonances. And just as a touched string moves a string similar to itself, so by adapting active things to passive things according to a certain harmonic analogy, they believed they would move the strings of the harmonic and mundane instrument in equal measure to produce miraculous effects in the nature of things. They thought this could not be done in a better way unless they had first solicited the supreme overseers of the World and the players of the world's many-stringed instrument <note>original: "polychordi mundani"</note> through sacrifices and hymns, using analogous and suitable things they had received. Once these were solicited, through a continuous plucking of the strings, as it were, which propagated to the lowest orders of things, they believed the many-stringed instrument of the soul would be moved above all others. Thus, the soul, snatched out of itself by a certain fury, would soon be invaded by the harmony of the divine breath, and from there lay open hidden things, predict the future, avert and guard against unfortunate outcomes of events, and finally obtain, by the necessity of infallible fate, those things which pertained to the public or private prosperity of anyone.

<margin>The Egyptians established divination in hymns.</margin>
And such were the hymns presented by the Egyptians through the schemes of hieroglyphics, by which they attracted the Spirit <note>original: "Genium"</note> set over a certain order of natural things through hymns, sacrifices, and the supplications of incantations; concerning which we have dealt in various preceding places, and shall discuss at length in the following.

<margin>The mystical hymns of Orpheus.</margin>
Such were those mystical Hymns of Orpheus, inscribed to the overseers of the parts of the world, to the Spirits, to Pan, Pluto, Jupiter, Saturn, Apollo, Hercules, Mercury, Rhea, Minerva, Pallas, Hecate, Proserpina, and similar Gods and Goddesses. To the Lyre <note>original: "Cÿtharam"</note> of these, the Priest-Prophet adapted his own with the greatest ingenuity; and indeed the sound, analogous to the celestial harmony, moved the celestial lyre by a certain fatal necessity; while the words solicited the Spirits to respond. Hence they believed it could not happen otherwise than that the Spirits, attracted by the vows of the Prophets, would satisfy them in every way. Thus, it was not without reason that the Ancients presented Orpheus as a Musician and Magician, drawing animals, woods, and even the very rocks by the magical sound of his Lyre.

<margin>The origin of the fabled song of Orpheus.</margin>
Regarding this, Claudian <note>A Roman poet, c. 370–404 AD.</note> writes quite elegantly in the preface of the second book of *The Abduction of Proserpina*, in these words:

Then the *Prophet*, rejoicing in the festive time of his fatherland,

<margin>What the story of the rocks and Orpheus teaches.</margin> Indeed, this miraculous attraction of animals, forests, and rocks is to be understood partly tropologically <note>A method of interpretation looking for moral or ethical lessons.</note> and partly allegorically. For the Ancients noted that the power of Music over the soul is greatest, and that the soul is changed according to its various sounds and harmonies, following them just like wax, whichever way you turn it. Therefore, they called the <gloss>soul</gloss> <note>original: "ψυχὴν" (psychen)</note> itself the principle of all things, and as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a 11th-century Byzantine philosopher and polymath.</note> says in his *Music*, <gloss>the ancients called it the Myrmindon</gloss> <note>original: "τὸν Μυρμινδὸν οἱ ἀρχαῖοι ἔλεγον"; likely a reference to a specific harmonic or rhythmic term in Greek music theory.</note>. Furthermore, they saw that this same Music was able to compose and vary character; for nothing flows so easily into tender and soft minds as the various sounds of singing, the power of which can scarcely be described in either direction. For they both incite the weary and make the excited weary; they now relax minds, and now contract them, as will be said a little later. Therefore, the rocks, forests, and animals—that is, men who were utterly hostile, beast-like, and monstrous in their cruelty—he led back to humanity and a political way of living, attracted by the divine sound of his Lyre. Others, however, understand the said attraction allegorically. For since, they say, Orpheus was a distinguished Astrologer <term>Astrologus: in this period, often used interchangeably with Astronomer</term> and Musician, being perfectly skilled in both arts, he so opportunely tempered and mixed sounds that he imitated the harmony of the celestial stars (which he himself understood best). He drew into himself and called down all their influence and power, relying on which, he might rouse or soothe whatever he wished by his playing. Some also add that since he knew best by what proportion and by what concord each thing was constituted by nature and composed, and which star it obeyed and was subject to, he adapted musical ratios to them. By their stars, he would entice inanimate things to movement through the power of the stars, which he brought forth from where it lay hidden in them by his own external harmony—not unlike how iron strikes hidden fire from flint, or a breeze brings forth the flame hidden in leaves. For there are in all things certain hidden sparks, as it were, and seeds of harmony or sense, so much so that the Ancients said God himself was <gloss>their own harmony</gloss> <note>original: "ἀρμονίαν ἑαυτῶν" (harmonian heauton)</note>.

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The human voice provokes imitation.</margin>
I truly do not know what hidden and hitherto impenetrable force of nature resides in motion, by which we see that one person is able to do what they see another doing. This happens not only in the external movement of the body, but most especially in that movement which occurs through the office of the tongue as it breaks forth into words and songs. For we see that even a single person singing excites others to do the same by a certain hidden force (whether this happens through fear, as in those struck by a panic, or by an instinct of joy, as happens in those dancing). While this occurs in other movements, it certainly takes place most of all in human voices. For since the human voice is nothing other than a certain skillful movement of the tongue, formed according to a person's intention to signify something, we see it produce in others exactly what the speaker performs. Experience has taught us that one person humming, or wailing, or whistling, or even yawning, excites others to do the same. Since this is true in sounds and voices that are raw and unpolished, it will certainly be verified much more so in a harmonious arrangement of words and voices. The Masters of primeval wisdom noted this hidden power of nature from the beginning; hence they did not compose the praises of the immortal Gods with just any random arrangement of words, but by casting "chains" <note>The author refers to the "chains" of poetic meter or rhythm that bind words together.</note> they constrained their Orations with a certain harmonic measure, so that the very measure of the words would precisely correspond to the internal affections of the soul. From this, you may recognize the first rudiments of sacred Poetry, which then, as in every age, maintained a certain divine quality among posterity in the minds of men. For they believed that by this means they could not only make Spirits and Gods draw near to them through a certain sympathetic alteration, but also that they could change the souls of men into whatever state they wished. All of these things that famous Horace <unclear>unlearns/teaches</unclear> <note>original Greek: ἀποδιδάσκει (to unteach/teach). The author likely means "demonstrates" or "explains."</note> so excellently, that it seems nothing else can be added to his words:

<margin>In what sense the Poets of old were said to draw wild beasts and rocks.</margin>

> And the way of life was shown, and the favor of Kings
> Was sought in Pierian modes, and games were discovered.

## CHAPTER IV.
We have explained more extensively elsewhere that speech does not have its origin except from harmonic motion; especially if that motion responds in a measured way to the internal affections <note>The term "affections" refers to the passions or emotional states of the soul.</note> of the soul. Moreover, it will correspond in a measured way if the Speech is drawn together into fitting and harmonious periods through the brevity or length of syllables; or, what is the same thing, if a quick and swift measure follows quick movements of the soul, and a slow measure follows slow ones. And although this possesses a wonderful power in the Metric or Rhythmic art, it is certainly found to have a much greater energy in Musical Poetry or Rhythm. For an infinite number of historical monuments testify that the former, when joined to the latter—a ruler complete in all its numbers—obtains utterly prodigious effects in the minds of men.

For there is, as I also said a little while ago, a certain sympathetic something between our soul and harmonic and rhythmic movements, so that as soon as metric harmony is presented to the ears, the mind, agitated by various affections, may now show signs of joy, now of love, now of sorrow, compassion, anger, groaning, and other passions. These sometimes increase to such an extent that the mind, unable to be contained within the internal cloisters of the soul, also excites the external limbs to acts responding to the passion. But since we have shown these things at length in our *Magnetic Art*, Book III, concerning the Magnetism of Music and Tarantism <note>Tarantism refers to a psychological illness or dancing mania popularly believed to be caused by the bite of a tarantula, which Kircher argued could be cured by specific musical frequencies.</note>, we refer the Reader there.

And these are the things which we thought should be said concerning Hieroglyphic Music; whoever desires more on this subject should consult the tenth book of our *Universal Musurgia* <note>Kircher's "Musurgia Universalis" (1650) was his most influential work on music theory and acoustics.</note>, which is titled *The Decachordon of Nature* <note>original: "Decachordon naturae"; literally "The Ten-Stringed Lyre of Nature."</note>; for there he will find a formal treatise on many other things which can be desired regarding this matter.

## SECTION IV.
### PREFACE.

<image-desc>A large decorative initial 'D' begins the first paragraph.</image-desc>In this Section, we shall present the twofold science of celestial matters practiced by the Egyptians. The first of these shall be *Astronomy*, the explorer of celestial motions and times; the second, *Astrology*, which reveals the decrees of fatal events depending on the stars and the fortunes established for individuals. The single difference between the two is this: the former measures much, while the latter mentions <note>original: "mentiatur," literally "lies about" or "falsifies"</note> much. We shall speak first of Astronomy; afterwards, we shall also discuss that particular part of *Astronomy* which they call *Computation* <note>The mathematical art of calculating calendars and celestial positions</note>, as far as the powers of our intellect permit.

<margin>The author's protestation regarding the interpretation of Egyptian Astrology.</margin>
<margin>Astrology is ruinous and vain.</margin>
Before I approach these matters, I protest before God and the holy court of heaven that I shall assert nothing contrary to the laws established by the Sacrosanct Roman Church. Rather, I shall perform only the office of a naked Oedipus <note>A reference to the mythological riddle-solver; Kircher views himself as the "interpreter" of Egyptian mysteries</note> or Interpreter in bringing forth these most recondite matters. Nor do I hold any faith in such a ruinous faculty as its practitioners persuade themselves of. For when I name Astrology, I do not mean that which measures the masses and motions of the stars by mathematical reasoning—certainly a noble art, most honorable in its own merits, and approved at all times by the greatest authority of the most learned men. Instead, I mean that which pronounces future events from the stars and brings force upon human will; an art forbidden by both civil and pontifical laws, mocked by Philosophers, cultivated by charlatans, and suspected by every good and prudent person. Regarding this art, relying both on reason and the judgments of the wisest men, I would not hesitate to affirm that among the deceptive arts, there is none that more greatly deceives the credulous and unskilled, nor any which, by deceiving the persuaded, does more harm. It is as much more deadly than other superstitions as it seems to approach closer to the truth. This art was first born in Egypt and Chaldea, raised in Greece, and reached maturity in the Roman Empire, from whence it spread its roots into all parts of the World—with an outcome all the more ill-fated as it brought greater ruin to the scepters of Kings and Emperors. And since "from a bad crow a bad egg is born," I do not see what good or fruitful thing can be born from such a pernicious root of such great superstitions. At first glance and from a distance, it offers some appearance and habit of wisdom; yet if you consider it closely, you will find it cherishes nothing in its bosom but a vault of infamy. Once examined more exactly, you would abominate it as a certain slave and a fallacy of darkness brought into the open light. From afar, it displays the heaven and the planets, whence you might easily believe that in such a sublime and lucid spectacle, everything could be most truly foreseen. But soon, when you have explored more attentively, you will see that the mirror is so sublime that the images of earthly things can by no means penetrate there; so bright that the weakness of our frail nature grows dim at its splendor. Then, if you approach its own details, you will see woven into its veil, instead of celestial things, monsters of portentous images and strange spectacles of stars transformed into exotic animals. In a word, you will gaze with stupor upon a heaven full of fables—indeed, instead of the true heaven, a counterfeit heaven not made by God, but fashioned by Astrologists. It is a wonder how, through these glooms and mists poured over the eyes of the unskilled, it represents an image of itself that is beautiful, venerable, and full of a series of authority. The books of the astrologers, with their daring fictions and the insane [works] of wicked men...

They taught their posterity that, having abandoned the sacred worship of the Divine Name, they should venerate and worship either the elements obscurely, or fire, or the demons of the air. Therefore, how this knowledge of curious things did not perish in the flood, and became known to succeeding ages, I think must be briefly touched upon. He was occupied with this one goal: to arrange the discipline according to the pious intention of the predecessor Fathers—chiefly Enoch, the first Idris <note>The Islamic name for the prophet Enoch</note>, or the first Hermes, whose name he also took for himself—which was directed toward the knowledge and worship of the true God.

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS CHAPTER I.

Whether you consider the immense capacity of his genius, his total knowledge of hidden things, or finally his desire to propagate his glory among posterity and to deserve well of the human race, he was the first. For here, as we have taught above, bringing back to the anvil <note>original: "ad incudem reuocans" — a metaphor for refining or reworking an idea</note> the laws of Astronomy which he had received by tradition from Enoch through the propagation of Noah’s lineage, he spared no effort to test the truth of the Ancients in the Astronomical Canons through the experiment of his own observation, and to reduce what was tested to that perfection which those unrefined times permitted.

<margin>The first division of the heaven into 12 parts.</margin>
These things being premised, I say that Mercury first divided the heaven into twelve signs, having invented particular characters for that purpose; he divided the year into 365 days, first detected the motions of the planets, and similar things, which will be discussed most abundantly in the following pages. It remains to be said by what method he accomplished this.

<margin>How Hermes was represented hieroglyphically.</margin>
First, it is likely that when he first observed the entire machine of the heavens revolving around two poles—of which Aratus <note>A Greek didactic poet (c. 315–240 BCE) famous for his poem on phenomena and stars.</note> is the author who states he invented the armillary sphere <term>armillary sphere: a model of objects in the sky consisting of a spherical framework of rings</term> as a model for it—he was the discoverer of the courses of the heavens and the sphere. Whence the Egyptians, intending to represent him hieroglyphically, painted a man with a canine face <note>referring to Hermanubis or Thoth-Anubis</note>, in whose one hand was held a caduceus <note>the staff carried by Hermes/Mercury</note>, and in the other a sphere; all of which you will find explained at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 294. For when he discovered that in the celestial machine, once a revolution was completed in the space of a natural day, certain fixed stars remained perpetually as if unmoved, some moved most swiftly, and the rest proceeded with a motion midway between speed and slowness; he thought the same thing happened as in a material sphere, which, when rotated, those parts that go around the poles are seen to be slow and as if unmoved, while conversely those which occupy the line of the middle globe proceed with the swiftest motion.

<margin>First observation of the poles and the equinoctial. Observation of the fixed stars.</margin>
Thus, by the said observation, he detected the poles in the heaven and the equinoctial <note>the celestial equator</note>. But when he noted one and the same immutable distance of all the stars from each other, from this he easily fashioned the globe of the fixed stars.

<margin>Observation of the planets.</margin>
Furthermore, when he noted that some stars held neither the same distance from each other, nor the same pattern of rising and setting, nor fixed places in the heaven, but were found to wander here and there with a certain perpetual variety spread out in the ethereal expanse; he judged them not to be fixed, but to be led around by motions attributed peculiarly to each: of which he found only seven subject to this instability; among which, since they held the principal place,

<margin>Observation of the motions of the Sun and Moon.</margin>
the Sun and Moon, he first applied his mind to scrutinizing their motion. Therefore, when he found that the Sun touched different points of the Horizon each day, and likewise marked different points of height or depression in the middle of the sky; he noticed that there was a certain and constant elongation of it toward the South and the North; and when it reached its furthest point, it soon receded in the opposite direction with a reversed motion. And from there emanated the invention of the Tropics, which he called the extreme "hostels" <note>original: "hospitia"</note> of the ascending and descending souls of the Gods, as will afterwards be proved from the *Cave of the Nymphs* described by Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher; Kircher refers to his work "De antro nympharum".</note>.

<margin>Observation of the Zodiac.</margin>
Again, when he noted that the Sun passed through certain alternating orders every month; from there flowed the distinction of the *dodecamoria* <note>Greek: "twelve parts"</note>, or the division of the Zodiac into twelve signs, which he called the mansions of the Gods.

In Egypt, however, Mizraim <note>The biblical son of Ham, traditionally associated with the founding of Egypt</note> first imbued his son and others with this same knowledge. Afterward, the second Hermes, known as Mercury Trismegistus <note>A legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with writing sacred texts</note>, cultivated it with the greatest zeal and passed it down to the Egyptian posterity in twelve books, as witnessed by <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> Clement of Alexandria in Book VI of the *Stromata* <note>original: "Stromatum," a work by the 2nd-century Christian theologian</note>. Therefore, it should seem a wonder to no one that the Egyptians, the Chaldeans (or Babylonians), and the Greeks competed for the primacy of *astronomical* <note>original: "Astronomica"</note> invention, since each of these nations claimed for itself the glory of discovering a matter they saw held in such high esteem and admiration by men. Thus, although the inventions of things may emerge in one particular region, they have always preceded them in other regions; since I show this in many other places, I did not wish to dwell on it any longer. Let it suffice for now, in a discourse perhaps longer than is fitting, to have demonstrated that Hermes was the first inventor, or rather the restorer, of astronomy in Egypt.

<margin>The method of observation established by Mercury.</margin>
Mercury Trismegistus, looking out for the human race and being intent on communicating the exact order of celestial things to posterity, described each detail in his books, as Clement of Alexandria testifies. And because he noticed that an influence is propagated into lower things from the star-bearing heaven in a continuous order, he took his beginning there for his astrological arrangement. Thus, when he had first noted—through long experience and frequent observation of the Sun, the Moon, and the other stars—the four principal cardinal points that effect all changes and the various seasons, he fashioned a circle. In this circle, he arranged the said points <note>The diagram shows the four cardinal points of the year: the equinoxes and solstices</note> through two diameters, *a-c* and *d-e*, intersecting normally <note>at right angles</note> at the center, namely *a, d, c, e*. Of these, those points which hold the middle line and are equally distant from the poles of the world, he wished to be called the points of equality <note>The Equinoxes</note>, because when the Sun reaches them, it makes the day equal to the night. He established the *Cynocephalus* <note>The dog-headed baboon, an animal sacred to Thoth/Hermes</note> as the symbol <margin>The symbol of the equinox is the Cynocephalus.</margin> for this, whose nature is such (according to Horus <note>likely referring to Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note>) that near the points of the equinox, it is accustomed to pass urine twelve times a day by a certain hidden and inborn instinct; more on this in its proper place. But those points *a* and *d*, which terminate the greatest elongation of the Sun as it travels back and forth, now to the South and now to the North, he called the limits of the Gods <note>The Tropics</note>, because the Divinities circling the Globe would never pass these boundaries, as if they were fixed for them, but with a reversed course would move now toward the South, now toward the...

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>

In that it was divided into four parts, it shows the four portions of the year, which the fourfold division of the Zodiac created. In that he asserts the heaven was divided into twelve parts, it indicates the division of the Zodiac into 12 houses or mansions of the Gods. <margin>The Decans of the signs.</margin>

<header>CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.</header>
<margin>Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note></margin>
<margin>Clement of Alexandria <note>An early Christian theologian who studied Egyptian customs.</note></margin>
### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS.
With these things thus distinguished, the doubts which you say you conceived in the Egyptian books you have read are easily resolved. For those things which speak in a <term>Gregorian style</term> <note>Likely referring to a specific rhetorical or ecclesiastical style of writing</note> circumscribed under the title of Mercury <note>original: "Mercurij"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, are nevertheless translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in Philosophy. See also Clement of Alexandria, Book 1, 5, and 6 of the *Stromata* <note>Miscellanies</note>, speaking amply concerning Mercury and his inventions, as well as Origen, Tertullian, and other authors whom I have often cited, discussing the same.

<margin><unclear>with greatest force</unclear></margin>
<margin>The First House or Citadel of his Zodiac.</margin>
*The first bright <note>original: "φαιδρώ"</note> and somewhat rough sketch of the Zodiac having been performed by Hermes, let us now see with what names, Divinities, animals, and characters he mystically adorned it.*

<margin>Anubis the hieroglyphic of Capricorn.</margin>
<margin>Clement of Alexandria.</margin>
<margin><unclear>zeal/study</unclear></margin>
<margin><unclear>Anubis</unclear></margin>
*Therefore, that starry circle which we call the Zodiac being divided into 12 houses or mansions, since he noticed that the lower things are subject to the higher, and that all influence flows into the lower World from the powers of the higher, he equipped each house with its own Powers or Divinities. And indeed, he attributed the first house to Anubis. Now Anubis was the dog-headed <note>original: "κυνοκέφαλον"</note> Divinity of the Egyptians, the guardian of temples, and the preserver of heat and moisture; whose hieroglyphic symbol was the goat-fish <note>original: "ἰχθυοτράγος"</note>, which Anubis held bound by a leash. The horns of the goat denoted the heat, or the fiery force of the Sun enclosed in the earth; but the tail of the fish denoted moisture, from which the first generation of all things proceeds; of which they said Anubis was the guardian. According to the testimony of Plutarch; who says he placed him in the middle between the upper and lower hemisphere for this reason: that when the Sun is in Capricorn at its greatest distance, and the solar rays are weakened, the earth, closed as if in a womb, contrives the preludes of a new generation through the arrangement of seminal principles, over which they said Anubis presided. Clement of Alexandria reports this expressly in these words in Book 5 of the *Stromata*: "The Egyptians were also accustomed in certain solemnities to carry around four statues of the Gods, whom they called Komasias <note>original: "Komafias"</note>, two of which shone in the shape of Dogs, the third a Hawk, and the fourth an Ibis. By the two dogs they understood the two hemispheres." And a little later: "Others, however, wished to suggest by the two dogs the two tropics, which are certain dogs appointed by nature as observers and guardians, preventing the further elongation of the Sun to the South and North." Thus this house was like a certain gate for the ascent of the Gods, about which more will be said later.*

<margin>II. House of Canopus.</margin>
*The second house was attributed to the care of Canopus. Now Canopus, or in Egyptian <term>Kanobos</term> <note>original: "κανώβος"</note>, was the Divinity or Genius who actuates the subterranean water and is the exciter for bringing forth fertility; concerning which see the very full treatment in Volume I, in the Chapter on Canopus. In his place the Greeks put Aquarius, in which, however, they do not differ from the Egyptians. For the water-jar, which the Greeks imagined was poured out by Aquarius, the Egyptians used to paint with Aquarius and Hydra joined into one image according to their usual custom. See the figure in the Scheme of the ancient Zodiac, which follows shortly after.*

<margin>III. House of the Zodiac was called Ichton and why.</margin>
*The third house or mansion was assigned to the Divinity Ichton, which Iamblichus explains in these words: "To this, Mercury sets before one indivisible thing, which he calls the first exemplar, or expression, or image, which he calls Ichton, in which is the first intellect and the first intelligible, which is worshiped by silence alone."*

# CHAPTER II. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

An exemplar, I say, not only in the intelligible World <note>The realm of pure ideas or divine thought</note>, but also in the starry world, and the idea for producing lower things. For by this, the seeds of conceived things are led into the light; with this as a guide, the gate of life assigned to all things is opened around this station of the year. Thus, they aptly indicated this by the hieroglyphic symbol of the fish; for fish at this time of year produce a most great and copious offspring, and swelling with seeds, they fill all the paths of moist nature. Consequently, the name of this Genius <note>A presiding spirit or deity</note> has remained derived from the etymology of "fish" even unto this day. *See the figure of this overseer in the diagram shortly following.*

<margin>IV. House of Amun.</margin>The fourth house or mansion was assigned to Amun, a Prince of great authority among the twelve Powers. His figure was <gloss>the mediating air</gloss> <note>original Greek: ἀὴρ ὁ μεσιτὴς</note> distinguished by ram's horns. By this, he indeed hinted at nothing other than the fertility of that station or mansion, through which the seeds that Ichthon <note>The previous deity mentioned, associated with Pisces</note> had arranged are produced by Amun into a varied harvest of general things. But since this Amun has been treated most amply in the first Volume, Treatise 2, in the chapter on Amun, and in Book 3 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk* concerning the hieroglyphic significance of the Ram, we refer the reader there, where he will find everything pertaining to this matter gathered from innumerable authors.

<margin>V. House of Apis.</margin>The fifth house or mansion in the Zodiac was destined for Apis the Bull. Now, Apis was the greatest deity among the Egyptians, the presiding lord of agriculture, by whose help they believed the abundance of all things necessary for human life was provided. For this reason, they believed him the prefect of this mansion, in which the harvest was gathered in Egypt and fruits were brought to maturity; these indicated nothing other than the effects of agriculture, of which Apis was the symbol. For the seeds which Ichthon had arranged <margin>Why the Bull was assigned to this sign.</margin> and Amun had produced into luxuriant offspring, Apis was believed to ripen into the fruits necessary for human life. He was represented hieroglyphically under the figure of a Bull, which Astrologers have preserved for this mansion even unto this day. Let the reader see what we have discussed most copiously concerning Apis in Volume I, Treatise 2, in the chapter on Apis, and in Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 256, regarding the hieroglyphic significance of the Bull.

For the Egyptians say that Isis lay with Osiris after his death, and from him conceived the twins Helitomenon and Harpocrates, and that they were afterwards translated into heaven and placed over this mansion. Hence the two stars in Gemini, which the Arabs call <gloss>Head of the Giant</gloss> <note>original Arabic: راس الجوز, Ras Elgeuke</note>, Abenregel calls <gloss>Garaklas</gloss> <note>original Arabic: غر قلس</gloss> for Apollo. Although these names are most corrupt, after the manner of the Arabs, they nevertheless indicate nothing other than Hercules and Apollo, or Horus; <margin>Horus.</margin> these two are equivalent to Helitomenon and Harpocrates. By them, nothing else is indicated hieroglyphically except the doubling of the strength of the Solar heat, which acquires its greatest power in this mansion. # CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER I.

<margin>The Hieroglyphic of June, the sign of Gemini.</margin>
...from the mountains of Ethiopia are released and adapted into the desired increase of the Nile; for this reason, Hercules and Apollo <note>The author associates these Greek deities with Egyptian counterparts governing the summer solstice</note> are considered its presiding deities. They are indicated hieroglyphically by two statues, one of which holds a pyramid in its hand, the other a club, with their other two hands mutually joined to denote concord, as will be explained in its proper place under June.

And thus far we have described the six houses of the ascending Gods; now from this point follow the seven houses of the six descending Gods, as the Egyptians maintain—or as Porphyry <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher</note> maintains, the mansions of souls (both views can be supported, since souls cannot descend without the guidance of the Gods, according to Proclus <note>Another influential Neoplatonist</note>). The symbol of this point, as well as of the opposite sign, was the Dog, whose boundaries were fixed there; either because the Dog-star, which we call *Sothis* in Egyptian, rose at this time as a kind of precursor to the coming Nilotic inundation.

<margin>The Dog Sothis rises in Egyptian [reckoning] at this time.</margin>
The seventh house or mansion was consecrated to the deity Hermanubis, that is, Mercury, whom they exhibited under the appearance of an Ibis. They believed his office was to heap up immense masses of vapors and, as if attracted and stolen from all the storehouses of human nature, dissolve them into rains; from which, subsequently, a great benefit proceeded from the inundation of the Nile. But as for why they placed the figure of a Cancer <note>The Crab</note> in the place of the Ibis, the reason was that the Crab among the Egyptians was not a symbol of any particular Spirit, but a hieroglyphic of the "turning" of the Sun. For just as it is natural for a Crab to observe a backward motion in its gait, so the Sun, after it reaches the furthest limit of its elongation, gradually fails from further motion and the days diminish, as if it seems to move backward by similarity to the motion of a Crab. However, the mansion was dedicated not to the Crab, but to Hermanubis, as was said, in the form of an Ibis <note>original: "Ibimorpho"</note>. Thus the ancient Egyptians did not paint a Crab, but an Ibis, the hieroglyphic of the Spirit ruling in this lodging. See more on this symbol below, and those things pertaining to this matter treated with curiosity in Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, in the chapter on the Ibis.

<margin>VII House of Hermanubis.</margin>
<margin>Why the Greeks placed the figure of a Crab in place of the Ibis.</margin>
The eighth house or mansion was consecrated to the God Momphra. Now, Momphra was nothing other than the Deity who presides over moist nature, the Spirit of the Nile's increase; concerning his name, origin, etymology, and hieroglyphic significance, consult Book 4 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk* regarding the Sacred Writing of the Lion. He was painted in various ways, sometimes in the form of a man <gloss>human-shaped</gloss>, sometimes under the simple figure of a reclining Lion, as will be explained in its proper time and place. He was a singular Deity among the Egyptians, held in the highest veneration, about whom frequent discourses were circulated; for they believed that all administration over moist nature was committed to him. But these things, as I said, we shall pursue most extensively in their proper places.

<margin>VIII House of Momphra.</margin>
<margin>The Office of Momphra.</margin>
The ninth house or mansion was given to Isis, whose figure was represented sometimes in the manner of a Virgin holding an ear of grain, sometimes under the form of a reclining Sphinx. By this, nothing else was denoted than the increase of the Nile, because that which took the beginnings of its flooding in Momphra (the Lion) would finish in Isis: and therefore, by the benefit of Isis, a great abundance of the future harvest was hoped for; for they believed Isis to be the discoverer of grain as well as the presider over the food supply. <page-num>156</page-num>
<header>CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.</header>

We have treated all these matters extensively in the first Volume, second Treatise, in the chapter concerning Isis.

<margin>X. The House of Omphta.</margin>
The tenth house or mansion was dedicated to a Spirit <note>Latin: *Genio*; Kircher uses "Genius" to mean a presiding spirit or deity</note> whom the Egyptians called **Omphta**. He was a beneficent Deity, because Omphta distributed in equal measure those things which **Momphtha** and **Isis** had set in motion through the moisture of the Nile's inundation. For this reason, the hieroglyphic of the Balance or **Libra** crept into this mansion; for Omphta was believed to be the just executor and weigher of arranged things, which they believed occurred at this station of the Zodiac. He was depicted in human form, holding a measuring rod in his right hand and a grain-measure <note>Latin: *modium*</note> on his head, as appears below in the Zodiac.

<margin>XI. The House of Typhon.</margin>
<margin>Osiris is shut into an Ark by Typhon.</margin>
<margin>Hieroglyphic.</margin>
The eleventh house or mansion was dedicated to **Typhon**, a Spirit of a malignant and wasting nature, by whose scorching power moisture was dried up, trees were stripped of their finery, and the earth was left parched, dry, and squalid, with its moisture driven deep into its bowels. And from this they tell the fable that **Osiris**, in this month of *Athyr*, was shut into an Ark by Typhon; and that snares were set for **Horus**, the beauty of the perceptible World; from which the Isiac lamentations and mournings found their origin. They aptly displayed this catastrophe of perishing fertility through a bull whose testicles are bitten by a **Scorpion**, to indicate that the generative moisture of the earth fails at this particular station through a certain wasting and Typhonian force, as has been explained elsewhere; so that from this very hieroglyphic it pleased posterity to honor this house with the symbol of the Scorpion.

<margin>XII. The House of Nephthys.</margin>
The twelfth house or mansion was called **Nephthys**, the Spirit presiding over subterranean heat, lest everything be destroyed by the power of Typhon. For, as **Plutarch** says, the Mistress of the lower earth does not permit the moisture to perish entirely by the adverse drying force of Typhon, wishing a temperate state to remain perpetually, since the complete adornment and harmony of the World could in no way exist if the fiery force caused it to perish. This is the Spirit to whose care the arms of Osiris—that is, of the Sun—were committed, which were (according to Plutarch) the dart, the spear, and the bow. By these nothing else was denoted than the tempered force of Solar heat, by which she strives to preserve the moisture that Typhon’s scorching power seeks to destroy; so that even from that time to the present day, the sign of **Sagittarius** has remained for this Station.

<margin>12 Deities arranged by the Egyptians according to the pattern of nature.</margin>
<margin>Who are the Decans in the Zodiac?</margin>
<margin>The Spirit of many forms, etc.</margin>
<margin>Authorities: Hermes in the Pimander and Asclepius.</margin>
And these are the twelve *dodecamoria* <note>term: dodecamoria (twelve parts/divisions of the zodiac)</note>, the houses or mansions of the twelve Spirits of the Zodiac, which the ancient Egyptians, by the tradition of **Hermes**, were accustomed to arrange according to the pattern of nature. The Greeks made this arrangement entirely their own, changing it slightly and veiling it with various other fables. Furthermore, to each of these Spirits of the twelve divisions, three other assistant Spirits were joined, whom they called **Decans**, so that the entire Zodiac is divided among 36 Spirits. To each of these, different duties in administering the worldly economy were committed by the supreme Spirit of all Nature, whom they therefore called *pantomorphos*, or <gloss>polymorphos</gloss> <note>original Greek: πολυμορφος; "of many forms"</note>. Moreover, Hermes, in the *Pimander*, calls the Zodiac a "tabernacle" constituted by a circle divided into twelve houses, according to the Ideas of all nature. But let us hear his words: *“But I would have you tell me this besides, how the twelve avengers of darkness are driven away by the twelve opposing powers.”* TRISMEGISTUS: *“That tabernacle...”*

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.

<page-num>157</page-num>

<margin>Who are the gods of the Horoscopes? Who are the Rulers?</margin>
That, O son, is established in the Zodiac circle which consists of the number twelve, and for each one of them there is one omniform <note>having all forms</note> being, according to the ideas of nature for the preservation and circuit of man. And in the *Asclepius* <note>original: "Alclepio"; a famous Hermetic dialogue</note> he describes them further in these words: There are many kinds of Gods, and they are arranged in a circle; of all of them, one part is called intelligible <note>perceived by the mind</note>, and the other part sensible <note>perceived by the senses</note>. They are called intelligible not as an idea, as if they were thought not to be subject to our senses; for we perceive them even more than those we call visible. For sublime and more divine reason, existing beyond the minds and intentions of men, will fly past and flow away—or rather flow back and mix itself with its own potent waters—if it does not receive the words of those speaking with the attentive obedience of the ears. There are, therefore, the Gods who are the Princes of all species. These are followed by the Gods whose Prince is the Idea. These sensible beings, similar to both their origins, make up all of sensible nature, one through the other: each one, or whatever it is that is encompassed by that name. *Solaex* is Jupiter (whom the Egyptians call *Hemphra*) for through the heaven Hemphra, or Jupiter, provides life to all. The light of the Sun is *sola* <note>unique/alone</note>: for the good of light is poured into us through the orb of the Sun: the thirty-six (who are called *Horoscopii* <note>the Decans; stars that mark the hours</note>) are of the stars fixed always in the same place; the Horoscopii are either Princes or he whom they call *narraq́;* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek or Egyptian term for "the narrator" or "the many-formed"</note> or the omniform one, who makes different forms for different species. These words are so clear that they seem to

<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
point directly to the doctrine of Hermes which we established a little while ago. Indeed, Iamblichus describes these things so beautifully that he might seem to have explained them himself. I, he says, will tell you the primary cause for which the sacred and ancient writers of the Egyptians felt various things about these matters: and moreover, why the Sages of this age do not speak of them with the same reasoning. Since there are many essences in the universe, and they differ among themselves in many ways, many principles of them have deservedly been handed down, having different orders—some by some Priests, and other principles by others—principles which are entirely universal, as Seleucus relates. Mercury <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> himself handed down twenty thousand volumes, or as Manetho recounts, he handed down thirty-six thousand five hundred and twenty-five volumes, and in them he perfectly demonstrated all things. But other ancients introduced different principles of particular essences here and there. It is necessary, therefore, to briefly declare the truth about all these things, and first regarding what you first asked. The first God, before being <note>original: "ens"</note>, and alone, is the father of the first God, whom he begets remaining in his solitary unity, and that is above the intelligible, and is the exemplar of him, who is called his own father, his own son, the sole-father, and the truly good God. For He is greater, and first, and the fountain of all things, and the root of those things which are first understood, and which understand, namely the ideas. From this one, certainly, the self-sufficient God unfolded himself. And therefore he is called self-sufficient, his own father, and his own prince. For he is the principle, the God of Gods, unity from the one, above

<margin>The most ancient principles of all.</margin>
essence; for from him comes essence, and therefore he is the father of essence with the name Being <note>original: "Ens"</note>, the principle of intelligibles. These are the most ancient principles of all, which Mercury places before the ethereal, empyrean, and celestial Gods: composing a hundred books about the empyrean ones, as many about the ethereal, and a thousand about the celestial ones. But according to another order, he places the God Emepht before the celestial Gods as a Leader, whom he says is the thinking intellect, turning intelligences into himself. Before him he places one indivisible thing, which he calls the first

<header>GYMNASIUM OF EGYPTIAN HIEROGLYPHICS</header>

## CHAPTER II.

<margin>Ichton.</margin>...the first model, or expression, or image, which he calls *Ichton* <note>original: "Ichton"; likely a corruption of a Greek or Egyptian term for the "First Image" or "First Being"</note>, in which is the first intelligence and the first intelligible thing, which is worshipped by silence alone. Besides these, however, other Leaders preside over the craftsmanship of visible things. For the craftsman-intellect, who is both the lord of Divinity and wisdom—insofar as he proceeds into generation and brings the hidden power of latent reasons into the light—is called <margin>Amun.</margin>**Amun** in the Egyptian language; but insofar as he accomplishes all things without falsehood, and with artistry combined with truth, he is named <margin>Phta.</margin>**Phta** <note>Ptah, the Egyptian creator god associated with craftsmen</note>: the Greeks, however, call him **Vulcan** <note>Hephaestus</note>, considering only his craftsmanship. Insofar as he is the bringer of good things, he is called <margin>Osiris.</margin>**Osiris**; and he has other names because of his different powers and actions. There is also another sovereignty among them over all the Elements placed in generation, and their virtues; four of which are masculine, and four feminine: a Sovereignty which they attribute to the **Sun**. Likewise, another Sovereignty over all nature involved in generation is attributed to the **Moon**. *Marsilio* <note>Marsilio Ficino, the Renaissance Neoplatonist</note>. In these matters, you can arrange the order according to *Proclus* <note>A major Neoplatonist philosopher</note> as follows. First is the One itself, existing above the entire intelligible realm. Second is the One Being, or the unity of Being, in which its unity is placed before its being: it can also be called the intelligible intellect, and its own father. Third is the intelligible intellect, which is simultaneously intellectual, and of the one intellect, and the first expression, *Ichton*. Fourth is the intellectual intellect already unfolded, the Leader of the celestial Gods, **Emepht**. Fifth is the craftsman-intellect, the nearest Leader of the Worldly craftsmen, who are the celestial, empyrean, and ethereal Gods: this perhaps is the intellect of the **Soul of the World**, which is named Amun, Phta, Vulcan, Osiris. *Iamblichus* <note>A Syrian Neoplatonist who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>. Dividing the heaven into two parts, or four, or twelve, or thirty-six, or doubles of these, or in any other way whatsoever, they also set Sovereignties over these, either fewer or more. Again, they place one Leader before these, and thus the Egyptian treatise on principles, proceeding from above to the last things, descends from the one into the multitude—governed, clearly, by one God—everywhere an indefinite nature is imperiously encompassed within a certain defined limit, especially by the exalted unity, the cause of all things. God produced Matter from materiality, namely derived from essentiality, which the craftsman, taking up as vital, made into simple and impassible spheres. But he took the last part of it to make generable and corruptible bodies. With these things thus distinguished, the doubts are easily solved which you say you conceived in the Egyptian books you have read. For those which are circulated under the title of **Hermes** <note>original: "Mercurii"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus</note> contain Hermetic opinions, even if they often speak in the style of Greek philosophers, for they were translated from the Egyptian language into Greek by men not unskilled in philosophy. I would wish, however, that whoever touches upon the first causes of worldly things would also declare the ultimate principles. Likewise, whoever treats the planets, the Zodiac, the **Decans** <note>term: Decans; thirty-six groups of stars (small constellations) used in Ancient Egyptian astronomy</note>, the **Horoscopes** <note>term: Horoscopes; here referring to the rising sign or the point of the ecliptic rising on the eastern horizon</note>, and the stars as powerful Leaders, should hand down the particular distributions of the principles. Furthermore, the dogmas which are in the *Salaminiaca* <note>likely referring to astrological or Hermetic texts associated with Salmeschoiniaka</note> contain in very brief parts the Hermetic arrangements. Likewise, those things which are treated concerning the appearances or disappearances of stars, or the waxing or waning of the Moon, have their assignment of causes among the last things for the Egyptians. Truly, the Egyptians do not think that all things are natural, but they distinguish both intellectual and animal life from nature, not only in the World, but also in men. And since they have placed intellect and reason, existing according to themselves, in charge, they believe that whatever happens, happens thus; and they assert that the craftsman is the father of those things involved in generation.

It explains the descent from the "One" into the material world and the role of Hermetic writings in preserving these ancient philosophical traditions.</summary>

...they assert. They also recognize a vital power, both that which is in heaven and that which exists above heaven. Likewise, they place a multiple intellect above the World, and one indivisible intellect in the whole World, and another distributed through all the circles. Now, they are not accustomed to contemplate these things with bare speech and reason alone, but they further admonish and teach that our nature progresses toward the higher commonalities, and those superior to fate, even to God himself and the <term>Artisan of the World</term> <note>original: "Deum Opificemque Mundi"; a reference to the Demiurge or Creator</note>, insofar as it carries neither matter with it, nor anything else except the observation of the opportune time; and they teach that they achieve this through sacred works, and at the same time they bring it to pass. <term>Mercury</term> <note>The Roman name for Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of Egyptian wisdom</note> himself also handed down this path to us: but the Prophet *Bitis* interpreted it for King Ammon, having found it in the sanctuary of the temple in the city of *Sais in Egypt*, inscribed in sacred letters.
