# CHAPTER II.

<margin>EXPLANATION of the Barberini Tablet.</margin>
The globe <note>original: "νυξο-πες μος" - likely a corruption of a Greek epithet for night-walking or nocturnal</note> shows the unity of the *three-fold Deity* <note>The "triformis Numinis" refers to the Egyptian concept of a god possessing three aspects or powers</note>, dwelling in solitary contemplation of itself. The principal figure, however, indicates the descent of the same all-formed *three-fold Deity* into the vastness of all nature. Upon its head, it wears a *Lion’s* head inserted into a crescent *Moon*, by which power and dominion over the *Sun* and *Moon* are shown; this power is also declared by its seated posture. It bears a ram’s horn to demonstrate its fertility and its *Ammonian* virtue <note>Referring to the god Amun, often depicted with ram horns, symbolizing generative power</note>. In its left hand, it holds a *Scorpion* and a dog; by which *Anubis* and *Typhon* are aptly indicated, according to the testimony of *Plutarch*, representing the drying force of the *Sun*, which arises most greatly when the *Sun* enters *Scorpio*, while the trees are stripped of leaves and the earth of its grasses. In its right hand, it holds two *Serpents* and the figure of a *Lion* entwined with a staff; by these, the force and power over life and death, over generation and corruption, over good and evil, and over the *Kingdom of Momphta* <note>Kircher's term for a specific divine or natural realm</note> are indicated. Thus, through the *Scorpion*, a fatal animal, the death and destruction of things—or the preparation of evils—is shown, according to *Horus* <note>Horapollo, an ancient author on hieroglyphs</note>; through the two *Serpents*, the double life of the *World*, both celestial and elementary; and through the *Lion of Momphta*, the presiding spirit of moist nature is aptly indicated. Furthermore, through the images placed around the many-formed *Deity*—serpents and others, such as staffs shaped like hoopoes <term>cucuphomorphis: shaped like a hoopoe bird, often associated with the 'was' scepter</term>, whips, and handled crosses <note>The Ankh</note>—under the figures of a *Boy*, a *Lion*, a *Hawk*, and an *Ibis*, they show the vital fertility which they flow into the *World*, the *Sun*, the *Moon*, and the *Elements* for the variety of things; all of which will be explained more fully in their proper places. It tramples the heads of two *Crocodiles* looking in opposite directions, by which it is beautifully indicated that it holds every pernicious force of *Typhon* and *Ahriman* <note>The Persian spirit of darkness/evil, equated here with the Egyptian Typhon/Set</note>, which extends to the East and West, perfectly subjected to itself. Beneath the *Crocodiles*, an arched surface is seen, full of the *Genii* <note>Attendant spirits or minor deities</note> who are followers of the all-formed *Deity* and tutelary ministers of affairs; by these, the entire *Kingdom of Momphta* is administered through a fit arrangement of times. Some of these are standing, others are sitting. The standing ones are the first three from the right and three from the left, with five intermediate ones in a sitting posture. Starting from the first on the right, <margin>The Spirit lyttnycalo, etc.</margin> is the *Spirit* <note>original: "λυττνικαλο"</note> holding a grappling hook in its hand, clothed in a sacred veil, and holding a globe on its head; by this, the *Spirit* is noted for conferring a corroborative strength and a reconciling solidity to things against the dissipative force of matters. There follows the *Spirit* <margin>The Spirit ineacdomorpho, etc.</margin> <note>original: "ινεακδμορφο"</note>, that is, with a *Hawk-like* face, distinguished by a hoopoe-shaped staff, by which the *Solar* force in heat and moisture—which is the cause of the variety of things—is indicated. There follows the third *Spirit* <margin>Ailyedromorpho, etc.</margin> <note>original: "αιλυεδρομορφο"</note>, or one with the appearance of a *Cat*, or what is the same, the *Dog-headed Lunar Spirit*. To these, three other *Spirits* respond from the opposite side, of which the first, with a *Hawk-like* face and a feather in its hand, shows the swift force of *Solar* motion; the second, in the form of an *Ibis* with a feather in its hand, the swift force of *Lunar* motion; the third, in its form of a dog, indicates *Anubis*, the protector of the *Horizon*, according to *Plutarch*. In the middle, the figure of a *Serpent* <margin>Symbols of the Zodiac.</margin> biting its own tail in a wavy coil is inserted, by which the year or the *Zodiac* is aptly indicated, according to *Horus*. It is wavy, or arranged in the figure of flowing water, to express the circuits which the *Sun* completes as if in the waves of the celestial sea through the twelve signs and as many months; while it performs its motion, it is the cause of the production of all things that are in the *World*. <margin>Intercalary days.</margin>
For the signs or Months are aptly indicated by circles. Because, however, five days are missing from the Solar year to reach 360, they wished to signify these by five principal circles, over which as many Spirits preside. The mythology according to the mind of Plutarch <note>Plutarch (c. 46 – 119 AD) was a Greek philosopher whose work "On Isis and Osiris" is a primary source for Egyptian myth.</note> is as follows: They say that Rhea, having secretly lain with Saturn, was cursed by the Sun—who had detected the crime—so that she should give birth neither in a Month nor in a year. But Mercury, captured by love for the Goddess, lay with her, and afterwards, playing at dice with the Moon, won and took away the seventieth part of each day; he added these to the 360 days of the year. These five days are now called *Misi* by the Egyptians and *Epagomenae* <note>original: ἐπαγομένας; "added days"</note> by the Greeks, or are celebrated as the birthday festivals of the Gods. On the first of these days was born Osiris, the Lord of all things; on the second day Arueris was born, whom some call Apollo and others the elder Horus; on the third day Typhon <note>The Greek name for Set, the god of chaos.</note> broke through, not at his proper time or place, but bursting out through a wound in the side; on the fourth Isis was born in the marshes; on the fifth Nephthys, whom they also name the End, and Venus, and Victory. We, however, have restored these five minor deities from hieroglyphic doctrine in such a way that we understand the first day to be dedicated to Hermanubis, the second to Anubis, the third to Isis, the fourth to Horus, and the fifth to Osiris, as the true guardians of Egypt, whom the figure expressed here denotes. For Hermanubis, or the Ibis-formed Hermes, is expressed by an Ibis-shaped statue; Anubis by a *Cynocephalus* <note>original: κυνοκέφαλον; "dog-headed"</note> or canine face; Isis by a female face with her veil; Horus by a boyish face; and finally Osiris by a leonine and maned countenance. They hold feathers in their hands to hint at the hidden motion of their activity. The circles on the heads of the first, second, and fourth indicate divine force and power over the World. The eyed Phallus placed upon the head of Isis in the middle indicates the multitude of seminal abundance, over which Isis stands as the passive principle of things. Finally, the fifth figure of Osiris carries a serpent-bearing globe on his head, to show that he is the active principle of worldly life.

And these are the moderators of the year, and the tutors and preservers of all things born in the lower World throughout the course of the entire year. Yet, because the happiness of lower things indicated by the said five guardian Spirits has opposing powers, by whose malice the things of nature could be variously disturbed; hence, aptly from the side, the guardian Spirits are averters of evil (as one of the small figures first pierces a Hippopotamus with a spear, and another a Crocodile, because the Typhonic Hippopotamus and Crocodile oppose things proceeding rightly and tending toward their end; which, however, the spirit of Horus and Osiris finally destroys and scatters). These things harmonize beautifully indeed with those which Plutarch recites in his book on Osiris and Isis at Hermopolis: namely, that an image of Typhon was shown: *“Typhon was an ass, and the ass is a symbol of slowness and ignorance. Upon the head of the ass was placed the hippopotamus, which is a symbol of impudence. Holding also the rod, which those in the Serpent festivals have, or indicating Typhon, receive the force and principle...”* <note>original Greek: Τύφων ἦν ὄνος...; Kircher translates the Greek into Latin in the surrounding text, identifying the animals as symbols of vice.</note>

See in this figure the Divinity of <gloss>Isis</gloss> <note>original: "Isæacæ"</note> holding a serpent in the left hand, while with the right hurling a javelin at a hippopotamus; for Osiris is the life of things, and by the power of his rays—as if by certain struck javelins—he easily overcomes that Typhonian <note>original: "Beboniam," referring to Bebon or Babys, a name for Typhon</note> force; and he kills that which is adverse to the end of natural things, against whom Mophta shows himself a diligent antagonist. This is indicated by the <gloss>Egyptian</gloss> statue of <margin>The meaning of the Egyptian form of Mophta.</margin> Mophta, equipped with a <term>cucuphomorphous staff</term> <note>A staff topped with the head of a hoopoe (cucupha), symbolizing alertness or spiritual protection</note> following him from behind and breaking his force. For they called all evil and harmful things, which have a certain repugnance to nature, the effects and works of Typhon; which the Sun, while he destroys them, simultaneously restores to a proper temperament within the World of <gloss>Isis</gloss>. Furthermore, by the dogs lying at the sides of the wavy serpent, the guardianship of the approach and retreat of the Sun is indicated; or as Plutarch wishes, the increase of the Nile, which the "celestial dogs" <note>The star Sirius, the Dog Star</note> move and promote by their rising. But that these things are so, Clement of Alexandria <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> demonstrates with clear words in the 5th book of the *Stromata* in these words: *There are those who wish the Tropics to be signified by the dogs, who guard and, like gatekeepers, observe the approach of the Sun to the South and the North.*

<margin>What the Divinities assigned to the Zodiac indicate.</margin>
These things having been explained, let us now set forth the offices of the individual Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note> described in the Zodiac. By Anubis, therefore, or the dog-headed Mercury, they understood nothing other than the guardian of the World's heat. By Canopus, the active power of the moist nature in the subterranean realms. By Ichton, the disposition of moisture for perfecting the generation of things. By Amun, the fertilizing power of heat. By Apis, the ripening power of fruits and the harvest. <margin>The effects which the Gods assigned to the Zodiac perform in the World.</margin> By the Twins, Hercules and Apollo, the heating power of the Sun. By Ibis, the rising of Sothis <note>Sirius</note>, the precursor of the Nilotic inundation. By Momphra, the disposing power of the Nilotic increase. By Isis, the abundance of the grain to follow. By Omphrad, the sowing of the seed and the equal temperament of the earth. By Typhon, the final drying out of the earth and the shutting up of the beneficial moisture into subterranean passages. Finally, by Nephthys, the vindication of moisture from all destruction. To these correspond just as many "Greater Gods" of the nations, whom you may contemplate as shown in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 251. The Hebrews and Arabs also, imitating the Egyptians, divide their Zodiac into twelve similar protections of Angels; since we have shown their names in the Kabbalah of the Hebrews and Saracens, we have thought it superfluous to repeat them here to the nausea of the reader.

### CHAPTER III.
*Concerning the Characters of the signs, and their origin.*
<margin>Why and in what manner the Egyptians place Capricorn as the first sign.</margin>
Almost all astronomers begin the order of the signs from Aries; which the Egyptians also do: whence someone might perhaps wonder why we have attributed the first sign or "twelfth-part" to Capricorn or Anubis. I answer, that we can consider the order of the signs in this place in two ways.

### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS.

<margin>The origin of the signs and characters of the 12 signs of the Zodiac.</margin>
The signs were considered either astronomically or mystically. Those considering them astronomically took their beginning from that point of the spring season which makes the days equal to the nights <note>The Vernal Equinox</note>; this is observed by astronomers even to this day. But those considering them mystically—that is, insofar as it concerns the administration of the worldly economy by Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note> and Gods—took the order of the signs and Gods from the point of the winter solstice. They called this the "ascent of the Gods," fearing that if they began the arrangement of the houses of the Spirits from the spring equinox, the order of the ascending Gods would be disturbed. And this is the reason why we, the initiates of the Egyptians, have preserved this order. Having explained these things, let us now see what the characters of the signs mean and from where they drew their origin.

Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth, credited with inventing writing and magic.</note>, after he had assigned his own Spirits to each of the twelve parts of the Zodiac, found it exceedingly laborious to always place hieroglyphic images in astronomical work whenever he wished to denote a sign. Therefore, he substituted certain abbreviations taken from the images themselves in place of the full figures; these have preserved the custom from that time until this day through a certain continuous succession and tradition. But let us explain each one, making a beginning with Aries, after the manner of the astronomers.

<margin>I Sign</margin>
The first sign in the astronomical manner is Aries <note>The Ram</note>, called in Egyptian <term>Σεεν</term> <note>original: "Seen"</note>, or Amun; it was depicted under the figure of a man conspicuous for having the horns of a ram. But in the shorthand business of astronomical calculation, so that they would not always be forced to write the entire image, astronomers placed only the two horns of the Ram in this manner: <image-desc>A woodcut image of a ram's head, facing left, with prominent curved horns.</image-desc> to which corresponds the symbol continued by later astronomers even into these times, which follows: ♈.

<margin>II Sign</margin>
The second sign is Taurus <note>The Bull</note>, which the Egyptians call <term>Απις</term> <note>original: "Apis"</note>, Apin, a most great Deity. It was exhibited under the form of an Ox, as is still in use today. Therefore, lest they always be forced to paint a whole ox whenever mention of this sign was made, they placed only the head of the Ox with its horns, as follows: <image-desc>A woodcut image of a bull's head, facing left, with large horns.</image-desc> to which corresponds the modern character of Taurus: ♉.

<margin>III Sign</margin>
The third sign holds the Gemini <note>The Twins</note>, whom the Egyptians call Hercules and Apollo, or Helitomenon and Harpocrates. There were two hieroglyphic statues of each, joining their hands to one another. Lest they be forced to paint these when mention of this sign was made, they found this abridged character in place of the statues: <image-desc>A woodcut image depicting two human figures, possibly embracing or holding hands, representing Gemini.</image-desc> by which the said Twins were expressed, and which astronomers use to this day, as follows: ♊.

<margin>IV Sign</margin>
The fourth sign is dedicated to Cancer <note>The Crab</note>, and to the Egyptians, to Hermanubis Ibimorphos <note>A composite deity combining Hermes/Anubis with the form of an Ibis</note>. Because the Sun is retrograde <note>moving backward</note> at the beginning of this sign, and the Ibis-shaped Deity presides over the same sign, they wrote a tail from the Crab and a head from the Ibis, from the positioning of which emanated the character...

composed of the head of an Ibis and the tail of a Crab; later generations, ignorant of the reasoning behind this, recorded it under this figure, which is not unlike an Egyptian hieroglyphic.

<margin>V. The Sign Leo ♌</margin>
<image-desc>A square woodcut depicting a lion's head in profile, facing left.</image-desc>
The fifth sign contains the Lion, which is called *Momphra* by the Egyptians. So that they would not always be forced to paint a whole Lion whenever it was mentioned, they painted a part instead of the whole—that is, the tail—as a symbol of Leonine strength in this manner <note>The author is explaining the origin of the ♌ symbol as a simplified lion's tail</note>, as they are accustomed to using the name.

<margin>VI. The Sign Virgo ♍</margin>
The sixth sign is the Virgin, whom the Egyptians name <insert>Isis</insert>, the discoverer of grain; they used to depict her hieroglyphically in the form of a Virgin made conspicuous by a triple ear of grain. Therefore, lest they be forced to paint this image every time she was mentioned, they formed three ears of grain bound by a tie, and the character of the Virgin emerged as follows:
<image-desc>A square woodcut depicting a swan or goose-like bird, facing left.</image-desc>
it is dedicated; whom the Egyptians call Isis the [grain-bringer]; whence also they [place] her under the Virgin.
<image-desc>A square woodcut depicting three stalks of wheat tied together at the bottom.</image-desc>
Later generations, not grasping the reasoning for this, placed this character in the place of the three ears of grain, which nevertheless does not deviate much from the ancient character. Moreover, they assigned three ears of grain because in Egypt the harvest was performed three times a year, on account of the supreme abundance of the earth, which she herself represented.

<margin>VII. The Sign Libra ♎</margin>
The seventh sign, the Scales, is attributed by the Egyptians to the Deity *Ompha* <note>Likely a reference to a localized or Hellenized name for an Egyptian deity associated with justice or measurement</note>, by whom the force of moisture was reduced to a temperate state and composed after an excessive inundation, as witnessed by Firmicus <note>Julius Firmicus Maternus, a 4th-century Christian writer and astrologer</note> and the Scholiast of Ptolemy’s *Tetrabiblos*; since the balance of a scale was the hieroglyphic for this, in place of the image of Ompha (which represented a man holding a measuring rod in his hands), they placed that same rod in this manner. Later generations, however, formed the Scales in this manner in place of it.
<image-desc>A square woodcut depicting a balance scale.</image-desc>

<margin>VIII. The Sign Scorpio ♏</margin>
The eighth sign, the Scorpion, the ancient Egyptians attributed to the Genius <term>Genius: a guardian spirit or presiding nature</term> of a stinging nature; since its symbol was the Scorpion—inasmuch as it possesses a certain poisonous and burning faculty, not unlike the operations of Typhon <note>Typhon was associated by the Egyptians with Set, the god of chaos and storms</note>—they placed the hieroglyphic character of that same Scorpion as follows. # CHAPTER IV. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>What is implied by the character of *Jesus*?</margin>

&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp; ♉ Taurus, the head of a *Bull* <note>original: "Babulum," likely a variant of bubulum</note>. ♊ Gemini, two small bodies with arms and legs entwined. ♋ Cancer, a distorted figure of a crayfish. ♌ Leo, the tail of a Lion. ♍ Virgo, the wing of a Virgin. ♎ Libra, the beam or scale with the tongue <note>the needle of a balance</note>, which the *Ancients* used to call the "moment"; hence the "momentary scale." ♏ Scorpio, needs no explanation. ♐ Sagittarius, likewise needs no explanation. ♑ Capricorn, is the coiled end of a fish's tail, into which that constellation tapers, which the Poets call *double-natured* <note>original Greek: "Διζωλο" (dizōlo)</note> in the figure of Triton. ♒ Aquarius, the pouring of water. ♓ Pisces, two fish facing away with their backs joined by bonds which the Greek Masters call *com* <note>original Greek: "κωμ"</note>. These twelve are, however, nothing other than hieroglyphic characters, explaining the effects of the twelve Spirits <note>Geniorum</note> assigned to these regions, and they are found everywhere among the hieroglyphic descriptions of the Egyptians, as will be demonstrated in the third Volume.

### CHAPTER IV.
->Concerning the origin, names, duties, and characters of the Seven Planets.<-

<margin>Manilius.</margin>
> Manilius sings truly and wisely in the first book of the *Astronomicon*:
> "Teachable ingenuity has conquered all things by trying,

<margin>Hermes was the first observer of the motion of the planets.</margin>
Our Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note> was the first among mortals who, after embracing the twelve-fold system of the Zodiac and seeing that some stars were not fixed, but moved to and fro in a wandering course through the spacious paths of the heavens, applied his burning mind to exploring the motions and the laws of those motions, so as to understand such an exotic thing. He discovered that seven stars in particular, out of the entire army of stars, were endowed with this wandering nature; yet with this condition, that all of them, following the slanted path of the Zodiac, completed their course only within a certain and defined period of years; some indeed faster, some slower; some treading the path of the Zodiac more straightly and precisely, some more irregularly. And first, indeed, he noted the Sun, with its constant and non-returning step...

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IV.

<page-num>169</page-num>

<header>CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IV.</header>

He observed with the greatest zeal and the experience of many years that the Sun held the middle line of the Zodiac; but that the Moon and the other five stars <note>The five planets known to the ancients: Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note> did not, but rather wandered back and forth across a breadth of six degrees. That this is the case is expressly testified by the Scholiast <note>An ancient commentator or annotator of classical texts.</note> on Hyginus, whoever he may have been. *Mercury,* he says, *was the first of mortals to show the obliquity of the Zodiac, and that the courses of the planets are completed beneath it.* Indeed, Trismegistus himself in the *Pimander* <note>The *Poimandres*, the first and most famous text in the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greek writings attributed to the legendary Hermes Trismegistus.</note> testifies to this in the following words:

AESCULAPIUS: *In what manner then, Trismegistus, are those things which are in the World changed along with those things which are moved? For you were saying that the wandering spheres <note>The planets.</note> are moved by the fixed sphere <note>The 'aplane' or the outermost sphere of the fixed stars.</note>.*

TRISMEGISTUS: *It is not motion itself, O Aesculapius, but a counter-resistance; for they do not proceed in the same manner, but in a contrary way. Indeed, this opposition creates a stable reverberation of motion.*

## CHAPTER IV.

<margin>The 3rd & 4th offices in the Worldly Economy.</margin>
...was shown at length. Furthermore, when he <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note> observed two other wanderers <note>planets</note> above the Sun, the perpetual and inseparable companions of the Sun; he distinguished the nearer one by the name of Mercury, as if he were the Sun's messenger and coadjutor—from which later emerged the fable of Mercury as the Messenger of the Gods. The following most brilliant star he called by the name of Aphrodite or Venus; for she completes and perfects with her fertility and grace that which the Sun, Moon, and Mercury had rightly arranged in the economy of the World. For this reason, even to this day, the office of fertility, grace, and love is attributed to her.

<margin>3rd & 4th offices.</margin>
<margin>5th office.</margin>
But because Venus, abounding in moisture, occasionally causes a certain imbalance in the sublunary world along with the Moon, he therefore established Mars—whom he knew as *Typhon* <note>original Greek: Τυφῶν</note>, of a malignant and perverse nature—and above him he placed Jupiter, whom he also called *Typhon* in the Egyptian manner <note>The author likely refers to a "good" aspect or a specific Egyptian deity name here</note>, endowed with all excellent faculties. By his beneficent and powerful virtue, Jupiter restrains the malignant nature of Typhon within his duty, lest by his wasting force he should turn everything upside down. Finally, over these he placed Saturn, whom he also called Rephan in the Egyptian tongue; his office is to temper the excessive heat in the World caused by Mars and the Sun with his own coldness, just as Mars tempers the humidity caused by the Moon and Venus. Since we have described their offices and virtues at length both in the preceding sections and in the work on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, we refer the reader there.

It remains to be explained by what apt hieroglyphic characters Hermes exhibited the offices and powers of each. Since he discovered that the entire lower material world was administered by the virtue of these seven principal Spirits <note>Genii</note>; he devised characters appropriated to the properties of each, five of which are composed chiefly from "kyriological" <note>proper or literal</note> hieroglyphics, namely from ☿ ♀ ♂ ♃ ♄. The first of these is the hieroglyphic character of the Sun <note>☉</note>; the second of the Moon <note>☽</note>; the third is the horn of the Ram <note>Aries</note>, the principle of heat, fertility, and the planetary course; the fourth is that of the bolt <note>or "fagina," perhaps referring to a spear or arrow</note>, signifying heat and dryness; and the fifth is the cross, the symbol of the elemental World. From these, he expressed the virtues of the individual planets with such ingenuity that by seeing the character of any one of them, one would immediately come to the knowledge of its virtue. But let us show the construction.

<margin>What the characters of the planets denote.</margin>
And first, I assume from Clement of Alexandria and Eusebius that the Egyptians had a twofold method of representing their symbolic mysteries: one through the virtues of animals, herbs, and plants; the other through Geometric characters, aptly representing the intended mysteries. Thus, in the first method, they represented the Sun and Moon by the Beetle <note>Scarab</note> and the Ibis; while in the latter method, they represented them by the simple characters of the Sun and Moon. Likewise, they represented the four Elements or principles of things by four animals which had qualities not unlike the Elements in the first method; but in the latter, they represented them by the cross †: a fact which Clement of Alexandria asserts in these words—

<image-desc>Symbol for Jupiter: The standard astrological symbol for Jupiter (♃), which resembles a crescent moon atop a cross.</image-desc>
**Jupiter** agrees in moisture with the Moon (☽) and the Earth (♁) <note>Kircher uses the globus cruciger symbol for Earth/Elements</note> by which he influences the Elements; hence he is composed of the Earth (♁) and the Cross (†).

**Mercury** agrees with all things (☿ ☽ ♁ †); hence he is composed of all: the Lunar, the Solar, and the Elemental.

"For by performing an anatomy of it, and dividing it into its parts, it will be clearly seen that it consists primarily of a perfect circle, the hieroglyph of the Sun; next, it consists of a semicircle, the mark of the Moon; of a cross, the symbol of the four Elements; and of the sign of Aries. The other four hieroglyphs thereafter—namely those of Saturn, Jupiter, Mars, and Venus—are formed either from the character of the Sun or that of the Moon, with the addition of the Cross, or part of it, or the mark of Aries. The hieroglyph of Saturn is composed of that of the Moon together with that of the Elements; that of Jupiter consists of the same, and is the same, except that it holds a different position; the character of Mars is composed of that of the Sun and that of Aries joined together by the straight line of the cross; the mark of Venus is formed from that of the Sun and the Elements; and finally, the hieroglyph of Aries is formed of two semicircles connected at a common point."

You see, therefore, how aptly that great <term>Trismegistus</term> <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the invention of writing and magic</note>, or the Egyptians taught by him, expressed the virtues of the planets through symbolic signs. Truly, see a copious treatise on these in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, folio 374, and in the *Alchemy of the Egyptians*. Moreover, with how much zeal the Ancient Egyptians were devoted to the worship of the planets, and how they ascribed all things to their influences, the Arabic historian Schiagia explains quite beautifully when he describes Egypt in these words:

->Regarding the mention of the Pharaohs of Egypt<-

<margin>Schiagia the Arab.</margin>
"And Egypt is in the region of wonders and the mine of rarities. Egypt is the garden of God the Exalted on His earth. The observer at this time still thinks that it remains in its original state, as if its cities were close together on the two banks like a single city. The gardens behind the cities are continuous, as if they were a single garden, and the farms are behind the gardens. Work could be done from Alexandria to Aswan in a single day, and the value of the gardens was handed from one to another. The people of Egypt were people of a great kingdom in ages past and bygone times. They were a succession of nations, including Copts, Greeks, and Amalekites <note>original: "علميتي" (Amalekites), a traditional Arabic identification for certain ancient peoples</note>. They used to worship idols and they turned away..."

And if they intended to survive the Flood, when they passed through it, they learned from the sciences specifically the knowledge of talismans <note>original Arabic: *al-talismat*</note>, sorcery, and alchemy. ### On the Excellence of Egypt and the Study of Astrology.

<margin>Monf, which is Memphis.</margin>
Egypt was a climate of miraculous things, a mine of wonders, the garden of the High God on earth; no one who considers it now believes it exists in its original state. Although it is one city, it appears as if many are clinging together along their shore. Gardens were seen behind the cities, merging into one another as if one; then fields were seen behind the gardens. Furthermore, the journey was a day's travel from Alexandria to Aswan, and the gardens extended their excellence to one another. The Egyptians were formerly masters of a very great kingdom, and though mixed from various nations—Copts, Greeks, and Amalekites—they likewise worshipped idols. After the flood, they were instructed in incantations, deceptive magic, and alchemy; their images [talismans] are easily found with a compass <note>or "needle"</note> according to the influence of the stars. Furthermore, the city of Monf <note>Memphis</note>, two miles distant from ancient Pheslad <note>Fustat/Old Cairo</note>, was the seat of the kingdom. Their priests excelled other priests in learning and wisdom, just as the Greeks say of them. When they applied themselves to the stars with their art of foretelling, they believed the stars infused them with knowledge, announced future events, and taught them the art of natural things and divination; just as in truth they taught them more abstract and hidden sciences. From these, they learned the most celebrated arts of divination and the most excellent laws; they made speaking statues, painted moving images, constructed buildings higher than all other buildings, and carved their sciences upon the hardest stones. Egypt consisted of 85 provinces, of which 45 were in Saida <note>Lower Egypt</note> and 40 in Upper Egypt. In each province, there was a leader of the priests or magi. However, among them, those who observed the seven moving planets for 7 years were called "the Ignorant"; but he who observed each one for 7 years (totaling 49 years), they called the **Infusing** or **Dripping** One <note>Latin: *Stillans* or *Infundens*</note>.
<margin>Dripping or Infusing is the same as Prophet.</margin>
And for the sake of honor, he sits as a King on high, and governed nothing except what belongs to the King. The priests, having entered with the craftsmen, stand before the **Dripping One**, and each of the priests, separated by the planet he serves, does not turn to his equal; he is called the servant of that planet, namely: Servant of the Moon, servant of Mercury, servant of Venus, servant of the Sun, servant of Mars, servant of Jupiter, and servant of Saturn. The **Dripping One** then questions each of them, saying: *In what state is your planet found?* and he answers: in such a sign, in such a degree, in such a minute. Thus he also questions one and then another, who instruct him; and when he has recognized the mansions of the seven planets, he says to the King: it is fitting for the King...

### CHAPTER V.
->Concerning the Spirits, powers, and qualities of the signs of the Zodiac, and how the Egyptians displayed the encompassment of all things through them.<-

<margin>The pyramidal influence from the celestial signs which must be considered.</margin>
The Egyptians, under the instruction of Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, conceived that from the twelve signs of the zodiac <note>original: "dodecamoriis"; the twelve 30-degree divisions of the ecliptic</note>, an equal number of bright and inverted pyramids were drawn down even to the center of the earth. The bases of these pyramids occupied the very length and width of the zodiacal signs, while the vertex rested upon the center of the earth, as I have said. They said that the entire order of nature was contained beneath these; and they displayed these hieroglyphically in the temple of Heliopolis <note>the "City of the Sun" in ancient Egypt</note>, which was constructed in the form of the Zodiac, by means of twelve Obelisks, as was proven in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on pages 171 and 179. Moreover, a presiding Principal Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> governed the influence of each pyramid upon the lower symbols; this Spirit moderated all things subject to the pyramid, and each thing according to the classes of natural objects appropriated to them. Indeed, these effects differed with a notable diversity as often as it happened that the seven *Vharchos* <note>a term used by Kircher for the planetary governors</note> or planets fell into these regions of the zodiacal signs. But because they saw that an entire sign did not always produce one and the same effect, but one at the beginning, another in the middle, and finally another at its end; they placed three other Spirits over each sign, having divided them into three parts. These they called sometimes "Decans," sometimes "Horoscopes," and later the Arabs called them "Faces" <note>astrological terms for 10-degree subdivisions of a sign</note>. Thus, thirty-six Horoscopes were contained within the entire circuit of the Zodiac—the stewards, dispensers, and administrators of all lower nature, whom we have shown above from the writings of Hermes and Iamblichus. And from here proceeded those twelve mystical chains of all things, by which lower things were connected with higher things in a certain wonderful proportion. And these chains, most frequent among hieroglyphic interpretations, were like twelve bonds of nature, by which they connected the lower or material <note>original: "hylaeos"</note> things with the intermediate grades of celestial nature, and these...

<summary>Kircher describes a ritual procession of planetary figures before the King and explains the Egyptian cosmological theory of "astrological pyramids" that connect the Zodiac to the center of the Earth.</summary>
<keywords>Zodiac, Decans, Hermes Trismegistus, Heliopolis, planetary influence, celestial chains, Memphis, astrology</keywords>

->CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS.<-

### CHAPTER V.

<margin>1. The chain of things.</margin>
And they believed these were so aptly joined with the supreme <term>dodecamorion</term> <note>A "dodecamorion" refers to a twelfth-part of the zodiac, or a specific zodiac sign.</note> choir of the **immortal Gods**, that whoever found a single chain corresponding to a certain zodiac sign was considered to have likewise discovered the entire economy of the classes of nature, which are analogous and subject to a specific <term>pyramid</term> <note>Likely referring to the geometric or hierarchical structure of celestial influence.</note> of that sign. Indeed, they believed that this knowledge was bestowed upon the soul by the supreme, **All-Formed Deity** <note>original: "Pantamorpho Numine"</note>—or the providence of all things—joined through love to the wisdom of those below. For, as **Proclus** says in his work **On the Soul and the Demon**, said providence is equally sincere and the decorator of all things; it is unhindered by those who are refined and runs through all things, especially because it is nowhere restrained. In no different a way, the presiding Deities subject to Him fill all things with themselves while remaining free from all things; they mingle with many things in various places and love their own offspring—that is, the series of subject things. For since Love provides for, warms, and contains the things divinely loved, the Gods love the super-celestial Gods; the celestial ones love the celestial spheres committed to them; and the Spirits of the spheres love each of the orders of the material worlds destined for them. But let us hear
<margin>Proclus on the Soul and the Demon.</margin>
the words of Proclus in the cited passage: *Therefore, all the sacred utterances indicate this love of the Lord, binding all things together and attending to all things. If this love truly connects all things, it joins*
<margin>Soul and Demon.</margin>
*us to the prefectures of the **Demons** <note>In this Neoplatonic context, "Demons" (daimones) are intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not evil entities.</note>. Diotius called this the great **Demon**, since it fills the middle everywhere between those things which desire and those which are desired. That which is to be loved claims the first rank for itself; the lover takes the third rank from the beloved; and finally, Love occupies the middle between both, gathering and binding together the desirer and the desired, and filling the inferior with the better.*
<margin>Grades of Demons.</margin>
*Now, among the intelligible and hidden Gods, he unites the intelligible intellect to the first and secret beauty through a certain life better than intelligence. Therefore, the **Theologian of the Greeks** <note>Likely referring to Orpheus or Plato.</note> calls that love blind. In those things which are outside the intelligible realm, he does not yet illustrate the indissoluble bond for all things perfected by him. For a bond is a certain unity, but one that exists alongside a great many things from the beginning. For this reason, the sacred utterances are accustomed to call the fire of this love the "joiner"; for proceeding from the intelligible intellect, it reconciles all subsequent things to one another and to that intellect. It therefore conciliates all the Gods to intelligible beauty. It joins the **Demons** to the Gods, and us to the Demons and the Gods. It subsists first in the Gods, second in the Demons, and third in souls through a certain process existing from the principles.*
<margin>Office of the Demons.</margin>
*In the Gods, it exists above essence (for every*
<margin>Diversity of Demons.</margin>
*genus of the Gods is of that kind); in the Demons, however, it exists through essence; and finally, in souls,*
<margin>to 12. Diversity of Demons.</margin>
*through the effect of illumination. And this triple order seems to be the triple power of the intellect.*
<margin>Grades of Demons.</margin>

Hence the **Egyptians**, weighing more exactly this so admirable
<margin>The principle of the amatory art.</margin>
marriage of the lower things with the higher, gradually arrived at a knowledge of the "philtrice" or the amatory art <note>The art of attraction or "sympathetic magic" based on cosmic love.</note>, which they described accurately under the hidden notes of hieroglyphics, as will be explained in its proper place. And first, they so aptly connected each of the zodiac signs, as well as the regions of the 36 **Horoscopes** <note>Referring to the "decans," or ten-degree divisions of the zodiac.</note>, to the **planetary Deities** who walk the fatal circuit of this circle with anxious step, urging the order of the fates, that they believed they could draw an infallible judgment regarding the events of future things from the disposition of the seven stars compared to the twelve **zodiac signs**. Hence the Birth-
<meta>Catchword: thlia- (completing "Genethliaca" or "Birth-horoscopes")</meta>

# CHAPTER V.

<margin>Astrological vanity.</margin> The <term>Genethliaci</term><note>Casters of birth charts or horoscopes.</note> believed quite superstitiously that one who was born under a certain influence of a <term>dodecamoria</term><note>A twelfth-part or sign of the Zodiac.</note> of the pyramid, with such-and-such a Planet ruling over him, was loved by his Spirit or Spirits as if committed to their faith and care. They believed that all talents, both of nature and of grace, which belonged to that same twelfth-part or ruling planet, were granted to him. If these Spirits were of a malignant nature, differing from the Spirits of the twelfth-parts, the person born would also be allotted a bad character; if they were of a beneficial and sympathetic nature, they asserted the newborn would be similar. Thus, the Egyptians ascribed the outcome of things not so much to the stars as to the Spirits presiding over them. Hence there was such great ardor in these quiet matters, and such great care and anxiety in propitiating them through sacrifices and preparatory ceremonies. This is quite different from what the Astrologers of our own time do, who rashly ascribe the fortune of men to a certain fatal necessity of the stars. But let us return to the subject at hand.

The twelfth-parts were therefore arranged in such a way that things celestial corresponded with things elemental, and these in turn with celestial and Angelic things, and finally all things corresponded with the supreme moderator of all by a certain exact analogy. According to the testimony of Psellus, they called these *Saras*, that is, *chains*, by which the highest things were connected to the lowest, the lowest to the middle, and the middle to the highest in a certain wonderful proportion, according to the twelve Classes of the nature of beings. Among these 
<margin>The Fiery, Watery, Airy, and Earthy Triangles.</margin> were the four Elements: fire, air, water, and earth. They assigned Fire to Aries, Leo, and Sagittarius, which formed the fiery <term>trigon</term><note>A group of three zodiac signs belonging to the same element; a triplicity.</note> in the Zodiac. Earth they assigned to Taurus, Virgo, and Capricorn, which formed the earthly trigon. Air to Gemini, Libra, and Aquarius, which formed the airy trigon; and Water to Cancer, Scorpio, and Pisces, which formed the watery trigon. To these they joined all the remaining orders of beings which in any way agreed with one of these four mentioned Elements. For example: all those species of things—such as stones, metals, flowers, plants, trees, four-legged animals, birds, aquatic creatures, and the human complexion—which by their nature were allotted a dry and hot temperament, they attributed to Aries, likewise a hot and dry sign. From those same most recent Classes, they assigned to the earthy sign (cold and dry) those things which 
<margin>From whence the triplicity of the Zodiac signs had its origin.</margin> expressed the nature and complexion of said sign; and so on for the rest of the airy and watery signs. And from this emerged that partition of the Zodiac into its trigons or triplicities. In like manner, they applied the nature and property of the seven Planets to the said twelve houses. But since we have taught these and similar things copiously and at length in the *Astrological Cabala of the Hebrews*, we refer the reader there; in this place, we only show how those things said according to the mind of the ancient Hebrews correspond to the mind of the Egyptians...

<meta>The text cuts off as the author prepares to compare Hebrew and Egyptian systems.</meta>

Indeed, according to the science of the Egyptians, there are twelve signs, and these dominate all things placed under them, from herbs even unto the animals and creeping things of the earth; and over each individual figure an Angel presides, ruling all things that are under him. Afterward, [the author] describes the signs in a long discourse, assigning the individual things which pertain to its dominion according to innumerable classes of things, in precisely that order which we described in the preceding table. Lest we be forced to transcribe entire books, we shall endeavor hereafter to reduce these into tables, so that we might compensate for the mass of material by a certain compendium. Furthermore, they proceed in a not dissimilar manner in describing the secrets of the seven planets, to each of which they first assign their own <term>Genii</term> <note>Guardian spirits or guiding intelligences associated with celestial bodies.</note>; then, under each, they connect chains of things analogous to the planets, taking the beginning of their discussion from the Sun. ...they would hold; and these they called <term>Decans</term><note>From the Greek 'deka' (ten); these are 10-degree subdivisions of the zodiac signs.</note> or "Faces." ->Concerning the Twelve Houses:<-

<margin>From Sextus Empiricus.</margin>
The Egyptians, not yet content with such a laborious apparatus of astrological science, noted certain wondrous effects which the stars—both fixed and wandering <note>The "wandering stars" are the planets.</note>—produced in certain regions of the sky. For they showed one effect according to the nature of the stars at rising, another at setting, another at the highest point of the heavens <term>Midheaven</term>, another at the point of midnight, and finally others in the intermediate places, both above and below the Horizon. Hence, following the division already established in the Zodiac, they divided the sky by another division into twelve intervals, six of which were above and six below the Horizon; these they called <term>Dodekatemoria</term> <note>original: δωδε (abbreviation for δωδεκατημόρια), meaning "twelfth-parts."</note>, or Bindings, houses, and mansions of the Gods. And in these houses they most diligently explored the position of both the signs of the Zodiac and the planets, as well as their configurations toward one another: oppositions, conjunctions, and aspects—trine, quartile, sextile, and wide <note>Kircher uses technical Latin terms for astrological aspects: trigonos (120°), tetragonos (90°), sexagonos (60°), and platicos (an aspect within a certain range of degrees rather than exact).</note>. And thus at last they would judge concerning lot, fortune, nature, and misfortune—in short, concerning the state of the whole of human life. They predicted storms, sterility, livestock health, the quality of the harvest, and similar matters used by Astrologers to this very day. And lest they should seem to attribute these things solely to the said regions of the sky and the virtues of the stars, they furthermore assigned to each house its own presiding, dominating, building, destroying, benign, and malefic Spirits <note>original: Genios</note>; to whose power and will all things were committed by the supreme ruler of the universe. Hence, just as they greatly feared the unlucky influences of opposing forces, so they desired with the greatest vows the beneficial influx of sympathetic Divinities. Having inspected and examined a particular theme <note>A "theme" here refers to a birth chart or horoscope.</note>, they strove to appease them with previous sacrifices and appropriate ceremonies (as will be said in its proper place and time): the malefic ones, indeed, so that they might not bring harm, and the benign ones, to render them propitious and draw them into their own fate. But let us confirm all that has been said so far with the words of <term>Sextus Empiricus</term> <note>A skeptical philosopher (c. 160–210 AD) who recorded many details of ancient sciences while critiquing them.</note>, who describes these things quite graphically. *First*, therefore:

<summary>This page describes Egyptian astrological archetypes (the negligent, the proud, and the lustful) and introduces the concept of the twelve astrological houses. It explains how the Egyptians used these divisions and planetary aspects to predict human fate and natural events through the mediation of spirits.</summary>

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER V.

<page-num>187</page-num>

It is established by them that earthly things possess a harmony—which they call *sympathy* <note>original: "fympathiam"</note>—with the celestial bodies, and that through the influences of the latter, the former are always renewed.

*The mind and thought of earthly men are such as the Father of men and Gods.*
*He wills the day to be such as the mind of the Father of men and Gods.* <note>This is a Latin translation of a famous passage from Homer's Odyssey regarding the influence of the heavens on human disposition.</note>

<margin>Concerning the 12 houses of the heavens.</margin>
The Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers.</note> have looked quite curiously upon that which surrounds us; they say indeed that seven stars <note>The five visible planets plus the Sun and Moon.</note> hold the account of the active causes for each of those things which occur in life, but that the parts of the Zodiac assist them. And we have received by tradition that they divide the Zodiac circle into twelve animals <note>The signs of the Zodiac.</note>; each "animal" consists of thirty parts (for on this point let us agree with them for the present); and each single part is divided into sixty minutes. (For so they call those things which are smallest and indivisible.) Of the animals, which they call *Casus*—that is, "little animals"—some they call masculine, others feminine; and some are "double-bodied" <note>Mutable signs like Gemini or Pisces.</note>; others truly are not; some are solid <note>Fixed signs.</note>, and others are *Corua*—that is, "changing" <note>Cardinal signs.</note>. And they call them masculine and feminine because they have a nature that assists in the generation of males and females; for Aries is a masculine sign, but Taurus is feminine; Gemini is masculine, and the rest follow in turn by a similar analogy, some being masculine and others feminine. Moved by these things, as I believe, the Pythagoreans call the number one "male," the number two "female," the number three "male" again, and the rest of the even and odd numbers by exactly the same proportion and analogy. Some, however, dividing each animal into twelve parts, use almost the same reasoning: for example, in Aries they call the first twelfth part both Aries and masculine; the second part Taurus and feminine; the third Gemini and masculine. They say the double-bodied animals are Gemini, Sagittarius, Virgo, and Pisces; the others are not double-bodied. And the "tropical" or changing signs are those in which the Sun, when it resides there, transforms and causes the turnings of the surrounding air; such signs are Aries and its opposite Libra, as well as Capricorn and Cancer: for in Aries the spring turning occurs, in Capricorn the winter, in Cancer the summer, and in Libra the autumnal. They consider Taurus and its opposite Scorpio, Leo, and Aquarius to be solid. Furthermore, of all these, those signs which hold dominion in each birth—which the <term>astrologers</term> <note>original: "ἀστρολόγοι"</note> speak of and from which they chiefly make their predictions—are said to be four in number, which they call by the common name of <margin>The Center of the houses.</margin> "centers." Specifically, one is the Horoscope <note>The Ascendant.</note>, another is the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "Μεσοράνημα"</note>, that is, <margin>Middle of the sky</margin> the middle of the sky; another is the West <note>The Descendant.</note>, and another is the <term>underground</term> <note>original: "ὑπόγειον"</note>, that is, the bottom of the sky, which is itself also a "middle" of the sky. And <margin>What the Horoscope is.</margin> the Horoscope is that which happens to be rising at the time the birth was completed. The Midheaven is the fourth sign from that one; the Subterranean is the sixth <note>The author likely means the fourth sign from the West, or the seventh from the Ascendant; traditionally the Imum Coeli is the 4th house.</note> opposite the Midheaven, which is diametrically opposed to the Midheaven—as (to make it clear by example) if Cancer is the Horoscope, Aries is in the Midheaven, Capricorn is setting, and Libra is under the earth. Furthermore, the animal or sign preceding each of these centers they call a <term>declination</term> <note>original: "ἀπόκλιμα" (Apoklima)</note>; but that which follows, they call a <term>relation</term> <note>original: "ἐπιναφορα" (Epanaphora)</note>; and this is indeed the <margin>Apoklima & Epanaphora</margin><margin>What animal.</note> following animal.

# CHAPTER V. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

That celestial animal or sign which is in the Ascendant <note>original: "Horoscopo"; the point of the zodiac rising on the eastern horizon</note>, if it be in the open, is called the sign of the Evil Spirit <note>original: "mali Daemonis"</note>; that which follows afterward (following that which is in the Midheaven) is said to be of the Good Spirit. That which precedes the Midheaven, they call the *Descent* <note>original: "κατωφερείας" (katophoreias)</note>, that is, the lower gate; and the *Height* <note>original: "υψηλείας" (hypsileias)</note>, that is, the *unique power* and God. That which comes to the Setting <note>the West</note> is the idle animal, or the sign and beginning of death. That which is after the Setting, and is not open, is called *Panam* <note>likely a corruption of a Greek or Coptic astrological term</note> and Ill Fortune; this indeed is situated diametrically opposite to the Evil Spirit. That which comes under the earth is Good Fortune, which is placed diametrically opposite to the Good Spirit. That which recedes from the point opposite the Midheaven is called the decline of the Evil Spirit. That which follows the Ascendant is called Idle, which again is diametrically opposed to the Idle sign.

Or to put it more briefly: regarding the Ascendant, the decline is called the Evil Spirit, while the *Succession* <note>original: "Epanaphora"; a house following a corner/angle</note> is called Idle. In the same way, the decline of the Midheaven is called God, and its Succession is the Good Spirit. Similarly, for the point opposite the Midheaven <note>the Imum Coeli or bottom of the sky</note>, the decline is called Goddess, and the Succession is Good Fortune. Likewise, the decline of the West is Ill Fortune, and its Succession is Idle. They believe these matters must be examined not lightly or as if doing something else: for they judge that the stars do not have the same power for doing evil or otherwise if they are situated in the centers <note>the angles</note>, or in the successions, or in the declines, but are in some places more effective, and in others truly less effective.

There were also certain Chaldeans <note>ancient Babylonian astrologers/astronomers</note> who attributed each part of the human body to a specific sign, as having a harmony with it and being affected by it. For they name Aries the head, Taurus the neck, Gemini the shoulders, Cancer the breast, Leo the sides, Virgo the hips, Libra the flanks, Scorpio the private parts and the womb, Sagittarius the thighs, Capricorn the knees, Aquarius the shins, and Pisces the feet, as is evident in the figure.

->[Image: A circular diagram of the zodiac wheel. In the center stands a nude human figure with arms outstretched. Twelve radiating segments contain the zodiac symbols. Lines connect the figure's body parts to their corresponding signs: Aries to the head, Taurus to the neck, Gemini to the shoulders, and so on, illustrating the "Zodiacal Man" or *melothesia*.]<-

And this is done, again, not as they themselves think, without reason; but because if any malefic star should be in one of these signs at birth, it causes a mutilation of that part which bears the same name. And these things have been shown in summary regarding the nature of those things in the Zodiac circle. It would not be absurd to speak next of their...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient astronomical and astrological methods, specifically focusing on the division of the Zodiac and the Chaldean method of casting horoscopes.</meta>

<page-num>189</page-num>
-># CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS.<-
->## CHAPTER V.<-

...I must say something regarding the division. For since there was no certain method of observation and inspection—because they did not contemplate the signs by their own boundaries, but by the perspective of the viewers—they observed with difficulty. Hence, they sought to divide the whole circle into twelve parts. Showing the way and the method, they say that when the Ancients had observed a certain bright star among those in the Zodiac circle, they then filled a perforated water-clock <note>original: "amphoram," here referring to a clepsydra or water-clock used for measuring time</note> with water and let it flow into another vessel placed beneath it until that same star rose again, concluding that the revolution of the circle went from the same sign back to the same sign. Again, they took a twelfth part of what had flowed out and considered how much time this took to flow: for they said the twelfth part of the circle sufficed for that amount, and it held the same ratio as a part to the whole circle, just as the part of the water which flowed out held to the total water. From this relation of the twelfth part, I say, they marked the final boundary by some notable star which was seen at that time, or by one of those which rose at the same time further North or further South. They did this same thing for the other twelve parts; such is the way and method by which they divide the Zodiac circle into so many parts.

<margin>By what method the Ancients measured the revolution of the Zodiac.</margin>

By analogy and proportion, that method seems to agree with the one by which the Chaldeans <note>Ancient Babylonian astronomers and astrologers famous for their celestial observations</note> observed the Horoscope <note>term: Horoscope (from Greek *horoskopos*), meaning the "hour-watcher" or the sign rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth</note> of each birth from the beginning. For he says that at night, the Chaldean would sit on some high promontory watching the stars; another sat by the woman in labor until she had given birth. As soon as she had given birth, he signaled this to the Master who was on the promontory; and he, when he heard it, observed the sign which was then rising as the Horoscope. Sometimes, however, he attended to the Horoscopes and the movements of the Sun. But these things concern the signs.

<margin>How the Chaldeans observed the Horoscope.</margin>

Regarding the stars, they say some are beneficent, others truly malevolent, and others common. For instance, the stars of Jupiter and Venus are beneficent, while those of Saturn <insert>and Mars</insert> <note>The Latin text omits Mars here, but the context of "maleficas" usually includes both Saturn and Mars in classical astrology</note> are malevolent; Mercury is common, since with the beneficent it is beneficent, and with the malevolent it is malevolent. Others, however, believe these same stars are sometimes beneficent and sometimes malevolent depending on different conditions. For regardless of the sign, or regardless of the aspects and figures of other stars toward them, a malevolent star is not entirely malevolent, nor a beneficent one entirely beneficent.

<margin>Some stars are beneficent, others malevolent, others common.</margin>

Furthermore, the Sun and Moon seem to preside over the seven stars <note>The seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn</note>, while the remaining five have less power over the events that are produced. They liken the Sun to a King and the right eye; the Moon to a Queen and the left eye. The five stars they liken to officers and attendants, and the other fixed stars to the rest of the people. And of the five, they say Saturn, Jupiter, and Mercury agree with and bring aid to the Sun; these they also call "diurnal" <note>belonging to the day</note> because the Sun, whom they assist, rules over those things born during the day. They say these same stars have greater power either because they are in their own houses, or in their exaltations <note>term: exaltation (Latin: *elatio*), a specific sign where a planet's influence is most harmoniously strengthened</note>, or terms, or because some are supported by others as if by attendants; or because they affect one another and take up certain figures between themselves, or because they are in the "centers" <note>the cardinal points of an astrological chart</note>.

As they themselves judge, the house of the Sun is Leo; of the Moon, Cancer; of Saturn, Capricorn and Aquarius; of Jupiter, Sagittarius and Pisces; of Mars, Aries and Scorpio; of Venus, Taurus and Libra; of Mercury, Gemini and Virgo. They call the "exaltations" of the stars (and similarly the "depressions" or "falls") those places in which they delight, or in which they have meager power. For they delight in their exaltations, but have meager power in their depressions...

# CHAPTER V. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>The aspects or conjunctions of the planets.</margin>
depressions or abasements. *For example*, the exaltation <note>original: "elatio in altum"; the point where a planet's influence is strongest</note> of the Sun is in *Aries*; specifically and perfectly at its nineteenth part or degree. Its depression, however, is in the sign diametrically opposite to it. *The Moon*, again, has its exaltation in *Taurus*; its depression is that which is situated diametrically opposite. For *Saturn*, it is Libra; for *Jupiter*, Cancer; for *Mars*, Capricorn; for *Venus*, Pisces; and their depressions, as I have said, are those which are opposite by diameter to their exaltations. They also call the "terms" of the *stars* <note>The author uses "stars" to refer to planets generally</note> those portions in each sign in which each star has the most power from one specific degree to another. Regarding these terms, there is no small disagreement among them, even in their tables. They also say that stars are "thronged as if by bodyguards" when they are in the middle of other stars in the succession of signs: as if, in the same sign, one star holds the first parts, another the last, and another the middle; the one in the middle is said to be thronged by bodyguards by those holding the extreme parts.

<margin>The aspects or configurations of the planets.</margin>
They are said to "look at" one another and to agree among themselves when they appear in a triangular or square figure. Stars are shaped into a triangular figure and look at each other when they have a space of three signs cast between them; and square when they have two. It appears that a beneficial star shaped in a triangle with a malevolent one <note>referring to "benefic" and "malefic" planets like Jupiter vs. Saturn</note> bestows a benefit and becomes more beneficial. A *beneficial* star with a beneficial one is only this; and a malevolent with a malevolent likewise. They are said to be "in the centers" when they are seen in any of the cardines <note>the pivot points of a chart</note>, either at the Horoscope <note>the Ascendant or rising sign</note>, or at the Midheaven, or at the Setting, or at that which is situated opposite the Midheaven. But since these things have been set forth by us simply and roughly, it must first be understood that the *Chaldeans*, moved by these things, bring forth their predictions of things to come, which they call *apotelesmata* <note>Greek: "effects" or astrological outcomes</note>. There is a difference among them: for some are simpler, others more accurate. The simpler ones are those from a sign, or from a simple and single star: such as, "this star, when it is in this sign, produces such effects." The more accurate ones are those made through a concurrence, and as they say, through the "tempering together" of many: as if one is in the Horoscope, another in the Midheaven, another in the opposite of the Midheaven, and others are held thus or so, then these things will happen.

And this is the opinion of *Sextus Empiricus* <note>A skeptical philosopher who recorded these systems to critique them</note> regarding the twelve domiciles of heaven; from whom, however, the *Egyptians* differ greatly; so that this may be made clear, it seemed best to begin a little further back.

<margin>The Egyptians divide the sky into 12 mansions.</margin>
The division of the sky into twelve mansions was an invention of the *Egyptians*, as was shown above from various authors; for just as they divided the *Zodiac* into twelve domiciles which they called "citadels," and which the Sun traveled through in its annual course, so also the celestial houses were divided equally, but in this manner: that in the space of one natural day, the Sun with its followers—the Moon, planets, and stars—would travel through each one. For since at any time one of the degrees of the *Zodiac* would hang over the *Horizon*, it followed that the remaining degrees of the signs of the *Zodiac* would also be found in some of the twelve mansions, which must also be said of the planets and stars. Since, moreover, different houses were open to different influences of light and heat, they believed that *Nature*, at the moment of birth, marked a person with various impressions according to the quality of each house; which is indeed the foundation of the entire *Genethliacal* <note>the art of casting birth charts</note> art. *And* first, indeed, the four principal cardines, in...

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS
## CHAPTER V

They considered those points in which a great force and power of celestial influences lay hidden; the Greeks called these *the highest points* <note>original: "ἀκροκέντρα"</note>, while the *Egyptians* <unclear>abundantly</unclear> called them the principal dwellings of the Gods. More recent authors call them cusps or angles. Truly, the remaining intermediate spaces <gloss>the results</gloss> <note>original: "ἀποτέλεσμα"</note>, of which there were eight, they called <gloss>in the middle</gloss>. Of these, four are <gloss>the rising</gloss> <note>original: "ἀνατολὴ"</note>, that is, the fallen or sluggish places; the other four are <gloss>the setting</gloss> <note>original: "δύσις"</note>, that is, the succeeding places. These are called "Ligatures" <note>Latin: *Ligaturæ*; refers to the magical binding or tying of spiritual influences</note> because no reliable judgment can be established unless all the positions of fortune are aptly combined among themselves, and, as it were, bind themselves together and mutually embrace one another. ## SOLOMON’S Conclusion <note>original: "ΣΟΛΟ Confectarium. ΛΩΔ" - Kircher often uses Greek or pseudo-Hebrew framing for his conclusions.</note>

In this figure, you first see a double hemisphere, upper and lower, divided into twelve equal parts, which they called *topoi* <note>Greek: places</note> or mansions. And indeed, at the four pivots <note>the "angles" of a horoscope</note>—the East, the South, the West, and the Bottom of the Sky—they placed four as if they were presiding officers and arbiters of all fortune. In the remaining angles, which they called the *octotopos* <note>the eight places</note> from the number eight, they placed the attendants of the principal Spirits <note>Genii</note>, some beneficial and some malevolent. Furthermore, they assigned certain lots of things pertaining to fortune to individual houses. In this way, they believed that **Mercury** presided over the first house of life, of the bodily constitution, and whatever pertains to the forming of character; in a word, they traced back every single thing that is "Mercurial" in any way across all classes of nature, and which could be recalled by a certain analogy to the goods of fortune, riches, honors, length of life, and the strength and beauty of the body. Likewise, they willed that **Rephan** or **Saturn** preside over the fourth house of the deep, sunken night, along with everything smelling of a Saturnine nature. Over the tenth house, or the Midheaven, they placed **Aphrodite** or **Nephthys** together with **Jupiter**; which they therefore called the house of dignity, honor, and Royal happiness. Finally, they believed that **Typhon** dominated the seventh house, the angle of the West, the house of death. To the other individual "eight-places," they attributed Spirits and natures suitable to them, as is clear from the figure.

The chart shows the positions of the planets and their Egyptian/Greek equivalents: **Typhon** (Set) in the West, **Saturn** in the depths, **Venus** and **Jupiter** at the Midheaven, and **Mercury** at the Ascendant. The houses are numbered I through XII.]<-

### *The application and use of the aforesaid matters in the business of Astrology, and their refutation.*

Since they kept the eyes of the mind continually intent upon the orders of the celestial motions, and noted various influences being led down from the Presiders of the supreme habitation of the heavens, through the intermediate choirs of the planets, into the ultimate seeds of the Elemental World; and since they saw changes emanating daily from the continuous motion of the heavens or the stars; they adapted the Zodiac to the expanse of the planets, and to these the houses and mansions in such a way that they might perceive from the System itself the encounter of qualities and influences, whether friendly or inimical. For if, at the hour of birth, they found happy and beneficial Presiders in the house of good fortune, they pronounced that person happy also from so many conspiring goods; but if they found beneficial ones ruling a certain house along with malevolent ones, they pronounced that such a lot of fortune would affect the person born; finally, if they discovered malevolent ones joined with malevolent ones in any house, they were of the opinion that the one born would be subject to an unjust and unhappy fate. Therefore, with the greatest zeal, they noted the four pivots and explored what relationship the presiding Spirits had toward one another. If they understood an inimical encounter anywhere, they immediately contended to appease the malevolent Spirits with the greatest prayers, sacrifices, and ceremonies so that they might not do harm; and the good ones, so that they might persevere in the favor of an influx of goods. And in this way, not only concerning the fortune of the Person Born, but in those things which [pertain to] sterility and fertili-

Indeed, they imagined they knew above all else that all human happiness and misfortune depended on the will of the Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note>. See more of what we have brought forward concerning these matters in the *Astrological Cabala* <note>original: "Gabala Astrologica"</note> of both the Hebrews and the Saracens. But as to why the Egyptians adorned the houses <note>astrological houses</note> in such an order, and with such meanings and promises, see Ibn Ezra <note>original: "Auenar," referring to the 12th-century scholar Abraham ibn Ezra</note> in his Astrology written in Hebrew; for since all such Egyptian delusions have long since been outlawed by the orthodox Church as the ruin and destruction of souls, I judged it not at all expedient to bring forward here the matter as it is described in more rambling words by Arabic and Hebrew authors.

# CHAPTER VI.
## *Concerning the 48 Constellations, or the Mansions of the Causal Gods.* <note>original: "αἰτιόχων" (aitiochon) – those who contain or hold the causes</note>

It is so ingrained in the human condition that as soon as people behold certain hidden and exotic things, they are snatched away into admiration, and once snatched, they scrutinize the reasons for the latent causes. This happened most especially to the Egyptians. Living as they did under a face of perpetual celestial serenity, while they assiduously contemplated those most orderly armies of the stars with the intentness and sharp edge of their eyes during the harmless vigils of the night, they were driven by a certain amazement. They persuaded themselves that it was impossible for that which was announced by such great portents to be idle, or for that which filled all things in the lower world with its irradiation to be fruitless in its wonderful effects. Hence, after many years of observations, they divided the entire star-bearing heaven into certain
<margin>The division of the starry sky into constellations made by the Ancients.</margin>
classes, which the Egyptians first called the "Mansions of the Gods," and later the Greeks called "Asterisms" or "Iconisms" <note>star-patterns or images</note>. For first, they uniquely worshiped the twelve choirs of the principal Gods enclosed in the Zodiac as the moderators of the Universe, as seen above, since upon their will and disposition all the lots of good or bad fortune in the lower world depended. To these, on both sides in both the Northern and Southern hemispheres, they joined certain subsidiary cohorts of Gods distributed into various offices. In the Northern realm of Typhon <note>the Egyptian god of chaos and storms</note>, they placed certain austere and—to speak with Zoroaster—certain "implacable" powers; but in the Southern realm of Osiris, they placed powers benevolent and highly favoring to the human race, as if set in opposition to the inclemency and austerity of the Northerners. From their technical opposition and perpetual movement, the seeds of the mixture of good and evil things arose. Hence, just as they strove with the greatest zeal to appease the Northerners for the averting of evils, so they tried to draw the Southerners into their protection through sacrifices and ceremonies established with singular industry. All these things were explained at length above in the treatise on the *Hieroglyphic System of the World*, as well as in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 206.

# CHAPTER VI. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>
The 48 constellations invented by the Egyptians.

<margin>
