# CHAPTER VIII. 224 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
...and they force numbers, which are otherwise immutable, to serve their own purposes through a strained and violent composition, whether the numbers will it or not. Oh, what donkey-like crudeness, worthy of nothing but a beating! I have deemed it necessary to refute these things at greater length so that the stupidity and madness of these idle men might be more clearly known. For I know not what "itch" for such seemingly beautiful dogmas of celestial scripture has excited the minds of the unskilled—especially at this time, when the more absurd the inventions are, the more plausible they seem to superstitious minds, being embraced greedily with both arms. I believed that no more effective remedy could be applied to these creeping errors than a demonstrative refutation of such insane dogmas; once their falsehood is suppressed, the truth may finally be restored to its integrity.

---

### CHAPTER VIII.

->On the Sun-dials, or the Shadow-Instruments of the Ancients.<-

<margin>The division of time was also in use among the Ancients.</margin>
If it is true what the School of the Stoics <note>A school of Hellenistic philosophy that emphasized logic and the natural order of the universe.</note> knew, and what I recorded in Book 3, Chapter 2 of *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*, that time is the standard and guardian of things—because it is the indicator and test of truth, and preserves the memory and duration of past deeds for posterity—then surely those men are worthy of no small praise who, binding the laws of time with chains of shadow, attempted by a truly ingenious invention to halt the fleeting years, months, days, and withdrawn hours, making them as present as if they were permanent things. For since time is nothing other than the *measurement of the first moved body* <note>original Greek: μέτρησις τοῦ πρώτου κινήτου. A reference to the Aristotelian definition of time as the measure of motion.</note> according to "before" and "after," as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies; and since this measurement is the rule for all human actions, adopted to avoid confusion: certainly Censorinus <note>A 3rd-century Roman grammarian who wrote on birthdays and time.</note> teaches at length that in ancient ages, while time was not yet established under the name of "hours," it was named and distinguished by daily actions. Thus they called the evening *the unyoking of the oxen* <note>original Greek: βουλυτὸν</note>, just as the Poet says:

> When Phoebus <note>The Sun god</note> took the yokes from his well-deserved horses.

<margin>Gnomonics existed from the beginning.</margin>
Likewise, designating the time before noon, they said *the filling of the marketplace* <note>original Greek: πληθύσης ἀγορᾶς</note>, namely because men gathered in the assembly at that time, as Hesiod says: *when the people, ceasing their work, gather together.* So Homer designates midday: *when the woodcutter prepares his meal.* Indeed, according to Athenaeus, the Ancients mostly noted the time of daily acts with the word *hour* <note>original Greek: ὥρᾳ</note>, such as *the hour of the snack* or *the hour of dinner*. Among the Latins it is also called *tempestas* [season/time]. You may judge the same regarding the ancient Hebrews, who divided the day into Morning, Midday, and Evening, which parts they called Hours. They also observed the entire *twenty-four hour period* <note>original Greek: νυχθήμερον, literally "night-day"</note> divided into four parts (which they called Watches): the first Watch was from Evening; the second from midnight; the third from dawn; the fourth from midday. From this, some conclude that the Ancients lacked the intervals of hours. They are wrong; for I am easily persuaded that the art of Gnomonics <note>The art of making sun-dials or using a gnomon to tell time.</note> and the distribution of hours existed from the beginning, while...

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHS
## CHAPTER VIII.
### PAGE 225

I consider more deeply the remarkable ingenuity of the ancients in discovering things. For since we judge those things which we cannot do without, and which we necessarily use, to be the most useful; certainly it is not likely that the first mortals discovered the use of Music and the more abstruse and less necessary intervals of voices, while neglecting the less difficult and more necessary art of Gnomonics <note>The art of using a gnomon (the pin of a sundial) to measure time by shadows.</note>. For if, as the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> testifies, *time is the measure of motion*, and thus the measure of our actions; it must be that either the Ancients lacked time by which to measure their actions, or they were not unskilled in Gnomonics. Almost everyone refers Astronomy, and indeed even Astrology, back to our first parents, Adam and his progeny, as we saw above and in Class II; but who is unaware that neither of these can stand without Gnomonics? For the partition of time is supremely necessary to both.

<margin>The use of Hours is most ancient.</margin>
Therefore, the division of the day into certain parts, *sha'ot* <note>original Hebrew: שעות, meaning hours</note>, which they called Hours, was most ancient; the principles of which sense itself designated. In the sacred books, the use of hours is clearly indicated in various places. In Exodus 9, Deuteronomy 28, and Esdras 3, chapter 2, and Job 11, mention is made of a half hour, and in chapter 12: *They prayed prostrate for three hours.* In Ecclesiasticus 12: *One hour he will remain with you.* and 30: *Every work in its own hour.* From which such an argument is constructed: If the Ancients had hours, they also had instruments by which they knew them; therefore they also cultivated Gnomonics: such instruments, moreover, were called *horologia* <note>clocks or sundials</note>; therefore [the conclusion follows]. But more on these things below in this same chapter. Furthermore, that Sciatheric Horologia <note>Shadow-measuring sundials; from the Greek 'skia' (shadow) and 'tithemi' (to place)</note> were in use in ancient times is demonstrated by the phrase *an eleven-foot shadow* <note>original Greek: ἑνδεκάπους σκιά</note>, for the hour of dinner; or *an eleven-foot element* <note>original Greek: ἑνδεκάπουν στοιχεῖον</note>, because the hours were distinguished by the marks of individual letters; it is also testified by an *epigram* <note>original Greek: ἐπιγραμμάτιον</note> concerning a Clock in Athenaeus, regarding which see section II following.

Herodotus in Book II writes that Geometry reached the Greeks from the Egyptians, but that Gnomonics and the breaking of the day into 12 parts flowed to them from the Babylonians. His words are: *For the Greeks learned the pole, and the gnomon, and the twelve parts of the day from the Babylonians.* <note>original Greek: Πόλον μὲν γὰρ καὶ γνώμονα, καὶ τὰ δυώδεκα μέρεα τῆς ἡμέρης παρὰ Βαβυλωνίων ἔμαθον Ἕλληνες</note>. 

<margin>What the Ancients understood by the name of Hours.</margin>
In this place, although some contend that hours should be taken not for the twelve parts of the day, but for civil signs assigned to business, and for the Solstitial times; we nevertheless think that the hours were truly 12 equinoctial and equal parts of the day, which they call *seasonal* <note>original Greek: καιρικὰς</note> and popular, which are twelve in every day and night. For it is certain that those Mathematicians who placed Horoscopes or Heliotropes <note>Instruments for following the sun</note> publicly and in the open, proposed them not only for the learned and those skilled in Astronomy, but for the common people; these pertained not only to discerning the Solstices by the ratio of shadows, but to the civil parts of the day and the governing of daily business. For what did it matter to plebeian men and citizens to know at what exact moment the Solstices occurred? Even if the use of such observation looked toward the management of certain rustic works, there was no need for such refined subtlety, but these could easily be discerned by a "rougher Minerva" <note>A Latin idiom meaning common sense or plain wisdom</note>, so that they might estimate the annual turning points from the civil months, as our Petauius <note>Denis Pétau (1583–1652), a Jesuit scholar</note> prudently noted in his *Work on the Heavens* <note>original Latin title: Ouranologicon</note> book 7, chapter 7. Furthermore, who would believe that those machines were [made] for only one day in the year, or the few on which those turning points happen—

He asserts that the 12-hour division of the day was a practical tool for common citizens, not just a theoretical pursuit for astronomers.</summary>

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
...were these their own specific properties? It would indeed be an opportunity worthy of great and public praise to know that one hundred or two hundred days ago the summer solstice had occurred, or would occur hereafter. On the contrary, the clocks of the Ancients were machines designed to distinguish the twelve parts of the day, which were named after the sun's revolution in such a way that nothing could be more absurd than to say such a massive structure served only one specific time, or even just one single day. Nor does it stand in the way that those clocks were called <term>therina</term> <note>original Greek: θερινὰ; meaning "summer-related"</note>, summer-clocks, or <term>cheimerina</term> <note>original Greek: χειμερινά; meaning "winter-related"</note>, winter-clocks; for by these terms they did not indicate the time of the summer and winter solstices, but rather equinoctial clocks. For these, being placed above the plane of the equinoctial, demonstrate the hours with their perpetual gnomon <note>The part of a sundial that casts the shadow</note> on the upper side when the Sun passes through the summer signs; but they show the same on the lower side during the remaining half of the year, when the Sun passes through the winter signs, as is well known even to boys studying the skill of gnomonics <note>The art of making sundials</note>. There were, moreover, various types of clocks used by the Ancients: <term>Gnomonic</term> (or <term>Sciatheric</term> <note>Shadow-measuring</note>), <term>Hydraulic</term> <note>Water-clocks</note>, and <term>Sympathetic</term>; and the Gnomonic types were themselves varied. We shall begin our discussion of each of these in order, starting with the Sciatheric clocks.

<note>Original Aramaic: הא אנא מתיב ית טול אבן שעיא דנחתת במסקנא דאחז שמשא לאחורוהי עשר שעין ותב שמשא עשר שעין בצורת אבן שעיא דנחתת</note>

"I will turn the sun back ten steps by which the shadow has gone down." <note>original Greek: στρέφω τὸν ἥλιον ἐπὶ δέκα ἀναβαθμοὺς ἐς κατέβη ἡ σκία.</note> Behold, I turn back the shadow of the steps, which the Sun, the father of its own house, descended by ten steps; I shall turn away the Sun by the ten steps which the shadow descended. <note>original Latin: Ecce ego verto vmbram...</note>

<margin>The Sundial of Ahaz was a shadow-measuring device, marked with hour lines.</margin>
We have, therefore, that this Sundial was a <term>gnomonic</term> <note>A device using a vertical rod or "gnomon" to cast a shadow.</note> or <term>Sciatheric</term> <note>From the Greek for "shadow-catching"; a sundial.</note> instrument; we have that it was in the house of Ahaz, the father of Hezekiah, King of Judah; and we have that it was marked with hour lines. However, what kind of device it was, and with what type of hours it was marked, remains to be explained.

Some think this Sundial was horizontal; they gather this from the <term>Chaldaic paraphrase</term> <note>The Targum, an ancient Aramaic translation/interpretation of the Hebrew Bible.</note>, where it is written: *Auen Schaia* <note>original Aramaic: אבן שעיא</note>, that is, the "stone of hours." Some think it was a semicircle, in the form of a bowl <note>original Latin: Scaphij</note>, placed before the King's doors. Most of the Rabbis believe it was on the wall of the Royal house. This is gathered from Radak in his exposition of this passage:

<margin>Rabbi Radak <note>David Kimhi, a prominent medieval biblical commentator.</note></margin>
"And the Sun returned backward, and the shadow was on the first step in the Sundial of Ahaz, because he himself had built those steps and arranged them so that the shadow descended upon the steps of Ahaz." <note>original Hebrew: וישב השמש אחרנית והיה הצל במעלה הראשונה במעלות אחז כי הוא בנה אותם המעלות ובדר ואשר ירדה במעלות אחז</note>

Or as Ralbag <note>Gersonides, a medieval philosopher and astronomer.</note> has it:

<margin>Rabbi Ralbag</margin>
"Which Sundial Ahaz had built in the Royal house." <note>original Hebrew: שבנה אחז בבית המלכות</note> Indeed, that it was vertical and looked directly toward the south, Rabbi Salmon shows in this place with these words:

<margin>Rabbi Salmon <note>Likely referring to Solomon Yitzhaki, known as Rashi.</note></margin>
"It was like a kind of staircase made facing the sun to determine the hours of the day." <note>original Hebrew: והיה כמין מדרגות עשויות כנגד החמה לבחון שעות היום</note> Since the sundial was intended for public use and for determining civil business usually carried out in the Royal house according to fixed times of the hours, it is likely that it was large, elegant, and open to all, located in the principal place of the City—that is, the Royal palace—both for ornament and for public utility, as I said, and for the convenient handling of business, positioned above the gate of the house. Nor do I see why some authors want it to have had the form of a bowl-shaped semicircle; since that, besides being small, could not have served public needs as well, as the hours can by no means be visible except to those looking closely into the concave stone. It remains, therefore, that it was drawn on a huge and vertical surface (as the Gnomonicists say) of polished marble, which faced precisely south.

<margin>The Sundial of Ahaz was vertical, directly facing south.</margin>
The only doubt occurring in this place is what kind of hours it was marked with; for it was clear from the Chaldaic Paraphrase cited a little earlier that it was described with hour lines. To explain this, it must be noted that four types of hours are commonly assigned by Astronomers.

<margin>Four types of shadow-measuring sundials.</margin>

is in use; the third counts 24 hours from noon to noon, as astronomers are accustomed to do, which is why they are called **Astronomical hours**; or they are even counted from midnight to midnight, the kind the Church is accustomed to use in the celebration of feasts. The fourth counts 12 hours from sunrise to sunset, and the same number from sunset to sunrise; so that an hour of this kind is nothing other than a twelfth part of the "artificial" day or night <note>An "artificial day" refers to the period of daylight, which varies in length throughout the year, as opposed to a fixed 24-hour "natural day."</note>. Although these hours are all equal in number, they are unequal in length when considering different days and nights—sometimes longer, sometimes shorter—concerning which, see page 215 of my work *The Great Art of Light and Shadow*. These are also commonly called **Ancient hours**, because all of antiquity is found to have always used them; Martial also elegantly describes them in Book 4 of his *Epigrams*. They are also called **Jewish hours**, because the ancient Hebrews used them and no others, as is proven from Holy Scripture. To this, the words of Christ our Savior allude: *Are there not twelve hours in the day?* <note>John 11:9</note>. To this also allude the "third hour" of the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the Disciples in the *Acts of the Apostles*, and the "ninth hour" of the death of Christ in the *Gospels*; the former corresponds to the ninth astronomical hour, the latter to the third astronomical hour. Furthermore, in the most celebrated Talmudic treatise *Sanhedrin*, mention is made of these kinds of hours, where they fabulously describe the limbs of Adam being produced by God according to a singular mystery of the distribution of hours: in the first hour, that is, from the rising of the Sun, God gathered his dust; in the second hour, the mass of his body was made; in the third hour, his limbs were extended; in the fourth, the spirit was breathed into him; in the fifth, he stood upon his feet; in the sixth, or at noon, he gave names to things; in the seventh, Eve was joined to him; in the eighth, they two ascended to the bed and four descended; in the ninth, he was forbidden to eat from the tree of knowledge; in the tenth, other precepts were given to him; in the eleventh, he signified the table; in the twelfth, at the setting of the Sun, Adam transgressed.

Therefore, the Hebrews had no other kind of hours than what we have described; from which it follows that the **Sundial of Ahaz** was marked with no other kind of hours than the "unequal" ones, as was common to all Eastern peoples. From this we gather that the shadow of the said sundial, at the time when the extension of life was promised to Hezekiah by the Prophet, showed the tenth hour, but by a supreme miracle the shadow retreated to the beginning of the first hour, as we have proven above from Radak <note>Rabbi David Kimhi, a medieval biblical commentator</note>. This could not have happened except by the course of the Sun being reflected back toward the sunrise by a stupendous miracle. This was not, as some think, an optical illusion, but a true and real retraction of the Sun from the west toward the east, by which the natural day was made ten hours longer than usual throughout the entire earth. This is also evident from the fact that the Babylonians, astonished by this unusual length of the day and informed of the retreat of the Sun on the sundial of Ahaz, sent men to Hezekiah to examine the reason for this miraculous event, as is recorded in the cited passage.

It is clear, therefore, from what has been said, that these kinds of hours were used at all times not only by the Hebrews, Chaldeans, and Romans, but also by the Egyptians. But now order requires that we show more closely the nature of the Egyptian sundials.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER VIII.

## § II.

->On Egyptian Clocks.<-

<margin>The Egyptians used three types of clocks: Shadow-based, Natural, and Sympathetic.</margin>
I read that three types of clocks were utilized by the Egyptians: the Shadow-based <note>original: "Sciathericum," from the Greek for shadow-tracking</note>, the Natural, and the Sympathetic. The first was that by which they learned the hourly times from the shadows of Gnomons <note>The pin or rod of a sundial that casts the shadow</note>. This type was moreover manifold. Some, from the shadows of Obelisks and pyramids—with certain fixed marks on the flat surface of the surrounding area which the shadow of the peak would reach—would say that it was such and such an hour. <margin>The shadows of Obelisks among the Egyptians showed the hours, noon, and the Solstices. Strabo. Solinus.</margin> We have shown elsewhere that in this manner the Obelisk erected at Heliopolis indicated the hours. Strabo and Solinus also teach that the largest pyramid exhibited the meridian time <note>noon</note> of the whole year, as well as the Solstices and equinoxes, with the midday shadows never falling outside the base. Furthermore, the expression <term>eleven-foot shadow</term> <note>original Greek: ἑνδεκάπους σκία</note>, meaning the hour of dinner, or <term>eleven-foot element</term> <note>original Greek: ἑνδεκάπους στοιχεῖον</note>, teaches that they learned the hours by the "feet" by which the shadow of a staff implanted in the ground was measured, and thus arrived at a knowledge of the time set for performing actions. This was because the hours were distinguished by the marks of individual letters, as <margin>The Egyptians learned the hours by measuring the shadow of a staff in feet.</margin> <margin>Athenaeus.</margin> Athenaeus left witnessed in the following Epigram:

> Six hours are most sufficient for labors; those following,
> shown for business, say "LIVE" <note>original Greek: Ζ Η Θ Ι (ZETHI). This is a wordplay: the letters also represent the numbers 7, 8, 9, and 10.</note> to mortals.

->*Six hours suffice for labors, the following are destined for business,*<-
->*But Z H Θ I, that is, 7. 8. 9. 10. they call the dining hours.*<-

So that A B G, that is, 1. 2. 3. were assigned to labors; D E F, that is, 4. 5. 6. to civil business; and finally Z H Th I, that is, 7. 8. 9. 10. to the refreshment of dinner.

<margin>The use of the quadrant in finding the hours among the Egyptians.</margin>
The quadrant <note>A mathematical instrument for measuring angles up to 90 degrees</note> frequently inserted among the hieroglyphics sufficiently teaches that the Egyptians also held the use of the quadrant in finding the hours, from which they elicited the given hour from the altitude of the Sun.

---

## § III.

->On the Egyptian Shadow-measuring Bowl.<-

<margin>Arazael. The Bowl-dial and its use in finding the hours among the Egyptians. Macrobius.</margin>
The Arab astronomer Arazael, in his book *On the Measurement of the World*, testifies that the Ancients, with truly supreme ingenuity, grasped the magnitude of the earth through shadows collected within Bowl-dials <note>original: "Scaphia," a hollowed-out sundial shaped like a bowl</note>. Ptolemy testifies that Eratosthenes also used these in Egypt. Moreover, the Bowl-dial was, as Macrobius explains in *The Dream of Scipio*, a certain stone vessel (which the Ancients therefore called the <term>hourly stone</term> <note>original Hebrew: אבן תשעות (Even Teshuot)</note> when they interpreted the clock of Ahaz described above) curved into the shape of a hemisphere...

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>CHAPTER VIII.</margin>
...hollowed out in a hemispherical shape, marked below by lines designating the number of the twelve hours of the day, which it distinguished by the shadow of a protruding pointer <note>original: "styli"</note> as the Sun passed by. For this was the function of such a vessel: that the shadow of the pointer would travel from one end to the other in the same amount of time that the Sun measured out half of the sky from sunrise to sunset—namely, the rotation of one hemisphere. For a complete rotation of the entire sky encompasses both day and night. And therefore it is established that as much as the Sun travels in a circle along any parallel, the shadow travels an equal amount within this vessel.

Vitruvius.
</margin>
I read that mention of this vessel was also made by Martianus Capella <note>A 5th-century author of an encyclopedia of the seven liberal arts.</note>: *The Scaphia*, he says, *are vessels made of bronze, in which they distinguish the paths of the hours by means of a pointer in the middle of the bottom, which pointer is called a gnomon.* See Pliny, Book 2, Chapter 2, and Vitruvius, Book 9, Chapter 9.

The Egyptians used this *Scaphium* <note>A bowl-shaped sundial; from the Greek word for "skiff" or "bowl."</note> above all others, as the hieroglyphics produced in their own time will demonstrate. Since they already perfectly understood the use of the sphere, and the *Scaphium* was nothing other than a concave hemisphere in which the divisions of the Sun's parallels—along with the tropics and the equinoctial line—as well as the unequal hours <note>In antiquity, "unequal hours" meant the day and night were each divided into 12 hours regardless of the season, meaning summer hours were longer than winter hours.</note> could be delineated with the greatest ease. In this manner, they first divided the equinoctial into twelve equal parts, and the Tropics of Cancer ♋ and Capricorn ♑ into the same number; if curved lines were drawn through these sections, the paths of the unequal hours necessarily emerged. The first of these, or the Horizon, held the twelfth hour <note>Kircher likely refers to the start of the count</note>, midday the sixth, and the last finally showed the twelfth again at the setting of the Sun. Truly, as to how Eratosthenes, Posidonius, and King Alammon investigated the size of the earth by means of the *Scaphium*, see the extensive treatise in our *Great Art of Light and Shadow*, page 722.

---

### § IV.
### *Concerning the Baboon Clock of the Egyptians.*

<margin>The Cynocephalus <note>The "dog-headed" baboon, sacred to Thoth.</note> measured the hourly times among the Egyptians by urinating.</margin>
There was, among other things, another device no less ridiculous than it was mysterious. They observed in the *Cynocephalus* (which is a certain species of Ape) I know not what hidden property, by which, when the Sun entered Aries ♈ and Libra ♎, it would pass urine twelve times during the day and twelve times at night by some concealed instinct of nature. From this arose the hydraulic clock <note>A water clock or clepsydra.</note> peculiar to the Egyptians. They fashioned a seated Baboon out of bronze, from whose member water glided down into an elongated vial placed beneath it; the rising level of this water, gradually ascending within the sides of a cylindrical glass machine divided into twelve circles, showed the hours step by step.

<margin>Horus.</margin>
So says Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, author of a treatise on hieroglyphs.</note> in Book 1, Hieroglyph 16, whom you may consult. You may also see the image of the Baboon on the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 300, where you will find everything described at length. You will find the clock itself below in the section on Egyptian Mechanics.

# SECTION V.

->*Concerning the Sympathetic Clock of the Egyptians.*<-

<margin>The water lily constituted a sympathetic clock among the Egyptians.</margin>
The Sympathetic Clock of the Egyptians was known only to the Philosophers and the initiates <note>original: "mystis," referring to those initiated into the secret religious mysteries</note>, which they used in their mystical consultations. This was the water lily <note>original: "Lotus aquatica"</note>; which is a marsh plant endowed with a hidden power of nature. As soon as the Sun rises, the plant itself, as if rising from the depths of the waters, gradually raises itself until midday. At that time, existing entirely above the waters in its upright position, it seems to emulate the Sun. However, as the Sun turns toward its setting, the plant follows the same laws from hour to hour through its own wonderful movement until it reaches the surface of the water. Finally, when the Sun goes below the horizon, the plant also goes beneath the waters, surrounding itself in such a persistent submersion that it sinks as far below the water as it had raised itself at noon, appearing to pine away for the Sun. The Priests understood this hidden impulse of nature; for that reason, they would place a wooden circle in the waters, as you see here, 

<column-break/>

imitating the solar circle and marked with its hours. It happened that they could perfectly discern the hours—which could otherwise scarcely be known by a sundial <note>original: "Sciatherico," a device using shadows to tell time</note>—through this hidden striving of the plant. But since we have already dealt with these matters in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>A reference to Kircher's 1650 work "Obeliscus Pamphilius"</note>, and shall again treat them specifically in the treatise on Egyptian plants, we refer the reader there. See also what we have said in the *Magnetic Art*, book 3, part 5, chapter 4.

# CHAPTER IX.

### *Concerning the Planetary Hours, and the Presiding Spirits of each.*

<margin>The Egyptians attributed individual planets to the individual days of the week.</margin>
As in all things, so especially in this, the Egyptians seem to have placed a great mystery in the seven planets that dominate the individual hours of the day. For they were the first who attributed the individual days of the week to individual planets. They believed, in fact, that for every hour from the rising of the Sun until the next sunrise, by night and by day, one of the presiding planets was in charge. From this source, even to this day, has flowed that astrological vanity <note>The author, Athanasius Kircher, often dismisses judicial astrology as "vanity" while still being fascinated by its history.</note>, because astrologers undertake almost nothing unless the hour of the dominant planet has first been inspected and thoroughly examined. But so that this hidden business may be more clearly revealed, it seemed appropriate to begin the explanation from a deeper level.

---

->§ I.<-

### *What the planetary hours are, and of what sort.*

<margin>What the planetary hours are, and of what sort.</margin>
The planetary hours described here are "unequal" hours <note>In ancient timekeeping, "unequal" or "temporal" hours divided daylight and night into 12 hours each, meaning an hour's length changed with the seasons.</note>. These are so called not in an absolute sense according to the course of the Sun, like equal hours, but are referred to the dominant planets. For since they listed the seven planets in this order: Saturn ♄, Jupiter ♃, Mars ♂, Sun ☉, Venus ♀, Mercury ☿, Moon ☽, each was thought to dominate and preside over the individual hours of the day in a retrograde <note>backward-moving</note> order. For if Saturn ruled the first hour of the day, Jupiter ruled the second, Mars the third, the Sun the fourth, Venus the fifth, Mercury the sixth, the Moon the seventh, and Saturn again the eighth, Jupiter the ninth, and so on; when these had revolved in such an order through the space of 24 hours, the first hour of the following day necessarily fell to the Sun, the second of that same day to Venus, the third of that same day to Mercury, and so on for the rest, until the revolution of 24 hours was completed and the third day [the first hour] fell to Mars; just as is exactly seen in the following table.

Thus, the twenty-fifth hour, which is the first hour of the following day, always falls to the planet that follows in retrograde order. For example, in the Table, on the day of the Sun <note>Sunday</note> at the first hour of the day, the lordship belongs to the Sun, from which the day is named; the second hour belongs to Venus, who immediately follows the Sun in retrograde order, and so on for the rest, up to the eighth hour. When the Sun reaches that point, the lordship of the seven planets having revolved through as many hours, the Sun begins its lordship again at the eighth hour; the remaining planets follow in order, as before, until the third hour of the night. At that point, the lordship of the planets having revolved again, the Sun begins its command anew, which it repeats at the tenth hour of the night. After this, the lordships of Venus for the eleventh hour and Mercury for the twelfth hour of the night follow. After these, the revolution of 24 hours having been completed, the first hour of the following day—namely, the day of the Moon <note>Monday</note>—falls to the lordship of the Moon in retrograde order. The same applies to the rest, as is evident from the Table. And from this, the reason is clear why the days of the week, marked by the names of the planets, follow neither the natural order of the planets nor the retrograde order as it appears in the Table, but always follow one another in an interrupted order.

<margin>The order of the days of the week, which are named after the planets, does not follow the order of the planets, and why.</margin>

I am not unaware that many who are ignorant of these matters devise various explanations for them. Indeed, having taken account of this kind of consonance and comparing it with the adornment of the heaven and the order of the celestial spheres and planets—noting a certain suitability and similarity in them—they decided that after one day was named after one planet, the following day should be named after the fourth planet after it, though in

## § II.
### Concerning the Governance or Lordship of the Planets.

<margin>The Governance of the Planets is an ancient fiction.</margin>
It was an **invention** of the Egyptians to arrange a substituted lordship of the Planets for each hour of the days, both diurnal and nocturnal; which even to this day the entire School of Astrologers embraces and kisses as if it were most sacred. It pleased the ancients so much that from it the very days of the Week took their names, as we have seen: a truly swollen and fertile nursery of superstitions, from which—just as in the past, so too today—innumerable monsters of portentous births have emerged and continue to emerge, as if from a certain Trojan horse. Hardly any Magical, Cabalistic, or Astrological operation is established which is not founded on this most vain observation of the planetary hour. We shall confute this more sharply once we have first shown the superstitious arrangement of this machinery from its foundations.

<margin>The Egyptians imagine seven Intelligences preside over the World.</margin>
The Egyptians thus imagine that in that great Hermetic year <note>A vast cycle of time in esoteric Egyptian chronology</note>, seven Intelligences preside over the World according to certain sets of seven, each of which governs for 354 years and four Months; and they all perform different duties and offices. Consequently, the World undergoes various and diverse alterations according to the influence and disposition of the seven wandering stars <note>The planets</note>. These things, according to the mind of the Egyptians, are recited by Abraham Auenar <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century Jewish scholar and astrologer</note>, the Hebrew Astrologer, in his *Book of Reasons* in these words:

<margin>Abraham Auenar.</margin>
> Behold, God has made seven rulers to reign over the world, and their names are Caphiel, Zadkiel, Camael, Michael, Anael, Raphael, and Gabriel; and behold, there are seven kings for the seven wandering stars, and each one shall rule the world for 354 years and 4 months. <note>original Hebrew: והנה המליך אלוה לעולם שבע שלטונים ושמותיהם כפיאל צדקיאל כמאל מיכאל ענאל רפאל גבריאל והנה שבע מלכים לשבע כוכבי לכת וכל אחד ואחד ימלוך העולם שנ"ד שנים וד' חדשים</note>

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER IX

among the Hebrews, these will be found to fall under the dominion of Anaël or another; so that the whole business must be judged by all those who are accustomed to weigh matters in the refined balance of reason as a fabrication, resting on no solid foundation of truth, and deserving of no merit or profit.

<margin>The Egyptians attributed individual ruling Planets to each hour of the day.</margin>
I find indeed in the ancient monuments of the Egyptians that they handed down something similar—as we shall later explain regarding the Sothiac or Canicular Year <note>The Sothiac cycle is a period of 1,461 years based on the rising of the star Sirius, which the Egyptians called Sothis.</note>—and as was touched upon in the preceding sections, and will be more fully explained in the following, where we shall treat of the Platonic Year and the <term>rebirth <note>original: παλιγγενεσία (palingenesia); the Stoic and Platonic concept of the periodic renewal of the world.</note></term> of things. It is certain, however, that the Egyptians were the first to distribute Spirits <note>original: Genios; refers to guiding spirits or tutelary deities.</note> to individual hours, who would have care of the things committed to their faith by night and day through the course of the entire week. Thus, the first hour of the first day fell under the dominion of the Spirit of the Sun, the second to the Spirit of Venus, the third to the Spirit of Mercury, the fourth to the Moon, the fifth to Saturn, the sixth to Jupiter, and the seventh to Mars. Once the dominion of this last one had revolved, the Sun repeated its dominion, and the others followed in the same order as stated; until, the revolution of 24 hours (that is, one natural day) being completed, the twenty-fifth hour—which is the first hour of the following day—fell to the Moon, from which that day also obtained its name. And so, another revolution of one day being completed, the dominion of the first hour of the third day fell to Mars, the first hour of the fourth day to Mercury, the first hour of the fifth day to Jupiter, the first hour of the sixth day to Venus, and finally the first hour of the seventh day to Saturn. The names of the Spirits, which we have extracted from the monuments of the Coptic Egyptians, are as follows:

<margin>Coptic Deities of the seven Spirits or Angels.</margin>

# CHAPTER IX. . 238 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>The Egyptians believe that individual Spirits are assigned to every hour of the entire week.</margin>
Once approved, this belief so infatuated the minds of men that, having taken root, it seems it can scarcely be pulled out. The Hebrews think that the Egyptians assigned not just seven, but as many different <term>Genii</term><note>In this context, "Genii" refers to guardian spirits or presiding deities, not "geniuses" in the modern sense.</note> to the individual hours of the days running in order through the whole week as there are hours calculated in one week; and they hold their names and offices as a great secret, being most superstitious.
<margin>Abraham Ecchellensis.</margin>
Indeed, these names and offices are contained in a certain book annexed to the *Yetzirah* <note>The Sefer Yetzirah or "Book of Formation," a foundational text of Jewish mysticism (Kabbalah).</note>, which book the most learned Abraham Ecchellensis <note>A Maronite scholar and linguist (1605–1664) who taught in Rome and assisted with the Paris Polyglot Bible.</note> once shared with me here, along with Jonah the Galilean, Professor of the Hebrew language at the Roman Lyceum. According to the testimony of the said Abraham, they were all translated into the Hebrew language from a very ancient Arabic manuscript, and they contain nearly everything usually treated in consultative and adjuratory <term>Astrology</term><note>Astrology used for seeking advice or summoning spirits.</note>. For this reason, I have judged that they should be suppressed in silence—as they are more worthy of fire than of light—lest they provide an occasion for stumbling to careless "philosophy-pretenders." I shall only set forth the names so that the reader, if he ever happens upon such names, may recognize from whose workshop they emerged and laugh at them as things involving open Egyptian idolatry.

It should be noted in this place that this Table contains only the disposition of the Spirits' dominion over the 12 nocturnal hours of the entire week; however, through the twelve hours of the daytime, the dominions of the Spirits follow one another in exactly the same order as they do in the nocturnal hours.

But let us expose this vanity a little more fully. The Ancients arranged the dominions of the planets according to the order of <term>unequal hours</term> <note>Hours that vary in length depending on the season, dividing day and night into 12 parts regardless of duration</note>; since these increase during the day when the Sun turns toward the North, and decrease at night—and conversely when the Sun turns toward the South—it necessarily followed that the planetary dominions were unequal in terms of duration. This was not the case regarding the day itself, but regarding the night compared to the day and other parallels of the Sun. Thus, at the Summer Tropic, when at Rome (for example) the hours of the day are almost twice as long as the hours of that same night, the planetary dominions lasted nearly one equinoctial hour and 15 minutes, while at night they lasted only 45 minutes.

Hence I ask: how could these <term>petty astrologers</term> <note>original: "Astrologastri," a derogatory term for superstitious or fraudulent astrologers</note> observe the hours so precisely as to invoke the Spirit presiding over that hour, especially at night, when the Sun did not illuminate the <term>sundials</term> <note>original: "Sciatherica," instruments for telling time by shadows</note> erected for this purpose? Certainly, they must have frequently fallen into the gravest errors, believing it was the hour of Mars while it still pertained to the empire of Jupiter. Truly, those monstrous names and offices of the planetary Spirits—who are imagined by the Arabs, Hebrews, and Egyptians to preside over the protection of things at individual hours—have no other origin than that drawn from the murky kitchen of the Devil. The horrendous superstitions they practice to draw a certain Spirit at a fixed hour, and to favor their prayers and solicitations, are such that I judge them more fit for stirring the fires of Vulcan <note>the underworld or a furnace</note> than for the commendation of public light; indeed, chaste Christian ears should shudder at them as most impious and as if invented by an <term>evil demon</term> <note>original: "Cacodæmone"</note>. Nevertheless, it seemed right to review them here, both to show the context of this substituted superstition and to more clearly demonstrate the systems of Egyptian superstition. In this matter, I have followed Saint Irenaeus, who, in order to show the unbridled lust and madness of the Gnostics in inventing such things, set forth a long catalog of those same "lesser gods" whom they call <term>Aeons</term>, along with their horrendous superstitions. ...the root of that *Key of Solomon* <note>original: "clauiculæ Salomonis"; a famous Renaissance grimoire of planetary magic</note>, as they call it; from which an entrance lies open to the eternal precipices of the infernal abyss, leading to the ultimate destruction of those who use them; from this source, Mages accomplish all their execrable crimes with the help of Demons. From this, Cornelius Agrippa, Paracelsus, Peter of Abano <note>Three influential figures in Western esotericism and alchemy</note>, and other masters of a damned and diabolical art, have drawn their dogmas, which I advise all men of fearful conscience to flee as they would Scylla and Charybdis <note>A metaphor for choosing between two equally dangerous evils</note>. # CHAPTER X.
->Concerning the Twenty-Eight Mansions of the Moon.<-

<margin>The Mansions of the Moon are a superstitious nursery, and are rightly called the stables of Demons.</margin>
Following the planetary hours and their Spirits <note>original: "Genijs"</note>, there are the 28 Mansions of the Moon, with Spirits appropriated to them. They are called in Coptic <term>ⲙⲁⲛϣⲱⲡⲓ ⲛ̀ⲓⲟϩ</term> <note>man-shōpi n-ioh</note>, that is, the dwellings or lodgings of the Moon; in Arabic <term>منازل القمر</term> <note>manāzil al-qamar</note>, the inns of the Moon. Some also call them the stations of the Lunar Gods. I should more rightly call them the stables of Demons; since they are filled with so many and such great superstitions that there is scarcely an Astrological invention into which the Mansions of the Moon do not enter. <margin>The 28 Mansions of the Moon are a fiction of the Egyptians.</margin> This is, however, a fiction of the Egyptians, who, defining the course of the Moon by the number of 28 days, assigned to it a single station for each natural day, together with the Spirit of that station as a kind of administrator and preserver. Thus, with the greatest zeal, they first sought out the planetary hour; then they considered in which station the Moon was at that same hour; and so, from the hostile or friendly meeting of the Spirits, they judged whether their work should be commenced or not.

<margin>The gate of the lunar mansions according to the Egyptians is the Milky Way.</margin>
But before we arrive at the explanation of the Mansions, it seemed best to explain their gate in this place. The Egyptians call the gate of the Lunar Mansions that circle which astronomers commonly call the Milky Way; in Coptic it is called <term>ⲡⲓⲙⲱⲓⲧ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉ ⲡⲓⲧⲟϩ</term> <note>pi-moit n-te pi-toh</note>, which word, as I said in the *Supplement to the Coptic Prodromus* class 5, is Egyptian or Coptic, and we interpret it as the "way of straw" or "chaff"; for by this name the Egyptians call that white circle which the Greeks call <term>γαλαξίαν</term> <note>galaxian</note>, or <term>τὸν γαλακτικόν κύκλον</term> <note>the galactic circle</note>, and the Latins call the *via lactea* [Milky Way]. Ovid, indeed, called it the path by which the Gods above approached Jove, in these words:

<margin>How the Milky Way is named by different peoples.</margin>
> There is a high way, manifest in the serene sky,
> It has the name "Milky," notable for its very whiteness.

# CHAPTER X.

> *By this path the Gods travel to the realms of the great Thunderer,* <note>original: "magni Tonantis," a poetic epithet for Jupiter/Zeus</note>
> *and to the royal palace, etc.*

The Milky Way is called the "milky circle" by the Poets because of the spilled milk of Juno; on this matter, consult Hyginus, Phornutus, and other mythologists. This path, I say, is called in Coptic the *way of straw or chaff*; a naming convention followed by almost all other Eastern peoples. It consists of two words, the first of which, **ⲙⲱⲓⲧ**, means *way*, and the other, **ⲧⲟϩ**, means *straw or chaff*; **ⲛ** is the grammatical marker of possession, as we have taught in Coptic Grammar. That our interpretation is the true one is shown by the Arabs, Syrians, Ethiopians, Hebrews, and other Easterners. The Arabs usually call the *galaxy* <note>original: "γαλαξίαν" (galaxian)</note> **المجرة** *Almagiret*, as if you were to say *a flow or trail of scattered straw*. The author of the *Scala* <note>A medieval Coptic-Arabic vocabulary</note>, as well as Abenregel, describes it thus: **المجرة هي طريق التبن** *Almagiret, and it is the way of straw or chaff*. Mor Isaac, in his Syriac Philosophy, likewise calls this milky circle the *path of straw* in these words:

<margin>
The author of the Scala, Abenregel, Mor Isaac.
</margin>

> **ܘܗܝ ܒܝܫܘܪܬܐ ܕܡܬܩܪܝܐ ܐܘܪܚܐ ܕܬܒܢܐ**
> <note>original Syriac: "And it is the belt which is called the path of straw."</note>

Indeed, the belt seen in the Circle of the 12 Signs <note>the Zodiac</note> is called the *way of straw or chaff*.

<margin>
The Egyptian fable concerning the Milky Way.
</margin>

The Ethiopians also, as I have heard from the Abyssinian priests here in Rome, call it *Chasara tsamangadu, the way of straw*; just as the Hebrews call it **נתיב התבן** <note>original: "Netiv ha-teven"</note>, all subscribing to the fables of the Egyptians. For the Egyptians imagine that Typhon <note>The chaotic deity Set</note> scattered a bundle of grain stalks, which had been placed in his way by the fleeing Isis, across the sky; from which event the name *way of straw* has remained for that region to this day.

<margin>
How the Egyptians name the 28 stations of the Moon.
</margin>

The Egyptians, therefore, as I was saying, establish 28 stations of the Moon—that is, as many constellations or places which the Moon reaches in each of its periods (a space of 28 days). They call these places by the Coptic name **ⲙⲁⲛⲙⲁⲛⲏ ⲛⲧⲉ ⲓⲟϩ**, which is to say, *the dwellings or lodgings of the Moon* (in Arabic **المنازل القمرية** *the lunar inns or lunar stations*). For **ⲙⲁⲛⲙⲁⲛⲏ** is the plural for *mansions*, **ⲛⲧⲉ** is the possessive marker, and **ⲓⲟϩ** signifies the Moon. We see that Astrologers, from the earliest times to this day, have observed these lunar stations as being opportune and worth knowing, both for investigating changes in the weather and for ensuring the success of beginning new works; this is because the influence of the stars in these specific locations of the zodiac introduces various effects upon worldly affairs.

<margin>
Each of the 28 stations of the Moon consists of 12 degrees and 24 minutes.
</margin>

Each station consists of exactly 12 degrees and 24 minutes, as will be evident to anyone dividing a circle into 28 parts. Although these stations used to begin at the "head of Aries" in the eighth sphere, modern Astrologers now begin them from the 22nd degree of Aries due to the motion of the apogees <note>the shifting of the stars over time due to precession</note>. The order of the lunar stations and their explanation follows.

<margin>
The order and explanation of the 28 stations of the Moon.
</margin>

**ⲕⲱⲧⲉ ⲙ ⲡⲓⲥⲓ** in Coptic means "fish," signifying in this context the *station of the fish*; in Arabic it is called **بطن الحوت** *The Belly of the Whale, or the Fish*. This is the first station of the Moon, so named for its harmful humidity; it used to begin at 0 degrees of Aries and end at 12 degrees and 24 minutes of the same sign. The Spirit <note>term: Genius (a guardian spirit or governing intelligence)</note> of this station according to the Arabs is **قيائيل** *Kyaiel*; it is a station associated with the harassment of an enemy.

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. 243 CHAPTER X.

II. *Piktōrion* <note>original: πικτωριον</note>, that is, the *Fish of Horus*, is in Arabic *Al-Sharatain* <note>original: الشرطين</note>, the *Station of the Moon*, which the author of the *Scala* describes in these words: *Al-Sharatain, which is the head of the Ram* <note>Aries</note>. Abenragel <note>A 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> says it thus:
->*Al-Sharatain is the station of the Moon in the sign of Aries, and it is commonly taken for the head of Aries itself.*<-
Its beginning is at 12 degrees and 24 minutes of Aries; its end is at the twenty-fifth degree of the same. Its Guardian Spirit is *Hiaiel*; it is the *station of the reconciliation of the Prince*.

III. *Kolion* <note>original: κολιων</note>, the *Connecting Station*, in Arabic *Al-Butain* <note>original: بطين</note>. Thus Chamus describes it:
->*Al-Butain is a station of the Moon, and it is a triangle near the belly of the Whale.*<-
We do not say this station is anything other than what the Triangle (or *Dilt*), the head of Aries, and the Northern Fish—being of nearly the same latitude—establish. The beginning of this station is from the start of the twenty-fifth degree of Aries ♈, and its end is in the ninth of Taurus ♉. Its Guardian Spirit is *Ginchiaiel*, and it is the *station of prosperity and good fortune*.

IV. *Horias* <note>original: ωριας</note>, that is, the *Station of Horus*, in Arabic *Al-Thurayya* <note>original: الثريا</note>; it is the lunar station which the Pleiades provide for the Moon. They called it the station of Horus from *Horias*, because Horus—by whom they signaled the fertility of the World through hieroglyphics <note>original: ἱερογλύφως</note>, according to Plutarch—exerts himself most in Taurus, the house of Venus, in the company of the Pleiades. Whence also the Hebrews call these same Pleiades *Gnasch* <note>original: עיש</note>, or *Succoth Benoth* <note>original: סוכות בנות</note>, that is, the *assembly*, or *daughters of the booth*, *covered and cherished daughters*. For just as a Hen cherishes and sustains her chicks, so Horus sustains the lower World in this sign; the station of the Bull <note>Taurus</note>. Whence they also say its idol was a Hen with her chicks. Thus Rashi <note>Rabbi Shlomo Itzhaki, medieval commentator</note> says in chapter 5 of Amos, and in Job:

<margin>Rashi</margin> *Succoth Benoth was the likeness of a Hen with her chicks.*
These *Succoth Benoth* are the same as the *Horias of the Egyptians*, and the *Al-Thurayya* of the Arabs, which is the same as the Taurine station. For *Al-Thurayya* finds its name from no other source than the Arabic word *Tzuor* <note>Thawr</note>, which signifies a *Bull*. Rabbi Jonah expressly teaches this in these words on Amos 5:

<margin>R. Jonah</margin> *Succoth Benoth are the seven stars in the Zodiac, which in the Ishmaelite language—that is, Arabic—are called Al-Thurayya.*
But concerning these matters, consult the *Egyptian Temple* (that is, the first volume of the *Oedipus* <note>Kircher's own work, Oedipus Aegyptiacus</note>), where many curious things are handed down. The words of Abenragel correspond to these, who in his *Astrology*, describing the mansions of the Moon, says of this one:

<margin>Abenragel</margin> ->*Al-Thurayya is the station of the Moon in the sign of Taurus, and it is called the Hen of Heaven with her daughters.*<-
There are some who confuse *Al-Thurayya* with the *Daughters of the Bier* <note>original: بنات النعش - Banat Na'ash</note>, that is, with the daughters of the funeral litter and the bier of Lazarus, which some call Arcturus and others the Little Bear <note>Ursa Minor</note>. But what we think of it, and what truly must be determined...

# EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>CHAPTER X.</margin>

Certainly, I find in Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian, circa 200 AD</note> that the Pleiades are called *peleiades* <note>original: πελειάδες</note> by Aeschylus, Pindar, and Simonides—that is, "doves." Nor does Homer look elsewhere when, in the description of Nestor’s Cup, he sings that the *peleiades* (doves) bring ambrosia to Jove, understanding them to be the Pleiades. But to return to our purpose, it is called *shastran* <note>original Coptic: ϣⲁⲥⲧⲣⲁⲛ</note> and by another Coptic name *exastran* <note>original: ⲉⲝⲁⲥⲧⲣⲁⲛ</note>, as if you were to say, *six stars*; by which words it is most clearly indicated that nothing else is understood but the Arabic *Al-Thurayya* <note>original: الثريا</note>, that is, the *Pleiades*. This agrees with that line of Ovid:

> The Pleiades begin to support their father's shoulders,
> Which are usually said to be seven, yet are only six.

The beginning of this station is the ninth degree of Taurus, and its end is the twenty-second of the same. But perhaps these matters are treated more diffusely than was proper. The Guardian Spirit <term>Genius: a protective spirit or planetary intelligence</term> of this station is *Delhaiel* <note>original Arabic: دلهيائيل</note>; and it is a station of enmity and vengeance.

V. **Pyrion** <note>original: πυριών - "The Fiery One"</note> and the station of the Greater Horus, in Arabic *Aldebaran* <note>original: الدبران</note>; it is called the station of Horus because, just as it occupies almost the same region of the sky as the preceding one, so it finds its name from the most effective operations of Horus in this station. Concerning this, Abenragel <note>A 11th-century Arab astrologer</note> says:

->*Aldebaran is a station in the sign of Taurus, and it is the Eye of the Bull.*<-

That is, *Aldebaran is the station of the Moon in the sign of Taurus, and it is called the Eye of the Bull.* All modern astrologers follow the Arabs, who thereafter take Aldebaran for the Eye of the Bull. By the Greeks it is called *lampadias* <note>original: λαμπαδίας</note>, named so evidently from its remarkable splendor. Its beginning is the 21st degree of Taurus, its end the 4th of Gemini ♊︎. The Guardian Spirit is *Huaiel* <note>original Arabic: هواىيل</note>; it is a station for the favor of Great Men.

VI. **Klados** <note>original: κλαδος - "The Branch"</note> and the *Cloister*; a station of the Moon called in Arabic *Al-Han'ah* <note>original: الهنعة</note>, and it is nothing other than two stars in Gemini, the first of which, preceding their feet, is called *meson* <note>original: μεσών - "middle"</note> by the Greeks (according to Geminius); the other, "the one on the head," of the second magnitude, is called by the Arabs *Ras elgiueze* <note>original: راس الجوز</note>, that is, the *head* of Gemini ♊︎. I find these stars described by the Arabs by two other names, namely *Garakles* and *Apullun* <note>original: فارقلوس واقولون</note>; which matter, while it left me perplexed, I finally discovered that they wished to indicate Hercules and Apollo by these corrupted Greek names (by which names I read the *Didymoi* or Twins are called among the Mythologists). This station begins from the fourth degree of Gemini and ends in the eighteenth of the same. Its Guardian Spirit is *Phigiaiel* <note>original Arabic: فيجاييل</note>; it is a station of benevolence and love.

VII. **Klaria** <note>original: κλαρια</note> and to the Arabs *Al-Henaah* <note>original: الهنعة</note>, is a station of the Moon which Abenragel describes thus:

->*Al-Henaah is the station of the Moon in the sign of the Twins, which they call the shoulders of the Twins.*<-

It begins at the eighteenth and ends at the thirtieth of Gemini. Its Guardian Spirit is *Zifaiel* <note>original Arabic: زساييل</note>; it is a station for the acquisition of goods.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS 247 CHAPTER X.

XXIV **Epechritos** <note>original Greek: ἐπεχριτος</note> *Happiness, or the swallowed arm*, in Arabic **Saad elbelàa** <note>original: سعد البلع</note>; this is a station of the Moon which begins at the 29th degree of Capricorn and ends at the 9th degree of Aquarius. This is also called **the tail of Capricorn** <note>original Arabic: ذنب الجدي, "Dhanab al-Jady"</note>, named after the first star of the first magnitude fixed at the root of the tail. Its presiding Spirit is **Chachaiel** <note>original Arabic: خخائيل</note>; it is the station for the fertility of flocks.

XXV **Hypexinestes** <note>original Greek: υπεξινεστής</note> *The happiness of happinesses, or the arm of arms*, in Arabic **Saad elsaaud** <note>original: سعد السعود</note>; this is a station of the Moon in the <term>dodecatemory</term> <note>a twelve-part division of the zodiac</note> of Aquarius, the beginning of which is the ninth degree of Aquarius and the end is the 21st of the same. Certain Arabs also call this region **the mouth of the fish** <note>original Arabic: فم الحوت, "Fom al-Hut"</note>; for it is, to speak with the Greeks, **the mouth of the so-called solitary southern fish** <note>original Greek: στόμα τοῦ ἰχθύος λεγομένου νοτίου μονάζοντος</note>. It seems, according to the mind of the ancients, that this star should be referred to the southern and solitary fish rather than to Aquarius. We, therefore, say that this station occupies that region which the Greeks called the **outpouring of water** <note>original Greek: χύσιν ὕδατος</note>, and because of its windings, the **steep-cut** <note>original Greek: ἀκροτόμον</note>. In Vitruvius <note>Roman architect and engineer</note>, the reading **akrotomon** is corruptly read in this place for **akrotomin**; which I would wish the learned to note; for Hesychius <note>Greek grammarian</note> expressly interprets **akrotomon** as **the outpouring from the gods, as he says** <note>original Greek: τὴν ἀπὸ θεῶν ὡς λέγων χύσιν</note>, that is, a fusion of the more obscure stars. Its presiding Spirit is **Dedaliel** <note>original Arabic: ددائيل</note>; it is the station for the abundance of the goods of the earth.

XXVI **Epestberian** <note>original Greek: επεσθεριαν</note> *The hidden arm*, in Arabic **Saad elachbieh** <note>original: سعد الاخبية</note>; this is a station of the Moon which begins from the twenty-first degree of Aquarius and ends at the fourth degree of Pisces. Presiding Spirit **Szafzaiel** <note>original Arabic: سزائيل</note>; it is the station of pleasures.

XXVII **Artiloch** <note>original Greek: ἀρτιλοχ</note> *The station of the first sprouting*, in Arabic **Alphara elmakoddem** <note>original: الفرع المقدم</note>; this is a station of the Moon whose beginning is from the fourth degree of Pisces and its end is in the 17th degree of Pisces. Its presiding Spirit is **Tatfaiel** <note>original Arabic: تطائيل</note>; it is the station of droughts.

XXVIII **Artilochia** <note>original Greek: ἀρτιλοχια</note> *The later sprouting*, in Arabic **Elphara elmuchur** <note>original: الفرع المؤخر</note>; this is a station of the Moon extended from the 17th degree of Pisces up to the 30th degree of the same. Presiding Spirit **Harchaziel** <note>original Arabic: هرخزيل</note>; it is the station of floods.

And these are the Names of the 28 stations of the Moon used by the ancient Egyptians, whose order was also followed by the Arabs and the <term>Brahmins</term> <note>priestly caste of India</note>, the Philosophers of the Indians, as is evident from their books, and as I have said in the Supplement to the *Prodromus* in the place cited above.

# PART II.

### On the Egyptian Computation, and the Reason and Method for Correcting the Year,

# C H A P T E R I.

### On the Origin of the division of time into years, days, and hours.

It has been shown more than enough above—from Plutarch, Diodorus, Herodotus, and others—that the Egyptians were the first of mortals after the flood to apply themselves to astronomy, to divide time into years and days according to the course of the Sun and Moon, and to discover the method for intercalating <note>The process of inserting extra days into a calendar to keep it aligned with the solar year.</note> days. So that this may now be more clearly evident;

<margin>The Egyptians divided the year into as many days as the years Enoch lived.</margin>
It must be known that there was a secret tradition of the Hierophants <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries.</note> (as we hinted at above in the section on Astrology, and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* on page 28) that the civil year of the Egyptians consisted of as many days as there were years in the life of Enoch—that first Hermes before the flood, whom the Arabs call Idris, and the Egyptians call the first Osiris, or even Hermes. Now, according to the sacred text of Genesis, Enoch had 365 years of life before he was translated <note>Taken up by God without dying.</note>. *And all the days of Enoch were three hundred and sixty-five years.* Since we reported above that the second Hermes, whom we called Trismegistus <note>Hermes "the Thrice-Greatest," a legendary Hellenistic figure conflated with the Egyptian god Thoth.</note>, established a year of that many days, it is probable that he obtained this method from the monuments of the first Hermes, which were communicated to the later world through Ham <note>The son of Noah, traditionally associated with the peopling of Egypt.</note>. Indeed, not only the ancient astronomers but also later mathematicians—and most importantly their prince, Ptolemy—used this full and simple civil year of the Egyptians. Others in this place say the author of the <term>epagomenal</term> <note>original: "ἐπαγομένων"; these are the five "added" days used to round out the 360-day lunar year to a 365-day solar year.</note> or intercalary days was Aseth, the thirty-first of the Kings of Egypt; so says Eusebius in his *Chronicle*. <margin>Eusebius makes King Aseth the author of the epagomenal days, but incorrectly.</margin> *Aseth, the 31st of the Egyptian Kings, reigned 20 years; he added the intercalary days to the year;* in those times, as they say, the Egyptian year of 365 days was brought forth, which previously was completed in 360. But since we have already attributed the invention of this thing above to Mercury Trismegistus, who was much more ancient, I do not see how these accounts can be consistent; since from Mizraim <note>The biblical grandson of Noah, considered the founder of Egypt.</note>, the founder of the Egyptian Monarchy, down to Aseth (whom we say is the same as Mispharmuthosis II), 924 years are counted, as Eusebius himself bears witness: <note>original: "Ἀπὸ τȣ͂ πρώτȣ Βασιλέως καὶ οἰκηστȣ͂ Μισρὲμ τῆς Αἰγύπτȣ ἕως τȣ͂ Κονχάρε ἔτη ἔσχατον πληρῶ θ ῆ ἔτη ψʹ. Βασιλέων κεʹ"</note> *From the first King and inhabitant of Egypt, Mizraim, until Concharus, 700 years were completed under 25 Kings.* From Concharus to Aseth, 224 years are numbered according to the same author, which added to 700 make 924 years; and thus the invention of the intercalary days would fall roughly at the time of the departure of the children of Israel from Egypt; which should not and cannot be said for any reason. For if we must calculate by the *Chronicle* of Eusebius from the fragments of Manetho <note>An Egyptian priest and historian who wrote a history of Egypt in Greek.</note>, it must be said either that Aseth has been confused with another King of this name...

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. 249 CHAPTER II.

Regarding the King whom we previously called *Maspharmutosin* <note>original: "Maspharmutosin" - likely a variation of Misphragmuthosis, a Pharaoh of the 18th Dynasty</note> II, this most intricate knot must be more accurately untangled. In order for that to happen:

I say that King *Afeth* was almost a contemporary of *Mercury* <note>The author uses "Mercury" to refer to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage-god of Egypt</note>; for *Eusebius* <note>A 4th-century Christian historian and chronologist</note> places him third before *Tutemosin*. This king, being of a curious nature, brought the inventions of *Mercury* back to the anvil <note>A metaphor for refining or reworking an idea</note> and organized the "epagomenal" days <note>term: epagomenal (from Greek ἐπαγόμεναι) — the five extra days added to the 12 months of 30 days to make a 365-day year</note> into a sequence. Rejecting the various opinions of a crude age regarding the form of the year, he retained this one alone as the most exact. To adorn it with a mysterious discovery, he distinguished each of these five intercalary days with the names of Gods; thus, among posterity, he was known as the inventor of this scheme. This was not because he was truly the first inventor of them, since *Mercury* was the first after the flood to publish the form of a 365-day year, which had been passed down from *Enoch* through *Ham* by successive tradition, as we have said. In this way, I believe this passage should be understood, saving the judgment of those better informed; for once this is established, both the order of *Chronology* and the reckoning of time will be more skillfully consistent.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the Sothiac or Canicular Cycle.

<margin>The Civil Year of the Egyptians of 365 days is twofold: fixed and wandering.</margin>
The Egyptians, becoming gradually more skilled through long experience of celestial observations, saw that the year of 360 days then commonly used did not correspond everywhere to the Sun's period in the Zodiac. Noting that the period exceeded it by five days, they defined the Solar year as twelve months with *epagomenals* <note>original: "ἐπαγομένους" - added days</note>—that is, twelve months of thirty days each, with an appendix of five epagomenal days at the end of the year, without defining any quarter-day <note>The extra 6 hours that lead to a Leap Year</note>. This was thereafter held by everyone to be the true civil year. This year was again either fixed or wandering and "loose"; the former served civil business, while the latter served the sacred rites of the Hierophants <note>term: Hierophants — high priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>.

<margin>The Egyptian year was always uniform.</margin>
Therefore, the Egyptian year was simple and uniform, without any additional hours or leap days, which are usually intercalated every four years in the Julian calendar format. Consequently, if compared with the Julian year, after four years the new moon of the months falls back by one day; after 8 years by two days; and so on gradually, until after 1460 Julian years have passed, the new moon of the first month returns to the same start of the Julian month and day from which it began. This circle of years some call the Canicular Cycle, or the *Dog-Year*, as well as the *Sothiac* <note>original: "ἐτος κυνικὸν, ἅτε Σωθιακόν" - The "Dog-Star" (Sirius) was called Sothis by the Egyptians</note>. The Lesser Canicular Cycle is a system of 4 Egyptian years, consisting of 1460 days. The Lesser Julian Cycle, however, is 4 Julian years of 1461 days, exceeding the Egyptian by one day due to the intercalation of the four quarter-days. For the simple Julian year exceeds the Egyptian by almost six hours, which in the space of four years grows into 24 hours, creating the intercalation of a whole day. Again, the Greater Egyptian Canicular Cycle is a system of 1461 Egyptian years, in which interval the civil *Thoth* <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar</note> returns to the Julian *Thoth* from which it started. The Julian Canicular Cycle, however, is a system of the smaller Julian cycles...

<margin>The Greater Canicular or Sothiac Cycle of the Egyptians.</margin>

# CHAPTER II. 250 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

365. That is to say, 1460 Julian years, but 1461 Egyptian years, in which interval the month of Thoth <note>The first month of the Egyptian calendar</note> returns to the same Julian day. And this space of time they call the <term>Great Canicular Year</term> <note>original: "ἔτος κυνικὸν μέγα"</note>, or the <term>Year of God</term> <note>original: "ἐνιαυτὸν Θεοῦ"</note>. This division and naming of years excited no small disputes not long ago between two men of great reputation; however, we have decided that this must be settled solely by the authority of ancient writers. For in this matter, as it is both abstruse and uncertain, only as much should be believed as can be proven from good authors, lest any place be granted to fictions and shameful commentaries.

<margin>The Year of God among the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>The status of the controversy regarding years and lustra <note>five-year periods</note>.</margin>
The hinge of the controversy, therefore, turns on this: First, whether the Egyptians, besides the common solar year which was loose and wandering, also employed four-year periods <note>lustra</note> or Sothic cycles? Second, whether they called it the <term>Year of God</term>? Third, whether they applied intercalation <note>adding leap days</note> to fix the years? I shall treat each of these briefly in order.

<margin>Theon of Alexandria.</margin>
Theon describes the Egyptians' use of a wandering and loose year in these words: *From which we take sometimes the day according to the Egyptians, or again in the manner of the Greeks; for the year given according to the Greeks, or rather according to Alexandria, is 365 days and one quarter, while according to the Egyptians, as we said, it is 365 only. It is clear that every four years one day is added according to the Alexandrian reckoning.* <note>original Greek: "Ἐξ ἧς λαμβάνομεν... καθ' Ἀλεξανδρείαν"</note> Thereafter, the month and day are used according to the Egyptians in this manner.

For since the specific year of the Greeks or Alexandrians consists of 365 days with one quarter, but that of the Egyptians is 365 exactly, it is evident that every fourth year one day is added to the Alexandrian year. In these words, he indicates that the Alexandrians had adopted a fixed year, namely the Augustan year; but the ancient Egyptians conducted a simple and uniform year without an intercalary day.

<margin>Ptolemy.</margin>
<margin>Censorinus.</margin>
All of these things are confirmed in Ptolemy's *Almagest*. Censorinus reports that they also used Sothic cycles, which they called the <term>Year of God</term>, in these words:

> The Moon does not pertain to the Great Year of the Egyptians, which the Greeks call <term>Canicular</term> <note>original: "κυνικὸν"</note> and the Latins <term>Dog-star Year</term> <note>original: "Canicularem"</note>; because its beginning is taken when the Dog-star <note>Sirius</note> rises on the first day of that month which the Egyptians call <term>Thoth</term>. For their civil year has only 365 days without any intercalary day; thus a four-year period among them is about one day less than a natural four-year period, and so it happens that in the 1461st year it revolves back to the same beginning. This year is also called the <term>Solar Year</term> <note>original: "ἡλιακὸς"</note> by some, and the <term>Year of God</term> by others.

<margin>The Egyptians had a double method of calculation.</margin>
So that these things may be understood, it must be observed that the Egyptians had a double method of calculation: one which was established for fixing years and reducing them to order, and was used indiscriminately by all of Egypt along with the Alexandrians; which the Coptic Christians observe even to this day.

<margin>The Hierophantic method of calculation among the Egyptians.</margin>
The other was peculiar to the Priests and Hierophants <note>interpreters of sacred mysteries</note>, whence it was called the mystical or hierophantic and secret method, known only, as I said, to the Sages of the priestly order. It used no intercalation like the civil year, but gave free rein to its years, and imputed the increasing days and years to the accounts of the Sun by a certain secret and mystical skill. But lest we seem to have said anything without cause, it remains for the statements to be declared by the testimonies of upright authors.

<margin>Geminus.</margin>
First, Geminus, a very ancient astronomer, discusses these Hierophantic years in his book *On the Sphere* as follows: *For they have held a conception and purpose contrary to the Greeks. For they do not lead the year according to the sun, nor the months and days according to the moon, but they have used a certain peculiar system of their own, for they wish the sacrifices to the Gods...* <note>original Greek: "Οἱ μὲν γὰρ τὴν ἐναντίαν... τοῖς Θεοῖς"</note>

*God willed that the year should not always occur at the same time, but that it should pass through all the seasons of the year, and that there should be a summer, a winter, an autumn, and a spring; and that the year should consist of three hundred and sixty-five days. For they lead twelve months of thirty days each, and they add five days; but they do not add the one-fourth of a day, for the aforementioned reason, so that their festivals might rotate for them.* <note>Original Greek: "Θεὸς μὴ ἐν τῷ αὐτῷ καιρῷ..." This passage explains the theological reasoning behind the "vague year" (Annus Vagus), where the lack of a leap year caused festivals to cycle through all seasons over a 1,460-year period.</note>

<margin>The wandering year of the Hierophants.</margin>
*For the Egyptians, he says, followed a sentiment and purpose contrary to the Greeks; for they do not direct their years by the Sun, nor their months and days by the Moon, but they rely on a certain peculiar foundation. For they strive not to have the same years represent the sacred rites of the Gods at the same seasons, but they wish those very rites to travel through all the seasons of the year, so that the same festival may be in summer, winter, autumn, and finally spring. Indeed, they observe a year of 365 days, and twelve months of thirty days; they further add five days twice <note>The text likely refers to the five "epagomenal" or added days</note>; nor do they insert the quarter-day, clearly for the stated reason, so that their solemnities might move backward. And this is the specific institution of the Hierophants <term>Hierophants: high-ranking Egyptian priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</term>, who industriously loosened the reins of their year, so that the solemn and festive days would be contained by no fixed season, but would be led around through them all little by little. Haly also mentions this in his Chronology in these words:*
<margin>Haly.</margin>

And again at that same time, the Alexandrians and Egyptians begin their year together; and for that whole year, the Alexandrians conduct their days and months plainly according to the Egyptian reckoning; but at the beginning of the following year, the Egyptians begin to anticipate the quarter of a day, and so on.* <note>Original Greek: "'Επειδὴ δὲ καθ' 'Ελληνας..."
