# CHAPTER II. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>Strabo.</margin>
...brings forward among other things. Their practice is this: to conduct their days not according to the Moon, but according to the Sun, so that to the twelve months of thirty days each, they add five supplementary days every year. Furthermore, since a small fraction of a day remains to complete the full year, they compose a fixed period from whole days and whole years, in which these remaining portions of individual years eventually make up a full day. <note>This refers to the leap year cycle where the extra quarter-day accumulates.</note>

<margin>Lucian.</margin>
On this point, some surprisingly contend that the years of the Egyptians were Lunar, persuaded by that passage of Lucian, who in his book *On Astrology* discusses it thus: <note>original Greek: "Καὶ οἱ μὲν ἐξ σφίσι μέτρον ἡ σελήνη..."</note> *And these indeed (the Egyptians) measure their months by the Moon and its conversion; but they define the year by the Sun and its circuit.* To explain this, it must be known that just as religion varied among different people in Egypt, so too the system of the Months <margin>The lunar year of some Egyptians was two months, three months, etc.</margin> was diverse. For some of the ancient Egyptians, noting that the Moon completes its orbit in individual months, used this orbit as a year, so that the Lunar Month, in which the Moon crosses the Zodiac, was called by them a "Lunar Year." However, when they saw that this method of reckoning was contrary to their established needs, they abandoned it and set a two-month, then a three-month, or a four-month year. But when they saw that even this did not satisfy them in the distribution of time, they made a Lunar year of precisely 360 days, so that individual months of 30 days corresponded precisely to the 12 signs of the Zodiac. <margin>Censorinus.</margin> But let us hear Censorinus: *And in Egypt indeed, the most ancient years were said to be two months long; afterwards they were made four months long by King Piso; and most recently they extended the year to 12 months and five days.* With this agrees the statement of the Hebrew Author in the book *On the Moledim* <note>The "Moledim" refers to the "Apparitions" or "Births" of the New Moon.</note>:

> Our Rabbis of blessed memory say that formerly they calculated their years according to the way of the Egyptians; that is, they calculated their years according to the Lunar cycles. And it is written in the books of accounts that our father Abraham, of blessed memory, delivered this method to the Egyptians. <note>original Hebrew: "אמרו רז״ל שמקדם חשבו..."</note>

<margin>Some Egyptians used Lunar years, others Solar.</margin> From these things it is clearly evident that the Egyptians also established their years according to Lunar cycles—not all of them, but some Nomes <note>A "Nome" was a territorial division or administrative district in ancient Egypt.</note> more devoted to the cult of the Moon. Nevertheless, the greater portion of Egypt used Solar years, as is testified by what we produced a little earlier, and will appear more clearly in what follows. But let us return to where we digressed.

It now falls to us to prove from Authors that both were called the "Year of God." And indeed, it was proven from Censorinus just a moment ago. Now, however, we bring forward a witness beyond all exception, Horapollo, <margin>Horapollo.</margin> who, dealing with the hieroglyphic representation of the year in Book 1, Chapter 5, discusses it thus: <note>original Greek: "ἜτΘ δὲ ἐνιαύσιον γράφοντες..."</note> *When they wish to write "a year," they draw a quarter of an aroura. Now, the "aroura" (from which the Latin word "arvum" for field is derived) is a measure of land comprising one hundred cubits. Therefore, wishing to say "a year," they say "a quarter," because they say that from one rising of the star named Sothis <note>Sothis is the ancient name for the star Sirius.</note> to the next, a fourth part of a day is added, so that the Year of God is 365 days.* For which reason, a quar- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword "quar-".</note>

# CLASS VII. MATHEMATICAL HIEROGLYPHICS. CHAPTER II.

<margin>The Year of God is the same as the Solar year among the Egyptians.</margin>
Every fourth year, the Egyptians calculate and intercalate an extra day, since four quarters of a day complete a full day. Since the Egyptians say the Sun is a God, it is not surprising that the Solar year <note>original symbol: ☉</note> was called **Ph-re** in Coptic, or **Pi-re** due to its "renewal" <note>The author suggests a Coptic etymology linking the name of the Sun to the concept of youth or renewal</note>. For it is better known than needs to be said that Osiris, or the Sun, was called the "Great God" by the Egyptians (according to the testimony of Plutarch), and Isis was called the Moon. Hence the historian Apion records that a statue of Osiris, or
<margin>Apion the Historian.</margin>
Serapis, was cast from an emerald of nine cubits <note>about 13.5 feet</note>—a stupendous miracle among them. All these things show that honor was given to this Solar Deity, Osiris, above all others.

<margin>Why the common year is signified by a fourth part of a field.</margin>
Now indeed (which is a matter of greater difficulty), it must be briefly declared why they expressed the common year by a "fourth part of a field" <term>arura: an ancient unit of area</term>, which comprised only one hundred cubits, and why they named that same year *tetarton*, as if you were to say "a quarter." For Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, the author of a treatise on hieroglyphs</note> describes a double
<margin>The double year among the Egyptians.</margin>
year in the place cited: one lesser year of 365 days, and another *Cynic* or "Dog-star" year, which encompassed four Solar years with one intercalary day added besides. They defined this year by the rising of Sothis <note>The star Sirius</note> repeated four times, so that when the three hundred and sixty-five days were finished, six additional hours were added each year to the course defined by the motion of the Sun. Those hours, after a rotation of four years, would create a solid day. The Egyptians, I say, finally intercalated one day in the fourth year of Sothis, and only then considered a "solid year" to be completed (which was in truth a four-year period, one day greater than a civil four-year period). This the Greeks call *Cynic*, the Latins (as Censorinus well notes) call *Canicular*, and the Copts call **Pi-re**, because its beginning is taken from the first day of the month the Egyptians call Thoth, when Sothis rises. For their own Solar year, being "loose" and wandering, has only 365 days without any quarter-day. Therefore, a four-year period is about one day less than a natural four-year period, and thus it happens that in 1,460 years it returns entirely to almost the same starting point. In Horus, therefore, the "turning year" is taken for the civil year, and they denote it by a fourth part of a field; and wishing to say "year," they say *tetarton*, a quarter. Why this, unless because six hours are the fourth part of a day? And just as the civil year is the fourth part of a Canicular or Sothic Lustrum <note>a four-year cycle</note>, so 365 years are the fourth part of a "Great Year." These 365 years, multiplied by four, produce 1,460—that Great Canicular Year which we defined above as the System of 1,460 Egyptian years. Again, just as six hours accrue to each single year, which after four years become a whole artificial day, so to every 365 years there accrue 91 days and one quarter, which after 1,460 years grows into a whole Great Canicular Year, which we defined as a System of 1,461 years <note>The difference between the 365-day Egyptian calendar and the 365.25-day solar cycle causes the calendar to "rotate" through the seasons over 1,460 years</note>. Moreover,
<margin>Horapollo.</margin>
Horapollo beautifully wove in this reasoning when he said: *From one rising of the star Sothis until the next rising, a fourth part of a day is added* <note>original Greek: Μετὰ τὴν ἀνατολὴν τοῦ ἄστρου τοῦ Σώθεος μέχρι τῆς ἄλλης ἀνατολῆς τέταρτον ἡμέρας προστίθεσθαι</note>. From one rising of Sothis to the next [besides the year], a fourth part of a day is added; from which, he says, they calculate an extra day every fourth year. This the Alexandrians call the Cynic year, and the Copts call the Sothic or even the Hermetic year, after Hermes its first...

<margin>Hermes is depicted in the form of a Dog.</margin>
...by the first teacher, whom they also depicted in the form of a Dog <note>The author refers to Anubis or Thoth/Hermes, often associated with the dog-star</note>, and they believed that once he was translated into Heaven, he shone in the form of Sothis <note>The star Sirius</note>. the Priests fixed their years, and by what reasoning they loosened the reins of the same: they fixed them, clearly, by the command of Princes for the direction of civil actions; but they loosened them for mystical reasons cited above from Geminus <note>Geminus of Rhodes, an ancient astronomer</note>. *The months of the Copts are 12, and their year is 365 days with 5 days of Nisi <note>The "forgotten" or epagomenal days</note>, and every four years an intercalary day at the beginning of the year Neuruz <note>Nowruz</note>, which is a Persian word.*

->The twelve months of the land of Egypt, and the year is the counting of the year, it is the 5 days of<-

That is, the twelve Coptic months, and the five intercalary days <note>original Greek term: ἐπαγόμεναι (epagomenai)</note>, the days of intercalation every four years at the beginning of the year, namely Nowruz. This is confirmed by a certain other Arabic manuscript, a treatise on the Computation of the Copts, which that distinguished man Abraham Ecchellensis <note>A Maronite scholar and linguist</note>, my singular friend, allowed me to borrow, who discusses the year of the Copts thus:

<margin>Arabic manuscript book on the Computation of the Copts.</margin>
->And the solar year, many of the scholars believe that it is three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter<-
->of a day, because of what they see of the months arranged in science—I mean the Coptic months whose beginning<-
->is Thoth and Paophi, or the months of the Greeks and Syrians whose beginning is Elul and Tishri; and it is said that this arrangement was made<-
->by the children of Adam from the first of his days.<-

*Many of the Wise believe the Solar year to be 365 days with a simple quadrant <note>a quarter day</note>; and therefore the months in this World are so ordered, that the beginning, for example, of the Coptic months is the month of Thoth and Paophi, or the beginning of the Greek or Syrian months is Elul and Tishri; and it is said that this ordering was made by the sons of Adam from the beginning of days.* By these words, the Solar year with its appendix of five hours <note>referring to the roughly six-hour quarter-day</note> is clearly described from antiquity. Moreover, the manner in which the Ancients instituted the intercalation follows:

->They established its measurement on the basis that the solar year is three hundred and sixty-five days and a quarter day.<-

...one day, and therefore the quarter-day accumulates every four years to become a full day; for this reason, they intercalate the fourth year so that it consists of three hundred and sixty-six days. ۞

And the founders fixed the year so that the Solar year was 365 days with an equal quarter of a day, and therefore, collecting this quarter every four years, they completed one day, and by intercalating it, they established a year of 366 days.

But if anyone is not yet satisfied by the passages already cited, we bring forward **Diodorus Siculus**, also cited above, who discourses as follows concerning the Thebans:
> For they do not conduct their days according to the moon, but according to the sun, setting the months at thirty days, and they add five days and a quarter to the twelve months, and in this manner they complete the annual cycle.

The days, he says, are not taken according to the Moon, but the Sun, so that they attribute 30 days to each month, and insert five days with a quadrant <note>a quarter-day</note> into the twelve months, and by this reasoning they complete the whole cycle of the year. Therefore, among the Egyptians, besides the wandering and loose year <note>the "vague year" of 365 days which shifted against the seasons</note>, a fixed and <term>intercalary</term> <note>embolismus: the insertion of a leap day to keep the calendar aligned with the solar year</note> year was also very much in use, since without it, the greatest confusion in the administration of public affairs would necessarily arise.
<margin>The Greeks received the method of intercalation from the Egyptians.</margin>
Indeed, so far is it from the truth that the Egyptians first received this intercalation from the Greeks and Latins, that rather the Greeks first learned the true reckoning of the year and the method of intercalation from those same Egyptians. But lest anyone think I am dealing only in words, I have on my side that most weighty author of the greatest reliability, **Strabo**, who in his 17th book near the middle, teaches that Eudoxus first introduced this method of intercalating the day and the reckoning of the year into Greece, having received it from the Egyptians, in these words:
<margin>Strabo.</margin>
> For Eudoxus traveled there with Plato; and they spent time there with the priests; they stayed there thirteen years, as some have said. These priests were superior in the science of celestial matters, but they kept it secret and were reluctant to share their time, though they were eventually softened by attentive service; thus they handed over some of their theorems, but the barbarians <note>the Egyptians</note> concealed the majority of them. These priests handed over the fractions of the day and night which run over the 365 days for the completion of the annual time. But the year was unknown among the Greeks until then, as were many other things; until the younger astrologers received them from those who translated the records of the priests into the Greek language, and even now they receive things from them and from the Chaldeans.

<margin>Eudoxus received the method of intercalation from the Egyptians.</margin>
**That is:** For Eudoxus set out there with Plato; and both were occupied with the Priests for 13 years, as some have handed down. These Priests, while they excelled in the knowledge of celestial things, otherwise kept it secret, nor did they wish to communicate it to anyone; yet, overcome by both time and obedience, they explained some precepts, while the Barbarians meanwhile concealed many things. They handed over the small portions of day and night running over the 365 days toward the completion of the year. The year was ignored at that time among the Greeks, just as were many other things; until the younger Astrologers received those things from those who translated the records of the Priests into the Greek language, and they still receive them both from them and from the Chaldeans. From which it clearly appears that long before the invasion of Egypt by Alexander the Great, the Egyptians knew and used the <term>intercalation</term> <note>original Greek: ἐμβολισμόν</note> of the year growing out of the four quadrants of the day; indeed, Eudoxus first handed down to the Greeks the secret received from the <term>Hierophants</term> <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>, who had been overcome by gifts and obedience.

# CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS 257 CHAPTER II.

Since the calendar could not consist with an intercalary day <note>An extra day added to the calendar, like a leap day</note>, they likewise detested it as being repugnant to the mystical sacred rites. For since the *epagomenae* <note>original: "αἱ ἐπαγομέναι" — the five extra days added at the end of the Egyptian year</note>, or the days of *Nisi* <note>The Coptic/Egyptian term for the intercalary days</note>, are named after certain Gods, and their birthdays were celebrated on the same day as those whose names they bore; if a sixth *epagomenal* day were added, to which God would it be dedicated, and which God's Epoch would they celebrate? For there were, as we have shown in the *Prodromus*, five Birth-giving Gods <note>original: "Θεοὶ Γενέθλιοι ε´"</note>.

-> OSIRIS ☩ ISIS ☩ NEPHTHYS ☩ TYPHON ☩ APOPHIS <-

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
according to the testimony of Plutarch. If, therefore, a sixth *epagomenal* day were added, there would be two *enaphrades* <note>original: "ἐναφράδες" — unlucky or "nefasti" days</note> or ill-omened days in a row; which was against the institution of the Hierophants <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>. They therefore relaxed the reins deliberately, so that when the course of 1460 years was completed, the ancestral Gods could be said to have traveled through the entire world, as Plutarch also clearly teaches in his book *On Osiris and Isis*. <margin>When the new moon of the Canicular Lustrum began.</margin> Moreover, when the said period was finished, the new moon of the Canicular Lustrum <note>A five-year period or cycle related to the Dog Star, Sirius</note> began on that night which followed the afternoon of the five days of *Nisi*, with the Dog Star rising at nightfall <note>original: "ἀκρονύχως" — at the beginning of the night</note> on the night preceding the month of *Thoth*, and that whole year was called *Sothis* <note>The Egyptian name for the star Sirius</note>. In the following year, on the same night that preceded *Thoth*, observing the rising of the Dog Star—which did not rise in the evening as in the first year, but at midnight—the year of the second Lustrum then began. In the third year, the rising of the Dog Star appeared before the Sun, and from this the third year of the Lustrum began. In the fourth year, the Dog Star could not be seen, because in the south of Egypt it rose in the opposite part of the other hemisphere; and so from the noon of *Thoth* the fourth year of the Lustrum began. Thus, between each year of the Lustrum, a quarter of a day was interposed, and without any intercalation <note>original: "ἐμβολισμῷ"</note> of a whole day. But gradually, one day would creep in. Therefore, the whole controversy among Authors seems to have arisen because they thought the Egyptian civil method of reckoning was different from the Alexandrian, which we say is the same. For just as the fixed year of the Egyptians is the same as the Alexandrian; so the wandering, free, and non-intercalated <note>original: "ἀνεμβολήματῷ"</note> year remained solely in the power of the Egyptian Priests and Astronomers, as has been proved at length in the preceding pages: and Geminus in chapter 6 clearly asserts that the festival of Isis, which in the times of Eudoxus coincided with the winter solstices, was afterwards in his own time a whole month distant from them; which would not have happened if the Egyptians had only a fixed year, and not a wandering and free one. <margin>How the festivals of the Egyptians wander through all the days of the year.</margin> For as Geminus himself testifies in the cited place, in 4 years the Egyptians fall short of the Sun by one day; in 40 years, ten days; and so their festivals anticipated by that many days, lest they should be held according to the same quarters of the year; so much so, that in the space of 120 years they anticipate the festivals by 30 days, that is, a whole month, by looking both to the year of the Sun and to the quarters. Hence, says Geminus, that error which is circulated among the Greeks, since on account of the length of time it was considered worthy of approval, was believed as true even up to our times. For many of the Greeks think that the winter solstices fall on the festival of Isis according to the Egyptians and according to Eudoxus; which is entirely false; for the festival of Isis is distant from the winter solstices by a whole month. ### CLASS VII. HIEROGLYPHIC MATHEMATICS. CHAPTER II.

We have added the festivals that occur in those months, collected from various authors; from the application of which to the first day of the month of Thoth, you will learn the day and year of the first wandering year <note>The "vague year" of 365 days which shifted against the solar seasons</note>, and the placement of the festivals throughout that entire year. Once the year has passed, the application of the first day of Thoth to the second day of the month of Thoth shows the placement and arrangement of all the festivals occurring in that year. Thus, for any given year, if you wish to know the placement and arrangement of the Egyptian festivals appropriate to that year, you will apply the first day of Thoth on the inner wheel to the given day or year on the outer rim, and you will have your goal. Note, however, in this place, that just as the Dog-star Lustrum <note>original: "Lustrum caniculare"; a period of four years</note> composed of a four-year period marks 1460 days, so the Great Dog-star Lustrum marks the years of that cycle. For according to what was cited above, the civil year is 365 days, which, when multiplied by 4, makes 1460 days—exactly the number of days the Sothiac four-year period contains. Moreover, 4 multiplied by 365 years produces that Great Dog-star Lustrum comprised of a course of 1460 years. Therefore, the outer circle, divided into 365 degrees, can be applied both to the days of the Sothiac four-year period and to the years of the Great Lustrum; so that the Egyptians showed a wonderful genius in such a beautiful arrangement. For the festivals which belonged to the Great Lustrum were adapted to the smaller Sothiac period composed of 1460 days; in such a way, indeed, that the Gods are not only thought to circle that Great Orb in the space of 1460 years, but could also be said to have circled the smaller Orb of days comprised in four years. And thus the Priests <term>Hierophantae: those who interpret sacred mysteries</term>, since they could not perform the worship due to the Gods in that Great Lustrum due to the brevity of human life, they performed it for the Gods in the Lustrum of 1460 days. Now let us explain the sacred rites and the use of the wheel.

<margin>Month 1: Thoth.</margin>
The first month, Thoth, signifies nothing else in Egyptian but Mercury, whom the Egyptians call sometimes Thoth, sometimes Thoyth, according to the testimony of Eusebius. The Phoenicians call him Tautus, but the Priests call him <note>original Greek: Σιωθ</note> Sioth, as if you were to say, "The Dog." Therefore, it is not without merit that the first month of the Egyptian year was dedicated by the ancients to Mercury as the author and inventor of the annual arrangement; concerning which, read more extensively in Diodorus, Book 2, Chapter 11, as well as Eusebius and Herodotus.
<margin>Diodorus. Eusebius. Herodotus. Plutarch.</margin>
In this month, the twelfth day was especially sacred to Mercury. But let us hear Plutarch: <note>original Greek: Τῇ μὲν οὖν ἐνάτῃ ἐπὶ δέκα τοῦ πρώτου μηνὸς ἑορτάζοντες τῷ Ἑρμῇ, μέλι καὶ σῦκον ἐσθίουσιν, ἐπιλέγοντες, γλυκὺ ἡ ἀλήθεια.</note> "On the nineteenth day of the first month, celebrating in honor of Hermes, they eat honey and figs, saying: Truth is sweet." Then, on the twenty-second day of the first month, they hold a festival for Mercury, eating honey and figs, saying: Truth is sweet.

<margin>Month 2: Paophi. Plutarch.</margin>
In the second month, which they call Paophi, the birthdays of the "Staffs of the Sun" are celebrated on the 22nd day; so says Plutarch in his book *On Osiris and Isis*: <note>original Greek: Τῇ δευτέρᾳ δὲ τοῦ Παωφὶ βακτηρίας ἡλίου γενέθλ. ἐν λύσει μὲν φθινοπωρινῆς ἰσημερίας.</note> "On the twenty-second day of the month Paophi, after the autumnal equinox, they celebrate a festival day, then calling it the birth of the Sun's staffs." By which, according to Plutarch, they imply that the Sun—as one who has suffered some diminution of heat and light due to his oblique descent toward the Winter Tropic—stands in need of a staff, as if for a kind of prop by which he may be supported. On the sixth day of this month, they celebrate the birth of Harpocrates <note>The child Horus</note>; which Plutarch records in the cited place with these words:
<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
"But they also speak of the love of Leto, and in the month of Paophi an amulet, on the sixth day of the beginning of the month Paophi. And on the <unclear>eighth</unclear> Harpocrates <unclear>... ...</unclear>"

<note>original: "την περὶ τροπὰς χειμερινὰς αὐτὴν κύεῖν."</note> ...that she conceived around the winter solstice. **Therefore it is said that when Isis felt herself to be pregnant, she hung an amulet upon herself on the sixth day of the month of Paophi <note>September/October</note>, and gave birth to Harpocrates <note>The child Horus, often depicted with a finger to his lips</note> around the winter solstice, imperfect and premature; this was because the early flowers and first buds spring forth at that time, and for that reason they offer the first fruits of sprouting beans. During this entire month they also celebrate the sacred rites of Omphta—whom Plutarch calls Omphis—the beneficent Deity:** <note>original: "Ἔτερον δ' ὄνομα τοῦ Θεοῦ τὸν Ὄμφιν εὐεργέτην ὁ Ἑρμαῖος λέγει"</note> **Hermæus says the other name of the God is Omphis, which he interprets as "benefactor"; concerning this, see the more extensive treatment in the description of the hieroglyphic Zodiac in the preceding sections.**

<margin>Month 3: Athyr <note>October/November</note></margin>
On the 17th day of the month of Athyr, the death of Osiris is celebrated: for they say that Typhon <note>Set, the god of chaos</note> trapped Osiris in a chest and cast him into the sea through the Tanitic mouth of the Nile; for which reason that mouth is still considered an object of dread by the Egyptians. <note>original: "Ταῦτα δὲ πραχθῆναι λέγουσιν ἑβδόμῃ ἐπὶ δέκα μηνὸς Ἀθὺρ..."</note> **These things are said to have been done on the 17th day of the month of Athyr, when the Sun enters Scorpio, in the twenty-eighth year of Osiris's reign. And elsewhere it is noted that his being shut in a chest is nothing other than the hiding and diminishing of the waters.** <note>original: "Διὸ μηνὸς Ἀθὺρ ἀφανισθῆναι τὸν Ὄσιριν λέγουσι..."</note> **Therefore they say Osiris disappeared in the month of Athyr when, the Etesian winds <note>Annual Mediterranean winds</note> having entirely ceased, the Nile recedes and the land is stripped bare.**

<margin>Month 4: Choiac <note>November/December</note></margin>
On the 19th day of the month of Choiac, the sacred *Cistophoria* <note>The "Festival of the Chest-Carriers"</note> are celebrated; Plutarch recounts the rituals of the solemnity in these words: <note>original: "Τῇ δὲ ἐννάτῃ ἐπὶ δέκα νυκτὸς ἐπὶ θάλασσαν κάτεισι..."</note> **On the nineteenth day at night, they go down to the sea, and the robe-bearers together with the Priests carry out the sacred chest, which contains a golden casket inside; into this they pour drinkable water they have taken, and a shout is raised by those present crying out that Osiris has been found. Then they mix fertile earth with the water, and having added a mixture of expensive spices and incense, they fashion a small moon-shaped image; this they clothe and adorn, signifying that they consider these Gods to be the very essence of earth and water.**

<margin>Month 5: Tybi <note>December/January</note></margin>
On the [7th] day of the month of Tybi, the return of Isis from Phoenicia is celebrated. Thus Plutarch in the cited passage: <note>original: "Διὸ καὶ θύοντες ἑβδόμῃ τοῦ Τυβὶ μηνὸς..."</note> **Therefore, sacrificing on the seventh day of the month of Tybi—which they call the arrival of Isis from Phoenicia—they fashion out of cakes the image of a bound hippopotamus. By this they imply that the Typhonian power <note>The chaotic force of Set</note> was defeated by Isis; in this same month, the solemnity of Nephthys is celebrated.**

<margin>Month 6: Mechir <note>January/February</note></margin>
In the month of Mechir, the Priests used to purify their inner sanctuaries and offer sacrifices to Canopus; for these rites and ceremonies, see the first volume of this *Oedipus*, in the chapter on Canopus.

<margin>Month 7: Phamenoth <note>February/March</note></margin>
In the month of Phamenoth, they celebrate the festival which they call the "Entry of Osiris into the Moon": thus Plutarch: <note>original: "Ὅτι τῇ νουμηνίᾳ τοῦ Φαμενὼθ μηνὸς ἑορτὴν ἄγουσιν..."</note> **Because on the New Moon of the month of Phamenoth they celebrate a festival, calling it the entry of Osiris into the Moon, at the beginning of spring.**

...they sing, believing that to be the beginning of *Spring*. For in this way, they obscurely suggest the power of Osiris—that is, the Solar power—within the Moon; for the Moon is Isis, the wife of Osiris. Therefore, they call the Moon the mother of the World, assigning to her a nature mixed from both sexes, because having been filled and made pregnant by the Sun, she in turn emits and scatters the generative principles back from herself into the air.

<margin>The 8th Month: Pharmuthi.</margin> In the month of Pharmuthi <note>roughly March/April</note>, they celebrate the festival of Ammon, as we showed above in the hieroglyphic of the Zodiac; for Amun is the Ram-Deity, the presiding spirit of fertility, whose signs exert themselves most greatly when the Sun is ascending in Aries near the beginning of *Spring*. At the same time, they celebrated a festival which, according to Pausanias, they called the "Driving out of Typhon": and according to Plutarch, they would kill a Crocodile, of which Typhon was the symbol. By these rites, they secretly suggest that when the Sun enters Aries (the house of Ammon), the darkness and the vehemence of cold—which are the effects of Typhonic power—are routed and dispelled by the Ammonian power. See what we have handed down concerning these things in the cited place, and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* regarding the significance of the Ram on page 269.
<margin>Pausanias. Plutarch.</margin>

<margin>The 9th Month: Pachon.</margin> In the month of Pachon (or *Pakhons*), which corresponds to May, they performed sacred rites to Serapis—that is, to the subterranean Osiris—whose benefit shines forth most greatly in this month, with the earth luxuriating in every kind of bud and herb. Hence Plutarch interprets this word *Serapis* as "joy": for the Egyptians call the festival of gladness *Saerei*. But see a more profuse treatment of these matters in Volume 1, in the chapter on Serapis. Furthermore, in this month the <term>sphragistae</term> <note>sealers or examiners of sacrificial victims</note> or "seal-bearers" sacrificed red oxen, according to Plutarch, <term>the seal</term> <note>original Greek: τῆς σφραγῖδος</note> (as Castor relates) <term>bearing an engraving of a man sinking to his knees with his hands tied behind his back and a sword held to his throat.</term> The sculpture of the seal was expressed as (*as Castor claims*) *a man sitting down on his knees, with his hands drawn back behind his back, and a sword threatening his throat*.

<margin>The 10th Month: Payni.</margin> In the month of Payni, donkeys paid the penalty for the sake of the detestable Typhon, whom they say resembled a donkey both in sluggishness and stupidity, as well as in color; hence <term>And making cakes in the sacrifices, in the months of Payni and Phaophi they imprint the seal of a bound donkey</term> <note>original Greek: Καὶ πόπανα ποιοῦντες ἐν θυσίαις, τῷ δὲ Παϋνὶ καὶ τῷ Φαωφὶ μηνὸς ἐπιπλάττουσι σφραγῖμον ὄνον δεδεμένον</note>. *In the months of Payni and Phaophi, making cakes in the sacrifices, they imprint upon them the figure of a bound Donkey*.

<margin>The 11th Month: Epiphi.</margin> In the month of Epiphi, which corresponds to July, the preludes of Momphtha <note>likely a reference to Ptah or a specific creative aspect</note> occurred, with the Sun entering into Leo; all the rites and ceremonies looked toward the happy rising of the Nile; concerning which I have written at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* in the hierogrammatic section on the Lion. On the last day of this month, they observe the birthday feast of the eyes of Horus, and they bring forth Songs invoking him who is hidden in the arms of the Sun. So says Plutarch: <term>In the sacred hymns of Osiris they call upon him who is hidden in the arms of the sun, and on the thirtieth day of the month of Epiphi they celebrate the birthday of the eyes of Horus, as they consider not only the moon but also the sun to be the eye and light of Horus</term> <note>original Greek: Ἐν δὲ τοῖς ἱεροῖς ὕμνοις τοῦ Ὀσίριδος ἀνακαλοῦσι τὸν ἐν ταῖς ἀγκάλαις κρυπτόμενον τοῦ ἡλίου...</note>. *In the sacred hymns of Osiris they invoke him who lies hidden in the arms of the Sun; and on the last day of the month of Epiphi they celebrate the birthday of the eyes of Horus, for they consider not only the Moon, but also the Sun to be the eyes of Horus*.

<margin>The 12th Month: Mesori.</margin> In the month of Mesori, they celebrate the solemnities of the Nile, specifically at that very time when the rising of the Nile begins. <term>And not only the Nile, but they simply call every liquid the "outflow of Osiris" in Mesori, and in the sacred processions the water-vessel always honors the God, and they draw the southern branch of the world, and the divine is interpreted as watering and the movement of all things, and it seems to resemble the generative part of nature; and they lead the festival of the Pamylia, which is phallic...</term> <note>original Greek: Οὐ μόνον δέ τὸν Νεῖλον, ἀλλὰ πᾶν ὑγρὸν ἁπλῶς Μεσορὶ Ὀσίριδος ἀπορροὴν καλοῦσι...</note>

# CHAPTER II. 264 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<note>The author is quoting Plutarch's "On Isis and Osiris" here.</note> ...next, they set forth and carry in procession an image whose male organ is threefold. <note>original: "ἑξῆς, ἄγαλμα προτίθενται καὶ περιφέρουσιν, οὗ τὸ αἰδοῖον τριπλάσιον ἐστιν"</note> Not only the *Nile*, but simply all moisture, they call the "outflow of *Osiris*"; and before the sacred rites in the procession, a vessel of water always precedes in honor of the God. They depict the King and the southern region of the World by a fig leaf; they interpret the fig leaf as the irrigation and movement of all things, and it seems by its nature to resemble the generative member. Furthermore, when celebrating the *Pamylia* festivals—which are performed using a phallus, that is, an image of the male member—they display and carry around an image whose penis is threefold. They are secretly suggesting that God is the beginning of all things; and every beginning multiplies that which is produced by it; and thus moisture is the beginning of all things, without which the sensible World, which they call Horus, cannot be preserved.

And these are the solemnities which the Egyptians were accustomed to celebrate throughout the course of the year in honor of the Gods they worshipped. These festivities, if you look at the common and civil year, were fixed and immobile; but they were wandering and free if you consider the method used by the <term>Hierophants</term><note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries.</note>. For they wished the Gods, in the space of 1460 years, to wander through all the regions of the World, and to pervade every degree of the Zodiac and day of the months in the succession of time, lest any part of the World or portion of annual time be deprived of the so necessary presence of the Gods, as we have shown above from Geminus. Moreover, they traced all sacred rites back to four principal Deities: namely, first to Sothis, who is Mercury; second to Isis; third to Osiris; and fourth to Horus, whom they also call Kemin. Thus, just as these four Deities are restored to their beginnings every four years (that is, 1460 days), so in 1460 years—that great course of the <term>Sothic cycle</term><note>A period of 1,460 Julian years (1,461 Egyptian years) required for the Egyptian calendar to realign with the stars.</note>—they return to the point from which they started. We have expressed these four Deities in the inner circle, each with their own hieroglyphics. And let these remarks suffice concerning the Great Sothic Year.

*   **Birthday of the Gods**

### The Sothic Cycles
*Two concentric textual bands explain the mathematical cycles:*
*   **The Fixed Sothic or Canicular Period of four years, consisting of 1461 days.** <note>The "minor" cycle account for the leap year shift.</note>
*   **The Wandering Sothic or Canicular Great Period of 1461 years.** <note>The "major" cycle where the Egyptian "wandering year" of 365 days eventually realigns with the solar year.</note>

### The Four Great Quarters
*The diagram is divided into four major quadrants:*
1.  **Year of THOTH**: 365 days / Hierophantic Year 1.
2.  **Year of ISIS**: 365 days / Hierophantic Year 365.
3.  **Year of OSIRIS**: 365 days / Hierophantic Year 730.
4.  **Year of HORUS**: 365 days / Hierophantic Year 1095.

### The Central Emblem
In the center of the wheel is the Earth globe, encircled by an **Ouroboros** <note>The serpent biting its own tail, representing eternity and cyclical time.</note>. Within its coils are four nodes featuring:
*   **Hermes** (ΕΡΜΗϹ) seated at the top.
*   **Aroueris** (ΑΡΟΥΗΡΙϹ) <note>Horus the Elder.</note> in a shrine at the bottom.
*   The inscription: **Venerable of the Gods** <note>original: "Θεῶν σεϐαστός"</note>.

Note, Reader: the fixed festivals of the Months show the specific day of the Month by their markers. However, the names of the 12 Gods displayed in Coptic letters indicate that these Gods have no fixed seats, but move forward through the calendar, so that in the space of 1461 years they complete the entire circle of 12 Months. This span is also called the Great Hierophantic Year or Period.

# CHAPTER II. 266 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

->Explanation of the Chronological Wheel, in which everything said thus far regarding the Months and Festivals is contained in a single synopsis.<-

The outer circuit contains the days of the entire expanded Egyptian year of 365 days; beneath which are contained the names of the Egyptian Months, each consisting of 30 days, along with the five intercalary days <note>original: "epagomenis"</note> which the Egyptians call the days of the Nile. Beneath this, however, a circle is placed divided into twelve months of the "yearly cycle" <note>original: "ἐνιαυτησιῶν"</note>, that is, of thirty days, together with the five intercalary days. And this is the **fixed year** of the Egyptians: four of these years constitute the Sothic period <note>term: Sothic period (Lustrum Sothiacum). A cycle based on the rising of the star Sirius, known as the Dog Star or 'Canicula'</note>, or the lesser Canicular cycle, or the cycle "of the August Gods" <note>original: "θεῶν σεβαστῶν"</note>; so that the first year is held sacred to Sothis, that is, Mercury; the second to Isis; the third to Osiris; and finally the fourth to Horus. Moreover, the aforementioned period corresponds to four Julian years containing a leap year; and it can be considered under a double rationale: either insofar as this four-year period is civil, or insofar as it is mystic and priestly <note>original: "hierophanticum"</note>. The former, after four years, is accustomed to intercalate one day; the latter, having spurned all intercalation, gives free rein to the preceding times. Hence we have arranged another wheel, movable at its center, upon which we have placed the festivals of the Egyptian Gods and other solemnities; it is called by Authors the "Great Year of the God" <note>original: "ἐνιαυτὸς μέγας τοῦ Θεοῦ"</note>, the great wandering Sothic year, or the Canicular Period, and it consists of 1460 years, at the end of which period it returns to approximately the first day of Thoth. For the Gods, and their festivals, wander through all the months of the fixed year over a span of 365 leap-year increments; and thus there is no day in the months which the Gods cannot be said to have traversed.

<margin>A serpent biting its tail signifies the year.</margin>
And this is the great priestly or hieroglyphic year, by which they mystically indicated that there is no part of the World which the Gods do not penetrate with their beneficent presence, animate, and preserve by necessary influence. They exhibit this aptly through a serpent going into a circle and biting its tail with its head, as Horus <note>referring here to Horapollo, an author on hieroglyphs</note> bears witness.

<margin>Horus. The four Divinities presiding over the Sothic Period.</margin>
In its revolution, it effectively created four circles, by which the lesser Sothic Period of four years was indicated, over each of which they placed a Divinity presiding, adorned with their own hieroglyphics. Here you see in the first circle Sothis presiding, that is, Mercury sitting and distinguished by a dog's head, as the Author of the arrangement of the year and seasons; in the second circle Isis occurs sitting, conspicuous with a female face, and she was said to preside over the second year; in the third circle Osiris sits upon a throne, distinguished by a Hawk's head, presiding over the third year; in the fourth circle Horus is seen in that figure which you perceive, the president of the fourth year. For just as these Divinities traverse the entire Sothic four-year period in a span of 1460 days, so they are said to complete the great period in 1460 years, together with the rest of the attendants and festivities assigned to them. Furthermore, just as one day is added every four years in the lesser period, so when the great period is finished, a year is added, so that they are restored to their original places.

Note also, that just as the year of the lesser period is 365 days, so one year of the great period is considered to be 365 years, which multiplied by 4—

It uses the Ouroboros (serpent biting its tail) to symbolize the divine presence permeating all time and space.</summary>

multiplied, they complete a circuit of 1460 years. This period—from its first institution, which we suppose was established by Hermes <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Egyptians attributed their science and laws.</note> in the year 1837 BC, as we showed in the Pamphilian Obelisk—has been completed twice up to our present year of 1653. Thus, today, the first day of the month of Thoth, according to the calculation of the Hierophants <note>term: Hierophants (priests who interpreted sacred mysteries)</note>, in the great wandering year, falls on the 25th day of the month of Phamenoth. For if you add 1653 years from Christ to the present year to the 1837 years BC (when, by hypothesis, Hermes established this calculation), you will have a total of 3490 years. When divided by the 1460 years of the greater Sothic luster <note>term: Sothic luster (the 1460-year cycle based on the rising of the star Sirius, or Sothis)</note>, the quotient is 2, with 570 days remaining. These days make up one year, six months, and 25 days, which correspond to the 25th day of the month of Phamenoth.

These things being established: if you wish to know which months the feasts and solemnities of the Gods correspond to today, proceed as follows. Turn the wheel of the great Sothic year (or Sothic luster) until its marker, which resembles a lily, is over the 25th day of Phamenoth; for by our hypothesis, the beginning of this Sothic cycle corresponds to this day at the present time. The days of the months to which the feasts and ceremonies arranged around the wheel correspond will give you the answer you seek. You shall operate no differently in this Sothic cycle when it is adjusted to the indicators of any other times. If, however, you desire to know which Deity out of the four August Ones <note>original: "Σεβαστῶν" (Sebastōn) - the Venerable or August ones, likely referring to the four primary deities governing the cycle</note> presides over this present year, do this: Divide the 570 days remaining from the previous division by 365; you will have a quotient of 1 and 205 remaining days, which are the days of the second year of the Sothic luster. You shall therefore pronounce that ISIS <note>original: "ΙΣΙΝ" (Isin)</note> presides over this present year; and that the beginning of the great wandering Sothic cycle falls on the twenty-fifth of Phamenoth, as was said, which corresponds to March 21st, the day of the equinox. We have handed these things down according to the mind of the Hierophants. But those who wish to adapt this greater luster to the Egyptian or Alexandrian years should divide the 3490 years since the cycle's institution by 1461; the result will be 2 and 578/1461. These fractions, resolved into days, will give one year, seven months, and eight days, which will be the 8th day of the month of Pharmuthi, corresponding to the third of April. Having premised these things, it now remains for us to say something concerning the modern calculation of the Copts.

Furthermore, the said *Supplement* has perhaps reached the notice of only a few, and it abounds in many errors due to the carelessness of the printer and the proofreader.

### CHAPTER III. 268 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<note>original: "تأريخ السنين ابونا آدم"</note> The *Era of the years of our Father Adam*, which the monk Maximus <note>Maximus the Confessor, a 7th-century theologian</note> calls the "Years of Adam," which they used in organizing both the Solar and Lunar cycles, and those things that follow the cycles. The second era begins from the start of the Kingdom of the Greeks <note>The Seleucid Era, beginning 312 BCE</note>; concerning these years, see the *Prodromus* <note>Kircher's earlier work, *Prodromus Coptus*</note>. The third is the instructional era from Diocletian, which they employ in inscribing books, letters, and monuments; Albateni <note>Al-Battani, a famous Arab astronomer</note> calls this <note>original: "تأريخ القبطي"</note> *Tarich Elkupti*, the *Coptic Era*. The Copts, however, call it <note>original: "ϯⲁⲣⲭⲏ ⲛ̅ⲧⲉ ⲛⲓⲙⲁⲣⲧⲩⲣⲟⲥ"</note> or in Arabic <note>original: "تأريخ الشهدا الظهار"</note> the *Era of the Holy Martyrs*. In Coptic <note>original: "ϯⲣⲟⲙⲡⲓ ⲛ̅ⲧⲉ ⲛⲓⲙⲁⲣⲧⲩⲣⲟⲥ"</note> that is, the *Year of the Martyrs*. Some add to these Eras or Epochs a fourth: that of Nabonassar, King of the Chaldeans; but since only astronomers use it, as it has no place in civil reckoning, we have deliberately chosen to omit it. For the Era of Nabonassar was not civil, nor commonly known to the Egyptians, but only to astronomers, who borrowed it from the Chaldeans. As our most learned 
<margin>Petavius.</margin>
Petavius <note>Denis Pétau, a Jesuit chronologist and contemporary of Kircher</note> proves in a certain letter given to me: namely, through the work and study of Callisthenes, who was a disciple of Aristotle. At his master's urging, while he was in the retinue of Alexander the Great, he sent the most ancient observations of the Chaldeans received at Babylon back to Greece. From there, they were brought into Egypt and employed by astronomers, especially by Ptolemy, who seems to have borrowed them from Hipparchus. Simplicius testifies to all these things in his commentary on 
<margin>Simplicius.</margin>
the second book of Aristotle's *On the Heavens*. Thus, whatever we said regarding this era in the *Prodromus*, we do not wish it to be understood otherwise than we have stated; nor do we think the era from the death of Alexander (which is also called the Era of Philip) should be confused with the era of <note>original: "دولقرنين"</note> *Dulkarnain* <note>Lord of the Two Horns, a title for Alexander the Great in the Quran</note>, since one differs from the other by nearly 12 years. These matters can be read more extensively in the works of Petavius, whom I praised above.

Regarding the Era of the years of the World, it must be noted that the Greeks and Latins, departing without any cause from the true calculations of the Holy Bible, reckon the years from the creation of things to the birth of Christ as 5199. This number exceeds the true accounts of Moses by one thousand two hundred and fifty years. But the Egyptian founders of the Greek Reckoning, having imitated them, interpreted the eras of the World in various ways so that they might accommodate them to the art of calculation. From this liberty were born three technical eras, which, having been devised or transformed by the Masters for the use of Calculation, posterity accepted as the true years of the World; these are the Dionysian, Alexandrian, and Antiochian eras, concerning which see Petavius in his work *On the Doctrine of Times*, and Scaliger. Since these eras are not natural but were invented to establish a calculation, they also differ greatly. The era of the Hebrews reckons 3760 years from the creation of the World to Christ. Thus says the Hebrew book of calculation, the title of which is:

-><note>original Hebrew: "לקט קציר לסוד העבור"</note> The Collector of Gleanings concerning the Mystery of the Calendar (or Intercalation)<-

That is, *The collector of ears of grain concerning the mystery of calculation, or of the embolism* <note>The insertion of leap months</note>; for what we call "Calculation," they call (naming the whole by a part) *embolism*, or in Hebrew <note>original: "עיבור"</note> *Ghibbur*, that is, *pregnancy*. This is a most elegant metaphor, as if the year carries an implanted month within itself, just as a pregnant woman carries a fetus in her womb. In this book, therefore, from the creation of the world to the era of Christ, they count 3760 years.

For since 25 Solar years (excluding leap years) contain 9,125 days, there occur within them 309 lunations <note>A lunation is the time from one new moon to the next.</note>. According to astronomical calculation, these consist of 9,124 days, 22 hours, 5 minutes, and 18 seconds; thus, all lunations will return after 25 years to the same day on which they previously occurred, anticipating the time by only one hour, 8 minutes, and 12 seconds. This result cannot be achieved by any logic if the nineteen-year cycle <note>The Metonic cycle, commonly used in the Julian/Gregorian calendars.</note> is applied to the aforementioned Egyptian years. From this also emerges the reason why the Ancients never intercalated <note>Inserted a leap day</note> their sacred years, whereas they did intercalate the civil or Alexandrian years every fourth year. But having discussed this cycle at length just before, let us now proceed to the Calculation used by the Coptic or Alexandrian Church. It uses a double cycle, Solar and Lunar; the former they call in Coptic <term>ⲡⲓⲕⲩⲕⲗⲟⲥ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲣⲏ</term> <note>pi-kyklos ente-pri</note> and in Arabic <term>دور الشمسي</term> <note>dawr al-shamsi</note>, meaning the **Circle of the Sun**; the latter they call <term>ⲡⲓⲕⲩⲕⲗⲟⲥ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲓⲟϩ</term> <note>pi-kyklos ente-pioh</note> and <term>دور القمري</term> <note>dawr al-qamari</note>, the **Circle of the Moon**. The Solar cycle consists of 28 years, and the Lunar of 19 years. *If you wish to know the day of the week for any month, take the character of the year, or the sign (in the column) corresponding to the solar cycle; to this add the character of the month (in its own column) and the sum will give the sought day of the week, after casting out 7 as many times as possible.* <note>The "character" refers to a numerical value assigned to years and months in medieval and early modern computus (calendar calculation).</note>

# PROPOSITION IV.

->To find the Paschal Cycle by another method.<-

If you want to know the calculation of the cycle <note>original: "kyqlas" (Arabic transliteration of the Greek 'kyklos')</note> of the year you are in, how much it is, subtract the years of our father Adam nineteen by nineteen; whatever remains that does not reach nineteen, that is the cycle of that year. Because the cycle grows from one to nineteen, and when it reaches nineteen, it returns to one.

*When you wish to know the number of the Lunar cycle of this year in which you are, and what it may be, cast away from the years of our father Adam 19 as many times as possible, and that which shall be the remainder, and is not 19, that will be the cycle of that year; because the cycle is a revolution of years from unity to 19, and from there back to unity.* <note>The "Years of Adam" refers to the Anno Mundi era, dating from the biblical creation.</note>

# PROPOSITION V.

->To find the Foundation of the Year.<-

And if you want to know the Base <note>original: "al-as" (the foundation or root)</note> and its calculation, which is the cycle of the Sun—this calculation grows from one to seven and from seven returns to one—and if you want the cycle of the year you are in, take the years of our father Adam and add to them their fourth part. If there is a fraction like a quarter or a half, leave it. When the quarter is added to the root, join the total and cast it out seven by seven; whatever remains that does not reach seven is the cycle of the Sun for that year you are in, and that is the Base. ۞

*That is, if you wish to know the foundation of the year (which is a certain cycle of the Sun, proceeding from one to 7, and from there returning to unity), take the years of our Father Adam, and add to them their fourth parts; and if there be fractions of numbers, you shall leave them; and if there be a complete fourth with the root, you shall join its sum, and cast away from it seven as many times as possible; and if there be any remainder, and it be not seven, that will be the cycle of the Sun for this year which is currently running, and this is the sought foundation.* <note>The "Foundation" or "Base" here refers to the Dominical Letter or the solar shift that determines which day of the week a year begins on.</note>

# PROPOSITION VI.

->To find the day on which the beginning of any month falls.<-

If you want to know which day will be the first of the month, look at the sign of the month you want and add to it the Base of that year. Whatever you have gathered, subtract seven from it; whatever remains of the seven—if one remains, the first of the month is Sunday; if two remain, it is Monday. ۞

*If you wish to know which is the first day of the month, see the character of the month you desire, and add it to the foundation of the current year, and from the total subtract seven; and the remainder of the seven, if it be 1, the first day of the month will be the 1st day of the week <note>Sunday</note>; if 2, the second day of the month will be the 2nd day of the week <note>Monday</note>, and so with the rest.*

### CHAPTER III. 274 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

And to these rules <note>original: "Canonibus"</note> the rules of the Ethiopian calculation correspond exactly <note>literally "to the fingernail," a Latin idiom for precision</note>, which I would gladly include here if the constraints of time permitted. For this same reason, I omit the expanded Arabic-Coptic-Latin Martyrology <note>a catalog of saints and martyrs arranged by their feast days</note>. However, so that the curious reader may know which day of the Julian months corresponds to which Egyptian day, I have decided to subjoin here a Table <note>original: "Pinacem," from the Greek word for tablet or map</note> of said days. Beneath this, we have placed another table of the months, in which we have set the months of the Hebrews, Syrians, and Arabs in a parallel arrangement, corresponding as closely as possible to the months of the Copts, so that if anyone wishes to compare one with the other, they might have the means to do so.

It must be noted here, however, that since most of the months of the Eastern peoples are lunar and arrange their days according to the New Moons <note>original: "Neomenias"</note>, they do not correspond in every respect to the days of the Coptic months—which are solar and fixed—but rather change their positions. Nor do the solar days of the Easterners always correspond to the Egyptian days, but they occupy different positions within the same month. The third Table contains the Nomenclature of the days of the week used by various peoples of the East; I have added this to the Monthly Table <note>original: "Menopinacio"</note> so that we do not seem to have omitted anything the reader might desire.

## Use of this Table.

If you wish to know which <term>Julian day</term> <note>The Julian calendar was the standard calendar of the Roman world and the precursor to our modern Gregorian calendar.</note> corresponds to any given day of an Egyptian month, look for the Egyptian day in the first column, then the name of the Egyptian month at the top of the Table, and the intersecting cell will give the corresponding day of the Julian month: thus, you will find that the sixteenth day of the month <term>Mechir</term> <note>The sixth month of the Egyptian calendar.</note> corresponds to the tenth of February; the twentieth of <term>Mesori</term> to the thirteenth of August, and so on for the rest.

# GYÖRGY LIPPAY
<note>Original: Georgio Lippay (1600–1666), a prominent Hungarian archbishop, alchemist, and gardener.</note>

### Archbishop of Esztergom, <note>Original: Strigoniensi</note> Privy Councilor to His
### Sacred Imperial and Royal Majesty, Primate of Hungary, and
### Grand Chancellor of the Kingdom.

<image-desc>A large decorative woodcut initial 'A'. The letter is constructed from architectural elements and foliage, with a figure of a saint or scholar holding a book and a staff standing within the central space of the letter.</image-desc>

*As I am about to hand down in this place that more secret "many-skilled" mastery <note>original: πολυτεχνίαν (polytechnian)</note> of the Egyptians, which posterity has called Mechanics, I found no one besides You, most sacred Prelate, to whom I might inscribe so noble, pleasant, and worthy an argument for the curiosity of Princes. For You, beyond the other aids of the disciplines with which you are equipped, have gained such a name and reputation for yourself through your knowledge of this wonderful and almost divine art, that in the opinion of all, you deserve to be called and held as "one of many devices and many skills" <note>original: πολυμήχανος καὶ πολυτεχνής (polymēchanos kai polytechnēs)</note>, just as Polybius <note>A Greek historian of the Hellenistic period.</note> once recorded concerning Archimedes. Those delightful retreats of Your gardens bear witness to this more than enough; they are equipped, as I hear, with such a variety of hydraulic machines that spectators testify to having seen few similar things in other places. Rightly, therefore, this present theme of discussion was owed to Your name; not because I hoped that I could add any ornament to Your fame (by which you are renowned in the world) through my writings, but so that the efforts of my studies, inscribed to Your name, might in this way obtain more authority, and that You might have some token of my respect for You. It is, I confess, a thin and crude service; but it will be held in value by Your Highness for this reason: that it was performed and presented not so much by my own will, as by the commanding will of the Great Emperor. Farewell, most worthy Prelate, and look with favor upon my studies.*

# CLASS VIII
## The Mechanics of the Egyptians.
### PREFACE.

<margin>How the Mechanics of the Egyptians are treated here.</margin>
Guided by the proper thread of order, we descend from the *Astrology of the Egyptians*—that is, from the *Heavens*—into their earthly dwellings, so that the wondrous fruits produced at all times by the ingenious industry of the Egyptians might shine forth from the marvels of this treatise. While we do this, let no one think we intend to provide Mechanics supported by mathematical demonstrations in this place, for that would be entirely outside our scope; rather, relying on historical accounts, we provide that which places the stupendous genius and prodigious inventions of the Egyptians before the eyes of the curious Reader. Furthermore, we shall explain the hieroglyphic principles shining forth within them; the remaining matters concerning mathematical principles are reserved for the great Work which we call *Universal Mechanics*.

<margin>Division of the treatise on Egyptian Mechanics.</margin>
We have titled this Class "The Mechanics of the Egyptians," and it is divided into three primary types used by them: the first was *Architectural*; the second *Organic* <note>In this context, "Organic" refers to the use of machines or "organa," such as pulleys and cranes</note>, which considers the various types of instruments customarily used in the erection of buildings, columns, and statues; the third is *Thaumaturgy* <note>original: "Θαυματουργική" - wonder-working or magic</note>, and it consisted of the fabrication of certain hidden machines drawn from the deepest springs of nature. These they adorned with such genius and subtlety that all posterity believed them to be not the work of men, but of Demons—utterly *unbelievable and paradoxical* <note>original: "ἄπιστα prorsus καὶ παράδοξα"</note>. And although I do not deny that the labor of Demons was occasionally involved with them, it will be my role here—that is, the role of Oedipus <note>Kircher casts himself as Oedipus, the solver of riddles</note>—to demonstrate through various modes and reasons that works of this kind by no means exceeded the limits of human power, but had their principles founded in the innermost recesses of nature. Let us therefore begin the business with the favor of God.

---

### PRELUDE I.
#### Concerning Egyptian Measures.

<image-desc>Decorative initial Q set within a square woodcut border featuring a central flower surrounded by symmetrical scrolling leaves and foliage.</image-desc>
Since mention will be made throughout this treatise of Egyptian measures and weights, it seemed best to first introduce each one here, lest the curious Reader be entangled in a confusion of measures used by other Nations with those of the Egyptians. In this way, one can form a more secure judgment regarding the authorities of the things to be cited, which ancient Writers describe everywhere.

Certainly, among the other subjects in which the tireless industry of scholars has sweated to determine until now, the subject of weights and measures occupies a significant place; it is indeed as abstruse as it is difficult, and by no one...

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 281 PROPOSITION I.

...matters penetrated this far by me. I find no other reason for this difficulty <margin>A treatise on weights and measures is difficult, and why.</margin> than the diverse uses and customs of different nations, by which I will not say only nations, but even individual towns seem to disagree among themselves. Added to this is the varying condition of times and the will of Princes, by which—as the necessity of public affairs demands—new laws are sometimes established while previous ones are annulled; at other times, the value of things to be acquired through civil contracts is increased or diminished. From this perpetual cycle of changes, a great uncertainty of things must necessarily arise. This holds true in all matters depending on the will of Princes, but especially in this subject of weights and measures, which are, as it were, certain instruments of justice by which that which belongs to each person is determined. Therefore, let no one wonder if they see such great inconsistency among authors disputing this <margin>Equivocation of authors regarding Ancient measures</margin> subject; for, if you except the names themselves, the determined quantity of weights and measures, especially those of the Ancients, is not only uncertain but so corrupted by the equivocation of authors that hardly any certain knowledge of them can be obtained. Since I beheld this calamity of literature not without pain, I decided that the sources themselves must be approached so that something certain might finally be established, as will appear from the following names. These have been extracted from the Coptic Nomenclator, which the Copts call the <margin>The Coptic Nomenclator or Great Scale.</margin> *Great Scale* <note>original: *Scala Magna*</note>, published by us in Rome in the year 1643, and are set forth more fully in this place.

Four kinds of measures are proposed in the *Scale*, of which those of the <margin>Four kinds of Egyptian measures.</margin> first kind are measures of intervals <note>distances</note>, which we use in commerce and the dimension of fields, such as: the foot, the palm, the ell, the arm, the pace, the cubit, the reed, the stadium, the mile, the parasang, and the league. Of the second kind are measures of dry goods, such as among the Hebrews were the Cor, the Omer, the Ephah, and the Kab; and among the Greeks the Medimnos, the Choenix, and the Kotyle; and among the Romans the Modius. Of the third kind are measures of liquids, such as the Hebrew Bath, Hin, and Log; the Greek Amphora, Urna, Metreta, and Congius; and the Roman Sextarius and Cyathus. Of the fourth kind are the names of various weights, such as the Hebrew Kikkarim <note>Talents</note>, Minas, Shekels, and Gerahs; and the Greek and Roman Talent, Pound, Ounce, Denarius, and Drachma. Although each of these is treated in the *Scale*, because they may lead the reader into various doubts, I have decided to describe them here more clearly.

The measures of the ancient Egyptians suitable for measuring intervals were: <margin>Egyptian measures for measuring intervals.</margin>

> **ⲡⲓⲗⲉⲕⲟⲥ ✣ ϣⲉⲣⲧⲱ ✣ ⲟⲩϣⲟⲧ ✣ ⲡⲓⲕⲁϣ ⲛ̀ⲧⲉⲡⲓⲙⲓⲛϣⲓ ✣ ϯⲥⲧⲁⲇⲓⲟⲛ ✣ ⲡⲓⲡⲁⲣⲁⲥⲁⲅⲅⲓⲟⲛ ✣**

*Pilekos* <note>Πιλεκοϲ</note> is an Egyptian measure, the same as what the Greeks call <term>Lichas</term> <note>Λιχὰς</note> and the <margin>Πιλεκοϲ Pilucos.</margin> Arabs call <term>Pheter</term> <note>فتر</note>; it is the interval between the thumb and the index finger when they are stretched out as far as possible. Thus Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note> says: *If you stretch the thumb against the part opposite the index finger, the middle space is called the lichas* <note>original Greek: Εἰ δὲ τὸν μέγαν δάκτυλον τῷ λιχάνῳ ἀντιτείνας, τὸ μέσον λίχας</note>, that is, it is a measure of ten fingers. Thus the cited author:

# PRELIMINARY I. 282 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>What an *orthodoron* is.</margin>
The distance from the base of the thumb to the tip of the [index] finger is ten digits. *The interval between the thumb and the highest part of the index finger makes ten digits. But the "orthodoron" is longer than the "lichas" <note>The lichas is the span between thumb and index finger</note>, specifically by one digit; I interpret "orthodoron" as the "straight palm," namely the distance between the first part of the palm, which they call the "karpos" <note>the wrist</note>, and the tip of the middle finger. So say Pollux and Hesychius.*

<margin>What *Shepto* is. What a *dochme* is.</margin>
The Egyptians call the Palm *Shepto* <note>Coptic: Ϣⲉⲡⲧⲱ</note>, which the Arabs call *Schabar* <note>Arabic: شبر</note>; it consists of four digits and is called a *dochme* by the Greeks. Thus Pollux: *A "dochme" is four fingers closed together.* For we measure by the hand held transversely. Aristophanes uses this measure in *The Knights*. The Sausage-seller, speaking of leather, mocks Cleon: *And before the day was out, it was larger than two "dochmai"* <note>about two palms' breadth</note>. Indeed, *dochme*, *daktylodochme*, *palaiste*, and *doron* all signify the same thing, and each is described by Hesychius as being *four digits wide*.

<margin>What *ohiot* is. The Cubit varied among the Egyptians.</margin>
The *ohiot* <note>Coptic: ⲟϩⲓⲟⲧ</note> measure, which the Arabs call *al-ba'a al-qama* <note>the fathom or stature</note>, is the same as the "ulna" <note>the reach of the arms</note>; it is the extension of both arms in length, which is equal to a man's height. From the Coptic, we interpret this as the "greater cubit." To understand this, it must be noted that the cubit was varied among the Egyptians. For one was 24 digits, another 32. One equaled a rod, or a reed, or a pole; another equaled the stature of a man. So says the Arab Abulfeda in the *Prolegomena* of his *Cosmography*; his words are:

<margin>Abulfeda</margin>
> <note>original Arabic: واعلموا ان بين القدما المصر والمحدثين ايضا اختلافا...</note>
> "And know that between the ancients of Egypt and the moderns there is also a difference in the convention regarding the cubit, the mile, and the parasang. As for the digit, there is no difference between them, for they all agree that every digit is six moderate barleycorns placed belly-to-belly. As for the cubit, the disagreement between them is real: for among the ancients it was thirty-two digits, and among the moderns it is twenty-four digits; thus the cubit of the ancients is longer than the cubit of the moderns by eight digits. And this is the secret of the priests."

<margin>The greatest cubit.</margin>
Furthermore, the Rabbis also affirm that a digit consists of 6 grains of barley in these words:

<margin>The Rabbis.</margin>
> <note>original Hebrew: ויש לאמה ו׳ טפחים וטפח אחד ד׳ אצבעות...</note>
> "And the cubit has 6 palms, and one palm has 4 digits by the thumb, and a digit has 6 grains of barley; and this is the true legal cubit of the Tabernacle, the Torah, and the Prophets."

<margin>The legal cubit.</margin>
*Every cubit has six palms, and the palms have four digits at the thumb, and the digit has six grains of barley; and this is the true legal cubit, and that of building—namely, that which the Law uses in the description of buildings and structures.* Rashi also affirms this in this place: *A digit has six grains of barley.* These things harmonize with the Syriac: *A digit is the measure of six grains of barley.* From these things it is clear that the lesser cubit, namely of 24 digits, is equal to the Mosaic cubit—

<margin>Rashi. The lesser cubit is equal to the legal cubit of 24 digits.</margin>

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 283 PROPOSITION I.

<margin>What a cubit is</margin>
...or legal cubit. Now, a cubit is a length as great as the distance from the bend of the arm, or the outer prominence <note>the elbow</note>, to the tip of the middle finger; or, what is the same thing, from the center of the chest to the elbow itself or the bend of the arm; which space, according to the testimony of Pollux <note>Julius Pollux, a 2nd-century Greek grammarian</note>, is exactly equal to the former: <margin><note>original Greek: Απὸ δὲ τοῦ ὠλεκράνου...</note> That is, from the bend of the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, the interval of a cubit contains one and a half feet, to which the interval from the middle of the chest to the bend of the elbow is equal.</margin> This kind of cubit contains, as I have said, six palms, and a palm contains four finger-breadths at the thumb; consequently, one cubit is twenty-four fingers long, which is the common Egyptian and legal Hebrew cubit we have already explained. From this it is clear that four such cubits, when taken together, perfectly fulfill the length of a man (which is measured by the extension of the arms) and his height or stature. These things being premised, let us now proceed to the rest.

<margin>
**Pikash**
**ntepiho-**
**sh**
Measuring rod.
</margin>
**Pikash ntepihosh** or also **Pikash ntepikhosh** <note>Coptic terms</note> I have interpreted in the *Scala* <note>Kircher's Coptic-Arabic dictionary</note> as a measuring rod; and applying myself to a more diligent scrutiny of this word, I finally discovered that it signifies the "reed of the Ibis" or the Egyptian Stork. Thus, this word is understood to be composed of **Pikash** and **Pi-hosh**, the former signifying a leg, shin, reed, or stalk, and the latter signifying the Ibis or Stork; as if you were to say, the "pace" or "ell" of the Ibis. For it was first discovered and observed from the gait of the Ibis. For as Clement of Alexandria <margin>Clement of Alexandria</margin> rightly says: <note>original Greek: Ἀριθμῷ δὲ ἐπινοίας...</note> <margin>The pace of the Ibis as an Egyptian measure</margin> *Namely, that among living creatures, the Ibis seems to have provided the Egyptians with the very beginning of the invention of number and measure.* For the ancient Egyptians were accustomed, for the most part, to use measures established from the movements of animals; since these animals always acted the same way by natural necessity, the measures adopted were also established on a more certain and solid foundation. What sort of thing this "pace of the Ibis" was, now remains to be investigated. Certainly, I find that it equaled the height of a man: and at the same time, it was the measure of the "Ibiac triangle." Thus says Abenephi <note>Ahmad ibn 'Ali al-Bunni, an occult writer Kircher frequently cites</note> concerning the sacred worship of the Egyptians; his words are as follows:

<margin>Abenephi.</margin>
->And the *Baa* of the Egyptians is the height of a man; its name is the Great Pace of the Crane and the measure of the Crane-triangle,<-
->and this is the secret of the Priests.<-

<margin>What the great pace of the Ibis is.</margin>
*The Baa is an Egyptian measure as great as the height of a perfect man; and this they called the great pace of the Crane, and the measure of the Ibiac triangle; and this was the secret of the Priests.* What the Ibiac triangle is, we have discussed elsewhere: but as for what or how great the Ibiac pace was, it can hardly be said how much I have sweated in finding it; nevertheless, God granting, I have extracted the secret, as I shall show. For since the height of a man consists of four common Egyptian cubits, and one cubit consists of six palms, and a palm of four fingers; one common cubit must necessarily consist of twenty-four fingers, and consequently the **Oushoti** or **Baa** (which above, as in our *Scala*, we interpreted as the measure perfectly filling the space of both arms extended in length) will consist of 96 fingers. But a mystical or sacred Egyptian cubit of just as many fingers, which they call the pace of the Ibis,

<meta>catchword: inue- (investigating)</meta>

<summary>This page defines the standard Egyptian and Hebrew cubit based on human anatomy and introduces the "Ibis pace" (Baa), a sacred measurement equivalent to a man's height or four common cubits. Kircher links these measurements to the natural movements of animals and the "Ibiac triangle," a secret of the Egyptian priesthood.</summary>
