# EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
<sig>N n 4</sig>
<meta>catchword PIS</meta>

<margin>
Abenephi. <note>Ibn Wahshiyya, an Arabic author often cited by Kircher for Egyptian lore.</note>
Abulfeda. <note>A 14th-century Syrian historian and geographer.</note>
</margin>
I find it by this reasoning. Since the leg or shin of the Ibis—according to the testimony of *Abenephi* and *Abulfeda*—is equal to the "greater cubit" of the Egyptians, namely 32 digits <note>A "digit" or finger-breadth was a standard unit of ancient measurement.</note>; <margin>The Ibiac triangle.</margin> and since the Ibis also forms an *equilateral triangle* <note>original: "τρίγωνον ἰσόπλευρον"</note> while walking, according to *Plutarch*; the "Ibiac triangle" will be 96 digits, *having the same perimeter* <note>original: "ἰσοπερίμετρον"</note> as three cubits of *thirty-two digits* <note>original: "τριάκοντα-δύο δακτύλοις"</note> each, which corresponds to the height of a human being, whose stature consists of four cubits. And this is that mystery of the Priests of which *Abenephi* speaks, which the Coptic name **MAHI** <note>Coptic for "cubit."</note> confirms. They were accustomed to write this in two ways: first, as **MAHI** and the cubit of 32 digits; then by this method: **MAHI**, by which they denote the "greatest cubit," which the *Scala* <note>A Coptic-Arabic dictionary or "ladder" of words.</note> calls **the land of the reaching** <note>original: "πικαϩ ι τ επι πωϩι"</note>, that is, the three-cubit pace of the Ibis, or the reed, or the cane, or the tripled leg of the Ibis—in Arabic **the measuring reed** <note>original: "القصبة الكرّي"</note>. This pace corresponds exactly to the length of a human; we can rightly call this a *six-foot* <note>original: "ἑξάποδον"</note> pace, for Geometers assign the stature of a proportionate man to that many feet. However, the mysteries hidden beneath this pace, and how they represented Mercury <note>Thoth, the god of measurement and writing.</note> under this measure, has already been discussed elsewhere.

<margin>
**PISTSAION**
The various stadia among the Egyptians.
</margin>
**PISTSAION** <note>A Coptic term for a stadium.</note> means the same as *stadium* <note>A unit of distance, roughly 185 meters.</note>, in Arabic **the heat or race** <note>original: "الغلوة"</note>. Among the Egyptians it was varied; some made it 65 canes or poles, others 85; nor are there lacking those who define it by a space of 400 cubits, as the author of the *Scala* says:

->**The stadium is sixty-five reeds; it was also found in an old manuscript once that the stadium is eighty-five reeds; it is also said that the stadium is four hundred cubits.**<-

That is: *The Stadium is 65 reeds, and it was also found in an ancient copy that the Stadium is 85 reeds or poles; it is also said that the stadium is 400 cubits or arm-lengths, and it is called an arrow's flight.* And this last measure corresponds exactly to the stadium of the Greeks, since <margin>Suidas.</margin> <margin>Herodotus.</margin> *Suidas* says *the stadium has 600 feet* <note>original: "στάδιον ἔχειν πόδας χ'"</note>, and *Herodotus* agrees with him in this; the foot, moreover, is 16 digits, or four palms, according to the words of the cited *Herodotus* in *Euterpe*: *The fathom is measured as six feet, or four cubits; the foot being four palms, and the cubit six palms.* <note>original: "Ἑξαπόδου μὲν ἡ ὀργυιὴς μετρεομένης, καὶ τετραπήχεος. τοῦ δὲ ποδῶν μὲν τετραπαλαίστων ἐόντων, τοῦ δὲ πήχεος ἑξαπαλαίστου."</note> Thus we measure a pace by six feet and four cubits; the feet are four palms, and the cubit <margin>Suidas.</margin> <margin>Plutarchus.</margin> is six palms. *Suidas* affirms this: *the foot has 16 digits* <note>original: "ὁ πούς ἔχει δακτύλους ις'"</note>. *Solon* uses this same measure in his laws, as found in *Plutarch*.

Therefore, since the Egyptian stadium is said to have 400 cubits, and the greater Egyptian cubit is (as proved above) 32 digits—that is, two feet, one of which equals 16 digits—then 400 cubits will equal 800 feet, which is indeed a stadium, as will be clear to anyone calculating them. Thus the Egyptian stadium will be equal to the Greek stadium, which was necessary to show. If, however, we take the "reed" for the pace of the Ibis, which we determined to be 96 digits, the stadium of 85 reeds would be a space of 340 smaller cubits, or what is the same, 510 feet. From this we gather there were three types of stadia among the Egyptians: the Greater, the Middling, and the Minimum. The Greater is 400 cubits; the Middling 340; the Minimum 260 cubits. The first, however, is the proper Egyptian one.

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. PRELUDE II.

<margin><note>original: πιελλιον</note> Mile.</margin>
**Piellion** <note>Coptic term for a mile</note> a mile, in Arabic *al-mil*; one mile consists of seven stadia <note>a Greek unit of length, roughly 600 feet</note>, and one parasang <note>a Persian unit of distance</note> consists of three miles. So says the Author of the *Scala* <note>A medieval Coptic-Arabic vocabulary manual</note>.

->The mile consists of seven stadia, and every three miles make a parasang. The parasang is one thousand four hundred cubits <note>the length of a forearm</note>, which amounts to a distance of three thousand paces.<-

*The mile contains seven stadia, and every three individual miles constitute one parasang; the parasang is 1400 cubits or "arms," and they are a space of 3000 paces. Abulfeda <note>Ismail Abul-fida, a 14th-century Syrian geographer and historian</note>, who defines the Egyptian mile in this way, agrees with this in all respects:*

->As for the mile, according to the Ancients it is three thousand cubits, while according to the Moderns it is four thousand cubits. The difference between them is merely verbal, for the actual extent of the mile is the same for everyone, even if the number of cubits differs. According to the explanations, a mile is ninety-six thousand fingers; if you divide this by thirty-two, the result is three thousand cubits, and if you divide it by twenty-four, the result is four thousand cubits. As for the parasang, according to both the Ancients and the Moderns it is three miles, but the difference arises in the parasang when it is measured by the cubit of the Ancients, making the parasang nine thousand cubits, whereas by the cubit of the Moderns it is twelve thousand cubits. According to the explanations, this is three hundred thousand fingers minus twelve thousand fingers. Know that the parasang according to the Ancients is nine thousand cubits and the mile is three thousand cubits, while according to the Moderns the parasang is twelve thousand cubits; and know that the mile in both explanations is one-third of a parasang, and every parasang is three miles.<-

*That is: A mile among the Ancients is 3000 arms, or cubits, and among the Moderns it is 4000. The only difference consists in this: that although the name "mile" is the same for everyone, the number of cubits varies. According to the interpreters, one mile is 96,000 fingers; if you divide this by 32, the result is 3000 cubits; and if you divide the same number by 24, the result will be 4000 cubits (one mile). The parasang, however, among both Ancients and Moderns, consists of three miles; the only difference is in the various naming of the cubit. For if you take the cubit to be the cubit of the ancients, one parasang will be 9000 cubits; and according to the cubit of more recent people, 12,000 cubits, which are (according to the interpreters) 300,000 fingers minus 12,000 fingers. You should know that the parasang among the Ancients is 9000 cubits, and the mile 3000 cubits; among the Moderns, however, the parasang is 12,000 cubits. Know also that the mile, according to both explanations, is 1/3 of a parasang, and a parasang is 3 miles. Truly, whoever compares these more exactly with the preceding accounts will find a remarkable agreement between the facts. But leaving these things aside, let us turn our attention to the measures of dry and liquid goods.*

->The *Sa'*, the *Makkuk* of wheat, is four *Mudd* measures.<-

# PART II. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

That is; *The Saa is a Corus, or a vessel of flour containing four modii* <note>A modius was a Roman dry measure, roughly 2 gallons.</note>. The Hebrews, however, describe it thus:

->The Corus is a measure of ten ephahs, and they are thirty sata.<-

> The Corus, a measure of dry goods, contains ten Ephahs, and there are thirty Sata. But before we proceed further, we must first explain what an Ephah and a Satum are: for since the Corus is the largest of all measures, not only for dry goods but also for liquids, all the others must be understood as parts of the whole.

<margin>Hesychius, Choenix.</margin>
That which the Egyptians call *Ouopi* <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩⲱⲡⲓ</note> or without the article *Ouop* <note>original Coptic: ⲟⲩⲱⲡ</note>, and the Arabs *Al-waibeh* <note>original Arabic: الويبة</note>, Hesychius corruptly calls the *Oiphin*; which he describes in these words: *A somewhat larger Egyptian four-choenix measure*, that is, the *Oephin* or *Ouopi* is a certain Egyptian measure containing four choenices. A Choenix, moreover, is equivalent to two Roman *sextarii*, weighing 40 Roman ounces in wine or water; therefore the Ephah or *Ouopi* measure would contain eight *sextarii*. 
<margin>Ephah. Satum. Cabus. Log. Author of the Yalkut.</margin>
The Hebrew Ephah, however, is the tenth part of a Corus, and is equal to a Bath; differing only in this, that the Ephah is a measure of dry goods, while the Bath is a measure of liquids. Furthermore, the Ephah contains three Sata. Thus says the Yalkut <note>A collection of Jewish midrash/commentary.</note>:

->An Ephah is 3 Sata, and a Satum is 6 Cabi, and a Cabus is 6 Logs, and a Log is 6 eggs.<-

<margin>The Egyptian Corus differs from the Hebrew.</margin>
*An Ephah contains three Sata, a Satum six Cabi, a Cabus six Logs, and a Log six eggs.* From these it appears that the measures of the Egyptian and Hebrew Corus are different: for the Corus of the Egyptians is a vessel containing four *modii* of flour; but the Corus of the Hebrews contains 47 *modii*—unless perhaps they take a *modius* for seven Sata, of which more below. Since therefore the Corus differs from the Corus, who does not see that the Ephah consequently differs from the Egyptian *Ouopi*? But even the Egyptian Bath differs from the Egyptian Ephah, though we said these measures were the same among the Hebrews; the Egyptians call the Bath *Pi-bathos neh* <note>original Coptic: ⲡⲓⲃⲁⲑⲟⲥ ⲛⲉϩ</note>,
<margin>Pi-bathos: The Egyptian Bath.</margin>
that is, *a Bath of oil*, for *neh* signifies oil in the Coptic language; which the author of the *Scala* <note>A Coptic-Arabic dictionary/thesaurus.</note> explains in these words: *A kaphiz of oil is sixty kost.* 
<margin>What a Kost is. Serapion the Arab.</margin>
But what a *Kost* <note>original Arabic: قسط</note> is, Serapion the Arab explains in these words:

->A Kost among the Romans is a pound with two thirds—that is, 20 ounces.<-

That is, *A Kost among the Romans is a pound with two thirds, that is 20 ounces*, to which Aben Sina <note>Avicenna, the famous Persian physician.</note> subscribes in almost the same words. 
<margin>Aben Sina.</margin>
Those among the Latins who distinguish between *Kist* and *Akfat* are merely distinguishing the singular from the plural; since *Kist* and *Akfat* are the same measure, differing only in number. I set these things down so that the reader, ignorant of the language, might not stumble when encountering such things. Therefore, since one *Kost* according to the Arabs is equivalent to 20 Roman ounces, 60 *Kosti* will be 1,200 ounces, which exactly fills 100 pounds. And such is the size of the Egyptian Bath according to the interpretation of our Author, when he says:

->The Bath of oil is sixty kost.<-

*A Bath or Kaphiz is a vessel of oil of 60 Kost.*

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. PROPOSITION II.

<margin>ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲙⲟⲣ Egyptian Ghomer.</margin>
We stated in the Supplement that the *Cor* <note>original: "Corum," a large Hebrew dry measure</note> and the *Ghomer* <note>original: "Ghomer," likely referring to the Omer</note> were the same measure; but I have discovered that among the Egyptians, this also differs from the *Cor*. For ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲣⲟⲥ ⲛⲥⲟⲟ <note>Coptic: Pi-koros n-soo</note> signifies a *Saam*, or a vessel of flour containing 4 *modii* <note>pecks or bushels</note>. The Egyptian ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲙⲟⲣ <note>Coptic: Pi-komor</note> is twofold, the greater and the lesser. The greater, which is called ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲙⲟⲣ, that is, the "greater modius," contains thirty other *modii*. Thus says the Author of the *Scala* <note>A medieval Coptic-Arabic dictionary</note>: **المد الكبير ثلثين** *The greater modius of 30 modii*; and the lesser modius ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲙⲟⲣ is of fifteen *modii*. Thus in the *Scala*: **المد الصغير خمسة عشر من** *The lesser modius capable of holding 15 other modii*. From these I gather that the *Komor* and the **المد** <note>Arabic: al-mudd</note> or "greater modius" is taken in this place for the *Cor* of the Hebrews, and the *modii* of which it consists are taken for *Sata* <note>Seahs</note>. By this reasoning, we shall reduce the Egyptian *Ghomer* to the Hebrew *Cor*, which we have proved consists of 10 *Ephas* and 30 *Sata*. Therefore, this *modius* is taken for one Hebrew *modius*, or one and a half Italian *modii*, which makes one *Satum*. Thus, the Hebrew *Cor* and the Egyptian greater *modius* or *Komor* are accepted as the same measure. The lesser *modius* or *Komor* consists of 15 *modii*, being exactly half of the greater. From these premises, we shall easily determine the remaining measures of the Egyptians.

<margin>ⲧϣⲁⲛⲓϣⲓ The Saa Modius.</margin>
The ⲧϣⲁⲛⲓϣⲓ <note>Coptic: T-shanishi</note> is the *Saa* modius containing 22 *Kost* <note>original: "Kost," from the Arabic "qist," a liquid measure</note>. Thus the Author of the *Scala* says: **الصاع تسع اثنين وعشرين قسطا وهذا الاسم في الايو غالميس ويذكر للجوهري ان المن مكيال ورطل عند اهل الحجاز ورطلان عند اهل العراق الصاع اربعة امداد** *That is: The modius contains 22 Kost, and this name is found in the Apocalypse <note>The Book of Revelation</note>, and Al-Jawhari <note>original: "Alhuari," a famous Arabic lexicographer</note> mentions it, saying: This modius is a measure which is worth a pound among the Hijazi Arabs, and two pounds among the Iraqis; but the Saa contains four modii.*

Let us now explain the words of the Author. He says first, then, that the modius or measure of the *Saa* contains 22 *Kost*. Since we have shown above from the Arab Serapion that one *Kost* consists of 20 ounces of a pound divided into 12 ounces; therefore, the *Saa* modius will consist of 36 pounds and 8 twelfths <note>8 ounces</note>. This modius, however, as Al-Jawhari rightly says, varies among different nations, so that the ambiguity of such measures produces no small confusion for those not paying attention to the specific circumstances of the terms. He adds at the end that one *Saa* consists of four such *modii*, namely of the kind where one consists of 36 pounds and 8 twelfths, so that one *Saa* consists of 146 pounds and 8 twelfths. <margin>Saa.</margin> From which it is clear that the ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲣⲟⲥ ⲛⲥⲟⲟ, that is, the Egyptian *Cor*, is equivalent to the *Saa*: for the *Saa* is a *cor* of flour of four such *modii*, one of which we said holds 36 pounds and 8 twelfths. It is also clear that the Egyptian measure ⲧϣⲁⲛⲓϣⲓ is the fourth part of the ⲡⲓⲕⲟⲣⲟⲥ ⲛⲥⲟⲟ. Finally, you may gather that the *Lecythus* <note>Greek: oil flask</note>, *Cantarus* <note>drinking vessel</note>, or the small flask of Elijah, which the Copts call ⲡⲓⲕⲁⲛⲑⲁⲣⲟⲥ ⲛⲧⲉ ⲏⲗⲓⲁⲥ <note>Coptic: Pi-kantharos nte Elias</note>, is worth four *Kost*. <margin>Lecythus.</margin> Thus the Translator: **قلة ايلياس اربعة قسط** which are 6 pounds and 8 twelfths; <margin>Hydria.</margin> the *hydria* <note>water jar</note>, however, which the Copts call ⲧϩⲩⲇⲣⲓⲁ <note>Coptic: T-hydria</note>, contains 19 *Kost*. Thus our Author: **وجره تسع عشر اقساطاً** *The hydria contains ten modii; that is,*

# PR. II. 288 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>The Skin.</margin>
16 pounds and two-thirds. Furthermore, the skin of wine, which the Copts <note>Egyptian Christians</note> call **ⲠⲚⲈⲂⲎⲖ ⲚⲎⲢⲠ** <note>original: "Pnebel n-erp"</note> and the Arabs describe thus:

-> The large skin for wine, which is one hundred and fifty *qists*. <-

<margin>Alabastrum.</margin>
The larger wine skin is 150 *Kost* <note>original: "Kost" or "Qist," a common Near Eastern measure</note>, that is, it weighs 250 pounds. Finally, the **ⲀⲖⲀⲂⲀⲤⲦRounding** <note>original: "Alabastron"</note>, or Alabaster jar of ointment, consists of 9 *Kost*, and weighs the same in pounds, that is, 24 pounds, or 24 Roman *sextarii* <note>a Roman measure roughly equal to a pint</note>. The **ⲠⲒ-ⲈⲢⲈⲄⲞⲘⲈ** <note>original: "Pi-eregome"</note> and the three water-pots, or measures of Cana in Galilee, each of which contains 72 *Kost*, according to the author of the *Scala* <note>A medieval Coptic-Arabic dictionary</note>:

-> The three jars which the Lord changed into wine each held seventy-two *qists*; and it is said that the *Saa* is thirty *mudds*, and the *mudd* is three *waibas*. <-

<margin>Three water-pots of Cana in Galilee.</margin>
The three water-pots or measures, in which the Lord converted water into wine, each contain 72 *Kost*; and it is said that the *Saa* contains 30 *modii* <note>pecks</note>, and the *modius* contains 3 *Ephi*. Therefore, the water-pot of Cana is 120 pounds, and the *Saa* of 30 *modii*, and the *modius* of 3 *Ephi*, is equivalent in this place to one *cor* or *ghomer* of the Hebrews containing 30 *Sata*, just as the *Ephi* contains 3 *Sata*, as has been said.

<margin>**ⲠⲒⲖⲞⲔ** Log.</margin>
**ⲠⲒⲖⲞⲔ** <note>original: "Pilok"</note> in Coptic seems to sound the same as the Hebrew לוג (*Log*), although the measure differs; for we have shown above that the *Log* holds six eggs; however, the **ⲠⲒⲖⲞⲔ**, or *Congius* <note>about 3 liters</note> here contains 9 *Kost*, which are 13 pounds and two-sixths. But the "sacred" **ⲠⲒⲖⲞⲔ**, as the Copts call it, contains 6 *Kost*, which are 10 pounds. But the reader will be able to compare these more extensively with the measures of the Greeks, Hebrews, and Romans; our task is only to faithfully interpret the measures according to the mind of the Egyptians.

### Concerning the Artaba.

<margin>Artaba.</margin>
The **ⲠⲒⲈⲢⲦⲰⲂ** <note>original: "Piertob"</note> is the most famous measure of the Egyptians, which is commonly called by the corrupted name *Artaba*, the Arabs call it *Alertob* (الأردب), and the Syrians <unclear>Ardubbo</unclear>. However, what kind of measure this was, and how great, is a matter of controversy among authors. <margin>Suidas.</margin> Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> says: "The Artaba is a Median measure, an Attic *medimnus* of grain." The Artaba is a measure of the Medes, that is, of the Medes, an Attic *medimnus* of grain; but the Attic *medimnus* is a measure of six *modii*, as witnessed by Cornelius Nepos in the *Life of Atticus*. <margin>Cornelius Nepos.</margin> Some say the measure is common to the Persians and Egyptians. Thus the interpreter of Aristophanes in *The Acharnians* says of the Artaba: "The name is both Persian and Egyptian." We say that the Egyptian *Ardab* (**ⲠⲒⲈⲢⲦⲰⲂ**) is a measure of liquids containing five *modii*. Thus a certain anonymous Greek on weights and measures in the works of Agricola says: "The Egyptian Artaba holds 5 *modii*, and the Egyptian and Italian *modius* contains 8 *choenices*." <margin>St. Jerome.</margin> I find that St. Jerome was of the same opinion, whose words in Book 11 of his *Commentary on Isaiah* are these: "And for the 30 *modii* which we have put for the *cor*, which in Hebrew is called *kor* (כור), the Seventy <note>The Septuagint translators</note> translate as six *artabae*, which is an Egyptian measure, and it makes thirty *modii*: for if six Artabae hold thirty *modii*, each one will hold five *modii*."

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 289 PROBLEM II.

Others, however, hold the opposite view. Thus Fannius <note>Rhemnius Fannius Palaemon, a Roman grammarian known for a poem on weights and measures</note>, who makes it smaller than we have stated.

<margin>Fannius.</margin>
> *There is also in the lands which the visiting Nile overflows,*
> *The Ardaba, which exceeds three modii by a third part,*
> *For a double Ardaba will be filled by ten modii.*

That is, the Egyptian Ardaba holds three *modii* <note>A Roman dry measure, roughly 2 gallons</note> and a third part of a *modius*. Epiphanius disagrees with this, claiming the Egyptian Artaba consists of 72 *sextarii* <note>A pint-sized measure</note>, or one Attic *Medimnus*; thus it would be equal to the Median Artaba. <margin>Epiphanius.</margin> *The Artaba,* he says, *was the name given to this measure by the Egyptians, consisting of seventy-two sextarii.* <note>original Greek: Ἀρτάβη... τοῦτο τὸ μέτρον παρ’ Αἰγυπτίοις ἐκλήθη ἐπὶ δὲ ἑβδομήκοντα δύο ξεστῶν.</note> By this reasoning, according to Epiphanius, the Artaba is the same measure as the *Ephi* <note>A Hebrew dry measure</note>. <margin>The Triple Egyptian Artaba</margin> However, so that such varying opinions on the Artaba may be resolved, I say that the Egyptian Artaba was threefold. The first, and larger one, held six *Choenices* <note>A Greek daily grain ration</note> more than an Attic *Medimnus*; Herodotus is the authority that the Persian Artaba was also this size, which is frequently confused with that of the Egyptians: <margin>Herodotus.</margin> *The Artaba is a Persian measure containing more than an Attic Medimnus by 6 Attic Choenices.* <note>original Greek: Ἡ δὲ Ἀρτάβη μέτρον ἐστὶ Περσικὸν χωρέον μεδίμνου Ἀττικοῦ πλέον χοινίξι ϛ’ Ἀττικῆσι.</note> Here a notable error of the translators comes to light, reading 3 instead of 6 <unclear>6</unclear>, deceived by the Greek numeral 6 (ϛ'), which is very similar to the mark for 3 (<unclear>τῷ</unclear> γ'); I would wish the learned to take note of this. We have said the second Artaba is capable of holding an Attic *Medimnus*, which was also used by the Medes. It was shown above that the third is of five *modii*. But let us now demonstrate this very thing from the sources. The Egyptians call these three Artabas *Ertob* <note>Coptic: ⲕⲉⲣⲧⲱϐ</note> as is clear from the *Scala* <note>A Coptic-Arabic dictionary or glossary</note>. The first is called *the great Ertob* <note>Coptic: ⲡⲓⲛⲓϣϯ ⲛ̀ⲕⲉⲣⲧⲱϐ</note>; the second *the middle Ertob* <note>Coptic: ⲡⲓⲙⲉⲧⲣⲟ ⲛ̀ⲕⲉⲣⲧⲱϐ</note>; the third is the *common Artaba* <note>Coptic: ⲡⲉⲣⲧⲱϐ</note> found everywhere; all of which the translator explains beautifully:

> And the large Ardab is one measure and six measures, and the middle Ardab is one measure, and the small Ardab is five measures. ۞ <note>Translated from the Arabic text provided in the manuscript</note>

*The large Artaba contains one large modius (which we said above was equal to a Medimnus) and six small modii in addition (which we equated with Choenices); and the middle Ertob is of one modius, that is, an Attic Medimnus; and the minor Ertob is of five modii.* All of these agree perfectly with what has been said; and the Hebrew description in the *Baal Aruch* <note>A famous 11th-century Talmudic lexicon</note> also agrees:

<margin>Baal Aruch.</margin>
> **The Ardab is a small measure; and its meaning is found as the daily ration for hiring laborers and craftsmen; and the large measure is used in the land of Egypt until this day.** <note>Translated from the Hebrew: ארדב מדה קטנה...</note>

*That is, the Ardab is a small measure of water: the middle is explained as the daily allowance for laborers or craftsmen: the third signifies the large measure used in Egypt even unto this day.* From all that has been said thus far, it is clear that six Artabas of the Seventy Translators <note>The Septuagint</note> were equal to the Hebrew *Cor*; a fact which the Greek Eupolemus <margin>70 Translators</margin>—a most ancient writer of great authority—left recorded in the works of Eusebius; consult him in the cited place. <margin>Eusebius.</margin> And let these remarks suffice concerning the Artaba.

### On the Weights of the Egyptians.

Since the Talent is the greatest of weights, we begin the starting point of our discussion from it.
<margin>ⲡⲓⲕⲓⲛϫⲱⲣ <note>Coptic: Pi-kinshor</note> Talent. Al-Samenudi.</margin>
Among the Egyptians, ⲡⲓⲕⲓⲛϫⲱⲣ is the same as a Talent, and it weighs 120 pounds. Thus says Al-Samenudi <note>A 13th-century Egyptian scholar known for Coptic-Arabic lexicons</note> in the *Scala* <note>A rhymed vocabulary or dictionary</note>:
-> The weight <term>Al-uazne</term> is one hundred and twenty pounds. <-
*The "Al-uazne" is the talent, or a weight of 120 pounds. The Talent of the Hebrews, however, is five pounds less: for the Hebrew <term>Kikar</term> <note>The biblical talent</note> is 125 pounds, according to the true opinion of the Hebrews, which Suidas <note>A 10th-century Greek encyclopedist</note> supports: <margin>Suidas.</margin> <note>original Greek: Το Ταλαντον ἑλκει λίτρας ρκε.</note> The Talent draws [weighs] 125 pounds. Among certain people, the talent holds one hundred and twenty-five pounds.*

<margin>ⲡⲓⲙⲉⲛⲁ <note>Coptic: Pi-mena</note> Mina.</margin>
ⲡⲓⲙⲉⲛⲁ is the same as the Mina, and it contains twenty ounces. Thus Al-Samenudi:
-> The Mina contains twenty ounces, and it is 28 denarii. <-
*The Mina indeed contains twenty ounces, and there are 28 denarii. And this is larger than the Ptolemaic and Italian Mina by two ounces, and is properly the Alexandrian Mina; concerning which Dioscorides <note>Ancient Greek physician and botanist</note> writes in "On Weights": <margin>Dioscorides.</margin> <note>original Greek: Μνᾶ παρὰ τὴν ἰατρῶν χρείαν ἔχειν ὄγκιας κ...</note> The Mina, according to the use of physicians, has 20 ounces, or 188 drachmas. The Italian mina has 18 ounces, or 140 drachmas. But the Mina of Alexandria has 20 ounces, or 160 drachmas.*

<margin>ⲡⲓⲥⲉⲕⲗⲟⲥ <note>Coptic: Pi-seklos</note> Shekel.</margin>
ⲡⲓⲥⲉⲕⲗⲟⲥ is the Egyptian Shekel, about which Al-Samenudi says: It is correctly a quarter of an ounce.
*The Egyptian Shekel is a weight, or a vessel, weighing a fourth part of an ounce, or four drachmas.*

<margin>ⲧϫⲉⲥⲕⲓⲧ <note>Coptic: T-sheskit</note> Drachma.</margin>
ⲧϫⲉⲥⲕⲓⲧ indeed, which Al-Samenudi interprets as a drachma, is the eighth part of an ounce. The words follow:
-> The Dirham <note>Arabic: Drachma</note> is an eighth of an ounce; and it is read in an ancient copy that it is two-thirds of an ounce. <-
*The Drachma is the eighth part of an ounce; and it is read in an ancient manuscript that it is two-thirds of an ounce. The Drachma was, however, as the name itself indicates, a weight proper to the Greeks, and a stamped coin, which when the Greeks were in power was transferred to the Romans and frequently used by them; just as, conversely, the weight and name of the Roman ounce was transferred to the Greeks and Arabs. It was, however, as among the Romans and Greeks, so also among the <margin>Fannius. Suidas.</margin> Egyptians, the eighth part of an ounce. Thus Fannius <note>A Roman poet who wrote on weights</note>: "An ounce is made of twice four drachmas." Suidas: <note>original Greek: Ἑκατόν δραχμαὶ ποιοῦσι μνᾶν μίαν.</note> One hundred drachmas make one mina. From which it is clear that the pound or "as" consists of 96 drachmas, to which if you add <margin>Dioscorides. Galen. Columella. Villalpando. Mariana. Agricola.</margin> four, you will have the Attic Mina of 100 drachmas; with which Dioscorides, Galen, Columella, and others agree, whom you may see in Villalpando, Mariana, Agricola, and others <note>Kircher lists several Renaissance scholars of metrology</note>.*

<margin>ⲥⲧⲁⲧⲏⲣ <note>Coptic: Stater</note> Stater.</margin>
ⲥⲧⲁⲧⲏⲣ or the Stater, used to weigh half an ounce. Thus Al-Samenudi:
-> The Stater, which Peter found in the mouth of the fish, is half an ounce, and it is a third of a denarius, or the small denarius. <-
*The Stater, which Peter found in the mouth of the fish <note>A reference to Matthew 17:27</note>, weighs half an ounce, and is the third part of a smaller denarius. And by this reasoning, the Hebrew Shekel and the Stater [weigh] the same—*

CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 291 CHAPTER I.

<margin>The Hebrew Shekel and Stater weighed the same. St. Matthew.</margin>
...they weighed the same, namely four Attic drachmas, or what they call a <term>tetradrachm</term> <note>original: "τετράδραχμον"; a silver coin worth four drachmas</note>; which is also evident from the words of St. Matthew, where it is stated: *Those who collected the two-drachma tax came to Peter and said to him: "Does your teacher not pay the two-drachma tax?" And a little later it is added that the Lord commanded Peter to go to the sea and cast a hook; "And the first fish that comes up," He said, "take it, and when you have opened its mouth, you will find a stater; take that and give it to them for me and for yourself."* <note>A reference to Matthew 17:24-27</note> By these words we have two things clearly witnessed: first, that it was customary for a <term>didrachma</term> <note>a two-drachma coin</note> to be paid by each individual; and second, that a <term>Stater</term> was equal to two didrachmas, since it was to be paid for both Christ and Peter. Since, therefore, eight drachmas constitute one ounce, a Stater will be half an ounce, or a tetradrachm is the same as a Stater. Our author therefore agrees with the Hebrews and Greeks; which is what we wished to demonstrate. There will also be

<margin>What the Census is.</margin>
† <term>Toki</term> † <note>Coptic: ⲧⲟⲕⲓ</note> Census <note>The "tribute" or "tax" coin</note>, the same as a Stater; because our author says † <term>Toki</term> † is half an ounce <note>original Arabic: "الجزية نصف أوقية" - The tribute is half an ounce</note>.

But † <term>Toki</term> † is the same as a <term>didrachma</term>; which is ten <term>quadrantes</term> <note>small Roman coins</note>: <note>original Arabic: "ربع أوقية وهي عشرين فلسا" - A quarter of an ounce, which is twenty fils</note> for it is the fourth part of an ounce.

Therefore, the <term>Stater</term> <note>Coptic: ⲥⲧⲁⲧⲏⲣ</note>, the Hebrew Shekel, and the <term>tetradrachm</term> <note>Coptic: ⲧⲉⲧⲣⲁⲇⲣⲁⲭⲙⲟⲛ</note> will be the same.

<margin>Stater, Shekel, and Census are the same thing.</margin>
† <term>Toki</term> † Census, the Roman half-ounce, according to the Egyptians, are the same thing, distinguished only by names.

# C H A P T E R I.
## *On the Architecture of the Egyptians.*

<margin>The Egyptians were outstanding in Architecture.</margin>
**T**he architecture of the ancient Egyptians shone forth most greatly in that prodigious magnificence of Obelisks, Colossi, Pyramids, Temples, Tombs, and Labyrinths. And if the things written about them by Herodotus, Pausanias, Diodorus, Pliny, and the histories of the Arabs—who were eyewitness inspectors of these things—are true, exceeding as they do almost all bounds of human belief; I do not fear to assert that these works were so great that, whether you look at their excellence and perfection or the difficulty of the efforts required to execute them, they seem to have taken away from all future architects any hope of ever reaching the same perfection. For if the work proves the craftsman, what kind of architects must we assert they were, and how endowed with divine genius? Certainly, the highest and singular symmetry and proportion of the parts, and the joining of the floorings, deservedly required a supreme Geometer and Arithmetician, just as the erection of such extraordinary structures required a supreme Mechanic and <term>Statician</term> <note>An expert in statics, the branch of mechanics concerned with bodies at rest and forces in equilibrium</note>. But so that we may proceed in order, it seemed best to begin first with the Pyramids, and then we shall follow with the remaining structures in order.

# CHAPTER I. 292 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

### §. I.
### *The Pyramids.*

<margin>The Pyramids of Memphis according to Herodotus.</margin>
**H**ow great the magnificence, splendor, and beauty of the Pyramids was—erected in Egypt through the supreme and most lavish generosity of Kings—may be gathered from this among other facts: that by the unanimous consensus of writers, even at that time when Roman pride trampled upon every corner of the world, they were numbered among the Wonders of the World. And although unusual masses of towers of this kind were seen established in various places in Egypt, those of Memphis, above all others, were the greatest cause for admiration, and were regarded as a miracle of the world. Herodotus, who, according to the testimony of Pliny, lived around the year 300 from the founding of Rome <note>approx. 450 BCE</note>, testifies particularly about one of those which he himself inspected in his book *Euterpe*: <margin>Herodotus.</margin> "Twenty years were spent in the making of this pyramid; it is square, each of its faces measuring eight *plethra* <note>a Greek unit of length, roughly 100 feet</note>, and its height is the same. It is made of polished stone, fitted together with the greatest care; none of the stones are less than thirty feet. This pyramid was built in the manner of steps, which some call 'battlements' and others call 'altar-steps'." <note>original Greek: "Τῇ δ' οὖν πυραμίδι ἀυτῇ... οἱ δὲ βωμίδας ὀνομάζουσι."</note> Truly, twenty years were consumed on this Pyramid, of which each face (for it was four-sided) is eight *plethra* or acres, with an equal height, made of hewn stones most decently joined together, none of which were less than 30 feet; moreover, this Pyramid was constructed in the appearance of steps, which some call ladders and others call little altars. <margin>Diodorus.</margin> Diodorus, four hundred years later than Herodotus, and himself an eyewitness inspector of the same, describes them in this manner: "Finally, the eighth King, Chemmis (called Cleobus by Herodotus), reigned in Memphis for 50 years and built the largest of the three Pyramids, which is numbered among the seven most famous works. These turn toward Libya, 120 *stadia* <note>approx. 14 miles</note> from Memphis and 45 from the Nile; they provide a wonderful astonishment to those who behold them, both for their craftsmanship and the magnitude of the work. <margin>A pyramid of wondrous magnitude.</margin> The largest of them has four sides, each of which contains seven acres at the lower part; the height rises more than six acres; the width of each side, as the height gradually decreases toward the summit, contains 65 cubits. The entire structure consists of hard stone, difficult to work but destined to remain forever. For nearly a thousand years, as some say—or as others hand down, more than three thousand four hundred years—that mass has remained intact until our time. They say those stones were brought from Arabia by a very long journey. It was built by means of earthen mounds, as machines had not yet been invented at that time. It is certainly a marvelous work, especially in a land sandy on all sides, where no traces remain of either a mound or the cutting of stone; so that the great mass seems to have been built not by men, but by Gods. The Egyptians attempt to tell certain wonders about these: that the mounds were made of salt and nitre, and later, when the Nile rose, they were melted away and vanished entirely without human labor. But this is far from the truth. For the mound was both constructed by a multitude of men and demolished by a multitude. For 360,000 men, as they say, were assigned to that work, which they finished in nearly 20 years." Then he describes the second Pyramid, erected by King Chabreus, similar in structure to the former but unequal in size, as the sides of the base encompass only one *stadium*: all the money was spent on the work of the first; so that for vegetables and herbs alone, one thousand six hundred—

<margin>Pliny.</margin>
...it is said that the expenses exceeded [thousands] of talents <note>A talent was a massive unit of weight and currency in antiquity</note>. King Mycerinus erected the third pyramid, but being prevented by death, he could not finish the work; thus one may admire the supreme genius of the Architects more than the idle display of wealth by the Kings. Strabo, nearly a contemporary of Diodorus, mentions these masses in Book 17:
> *Forty stadia <note>A stadium was roughly 600 feet</note> from the City, he says, is a certain mountain ridge on which many pyramids stand. Three of them are memorable; two are numbered among the seven wonders of the World, each a stadium in height, square in shape, having a height slightly greater than any side, and exceeding each other slightly in mass. And a little later: Further up on a greater height of the mountain is the third, much smaller than the first two, yet built with greater expense. For from almost the foundations up to the middle, it consists of black stone <note>original: "nigro ex lapide"; likely referring to granite</note> from which they make mortars, brought from the furthest mountains of Ethiopia; since it is hard and difficult to work, it rendered the work more costly—the burial place of the courtesan Rhodopis, or Doricha.*

Pliny, then weighing each detail more exactly, brings forth these points among others in Book 35, Chapter 12:
> *Let the pyramids in that same Egypt also be mentioned in passing, an idle and foolish display of Royal wealth; indeed, the reason for making them is handed down by most as being so that they might not provide money to successors or plotting rivals, or so that the common people would not be idle. There was much vanity among those men regarding this, and traces of several unfinished ones remain. One is in the Arsinoite Nome, two in the Memphite district not far from the labyrinth, about which we shall also speak. Just as many where Lake Moeris was, that is, a great trench. But Egypt narrates among its wonders and things to be remembered the extreme peaks of these, which are said to stand out. The remaining three, which filled the World with their fame, clearly visible from all sides to those sailing toward them, are situated in the part of Africa on a rocky and sterile mountain, between the town of Memphis and what we said is called the Delta, less than four thousand paces from the Nile, and six from Memphis, with a village nearby which they call Busiris, from which people are accustomed to climb them.*

And a little later:
> *But the largest pyramid consists of stone from Arabian quarries; it is recorded that 360,000 men constructed it over twenty years.*

And below:
> *The largest occupies eight acres of ground, with the four corners at equal intervals of eight hundred and eighty-three feet for each side; the height from the peak is 25 feet <note>Pliny's measurements here are historically debated for their accuracy</note>.*

Thus says Pliny. And although the cited Authors agree regarding the location, there is hardly one who agrees with another in measurement; which I believe happened because of the different systems of measures used by different nations.

<margin>Pierre Belon.</margin>
To these have been added the modern measurers of the pyramids; among whom Pierre Belon <note>original: "Petrus Bellonius"; a 16th-century French naturalist and traveler</note> deservedly holds the first place, who went to Egypt with the express purpose of measuring the pyramids. He speaks thus:
> *The pyramids of Egypt, so celebrated by the Ancients, are in an elevated place, and they begin to appear from 40 miles away. The Egyptians call these "Pharaohs." These indeed seem more admirable to those inspecting them closely than they were described by the Authors: for they seem to be mountains of immense magnitude, whence the Roman buildings and ancient works approach nothing of the splendor and magnificence of these pyramids. They are placed, moreover, in a very deserted place, or solitude, four miles distant from Cairo across the Nile by a third stone's throw; and the largest of them surpasses the others even in excellence, which all Ancient Writers wrote was wonderful to behold. It is built with steps projecting outward, and is 324 paces*

Its summit ends in a flat area 2 paces <note>A "pace" (passus) was a Roman unit of length, roughly 5 feet.</note> wide in diameter, upon which 50 men can stand. Besides these three, many other smaller ones are scattered here and there through that sandy soil, more than a hundred, of which not a single one is seen to be as damaged as the Roman one. <margin>Marco Grimani.</margin>
The measurement of this pyramid in exact intervals of paces, the size of which is thought to have slightly exceeded the modules of three ancient palms. Each side of the square base is completed by about 270 paces; and the entire pyramid consists of reused and very hard stone, and its tiers <note>original: "praecinctiones," referring to the stepped layers or ledges of the pyramid.</note> extend to a sufficiently convenient length, and are so fitted and arranged throughout the whole work that they provide an ascent all the way to the highest peak, although it is extremely difficult and inconvenient; for each step is about three and a half palms high, and they did not possess enough of a protruding flat surface for the feet of those climbing to rest upon them comfortably and safely. From the base to the summit there are about 210 tiers, and each maintains exactly the same height, so that the height of the entire structure seems altogether equal to the width of the base placed beneath it. Above all others, however, I find that Prince Radziwiłł <note>Mikołaj Krzysztof "the Orphan" Radziwiłł (1549–1616), a Polish-Lithuanian noble who wrote a famous account of his pilgrimage to the Holy Land and Egypt.</note> observed these things most closely and exactly in the history of his travels on page 161. <margin>Radziwiłł.</margin>

*...large enough for a body to have been placed within it. Furthermore, by which Kings, at what expense, or by what method or skill these masses of pyramids were raised—and whether by the Jews established in Egyptian servitude (an opinion which pleases almost all Authors)—or whether those same Hebrews completed the embankments and trenches by which the Nile is diverted (for all these things appear to have been made by art, not by nature), I leave for historians to judge. It is right to marvel greatly at this: since the said pyramids were erected upon a high mountain which consists entirely of living rock <note>Natural, unquarried bedrock</note>, yet as far as can be gathered from the type of stones, it appears they were not fashioned from the stones of that same cliff. Nor can it be easily investigated from where, or by what reasoning, such a vast heap of stones could be carried there, especially since the flooding Nile runs three miles distant from the structure. But neither can it be fathomed by what labor and skill stones—each three cubits <note>A cubit is roughly 18 inches, the length of a forearm</note> long and wide, and more than one and a half high—could be dragged up such a high mountain and placed at the summit.* <margin>The size, shape, etc., of the largest pyramid according to Radziwiłł. <note>Mikołaj Krzysztof "the Orphan" Radziwiłł (1549–1616), a Polish-Lithuanian noble who wrote a famous account of his pilgrimage to the Holy Land and Egypt.</note></margin> *The largest pyramid of all is fabricated from stones of this kind, cut and squared, into the form of a certain natural mountain by a singular skill; and although it rises from the bottom part gradually to the peak in a quadrangular shape, nevertheless those squared stones are seen to be composed in an unequal order with such marvelous art that the whole mass represents the appearance of a mountain formed by nature. The ascent, on account of the thickness of the stones, is heavy and laborious, yet secure; and although I used a convenient pace, I barely ascended the summit of the pyramid within one and a half hours, where there is a square level area, encompassing a space of ten cubits on each side.*

*The second pyramid, a little smaller than the former, stands at a distance of two arrow-shots from it; the interior entrance into it is not open, though they claim it is hidden. On the exterior, one can climb it as far as the middle, since it has stones composed in the same manner as the first, except that they are a little smoother and smaller. From the middle, however, the stones rise up so smoothed that it is impossible to proceed further; which appears to have been done with that specific purpose. From there, the third part of the same pyramid, all the way to the summit, has stones placed as if neglected and disorderly, just as in the lower part; so that if that smooth series of rocks, which rises for several dozen cubits, did not impede it, the summit could easily be climbed just like the first.*

*The third pyramid, at the side of the second toward the city, belongs to that Rhodopis <note>A famous Greek courtesan who, according to legend, had a pyramid built for her</note> whom we have already mentioned; it is fabricated entirely of hewn stone so that it cannot be climbed. From this, at three bow-shots also toward the city, is a head with a neck and shoulders projecting, belonging to the same harlot <note>The author is identifying the Great Sphinx as a statue of Rhodopis</note>, seven cubits in height, of marvelous appearance, carved from a single piece of living rock. Some claim that from that larger pyramid which we entered, through a subterranean cavern cut into the cliff (which we saw overwhelmed with stones), a narrow and hidden passage lay open into this head, and from there oracles were delivered, with the common people of the Heathens believing that they were brought forth through the mouth of the head itself. Thus far Radziwiłł: who indeed described everything so exactly that it seems nothing can be added to or taken away from it.*

<margin>Pietro della Valle <note>A famous Italian traveler (1586–1652) who explored the Orient.</note></margin>
> *Thus, twelve miles from the river, one finds the first pyramids, which are those three great ones described by Belon <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist who traveled to Egypt.</note>, my guide; and those same ones that we discovered coming to Cairo, with an innumerable quantity of other smaller ones. Regarding the beauty of these—that is, the great ones—it will suffice to say to Your Lordship that Belon has spoken little of it, and that I esteem them worthily as wonders of the World; and when I say it, coming as I do from Italy and from Rome, Your Lordship can believe it to be true.*
<margin>Architecture of the pyramids.</margin>
> *There is no great charm of architecture, nor elegance of relief members, of whimsies, or other ornaments with which we are accustomed to adorn our buildings; nor even the difficulty of supporting great vaults in the air, like our domes and other structures which among us are considered ingenious. For it was not the intention of those people to make something pleasing to the eye, but to make a structure that would be eternal—as it has been, and will be in my opinion. For this purpose, there was no better form than that solid shape of the pyramids, which is nothing other than a square body of very large pieces of marble <note>The author likely refers to the limestone casing or the massive blocks themselves as "marble" due to their hardness and finish.</note> which, the higher it rises, always diminishes by steps; according to which proportion, in respect to its vastness, it does not rise very high. From these three conditions—namely, being composed of solid material like fine and very hard marble; having a foundation little burdened; and the body being a full Pyramid that always tapers upward—it follows that it is rendered most firm against every movement of the sky, the earth, and time, taking on no less the firmness than the form of a natural mountain. This seems, at first sight, a small thing: because gathering so many marbles in a sandy plain where there are none is no great feat. Egypt has very large mountains not far away; conducting them by the Nile is very easy; and thus from the Nile to there, which is a short distance, it is all plain; and in the pyramid, composing them simply in a square figure one above the other is not great craftsmanship. The size of the pyramids does not seem less excessive; for in fact I would believe that in height it does not much exceed the dome of St. Peter's in Rome. I truly had neither time nor patience to measure; but thus by eye, and as much as I understood also from various curious people who have taken the trouble, I believe that Belon's measurements are correct: that is, that the pyramids are about three hundred or three hundred and fifty paces wide at the base on each of the four sides; and high around two hundred and ten up to two hundred and fifty steps, which it is impossible to count exactly because they are ruined in some places; and each step will be a little more than two palms wide and a little less than four high.*
<margin>Quantity of the pyramids.</margin>
> *So, for the things already said, they do not appear so marvelous at first sight; and they had this same effect on me. However, when a man approaches closely and considers better the immensity of the stones—much larger than the architraves of the portico of the Rotunda <note>The Pantheon in Rome.</note>, the stones of the Colosseum, and any others I have seen—and I think how with such ease they were handled up to the very top, where they must have been carried either with ropes or with bridges; and moreover, that they were composed with such accuracy of measurement, each placed in its spot so precisely and with such judgment; I begin to recognize the artifice, and to understand that those men knew quite a lot.*

All of which agree with what has already been said by other Authors. He proceeds afterward to describe the entrance into the interior of the pyramid—

*“But when one climbs toward the middle, and finds the door, carved with a marvelous precision amidst a mass of stones of extraordinary size; which, although so immense, are composed above in an arch, and provide ornament with very beautiful architecture; it must be confessed, that there is something of great merit there. For, if we admire in Rome the door of the Rotunda <note>The Pantheon</note>, which is erected on level ground, for its size—being all one piece (as many believe), the jambs with the architrave; much more must we admire in the pyramid those seven or eight stones (each of which, in length and width, is perhaps no less than the entire width of the door of the Rotunda) which, pulled so high up, and with most beautiful design fitted together by the corners, form an arch and vault for a small little doorway. The wonder increases upon entering inside, and walking through that path, which Belon <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist and traveler</note> describes, which goes right to the center, where they placed the body in the sepulcher: which path, as he says, is square in the manner of a well, not plumb <note>vertical</note>, but sloping, and quite steep, so that one can walk there only with difficulty; and they did this because, in effect, they did not want anyone to go there to move and disturb those corpses: indeed the door, when the body was placed, was closed, and covered with the same large stones in such a way, that from the outside it did not appear where it was; and the rest of the pyramid being solid, even if it had been searched for, it was almost impossible to find it, unless the pyramid was dismantled. This path, where one enters with lights, because there is no vent or opening at all, I do not believe to be less than two hundred paces long, because it goes, as I have said, right to the center; and it goes, not plumb, but sloping, which makes the line longer. It is very straight, and is carved entirely between four very equal orders of stones, one of which makes the roof, one the floor, and two the sides. The width and height are such that a single man, bent over, can walk there, but not standing upright; and this I believe also that they did to make the entrance more difficult. The stones around are so large, that very often one finds them, and thus almost all of them, of twenty, twenty-five, and thirty palms <note>A 'palmo' or palm was a historical unit of length, roughly 22-25 cm</note> in length, and even more. At the end of the path one finds something like a little room, to rest a while, which is necessary; since that descent by a very steep way, and bent over, and sometimes, where the stones fallen from the door obstruct the path, with one's belly on the ground, makes one tire a little; besides which, being in a closed place, between the breaths and the heat of the lights, it becomes so hot, that when I reached that place, my sweat had soaked through even my doublet, and all the others who were with me had done no less. From the little room there begins on the left hand a quite steep passage, which goes upwards, returning again to ascend, and it is exactly like one of our vaulted staircases: the vault of it, however, is not round, but ends in an angle; and it is formed in the mass of the pyramid by stones, which, very large, very equal in several orders one above the other, and arranged with excellent architecture, with each order always coming out further than the one below it, gradually narrow, and leave in the middle the vacuum of the little room and of the passage that I speak of: in which, to climb, there are no steps; but only some very steep ledges of the same stones on this side and that, upon which one grips a little with the hands; and for the feet, there are lower down, arranged in order, some holes, by which one can climb: but it is necessary to spread the legs as much as possible from one ledge to the other, which will always be five or six palms in width; and in putting from one hole to the...”*

*...the foot, making the step very long. In such a way, that climbing this passage, although it is not extremely long nor high, nevertheless turns out to be very exhausting; and one can argue from this either that they made it so on purpose to make it difficult to climb, or perhaps that in those times the men of Egypt were of greater stature than they are today, if indeed it was easy for them in this manner. But I went there, and I examined it minutely with great pleasure: and in fact, considering well the handling of those pieces of stone so thick, and the arranging and adjusting of them with such beautiful order, it seemed to me that I found there an architecture and a level of skill such as I, for my part, could not desire any greater. Having climbed this like a staircase, one enters the chamber of the tomb, which is somewhat square; and measured by me, I found it to be about twenty-one of my feet wide, and about forty long. Seven stones alone cover it entirely, each of which rests on one side and the other of the width; and the rest is sustained in the air, forming a very flat vault, like one of our ceilings. The tomb stands at the head of the room crosswise in an isolated position, and it is a very large and quite thick basin, made of a single piece of that hardest stone of Egypt, which Belonio <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist who traveled to Egypt and wrote extensively on its monuments.</note> in several places calls Thebaic <note>A type of red granite or porphyry from the region of Thebes.</note>. I tested its hardness, because with a steel hammer that I had, it was not possible to break off a scale; and what pleased me greatly, striking it with the same hammer, it rang exactly like a bell, giving off a sweet sound, and so loud that if it had not been in a closed place, it would have been heard from very far away. There is no lid to the tomb, either because it was broken, or perhaps because it was never put there; if indeed it is true, as the ignorant locals say, that the King who had that pyramid built was not buried there; and that it is therefore open, and not like the others nearby, which are all closed, and the door cannot be found. Be that as it may, the tomb was placed in there while it was being built; because to bring it there afterward, due to the narrowness of the entrance and other difficulties, was not possible. I had no less pleasure in seeing the pyramid from the outside; because I climbed with some little effort to the very top, where one enjoys a most beautiful view; discovering the sea, and Egypt with much of the surrounding country. Up there at the highest point, in that part which looks toward Italy, I took pleasure in leaving my name carved there, along with that of some other person to whom I wish no ill. I also took pleasure in having my Capigi <note>A Turkish gatekeeper or guard (from the Turkish 'kapıcı').</note> and other Turks who were there with us shoot several arrows from that summit with the greatest force possible; which nevertheless, despite whatever effort was made, always fell back onto the steps of the pyramid; nor was there ever anyone who could push even one of them beyond the steps, nor make it reach the end of them by a long shot. Having then climbed down, I took another look from the outside at the smaller pyramids, which cannot be climbed; and also nearby at the Sphinx, which truly is a fine piece of stone, carved as it is depicted. I do not remember having read whether it is natural stone in that place, or if it was brought from elsewhere; as seems more likely, the countryside being flat and sandy. In that place one cannot tell, because the sand has increased greatly, and the Sphinx stands, perhaps half of it, buried within it; only the head and the neck being visible outside, with a little of the shoulders and the back. # CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. CHAPTER I.

The following day, which was the ninth of December, we rose early in the morning and, having struck our tent, set out to see certain other pyramids further off, which Belonio <note>Pierre Belon (1517–1564), a French naturalist who traveled to Egypt and wrote extensively on its monuments.</note> likewise mentions—that is, many of them; but he does not mention another quite large one, to reach which one must travel a great distance across the sandy plains toward the South. These pyramids are called those of the Mummies, because they are near—indeed, within—the sandy region where the mummies are found. Throughout the journey, one sees nothing but plains of very fine sand, yellow like that which we use for [blotting] letters, and extremely arid; and all around, step by step, are scattered pyramids of various sizes, but all of one shape. This larger one, which I went to see, stands many miles inland and is quite large and beautiful; but it has been so consumed by time on the outside that the steps are ruined, and it is difficult to climb to the top, nor did I care to go there. I did wish to see the inside, as it has an open mouth; and I found it, to my taste, much more beautiful than the other one seen before: because that downward passage, made in the manner of a well, begins a bit higher up; and whether for this reason or another, it is undoubtedly twice as long as the one in the other pyramid. It is also flatter and easier to walk; but it goes down so far that I certainly believe it reaches the very bottom among the foundations. Even though it is so flat, the journey nonetheless proved very troublesome for us: because, as the pyramid is more decayed on the outside, a great multitude of large stones have fallen inside from the mouth, which in many places have so obstructed the path that several times we had to "swim" over the stones, as the Doctor in Naples does upon the water <note>A likely reference to a local Neapolitan character or a specific swimming technique known to the author's contemporary readers.</note>. And sometimes we passed through such narrow straits that they gave me pause; for if by chance one of those stones had moved a little, or through the malice of someone above (for after all, one is in a land of infidels) another had been thrown down that blocked the entrance a bit more, we would have been finished, and would have had to remain there dead and buried alive. Truly, this thought occurred to me, and if I had to return another time, I would want to leave a good guard at the door for every precaution; with orders also that if we delayed too long, they should come down with good pickaxes, because those outside, being in a superior position, could help; but those inside, even if they had pickaxes and every other tool, it would not be possible; because a weight cannot be pushed upward by a single man, who can only fit one at a time; and as for being heard shouting, there would not be a hope in the world. Enough, we others passed through well enough without such diligence: and at the foot of the descent we did not find a climb, as in the other pyramid; but immediately and directly the burial chamber, quite large and very high: and the vault is not flat as in the other; but made at an angle at the top, narrowing as it goes up. From this chamber, through a very low little door, one enters another similar chamber of the same size and workmanship; perhaps the pyramid was made for more than one person: but, neither inside the one nor the other chamber did I find any tomb <term>avello: a formal tomb or sarcophagus</term>; and it must be that either they were not there, or they have been broken and destroyed. It is quite true that in the second chamber, one sees a door left among the marbles very high up, into which I threw a stone and heard it go quite far inside: but the height is such that it would require a large ladder to climb there; and some of the locals say that up there in that third chamber lies the sepulcher: I do not know, as I could not see it; but it could be; placed there perhaps so that the body, through the difficulty...

->On the mention of ancient monuments and great buildings in the land of Egypt<-

The pyramids which are in Egypt are great and numerous, and the largest of them are the two pyramids which are in Giza, Egypt, west of the Nile. It is said that their builder was Shur, son of Shaluk, son of Sharbak, before the Flood. And it is said that Hermes, thrice-great in wisdom <note>Hermes Trismegistus</note>, whom the Hebrews call Enoch—and he is Idris, peace be upon him—when he knew of the coming Flood, built them and deposited within them wealth, scrolls, and everything he feared for throughout the ages and from destruction. Every pyramid has a square base and a conical <note>tapered</note> shape; the height of its pillar is three hundred and seventeen cubits. It is surrounded by four surfaces of equal sides, each side being four hundred and sixty cubits. Despite this greatness, it is of such perfection of workmanship, mastery of structure, and beauty of proportion that nothing of it has changed, even though winds blast and earthquakes shake. The masonry does not allow even a hair to pass between it, and the length of a stone therein is five cubits by a thickness of two cubits. It is said they have doors upon vaults <note>arched passages</note> underground, each vault twenty cubits long, and it has a door of a single stone that rotates on a pivot; when closed, it is not known to be a door. The eastern vault faces the south and the western vault faces the west. You enter from each into seven rooms, each room named after one of the seven planets. The rooms are all locked with a single lock, and in each room is a hollow golden idol, one of its hands upon its mouth, and on its forehead is an inscription; when read, its mouth opens and the key to the locks is found therein. In the Eastern Pyramid, King Shurid was buried; in the Western Pyramid, the brothers of Hujit; and in the Colored Pyramid, Aphrus son of Hajrit. The Sabians claim that one of them is the tomb of Agathodaimon <note>original: "Agithimon"</note>, who is Seth, and the other is the tomb of Hermes, and the Colored one is the tomb of Wasab son of Hermes.

---

### Concerning the Antiquities of Egypt.

The Pyramids which are in Egypt are very large, especially two which are in the trench <note>or site</note> of ancient Cairo <note>original: "Mesrae"</note> on the western side of the Nile. It is said that Shur, son of Shabaluaq, son of Shariak, built them before the Flood; and it is said that Hermes Trismegistus, on account of his wisdom—who is also called Enoch in Hebrew, and is Idris, peace be upon him—when he knew of the future Flood, built it and stored in it all his goods, and books, and whatever precious things he had. Moreover, every pyramid is square and of a polished figure; if you look at the perpendicular elevation, it is 317 cubits; it is surrounded by four equal surfaces of sides, each side being 460 cubits. Furthermore, it was constructed with such skill by ingenious architects that nothing in it is subject to alteration: for whether violent winds rush in, or earthquakes shake it, yet nothing is ever taken away from it. The individual stones of which it consists are 5 cubits long and two high. It is said to have doors above hidden subterranean channels, each channel being 20 cubits long, and they have doors made of stones, through which an entrance lies open by a screw-mechanism <note>original: "cochleam"</note> into a small chamber; nor is it known that that door and the eastern channel look toward the South,

# THE DECREE or *Calculation of the entire Architecture of the Great Pyramid.*

Among so many authors, we find *Herodotus* and *Pliny* to agree most especially; of whom the former stands out for his antiquity (for he lived about 300 years from the founding of the City [Rome], according to the testimony of *Suidas* and *Pliny*), while the latter deservedly holds the chief place among those worthy of trust due to the excellence of his writing and his curious investigation of matters. From his words, therefore, we have established a *calculation* <note>original: "ψηφισμὸν" (psephismon); a Greek term for a mathematical reckoning or decree.</note>. *Pliny* says, therefore, that the base of the pyramid was 8 *jugera* <note>A Roman unit of area, roughly 0.6 acres.</note>, and each side was 883 feet; if these are multiplied by each other, a square number of 779,689 feet is produced. We have, therefore, the area of the base, the cube of which—if you wish to know it—requires one side to be cubed; that is, 883 must be multiplied into the square (assuming, however, that the height is equal to the base of the pyramid), and 688,465,387 will result, which is the <term>prism</term> <note>The volume of a rectangular solid with the same base and height.</note> of the said base. Since a pyramid is truly the third part of its prism, as *Euclid* demonstrates in Book 12, divide the given pyramid cube of 688,465,387 by 3, and the quotient 229,488,462 will give the solidity <note>volume</note> of the Great Pyramid in cubic feet. If you desire to have its weight, multiply the weight of one cubic foot—for example, 200 pounds—by 229,488,462, and the product will give the sum of pounds which the entire mass would weigh if it were entirely solid.

<image-desc>A geometric diagram of a pyramid used to demonstrate calculations of height and area. The square base is defined by points a, b, c, d. The apex is marked e. A vertical altitude line is drawn from e to the center of the base f. A point g is marked at the midpoint of base edge bc. Lines are drawn connecting e, f, and g to form a right-angled triangle (efg) within the pyramid. Numerical values 45 and 44 1/2 are written near the center f.</image-desc>

Furthermore, those who say that the four surfaces of the said pyramid are equal and equilateral must necessarily assert, by the force of geometric reasoning, that the height of the pyramid is less than the length of its side; I demonstrate the matter thus. Let the base of the pyramid be *abcd* and the surfaces be *eac*, *edb*, *ecd*, *eab*, the sides of which are equal to the sides *ab*, *bd*, *cd*, *ca*, and consequently equilateral. These things being established, imagine within the solidity of the pyramid a right-angled triangle *efg*, whose side *eg* is in the middle of the equilateral triangular surface, *ef* is perpendicular to the base *cb*, and *fg* indicates the semi-base, or half the width of the said pyramid, which is *bg*, up to the axis *fe*, which shows the perpendicular of the pyramid or its height. Since, therefore, in this right-angled triangle those sides are smaller which form the right angle, such as *fe* and *gf*; it necessarily follows that the line *fe* is smaller than the line *eg*, which subtends the right angle; and thus it is clearly evident that the height of the pyramid is less than...

to be of that width, assuming the necessary premises—that is, if each of the four surfaces is understood to be an equilateral triangle.

You shall investigate the quantity of the individual sides of the said triangle *e f g* in this manner. Since the sides of the pyramid *a b, b d, d c, c a* are each 883 feet according to Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, Roman author of Natural History</note>, the segment *f g* will necessarily be half of said sides, or 441 1/2 feet. This being established, let it be that as the sine of the complement of the inclination of the pyramid's side is to the right sine <note>The standard sine value</note> of the same inclination—that is, as the sine of 30 degrees is to the sine of 60 degrees—so is 441 1/2 to the other value; and once the operation is performed, the line *f e*, the sought-after altitude of the pyramid, will be produced. You will find the side *e g* thus: Let it be that as the sine of the complement of the pyramid's inclination is to the total sine <note>The radius or sine of 90 degrees</note>, so is 441 1/2 to the other; and the line *e g*, the sought-after slant height of the side of the pyramid, will be produced. Or, let it be done through tangents or secants: as the total sine is to the tangent or secant of 60 degrees, so is 441 1/2 to the other; once the operation is performed, the same result as before will be produced, namely the height of both sides *e f* and *e g*. And this is the calculation according to the account of Herodotus <note>Greek historian, often called the Father of History</note>, which nevertheless can hardly stand if it is compared with those things which other authors observe regarding its height.

->[Figure I: A geometric diagram of a pyramid. A vertical line (altitude) drops from the apex 'e' to the center 'f'. A line 'fg' connects the center to the midpoint of the base edge. Angles of 30 and 60 degrees are marked.]<-

Others suggest that the height of this pyramid was equal to the length of the base: if that were so, let the axis of height *f e* be 883 feet, as in Figure II; and the quality of line *e g* will be obtained in the following way. Let the number of line *e f*, 883, be squared, and likewise the side *f g*, which we said was 441 1/2 feet; let the squares be joined into one; if you extract the square root from that sum, it will show you the quantity of line *e g*, the sought-after slant height. But since this height, given the premise, exceeds what is reasonable, we have decided that a middle opinion must be held, which in this matter considers the perpendicular height least of all, but rather that which the line *e g* expresses in the figure.

->[Figure II: A second geometric diagram of a pyramid with different proportions. The vertical altitude is 'ef', the slant height is 'eg', and the distance from center to edge is 'fg'. Angles of 35 and 55 degrees are shown.]<-

Therefore, let us suppose the angle of the slope of the surface to be 55 degrees, and let it be that as the sine of the complement of *f g* is to the total sine *e g*, so is 441 1/2 to the other; once the operation is performed, the quantity of line *e g*, the sought-after height, will be produced. If you now desire to have the perpendicular height, that is, of line *e f*; let it be that as the sine of the complement of 55 degrees is to the right sine *e f*, so is 441 1/2 to the other; and once the operation is performed, the sought-after perpendicular height will be produced, that is, the quantity of line *e f*.

## Architectural Conclusion.

And from these things demonstrated—perhaps more extensively than was necessary—the wonderful genius of the Architect clearly lies open, both in decorating the marvelous structure and in moving such vast individual stones into their places. For the matter could by no means be accomplished without machines constructed with the highest industry and a truly Archimedean <note>Referring to Archimedes of Syracuse, implying advanced mechanical engineering</note> skill. But what pulling-machines shall we think were used to transport stones from the mountains of Arabia, separated by such a great distance, through such pathless and obstructed routes, to the appointed place? Who could find an Architect in the present day whose spirit would suffice to attempt such a thing? For it is joined together with stones, each 30 feet in length according to the testimony of Herodotus, so that it remains intact to this very day without any tearing apart of the stones; it has a circumference of 3,532 feet, of which each side occupies almost as much space as the length of the Piazza Navona <note>original: "fori agonalis"; the author compares the pyramid's footprint to this famous Roman square</note> in Rome. Thus, this fabric surpasses all the sumptuous buildings of the Romans—such as the Baths, Amphitheaters, etc.—by many parasangs <note>A Persian unit of distance, used here metaphorically to mean "by a long shot"</note>, whether you look at the magnitude, the exorbitance of the expenses, or finally the magnificence and genius.

While I am writing these things, Tito Livio Burattini <note>1617–1681, an Italian inventor and Egyptologist</note>, a distinguished Architect who traveled to Egypt for the express purpose of investigating all the monuments of antiquity with the greatest diligence, sketching what he investigated, and thus entrusting a treasure to posterity, has sent me, among many other things, a sketch of this pyramid. This includes a ground plan <term>Ichnographia: a scale ground plan or map</term> of the desert in which it is found and of the subterranean vault where the entrance to the Mummies lies open; which I have decided to place here along with the letter given to me.

This letter of mine will be accompanied by the drawings of the Mummies and the Pyramids, near which the famous Memphis once stood; you shall have their measurements and the interior drawing together with those of Giza, placed among the seven wonders of the World. In the past weeks, I received two most dear letters from Your Most Reverend Paternity, from the last of which I see the desire you have to know something of the City of Chanea <note>Modern Chania, on the island of Crete</note>, of which Father Marco tells you so many things. Likewise in the most ancient Sais, now called *Sa l’haiar*—that is, "Sais of the stones," just as the aforementioned *Bebet* is "of the stones"—so called because of the very great ruins seen in both, which denote the greatness of Egypt's ancient prosperity. In *Sa l’haiar* there are many antiquities, as I say, among which are various Sphinxes of white stone and also of Granite, all covered in Hieroglyphics. However, the one at Thebes surpasses all others in size, excepting that of the Pyramids of Giza, as I shall show in due time. That of Thebes is about 30 feet long, and its base is adorned all around with Hieroglyphics, as are also two great Idols <note>Likely referring to colossal statues</note> that are near it, each about 20 feet long.

Many other things besides these I have lost, to my supreme sorrow, which has been the reason I no longer applied myself to regularly organizing the little that remains to me, which I indicated to Your Most Reverend Paternity in my first letter. I humbly kiss your hand and remain, Warsaw, September 15, 1652.

Of Your Most Reverend Paternity,

->Temples and Shrines<-

**A**mong the other memorable things of the Egyptians established by King Amasis <note>Amasis II, a pharaoh of the 26th Dynasty who reigned shortly before the Persian conquest.</note> is this: that he transported a certain shrine made of a single, solid stone over a period of three years, with the help of two thousand men, from the city of Elephantine to Sais, a journey of 20 days' distance. Herodotus writes accurately about this in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's *Histories* is named after Euterpe, the Muse of music.</note> near the end. <note>The following Greek text is a citation from Herodotus, Book II (Euterpe), Chapter 175.</note> *And of these things, I wonder not the least, but the most, at this: he brought a monolithic chamber from the city of Elephantine. And he brought this over three years, and two thousand men were assigned as transporters, and these were all pilots. The length of this roofed chamber on the outside is twenty-one cubits, the width fourteen, and the height eight. These are the measurements on the outside of the monolithic chamber; but on the inside, the length is eighteen cubits and a span, the width twelve cubits, and the height five cubits.* <note>original Greek: "Τὸ δὲ οὐκ ἥκιστα αὐτέων... πέντε πηχέων ἐστί."</note> *In addition to these things, what I admire not the least, but the most, is this: he brought a building made of solid stone from the city of Elephantine; in bringing which two thousand selected men, who were all pilots, spent three years. The length is eighteen ells and a cubit, the width twelve, and the height five. <note>These measurements refer to the interior of the monolithic chamber.</note> This house was intended to be carried into a most magnificent temple, or rather the vestibule of Minerva <note>The Greek goddess Athena, whom the author identifies with the Egyptian goddess Neith.</note> which Amasis had built in Sais. And this is that admirable fabric cut from a whole rock, or rather a mountain; it is difficult for anyone to conceive in their mind by what machines they were able to move it from a distance of 20 days' journey from Sais. This mass was brought from that distance over a period of three years, as has been said. However, how much the mass was moved each year, month, or day by the machines, I leave to be calculated by the Arithmeticians.

### *The Labyrinth, and the Tomb of the Kings.*

**W**hat the most ancient Authors—Herodotus, Diodorus, Strabo, and after them Pliny—write concerning the Egyptian Labyrinth seems to surpass all human belief.
