--- Page 313 ---
<meta>This page continues the discussion of Egyptian engineering and architecture, specifically focusing on the Great Labyrinth. It follows the general introduction to Egyptian mechanics.</meta>

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. CHAPTER I.

The size, arrangement, and magnificence of this structure are described differently by various authors; nor should this seem strange to anyone, since those who entered the Labyrinth—amidst such a vast multitude of things to see—each thought it best to report on whatever drew their greatest admiration. Thus, while new and more wonderful sights continually appeared to be surveyed, the minds of the observers were easily confused by the innumerable details; as they were unable to observe each part distinctly, they recorded them for posterity in a confused and indistinct manner. Certainly, Pliny asserts that Daedalus <note>The mythical Greek architect and craftsman.</note>, captured by admiration for this building, took the opportunity to build another Labyrinth in Lemnos, although he imitated only a hundredth part of it, as he was unable to disentangle himself from the inextricable structure of the building even with the supreme genius he possessed.

<margin>Location of the Egyptian Labyrinth.</margin> The Labyrinth is located at Lake Moeris toward Crocodilopolis <note>original: "Crocodilopolim"; an ancient city in the Faiyum dedicated to the crocodile god Sobek.</note>, according to the testimony of Herodotus and Pliny, who also maintain that it is the Tomb of Moeris. <margin>The dwellings of the Labyrinth.</margin> It is divided first into twelve dwellings according to Herodotus, and into sixteen according to Pliny; these were evidently as many halls, or rather ample reception rooms and vast buildings, as there were once administrative districts—which they call <term>Nomes</term> <note>From the Greek 'Nomos', the territorial divisions of ancient Egypt.</note>—into which all of Egypt was divided. It contained, moreover, the temples of all the <margin>Temples of the Labyrinth.</margin> Egyptian Deities; within which were included several pyramids of forty cubits each. Furthermore, according to Strabo, the individual halls of the Nomes were surrounded by columns and were continuous with one another; the paths leading to them are opposite the wall which surrounds the halls arranged in order. <margin>The crypts of the Labyrinth.</margin> Before the entrance gate, however, there are many long crypts <note>Hidden or underground chambers.</note>, which hold paths entangled with such great and marvelous tortuosity that no one can enter any hall, nor exit, without a guide, being deceived by that inexplicable wandering of the paths.

<margin>The dining rooms and porticos of the Labyrinth.</margin> Here there are also very high dining rooms, and porticos each built with ninety steps, supported by columns of porphyry stone <note>A prized purple-red igneous rock.</note>, among which are images of the Gods, statues of Kings, and a vast collection of monstrous images. Indeed, the site and arrangement of certain houses is such, by the ingenious invention of the Architect, that as soon as their doors are opened, a formidable thunder seems to be heard. <margin>The roofs of the Labyrinth.</margin> Truly worthy of admiration above all else is that the floors or roofs of the individual houses, as well as the widths of the crypts, were constructed—according to Strabo—from single stones of an altogether unusual size, without the intervention of any wood or other material.

In a word, the entire extension of the structure comprised three thousand houses, which could equal even a huge city. But let us hear Herodotus describing the details exactly in his *Euterpe* <unclear>Book II</unclear>. His words are: <margin>Herodotus. Description of the Labyrinth from Herodotus.</margin>
*When the twelve Kings were reigning in Egypt, they decided to leave some monument common to them all, and from that decision they made the Labyrinth a little above Lake Moeris, especially toward the city called the City of Crocodiles, which I beheld as being greater than its fame. For if anyone calculates the walls and the appearance of the work from the narration of the Greeks, he will conceive of less than the labor and expense of this labyrinth; for although the temple at Ephesus is worthy of mention, and that in Samos; nevertheless the pyramids were greater than the telling, each of which is equal to many and great works of Greece. But the Labyrinth surpasses even those. For it has twelve halls covered by a roof, with gates opposite one another on each side: six facing the North—*

# CHAPTER I. 308 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>The 3,500 dwellings of the Labyrinth.</margin>
...[the rooms] are contiguous, with just as many facing South, all enclosed by the exact same wall. The dwellings within are of two kinds: one part is subterranean, and the other is the upper structure placed above them. There are three thousand five hundred of each <note>Herodotus actually cites 3,000 total (1,500 above and 1,500 below); the author here may be using a variant manuscript or calculation.</note>. We ourselves saw those which are above ground, and we relate what we beheld; however, we learned of the subterranean ones only by report. For the Egyptian overseers of the Labyrinth were unwilling to show them by any means, saying that the tombs of the Kings who were the authors of the Labyrinth's construction were there, as well as the tombs of the sacred Crocodiles. Thus, we found out about the lower parts by instruction, but we saw the upper parts ourselves, which are greater than any human works. For the winding passages or exits through the roofs, and the returns through the halls, being so exceedingly diverse, filled me with infinite admiration. One passes from a hall into chambers, from chambers into bedrooms, from bedrooms into other terraces, and from chambers into other halls. The ceiling of all these, just like the walls, is made of stone, adorned everywhere with carved figures; each hall is for the most part laid out with white stone and encircled by a perimeter of columns. At the corner where the Labyrinth ends, there stands a pyramid of forty paces, upon which large animals are inscribed, and to which a path leads underground. This is the description observed by Herodotus, a curious inspector and admirer of all things. Following his description, I would have gladly exhibited here at least some rough and superficial ground plan <term>Ichnographia: a floor plan or map</term> of the entire fabric if time had permitted, so that the reader might "gather the Lion from its claw" <note>original: "ex ungue Leonem" — a proverb meaning to judge the whole by a small part</note> and might conjecture the excellence of the genius of the Architect of such works. But perhaps we shall provide that elsewhere.

<margin>The Tomb of Ismendis is distinct from the Labyrinth.</margin>
Furthermore, what Hecataeus relates in the writings of Diodorus concerning the Tomb of Ismendis does not seem to agree with the account of Herodotus and Pliny, since he makes no mention of the halls which they call "Nomes" <note>The administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note>; nor does he arrange the dwellings in the same order as Herodotus; nor does the location, which the cited authors assign near Lake Moeris, agree. For he says that it was built in the territory of Thebes; since this is distant from Lake Moeris by a journey of many days, we are necessarily forced to assert that it was undoubtedly a different structure (whatever some authors may say who confuse the construction of the Tomb of Ismendis with the Labyrinth). Yet, because from the account of Hecataeus this structure of Ismendis is by no means inferior to the Labyrinth, whether you look at its magnificence or its vastness, we shall set down here its description also, from the very words of Hecataeus, an eyewitness, as found in Diodorus.

# CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

Next were the images of all the Egyptian Gods; also of the King offering gifts, such as were appropriate to each God. <margin>20</margin> Behind the Library was situated a magnificent house, in which were the <term>lectisternia</term> <note>A ritual banquet offered to gods where their images were placed on couches.</note> of Jupiter and Juno. Around the monument ran a golden circle of 365 cubits in circumference and one cubit in thickness, in which were inscribed, cubit by cubit, the days of the year, and the Risings and Settings of the stars, and what those observations signified according to the Egyptian Astrologers. They say this circle was carried away at the time when Cambyses and the Persians ruled the Egyptians. This monument of Osymandias <note>The Greek name for Pharaoh Ramses II.</note> was not only more costly than all others, but also more excellent in craftsmanship. Thus far Hecataeus according to Diodorus.

<margin>Three things especially to be wondered at in the Tomb of Ismendis. First, the multitude of Statues.</margin>
In this unusual construction of a prodigious work, three things especially occur as worthy of admiration. The first is the craftsmanship of so many statues constructed from a single stone, each of which was 32 feet in height, and which supported the roof of the peristyle in place of columns. These were exceeded by many <term>parasangs</term> <note>A Persian unit of distance; here used metaphorically to mean "by a great deal."</note> by the middle one of three at the entrance of the second peristyle, whose foot alone almost equaled the height of those serving as columns, being 28 feet, or seven cubits in length. Since, therefore, the length of a foot is one-sixth of the total height of the body, the said statue, if it had stood upright (for it was represented in a sitting posture), would have been 168 feet; which not even the Colossus of the Sun at Rhodes would have equaled. Two other prostrate statues are also mentioned, each of which was 108 feet in length; though these yielded to the former in size, they far surpassed it in the excellence of the stone.

<margin>Second, the square building.</margin>
Second, the square building resting on columns, each side of which was 480 feet long, supported by 27 columns of solid stone; to which corresponded an equal number of wooden statues of immense size on the upper roof.

<margin>Third, the golden circle of 365 solid cubits.</margin>
The third was the golden circle which surrounded the monument of Simendis, of 365 cubits, which contained the days of the entire year, the Risings and Settings of the Stars, and the elections <note>Astro-chronological determinations of favorable times.</note> and observations of the Astrologers; and each degree was one cubit, that is, 4 feet, in length as well as in width and thickness; its diameter, by Mathematical reasoning, was about 120 cubits, that is, 480 feet; from which the size of the place it occupied can be sufficiently gathered. Furthermore, if it was of gold, as Diodorus records, and not of gilded bronze; the total mass of the circle weighed 3,650,000—that is, three million, six hundred and fifty thousand pounds—assuming that a solid cubit of gold, or a golden cube measuring 4 feet in width as well as height, weighs 10,000 pounds. This is a thing that can hardly be conceived by the mind.

# SECTION VIII. THE MECHANICS OF THE EGYPTIANS. 311 CHAPTER II.

<margin>The excellence of Egyptian Architects.</margin>
...formed by maintaining the perfect proportion of the human body, and the quantity of gold used in the construction of a single celestial Sphere, demonstrated with no less brilliance of genius than of wealth. Indeed, if I consider these works a little more deeply, I would dare to solemnly affirm that just as nothing of human science was hidden from these men of supreme intellect, so by the help of those sciences they achieved things greater than even other human works; for I see all arts and sciences—Physics and Mathematics—conspiring together in the formation of even a single structure. For who today would dare to attempt anything similar, unless they were consulted in the whole of nature, and endowed to a miraculous degree with skill in all of Arithmetic, Geometry, Optics, Astronomy, Mechanics, Statics, and the other related arts? Let no one wonder, therefore, that the system of the entire Art of Architecture, having devolved first from the Egyptians to the Greeks, and from them to the Romans, still maintains its high reputation to this day.

<margin>Lake Moeris. Herodotus.</margin>
<margin>The wonders of the city of Thebes.</margin>
I shall say nothing here of Lake Moeris <note>A vast ancient artificial reservoir in the Fayyum basin</note>, which, according to the testimony of Herodotus, inspires more admiration than all the works described thus far. It measures three thousand six hundred stadia <note>An ancient unit of distance; 3,600 stadia is roughly 400 miles</note> in circumference; where it is deepest, it is 50 paces; it was excavated by human industry both to receive the stagnant waters of the Nile and to irrigate the land when those waters failed. Regarding its wonders, see the cited Herodotus in *Euterpe* <note>The second book of Herodotus's Histories</note>, who describes every detail most exactly. I do not mention the wonders of the city of Thebes, which may be seen in the works of Strabo, Diodorus, and the previously cited Herodotus; these are truly so great that, by the testimony of the authors themselves, nothing greater or more excellent could exist in human affairs. And these are the things we thought should be said regarding the Architecture of the Egyptians; now let us turn our pen to their machines.

## CHAPTER II.
->On the Mechanics of the Egyptians.<-

<margin>Herodotus.</margin>
<margin>Machines necessary for constructing the works of the Egyptians.</margin>
We have seen the immense structures of the Egyptians, we have marveled at the inextricable wanderings of the Labyrinth and the towering masses of the Colossi; it remains now for us to show by what industry of intellect and craftsmanship they erected such unusual structures. Certainly, this could by no means have been accomplished without machines constructed with the highest art. And first, indeed, I do not deny that a vast multitude of men was necessary to build such edifices both more quickly and more easily. For Pliny records that three hundred thousand men labored in the building of the Great Pyramid alone; in the same way, no one should doubt that the same occurred in the construction of the Labyrinth and the other described works, unless they are ignorant of the fact that Egypt, above all other nations of the world, always abounded in a nearly innumerable supply of men. But notwithstanding that excessive multitude of men, I say nonetheless that those works could not have been done without the employment of machines; nor can the claim of Diodorus stand, that it was built with earthen ramps, machines not yet having been discov—

found. Pliny <note>original: "Plinius"; referring to Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist</note> asserts that brick bridges <note>ramps</note> were constructed, over which immense rocks were rolled to their designated places by the force of laborers; but this cannot be maintained, since the weights were greater than what could be moved by the direct application of hands. Statics <note>The branch of mechanics dealing with loads and balance</note> teaches us that a weight which cannot be moved by the work of two hundred men applying their strength by hand, can be moved without difficulty by the work of eight or ten men using machines. Therefore, they necessarily used machines for both moving and erecting such monstrous masses; what kind of machines these were remains to be explained.

<margin>
Knowledge of tempering iron among the Egyptians.
</margin>
I suppose, first, that the Egyptians had a perfect knowledge of tempering both other metals, such as gold and silver, and especially iron—a knowledge handed down from the first Fathers. For how could they have cut, hewn, and polished such immense masses of statues, even those constructed from a single block of porphyry <note>A very hard, purple-red igneous rock</note> (the hardest kind of stone, as we have seen), without the quality and tempering of the finest iron? We know how much our own craftsmen sweat even in the crafting of small porphyry vessels. It is likely, therefore, that they possessed a marvelous tempering process, entirely unknown to us, for penetrating those porphyry mountains and for cutting, hewing, and polishing the stones.

<margin>
Mechanical principles implanted by nature.
</margin>
I suppose, secondly, that the Mathematical Mechanics—a large number of whom were maintained at public expense for this purpose—devoted themselves solely to this: that by inventing new machines, they might advance the proud undertakings of the Kings.

I suppose, thirdly, that mechanical principles are implanted by nature, as experience teaches from the movements of bodies, the lifting of heavy weights, or the striking of objects; from this, the principle of levers and hammers found its origin. For when we attempt to drive a nail into a wall, we do not use the hand or any hard object held in the hands, but a hammer, which acts like a lever; so also we attempt to push and raise a rock more easily not by the direct application of hands, but by placing a piece of wood beneath it. These things are too well known to need further mention. These things being established, we come to:

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 313 CHAPTER II.

<margin>The method of dragging stones. Vitruvius.</margin>
...they relate of him. Furthermore, for dragging and carrying massive stones over long distances, he prepared two rollers or cylinders proportioned to the weight to be carried, with a frame made of the sturdiest trees laid over them, yet in such a way that they did not touch the cylinders; and upon these, he placed the firmly secured stones. By attaching ropes only to the axles of the cylinders, a great multitude of men pulled them to the designated place across mounds of earth piled up like mountains. To ensure no obstacle was encountered on the way, all pits and inequalities of the paths through which the stones were to be conveyed were first filled with stones, sand, and earthen masses. Vitruvius <note>Marcus Vitruvius Pollio, a Roman author and engineer</note> records that Ctesiphon and his son Metagenes used this same device for transporting the columns intended for the Temple of Ephesus.

<margin>A triple method for moving larger machines from their place.</margin>
There was, moreover, a triple method and system commonly used for moving larger machines: for they either had to be transported from the quarry to the established location, whether by land or by river; or immense Colossi had to be erected; or finally, stones of the loftiest mass had to be set in their designated place. The first was called *helktike* <note>original Greek: ἑλκτικὴ</note>, that is, performed by **tractive force**; the second *exagogike nautike* <note>original Greek: ἐξαγωγικὴ ναυτικὴ</note>, that is, **exportive or nautical**; the third was called **manganaria** <note>The art of using engines or cranes; from the Greek 'manganon'</note>. I shall speak of each.

->§ II.<-

->*Concerning the Machines by which huge masses of stone*<-
->*were carried by land.*<-

<margin>Philo of Byzantium. What a sledge is.</margin>
**F**irst of all, as we mentioned above, the path through which the masses were to be rolled was leveled with the greatest zeal and industry, by filling in ditches and smoothing down the higher parts of the earth, so that no impediment or stumbling block might be encountered. This being established, they brought the stones and similar masses through the prepared path to the destined station by a twofold device. Philo of Byzantium <note>A Greek engineer and writer on mechanics</note> asserts that the Ancients used a **sledge** <note>original: "traha"</note> in conveying stones. Now, the sledge was a type of vehicle consisting of two huge parallel beams, which were firmly connected by transverse rungs, and were covered on the underside with polished iron plates, with the ends <note>literally "horns"</note> slightly curved and turned back. Upon these they placed the huge stones, and thus, with a vast multitude of men or beasts of burden attached to the cables, they led them to the destined place; this method found its greatest use after the receding of the Nile, while the earth was still muddy and slippery.

<margin>Chariots for conveying huge masses of stone. Vitruvius.</margin>
The second type of vehicle was a chariot equipped with four very thick cylinders or drums, likewise covered with polished iron plates around their circumference; through the centers of these, two axles forged from very thick iron or another metal were passed. Above these axles, a framework <note>term: "pegma" - a wooden scaffolding or platform</note> of beams was constructed according to the size of the masses, upon which the load to be transported was placed, and then, by the aforementioned multitude of men or beasts, they were carried to their place with straps and very thick ropes. <margin>How Ctesiphon transported columns into their place.</margin>
He used a not dissimilar artifice; for when he was about to transport huge columns into their place, once the individual columns were finished, he soldered bronze axles into the ends of the columns, corresponding to their centers. Then, he fitted these axles into enormous wheels, and thus at last the load was rolled along at the Architect's will by the aid of the wheels. These bronze axles then served to stabilize the columns more firmly within their bases and capitals. Examine the accompanying figure:

<note>The illustration depicts the method used by the Greek architect Chersiphron (here called Ctesiphon) for the Temple of Artemis at Ephesus. By turning the column itself into an axle for a giant wheel, he avoided the friction of dragging it.</note>

*A woodcut illustration showing the engineering process for transporting a large stone column. The cylindrical column segment is mounted horizontally within a heavy wooden framework supported by a massive wheel. A man on horseback, wielding a whip, leads a team of horses pulling the mechanism along a path.*

<margin>The use of rollers.</margin>
Others say that the Ancients used <term>rollers</term> <note>original: "scytalis"</note>, upon which polished and smooth wooden planks were spread; the weight placed upon these was turned by levers toward the desired station. I would not wish this to be understood as a method for a journey of great distance; for that perpetual agitation of the rollers and the changing of the planks thrown over them almost every fifteen paces would have been very inconvenient. However, in a small space, they were able to provide no small use for rolling a load along.

### §. III.
### *By what machines the said masses were conveyed by water and sea.*

<margin>The method of transferring Obelisks from the quarries to the appointed place.</margin>

In this trench—or more truly, a river—according to the witness of Callixenus the Phoenician in the writings of Pliny, they arranged two very large ships, which they loaded with stones to such an extent that the weight of the stones was double the weight of the Obelisk...

These are the words of Pliny. By a similar industry, undoubtedly received from their ancestors through tradition, the rest of their descendants used it in transferring great masses. Some maintain that the Obelisks were transferred to the appointed places at that time when the inundation of the Nile in Egypt was at its greatest; for with the waters rising high above the lands, nothing was easier than to carry a burden outside the channel of the Nile into any level place in Egypt. If, however, necessity so required, they rolled the Obelisk, placed upon <term>chamulci</term> <note>low carriages or sledges used for heavy weights</note> or cylinders, to the place of erection; in which place, the foundation having first been set—which for the most part was a stone or native rock—they finally erected the Obelisk with the help of capstans and pulleys, protected against all violence by wooden beams and planks stuffed with wool, hay, and straw.

# CLASS 8. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. 317 CHAPTER 2.

...to explain the names commonly used by the Egyptians. It has been handed down by Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a 1st-century engineer</note> and by Philo <note>Philo of Byzantium, a writer on mechanics</note> why the aforementioned powers are reduced into a single nature, although they differ greatly from one another in their shapes. These names, therefore, are: the wheel and axle <note>original: "axis in peritrochio"</note>, the lever, the pulley <note>original: "polyspastos"</note>, the wedge, and finally that which is called the infinite screw. And to begin with the simplest, the lever:

<image-desc>A diagram illustrating the use of a lever. A man stands on the right, applying downward force to one end of a long wooden or iron pole (labeled B). The pole (lever AB) rests on a small triangular support (fulcrum C) and acts as a lever to lift a large rectangular stone block (stone D). The letters A, B, C, and D are used to label the specific parts of the lever mechanism.</image-desc>

<margin>What a lever is.</margin>
A lever is an instrument, either of wood or iron, of an oblong shape, which, when placed under a weight at one end and pressed downward by a moving force at the other, lifts the weight with no difficulty. This is seen in the figure, where **D** is the stone, **AB** is the lever, and **C** is the fulcrum <note>original: "hypomochlium," the pivot point</note>. For as Hero rightly discusses in the works of

<margin>Hero the Mechanician.</margin>
Pappus <note>Pappus of Alexandria, a mathematician who preserved Hero's work</note>, when the Ancients wished to move great weights, it was first necessary to raise them from the earth; however, they had no handles because all parts of the base of the weight itself rested upon the ground. By digging out a little space and thrusting the end of a long piece of wood under the load, they placed a stone—which is called a fulcrum—under the wood near the load itself, and in this way they moved the load. And since this motion seemed very easy to them, they persuaded themselves that it was possible for any great weights whatsoever to be lifted in this manner. Moreover, they discovered that the closer the fulcrum was to the stone, the more easily the weight was moved; for by this reasoning, the lever acquired a greater length <note>referring to the effort arm</note>. As the mechanics demonstrate, the longer the lever was, the more easily the weight was moved.

<margin>The use of the lever provided the first foundations of Mechanics.</margin>
And these are the first foundations of Mechanics, which we all use, not so much by art as by a certain instinct of nature. Indeed, no human action involving any force can be identified which is not—even without us noticing—accomplished by the help of the lever.

Furthermore, since the scale of weights was sometimes such that levers could not perform their duty (as happens in lifting massive structures), they engineered another kind of machine. In this, a multiple arrangement of levers set in a circle would perform the same task in lifting masses to a great height as levers do for masses resting on the surface of the earth.

<margin>The wheel and axle.</margin>
And this they called the wheel and axle <note>original: "axis in peritrochio"</note>. It was an instrument consisting of a cylinder and a wheel, on the circumference of which spokes were arranged to take the place of levers, as appears in the following figure. For they wrapped ropes around the cylinder AB, to which the wheel S was fixed, and from the end of these ropes the stone L hung. It happened that when the wheel was turned by its spokes, the cylinder, revolving the ropes along with it, finally lifted the stone. They usually placed this machine on the walls onto which the stones were to be raised; and thus, firmly...

The use of this instrument was twofold: upright and inverted. It was "upright" when weights were raised high by its help; it was "inverted" when they dragged said weights from a distance, or even pulled them upwards; and then it was called a <term>capstan</term> <note>original: "ergata," a Greek-derived term for a vertical winch</note>. It is called inverted because, just as in the upright position the cylinder is parallel to the horizon, so here it was established as normal or perpendicular to the same. However, for this position, certain other things were required, such as pulleys and beams equipped with <term>compound pulleys</term> <note>original: "polyspastis," a system of multiple pulleys for lifting heavy loads</note>: of which more will be said at length as soon as we have understood what is meant by pulleys, wedges, and similar mechanical powers.

## The Egyptian Wedge.

<margin>The Egyptian Wedge.</margin>
<margin>Philo of Byzantium. The use of the wedge in splitting stones.</margin>
The wedge was used most especially in stone quarries; it is a wooden or iron instrument of pyramidal shape, by which immense rocks are split. For when this is placed within the crack of some stone and struck by a violent blow of a hammer, while it violently introduces itself into the crack and powerfully presses against both sides, it finally splits the rock. Moreover, they had many instruments of this kind which, when placed in order within the fissure and struck, the stone was split. Indeed, in those mountainous places where immense masses for columns, obelisks, and statues were to be extracted from a single stone, Philo of Byzantium <note>A Greek engineer of the 3rd century BCE</note> reports in his booklet *On the Five Statical Faculties* that the ancients used this industrious method. They established a wooden machine upon the rock, or rather a <term>scaffold</term> <note>original: "pegma"</note>, adorned with a transverse revolving cylinder; to this cylinder they hung a steel column of immense weight by a very thick rope; and below, within the crack of the rock, they placed a wedge proportioned to the size of the steel cylinder. And so, by pulling the rope, the cylinder was raised; once it was elevated to a certain height, the workmen, loosening the rope, allowed it to fall onto the wedge. Pressed by the immense weight of this, the wedge split the rock with great force, and thus following the fissure of the crack by a new adaptation of the instruments...

### *The Egyptian Compound Pulley*

<margin>The Egyptian Compound Pulley</margin>
The second capability was achieved through the compound pulley <note>original: "polyspastus"</note>, with a pulley-wheel inserted into a frame <note>original: "manganum"</note>, around which a rope was wound; by this, a weight could be pulled and moved with no effort. Furthermore, the arrangement of these pulley-wheels varied according to the size of the weights. When a single pulley-wheel was used, as happened with smaller weights, it was then called a <term>monopastos</term> <note>Greek: "single-pulley"</note>; if two pulley-wheels were used, a <term>dipastos</term> <note>Greek: "double-pulley"</note>; if three, a <term>tripastos</term> <note>Greek: "triple-pulley"</note>; and so they were named on to infinity. <margin>The use of the compound pulley on flat ground</margin> Moreover, the use of these compound pulleys was twofold; for they served either for lifting weights on high, or for dragging them across the ground. Indeed, I have decided to set forth the mechanism of both here before the eyes of the reader, so that by the representation of the machine itself, I might compensate for a lengthy description of the same.

<margin>What the disadvantages of the compound pulley are.</margin>
This machine did indeed have this disadvantage: that for every hundred paces, the locations of both the compound pulley and the windlass <note>original: "ergatæ"</note> had to be changed simultaneously until the load was transferred to the designated place. Otherwise, enormous weights were transported with almost no effort by the help of this machine. And no one should doubt that by the power of this machine, that prodigious temple fashioned from a single stone—which we mentioned above from Herodotus—was transported from Elephantine all the way to Sais (a distance of twenty days' journey) over a period of three years; for no better or more efficient method could be found. Let these remarks suffice regarding the moving of weights on a level plane by means of the compound pulley.

# THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
### CHAPTER II.

lest the overburdened tree <note>original: "arbor"; here referring to the central mast or beam of the lifting machine</note> should break, four or five ropes (marked X, T, Y, F, G) were drawn down from the top of the tree and fixed firmly into the ground. In this way, the machine was stabilized by these cables, much like the mast of a ship, along with its rotating platform. However, because the machine often had to be moved, wheels or rollers (C, D, V, E) were fitted to the platform so that they could transport the entire machine wherever they wished with no trouble. But observe the figure placed here. <note>The author refers to an illustration likely appearing on the original page or facing it.</note>

In this manner, they raised any weight, however vast, to a great height. But if the weights were too great to be lifted by the power of a single capstan <term>ergata: a vertical-axle windlass or capstan used for hauling or lifting</term> and pulley system <term>polyspastos: a compound pulley system with many sheaves</term>—as was the case with the mass of the Obelisks and the huge Colossi—then they would multiply the pulley systems to match the number of capstans. Thus, by employing a vast multitude of men or pack animals, with each moving their individual capstans equally and in unison, they finally raised the masses. These masses were first enclosed in scaffolding or a wooden "garment" to prevent damage to the statues or Obelisks, and they were lifted with as much ease as there was harmony in the effort.

<margin>A bifurcated wooden machine used in the construction of pyramids.</margin>
In the construction of the pyramids, however, they did not use a "tree" implanted into a platform, but rather employed a certain bifurcated <note>two-pronged or fork-shaped</note> wooden machine. A pulley attached to its upper part would take the ropes; meanwhile, outside the base of the pyramid, another machine was applied (which I would interpret as a capstan), around which the other end of the cord was wound. This machine, rotated by the labor of men or animals, gradually placed the stone in its designated spot. They would move the aforementioned bifurcated wooden machine to each successive level of the pyramids, completing the work step-by-step. Thus, there were either as many machines as there were levels of the pyramid, or certainly the same machine was moved from level to level. Indeed, let us hear the words of Herodotus himself in his second book, where he discusses the pyramid of Cheops:
> This pyramid was built in the form of steps, which some call "stairs" and others "altars." After they had first made it in this shape, they raised the remaining stones with short machines made of wood, lifting them from the ground to the first row of steps. When the stone was on this step, it was placed onto a second machine which stood on that first level; from there it was dragged to the next row onto another machine (for there were as many machines as there were rows of steps), or perhaps they transferred the same machine—if it was a single one and easy to carry—to each row whenever the stone was moved.

And from this it is clearly evident that these machines were first successfully devised by the Egyptians, who above all nations of the world always had their minds intent on erecting the greatest and most prodigious structures. <margin>Herodotus, Philo.</margin> These inventions were then passed to the Greeks through Daedalus <note>The mythical master craftsman</note>, as Herodotus and Philo testify, and from there were transferred to the Romans. It is so true that Archimedes, Vitruvius, and Pappus derived all their knowledge from here that even Archimedes himself admits it, <margin>David Rivalt.</margin> according to Rivalt in his *Life of Archimedes*, where he sincerely confesses that he learned many things regarding Mechanics while in Egypt through his association with Hero. <note>Hero of Alexandria, a famous Greek mathematician and engineer.</note>

There remains the final power concerning the screw <note>original: "cochlea"</note>. Since it possesses some difficulty both in its construction and its use, I do not think it was so frequently used by the Egyptians, nor could it have much use in lifting weights from the ground. <margin>What a screw is.</margin> According to Pappus, a screw is nothing other than...

# CHAPTER III.

## Concerning the Wonder-Working Machines of the Ancient Egyptians.

<margin>Wonder-working machines of the Egyptians.</margin>
This chapter is entitled "Concerning the Wonder-Working Machines of the Ancient Egyptians," that is, concerning structures built with such miraculous and great industry that all authors who have mentioned them have judged them to be constructed not by human art, but by the magical help of demons. For it is the nature of such machines that while their hidden and concealed devices are not visible, they nevertheless breathe motion and life, and hold spectators astonished by the novelty of the thing, as if struck by lightning.
<margin>They were of many kinds.</margin>
They are, moreover, of many types. Some displayed the miracles of art by sound alone, such as the statue of Memnon; others feigned life by motion alone; some were adorned by the artifice of waters. There were not lacking those which were constituted with such industry—by sound, motion, and other circumstances—that they were not undeservedly called <term>thaumaturgi</term> <note>original: "θαυματουργοὶ," meaning wonder-workers or miracle-performers</note>, that is, workers of miracles, among posterity.
<margin>Who was the author of the wonder-working machines.</margin>
Furthermore, who the architect of all these was is as uncertain as the inaccessible antiquity of this invention is uncertain, since the Arabs assert they were in use even before the Deluge, as will be said later.
<margin>Hesiod.</margin>
Hesiod, the most ancient of poets, makes Vulcan the inventor of these, when he recites that golden statues moving themselves in every direction were fabricated by him.
<margin>The tripods of Vulcan.</margin>
He also skillfully describes how he fabricated tripods mobile in various directions, contending among themselves, and returning to the place from which they had come.
<margin>The statues of Daedalus.</margin>
Some wish it that Daedalus, instructed by Vulcan, drew all of Greece into admiration of himself by the prodigious works of these machines.
<margin>Homer.</margin>
He had constructed, according to the testimony of Homer, with the help of Ariadne, boys who performed dances with outstretched hands;
<margin>Dionysius, interpreter of Homer.</margin>
furthermore, a golden dog, seemingly animated, according to the testimony of Dionysius, the most ancient interpreter of Homer, concerning which see Julius Pollux.
<margin>Julius Pollux.</margin>
<margin>Plato.</margin>
Plato also makes mention of the structures built by Daedalus in the dialogue entitled *Meno* <note>The text says "Memnon," likely a slip for "Meno"</note>, which, if they were not tied down, would flee away.
<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle alludes to this in Book 1 of the *Politics*, where he openly says there would no longer be a need for slaves if instruments obeyed the craftsman, just as the machines obeyed Daedalus.
<margin>Daedalus instructed by the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>Diodorus.</margin>
But Diodorus asserts that Daedalus received all his knowledge from the Egyptians; it was their peculiar trait to draw everyone into admiration with ingenious and unheard-of machines.
<margin>Heron learned his pneumatics from the Egyptians.</margin>
From these, Heron drew whatever he wrote concerning pneumatics and automata, while he sincerely confesses that he received them from his predecessors. Hence Pythagoras, Archytas, Eudoxus, Apol-

# CHAPTER III. 324 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
It is too well known to need repeating that Apollonius <note>Apollonius of Tyana, a famous Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker.</note> and other philosophers celebrated for their reports of marvelous things drew their knowledge from these sources. Even Aristotle himself seems to have acknowledged this in the Preface to his *Mechanics* with these words: *“And so, by making use of the nature found in the circle, craftsmen construct various instruments, concealing the principle so that only the marvelous part of the machine appears, while the cause remains hidden.”* He confirms this in the second book of *On Generation* and in his book *On the Motion of Animals*, where he explains the movement of animals through a certain comparison drawn from automated machines. Thus, the use of these automata existed long before Aristotle, from time immemorial. For the sorts of things Philo of Byzantium and Archimedes made by these means—and those of Ctesibius (the son of an Alexandrian barber and teacher of Heron)—are well known from their works on hydraulics, organs, water-clocks, and other automated machines animated by the help of toothed wheels and <margin>Pappus.</margin> screws, as Pappus reports in his eighth book. Indeed, over the course of time, these have been brought to such excellence and perfection that it seems nothing is denied to modern craftsmen in that faculty, as we shall describe more fully, God willing, in our own *Universal Mechanics* in due time. Therefore, let us return to the automated machines of the Egyptians; in describing them, we shall first cite the Authors, and then we shall reveal the hidden methods of constructing such machines—as far as it is possible to conjecture—through an equal number of problems.

## §. I.
### The method and reasoning of the Statue of Memnon.

<margin>The statue of Memnon, its appearance, and location.</margin>
There is no one who does not know of Memnon, so often sung of by the Poets; regarding him, we have discovered certain things that must clearly be numbered among those most worthy of admiration in the contemplation of nature, or even those which, by the novelty of the matter, can scarcely gain belief. I find this image discussed in various ways by various authors. <margin>Pliny.</margin> Pliny, in Book 35, Chapter 7, relates that it was constructed from basalt stone and placed in the temple of Serapis, and that it sounded when struck by the rays of the sun at every sunrise. <margin>Philostratus.</margin> Philostratus, however, in his *Images*, says: *“Memnon, in Ethiopia, was transformed into a black stone in a sitting posture; when the statue is touched by the solar rays, the Sun, falling upon Memnon’s mouth like a plectrum <note>A small tool used to pluck a stringed instrument like a lyre.</note>, draws forth a voice from it.”* In his *Toxaris*, Lucian records that Demetrius of Sunium made a journey to Egypt to see the pyramids and Memnon, because he had heard that the pyramids, though very high, cast no shadow, and that Memnon <margin>Strabo.</margin> calls out to the rising sun. Strabo writes that he was present there with Aelius Gallus and a multitude of friends and soldiers, and heard the sound around the first hour, though whether it came from the base, the Colossus, or was made intentionally by those standing around, *“I could by no means affirm,”* he says, *“since, the cause being uncertain, I would believe anything rather than that a sound could be produced from stones so composed and <margin>Pausanias.</margin> arranged.”* Pausanias marvels at a stone in the mountains of Megara which, if someone struck it with a pebble, would ring out just like a lyre;

But he said, "The *Egyptian Colossus*, which is at *Thebes* in *Egypt* after you have crossed the *Nile*, affected me with much greater admiration; for I saw even to this day a seated statue near that place which they call the *Syringes* <note>The "Syringes" refers to the rock-cut tombs of the Valley of the Kings, named for their long, pipe-like corridors.</note>; most people call it *Memnon*, whom they believe came into *Egypt* having set out from *Ethiopia*. But the statue of Memnon reflects the image of a beardless youth; it is moreover fashioned from black stone, and turned toward the rays of the Sun, with both feet touching the ground, while the upright hands rest upon the seat in the likeness of a man wishing to rise, and the habit of the eyes and the whole body is like that of a man speaking; but when it is struck by a ray of the Sun, which happens in the morning, then indeed it produces the greatest admiration, for they claim it speaks then, when the first ray reaches its mouth. For the eyes are shining and joyful as they are exposed to the Sun, like those who can greatly endure the sight of the Sun, whom the Greeks call *Euhelios* <note>original Greek: ἀηλίους (sun-blind) corrected to εὐηλίους (sunny/well-sunned).</note>, that is, *Sun-favored*. Of which the Satirist also makes mention while he sings:

<margin>Juvenal.</margin>
> *The golden image of a sacred long-tailed monkey shines,*
> *Where the magic strings of the halved Memnon resound.* <note>A quote from Juvenal's Satires (15.4-5) mocking Egyptian superstitions.</note>

<margin>The statue of Memnon produced sound by magic art, or by the help of a Demon.</margin>
We have seen the appearance and position of Memnon’s statue; it remains for us to explain what produced that prodigious sound. Most authors think it was a work of magic; which I also believe, persuaded both by the antiquity of the work and the condition of the statue; for if it had been something artificial, and an industrious invention of genius, it certainly could not have continued its effect through nearly eleven hundred years, during which it persisted from its origin until the times of Apollonius of Tyana. Therefore, it is more likely to have been a Talisman <term>Talisma: a consecrated object believed to hold magical or astrological power</term>, if the things which the authors cited a little earlier commemorate about it are true, or a Demon <note>In this context, a "daemon" refers to a spirit or supernatural entity inhabiting the statue, not necessarily a "demon" in the modern evil sense.</note> confined within the said Statue by the usual incantations, who would produce the said effect. Nevertheless, let us see how the same effect might be accomplished by natural industry.

# PRACTICAL STUDY I.

->*To construct a Memnonian statue which, at the rising of the Sun, emits the sound of a stringed instrument.*<-

---

<margin>How the Memnonian statue is able to emit a sound by natural means.</margin>
Since historical accounts say that the statue of Memnon <note>A colossal statue in Thebes, Egypt, famous in antiquity for "singing" at dawn.</note> emitted a sound similar to a lute <note>original: "cythara," a lyre-like ancient instrument</note> at sunrise, I have decided to show in this place, through physical-mathematical reasoning, how that could have been achieved. No one is ignorant of the fact that rarefaction <note>The process of air becoming less dense and expanding when heated.</note> possesses great power in the nature of things. Let there be a base or pedestal <note>original: "Abacus"</note> proportioned to the Memnonian statue, labeled ABCD, and divided by a diaphragm <note>A horizontal partition or shelf.</note> EF. Next, let the side of the pedestal DF be made of a thin metallic plate that easily absorbs the heat of the Sun, and let it be turned toward the sunrise. Furthermore, let a hole R be made in the bottom of the diaphragm, through which a pipe is led. Within the upper receptacle of the diaphragm ABEF, let a delicate, thin, and very easily moved wheel be arranged, with its axle inserted into each side of the receptacle. This wheel, rotating on its axle, should have wooden slats or paddles inserted around its outer circumference, and these should be equipped with quill-like points <note>original: "penneo cuspide," acting like the plectrum of a harpsichord.</note>. Across the circumference of this decorated wheel, let metallic strings be stretched in a circuit—as many as you wish for a greater variety of harmony—of both large and small thickness, fastened to the sides. You will then have a machine adapted for producing the sound of a lute. For as soon as the side of the pedestal DFB, turned toward the rising Sun, grows warm from the presence of the Sun, it will rarefy the air hiding within (which had cooled during the night). This air, unable to remain compressed, will seek escape through the pipe R with considerable force. The pipe, being positioned against the paddles of the wheel, will turn the wheel in a circle. As the wheel turns, its quill-points will strike the strings stretched over it with some force, and will finally present to those standing by a sound similar to a lyre or lute, with no one [suspecting] the hidden machine—

...conceiving the machinery. If, however, you wish to accomplish the task with strings or chords, let small paddles be attached to the side of the wheel, and let the circumference of the wheel be thoroughly rubbed with a fairly thick resin, so that the stretched strings lightly touch the wheel; it will then happen that as the wheel turns, it will produce the desired sound by friction against the strings.

<margin>How the statue of Memnon may exhibit both sound and motion.</margin>
If you wish to animate a statue placed upon a pedestal with both motion and sound, another pipe must be arranged, secretly led from the bottom of the diaphragm through the middle of the statue. This statue should have one of those pipes inserted in its mouth which they call <term>anthropoglossas</term> <note>original: "anthropoglossas, id est, humanam vocem mentientes" — literally "human-tongued," pipes designed to mimic the timbre of the human voice</note>, along with movable eyes. For through this pipe, the air escaping with great force will animate the reed-pipe and provoke the eyes into motion, whereby the statue will aptly mimic life through both sound and movement. Experience has taught that these things succeed in a similar machine which I took care to have constructed; when exposed to the Sun, it produced a very clear harmony and all the motions I have described. Indeed, I have decided to hand down nothing in this place that was not first made known to me by experiment. Nevertheless, it is evident that the original Statue of Memnon was not constructed by this art, but by magic, or by the device of an enclosed Demon, because strings could not have lasted for such a long time. Hence, so that they might last, it would perhaps be more advisable to adorn the circumference of the wheel with fine quills inserted into it, as is done in <term>harpsichords</term> <note>original: "clauicymbalis"</note>; for these, when the wheel is rotated, will strike those strings and produce a long-lasting sound not unlike a lute. However, so that the enclosed sound can be perceived by those standing around, it would not be useless to make holes in the upper or lateral part of the reservoir; for in this way the escaping sound will present itself more clearly to the ears.

The movement of the beak, tail, and wings is established by this artifice. Thus, as the wheel O X is driven around by the air duct, it will depress the handle M with its teeth; once depressed, it likewise pulls down the iron wire, and at the same time the joint Y Z, which at Y will open its beak, and at Z will raise the tail resting on the joint; hence the bird will seem to be alive by the movement of its beak, tail, and sound. But since the artifice appears clearly from the figure itself, I did not wish to be longer in describing it. ## PRACTICAL APPLICATION IV.

->An Echo which produces the sound of thunder upon opening a chamber.<-

<margin>How thunder may be artificially produced.</margin>
We recalled above, citing Pliny, that certain chambers of the Theban Labyrinth were so arranged that as soon as a door was opened, a very violent sound like thunder was perceived. We have decided to explain how this was done and by what artifice. The whole matter depended on the arrangement of the vault, which, being winding and having various cavities suitable for multiplying sound, caused the creaking of the door to be amplified within the sinuous coils of the walls, producing the thunder I mentioned. <margin>The Ear of Dionysius at Syracuse.</margin> Anyone who understands the artifice of the "Ear of Dionysius" constructed in the city of Syracuse will easily grasp the principle of the said thunder. It has a winding entrance adapted into the shape of a spiral <note>literally "snail shell"</note>, constructed with such skill that someone clearing their throat or shaking a cloak at the entrance clearly perceives the sound of thunder or the blast of a cannon. However, he who wishes to understand the principle of this hidden mechanism described more clearly should consult Book IX of our *Musurgia*. There, since we demonstrate the architectural principles of the Ear of Dionysius and other Echo-producing places occurring throughout Europe with mathematical reasoning, he will easily see how the structure of the Theban Echo was built to produce thunder.

The *Serapeum* <note>The temple of Serapis</note> was built in a round shape, as are all shrines of the Sun, and was notable for its hemispherical dome. In the middle of this, the statue of Serapis was placed, of such size that it touched the sides of the shrine on both ends. Thus, so that throughout the entire course of the year the rays of the rising Sun might touch the mouth and face—

### CHAPTER III. 330 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>The mechanism of the solar kiss</margin>
...they would touch; in a circular domed base <note>original: "bafitholi"</note>, they had intentionally constructed circular openings like windows, aligned with the rising and setting widths <term>amplitude: the angular distance of a celestial body from the true east or west point of the horizon</term> of the Sun. These were arranged according to astronomical calculation—that is, according to the Sun's deviations from the equinoctial point, positioned as much toward the South as toward the North—so that the rising Sun would always strike directly into one of the said cracks according to its rising or setting width. Consequently, it would necessarily and infallibly touch the mouth of the statue positioned in the center of the round structure. From this, the common people, ignorant of the mystery, came to the opinion that Serapis was being greeted with a kiss by the Sun, whose soul they believed he possessed. Indeed, as the Sun set, so that it would not seem to have departed below the horizon without greeting the Deity, it would strike a kiss upon him as if paying a perpetual tribute to its lord. But let us demonstrate the matter by mathematical reasoning. Let there be a circle or spherical base:

->[Image: A geometric diagram showing a central face (A) inside a circular room (B-E-C-D). Lines of sunlight pass through specific holes in the wall (F, C, G) to strike the lips of the statue.]<-

**B E C D**, within the center of which, **A**, imagine the head of Serapis to be fixed. Let round holes be arranged in the circumference of the base, placed within the maximum rising and setting widths so that they perfectly represent the Horizon. Let the rising width be contained between **F C G**, of which **F** represents the winter, **C** the equinoctial, and finally **G** the summer—the maximum width of the Sun on the Horizon. Let all things be considered arranged in the same manner on the setting side. Between the said breadth of the widths **F G**, let those cracks be placed like windows, so that between any given sign <note>Zodiac sign</note> two cracks intervene. It will happen that while the Sun rises in the first point of Capricorn, the ray entering through hole **F** will necessarily illuminate the face of Serapis. It will do the same when positioned at point **C** of Aries and Libra while rising; the same at the summer point **G** of Cancer; and it will perform the same at any other intermediate point, as well as at the points of the setting width. Since the base of the dome corresponds perfectly to the plane of the Horizon, and the Solar rays are carried directly into the holes which correspond exactly to the Solar stations on the Horizon, they will necessarily always strike the central portion of the statue, as appears from the figure; and thus, at its rising, the Sun will always seem to kiss the face of the statue. Thus, the proposition is clear.

But if anyone should wish, at any hour of the day throughout the course of the entire year, to have this sort of...

# PRAGMATIA VI.

->*A Statue placed atop a Shrine that turns itself toward the Sun.*<-

The Arabs report that this machine was constructed by King Nacraus, as the curious reader may see in the first volume, Treatise I, where the Arabic words are found, the translation of which is: *And he built a city in Egypt, the name of which was Salgia, and he made in it a garden, and surrounded it with a wall made of stones of various colors and covered in gold, and he planted in it various kinds of fruits, beneath which a river flowed, and he planted in it a tree fertile with every kind of fruit, and he made in it a pavilion of red stone, on the peak of which was an idol that turned with the Sun, etc.* However, how this image was rotated with the Sun remains to be explained.

<margin>A statue can be turned with the Sun in two ways: sympathetically or mechanically. Theophrastus. The Egyptian Lotus.</margin>

A twofold method for this mechanism can be assigned here: either sympathetic or artificial. The sympathetic method could be achieved by some material having a sympathy for the Sun, just as Theophrastus writes concerning the Egyptian Lotus; for if this were inserted into the more prominent parts of the statue (acting as limbs), and the statue were balanced very lightly and exactly upon a sharpened iron point, the material, being attracted by the Sun, would cause the statue to turn. See more of what we have treated concerning these and similar matters in the third book of *The Magnetic Art* regarding Heliotropic Clocks. The other method, as it is more readily available, so it is more solid: it is likely that it performed its rotation by means of wheels, in much the same way that clocks are driven today. Since we have shown in the preceding pages that the Egyptians had knowledge of geared machines, nothing was easier than to animate an image—previously exactly balanced—into a motion corresponding to the motion of the Sun, using wheels that measure the Sun's movement by their rotation and attached weights. As these things present no difficulty, we did not wish to dwell on them further.

## § II.

->*Concerning the machines pertaining to sacrifice:*<-

<margin>Various machines of the Egyptians pertaining to sacrifices.</margin>It was so arranged by the ingenuity of the Egyptians that they did not only adorn altars, temples, and statues transformed by a certain mystical and exotic metamorphosis, but they also believed it contributed greatly both to reverence and to inspiring admiration for the sacred rites to bestow motion upon statues in imitation of the all-transforming nature of the universe. They intended that men ignorant of the mysteries might, at least from the movement, gestures, and actions of the Gods—or more truly, Demons—recognize their will. Truly, this was a marvelous invention of the Priests for perverting the blind hearts of mortals. There were, moreover, various types of machines. Some were displayed at the entrance of the temple, others upon the altars. These were indeed fashioned with such ingenuity that not only did the common people think something divine was within them, but even as many Authors as have made mention of them judged them to have been finished by an art superior to human genius. Such are most of those which Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a 1st-century mathematician and engineer famous for his steam-powered inventions and automata.</note> hands down in his *Pneumatics*, which he testifies to have organized from the ancients in these words:
<margin>Hero of Alexandria</margin>> *Since the study of pneumatics was deemed worthy of the greatest zeal by the Ancients, both Philosophers and Mechanics—the former treating its power and faculty through reason, the latter even through the sensible action itself—we have deemed it necessary to put into order those things handed down by the Ancients, and to set forth what we ourselves have discovered.*
Hero, therefore, wished to consign to posterity those things handed down by the Ancients which he had found worthy of admiration and put into practice; wherefore we have thought it best to explain each machine in order in this place.

---

# PRACTICAL DEMONSTRATION I.

->*On the Altar of the Great Mother of the Gods with many breasts: as soon as the candles were lit, the breasts poured forth a copious amount of milk.*<-

<margin>The Great Mother of the Gods scattered milk through the fraud of the Priests.</margin>Many Authors think this work was constructed by the art of jugglers and the Demon; but we shall openly show in this place that it was a deceitful machination of the Priests. They proceeded in this way. A structure A B C K L was made, furnished with its columns B K and L C, upon which a hemispherical concave dome A B C was placed; inside this was a vessel G H, upon which the idol F, fashioned with protruding breasts, was established. The columns B K and C L had movable arms S and T, which could be moved up and down, furnished with candle-holders. The dome A B C was closed by a pulley placed at position A. This being completed, a small altar-receptacle M N was filled with milk; inside this, a siphon <note>A tube or pipe used to move liquid via air pressure or gravity.</note> X B K I was led from the dome through the bottom of the vessel K L all the way into the highest point I of the altar-receptacle N M; from the bottom of the altar-receptacle, however, another siphon N M was extended inside the statue, and at point F was divided into small channels according to the multitude of the breasts; and thus the machine was prepared.

At the time of the sacrifice, once the candles E and D were lit, the base of the dome B-C became heated, which caused the air hidden inside the dome to expand <note>The author uses the term "rarefy," describing how heat causes air to take up more space</note>. This expanded air, finding no way to escape because the dome was sealed by a pulley system, sought a way out through the pipes X-B-K-I. When it reached the interior of the small altar, which was already filled with milk, the air's pressure pushed the liquid through the channel N-M into the breasts of the statue. These breasts then dispersed the flowing liquid into the basin of the altar G-H. This happened to the great wonder of the watching people, who believed it was a singular blessing granted by the Gods; the effect lasted only as long as the sacrifice was burning. Thus, the purpose of the device is clear from what has been said.

Two other siphons were led along, bent at the top, marked H-O and S-V, which ended in the bowl of the small altar itself; they possessed a machine prepared for exhibiting mysterious actions. For at the time of the sacrifice, as soon as the fire was kindled on the small altar C-D, the air within the altar became rarefied <note>original: "rarefactus"; meaning the air expanded due to the heat</note> and, seeking more space, sought its escape through the siphon D-E. From here, it was first carried down through the Dragon's siphon F-Y, where, through a specific pipe in which it ended, it caused the Dragon to hiss. 

However, being carried through the two lateral siphons G-M and N-X into the small vessels O-H and S-V, and there pressing upon the liquid—milk in one and wine in the other—it pushed them through the siphons into the bowl of the altar. From this, Dionysus and Diana <note>The author uses the Roman name Diana for the Egyptian Isis, and Dionysus for Osiris, following the "interpretatio graeca" common in Renaissance scholarship</note> seemed to pour out milk and wine, while the Dragon, as if applauding their actions, hissed. 

Since these things were not perceived by the standing common people, nor was the method of the hidden mechanism known, it is no wonder that they believed it happened by the favor of the Gods. For since Osiris (or Dionysus) was considered the inventor of the vine and milk, and Isis the Spirit <note>original: "Genius"</note> of the Nile waters, and the Asp the Solar *Agathodaimon* <note>original: "Ἀγαθοδαίμων"; a "Good Spirit" or protective deity often depicted as a serpent</note>—the cause of all things mentioned, as we have explained elsewhere—and since sacrifices were made to obtain benefits common to all and to appease the Gods; then, once the sacrificial fire was lit, the Gods seemed to demonstrate by that very act that the requests were granted, both by the pouring of milk and wine (or water) and by the hissing of the Dragon. Thus, the proposition is clear.

## §. III.
### **Concerning the Clepsydras, or clocks of the Egyptians.**

<margin>Hydro-pneumatic clocks of the Egyptians.</margin>
Just as the Egyptians thought it was of great importance for the proper establishment of their elections <note>likely referring to the timing of ritual or astrological selections</note> to have an exact observation of time and hours; so too, the many and diverse clocks they used sufficiently declare that they possessed a remarkable knowledge of the science of timekeeping <note>original: "horographicæ doctrinæ"</note> beyond other nations, and were uniquely devoted to it. Indeed, Hero <note>Hero of Alexandria, a Greek mathematician and engineer</note> reports in his *Pneumatics* that he described these in an entire book; but this has perished through the passage of time. However, as much as can be gathered from the words of Pappus <note>Pappus of Alexandria, a major Greek mathematician</note> and Hero himself, most were constructed with hydro-pneumatic art <note>using both water and air pressure</margin>Hero, Pappus.</margin> as will appear more clearly from the mechanical devices <term>technasmatis: clever feats of engineering</term> to be introduced shortly. It should be noted, therefore, that the Egyptians had a threefold...

# CLASS VIII. EGYPTIAN MECHANICS. CHAPTER III.

<margin>Three types of clocks used by the Egyptians</margin>
...that three types of clocks were in use: the Artificial, the Natural, and the Mixed. The Artificial was divided into the Sciatheric <note>original: "Sciathericum" — a sundial or shadow-measuring device</note> and the Hydraulic. The Natural was constructed from things having a hidden instinct for motion synchronized with the Sun. The Mixed was prepared from both. Regarding the Sciatheric, it has already been treated extensively above in the section on Egyptian Astronomy; it remains for us to discuss the others in this place.

# PRACTICAL APPLICATION I.

->*An Egyptian Baboon pouring water from its member, demonstrating the hours in a vessel placed beneath it.*<-

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a mechanical water clock (hydrologium). At the top sits a Cynocephalus (baboon), which functions as a fountain, urinating into a tall glass cylinder below. The cylinder is housed within a classical pedestal consisting of four columns (tetrastylon). The various components are labeled with letters: the pedestal (A, B), the glass cylinder (C, D), an internal siphon or "diabetes" (E, F), a receiving vessel (G, H), and an opening in the baboon's back (M).</image-desc>

<margin>Horapollo.</margin>
Horapollo <note>A 5th-century author of a treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs</note> indicates the mechanism of this Clock in these words: "Again, to signify the equinoxes, they depict the same animal, a seated Baboon <note>original: "Cynocephalum"</note>; for during the two equinoxes of the year, it releases urine twelve times a day, specifically once every hour; it does the same at night. Therefore, not without reason, the Egyptians carve a seated Baboon on their water-clocks <note>original: "hydrologijs"</note>, from whose member water flows down. This is because it signifies the twelve hours into which, as I have said, the days and nights are equally divided at the time of the Equinox." Furthermore, lest that opening—constructed with sharp skill through which the water flows and is excreted into the clock—be either too wide or too narrow (for both are of great consequence: if too wide, it pours out water with great speed and does not correctly achieve the measure and proportion of the hour; if too narrow, it releases the water flow more slowly and gradually than is proper), they devised this remedy: shaving off all the hair down to the tail, they fabricate an iron pipe according to its thickness for the aforementioned use. This seemed to them to be done not without some reason, just as in their other works; and also because it is the only animal of all that barks twelve times a day, once every hour, during the equinox. We have heard the method of the hieroglyphic water-clock recited by Horapollo; it will further be our task to show in this place with what industry it was constructed. <margin>The hydrological Baboon.</margin> First, therefore, they made a seated Baboon out of bronze, hollow inside, such as is shown today in the Royal Museum of the Pincian Hill, provided by Francisco Gualdo, a Knight of Rimini. They placed this upon a four-columned pedestal <note>original: "Abacum tetrastylon"</note> AB, supported by four columns, within which was placed a glass cylinder CD, the base of which was closed and the upper part open. Inside this glass cylinder, a <term>diabetes</term> <note>A siphon or water-regulating pipe used in ancient hydraulics</note> EF was arranged, whose interior channel IK, perfectly joined to the base of the cylinder, ended in a vessel GH placed below. On the circumference of the glass cylinder, or even on the siphon itself, the twelve hours were described within as many circles, as the following figure shows. This being completed, the Baboon was filled through the orifice M with Nile water (of which it was a symbol), which is emptied through the Baboon's member into the glass cylinder. And since the channel of the member was constructed with such industry that the water would be exactly emptied through it in the space of twelve hours (which they verified was done exactly according to the Sundial), therefore the siphon EF, together with the glass cylinder...

# CHAPTER III. 340 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

They were arranged in such a proportion that, within the space of 12 hours, both the cylinder would be filled and the siphon <note>original: "diabetes," a term used here for a U-shaped siphon or water-regulator</note> would be emptied, as we shall now describe.

<image-desc>An engraving of a complex Egyptian water clock (hydrologium). At the top, a seated Cynocephalus (baboon-headed deity) with raised hands sits upon a platform labeled A and B. Below this, supported by two columns, is a glass cylinder (CD) marked with a grid and numerals 1-12 in two columns. This cylinder rests on a large rectangular pedestal base (GH). On the right side of the base, there is a small faucet or pipe labeled L. Labels I and K designate internal plumbing connections.</image-desc>

For the water, falling from the <term>urethra</term> <note>original: "veretillo," referring to the anatomical source of the water flow in the statue</note> of the **Cynocephalus** <note>The dog-headed baboon associated with Thoth, the god of time and wisdom</note> into the glass cylinder **CD**, gradually worked its way into the siphon **FE**. Over the space of twelve hours, it rose as far as **E**, and from there, falling through the opening of the small pipe **I** into the vessel **GH**, it discharged itself through the opening **K** over another twelve hours. Thus it happened that, by the twelve circles of the glass cylinder, the water—first by rising—would show the twelve hours of the day within the sides of the cylinder; and within those same sides, the water—discharging itself through the siphon—would show the hours of the night by falling. When the natural day had passed, new water was poured into the **Cynocephalus** to continue the clock's operation, after first removing the water from vessel **GH** through the pipe **L**. And this was the method of the Egyptian water clock described by **Horus** <note>Likely referring to Horapollo</note>. It must be noted, however, that the hourly spaces of the cylinder are unequal, and one division must be made for the day hours, and another for the night. For as the water discharges itself through the siphon **IK**, the hourly spaces must necessarily be larger, decreasing proportionally down to **D**. The opposite occurs with the water rising within the siphon. Note also that the pipe **IK** must not be of just any size, but so proportioned that the space **IK** between the hourly lines exactly equals the flow of twelve hours. See the figure of the **Cynocephalus**, depicted according to the custom of the Ancients (a bronze figure of which is found today in the Royal Museum of the Pincian Hill, belonging to **Francesco Gualdi**, Knight of Saint Stephen, as we mentioned above), in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's 1650 work on the Obelisk of Agonalis</note>.

# EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
### CHAPTER III.

<margin>
This clock, and the one preceding it, showed only equal hours.
</margin>

This water clock <note>original: "hydrologium"</note> was indeed ingenious and very well suited for showing astronomical hours <note>Hours of equal length (60 minutes), used by astronomers rather than for daily civil life</note>. However, like the one before it, it only demonstrated the hours perfectly on the days of the equinox, when the artificial day is equal to the night. Since the ancient Egyptians followed a system where each day was divided into twelve hours, as were the nights, these hours were consequently longer or shorter depending on how close the sun was to the tropics. Therefore, it was impossible to have a stable and constant measurement of flowing water. We shall now attempt to explain how a clock might be constructed so that the aforementioned hours of the days and nights might be shown according to a constant law throughout the entire course of the year.

# PRACTICAL APPLICATION III.

->An ancient Egyptian water clock which demonstrates unequal hours.<-

<margin>
A clock for unequal hours.
</margin>

Let the machine be set up in a suitable place where there is a perpetual supply of water. Let there be a Lion’s head, or *Momphta* <note>A symbolic Egyptian name for a water-source or the spirit of the Nile</note> marked **A**, which pours water into the receptacle **B C**. To prevent the said vessel from overflowing, let it be drained through the channel **T V**. However, let the vessel **B C** have a curved siphon **D** inside, through which the water drains into a glass vessel placed within a four-columned structure <note>original: "tetrastylon"</note> **G G H I**, upon whose columns the receptacle **B C** rests. Let this four-columned structure stand upon another receptacle **H I K L**, into which the water, having fallen from the siphon **D** of vessel **B C**, drains through a float-gauge <note>original: "diabetem," a device used to measure water levels</note> **E F** inside the glass cylinder. This is the construction of the machine; there follows the method for drawing the unequal hours upon the glass cylinder. To ensure that the water inside the glass cylinder exactly demonstrates the unequal hours throughout the course of the entire year, proceed as follows:

First, take a piece of paper equal to the height of the glass cylinder **E F**. Upon this, you will separately paint the hour lines in this manner: Observe the maximum and minimum length of the day for the place where the water clock is to be set up; at Memphis, this was fourteen and ten hours <note>In the ancient world, "unequal hours" meant the period of daylight was always divided into 12 hours, meaning a summer hour was much longer than a winter hour</note>. Then, let a parallelogram **A B C D** be described, whose sides **A C** and **B D** are each to be divided into 24 equal parts. Divide the top side **A B** into six equal parts by seven lines, which descend parallel to the base **C D**. On each of these, let the characters of the Zodiac signs be inscribed, as appears in the following figure. Once this is done, on side **A C**, starting from the bottom, count ten spaces, and on side **B D**, fourteen; and let a straight line **E F** be drawn through these points. This being established, let the space **E C**, as well as **F D**, be divided into twelve equal parts, and let straight lines be drawn through the corresponding hours.

In the same manner, you will divide the spaces E A and B F; this is done by transferring the hour-spaces F D into E A, and the hour-spaces C E into the line F B. Once the straight lines are drawn, you will have the lines of the <term>hydrolegium</term> <note>A water clock; from the Greek 'hydro' (water) and 'legein' (to tell/collect).</note> ready to show the hours. You shall paint this entire parallelogram onto the surface of a glass cylinder, and you will have the whole business completed. For as the water discharges itself through the curved <term>siphon</term> <note>original: "syphonem D reflexum"</note> into the glass cylinder, in such a proportion that the water precisely fills the cylinder up to A B in the space of 24 hours, it necessarily follows that the water in side A C—while it runs from C to E—measures the length of the shortest day of ten hours through the twelve hour-spaces into which part C E is divided. At **V**, however, it exactly demonstrates the twelve hours of the equinox; and finally at F, it shows the length of the longest day of fourteen hours through the twelve spaces into which part D F is divided; and you will judge the same to occur consequently in the remaining lines of the zodiac signs.
