After E F, however, the water—gradually rising—will begin to show the night hours. When the water reaches the final line, it will begin to enter the <term>diabetes</term> <note>A Greek term used here for a specific type of siphon or drainage pipe that regulates the water level.</note> E F, and through it, by the same proportion of motion with which it had risen within the glass cylinder, it will empty itself into the vessel placed beneath, H I K L. This is done with this precaution: that the water which had shown the hours while the Sun was in Capricorn by rising in space C E, should show those same hours by falling in space B F. In like manner, the water which had shown the hours while the Sun was in Cancer by rising in space F D, should show the same by falling in space A E, as the added numbers clearly demonstrate. The same logic applies to the remaining lines of the signs; so that as the water is falling, the line opposite to that through which it had risen must always be used, as the characters of the signs at the base show.

This clock is perpetual.
</margin>

Therefore, this clock is perpetual, on account of the flow of water flowing perpetually through the lion's mouth. Thus, the whole ingenuity consists in the construction of the curved siphon and the <term>diabetes</term>, both of which must be reduced to such thinness and precision that the water from reservoir B C, through siphon D, precisely fills cylinder G I in the space of 24 hours, and at exactly the same time empties itself through the <term>diabetes</term> E F into the vessel H I K L. This indeed cannot be achieved except through observation over the said space of time: then, the greatest care must be taken regarding the proportion of the vessels—

must be maintained. However, since the water flows perpetually, the cylinder would always remain full; for this reason, the lion's mouth should have a <term>stopcock</term><note>original: "epistomium"; a valve or plug to control flow</note>, so that when the glass cylinder has been filled with water, it may be closed until the entire volume of water has depleted itself over the space of twenty-four hours. Then, for a new demonstration of the hours on the following day, it is opened again; and thus, on alternating natural days, the stopcock is closed and opened. We have provided for a perpetually flowing supply of water for this reason: as long as the reservoir B C remains full of water, the water consequently falling through the siphon with a completely equal pressure will cause an equal increase within the glass cylinder. This would not happen if the water in vessel B C were gradually to fail, as we shall demonstrate at length in our *Hydrostatic Mechanics*.

### *The Use of the Clock.*

If you wish to know the hour, first look for the line of the Zodiac sign in which the Sun exists at the current time, and see where the water in the vessel intersects said line; for the hour line which it touches there is the <term>unequal hour</term><note>Also known as "temporal hours," these divided the daylight into 12 equal parts regardless of the season, meaning summer hours were longer than winter hours.</note> you seek. Indeed, while the water is rising within the glass vessel, use the signs marked on the front A B; but when the water is decreasing, the signs described on the base C D must be used, just as we have handed down in the preceding sections. And so, we have constructed a Water-Clock which demonstrates the unequal hours throughout the entire course of the year. These are the things concerning Egyptian Mechanics which I considered necessary to point out. Whoever desires to know more of the wonders of Egypt should read the histories of the Arabs, especially the celebrated author Schiangia; Salamas Kandati, in the work he names the *Garden of the Wonders of the World*; Joseph Ben Altiphasi, and countless others cited here and there in the preceding pages. I would gladly include their narrations of Egyptian portents in this place, had I not already provided them in the first volume of *Oedipus*. Furthermore, since many of these mechanical marvels are said to have been constructed by the help of demons and the magic arts, we have judged it best to omit them intentionally.

You have long since begun to dictate the themes for them, through which posterity shall know with what great counsel, prudence, and authority You have conducted Yourself in the August theater of the Empire, and with what great dexterity You have prevailed in handling matters of vast importance. # CLASS IX.
## Iatrics, or Hieroglyphic Medicine.
### P R E F A C E.

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap 'C' with a landscape scene featuring buildings and a river.</image-desc>

<margin>The triple method of healing among the Egyptians: Physical, Prayerful, and Amuletic.</margin>

*Since a great portion of the hieroglyphic inscriptions is filled with the secrets of Egyptian Medicine, I have deemed it appropriate to discuss its origin, invention, and application in this place, so that the elements of which it chiefly consists may become known. There were, moreover, three systems of medicine in use among the Egyptians. The first was* Physical or Economic, <note>The author uses "Economic" here in the classical sense of managing the household or the natural constitution of the body.</note> *by which the infirmities of the human body were driven away through remedies of a vegetable nature common to all. The second was called* <term>euchetikon</term> <note>original Greek: ευχετικόν</note> *or* prayerful, *by which they believed they could put any diseases to flight through prayers and hymns to the Gods. The third was* <term>phylaktikon</term> <note>original Greek: φυλακτικόν</note> *or* Amuletic, or characteristic, or sidereal or astral, *by which they persuaded themselves that a person could be restored to their former health—from whatever infirmity they might be held by—through the figures of the Gods assigned to individual diseases, adorned with various hieroglyphic symbols, and through the addition of an incantation to attract the lesser stars. We have led ourselves to treat each of these in order, intending this one thing: that the dogmas of the depraved arts, which have spread their roots even unto these times by the* sowing of the Demon, <note>A reference to the idea that superstitious or magical practices were planted in human culture by evil spirits.</note> *may be uprooted; and thus, which is our* sole purpose, *the secrets of hieroglyphic learning may be opened through a truthful interpretation.*

<margin>
The Egyptians sought the use of green plants born in their own soil.
</margin>
By no means content with the knowledge handed down to them by their predecessors, they left nothing undone to penetrate the innermost natures of things. Hence, when they were about to examine the individual properties of pebbles, plants, and herbs, they did not scrutinize Indian, Assyrian, or European plants, but those which had been born and raised in their native soil; they placed great power in the disposition of climates. For since these plants had received from the liberality of benign nature the same temperament <note>In this context, "temperament" refers to the balance of the four humors or qualities—hot, cold, moist, and dry—believed to govern health.</note> of which they themselves were composed, they cared for no others besides them; indeed, they rejected others as being of a degenerate character. They did indeed possess many traditions concerning the "characters" <note>The "signatures" or physical marks on plants believed to reveal their medicinal use.</note> impressed by nature upon individual things, but access to the application of this art was not easy for everyone; therefore, taught by industry, continuous exercise, and experience, they finally arrived at what they desired through a constant—as I have said—investigation of the mind. Let us therefore explain the method by some examples.

<margin>
The Egyptians scrutinized the chains of worldly things.
</margin>
It must first be noted that the Egyptians were entirely occupied in investigating the chains of worldly things, by which the fourfold World—the Archetypal, the Angelic, the Sidereal <note>The world of the stars and planets.</note>, and the Elemental—were tightly connected. Their entire study seems to have been placed in this: to know which stars and which presiding Spirits <note>original: "Genijs Præsidibus"</note> governed each elemental thing. Elluchasen <note>Likely referring to Ibn Butlan, an 11th-century Christian physician from Baghdad known in Latin as Eluchasem.</note> recounts all these things in clear words, consistent with his own calculations, in his book on the rites of the Egyptians.

# CHAPTER III.

**Concerning the method and reasoning by which the Egyptians arrived at the knowledge of the powers of things; that is, how the Egyptians recognized the powers of every natural thing through Characters and similarities impressed upon those things.**

<margin>The Ancients explored the powers of natural things in three ways.</margin>
It is certain from the Cabala <note>original: "Cabala"; here referring to a tradition of secret or mystical knowledge passed down through generations</note> of the Primeval Patriarchs of the World, that they learned this art through tradition, which they afterwards advanced with the greatest zeal through long use and experience. Therefore, when they were about to investigate the virtues of things, they employed a triple method: the first of which was through the manifest qualities inherent in the things themselves; the second was through signs or Characters impressed upon individual things by wise Nature; the third was through the similarities of things to other things; each of which will be treated in order.

## §. I.

**Concerning the recognition of the powers of herbs through elementary qualities, which is the first method used by the Egyptians.**

<margin>The Egyptians used only indigenous herbs in curing diseases.</margin>
It must be known that the Egyptians used no herbs except those which their native soil supplied to them (rejecting foreign and exotic plants as being of a degenerate nature); for only Egyptian plants were held in price and esteem, as if they were a gift of the immortal Genii <note>guardian spirits or divine influences associated with a specific place</note> granted to the natives. This was also the practice regarding animals and stones; indeed, they deemed no animal worthy of either divine honors or inclusion in the catalog of hieroglyphics except that which, produced by the bounty of the native soil, had grown up in that same place; the cause of which matter we discuss more fully elsewhere. It has also been extensively proven in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>A reference to the author's own work on the Roman obelisk moved by Pope Innocent X</note> that they assumed no stone for the construction of an Obelisk or other sacred images except a "nursling of the Nilotic earth" <note>stone quarried from the banks of the Nile</note>. Therefore, they determined that the same must be held true for plants; these they sought out with the greatest study, and in the manner of an anatomy, they resolved them into roots, flowers, fruits, and leaves, as being of a heterogeneous nature and thus of diverse use in medicine. <margin>The Egyptians learned the virtues of herbs through the service of the five senses.</margin> Furthermore, they learned the virtues inherent in individual plants through the service of the five senses. Sight sought to recognize the powers from the colors—white, yellow, red, scarlet, flame-colored, purple, green, blue, pale, ash-gray, and black or dark—all of which revealed the different proportions of the temperaments hidden within the plants. Hearing [judged] from the sound with which they were struck, whether sharp, heavy, tinkling, dull, harsh, or smooth,

It emphasizes their strict reliance on native Egyptian flora, fauna, and minerals, which they viewed as divinely gifted to their specific land.</summary>

### CHAPTER III. 352 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS. THE HIEROGLYPHIC SCHOOL.

...the student learned the temperament of the joined stock. **Taste**, through their flavors—sharp, harsh, sour, bitter, sweet, salty, fatty, or austere—judged the powers of the plants. **Smell** also, through their odors—troublesome, pleasing, unpleasant, dull, sweet, styptic <note>binding or contracting</note>, or piercing—revealed hidden qualities. Finally, **Touch**, through lightness, roughness, softness, hardness, scabbiness, and hairiness, perceived the latent virtues. And from these qualities manifest to the senses, they judged the levels of heat, cold, dryness, and moisture. Indeed, from a white or pale color, they took an indication of the weakness of a moist temperament; yellow was an index of heat; red and saffron-colored plants offered signs of immoderate dryness and moisture; conversely, herbs of green and leek-like color were established as symbols of excessive moisture. Again, a sharp taste showed a sign of vehement heat lurking within; a harsh taste manifested a mark of a cold, dry, and earthy nature; a sour taste was a sign of a nature more moist than cold, for it occurs when more moisture is mixed with the austere; from bitterness they noted a sign of aridity and heat (namely, an earthy dryness lurking in the herbs); in an oily taste, an airy power; and finally, in an insipid taste, an excess of cold and moist quality. Likewise, a good odor uncovered good qualities, while a stinking one uncovered bad qualities and those of excremental moisture.

<margin>Avicenna.</margin>
All of these things are confirmed by Avicenna <note>original: "Abensina"; the famous Persian physician Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037), whose "Canon of Medicine" was a standard textbook.</note> in Book 2 of the *Canon*, chapter 3.

<margin>
Other ways in which the Egyptians came to the knowledge of the virtues of herbs.
</margin>
Furthermore, **Touch** discovered an abundance of earthy parts, moist and congealed by cold, through thickness; and through thinness, it discovered the presence of fiery and airy parts. Just as hardness was held to be the companion of earthy dryness, so softness was the companion of moisture, to which gravity and levity <note>heaviness and lightness</note> correspond. Beyond the aforementioned, they recognized the qualities of things from their disposition or mutability, and the easy or difficult way they received change. Thus, a thing of faster freezing was judged cold; one of faster inflammation, hot. From **age**, they said younger things would be moister, and old things drier. From **location**, they also considered marsh plants to be moist and cold; river and sea plants to be cold-dry; but those which have their birth in sterile soil, or in the mountains, or in sandy places, they reputed to be hot-dry. Finally, from **operations** <note>the effects the plant has on the body</note>, they called that "hot" which rendered subtle, resolved, cleansed, opened, softened, ripened, digested, cut, attracted, reddened, or scorched. "Cold" was that which repelled, thickened, or made raw. "Dry" was that which constricted or squeezed out. "Moist" was that which inflamed, washed away, lubricated, or smoothed. And this was the first method by which the Egyptians arrived at the knowledge of the hidden qualities lurking in herbs.

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER III.

<margin>The method of learning the virtues of natural things through the seals of likenesses impressed upon them: how ancient it is, and in what it consists.</margin>
We shall now review only by what means the Egyptians attained knowledge of the virtues of natural things through the hidden seals of likenesses <note>This refers to the "Doctrine of Signatures," the belief that plants resemble the body parts they cure.</note> impressed upon individual objects. For this science was not, as many suppose, invented by more recent authors, but was revived anew from the monuments of the Orientals, as Cornelius Agrippa <note>Heinrich Cornelius Agrippa (1486–1535), a famous German polymath and occult writer.</note> beautifully teaches, and to which Quercetanus <margin>Cornelius Agrippa. Quercetanus.</margin> subscribes in his book *On Ancient Medicine*; it is a part of the Cabala, handed down orally by the Sages of Egypt or their descendants, or proposed to men of their own order wrapped in hieroglyphics. It consisted, moreover, in a certain hidden analogy of the members of the human body to the various characteristics of herbs, by which the said members were represented. But let us demonstrate the matter with examples. The Egyptians, therefore, <margin>Plants having a likeness to the head heal the head.</margin> wishing to heal diseases of the head, sought an herb whose fruit or calyx <note>The protective outer layer of a flower bud.</note> represented the shape of a human head, and they said this was an appropriated medicine for the head; such was the flower of the Peony while still enclosed in its calyx, which they used especially for the disease of epilepsy, prepared in various ways. In this category, the poppy, walnut, nutmeg, squill root, agaric, lily of the valley, and similar things were also reckoned. These they did not use raw, but variously corrected and prepared for use as medicines. In this same way, since in the flowers of eyebright, marigold, hawkweed, and scabious <margin>Eyes for eyes.</margin> they found some sort of rudimentary ocular likeness, they similarly persuaded themselves that these, rightly prepared, benefited the eyes. Those things which resembled teeth, such as henbane, <margin>Teeth for teeth.</margin> pomegranate seeds, pine nuts, toothwort, and the root of lesser celandine, they believed healed the pains of the teeth. Thus the leaves of asarum and snails, and the leaves <margin>Ears for ears. The rest for the rest.</margin> of water mint—of which the latter resemble the nose and the former the ears—they maintained benefited the said members through a hidden sympathy. In like manner for diseases of the throat, they applied wintergreen, throatwort, and cassia fistula; for the lungs, lungwort (both the stony and spotted varieties) or that which has its origin on oaks; for the heart, the fruit of the citron, the root of anthora, the fruit of the cashew, and the persea; for ailments of the liver, lichen, birch fungus, oak, and liverwort; for the spleen, scolopendrion, hart's-tongue fern, asplenium, and ceterach; for the stomach, the leaves of cyclamen, ginger, and galangal; for the intestines, bindweed, aromatic calamus, cassia fistula, and vine tendrils; for the bladder, winter cherry, bladdernut, bladder-herb, and nightshade; for the private parts, arum and beans; for the genitals, all orchids and types of satyrion; for the womb, round birthwort, of which both the leaves and root exhibit the womb; for the kidneys, purslane and cyclamen root; for the joints, hermodactyl; for the hands, the *Palma Christi* <note>Castor oil plant, named for its hand-shaped leaves.</note>, palmago, etc. Indeed, contemplate a Synopsis of all those reviewed so far, expressed with their figures in the following diagram. If anyone truly desires to know what Egyptian Nomenclature these herbs are assigned, and what power they possess for drawing down the chains of the Gods <note>A reference to theurgy, or the ritual practice of connecting with divine forces through natural objects.</note>, let him go to Volume III, Chapter 8, where he will find everything treated at length, so that it would be superfluous to deal with them more extensively in this place.

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE.
## CHAPTER III.

->**The juices of herbs that resemble the humors of the human body heal those same humors.**<-
<margin>The juices of herbs heal the humors of the human body when they reflect a likeness to them.</margin>
In a similar manner, they employed those juices of herbs which reflected the juices or humors of the human body in color for the purging of that specific faulty humor. Hence, the saffron-colored juices of plants—such as cumin, saffron, aloe, senna, wormwood, colocynth <note>bitter apple</note>, castor oil plant, and rhubarb—which reflected yellow bile, were also held to cure it. For purging black bile, all those herbs which grow dark or purple in their flowers, leaves, or juice, or are of a blue color, are beneficial, such as beans, bindweed, orach, and borage. Plants with white flowers, gourds, white mushrooms, lettuce, and larch agaric <note>a medicinal fungus</note> evacuate phlegm, because they reflect the phlegmatic humor in their own moisture. Truly, plants of a red color and juice—whether the color shines in the flowers, the stalk, or the sap—such as red sandalwood, fern root, and the stalks of orach and red beet, are held to purify the blood. They believe that plants of mixed colors, such as the iris, cure mixed humors. Finally, for milk and semen, they use lettuce, sow-thistle, *beitalzar* <note>likely a transliteration of an Arabic plant name</note>, spurge, and all species of milk-bearing herbs. Indeed, they did not use these juices raw, but applied them for medical use prepared and preserved with the highest art.

->**Those things which represent a certain disease heal it.**<-
<margin>Things that represent a disease heal it.</margin>
The Egyptians did not stop here, but reasoning further, they examined the signatures and characteristics of diseases with all zeal. It happened that through continuous use and experience, they discovered that whatever seemed to represent a certain disease contributed to the curing of that disease and its morbid condition. Thus, they found by experience that those things which mimicked stones and pebbles were beneficial to those suffering from "the stone" <note>calculus/kidney stones</note>. Thus, they asserted that the eyes of fish and stones found in the bodies of animals, and among herbs, "Sun-millet" <note>Gromwell, *Lithospermum officinale*, known for its stone-like seeds</note> and others dwelling in stony places, were appropriate means for crushing stones lurking in the bladder and kidneys. Thus, they believed that herbs naturally perforated, such as *hypericon* <note>St. John's Wort, which has translucent spots looking like holes</note>, healed wounds, that is, perforations of the body. In the same way, spotted herbs healed skin spotted by tetter <note>a skin disease like eczema or psoriasis</note>; scaly plants healed scales; and they said that swelling plants and animals benefited swollen limbs. In like manner, they drew medicine from venomous animals, such as serpents, scorpions, spiders, and bramble-toads, which destroyed any kind of poison swallowed either by drink or bite. Thus, sterile herbs, such as lettuce, willow, savin, and *vibex* <note>likely a reference to a marking or specific plant variety</note>, were thought to bring sterility to man. On the contrary, lustful and fertile things were thought to bring fertility, such as *satyrium* <note>an orchid variety</note>, the sparrow, and the skink <note>a type of lizard</note>.

->**The use of herbs and animals in healing.**<-
<margin>The use of herbs and animals in healing.</margin>
Truly, long-lived and ever-green plants were said to procure vigor for man. Voracious herbs and animals, such as the Wolf and the Pike <note>original: *Lupus & Lucius*</note>, were thought to provide men with the faculty of digestion. In this way, they persuaded themselves that animals endowed with wit and docility contributed to intelligence and memory; that gloomy animals made men gloomy; sleepy ones made men sleepy; watchful ones made men watchful; fierce ones made them fierce; and angry ones made them angry. Thus, those about to fight against enemies, by drinking the warm blood of animals previously driven into a rage, were rendered most fierce; and so with others. Nor was this without reason: for as they were of great and subtle wit, and knew how to apply the analogies of things aptly and neatly to circumstances, so they also searched out the reasons and causes of individual things. For they knew that every single thing moves and turns itself toward its like. Therefore, being about to operate toward some specific—

It details how specific colors correspond to bodily humors and how physical resemblances are used to treat specific ailments like kidney stones or skin diseases.</summary>

property or virtue, they sought those things and animals in which such a property or action was most excellently present. Moreover, they called "action" a certain mode of being born, flourishing, generating, growing, proliferating, fruiting, ripening, and bringing forth, by which individual things—driven as if by an implanted weight and a natural stimulus of appetite—mutually pursue, recoil from, or entice one another. Configuration, or "characterization," is the similarity of a signature <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that the physical appearance of plants or animals indicated their medicinal use.</note> or characteristic shining forth in one thing and another; for a similar effect presupposes a similarity of the internal agent or cause in both, and this is all the more evident the more distinct that signature is. Thus, "Alexipharmics" <term>Alexipharmics: medicines used to neutralize poison or venom</term> are conjectured to be those things which mimic the horn of a deer or represent serpents, etc. This is based on the principle that whatever bears the shape of a deer's horn was produced by a similar internal principle as the horn itself. Therefore, a similarity of the principle allows one to conjecture a similarity of powers. The Egyptian philosophers penetrated this secret of nature most excellently,

<margin>The limbs of animals heal the afflicted limbs of men.</margin>
who cured a diseased limb by taking a similar limb from animals and giving it as food. Thus, those with liver disease were cured with the livers of goats, pigeons, and other animals redolent of a "hepatic" nature. Those with consumption <note>Original: "Phthisicis," referring to pulmonary tuberculosis or wasting of the lungs.</note> were healed with the lungs of animals that had been fed for some time on pulmonary herbs, and also with decoctions and preparations of herbs resembling the lung. They aided those with heart trouble with "cardiac" things and the hearts of animals reflecting the nature of the heart; and head infirmities with the brains of appropriate birds. And so, for each individual part, they established the care of different limbs. And lest physicians be distracted by the sheer mass of such matters, it was provided by law that no single physician should undertake the cure of all infirmities of the human body; rather, individuals applied themselves to the care of individual limbs, as if the burden were distributed among many. Hence, Ophthalmic physicians sought means fit only for healing diseases of the eyes. Cephalic physicians explored diseases of the head and sought fit remedies for them. Likewise, Cardiac physicians treated the heart; Splenetic physicians the spleen; Hepatic physicians the liver; Stomachic physicians the stomach; Pectoral physicians the chest; and Pulmonary physicians the lung. Thus it happened that they progressed most successfully in their destined care. Indeed, this method, propagated from the earliest ages until the present day, still endures in Egypt, as

### **Concerning the Astral or Starry Philosophy, which the Egyptian Philosophers and Physicians used in the cure of diseases.**

This Medicine was entirely hieroglyphic, and known only to the Priests and Sacred Diviners <note>Original: "Hieromanthis."</note>, which the previously cited Arab, Elluchafen <note>Likely referring to Ibn Butlan, an 11th-century Christian Arab physician known in Latin as Elluchasem Elimithar.</note>, also describes amply in his truly golden booklet on the customs of the Egyptians. It consisted, moreover, in the arrangement of the "world-chains" which we have explained above.

<margin>The astral philosophy of the Egyptians consisted in the arrangement of Worldly chains.</margin>
Indeed, it was a dogma—not only of the Hebrews, but most especially of the Egyptians—that there is no member of the human body which does not have its own herb, plant, or stone as a protector of its health. These are therefore "friendly" or sympathetic, and by a certain natural inclination, they concur to preserve said member if it should ever fail. Furthermore, there is no species in the lower economy of the sublunary World <note>The "sublunary world" refers to the Earthly realm below the moon, subject to change and decay.</note>—among herbs, plants, stones, or animals—which does not have its own specific star. By the influence of this star, the species perfects its functions of natural gifts and powers. Nor is there any star that does not have its own assigned Genius <note>A guiding spirit or angelic intelligence.</note>, by whose protection it is supported, and by whose command it communicates the gifts of its influences to the species committed to its care. These Geniuses rest in that abyssal center of divinity from which all things flow, ready to execute the will of the Supreme Deity, who foresees for every single thing the means sufficient for its own preservation. This dogma was held in such high value by the Priests as a celestial secret that they rightly judged it should be hidden behind hieroglyphic symbols, as will be demonstrated later. But lest we seem to have fabricated anything, I will set down in this place the authority of Abenrahhmon <note>Likely referring to Ibn al-Rahman, an Arabic source used by Kircher.</note>, son of the excellent Elder Elmorgum, an Arab Philosopher, who extensively hands down the doctrine proposed by us here in the work he entitles <term>Instruction for the Sages of Egypt</term> <note>original Arabic: تعليم للحكما مصر (Ta'lim lil-hukama Misr)</note>. He speaks as follows:

<margin>The dogma of the Egyptians concerning the agreement of the higher things with the lower.</margin>
<margin>Abenrahhm.</margin>
> It was characteristic of the sages of Egypt to be diligent in the use of medicines from all types of nature, category by category, and from every level of all beings which have a likeness and property with the seven wandering stars <note>The seven classical planets: Sun, Moon, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, and Saturn.</note>. For example, they selected all those which have a likeness to the Sun from its sphere: from the earth its minerals and stones, its wild and sea animals, and from its plants. They drew down their influences and properties from all their actions, applying them all to the use of medicine for the heart, which is like the Sun of the "lesser world" <note>The "lesser world" or Microcosm refers to the human being as a reflection of the universe.</note>. And in this way they acted for all types of pains and diseases of the head, the liver, the stomach, the lungs, and others.

*It was characteristic of the Egyptians, for the use of Medicines, to select from all species of nature and from all levels of beings those things which obtained some similarity and property with the seven planets; for example, all species which had some similarity to the Sun, they selected from minerals, metals, stones, animals (both of the forest and the sea), from plants and herbs, and from those properties concerning their influence; finally, they adapted all operations of "Solar" things for the use of Medicine for the heart, because the heart is like a Sun of the lesser World. And in this manner they operated in every kind of infirmity, for example <note>v. g. = verbi gratia</note>, in the cures of the head, liver, stomach, lungs, and the rest of the members.* Then he proceeds to particulars: to select from all the reviewed things and adapt Solar things to Solar diseases, Lunar to Lunar, Saturnine to Saturnine, Martial to Martial, Venereal to Venereal, Jovial to Jovial, and Mercurial to Mercurial, and to show the power, composition, and force of the Medicines. Since we have shown these in the preceding sections, I have judged it superfluous to repeat them in this place. Since, therefore, he subjects the individual members of the human body to one of the planets and signs of the Zodiac, and from the individual levels of nature, be-

And among the classes of worldly things, he assigns those matters which agree by similarity to such and such a planet and sign, and puts forth the following pronouncement:

<note>original Arabic: "كل وحدة من انواع الحيوانات والنبات والمعدنات الذين لهم المثل وصفه مع الكواكب مذكورين وهو باستعمال الدوا ينفع من عضا الذين لهم مثل مع النجوم الذين ذكرنا ."</note>
*Every species of animal, plant, and mineral possesses a certain similarity to the aforementioned planets; and these, when used in medicine, benefit those limbs which have a similarity to the stars we have mentioned.*

<margin>Marsilio Ficino</margin>
All of these things Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century Italian scholar who translated Plato and led the revival of Neoplatonism.</note> confirms from the tradition of the Ancients with these words: *By applying those things which pertain to a specific star, one undergoes the particular influence of that star and its Spirit <note>original: "Daemonis," referring here to a guiding spirit or mediating entity, not an evil demon.</note>, just as wood prepared with sulfur is drawn to a flame present everywhere. And this occurs not only through the rays of the star and Spirit themselves, but also through the Soul of the World <note>original: "Anima Mundi," the vital force connecting all living things.</note> present everywhere, in which the "reason" or "pattern" of every star and Spirit flourishes—partly as a seed for generating things, and partly as a model for knowing them. For according to the older Platonists, the Soul built these patterns by its own reasons beyond the stars in the Heaven, forming shapes and parts of such a kind that they themselves are also specific figures; and it impressed properties upon all of them. Within these celestial stars, figures, parts, and properties, all species of lower things and their properties are contained.*

<margin>Celestial figures established by the Ancients.</margin>
*Indeed, he established forty-eight universal figures: namely, twelve in the Zodiac and thirty-six outside of it. Likewise, in the Zodiac, there are thirty-six according to the number of the "faces" <note>A ten-degree division of a zodiac sign, also called a decan.</note>. Again, in the same place, there are three hundred and sixty according to the number of degrees: for in any given degree there are several stars from which images are composed. Similarly, he divided the images outside the Zodiac into many figures according to the number of their faces and degrees. Finally, he established certain relationships and proportions from these universal images to other universal images, which themselves also exist there as images. Each of these figures maintains its own continuity from the rays of its stars cast upon one another by a certain peculiar property; from these orderly forms, the forms of lower things depend, being ordered from that source. But even those celestial forms, though distinct among themselves, proceed from the reasons of the soul joined together, and are in a way changeable things coming from stable ones. But insofar as these do not comprehend themselves, they are referred back to forms in the Mind—whether animal or a higher mind—which comprehend themselves; these, being manifold, are reduced to the most simple One and the Good, just as the celestial figures are reduced to the pole.* Just as individual species of things on earth were not subject to the same Spirits, but to different ones according to the nature of the Nations over which they presided; so too the specific types of Egyptian things were thought to have obtained their own proper Egyptian Spirits. For the domains of the Spirits were diverse, as they themselves hand down, just as there are diverse legal jurisdictions.

<margin>The Egyptians worshipped proper Spirits in each Prefecture.</margin>
Hence, they judged that foreign plants, living as if under a foreign jurisdiction, should never be adopted for either medical use or for mystical Sacred Rites, as was hinted at above; indeed, they had individual species distributed among individual prefectures <note>Administrative districts of ancient Egypt, also known as Nomes.</note> under appropriated Spirits, as Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note> teaches in his book on the Mysteries of the Egyptians, in these words:

<margin>Iamblichus</margin>
> Therefore, having contemplated this Sacred wisdom, and thus according to the congruence of things, having discovered the fitting receptacles for each of the Gods...

*...carefully discovering, he often composes into one: stones, herbs, animals, spices, and other similar things that are sacred, perfect, and God-like; and thereafter, from all these, he fashions a pure and complete spectacle. For it is not right to despise all matter, but only that which is foreign to the Gods. It is proper to choose matter that is appropriate to them, as it is able to harmonize with and contribute to the buildings of the Gods, the foundations of statues, and the works of sacrifice. For in no other way can a portion of divine possession reach earthly places and the men dwelling here, unless such a foundation has first been laid. One must believe the secret discourses <note>original: "Arcanis sermonibus"; likely referring to Hermetic or Neoplatonic mysteries</note>, which testify that a certain matter was handed down from the Gods through blessed visions. This matter is therefore kindred to those who handed it down. A sacrifice of such matter rouses the Gods to manifest themselves, and immediately calls them to be understood, and captures them as present, and demonstrates them perfectly. One can learn these same things even from the distribution of divinity effected according to locations, and from the very prefecture <note>term: "prefecture" (praefectura) refers to the spiritual jurisdiction or governance over specific regions or objects</note> which is divided through individual things, which, according to various orders—whether greater or lesser—have obtained such lots everywhere. For it is established that for the Gods who are rulers of certain places, a sacrifice made from the very things that grow there will be most harmonious; the governed things please the governors, and those things belonging to them are pleasing. Works are always most grateful to their makers, and those who first procreate something find such things especially acceptable in return. Therefore, whether they be certain animals, or plants, or other things which are seen to be dispensed by the powers above, they have simultaneously obtained a prefecture under them and procure for us an indivisible communion with the powers above. Some of these things, insofar as they are preserved and held, increase the familiar property of those holding them toward the Gods; namely, because they remain whole, they preserve the power of communion between men and Gods. Such are certain animals among the Egyptians, and everywhere the sacred man; other things, however, when slaughtered and burned, make the familiarity clearer, namely because they effect a resolution into the principle of the first elements, making them more kindred to the causes of the powers above, and more sacred according to the rite. For everywhere, the more the property and familiarity are perfected, the more perfect are the goods that descend to us from there. Nor are these merely the inventions of men, nor did they gain authority through human customs, but God himself, duly called among the sacred rites, is the Author of such laws, around whom many Gods and Angels dwell, and under whom, through whatever nations on earth, some Divinity has obtained a Prefecture and a common Province. From there, a specific Divinity is also assigned to every temple. Likewise, of the sacred rites we perform for the Gods, some God is the spectator and governor; of those for the Angels, an Angel; of those for the Demons <note>note: "Demons" (Daemon) here refers to intermediary spirits or tutelary genii, not necessarily evil entities</note>, a Demon; and in others, in the same way according to their own kind, a perfect being has obtained a kindred Prefecture. And although in the Egyptian Astrology we have shown the chains of herbs linked with the planets, the twelve signs of the Zodiac, as well as their Decans <note>term: "Decans" are 36 sub-divisions of the Zodiac, each spanning 10 degrees</note>, together with the presiding Genii through extensive tables, it nevertheless seemed right to present them here more diffusely and specifically, as if by profession, lest we should seem to have omitted anything profitable to our Physicians in this Work. I here place a figure of the things said and to be said, from which the mind shines forth more clearly than the midday light.*

**The Correspondences of the Body and Nature**

Starting from the top and moving clockwise, the substances of the natural world are aligned with human anatomy and ailments as follows:

**FOR THE HEAD**
Peony, Walnuts, Squill <note>original: "Squilla," or sea onion</note>

**FOR THE CHEST**
Hyssop, Elecampane, Coltsfoot

**FOR THE ARMS**

**FOR THE STOMACH**

**FOR THE HEART**

**FOR DISEASES OF THE ANUS**

**FOR THE HYPOCHONDRIA**
<note>The "hypochondria" refers to the upper abdomen, below the ribs, where the liver and spleen are located.</note>

**FOR GOUT**

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER III.

*The characteristics of plants compared to the characteristics of the twelve signs, and the members of the human body, according to the method of both the Hebrews and modern Physicians; of whom the latter received everything from the Hebrews, and the former from the Egyptians by tradition.*

<margin>Characteristics of plants compared to the 12 Signs of the Zodiac and the members of man.</margin>
But because not all herbs that are referred to a certain sign possess the same degree of quality, nor do they obtain their full value of virtue at just any time; for this reason, we shall present the individual plants belonging to each sign, distinguished into four degrees. We shall declare in what place and at what time they are to be gathered so that they may serve the body part they regard, and furthermore, what antipathies <note>Antipathy: in early medicine, a natural repulsion or opposing force between substances or celestial influences.</note> they have toward the remaining signs. Thus, this botanical argument may come forth for use, perfected in all its parts; which we have extracted partly from Avenar the Hebrew <note>Likely Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century scholar and astrologer.</note> and partly from the Astral Botany of Carichter the German <note>Bartholomäus Carrichter (1510–1567), physician to Emperor Maximilian II.</note>. We shall therefore make the beginning of our discussion with Aries.

### I. Aries ♈

<margin>Plants related to Aries ♈.</margin>
Aries is a masculine sign, fiery, hot-dry, and sympathetic to the head. Plants in the first degree are hot and dry.

<margin>Degrees of hot-dry things</margin>
**I Degree.** Red Mugwort, Betony, Chicory, Larkspur, Dwarf Elder, Mint, Coltsfoot, Speedwell. They are to be gathered at the end of the Dog Days <note>The hottest days of summer, usually July and August, associated with the star Sirius.</note> after the full moon.

**II Degree.** Plants in the second degree are hot and dry. Asparagus, St. John's Wort, Yarrow, Plantain, Peony. They are to be gathered while the Sun and Moon are existing in Cancer ♋.

**III Degree.** Larch Agaric, Spurge, Mezereon, Bitter Apple, Coltsfoot <note>original: "Farfara," often used interchangeably with Tussilago.</note>, Gentian, Privet, Castor Oil Plant, Elder. They are to be gathered at the end of July and the beginning of August.

**IV Degree.** Southernwood, White Hellebore, Marjoram, Horehound, Wild Tansy, Rosemary. They are to be gathered partly in the month of April and partly in September.

### II Taurus ♉

<margin>Plants related to Taurus ♉.</margin>
Taurus is a feminine sign, cold and dry, earthy; it is sympathetic to the neck and throat.

# CHAPTER III. 360 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Cold-dry species.</margin>
**1st Degree.** Cold-dry plants of the first degree: Spleenwort <note>original: *Asplenion*</note>, Ceterach, Wall Germander, Ground Ivy, Lily root, Narcissus, Polypody fern, Roses, Valerian, and Violet. These soften tumors of the throat and spleen.

**2nd Degree.** Maidenhair fern, Winter Cherry <note>original: *Akakengi*</note>, Columbine, Wall Ivy, Solomon’s Seal, Oak, and Mistletoe of the oak. These are beneficial for wounds.

**3rd Degree.** Bugloss, Blessed Thistle <note>original: *Carduus benedictus*</note>, Hound’s-tongue, Agrimony <note>original: *Eupatorium*</note>, Lesser Burdock, Oregano, Parsley, Sanicle, Figwort, Tormentil, and Periwinkle. All of these are wound-healing herbs <note>term: *vulnerariæ* — herbs used specifically for treating external wounds</note>.

**4th Degree.** Mouse-ear Hawkweed, Greater Burdock, Greater Celandine, Ash tree, Mallow, Lungwort, and Scabious; these have an antipathy <note>term: *antipathiam* — a natural or astrological opposition</note> with sub-lunar things belonging to Libra and Scorpio, but a sympathy with those belonging to Cancer and Sagittarius.

Avenar <note>Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous 12th-century scholar</note>, in his *Astrology of the Egyptians*, ascribes the following species of things to Taurus:

->And of the animals, all that have four legs; and of the trees,<-
->the tall ones, and every tree that bears fruit, and every tree that has no need<-
->for much water; and every tree whose fruit is used, and whose taste and scent are good.<-
<note>original Hebrew: ומן החיות כל שיש לו ארבע רגלים ומן אילנות הגבוהות וכל אילן עושה פרי וכל אילן שאין לו צורך למים וכל עץ שישתועלו בפריו עץ טעמו וריחו טובים</note>

> *Of the animals, he says, all quadrupeds; and of the trees, the tall ones, and every fruit-bearing tree, and every one requiring little water, such as mountain trees, strong in fruit; finally, all plants and trees sweet to the taste, flavor, and smell.*

The Egyptians truly, as Auenar <note>Abraham Ibn Ezra</note> recites, subject the following to Cancer:

The Crab: and it is cold and moist with a little directness; and of its taste, sour and salty; and of the appearance of the eyes, white and the color of dust, and like smoky eyes and what resembles them. And in its portion of living things are all swarming creatures, the small fish, the creatures of the dry land, scorpions, and the creeping things of the earth. In general, it indicates water that has much movement, and every plant that is by the water, and rainwater, and all sweet waters.

*Cancer is cold and slightly moist; of flavors, it possesses the sharp and the salty; of visible things, it has the color white and ash-gray, and what is similar to it. Its portion of animals includes all aquatic things, serpents, and small fish, and dry animals, and scorpions, and everything that creeps upon the earth; in short, it signifies much-moving water, and all things budding upon the banks of waters, and those which come forth upon torrents or rain and sweet waters.*

### CHAPTER III. 362 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Degrees of hot-dry plants.</margin>
**1st Degree:** Basil, Saffron, Cypress, Clove, Hyssop, Lavender, Water Plantain, Sundew, Thyme.
**2nd Degree:** Wild Angelica, Twayblade, Centaury, Galangal, Gentian, Devil's-bit.
**3rd Degree:** Stinking Chamomile, Parsnip, Mint, Garden Cress, Pennyroyal, Buttercup, Nettle.
**4th Degree:** Birch, Broom, Boxwood, Laurel. Herbs of the first degree are gathered when the Sun is in Pisces and the Moon is in Cancer. Species of the second degree are gathered at the beginning of May before sunrise, or toward the end of August; or when the Sun is in Taurus and the Moon is in Gemini, before sunrise. Species of the third degree are gathered when the Sun is in Leo and the Moon is in Virgo at the last quarter, or for cooling, while the Sun is in Taurus and the Moon is in Gemini, before sunrise. Species of the fourth degree are gathered when the Sun is in Pisces and the Moon is in Aquarius; for by an influence of this kind, they are reduced to a temperate state. But let us hear Aben Ezra <note>original: "Auenar"; likely referring to Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous medieval scholar</note> discussing these matters according to the mind of the Egyptians:

> <note>original Hebrew: "And its nature is hot and dry, and its humor is red bile, and its taste is bitter and sharp, from the sight of the eyes the blessed and the yellow, and from the animals the lions and the leopards and the hyenas and the bears and the wolves, and from the metal vessels gold and silver and precious stones and the piercing stone, the stones called diamonds, and the stone that gathers straw called El-Sari, and all work of fire."</note>

> *That is, in complexion hot and dry; of the humors it possesses red bile <term>choleram rubeam: one of the four ancient humors, associated with a fiery temperament</term>; of tastes, the bitter and sharp; of colors, saffron, reddish, and those inclining toward red; of animals, it possesses Lions, Leopards, Basilisks, Bears, Wolves; of metals, Gold and Silver, and precious stones, Diamond, Chrysoprase, and that which is called Eljari <note>likely a transliteration of an Arabic name for a specific mineral</note>, and all work of fire.*

### XI Aquarius ♒.

<margin>Plants related to Aquarius</margin>
Aquarius is a masculine sign, belonging to the element of air, warm and moist, having a sympathetic relationship to the shins, and is adorned with all these species:

**Grade I.** **Angelica**, **Wild Carrot** <note>original: "Daucus"</note>, **Fig**, **Ash flowers**, **Walnut**, **Sweet Clover** <note>original: "Melilotus"</note>, **Sanicle**, **Solomon's Seal**.
**Grade II.** **Larkspur** <note>original: "Consolida regalis"</note>, **Cumin**, **Dodder of Thyme** <note>original: "Epithymum"</note>, **Geranium**, **Burdock** <note>original: "Lappa"</note>, **Rose Root**, **Pellitory-of-the-wall**.
**Grade III.** **Agrimony**, **Wall Fescue** <note>original: "Myuris"</note>, **Clary Sage** <note>original: "Horminum"</note>, **Saxifrage**, **Dragonwort** <note>original: "Serpentaria"</note>, **Wood Sage**.
**Grade IV.** **Asarabacca leaves**, **Motherwort** <note>original: "Cardiaca"</note>, **Hemlock**, **Medlar**; to which **Avenar** <note>likely referring to the Hebrew scholar Ibn Ezra</note> adds: from the humors, blood; from the flavors, sweet; from the colors, green and lemon-yellow.

### XII Pisces ♓.

<margin>Plants related to Pisces</margin>
Pisces is a feminine sign, belonging to the element of water, cold and moist, having a sympathetic relationship to the feet; its species are:

**Grade I.** **Beech**, **Birthwort** <note>original: "Aristolochia"</note>, **Cabbage head**, **Gourd**, **Myrobalan**, **Turnip**, **Water Lily**, **Purslane**.
**Grade II.** **Artichoke**, **Snapdragon**, **Cornflower**, **Yellow Chaste-weed**.
**Grade III.** **Black Cumin** <note>original: "Nigella"</note>, **Horned Poppy**, **Sow Thistle**.
**Grade IV.** **Hemlock**, **Henbane**, **Monkshood** <note>original: "Napellus"</note>, **Nightshade** <note>original: "Solanum"</note>, **Serpent-herb**; to which **Avenar** adds: from the flavors, salty; from the colors, green, white, and variegated; from the animals, all aquatic creatures; from the plants, likewise those that grow in water; from the stones, coral.

And these are the species which several modern authors <note>original: "Neoterici"</note> have subjected to the twelve signs according to the Egyptian rule; but whoever examines these with a deeper scale of judgment will find many gaps, and that they cannot satisfy the mind, since they have subjected species of entirely contrary qualities to one and the same sign, and have mixed poisonous plants with healthy ones entirely without reason. Not so the Egyptians, who with the highest judgment selected some single plant which, by its <term>signature<note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" was the belief that a plant's physical appearance revealed its medicinal use.</note></term>, expressed the limb and its quality, and was collected at the same time. In a word, they arranged every single thing subjected to each sign—whether you look at the flavor, the scent, or the form and figure—so exactly that there was nothing in any way that did not correspond in every respect to the celestial sign and the limb it denoted, as will be seen shortly after, when we have examined the first class of planetary species.

# CHAPTER III. 366 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

## Characteristics of Plants compared to the seven Planets.

<margin>Characteristics of plants compared to the Planets.</margin>
The influences of the stars are outpourings endowed with peculiar powers. When the stars are robust and in their full strength, these influences strengthen, fertilize, and promote the things familiar to them; conversely, they weaken, corrupt, and hinder those things contrary to them. Indeed, according to the thought of Plato and Paracelsus <note>Paracelsus (1493–1541) was a famous physician and occultist who popularized the idea that every earthly thing has a celestial counterpart.</note>, the "familiarity" or connection of the stars with sublunary things <note>Things "under the moon," meaning the physical world on Earth.</note> should be established according to individual stars and individual types of earthly things; (for they maintain that individual stars preside over individual species of earthly things, and pour their powers into them through a peculiar influence.) However, since it would be difficult to assign individual stars to every single individual thing, perhaps for this reason some—with better judgment—have aptly assigned to the stars not individual things, but rather the faculties and powers with which each thing is endowed by nature. Hence, they aptly named things expressing the nature of the Moon "Lunar"; those belonging to Mercury, "Mercurial"; to Venus, "Venereal"; and to the Sun, "Solar," as the previously cited Arab, Aben-elrahhmon <note>Likely referring to the 12th-century scholar Ibn al-Rahman, used as a source for astrological lore.</note>, learnedly demonstrates. We have decided to display these categories in this place, beginning with Saturn.

### I. Saturn ♄ and its species, extracted from Avenar.

<note>Avenar refers to Abraham ibn Ezra, a famous medieval Jewish scholar and astrologer.</note>
Just as Saturn is by its very nature malignant, extremely cold, melancholic, a friend to Mars but an enemy to the rest; so its progeny is equipped with similar qualities. Therefore, in the Microcosm <note>The human body, viewed as a miniature version of the universe.</note>, they specifically correspond to the spleen, an organ marked by similar qualities.

->Saturnine and Splenetic Things.<-

From the animals, the solitary, nocturnal, and sad ones, such as the Donkey, Bear, Toad, Camel, Mole, and Scorpion. From the birds, the Eagle Owl, Raven, Little Owl, Bat, and Hoopoe.

# C H A P T E R IV.

## The application of what has been said, or Egyptian Medicine in practice; and first concerning Botanical remedies, and the classification of diseases.

<margin>The Egyptians classified diseases according to the number of the members of the human body.</margin>
The Egyptians applied the aforementioned analogies of things to the species of higher beings <note>referring to the celestial bodies and spiritual hierarchies</note> in their own times, places, and other circumstances so cautiously and solicitously for medical use, that if they bypassed even one detail, they believed the entire undertaking would fall into failure. Indeed, they distinguished all diseases according to the number of the members of the human body, compared to the twelve signs and the seven planets; thus, they referred head diseases <note>original: "Cephalicos morbos"</note> to Aries and the Moon;

<note>The following image description refers to a "Zodiac Man," a common historical diagram showing how astrological signs govern specific body parts.</note>
*A circular astrological diagram, often referred to as a "Zodiac Man" (homo signorum). In the center of a double-bordered circle stands a nude male figure with arms outstretched. The outer ring is divided into twelve segments, each containing a zodiac symbol. Starting from the top and moving clockwise, the symbols are: Aries, Taurus, Gemini, Cancer, Leo, Virgo, Libra, Scorpio, Sagittarius, Capricorn, Aquarius, and Pisces. The diagram serves to illustrate the correspondences between the zodiac signs and specific parts or diseases of the human body.*

<margin>Rabbi Sola. Haly the Arab. Prosper Alpinus.</margin>
<margin>Five classes of head diseases.</margin>
Pulmonary diseases to Cancer and Mercury; Cardiac diseases—that is, infirmities of the heart—to Leo and the Sun; and so they referred each of the other diseases to their own signs and planets, as if to the sympathetic causes of the same. Once this was done, if anyone suffered from a certain infirmity of the head, they diligently examined the causes and quality of the disease, whether it had its origin from moisture or cold. But if the limb had been attacked by some excessive inflammation <note>term: phlegmone — a type of hot, painful swelling or inflammation</note>, they applied a "chain" of moist-cold remedies for the cure of said infirmity. If, on the contrary, cold and dryness had been the cause, they thought they must consult a "chain" of moist-warm remedies. And this was the first degree of Egyptian medication, by which they applied opposites to opposites. All of these things are deduced at length by Rabbi Sola, Haly the Arab, and Prosper Alpinus <note>A 16th-century Venetian physician and botanist famous for his study of Egyptian medicine</note> in their records on the Medicine of the Egyptians. Those who reasoned a little more subtly about medical matters divided the previously described diseases more precisely. Thus, they divided diseases of the head into five Classes, so that the primary Class contained rheumatic diseases, or those which depend on rheum or catarrh <note>term: catarrh — an excessive buildup of mucus in the nose or throat</note>; of which kind are catarrhs, dizziness <note>original: "scotomia"</note>, vertigo, paralysis, epilepsy, and apoplexy; for the curing of which they employed specialized physicians—

# CHAPTER V. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

<margin>Diseases of other parts of the human body.</margin>
<margin>Specific diseases had specific Doctors among the Egyptians.</margin>
...they maintained those who, throughout their entire lives, labored at nothing else but to scrutinize the causes and origins of these evils, and to discover opportune and appropriate remedies for each individual case. The Second Class contained diseases of the eyes; the Third, of the ears; the Fourth, of the tongue and throat; the Fifth was occupied with external ailments, such as the itch <note>original: "scabies"</note>, mange <note>original: "psora"</note>, and wounds inflicted from without. For the curing of each of these, they appointed just as many Doctors; so that some were Doctors of Rheumatic conditions; others for the Eyes; others for the Ears; and finally, others were appointed to cure other ailments. Nor was it permitted by law for any to attend to other matters, as we have deduced at length above in the *Egyptian Politics*, chapter 3. Others, furthermore, were occupied only in the care of the chest and lungs; others were destined for the healing of heart diseases, of which again there is a great variety. Some focused solely on the care of the liver, kidneys, and bladder, the spleen, and the flanks; others on the stomach and intestines; and finally, others on the cure of fevers; so that as many Doctors were deputed as there were species of diseases. Thus it happened that each individual, with the greatest zeal, undertook the care of the limb committed to him through opportune and highly appropriate remedies—extracted from their own "chains" <note>A reference to the "Chain of Being" or Hermetic correspondences where plants and minerals are linked to specific celestial bodies and body parts.</note>—and the effects that followed in the cure of said diseases were utterly prodigious. However, because there is a great connection between the diseases of one limb and another, they were bound by law first to learn universal Medicine and anatomy; and finally, being instructed with sufficient knowledge of the same, to apply their minds to healing particular diseases according to each person's inclination. See what we have discussed regarding these matters at greater length above in the *Egyptian Politics*. Furthermore, since Egypt, by its natural constitution, produced certain specific and epidemic diseases—concerning which see Prosper Alpinus <note>A famous 16th-century Italian physician and botanist who wrote "De Medicina Egyptiorum."</note> cited above—they first investigated the causes of these diseases with diligent inquiry, and then applied suitable remedies. For at certain times of the year, winds sent from the South with the burning heats of the sandy soil produced various diseases, just as they produced exotic symptoms in bodies. These things having been established, they approached the care of the limbs by a triple path: the sympathetic, the astral, and the characteristic (or hieroglyphic); concerning each of which we shall discourse.

## CHAPTER V.

### *Sympathetic Medicine:*

<margin>The sympathetic Medicine of the Egyptians.</margin>
The sympathetic Medicine of the Egyptians consisted in this: that things or species of those items which were known to have some hidden "consent" <note>A term in early modern medicine referring to a shared resonance or harmony between a remedy and a body part.</note> for curing a limb were applied with a singular preparation. Moreover, they drew these from the "worldly chains" by which things of the same nature—such as a plant—were connected by a similarity of hidden nature to some sign of the Zodiac that presided over the limb to be cured. For they knew that some species, by a certain natural inclination, were connected with a specific star and sought the preservation of the limbs whose seals they expressed; so that the more such things concurred, the greater the effects in the cure of the limb...

For as the Arabs rightly say, following the <margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> mind of the Egyptians in Marsilio Ficino <note>A 15th-century Italian scholar who translated Plato and wrote extensively on "natural magic."</note>, chapter 2 of *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*: "Indeed, no one ought to distrust that we, and all things around us, are able to claim celestial things for ourselves through certain preparations; for these things were made from heaven and are constantly governed by it, and they are especially prepared for those influences." Therefore, just as in us the quality and movement of any member—especially a principal one—pertains to others, so the acts of the principal members in the World <note>The "Macrocosm" or the universe as a whole.</note> move all things, and the lower members easily receive from the higher ones which are ready to give of their own accord. For the more powerful a cause is, the more principal it is in acting, and the more inclined toward giving. It is also expedient to know which members each Planet governs in any given sign. All of these things were believed by the Ancient Egyptians to be animated by a single spirit of worldly life. <margin>Abu Rhodam: The Egyptian dogma concerning the Soul of the World.</margin> For as Abu Rhodam <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic astrological authority.</note> rightly asserts, it was a dogma of the Egyptians that the Soul of the World, which they called *Ruach aldonia* <note>original: "روح الدنيا" - Spirit of the World.</note>, has as many divinely implanted reasons within itself as there are Ideas in the Divine Mind, by which it fashions the species in matter. Whence every species, through its own "seminal reason" <note>A Stoic and Neoplatonic concept of "seed-germs" or formative principles that organize matter.</note>, properly corresponds to an Idea; and through this, it can often easily receive something from that source, since it is influenced from there through this link. Therefore, if it should ever degenerate from its proper form, it can be formed anew through this nearest medium, through which that medium can easily be reformed from above. But if you rightly apply many things that are scattered but conform to the Idea to a certain species of things, or to an individual of it, you will soon derive a singular gift from the Idea into this matter (prepared opportunely in this way) through the seminal reason of the soul. For it is not the Intellect itself that is properly drawn down, but the Soul; for the ancient Sages did not think that certain Divinities entirely segregated from matter were drawn to specific worldly materials, but rather Spirits <note>original: "Dæmones" - here meaning intermediary spirits or guiding intelligences, not "demons" in the modern sense.</note> and those animated by the gift of the living stars, as they used to say, were drawn down. Therefore, when the soul generates the special forms of lower things and effects those powers through their proper reasons, it does so under the support of the stars and celestial forms. However, it exhibits the singular endowments of individuals—which are as admirable in some as they usually are in species—through seminal reasons, not so much under the support of celestial forms and figures, as by the position of the stars, the habit of the degrees <note>original: "morionum" - likely referring to the 'moira' or specific degrees of the zodiac.</note>, and the aspects of the planets both among themselves and toward the stars higher than the planets. For just as our soul, beyond the proper powers of the members, brings forth a common virtue of life everywhere in us, it does so especially through the heart as the proper fountain of the soul's fire.

<margin>The Soul of the World exerts its powers through the Sun.</margin> Similarly, the Ancients said that the Soul of the World, flourishing especially through the Sun, explains its common virtue of life everywhere; whence they judged that the soul, both in us and in the World, is whole in any part, but is located chiefly in the heart and the Sun. For just as the virtue of our soul through the spirit...

They believed this power was especially infused into those things which had drawn in the greatest amount of this spirit.

<margin>The fifth essence of things.</margin>
Hence, they skillfully separated this fifth essence from both the elements and from mixed substances, making use primarily of those things which abounded in this kind of fifth essence and spirit, such as wine, sugar, balsam, gold, precious stones, and myrobalans <note>A dried fruit used in apothecary and tanning</note>, which smell most sweet, shine brightly, and possess a warm, moist, and clear quality in their subtle substance. Furthermore, just as food properly taken into us is not alive by itself, yet is reduced to the form of our life through our spirit; so also must our bodies, when properly applied to the worldly body and spirit—namely through worldly things and through our own spirit which is sympathetic to them—draw as much as possible from that worldly life. Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonic philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note> shows all of this beautifully in his work *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, which the reader should consult.

<margin>The Egyptian method of healing.</margin>
For this reason, the Egyptians, in order to more effectively uproot the seeds of diseases, would place medicines into an alembic <note>An early chemical still used for distillation</note>. These medicines were specifically tailored to individual limbs and composed of herbs, plants, and animals analogous to said limbs, prepared under the corresponding position of the heavens and at the proper hour. Through continuous distillation, they extracted with the greatest industry a water that was most pure, most subtle, and very similar to the worldly ether or "fifth essence," which they called the spirit of the Soul of the World. For example, if they were about to purge the head of harmful rheums <note>Latin: *rheumatismis*; here referring to excess bodily fluids or "catarrh" believed to cause illness</note>, they would draw a liquor from species that correspond to the head. When this was taken at the appropriate time according to Astrological laws, it would fly immediately to the limb for whose sake it was produced, to preserve it and to strengthen it against the hostile machinations of diseased qualities dwelling there. Thus it happened that, through both the penetrating power and the efficacy of the medicine, the sick person was soon freed from the hidden enemy. The same must be said for medicines for the heart, spleen, liver, seed, chest, and so forth. For they said that this most subtle liquor was miraculously strengthened by the worldly spirit, the author of lives; this liquor, uniting into one with the ethereal spirit and being further tinged with the specific virtues of the species mixed into it, could not fail to produce great and prodigious effects in driving away diseases. This is because in such liquors—the raw materials and any existing malignancies having been cast aside and stripped away—there dominates only the power of things and the natural, specific gift and quality emanating from the property of the whole substance.

<margin>Three things are elicited by distillation: Spirit, Oil, and Salt.</margin>
And since in every distillation three things especially emerge through the marvelous artistry of dissolution—spirit, oil, and salt—just as the spirit obtained a marvelous power in strengthening the limbs sympathetic to it, so the salt was held to be of wonderful efficacy in opening the obstructions of the channels of the microcosm <note>The human body, viewed as a miniature reflection of the universe</note>, and the oil in the cure of external evils, each according to the affection of the part for which it was a symbol. Some presented these things first macerated in choice wine and then distilled. Others fashioned electuaries <note>A medicinal paste made with honey or syrup</note> from them, according to the inclination and judgment of the Physicians, who nevertheless never [departed] from the chain of things [required] to drive away some disease...

->*Concerning the Panacea, or the Universal Medicine of the Egyptians, most suitable for driving out all diseases.*<-

<margin>The Panacea of the Egyptians. What Hippocrates understands by the healing power of nature.</margin>
Hippocrates calls that "healing power of nature" the instrumental cause which the soul uses immediately to exercise its principal faculties, or for the sake of restoration and preservation. <margin>The primordial virtue of the radical moisture and heat.</margin> You should understand this not merely as an elementary mixture of parts or a temperament of the primary qualities, but as that substance forged from the <term>radical moisture</term> <note>The essential fluid believed to sustain life and vitality in medieval medicine.</note> and the <term>primordial heat</term>, and the indwelling spirit—the bond between soul and body, the foundation of things celestial and terrestrial, which in preceding chapters we have called the <term>fifth essence</term> <note>The "Quinta Essentia" or ether, the purest element beyond the four earthly ones.</note>; the Ancients also named it the elementary heaven and the celestial element. According to the mind of Hippocrates, this substance, falling away from the individual members of the human body, forms the seed, ferments it, disposes it, and shapes the body for the soul that is to enter it from the matter subject to it, creating a new harmonic mixture of offspring from the very parts from which it flowed. For a part cut off from the head conforms a new head, the idea of which it retained; that from the heart, a new heart; that from the liver, a new liver; that from the lungs, a new lung; and so with the rest. Moreover, the duty of that member which it formed for itself in the unborn fetus is the same in the already born: to preserve it unharmed in all things, or to restore it to health if it should happen to fall away from it. <margin>The healing power of nature.</margin> Although that entire nature concurs toward the integrity, preservation, and safety of the whole body, its various particles nevertheless bring aid and assistance to the different parts of the body in which they are innate through a certain occult <term>sympathy</term> and consensus; this is what Physicians are accustomed to call a <term>disposition</term> of the parts proceeding from the whole substance. For although they differ very little from one another in nature, being innate substances, they nevertheless have a certain specific <term>sympathy</term> <note>original: "συμπάθειαν"</note> with the parts of the body in which they reside, by which they preserve and strengthen the member of the body to which they are related, and rescue it from diseases as if from things contrary to its preservation. <margin>The Egyptians applied different members of animals to different suffering members.</margin> Hence, for those suffering from a disease of the head, the Egyptians offered the heads of birds and various brains of animals that were most suitable; for those with liver complaints, livers; for those with heart trouble, hearts; for the splenetic, spleens; for the consumptive, the lungs—as I have said—of appropriate animals, to be devoured either cooked or prepared with appropriate herbs (cephalic, cardiac, hepatic, pulmonary, or splenic). They were not unaware that nourishment of this kind would properly perform its duty in curing the member whose <term>signature</term> <note>The "Doctrine of Signatures" held that herbs or organs resembling body parts could cure those parts.</note> it possessed, and toward whose preservation it was uniquely inclined. And although these similar things were offered with great benefit to the sick, because they had learned by experience that medicines would achieve a greater effect the more they were similar to the parts—indeed, to the whole—and were the same according to their species, they therefore devised something even more sublime. # CHAPTER VI. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

<margin>The Egyptians selected medicinal liquids from the members of the human body.</margin>
From the individual members of the human body, they separately extracted certain liquids using the chemical art <note>original: "Chymicâ arte," referring to early alchemy and pharmacology</note>; with these, they produced wonderful and almost prodigious effects in the cure of that specific part from which they had been extracted. They proceeded in this manner: To strengthen the vital spirit, they would remove the heart of a recently killed and still warm man, or the liver, or the lungs, or the brain, and so on for the rest. This was crushed into minute parts and mixed with herbs—if it were the heart, with cardiac herbs; if the liver, with hepatic herbs; if the stomach, with stomachic herbs, and other things regarding the said member. This mixture, enclosed in an alembic <note>a chemical distilling apparatus</note>, they distilled over a slow fire. For the liquid that came forth from it was for them an appropriated and specific medicine, destined for the cure of the intended member; they gave this to the sick person either alone, or mixed with other things, or in a broth well diluted with the liquids, at a competent time and hour.

<margin>How the Egyptians prepared the Panacea.</margin>
Indeed, they prepared the Panacea <note>a "universal remedy" believed to cure all ills</note> in this way: They took corpses, which they call Mummies, previously preserved in the proper rite with balsam, myrrh, asphalt, and other spices, and cut them into small pieces. To these they added grain, wine, myrobalans <note>a type of plum-like fruit used in tanning and medicine</note>, gold leaf, and similar universal medicines. The entire mass was placed inside a chemical vessel, and from it they elicited either a salt or a liquid, which they called Panacea, beneficial for all diseases. For since all members lie hidden by virtue in the said body, and prevail by their own specific virtues, and each individual part has a natural inclination toward that which is sympathetic to it; they certainly persuaded themselves that the latent virtues of each individual part were extracted in this, and acted in an unconfused manner upon the members corresponding to them, just as they act when separated. And thus they believed that this universal liquid, as it was extracted from the mass of the whole body, likewise obtained a universal virtue to protect and deliver the whole body to which it was applied from all violence of diseases, for the reasons indicated shortly before.

<margin>Eben Rhodâ.</margin>
The aforementioned Eben Rhodâ <note>likely Ali ibn Ridwan, an 11th-century Egyptian physician and astrologer</note> pursues all these matters more extensively in his treatise on the Medicine of the Egyptians. I would willingly place his Arabic words in this spot, were it not that the bulk of the book and the weariness of transcribing deterred me; let it suffice to have introduced his mind in these few words.
