# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER V.

<margin>How the Egyptian priests prepared themselves for metaphysical Medicine.</margin>...incantations and spells, whether through dreams, or manifest apparitions, and in other ways which we have described in *Hieroglyphic Magic*. And this was the specific institution of the Egyptian Hierophants <note>High-ranking priests who interpreted sacred mysteries</note>; to obtain which gift of grace, they knew how to prepare themselves in a wondrous manner through fasts, a chaste life, and temperance in food. Indeed, they firmly believed that they could attain this through natural means, intellectual operations, and the perpetual contemplation of the Gods. Furthermore, there were ten Gods whom they were chiefly occupied in adjuring and petitioning to obtain the revelation of medicines appropriated to individual diseases, as we shall show below. To these Gods they also consecrated individual numbers, as if they were indicators of the world-chains <note>The "Great Chain of Being" or the links between the divine and material worlds</note>. <margin>The Gods from whom the Egyptians requested skill in healing.</margin> These numbers they applied to natural things in a certain wondrous ratio to produce prodigious effects, which was most evident in the subject of vegetables. Indeed, they dedicated one to the supreme Deity and Cause of causes, from whom all things flow as if from a perennial fountain. They attributed the dyad <note>the number two</note> to Nephtha, the triad to Minerva, the tetrad to Apollo (or Horus), the pentad to Isis, the hexad to Osiris, the heptad to Mercury, the octad to Ammon, the ennead to Typhon, and finally the decad to Momphta.

<margin>Which vegetables the Egyptians attributed to which Gods.</margin> Truly, to demonstrate the method of proceeding established in the workshop of vegetable nature (to say nothing for now of other levels of nature), they first inquired what number the leaves of herbs expressed. If an herb matched a certain fixed number dedicated to a specific Deity by the numerous offspring of its leaves, they preserved it as if under the protection of the corresponding Deity, as belonging to the economy of said Deity. They also examined the flowers according to the number of leaves <note>petals</note> with which they were adorned, together with their shape and color. If they found a flower corresponding to some Deity in number, shape, and color, they considered it most appropriated to that same Deity. With this same flower, they performed sacrifices, as if it were most effective for swaying the Deity. They did the same with the number of seeds in a fruit. All these things, having finally been learned through long experience, they recorded in the sacred register of hieroglyphics as belonging to the chains of the said Deities. In a similar manner, they duly investigated the number of nodes in the stalks of plants, and the shape of the stalks—whether they were round and smooth, or triangular, or square. These they consecrated as if they were scepters to the appropriate Deities, as will be clear in the demonstration of the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian mysteries, also known as the Mensa Isiaca</note>. By employing these ceremonies according to the analogy of the said things, they persuaded themselves that they could exhibit marvelous effects both in Medicine and in divinations through dreams. <margin>Through dreams the Egyptians recognized the characteristics of herbs.</margin> Indeed, when they were about to consult concerning the cure of some disease, before committing themselves to bed, having first duly disposed and purified the mind through various lustrations, they would consider several such characteristics of plants and flowers placed before them with intense and fixed imagination. Then they would solicit heaven and the Gods with songs, so that they might show through a dream which of the said vegetables would lead to the cure of a particular disease. Then, girding themselves to catch sleep, whichever Deity first appeared to them in sleep, they [believed] the plant committed to that Deity's faith [would provide] the desired cure for the proposed disease...

What Astral medicine is.

**Astral** Medicine was nothing other than the administration of medicines at a fixed time and hour, and under a suitable positioning of the Heavens; since we have spoken sufficiently of this in the section on Astrology and the preceding parts, we wished to be briefer here. For the whole business consisted in the application of lower things which had a necessary connection and harmony with the superior stars, as well as with the members of the human body, and even with supramundane ideas and spirits <note>original: "genijs" - guardian spirits or guiding intelligences</note>; concerning this, see Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous 15th-century Italian scholar and priest who led the revival of Hermetic and Platonic philosophy</note> in his book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens*, where he delivers many things according to the mind of the Ancients—truly curious and proper to our purpose—as well as other authors, both Arab and Hebrew, cited above.

## § III.
### *Concerning Characteristic Medicine.*

<margin>
Characteristic Medicine, or the use of amulets.
</margin>
**Characteristic** Medicine is the faculty by which they believed a disease was necessarily put to flight through the use of hieroglyphic marks, carved according to astrological laws into a stone or a medicinal vessel made of that same stone, analogous to the specific disease. It was the custom of the Egyptians to proceed with stones just as we described above regarding herbs, while they would engrave certain figures upon them for the individual signs of the Zodiac and the planets—figures entirely analogous to the Spirits, Signs, Stars, and diseases—at the opportune hour and time, namely when they were dominant. For in this way, they quite simply persuaded themselves that the presiding Spirit [acted] through the star subject to it, the star through its influence into the figures, and these acting upon the disease, would finally confer an infallible effect upon the sick person. And although such things are proscribed by the laws of the Church as the vain and superstitious inventions of astrologers, we nevertheless judged that they should be dealt with in this place as an opportune moment, both so that the roots of astrological superstitions might be more clearly shown and uprooted, and so that the truth of hieroglyphic doctrine might be more solidly proven. *There are in the Heavens various forms derived from the Egyptians and Chaldeans, or at least devised by them. For example, in the first face of Virgo, a beautiful Virgin sitting, holding twin ears of corn in her hand and nursing a boy; which the Arabs say, when engraved on an agate, has great power in procuring an excellent habit of body and the goodwill of Princes. There are also other characters of the signs and planets designated by the Egyptians. They wish, therefore, for all these to be inscribed in images, so that if anyone expects a specific benefit from Mercury, he ought to place him in Virgo, or at least have the Moon there in aspect to Mercury, and then fashion the image out of tin or silver, in which is the whole sign of Virgo, its character, and the character of Mercury. For length of life, the Ancients made an image of Saturn on a sapphire stone in the hour of Saturn, with Saturn himself ascending and fortunately positioned. The form was an old man sitting on a high chair or a dragon; his head covered with a certain dark linen cloth, raising his hands above his head, holding a sickle in his hand, or fish, clothed in a dark garment. For a long and happy life, they fashioned an image of Jupiter on a clear white stone; it was a man sitting upon an eagle or a dragon, crowned, in the hour of Jupiter, with him emerging happily in his exaltation, clothed in a saffron garment. Against fearfulness, images were manufactured in the hour of Mars with the first face of Scorpio rising, showing Mars armed and crowned. To cure diseases, they fashioned an image of the Sun in gold during the hour of the Sun, with the first face of Leo ascending with the Sun: a King on a throne in a saffron garment, a crow, and the figure of the Sun. For joy and bodily strength, a maidenly image of Venus holding apples and flowers in her hand, clothed in saffron and white, in the hour of Venus, in the first face of Libra, or Pisces, or Taurus, for they said she prospered greatly in these signs. They carved the image of Mercury for intellect and memory in the first face of Gemini. Likewise, against fevers, Mercury was carved in marble as a man carrying weapons in his hand, in the hour of Mercury rising; sometimes they impressed this on a certain material to be taken by the weak. Hence they said it cured every kind of fever. The form of Mercury, however, was a man sitting on a throne, wearing a cap and crested, with eagle's feet, holding a cock or fire in his left hand; sometimes winged upon a peacock, holding a pen in his right hand, in a variegated garment. The Moon was a beautiful girl with a horned head sitting upon a dragon or a Bull, with serpents entwined both at her head and feet; she was thought to obtain a miraculous power against the stone <note>Kidney stones</note>, pains of the genitals, and for stanching blood, in the hour of Saturn. Likewise, they impressed a Lion in gold, which they believed conferred a miraculous benefit when worn for expelling diseases. They made the image similar to the disease, with the Sun in the heart of the Lion occupying the middle of the Heaven. # CHAPTER VI. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

From the seventeenth degree of the Virgin <note>the zodiac sign Virgo</note> to its end, they made images against diseases, hatreds, and for a successful journey. In the station of the Ram <note>Aries</note>, from the first degree to the twelfth, against diseases and discord. In the station of the Goat-Horned <note>Capricorn</note>, from the twelfth degree to the twenty-fifth, against weakness and imprisonment. In the station of the Fishes <note>Pisces, marked as ♓</note>, from the fourth degree to the seventeenth, for curing diseases, for profit, and for increasing the harvest; and in other signs similarly, they often devised other things with a vain curiosity that smelled less of the Physician than of the Magician. Thus says Marsilio <note>Marsilio Ficino, the 15th-century Neoplatonist who translated the Corpus Hermeticum</note>. These things indeed agree with the reports of the Arabs, but they do not reflect the pure doctrine of the Egyptians, as they are contaminated by the various superstitious opinions of other nations. Therefore, it seemed appropriate to explain what method was used by the Egyptians in <term>characteristic Medicine</term> <note>Medicine using specific signs, characters, or talismans</note>.

<margin>The method of the Egyptians in characteristic Medicine.</margin>
It was said in the preceding pages that they most strictly observed the dominion of the twelve Genii <note>guardian spirits or intelligences</note> presiding over the signs of the Zodiac, as well as the seven planets. For since they knew, through a certain successive tradition, the Genii presiding both over the said signs and planets, and over individual bodily diseases, they would begin their business thus: For example, against diseases of the heart, they would take a round gold plate during the hour of the Sun, with the Sun positioned near the <term>Basiliscus</term> <note>the star Regulus</note>—which moderns call the Heart of the Lion—and they would engrave the figure of a Sphinx, which represented a human in its head and a Lion in the rest of its body,

I now proceed to explain what all these things signify. On the front part, there appears a human figure ending in the body of a Beetle <note>original: "Scarabæus"</note>, notable for its fourfold spread of wings; by which nothing else is designated hieroglyphically but the Solar Intelligence. It bears a globe on its head because it partakes of divinity. It is seen with a human face and a bare chest because it understands and sees through all things, although it is free from any mixture of earthly and material contagion. It ends in the body of a Beetle because, just as the Beetle expresses the operations of the Sun by rolling its material pellet from east to west—both in its body and its actions—so the Solar Intelligence moves that Solar globe from east to west, by which revolution all lower things are moved, animated, and generated. Since all these matters have been explained most extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, in the sacred writing concerning the Beetle, I refer the reader there. It is marked by a fourfold spread of wings because it diffuses the power of its motion into the fourfold face of the World with the greatest speed, as was handed down in the cited place. In its hands, it holds ears of grain, because they believe that a suitable method of nourishment proceeds from them, as if from kindred and Solar species: for grain is the unique and supreme sustenance of men, possessing great strength in Medicine. Immediately following this figure is the image of an Ibis, by which the conjunction of the Sun and Moon is expressed, at which time a medicine should be opportunely taken; this conjunction is aptly signified by the bonds derived from the Beetle-shaped Intelligence into the Moon, to which a globe is attached, for at this time the Sun acts especially upon the globe of the Moon, impregnating it with its power. Moreover, that the Ibis signifies the Moon was demonstrated copiously in the book cited a little earlier, in the sacred writing of the Ibis. It has expanded wings to signify the joy and readiness with which it desires to be impregnated by the Sun for the good of the lower World. Then follows a kneeling figure, holding with one hand a sextile Moon <note>A "sextile" Moon refers to an astrological aspect where two heavenly bodies are 60 degrees apart, often considered harmonious.</note> placed upon its head, and with the other sustaining a <term>ram-shaped</term> <note>original: "κριομορφόv" (kriomorphon)</note> scepter—that is, marked with a Ram's head—by which is indicated Nephta, the Preside of sublunary moisture. She perfects the influential power of the Sun and Moon upon the grain in the sublunary World, and according to the three seasons of the year—which the three ears of grain placed in the cavity of the sextile Moon show—she provides a joyful and fertile harvest, with the help and dominance of Ammon, whom the Ram-shaped scepter expresses. She kneels in the manner of a suppliant to show the order of the Spirits <note>original: "Geniorum"</note>, by which these lower Spirits revere the higher ones as their Presides. Since, however, Ammon (or the Spirit of the Ram) as well as the Moon preside chiefly over the head, it is beautifully shown by this sacred writing how, when the Moon is positioned in Aries <note>The Ram</note>, a Medicine should be prepared from grain and the Water Lily <note>original: "Nenuphar" or "Nymphæa"</note>, so that the head, and indeed the whole body, may be freed from all infirmities; or, having been prepared rightly and according to the laws of sacrifices, the Spirits of both the Sun and the Moon may be attracted to dispel the aforementioned infirmities, as if by a certain lure and sympathetic enticement. Indeed, the Water Lily prepared with the grain-based Medicine, which the figure of the Water Lily itself shows between two ears of grain, should be tak—

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. 381 CHAPTER VI.

<margin>Avicenna</margin> Avicenna <note>original: "Abensina," the Latinized name for the Persian physician Ibn Sina</note> teaches that the supreme medicine for diseases of the head was discovered by the Egyptians, using these words:

> The Egyptian Water Lily is the cabbage of the water; in Egypt it is called "the bride's seed." It induces sleep and soothes headaches caused by heat and bile. Its syrup, prepared with grain, benefits all pains of the head. It is a great medicine, especially for the Egyptians. <note>Translated from the original Arabic and the author's Latin translation provided below it.</note>

*The Water Lily, that is, the Nymphaea, is to the Egyptians an aquatic stalk; it is called in Egypt the "seed of the Bride." It procures sleep and settles headaches caused by hot and choleric matter. Its syrup, prepared with wheat, assists in all pains of the head, and it is a great medicine, especially for the Egyptians.*

<margin>The back part of the vessel.</margin> The back face of the vessel contains these hieroglyphics: A half-naked man carries above his head, with arms outstretched, the image of a Sphinx placed upon an altar. By this they signify the **Solar Intelligence**, the strengthener of the heart, and the rites and ceremonies by which things similar to the Solar Deity ought to be consecrated in the inner shrines. For they believed that in the administration of medicines, the heart, above all other members, must be strengthened; they believed that once the heart was comforted and the spirits fortified, all the malice of diseases could be easily expelled. Indeed, they thought that through ceremonies analogous to the disease, the Solar Sphinx would be infallibly drawn to strengthen the limb committed to its faith. For this reason, as we showed a little earlier, they wore another image of the Sphinx engraved on a gold plate for the same purpose, fixed outwardly to the region of the heart as the sole healer of cardiac diseases.

To ensure that cardiac medicines obtained a greater effect, they carved two <term>Cynocephali</term> <note>Dog-headed baboons, often associated with the god Thoth</note> on the sides, carrying a leaf of the Lotus or Egyptian Water Lily in their hands. They stand upon columns decorated partly with Water Lilies and partly with stalks of wheat. By the Cynocephali, they signify the Moon both after and before its conjunction with the Sun (as the six-day-old Moon placed upon their heads shows), indicating in which phase the medicine ought to be administered. For the Cynocephalus, according to Horus <note>referring to Horapollo, an author on hieroglyphs</note>, is a symbol of the Moon; see a very full treatment of this in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, in the chapter on the Hieroglyphic Writing of the Cynocephalus.

The Water Lily is truly a Lunar herb, possessing the greatest power for drawing out humors both from the head and from all the limbs. They sit upon columns conspicuous with the Water Lily flower, as if the things were committed to their faith; alternating stalks, now marked with an ear of grain, now with a Water Lily flower, surround them in the form of a candelabra. These indicated that a composition of Lunar and Solar species (such as the grain and the Water Lily were) was necessary for the proper temperament of the medicine. This is more than sufficiently taught by the lower rim of the vessel, in which we always see the Water Lily crowded with ears of grain. Furthermore, a small altar seems placed by each one, upon which is set a small vessel with a Water Lily flower and an ear of grain joined into one column; by this, they silently hint at the ceremony to be used both for the vessel and for consecrating the compounded potion. On the rear altar, above the Water Lily flowers extended in the shape of arms, an outstretched hand is seen, by which they hoped the beneficial Deity would be present for them through these kinds of analogous ceremo-

<margin>
The use of the aforementioned vessel in driving away diseases.

Therefore, they would fill this vessel, duly consecrated both by symbols and ceremonies, with a "Lunar-Solar" potion <note>A chemical or alchemical preparation associated with the properties of the Sun and Moon</note> and offer it to the sick person to drink, either when the Sun was joined with the Moon, or at least when the Moon looked upon the Sun in a sextile aspect <note>An astrological position where two planets are 60 degrees apart, considered harmonious</note>. Once this was done, they persuaded themselves that the Divine Powers, infallibly attracted through these Lunar-Solar forms, would restore the patient to their former health. However, the reader should know that hieroglyphics of this kind had different meanings in different orders of the World: for whenever they were engraved on medicinal vessels, they showed what effect they would have in procuring health for a human being. In this same way, they denoted the secrets of worldly things on Obelisks; but on Tablets, such as the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet with Egyptian-style motifs, much studied by Kircher</note>, they signified the mysteries of secret Theology and the archetypal patterns by which the said Divine Powers were attracted to analogous proportions; about which we treat more extensively in Volume III.

May the venerable Isis, mistress of the waters of the Nile and protector of the fields, be present.

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. 383 CHAPTER VI.

<margin><note>original: "Aegyp. Hierog. vafis medicinalis expos."</note> Explanation of the Egyptian Hieroglyphs on a medicinal vessel.</margin>
In the first row, these hieroglyphs are found: a tiller <note>or pole of a carriage</note> with three lines, with a scepter placed above it; there follow these images of two Spirits <note>Genii</note> together with a ram-headed scepter <note>original: "κριοφόρῳ"</note>, that is, marked with the head of a Ram; then two inverted pyramids with a circle between them. By the tiller, they indicate the vehicle by which the Solar Spirits are led through the three lower Worlds as if through moisture, which the images conspicuous for their Hawk-heads indicate, with the help of the Ammonian force signified by the Ram-headed scepter, which grazes both the upper and lower World with its rays, as is noted by the inverted pyramids. Please see the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, book 3.

In the second row, in the first place, is the ram-headed scepter, with two curved staffs, with the head of Horus, a scepter, and a circle in between; there follows an extended hand, with a serpent and a triangle; by which the Ammonian force ruling the East and West, and its influence into the sensible World, provides life to things.

In the third row is a female head, with a bier <note>or coffin</note> placed above, by which the cult of Isis is noted; there follows the Hawk, the symbol of Osiris, with the figure of water; then two scepters with two oblique lines, by which the dominion they possess over the waters is indicated, just as we demonstrated in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*.

In the fourth row is a Nilotic vessel, with the scepter of Momphtha; with two curved scepters and the scepter of Ammon in between, and two squares; by which it is indicated that by the benefit of Momphtha and Ammon, heat and moisture are aptly tempered for the generation of vegetable nature, and by their influence, it is defended from all adverse and unfortunate things; which is aptly signified by the handled cross <note>the Ankh</note> and the Owl. I do not bring forward authorities in this place, since they will be cited from Volume III as their proper place. And indeed, these things ought to be understood according to the physical sense; according to the medical sense, they wish to indicate that the liquid composed of various species enclosed in the vessel is under the power of Ammon, Isis, and Osiris, whence they believed that whoever of the sick drank from it would, by their help, be infallibly freed on account of the sympathetic reasons both of the hieroglyphs and of the species from which the Medicine was composed.

<margin>Interpretation of a medicinal vessel taken from the Museum of Pietro Stefanoni, the figure of which see on the following page.</margin>
Such was the small medicinal urn made of Helite stone <note>likely a reference to a sun-stone or specific Egyptian mineral</note>, which Pietro Stefanoni once kept in his Museum, on the surface of which, fashioned in the shape of a heart, these hieroglyphs are depicted: a winged globe, a human figure in the shape of a hawk <note>original: "ἱερακόμορφος"</note> sitting, the figure of the Sun, which is followed by a pyramid, and this by a Lion's head, which a Hawk receives, with a Lotus flower, and finally a circle with two segments terminates it, as is clear in the following figure. These hieroglyphs indicate nothing other than the chain of Solar things, in which in the first place the winged globe shows the triple-formed Divinity <note>Numen</note>, the hawk-shaped statue with a star placed near it represents the Solar Spirit, the circle represents the Sun itself, the pyramid represents fire, the Lion's head represents the four-footed Solar animal, and the Hawk represents the Solar bird. The Lotus represents the Solar plant; the circle with two segments represents the subterranean Sun, namely gold; and they indicate nothing else but a cardiac <note>heart-related</note>

<image-desc>A tall, ornate ceremonial vessel (poculum) with a lid shaped like the head of a bird, likely an ibis. <margin>The Egyptians and Arabs mark medicinal vessels with hieroglyphic signs.</margin>
It was therefore familiar to the Egyptians to mark medicinal vessels with certain hieroglyphic schemes of the Deities regarding specific diseases; by these, as if drawn by sympathetic forces, they might cure the illnesses they noted. The Arabs received this kind of invention from the Egyptians, and among them nothing is more frequent than these "characteristic" vessels. This can be seen in the museums of Angelomus, Carlo Antonio Magnini, and my own, which contain vials of this sort prepared for medical use. There is, however, this distinction: the Arabs, besides figures of the Scorpion, Serpent, Lion, etc., also add prayers or incantations <note>original: "Ensalmos"</note> taken from the Alcoran <note>The Quran</note> written in Arabic characters. From them, this custom has descended even to our own times, providing various cups marked with superstitious characters against the power of certain diseases. For example, against jaundice <note>original: "icteritiam"</note> they take a cup made of yellow virgin wax, upon which they impress the figure of the *Galgali* bird <note>The Golden Oriole, traditionally associated with curing jaundice due to its yellow color</note>; they assert that as many as drink from it while afflicted by jaundice are soon freed from it.

<margin>Various cups marked with superstitious characters.</margin>
<margin>Paracelsus.</margin>
The superstitious Paracelsus <note>A famous 16th-century Swiss physician and alchemist</note> treats these matters at length in his *Archidoxes*; since these are unworthy of the light of day, I deliberately omit them.

<margin>Medical rings and plates of the Egyptians.</margin>
Furthermore, the Egyptians did not only use the aforementioned vessels, but for the most part, they engraved the said hieroglyphics onto appropriate plates and "potable" rings <note>rings intended to be dipped in liquid or worn for healing</note> against the power of diseases. They wore the plates applied to the neck, chest, head, loins, belly, genitals, and other members according to the location of the ailment; the rings they wore on different fingers corresponding to different diseases.

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC MEDICINE. CHAPTER VI.

...it was not possible to know, since the lid of the small box had, through the long passage of time, become so fused by the intervention of tartar <note>original: "tartari interuentu"; likely referring to mineral encrustation or calcification</note> that it could be opened by no means except by cutting it; nor could its owner be induced by any prayers to open it. But to return to our purpose: the Egyptians revered, above all other Divinities, especially Isis, Osiris, and Horus (or Harpocrates), as <term>Healing Spirits</term> <note>original: "Iatricos Genios"; from the Greek 'iatrikos' meaning medical or healing</note>.

<margin>Gods engraved on various materials against diseases by the Egyptians.</margin>
Hence, they everywhere engraved them upon various materials, such as wood, bone, metal plates, and various precious stones, according to the nature of the diseases. This was done with the utmost rigor, observing the proper time and other astrological circumstances, as the following amulets demonstrate. I find that they also made small boxes <note>original: "capsulas"</note> shaped like the limbs they were intended to protect; one of this kind was shown to me not long ago by the previously praised Captain Torquatus Alexander.

<margin>A Medical Box.</margin>
The box is in the shape of a heart, mimicking the fruit and leaf of the Persea tree <note>The Persea was a sacred Egyptian tree, often identified with the Mimusops laurifolia</note>. In its very center, Harpocrates is seen placed—naked, an infant, urging silence with a finger pressed to his lips. He is depicted with the exact same symbols with which he is elsewhere distinguished, formed right upon the box. Indeed, they believed this to be a most powerful <term>prophylactic</term> <note>a preventative charm or medicine</note> for the heart when worn. We have thought it proper to include the figure here for a better understanding of the matter, so that from this you may see

By what methods and industries the Egyptians were engaged in the cure of diseases. Moreover, Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note> assigns the cause for which the Egyptians so greatly worshiped the three aforementioned Spirits in these words:

<margin>Diodorus.</margin>
<margin>Why the Egyptians so greatly worshiped Isis, Osiris, and Horus.</margin>
> *The Egyptians assert,* he says, *that Isis was the primary discoverer of many medicines for diseases and contributed greatly to the art of medicine; and that, having attained immortality, she delights in the worship of men and is especially concerned with their health. For even in sleep, she openly brings aid to those she deems worthy, both manifesting her Divinity and her benevolence toward those needing cure. They say the proofs of these things are not Greek fables, but certain works; for almost the entire world worships this Goddess on account of her manifest cures of diseases. For they say that in sleep she provides assistance for the diseases of those not in good health, and those who obey her warnings are cured beyond expectation, even those whose safety the Physicians had despaired of. Also, those weak in sight or any other part of the body, by imploring the Divinity of this Goddess, are restored to their former health. They say that by her, too, the remedy for attaining immortality was discovered. Thus, when her son Horus was killed by the Titans and found through the water, she not only restored his life but also made him immortal. This Horus, they say, is interpreted as Apollo, and having been taught the art of healing and divination by his mother Isis, he brought much utility to men both through oracles and cures.*

From these things, it is clear why they worshiped Isis, Horus, and Harpocrates with such intense devotion; since, as has been said, they everywhere wore the images of these deities engraved on various metal plates and gems against the force of diseases. # CLASS X. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY,
# Or the Gold-Making Art of the Egyptians.

---

->TO THE MOST SERENE PRINCE<-

## FERDINAND II

->Grand Duke of Tuscany.<-

->MY MOST MERCIFUL LORD.<-

<image-desc>Historiated ornamental drop cap 'Q' depicting a scholar or alchemist seated at a desk with an open book and various scientific instruments.</image-desc> AS OFTEN as I ponder deeply within myself, Most Serene Prince, the admirable and nearly divine virtues of Your truly Heroic soul, so often do I see that famous *exclamation of Plutarch* <note>original: "Epiphonema"</note> proven true in You:

> Nothing is more brilliant than a ruler who is also wise. <note>original Greek: Μηδὲν λαμπρότερον τοῦ ἄρχοντος ϗ σοφοῦ.</note>

Namely, that nothing is more beautiful, more splendid, or more excellent than a Prince distinguished by the praise of wisdom and wide-ranging learning <note>original Greek: πολυμαθείας (polymatheias)</note>. Indeed, such is the vastness of Your mind and the energy of Your great intellect, that You so flourish and so illuminate the World with it, that I have found no one to place before You—whether one considers Your knowledge of abstruse matters or Your science of things divine and human. Your *Treasury* <note>original: "Gazophylacium"; likely referring to the Medici collections in the Uffizi or Pitti Palace</note> bears witness to this, being by far the best furnished with a variety of everything the mind can conceive. In it, as if in a true *Theater of Art and Nature*, You hold enclosed—to the greatest admiration of visitors—whatever rare and foreign things *India* possesses, whatever unseen things *Asia* offers, whatever monsters *Africa* brings forth, or whatever exotic artistic miracles *Europa* produces, all as if in a certain epitome of the greater World. Therefore, since by the command of the Great *Caesar* <note>Referring to Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III, Kircher's primary patron</note> I have begun to commit the *Oedipus*—the restorer of the hieroglyphic discipline—to the public light; and since among its other subjects the Alchemy of the ancient Egyptians holds no lowly place; I have rightly deemed that it should be inscribed to the glorious honor of Your Name, as to the sole Judge of hidden things. I do this so that a grateful posterity may finally know how much I owe to Your supreme liberality and munificence, from which not only this present Work, but also whatever other offspring of my talent, have at all times drawn such great aid and benefit for the illustration of recondite knowledge. Receive therefore, Most Serene Prince, this argument of abstruse matters, offered to You not with the thought that any increase of science could be added to You who are already knowledgeable in all things; but rather that it may be a proof <note>original Greek: τεκμήριον (tekmerion)</note> of my esteem for Your great mind and of my highest and most sincere goodwill, more lasting than cedar; and so that those things which flowed forth from the immense sea of Your treasures may be restored to the same by right of return. Farewell, Great Duke, the Ideal of Princes, and the eternal glory of men of letters, and look with favor, as is Your custom, upon my writings.

# CLASS X.
## Hieroglyphic Alchemy, or the Gold-bearing Art of the Egyptians.
->P R E F A C E.<-

<image-desc>A decorative square woodcut initial 'M' featuring a floral landscape with a bird, possibly a crane, standing amidst foliage.</image-desc>
The reader will perhaps wonder that I have undertaken this subject in this place, removed so far beyond the limits of my original plan; nor will there perhaps be lacking some <term>Aristarchus</term><note>A reference to Aristarchus of Samothrace, a rigorous critic; here meaning a harsh or pedantic critic.</note> who might pierce me with an <term>obelisk</term><note>A critical mark used by ancient grammarians to indicate spurious or doubtful passages.</note>, because I set out to treat an art that is to many hateful, sophisticated, deceptive, and "selling smoke"—in a word, full of risk—yet to not a few the very pinnacle of divine and human wisdom, filled with the happiness of all good things.

<margin>Why the Author treats Alchemy, and in what manner.</margin>
Let him know, however, that the logic of the proposed argument has claimed this for itself by a certain right, so that in acting the part of <term>Oedipus</term><note>The mythical riddle-solver; Kircher uses this as his persona for decoding Egyptian mysteries.</note>, whose proper role is to loosen the hidden knots of abstruse things, I might—according to my small measure—unroll from its darkness this art, which was presented to the mind of the Egyptians through various coverings of hieroglyphics. I do this not because I approve of it, or because I believe any utility or profit can be drawn from it regarding the part that insists on the making of gold; but so that I might bring into the light, through a faithful and sincere exposition, that which venerable antiquity believed should be consigned to posterity by so many symbols and symbolic marks; leaving full liberty to everyone to hold, believe, and judge what he wishes. Certainly, among those arts and sciences which human curiosity so studiously pursues and so ardently desires, I have found none harassed by sharper lashes, yet none more stubbornly defended.

<margin>How ardently Alchemy is cultivated by many.</margin>
And no wonder; for "to what do you not drive mortal hearts, O cursed hunger for gold?" <note>original: "quò enim non auri sacra fames mortalia pectora cogis?" — A famous quote from Virgil's Aeneid.</note> There are those who, while they have consumed their entire age, life, and substance in this smoky business without any fruit or utility, <margin>It is condemned by others.</margin> driven headlong into desperation, do not hesitate to provoke with insults and slanders not only the art itself, but even Nature herself, as if she were spiteful with a stepmother's hatred. Others, through ignorance of natural things, or by a distorted judgment, or stimulated by other private <margin>It is commended by others.</margin> passions, do not understand what they are carping at and attacking while they rise up too high. Finally, there are those who, in vast volumes, extol the excellence and divinity of the art to the heavens with innumerable praises of words; and as is the custom of impostors, they so veil their own ignorance with exotic characters, symbols, and pronouncements—or more truly with a certain fox-like cunning—that by the very fact of what they themselves do not know, they show they wish others not to know. Lest they be accused of the fraud they have imposed, they use I know not what pompous words and affected <margin>And to what end.</margin> "bottles" of exotic names, being more prideful than a <term>Sophoclean buskin</term><note>A high-heeled boot worn by ancient tragic actors; a metaphor for a grand, tragic, or overly-inflated style.</note>, and they more truly sweep out an <term>Augean stable</term><note>A reference to the Herculean labor; here meaning a task involving a massive amount of filth or confusion.</note> of a common art that is dreadfully confused and filled with intolerable filth. <margin>Especially by those ignorant of philosophy.</margin> They are compelled by this sole intention: lest they prove to posterity that they were ignorant of that which they see held in such high esteem among men and in such great value among Kings and Princes; which is the characteristic of the Alchemists of this time. And although Chemical Philosophy, enclosed in the innermost shrines of nature, has fixed roots, I find it so arranged that there has never been any art which a greater number of the most ignorant men—

# CLASS X. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY. CHAPTER I.

<margin>Alchemy held in honor and value among the Egyptians.</margin>
...a multitude of the most vile and filthy men has rushed in, taking it up to be handled with "unwashed hands," as the saying goes <note>original: "illotis manibus"; a proverb meaning to approach a sacred subject without proper preparation or reverence</note>. Since these men are destitute of all scientific equipment, and possess no natural talent for rightly perceiving the innermost principles of nature, they are nevertheless of such great and shameless audacity that they do not blush to treat, teach, and prescribe laws for a science that is impassable even to the sharpest Philosophers due to the hidden recesses of nature. O, foolish little philosophers! Truly worthy to be sent away, not to a Chemistry lab, but to the "clanking-shackle" workshop of Plautus <note>original: "ferricrepinam Plauti officinam"; a reference to the Roman playwright Plautus, implying a place where slaves were punished with chains—a pun on "ferrum" (iron) and the noise of the forge</note>. Greater honor was held for this secret science by the Egyptians, who—excepting Kings, Priests, and Philosophers endowed with the highest and sharpest intellect—considered it a crime expiable only by death for any other man to be skilled in it. Hence, not without reason, they veiled the same with so many and such abstruse marks of symbols, lest it happen to be turned to the abuse of plebeian ignorance, to the notable prejudice, indeed the ruin, of the Kingdom. Therefore, I have decided to explain this now in this Class, so that the curious Reader may understand what it was, in what it chiefly consisted, and what benefits it brought to the Kingdom, beginning the account from the very origin of the whole business.

## CHAPTER I.

### On the Origin of the Alchemy of the Egyptians.

<margin>Names, definition, and origin of Alchemy.</margin>
ALCHEMY—which the Egyptians call <gloss>Hermetic Wisdom</gloss> <note>original Greek: "σοφία ἡερμηϰή"</note>, the Greeks call <gloss>gold-making</gloss> <note>original Greek: "χρυσοποιΐαν"</note>, the Arabs call <gloss>the universal science</gloss> <note>original Arabic: "لحكمة الكلية" (al-hikma al-kulliya)</note>, and others call by other names—is nothing other than the art of making gold. Various men dispute its origin in various ways. There are those who wish Alchemy to be so named from *Alchimus*, its first inventor, or from the Greek words for "pouring" and "metals" <note>original: "χύω & μέταλλα"</note>. Others make Hermes Trismegistus its inventor, as do the Egyptians and their followers, the Arabs. Certainly, the unanimous consensus of all Philosophers testifies that it is a most ancient art. Nevertheless, it falls to us to demonstrate from whence it had its primordial origin.

<margin>The primeval Patriarchs possessed knowledge of all sciences.</margin>
I suppose, therefore, first: that the primeval Patriarchs before the flood—distinguished by the science of all natural things infused into them by God from Adam—were most skilled in the philosophy of metals, so necessary to the human race, just as they were in the rest of the arts. Nearly all commentators on the sacred book of Genesis agree on this. And indeed, that gold was known at that time is shown from the second chapter of Genesis, where in verse 12 it is held thus: > The name of the one (namely, of the four rivers) is Pishon; it is that which circles the entire land of Havilah, where gold is born; and the gold of that land is the best. Indeed, mention is made of the remaining metals in the third chapter <insert>actually the fourth</insert> of the same, verse 22: <margin>The metallic art is most ancient, before the flood.</margin> Zillah also bore Tubal-cain, who was a hammerer and smith in every work of brass and iron. From these things it is clear that the metallic art was cultivated immediately from the first cradles of the rising World by the sons of Adam—as being that without whose help they would be destitute of every aid for rightly administering life—nor should there be any doubt to him who considers the very long life of the first men,

# CHAPTER: THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS, HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Handed down by later tradition.</margin>
If one considers more deeply a life administered under such a great instructor as *Adam* was, there is no doubt that they possessed an exact knowledge of the nature of individual metals. It is also certain that they held a singular skill in smelting, dissolving, purifying, alloying, hardening, and polishing metals. For what could not be accomplished in such a long course of age and life, when continuous and lengthy experience of things was joined to the theory handed down concerning them? See what we have deduced at length concerning the science of *Adam* in Class I. And lest the metallic art, so necessary to the human race, be given over to oblivion, it will be evident to anyone that it was propagated by tradition all the way to *Noah*. We have shown from various authors in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>A reference to Kircher's own work on the Roman obelisk in the Piazza Navona</note> how *Ham* <note>original: "Cham"</note> had inscribed the inventions of arts and sciences upon metallic plates before the flood, and took them with him into the ark so that what had been prepared with such great zeal might not perish in the imminent deluge, but be propagated to posterity. To this also pertains what we cited above in the Architecture of the Egyptians regarding the immense gold works of the first Kings, based on the accounts of the Arabs.

<margin>And after the flood, it was excellently cultivated by the first men.</margin>
<margin>Diodorus;</margin>
<margin>Semiramis erected three huge statues.</margin>
I suppose, secondly, that after the flood this metallic art was most highly cultivated; and this is more than sufficiently demonstrated by the most proud works, both of the *Tower of Babylon* and the monuments of *Semiramis*, which are to be admired by all past ages, and which certainly could not have been made without an exact knowledge of the metallic art. For as *Diodorus* <note>Diodorus Siculus, a Greek historian</note> relates: *Semiramis* erected three huge golden statues of *Jupiter, Juno, and Ops* <note>original: "Iovis, Iunonis, Opisque"</note> at the top of the temple; that of *Jupiter* still stands at a length of 40 feet, weighing a thousand *Babylonian* talents. *Ops* sits in a golden chair of similar weight, at whose knees stand two lions, and nearby are silver serpents of immense magnitude, each weighing thirty talents. The statue of the standing *Juno* weighs 800 talents. Common to all these was a handcrafted golden table, 40 feet in length and twelve in width, weighing 50 talents. There were besides two drinking vessels <term>Carchesia: high-handled Greek drinking cups</term> of 30 talents, and as many censers, each of 30 talents. There were three mixing bowls <term>Crateres: large vessels used for mixing wine and water</term> made of gold, of which the one dedicated to *Jupiter* weighed 1200 talents, and each of the others 600; all of which the *Kings of the Persians* later plundered. Furthermore, how much iron, bronze, and lead shall we estimate was spent on the immense and nearly innumerable armies of men?

<margin>The abundance of arms and the number of armed men under Ninus.</margin>
For as *Ctesias* mentions in *Diodorus* Book 2, Chapter 2, *Ninus* led against the *Bactrians* an army of one million seven hundred thousand infantry, 200,000 cavalry, and 10,600 scythed chariots. To pass over for a moment the huge abundance of arms necessary to equip such a multitude: for it is likely they fought not just with clubs and stones, but each with swords, spears, and bows. Certainly, the sacred scriptures testify above all that *Abraham*, a contemporary of that same age, was wealthy in the possession of gold and silver.

<margin>Exodus chapter 37.</margin>
The expenditure of gold, as held in *Exodus* 37, offered for the construction of the tabernacle, was 29 talents and 730 shekels <note>original: "Siclorum"</note>, which make 131,595 pounds of gold.

The expenditure of silver for the same work was 100 talents and 1,775 shekels, which make 37,722 pounds.

The contribution of the Princes toward the structure of the same temple was 5,000 talents and 10,000 <term>adarconim <note>A Hebrew term for darics, ancient Persian gold coins.</note></term>, which makes 22,507,500 pounds; furthermore, 10,000 talents of silver, which makes 3,750,000 pounds. All these riches of Solomon, cast into one sum, total 873,358,500 pounds—that is, eight hundred seventy-three million, three hundred fifty-eight thousand, and five hundred pounds. This sum is certainly so great that it might rightly seem a <term>paradox <note>In this context, an unbelievable or contradictory statement.</note></term> to anyone, and would exceed all belief, were it not for the testimony of the Sacred Scriptures. And certainly, if we were speaking of the "greater talent" of 125 pounds, which the Hebrews call a <term>Kikar <note>The Hebrew word for a talent-weight.</note></term>, it seems impossible to say, since the total sum of gold, if melted into one mass, could equal the temple itself or even an entire mountain. Certainly, the Sacred History reports that there was no counting of gold and silver in the days of Solomon, and that silver was as common as stones.

<margin>The huge abundance of gold in the time of Solomon from the Chemical Art.</margin>
<margin>Solomon is believed to have had perfect knowledge of the gold-bearing art.</margin>
These things being established, it is asked from where such a great abundance of gold and silver, and such a quantity of copper, lead, and iron originated. Certainly, it is clear from the Sacred Scriptures that Solomon did not "make" it <note>i.e., create it from nothing or solely by alchemy</note>, since such a sum was gathered partly from Ophir and Tarshish, partly from the contributions of Kings and Governors, and finally partly from taxes and Solomon's own industry. I truly believe that at that time, there flourished an art—perhaps unknown to our own times—for extracting gold, silver, and other metals from all parts of the earth with the greatest ease. I believe this knowledge was left to those ages by a kind of successive tradition and was refined both by others and especially by the wisdom of Solomon. The Rabbis, commenting on this passage, report that he perfectly knew all the veins of gold and silver and the hidden gold and silver mixtures in all parts of the earth, even in the vilest sand—a claim supported by many conjectures. But we shall speak of these things more extensively in what follows; now let us return to the goal we proposed at the beginning.

# CHAPTER I. 392 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>
Ammianus.
A vast quantity of gold was found in Egypt after it was conquered by the Persians.
Diodorus.
The annual revenues of King Simendis.
A golden circle in the monument of Simendis;
The riches of the Egyptians surpassed the wealth of all other Kings.
Pliny.
</margin>

In the city of Thebes, there was such a great supply and abundance of gold and silver that after the fire which Cambyses <note>The Persian King who conquered Egypt in 525 BCE.</note> set to that city—memorable throughout all ages—the total amount of gold that had melted and flowed away, collected by the Persians, was (according to the testimony of Diodorus) 300 talents; and of silver, 2,300 talents. This amounts to 37,000 pounds in gold and 287,500 pounds in silver. In the excavation of Lake Moeris, an innumerable force of gold is said to have been spent, so that according to Diodorus, the tax from the fish alone reached 365 talents of gold in annual revenue. The annual revenue in gold paid to King Simendis <note>Likely referring to Smendes or a Hellenized name for a Pharaoh mentioned by Diodorus Siculus.</note>, as Diodorus testifies, was one hundred and thirty-one thousand, one hundred million, and additionally two hundred million <note>original: "Minæ centies trigesies semel millies millena millena, & insuper ducenties millena millia"</note>, or 131,200,000,000; and it is maintained that this was written on his monument. A golden circle surrounded this monument, with a circumference of 365 cubits, so that each individual degree consisted of a golden cubit. Since a cube cast from pure gold and measured cubically weighs at least 10,000 gold pieces, it is clear that the whole circle amounted to 3,650,000—three million, six hundred and fifty thousand gold pieces. I shall say nothing here of the other sumptuous monuments which we have treated above in the *Architecture of the Egyptians*, which are read to have been constructed with an innumerable supply of gold and silver. Nothing of the armies of Sesostris <note>A legendary king of Egypt said to have conquered the world.</note> numbering three hundred thousand men; nothing of the expenses paid for the erection of Obelisks and Statues; for from what has been said, the immense riches of the Kings of Egypt are more than sufficiently evident, which seem to have far exceeded all the treasures of Emperors, Kings, and the most powerful Princes. Thus, not without cause, Pliny, while recording the structures of these most proud masses, says they were an idle and foolish display of money.

<margin>
The Egyptians extracted gold from all things.
The Alexandrian Chronicle
</margin>

Since, therefore, there existed such a great supply of gold and silver in Egypt as we have described, someone might rightly wonder from where they acquired such a great force of money, especially since Egypt is not celebrated as being particularly filled with gold mines. To satisfy this doubt, I begin the matter "from the egg" <note>A Latin idiom meaning "from the very beginning."</note>. It is certain that the Egyptians, taught by Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary father of alchemy and Egyptian wisdom.</note>, possessed the art of extracting gold from all earthly things. The *Alexandrian Chronicle* clearly teaches that the said Trismegistus, instructed by the "Janigenae" <note>Literally "descendants of Janus," referring to early inhabitants of Italy in Kircher's historical framework.</note> with whom he was contemporary, propagated this art to posterity. For it says that Mercury <note>Identified here with Hermes/Trismegistus.</note>, having been taught by King Picus Jove of the Janigenae in Italy, discovered the method of detecting gold ores and smelting gold; then, having set out for Egypt to join Mizraim <note>The biblical progenitor of the Egyptians.</note>, he practiced philosophy clothed in a golden cloak and taught the Egyptians the art he had discovered. Because of this benefit, he was held in the admiration of all, called Mercury, and attained the title of the Golden Deity. Contemplate the text of the Chronicle placed at length in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, folio 105. It is so certain that the first men possessed a certain gold-bearing art—entrusted to no one except Kings and heads of families, and handed down not in writing but by word of mouth—whether it consisted in extracting gold from all things or in transmuting other metals one into another, that no one can doubt it unless they are ignorant of all history. However, it was suppressed with the greatest silence by its possessors with the intent <unclear>lest</unclear>

# CLASS X. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY. 393 CHAPTER II.

<margin>The gold-making art was known only to the Kings and heads of families among the Egyptians.</margin>
...lest the more secret storehouses of nature, if opened to the ignorant masses, should lead to the loud-cried destruction of the Republic and deservedly bring ultimate ruin upon the kingdom. For this reason, the most ingenious Mercury <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage</note>, foreseeing such great damages, veiled the more divine portion of philosophy concerning God, Angels, and the World in the most hidden symbols so they would not be open to common use. Likewise, he concealed this gold-making art <note>original: "artem auriferam," referring to alchemy</note>—which is deservedly considered the most secret and divine among those sciences that contemplate the economy of the sublunary and subterranean world—by wrapping it in the same obscurities of hieroglyphic signs, far removed from the reading of the profane. What truly this art was, and with which hieroglyphics it was adorned, time and order now demand that we reveal.

## CHAPTER II.

### Concerning the hieroglyphics by which the gold-making art was presented by Trismegistus.

<margin>Trismegistus, the Author of the hieroglyphics.</margin>
Mercurius Trismegistus, the Author of all hidden learning, when he had penetrated with the highest subtlety of genius whatever secrets shine forth in the majesty of nature, undertook that ingenious architecture of hieroglyphics so that such great sacraments in the recesses of the world would not be encountered by just anyone. By this means, he hid individual mysteries of great importance under certain symbols devised in the likeness of "all-forming" nature <note>original: "pantamorphæ naturæ"</note>, yet in such a way that they were not left impassable to those whom he judged worthy and similar to himself in the perspicacity of their genius. Hence, he communicated the secrets of his mind expressed through said symbols to the Priests, Philosophers, and Prophets elected for this purpose (who were the only hope for the throne of the Kingdom), lest such great benefits of discovered things perish along with him; and he took care to have them carved into stone against every injury of time. Since, truly, the knowledge of such great things could not be expressed in few words, he devised with subtle investigation certain Ideal symbols which held a certain analogy embracing many things—of which kind are the hieroglyphics—by which all those things that could not be described without many discourses might be made clear by the single and mystical concept of one symbol.

<margin>Trismegistus distinguished a fourfold World.</margin>
Therefore, since he perceived all things to lie hidden in all things under a certain fixed analogy—indeed, seeing that higher things are contained in lower, and these in the higher and middle things by a certain wonderful reason—he distinguished a fourfold World: the Archetypal, the Genial <note>the world of spirits or intelligences</note>, the Sidereal <note>the world of stars and planets</note>, and the Elementary. This was amply demonstrated above in the *System of the World* and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>references to Kircher's other published works</note>. In these, he arranged the orders of things and the grades of beings with such genius that no being of the lower world exists which does not have its consonant and proportioned being in both the Sidereal and Genial worlds, according to the intended analogy; which things in the Archetypal world are distinct by a certain ideal analogy according to our way of conceiving, yet in reality [are one].

<summary>This page explains that Hermes Trismegistus created hieroglyphics to hide the secrets of alchemy and philosophy from the unworthy. It introduces his "fourfold world" theory, which links the earthly realm to the celestial and divine through symbolic analogies.</summary>

# CHAPTER III. 394 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>
The origin of the worldly chains.
</margin>
...nevertheless, they are considered under the reasoning of a single, simple divine essence. And from this, those chains which the Egyptians call *seiras* <note>original: "σειρὰς" - meaning cords or strings of connection</note>, about which we spoke in the preceding Class, found their origin. The higher World has its Sun, Moon, and other Planets, to which just as many presiding Spirits <note>term: Genii - guardian spirits or governing intelligences</note> from the higher World of Intelligences are assigned; the lower World has these things as well. Thus, since in the Starry World nothing more excellent, more outstanding, or more divine than the Sun could be found, and in the mixture of the lower elemental World nothing more beautiful, effective, or excellent than gold was known, they called the latter the Sun of the lower World on account of its powers being analogous to the Sun.

<margin>
Gold is the terrestrial Sun.
</margin>
In this way, seeing that the Moon was closest to the Sun in excellence, they willed that the silver of the lower World be the Moon; and so for the rest of the Planets, connecting each one proportionally <note>original: "ἀναλόγως"</note> to the individual corresponding metals of the lower World. From this it came to pass that through the symbol of the Sun, for example, a fourfold sense was displayed; or rather, that the secrets of the Archetypal, Spirit-led, Starry, and Metallic or Elemental Sun were considered as one thing under a fourfold analogy. Thus, whatever mysteries of the divinity of the supreme Deity were handed down, the same could be understood in their own way regarding the mysteries of the Spirit World, the Starry World, and the Elemental World. Truly, since they knew nothing in all of nature more wonderful than metallic operations, they displayed this art under the same mysteries as the sacraments of the supreme Deity and the other Worlds; the Greeks later followed them in all things and hid the nature of things in not dissimilar enigmas, as we shall see shortly. Now, we must speak of the manner in which they displayed this gold-bearing art in their hieroglyphics.

---

### CHAPTER III.

->Concerning the hieroglyphic symbols by which Chemical secrets are expressed, represented under the history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon.<-

<margin>
The Chemical world under the history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon among the Egyptians.
</margin>
It is evident from many arguments in this *Oedipus*—most especially from the *Egyptian Mystagogy* of the Pamphilian Obelisk—that the history of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon involved various meanings. There, we explained this history not only according to the historical sense, but also the physical, medical, tropological <note>interpretive: moral or figurative</note>, anagogical <note>interpretive: spiritual or mystical</note>, and allegorical; and in the second Treatise of this work, according to the political sense. It remains now for us to show how the Egyptians indicated the Chemical World by that history, always preserving the same tenor of analogy.

Just as the Egyptians indicated through Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon the labors of the Sun and Moon in this worldly house through various struggles of nature; so also they indicated analogically the most excellent effect of all to be produced through the various and diverse operations of the subterranean Sun and Moon—which (as many falsely believe) is the end of human happiness. For considering the art which they cultivated with such zeal, they saw that its object, form, efficient cause, and effects had a certain community with the principal parts of the World: namely with the Sun, Moon, fire, air, water,

For in the subject of this art they considered two things, one of which holds the role of the male, the other of the female; and therefore they called the former Osiris or the Sun, and the latter Isis or the Moon. Mercury, who is joined to the Sun and Moon, they called common to both; since no conjunction of the Sun and Moon occurs in the Greater World <note>the Macrocosm/Universe</note> unless Mercury, the satellite of the Sun, is present.
<margin>Plutarch</margin>
Indeed, Osiris and Isis are not only spouses, but also brother and sister, as Plutarch testifies, held under a certain mystical reasoning; to these is added a certain third, Typhon, a black and burning spirit, who cuts his uterine brother Osiris into tiny pieces. To these they add Vulcan, or external fire; Pallas, or the Wisdom of working; the Ocean or Mother Tethys, or in place of both, the Nile—that is, water and earth, the mother of all things, who according to Orpheus bestows riches—along with the remaining types of metals and minerals, which they signified through Saturn, Jupiter, Venus, Apollo, and Pluto, as can be seen in the writings of Diodorus.
<margin>Diodorus. Vulcan in the Chemical art.</margin>
Who is this Vulcan? Is he not the Fire, the Master of the works? Who is Mercury? Furthermore, just as Vulcan is said to have been the first to reign in Egypt, so Mercury was held to be the inventor of letters and arts: for in the Hermetic art <term>Hermetic art: Alchemy, named after Hermes Trismegistus</term> nothing can be rightly accomplished without a universal knowledge of the arts; for Hermes is the interpreter of all, whose counsel Osiris uses most frequently, and without whom nothing happens. Truly, the reason is obvious why Isis fashioned everything from gold—indeed, entire temples for her parent and the rest of the Gods—or why she held the smiths of copper and gold in such high honor; for she is the golden Goddess, and for that reason was called the "Golden Venus" by all of Asia. For she is said to be both sister and spouse of Osiris, just as Juno is to Jupiter, and Rhea to Saturn, their progenitors. If anyone truly possesses any knowledge of the art in question, they will admit by this allegorical art that Osiris and Isis are nothing other than the **agent** and the **patient** <note>the active and passive forces</note> in a single subject. Indeed, by the "expedition of Osiris" is denoted the most secret **solution** of the work, where one first arrives at the "black Ethiopians" and afterwards at the "Red Sea"—colors which must necessarily intervene first and last, passing through intermediate colors into whiteness, and afterwards into redness.

<margin>The parallelism of the Egyptian and Greek minor deities in the chemical art.</margin>
So that the story of Osiris, Isis, Horus, and Typhon harmonizes entirely with the fabulous narration of the Greeks, which they devise concerning Jupiter, Juno, Alcmena, Hercules, Amphitryon, and others. For if we apply these to our purpose, Alcmena or Isis is nothing other than the *metallic earth*, which is joined to Osiris or Amphitryon in a conjugal bond. Jupiter, captured by love for Alcmena, through deceits and crafts prepared for this, represents a certain proper and peculiar species of metal which, by the industry of the Hermetic art, is insinuated and mixed into the borders of Isis or Alcmena (that is, the metallic earth). While they enjoy their desired embraces, Mercury or quicksilver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note>, who is the *servant of the Philosophers*, plays the part of Sosia <note>A character from the myth of Amphitryon who is impersonated by Mercury</note>—that is, he dissolves the radical moisture of the gold. As Jupiter enters into Alcmena, the metallic earth swells, pregnant with a copious metallic moisture, which at the time of birth, by the lightest distillation, drips into a most white water, highly smoky and airy, which is decorated with the name of Hercules because of its signal and most powerful virtues and energies. Indeed, what else is indicated when twin serpents are thrust upon Hercules by Juno while he is still crying in his cradle to be killed, if not the two metallic salts, which are called the Sun and the Moon <note>Gold and Silver</note>, or brother and sister, which are crushed and killed by the efficacy of the said Herculean water? What do they indicate here by the adult Hercules, if not the Mercury of the Philosophers? This Mercury, after its legitimate preparation, is supported by a remarkable and wondrous strength to overcome the raw and as-yet undigested metallic seed. This seed is not incongruously represented by the snakes sprouting back with formidable heads, arising in almost infinite ways. In the Lernean marsh—that is, in the Chemical water prepared by singular art, which is enclosed in a round glass vial like a kind of swamp—it raises its poison. This is the metallic seed, called the Chemical Hydra, arising from the water, exerting itself through a variety of colors as if they were a brood of heads. These can never be killed unless we cut them away with continuous fire and iron—that is, Mars <note>The alchemical term for Iron</note>—and in this way restrain the variety emerging and sprouting from the rawness of the Mercury. This continues until, having cast off its false colors, it is reduced into a single, perfect, and final red color that is permeating and stable. Unless this Hydra is killed and the Typhonian force cut away, no one can hope to preserve Horus from destruction; that is, no one should think they will reach the desired goal in the Chemical business. ## CHAPTER IV.

->*Concerning the Hermetic Cross, which we frequently call the Handled Cross in this work, and its secret significance in the Hermetic Work.*<-

<margin>The Hermetic Cross, the Handled Cross of Isis, and why it is so named.</margin>
<margin>Marsilio Ficino on the handled cross.</margin>
Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the invention of writing and magic.</note>, being either the first inventor of letters or the restorer of those already invented, was likewise the founder of Hieroglyphic characters. In order to express the most hidden things lurking in the world through a wonderfully devised symbol, he expressed everything in a single character, which they call the Hermetic Cross. (We call it the Isiac or "Handled" Cross <note>The Ankh</note>, because it is seen carried in the hand in almost all Egyptian images). They held this character in such great veneration that they believed nothing could be rightly accomplished without it. It was a most powerful amulet, a character fashioned with marvelous subtlety of intellect according to the pattern of nature, and the sole guide and light for demonstrating the way to happiness. Marsilio Ficino <note>A famous Italian Renaissance philosopher.</note> describes its power excellently in his book *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* <note>original: "De vita coelitus propaganda"</note> in these words:

> *The ancient Egyptians, as we read in a certain College of the Arabs, placed the figure of the Cross before all others. Through this figure, bodies act by a Power already spread to the surface; for the first surface is described by a Cross, as it possesses primarily length and breadth. This is the first figure, the straightest of all, and contains four right angles. Indeed, the effects of the celestial bodies result chiefly through the straightness of rays and angles; for the Stars are greatly powerful when they hold the four angles of the Heaven—namely the hinges <note>The "cardinal points" of an astrological chart.</note> of the East, the West, and the Midheaven on both sides. When arranged thus, they cast their rays into one another in such a way that they constitute a Cross. Therefore, the Ancients said the Cross was a figure formed from the strength of the stars and a receptacle for that same strength, and they signified all the secrets of the world through it.*

However, since I have demonstrated all these things most fully in Book 2 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>Kircher's own 1650 work on the Obelisk in Rome.</note> concerning the Handled Cross, I have judged it superfluous to repeat them in this place. Therefore, we refer the reader there. It is our task here to explain what mysterious secrets of the Great Art the said Cross indicates; this will be done opportunely once we have first shown the structure of the entire Hermetic or Mercurial character.

# CHAPTER IV. 400 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>
The structure of the Hermetic Cross.
</margin>
It must be understood, therefore, that Hermes <note>Referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage to whom the Egyptians attributed their sacred knowledge</note>, when he observed the profound connection of the celestial bodies—and indeed how all things lie hidden within all things in a certain manner—established a twofold Astronomy: the celestial and the elemental. In the celestial, he considered the order, connection, properties, and influences; in the elemental, he considered all these same things, but in their own specific way. Thus, he contemplated that there is nothing in the lower world of the elemental mixture which could not be found, through a certain analogical comparison, in the celestial world.

<margin>
The analogy of the lower world with the superior.
</margin>
There are in the superior world the signs of the Zodiac and the seven Planets, along with their presiding Spirits <note>original: "Genijs"</note>; these same things exist in the lower world, as has been demonstrated copiously in various places throughout this work. Therefore, when he had considered these things, he devised a hieroglyphic character, which he called after himself the Hermetic, Tautic <note>derived from Thoth, the Egyptian god of wisdom</note>, or Mercurial character, in which he encompassed the secrets of both Astrologies by a certain mystical reasoning and marvelous artistry. And although in hieroglyphics this character is presented with a somewhat simpler skill <note>original: "rudiori Minerva," a Latin idiom for a plain or unrefined approach</note>, it nevertheless possesses its own hidden proportions, by which the innermost actions of the World-Spirit are expressed. But let me show its structure.

<note>The following diagram illustrates the geometric construction of an Ankh-like cross, used here as a universal symbol of the "World-Spirit."</note>

[A technical diagram illustrating the geometrical construction of a Hermetic cross (a variant of the Ankh). A vertical axis labeled A-B is divided into nine equal segments, numbered 2 through 9 starting from the bottom point A. A circle labeled P-M-N is centered at point I (level 6). A horizontal line C-D intersects the axis at point E (level 4). At the top point B, an upward-curving arc X-B-Z is drawn. At the bottom point A, two downward-curving loops, R-V-A and A-H-G, are centered on points S and T respectively. Points Y and H are also indicated within the arcs.]

Let a straight line A-B be drawn on any plane, which you shall distribute into nine equal parts, in much the same way the Egyptians divided the expanse of the Starry World. This being done, count three parts out of the nine upward from the bottom at A to point E; through this point, draw the line D-C, intersecting line A-B at right angles. This line should occupy two parts out of nine on each side, such as the lines E-D and E-C. Again, from point E, count three parts out of nine upward to point I; there place the compass, and with a span of two parts (of which the whole line A-B has nine), let the circle P-M-N be described. This also being done, let the compass be placed again at the endpoint B, and with a span of two parts, let the semicircle X-Y-Z be described. With the semicircle described, let a line R-G be drawn from the other endpoint A, four parts out of nine in length, so that two parts exist on either side; and with the compass placed at points S and T, with the span T-A and S-A, let the semicircles R-V-A and A-H-G be described on both sides. You will then have the Hermetic character described according to its proper proportion, and agreeing in every way with the body of worldly symmetry. Nothing further remains except that we now explain its mysteries step by step; which we shall indeed perform part by part.

# CLASS X. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY. 401 CHAPTER IV.

->*Interpretation of the Hermetic Character.*<-

<margin>The mysteries and interpretation of the Cross or Hermetic character.</margin>
First, therefore, Hermes <note>original: "Mercurius"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary founder of alchemy</note>, considering the structure of the world-machine more deeply, and seeing that it was composed of straight and cyclic lines, decided that his own character should be prepared with a similar mixture of lines, so that this hieroglyphic monad <note>term: monad; a single, indivisible unit representing the unity of all things</note> might correspond to the great cosmic monad in exact proportion. For just as the first and simplest production and representation of all things was brought to light through the straight line and the circle; so also in this "sharply-variegated" <note>original: "ὀξυποικιλόγραμμῳ" (oxypoikilogrammō)</note> characterization, the order and series of all things is displayed. In this, the central point represents the Earth, around which both the Sun and the Moon, as well as the rest of the Planets, complete their courses. The Sun was represented by the Egyptians through the hieroglyphic of a circle, while the Moon was represented by a segment of the same, as is evident in the figure. For as we have said elsewhere, they connected the Moon to the Sun, not only because of the proximity and position it holds in the worldly system relative to the Sun, but also because of the excellence of these luminaries. The Sun acts as the active principle, while the Moon acts as the passive principle; they perform the office of male and female in this economy of the World, from whose congress and most fruitful influence the entire nature of the lower World is nourished and preserved. Furthermore, what the Sun and Moon do in the Starry World, the Sun and Moon—that is, gold and silver—perform the same in the Elementary or terrestrial World. Rightly, therefore, in this characterization, they are seen to nourish themselves by the union of a mutual bond.

Furthermore, while our Hermes saw that all actions and influences of the Stars emanate into the lower regions only by the straight diffusion of rays; and moreover, that elements moved out of their natural places perform their returns to them, led by nature, through straight lines; he rightly placed a rectilinear cross beneath the Sun and Moon, so that he might more clearly express the actions of the Elementary World, animated and impregnated by the starry rays. For just as a line arises from the flow of a point, a surface from the flow of a line, and a body from the flow of a surface; so it happens entirely in the economy of both the superior and inferior World, and indeed even in the Chemical World. In this process, while the elementary lines in the Chemical business are produced from the "star" <note>likely referring to the 'regulus' or a specific crystalline starting point</note> as if by the continuous course or flow of a physical point, and light things are mixed with heavy things, a cross necessarily emerges. One straight line of this cross, descending downwards, represents the simply heavy and light; while the line cutting the perpendicular line at a right angle appropriately designates bodies mixed from heavy and light elements. The followers of Hermes demonstrate all these things clearly when they dissolve a body enclosed in a vessel, by the power of heat, into the four primary natures in a wonderful manner according to what has been said, with a most exact separation made into their lines; so that finally, through the circular perimeters of those same lines, a conjunction may occur in the Solar completion.
