<margin>A word-puzzle concerning the Elixir, and its explanation.</margin>
which they speak in the manner of a word-puzzle <note>original: "Logogriphus"</note> thus: "The matter of our stone, *Xir*, in its preparation becomes *Ixir*, and when fermented it becomes *Elixir*"; which I explain in this way. *Xir* is said to be any medicine that binds Mercury prepared chemically, when cast upon it. Therefore, first extract the oil from the earth, and dissolve in it the dissolving and coagulating Medicine—that is, the earth—and sublimate it again through the alembic; calcine <note>Reduce to powder by heat</note> the sublimated material, and the expressed calcination remains; dissolve, distill, coagulate, and coat it with its own oil, and cast it upon the fermented Mercury called *Xir*; and it becomes *Ixir*, fit for making the *Elixir*. From these things it is clearly evident that the Sages expressed the work of the art through various metaphors and similarities, in which, however, they looked toward exactly the same thing. But let these things said briefly concerning the theory and practice of the Great Art suffice; concerning all of which, God willing, more copious material for discussion will be given in *The Subterranean World* <note>A reference to Kircher’s famous work *Mundus Subterraneus*</note>. That the Egyptians knew the gold-bearing art <note>Alchemy or gold-making</note> more than other mortals is so certain that whoever dares to deny it would deservedly seem to contradict the account of all historians. Yet what kind of art that was is as uncertain as it is certain that they possessed it. Modern Alchemists think that their fabricated stone <note>The Philosopher's Stone</note> was first

# CHAPTER VII. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
<note>The title refers to Kircher's massive work *Oedipus Aegyptiacus*, where he attempts to "solve the riddle" of Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>

...do they not weave fables to establish its truth? With what tortures and torments of distillation, dissolution, coagulation, and fixation do they rage against wretched metals? They turn, return, revolve, and revolve again; they cook and re-cook, fix and un-fix—in a word, they *change squares into circles* <note>original: "mutant quadrata rotundis" — a Latin idiom for attempting the impossible or creating chaos</note>, so that they might finally reach that longed-for end which they never attain. Certainly, gnawed by so much smoke, blackened by so many coals, scorched by fire, and intoxicated by the breath of pestilential spirits—with their substance, age, and life eventually vanished into smoke—while they lead a miserable and calamitous life, they are held worthy of pity rather than envy. I shall not speak here of the useless prolixity of the books in which they describe this stone, nor of their vain—not to say ridiculous—structure, leaning upon foundations made only of fragile reeds and sterile stalks <note>original: "thyrsis" — the staff of Bacchus, here implying something hollow or fruitless</note>, with such horrendous confusion that even at the first reading it provokes both nausea and despair in the reader. In these books, besides tasteless commentaries, there is a thoroughly affected and ignorant obscurity; with an execrable barbarity of style, it so binds the mind that when you have read and weighed everything, you can scarcely see what you finally can or should conclude. Where contradiction involves contradiction, principles previously established are destroyed by those placed later, with an inextricable hodgepodge of ambiguities; so much so that even *Proteus* <note>The Greek sea-god capable of changing into any shape</note> could not transform himself into as many forms as the Alchemists transform their ridiculous stone. Thus, not without merit among all more sensible Philosophers, Alchemy has earned the title of an infamous science. Certainly, in my various travels, I have made it my one business to find out if any men celebrated for the fame of this science were to be found anywhere; yet it was never permitted to find even one who performed any of the promises of the art. I have known indeed most excellent Philosophers, not only ancient but modern, who have brought forth many outstanding things concerning this science and discussed it with the greatest perspicacity of intellect; but in this they seemed least of all to intend what the Alchemists do—that is, the construction of the stone—but rather they only explained the gifts of nature and her wonderful operations.

<margin>The Egyptians did not intend to manufacture the Philosophers' Stone.</margin>
Neither is it certain that the Egyptians intended the practice of this stone, for although they sometimes touch upon the preparations of metals and open the treasures of mineral secrets, they do not pretend to that which the Alchemists of our time and of the past do. Rather, they indicate a certain thing in the lower World analogous to the Sun, imbued with exotic powers most excellent and beyond human grasp—that is, a certain *quintessence* <term>Quinta essentia: the "fifth element" or purest essence of a substance</term> hidden in all mixtures and impregnated by the virtue of the World-Spirit, and a *symbol* <note>original: "σύμβολον" (symbolon)</note> to the same. They believed that whoever, inspired by the divine Will, unearthed this, would live a life free from all infirmity and full of all happiness; nor do I ever find them to have taught the method of making the gold-bearing stone in the manner that has been described, but rather they spoke of the *Elixir* of all things.

But perhaps someone at this point might object that the *Emerald Tablet of Hermes* <note>The Tabula Smaragdina, a foundational text of Hermeticism</note> dictates nothing other than the art of the transmutation of metals into gold and its multiplication from seed. To respond to these people, and so that it may be known what that Emerald Tablet truly is, it seemed best to begin a little further back.

<summary>Kircher critiques the futility and physical toll of laboratory alchemy, arguing that ancient Egyptian "alchemy" was actually a pursuit of a spiritual quintessence rather than literal gold-making.</summary>

# CLASS IX. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY. 427 CHAPTER VII.

## Whether Hermes Trismegistus, properly so called, was the Author of the Emerald Tablet.

<margin>Why it was called the Emerald Tablet, and who its Author was according to the chemists.</margin>
Nothing is more celebrated among the Chemists <note>The author uses "Chemists" to refer to Alchemists</note> than the Emerald Tablet of Hermes, in which they persuade themselves that the absolute mastery of the Philosopher's Stone is contained under hidden riddles of words. It is called "Emerald" because the laws of the art were said to be engraved on an Emerald and propagated to posterity in eternal memory of the matter. However, as to who that Hermes was, where or when he lived, in what place the tablet was stored or found by posterity, or in what language or letters it was written—there is a deep silence regarding all these things; which is a manifest sign of I know not what fraudulent offspring <note>original: "supposititij partus"; implying the text is a forgery or "supposititious"</note>. Is it possible that such a famous monument of Hermes could have escaped the notice of the most curious Greek Philosophers, who traveled to Egypt as if to a marketplace of the arts for the sake of seeking out secrets of this kind? Certainly, the architects of this so-solemn fiction seem to have rightly abstained from every circumstance of time and place lest they be accused of imposture, although they were by no means able to escape that mark. Thus, they assert Hermes—the most ancient of all Philosophers who ever existed—to be the Author, both to commend the antiquity of the art and to win authority for it by the title of a magnificent name.

<margin>Hermes Trismegistus is not the Author of the Emerald Tablet.</margin>
There is a twofold opinion concerning Hermes; some assert him to be Egyptian and "Thrice-Greatest" <note>original: "Trismegistum"</note>; but while they make him a contemporary of Plato, they seem to utterly rave in their Chronology. Others say he was a Greek King of Constantinople; but these err so much worse than the first, as they babble this out more inconveniently against the sense of all Chronologists and Historians: read all the books of Constantinopolitan History, and you will find no King of this name. It adds to this that he could not have existed (if he could exist at all) except in the times following Constantine, from whom Constantinople found the first origin of its name; but since all Historians are silent about this Hermes, it is rightly gathered, clearer than the midday light, that he is a fictitious Author.

<margin>Albertus Magnus.</margin>
Only **Albertus Magnus** in his book on Chemical secrets—which is nevertheless numbered among the forged books of Albertus—recites the origin of this Tablet; for he says that Alexander the Great, in his travels, found the tomb of Hermes, the parent of all Philosophers, full of all treasures, not metallic, but golden writings on a Tablet of Zatadi <note>A term sometimes used for green stone or jasper</note>, which others call Emerald. Where, I ask? In what place? In what region? In what characters and language was it inscribed? Who does not see openly that these are mere fictions of the "Chemists" <note>original: "Chimiastrorum"; a derogatory term for pseudo-alchemists</note>, since nothing similar is held in the life of Alexander, nor before the time of Albertus was any mention made of this said Tablet among the Greek, Latin, or Arabic Chemical writers.

<margin>Bernardus Canesius the Alchemist first brought forth the Emerald Tablet.</margin>
**Bernardus Canesius the Alchemist** was the first, as far as I know, who offered it to the World, and he says that in it the whole work and the treasure of the whole World is contained. The inscription of the Tablet follows.

### CHAPTER VII. 428 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

### *The Emerald Tablet of Hermes*

<margin>The words of the Emerald Tablet.</margin>
> It is true, without falsehood, certain, and most true: that which is below is like that which is above; and that which is above is like that which is below, to accomplish the miracles of one thing. And just as all things were from one by the mediation of one, so all things were born from this one thing by adaptation. Its father is the Sun, its mother the Moon; the wind carried it in its belly; its nurse is the earth. This is the father of all <term>telesmus</term> <note>original: "telesmi"; a term derived from the Greek "telesmos," meaning completion, perfection, or a consecrated talismanic power</note> or the consummation of the whole world. Its power is complete if it be turned into earth. You shall separate the earth from the fire, the subtle from the gross, gently, with great ingenuity. It ascends from the earth to the heaven, and again it descends to the earth, and receives the power of the higher and lower things. Thus you have the glory of the whole world; therefore all obscurity flees from you. This is the <term>strong fortitude</term> <note>original: "fatitudo fortis"; Kircher later mocks this specific phrasing as "barbarous" or nonsensical Latin</note> of all strength, which will overcome every subtle thing and penetrate every solid thing. Thus was the world created. From this shall come wonderful adaptations, the method of which is this. Therefore I am called Hermes Trismegistus <note>meaning "Thrice-Greatest Hermes"</note>, having three parts of the philosophy of the whole world. That which I have said concerning the operation of the Sun is completed.

<margin>The Emerald Tablet is a fiction.</margin>
And this is the inscription of the most celebrated Emerald Tablet of Hermes, which is the supreme oracle of the <term>Alchemists</term> <note>original: "Chimiastrorum"; a somewhat dismissive term for those obsessed with the chemical arts</note>. If anyone examines these things a little more closely, he will soon find that almost every single word has been extracted here and there from Hermes' *Pimander* and *Asclepius*, from Iamblichus, and from Proclus, and compiled into this epigraph. Furthermore, some barbarous words are added, of which you will find no trace in Hermes, such as <term>strong fortitude</term> <note>original: "fatitudo fortis"</note>; what this word indicates, I have not been able to guess, unless perhaps they wished to indicate a "fatuitousness" <note>a pun on "fatitudo" and "fatuitas" (foolishness)</note> suitable to the heads of the Alchemists, which I gladly leave to them. Truly, what that "greatest treasure of the whole world" is, which they think lies hidden under these words, I do not understand. Certainly, as easily as they assert the miraculous virtues of their "Stone" are hidden under these words, I just as easily adapt the whole thing to the universal force of nature. For what else is indicated by that phrase, *that which is below is like that which is above, and vice versa*, except that all things are in all things?

<margin>Explanation of the Emerald Tablet.</margin>
<margin>Proclus.</margin>
For as Proclus testifies in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, earthly things are in heaven according to their cause and in a celestial manner, while in the earth there are celestial things, but in an earthly manner. That all things are from one by the mediation of one, and all things from one by adaptation, is quite aptly proved by the Platonic Parmenides, and by Hermes in the *Asclepius*: a certain very great power of the "World Spirit" <note>original: "Mundani spiritus"</note> lies hidden in the innermost marrow of all things, whose principal instruments are the Sun and Moon, and which consists in a certain moist vapor. And this is what the tablet says: *the wind carried it in its belly*. Moreover, this greatest power, enclosed in earthly materials, is the parent of the perfection of all things and of the whole world; these things are aptly suggested by these words:
<margin>Plato. Hermes.</margin>
*the earth is its nurse, the father of the perfection of the whole world; its power is complete if it be turned into earth*; which is possessed by the ministry of fire, by separating the earth from the fire, the pure from the impure, with moderation and singular industry. For by the ministry of fire it soon ascends from the earth to the heaven, and if anything remains mixed with the dregs, it descends again to the earth; which the Hermetic *Asclepius* explains at length, and in this place it indicates nothing other than a certain digestive and refining power of nature for the perfecting of the generation of things—

<summary>Athanasius Kircher presents the text of the famous Alchemical "Emerald Tablet," but argues it is a later compilation of various philosophical sources rather than an ancient Egyptian original. He interprets its cryptic instructions as metaphors for the universal "World Spirit" and natural processes rather than literal gold-making.</summary>

necessary to be performed, with the light of heaven cooperating in the arrangement of earthly things. And this is that **fifth essence** <note>The "quintessence," or the purest element beyond the four earthly ones.</note> of all things, and the treasure of the World evolved from the darkness—that is, purified from all earthly contagion; according to whose model the World itself was produced by a certain wonderful series of adaptations. This is the exposition of the tablet, in which the natural force in the production of things toward the best and most excellent state of things is described by a certain universal reason; and it can be most excellently applied, according to a certain analogy, not only to earthly and metallic things, but also to vegetables, elementary animals, and celestial bodies.

<margin>What the meaning of the Emerald Tablet is.</margin>
Therefore, the entire meaning comprised in this Emerald Tablet is nothing other than a certain Theory of that most excellent essence, endowed with miraculous virtues, which some call the **Elixir of Life**, some the treasure of all nature, some **potable gold** <note>Liquid gold, believed to be a universal medicine.</note>, and most say is the **fifth essence**. For it is most certain that the meaning of the tablet can be applied to each of these individually; for whatever power the Mundane Spirit possesses in the Sun, it possesses the same in the Sun of moist things (wine), and in the Sun of minerals (gold), according to a certain analogy; one and the same virtue operating in different subjects according to the condition and property of each.

<margin>The Egyptians did not know the art of transmuting things into gold.</margin>
Since these things are so, it must now be discussed whether the Egyptians possessed the true knowledge of the transmuting art, and whether by its help they amassed such a great abundance of gold and silver as we described in the first chapter. I respond that it cannot be denied that the most subtle Philosophers of the Egyptians possessed the doctrine of the transmuting art, speaking always *in theory* <note>original: "εν τω θεωρειν" (en tō theōrein) - in the realm of contemplation or theory.</note>; yet the practice was so difficult and so dangerous that they thought it by no means sufficient to support a kingdom by its help for the immense expenses they required. For they either practiced that art publicly or privately; if the former, then the art was no longer hidden, but prostituted to public uses, which would stimulate every private citizen to provide for his own profit and amass huge treasures by its help. Thus things would reach a point where, in a short time, everyone could be equal to Kings in the flow of riches and abundance of gold, to the greatest and inevitable danger and prejudice of the Kingdom. Only one who is ignorant of what we have treated in the *Politics of the Egyptians* could be unaware of how contrary this would be to political reason. If the latter (practiced privately), it undoubtedly flourished among only a very few; who, in a most laborious and dangerous work, could by no means suffice to provide an abundance of gold and silver sufficient for the Kingdom.

<margin>The objection of the Chemists is resolved.</margin>
But the Chemists <note>The author uses "Chemists" here to refer to practicing alchemists.</note> will object that such an inestimable abundance of gold was supplied to the Egyptians from that miraculous stone, by whose "projection" the power of gold would be increased almost unto infinity. But since all these things are the ravings of the Chemists, they are to be utterly rejected. For if such an art of multiplying gold had ever existed in the nature of things, what would have prevented the craftsman from converting everything into gold by its help? Certainly, there has never been any Alchemist who performed this (unless perhaps they thrust forward the fabled Midas), or who abounded much in riches, as modern experience, as well as that of the ancients from so many thousands of years, has clearly taught. O happy...

# CHAPTER VII. 430 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

Kings and Princes, by the aid of such a divine art, would no longer need to provide for the strength and sinew of the state by digging gold out of the bowels of the earth with the greatest labor and expense. Instead, as if by a children's game—that is, with no effort at all—by casting the "leaves of the golden soul" <note>original: "foliis animae auriferae"</note> upon imperfect metals, gold would sprout forth unto infinity. Thus, all trees would no longer offer apples and pears, but golden fruits; and so, mineral nature having been transmuted into vegetable nature, gold would compete with the luxury and fertility of fruit-bearing trees. Happy are the people for whom these Divinities grow in their gardens! But what historian has ever observed such portents to have happened?

<margin>The Egyptians extracted an elixir from the most excellent things.</margin>
Therefore, I shall reveal what the Egyptians understood by this "multiplication." We have said in the preceding sections that the Egyptians were skilled in a certain method of extracting a particular Elixir <term>Elixir: here referring to a concentrated medicinal or alchemical essence</term> from the most excellent materials, which I find they also called "Heaven" because of its supreme subtlety and perfection. This Elixir, or "fifth essence" <note>The quintessence, the purest element beyond earth, air, fire, and water</note>, was of such eminent virtue that into whatever water distilled from any herbs it was poured, it would increase tenfold the virtue of that herb which corresponded to a specific member of the body. For example, if it were added to water extracted from Liverwort <note>original: "Hepatica," a plant traditionally used to treat the liver</note>, that water would provide an effect ten times more powerful in the cure of the Liver. This water was reduced to such a temperament through continuous circulations <note>A process of repeated distillation and condensation</note> that when added to cold things, it made them ten times colder; added to hot things, ten times hotter; joined to dry things, ten times drier; and finally, mixed with moist things, it made them ten times moister. The Arab Balsan <note>Likely a reference to an Arabic alchemical source or author known to Kircher</note> pursues all these matters at length according to the mind of the Egyptians in his book *On the Composition of the Elixir of Life*; for this was a certain extraordinary and most excellent panacea for preserving the body immune from any infirmity, not that metallic Medicine for the multiplication of gold.

<margin>
Balsan the Arab.
The Elixir of Life is the Philosopher's Stone of the Egyptians.
</margin>
And I judge this to have been that admirable and plainly heavenly water, fit for driving away all diseases, which they also called the "Stone," for the reason that it had been extracted from most precious stones of wondrous virtue. They also called it the "Water of Life," the "Vegetable Seed of Nature," the "Solar Soul," and by similar names bestowed upon the Hermetic Stone. Just as they most studiously concealed this secret as the greatest of all, so they introduced fabulous stories everywhere concerning a "Stone" prevailing by a certain power of gold to transmute other metals into gold. These things having been duly weighed, let us now see what that "gold-bearing art" of the Egyptians properly was, by whose help they arrived at such great riches.

<margin>What the gold-bearing art of the Egyptians was.</margin>
I answer that it was the art by which they knew how to extract gold and silver from all terrestrial materials prepared with the highest industry of wit. Since in this business nearly all the operations prescribed in the "Mastery of the Stone" are employed, the transmutatory art is easily confused with the metallic art, so that consequently all the hieroglyphic symbols set forth above seem to allude to this metallic art.

<margin>
The gold-bearing art of the Egyptians is explained.
Materials from which the Egyptians extracted gold.
</margin>
Let us explain, however, what kind of art it was. I find two materials from which they are said to have extracted gold: the mud or earth of the Nile, and rocks of every kind. The mud of the Nile, or Nilotic earth, was especially full of golden sands. For since in the Ethiopian mountains, through which the Nile was diverted, there lies hidden a great force of gold-bearing mines, and consequently from the continuous flooding of the river...

# CLASS X. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY. CHAPTER VII

<margin>The Egyptians extracted gold from sand.</margin>
...particles of gold were worn away; it could not happen otherwise than that the river, rushing headlong into Egypt through the cataracts <note>original: "catadupas," referring to the famous waterfalls of the Nile</note>, would carry down with it a great force of gold. By this process, the silt—and indeed the very earth involved—supplied a sufficient mass for the copious extraction of gold. It is well established that the Nile silt most suited for this business was that found from the cataracts down to the Island of Elephantine <note>An island in the Nile, part of the city of Aswan</note>, rather than that collected near Memphis or the fields closer to the sea. This is because, due to the river's precipitation over immense crags, the golden sands mixed with the silt were separated in the underlying bed of the precipice and soon mingled with the earth. They were subsequently found collected in entire masses, which were then separated by a skill known to them (as we shall describe later) and destined for smelting in suitable furnaces. The silt collected in this manner was extracted by a vast multitude of men who, having been condemned for crimes, were assigned to this labor. It was first processed through very frequent washings until the earthy parts were separated from the gold and flowed away; the golden sand alone, being heavier by its natural weight, remained in vessels constructed with the greatest industry for this purpose and set at a slight incline. Once collected, they placed this sand in earthen pots, properly sealed, with a certain quantity of Mercury <term>Mercury: used here in the context of amalgamation, a process where mercury binds to gold to separate it from impurities</term> or lead added to them. They exposed these to the furnaces to be cooked for three or four days at first, or as the work required, so that a perfect mixing and penetration of the gold with the Mercury or lead might occur. When this was finished, they brought it into common use by casting it into golden plates. And this was the method of extracting gold from sand.

<margin><unclear>Faded Greek and Latin reference</unclear></margin>

<margin>The Egyptians extracted gold from stone quarries.</margin>
The other method of extracting gold from stone quarries was as follows. Above the Theban Prefecture <note>The region around Thebes/Luxor in Upper Egypt</note>, and throughout all the surrounding regions, many stone quarries are found, especially swollen with gold, from which stones of every kind were dug out both for buildings and for the construction of statues.

<margin>The method of extracting gold from stones used among the Egyptians.</margin>
An infinite multitude of men, condemned for crimes, dug these out. There were those who applied their labor to cutting the stones; to some was committed the care of carrying them outside; some cut them into very small pieces; others ground them into dust in mortars by driving mills. A portion of the material prepared in this way was placed on sloping boards and cleansed with very frequent washings. By this frequent cleansing, the gold was finally separated from the earthy parts and remained on the boards. Collecting it then, and squeezing it through sponges and amalgamating it, they placed it in earthen pots. Having mixed in a certain quantity of lead or another metal related to gold according to the art known to them, they first sealed these pots properly with clay so that the spirit <note>original: "spiritus," referring to volatile vapors or gases during the heating process</note> would not exhale, and delivered them to the furnaces to be cooked. When this was finished, they had gold reserved for human uses. So great was the multitude of these pots that they received from them several millions of pounds of gold every month, to the greatest benefit of the entire Kingdom.

<margin>Diodorus Siculus <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BCE</note>.</margin>
But let us hear Diodorus Siculus, who writes that he surveyed everything with his own eyes and described the scene of the entire operation as accurately as possible; he reports it thus in Book 3, Chapter 2:

> On the borders of Egypt, which verge toward Ethiopia and Arabia, there are places fertile in metals, from which gold is drawn with great labor and expense. For the black earth has natural passages and veins of the whitest marble, which shines beyond all splendor. To this work...

# CHAPTER VII 432 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin><unclear>Diodorus, Book 3 of the Historical Library, chapters 11, 12, & 13.</unclear></margin>
Those who oversee the work employ a vast multitude of men for the extraction of gold. For the Egyptian Kings assign all those convicted of crimes, those captured from enemies, and furthermore those thrust into prison due to some false slander or the anger of the Kings—sometimes the individuals themselves, sometimes their entire extended family—to the digging of gold. This serves both as a punishment for their crimes and as a means of reaping great profit from their labor. Bound in fetters, this great number of men works without any intermission day and night; no rest is granted, and every opportunity for escape is removed. For barbarian soldiers, who speak different languages from one another, stand guard over them, so that no one, being deprived of the exchange of speech, can be corrupted by entreaties or by affection. The gold is extracted from the hardest earth, which has been baked by much fire. Nearly infinite thousands of men dig out the softer rock, which is broken with moderate labor, using iron tools.

<margin>The method of producing gold among the Egyptians according to Diodorus.</margin>
The one who discerns the veins of gold precedes the laborers, showing them the places to be dug; they split the indicated stony marble not by art, but by great force with iron wedges, using the strength of a powerful body. Indeed, they drive the tunnels not in a straight line, but wherever the nature of the marble gleaming with gold leads; because of various bends and circuits, these tunnels are dark. The workers, carrying lights fixed to their foreheads, throw the stones—cut into pieces with great effort—down to the floor. They never rest from this labor, being forced to continuous work by cruelty and lashes. Young boys are divided into two groups: some indeed break the thrown pieces into small bits, while others carry them out. Those who exceed their thirtieth year take these measured pieces and crush them in stony vessels with iron hammers; then, these are cast into mills, of which there are many, where two or three women or old men are stationed at a mill and grind them until they are reduced to the consistency of flour. With the filth of these bodies manifest to all, and with no garment covering their private parts, there is no one who, moved by such a foul and hideous sight, would not pity such great calamity. But no mercy, no rest, no pardon is given to them, whether they be sick, feverish, elderly, or weak women; instead, all are driven to continuous work by blows, until the wretched ones collapse from weakness. Finally, the workers place the ground material from the mill on wide, slightly sloping boards and rub the marble again with water poured over it. In this way, as the earth flows away, the gold remains on the boards due to its weight. Repeating this often, they rub the gold with their hands; then, with thin sponges, they press out the soft earth until it is rendered like golden sand. Lastly, other workers, casting it by weight and measure into earthen pots, add a certain measure of lead, sea-weed, and barley bran. When these are mixed in proportion, they carefully smear the pots with clay; finally, after being cooked in a furnace for five continuous days and nights, and the other substances being consumed, only the gold is found in the vessels, with its previous weight only slightly diminished.

<margin>The Alchemy of the Egyptians.</margin>
And this is that celebrated Alchemy of the Egyptians, this method of extracting gold from earthly materials; not that which we described above resulting from the <term>Philosopher's Stone</term> <note>The legendary substance capable of turning base metals into gold; Kircher distinguishes here between industrial metallurgy and mystical alchemy.</note>, which was nothing but a certain theory of this practice.

<margin>Diodorus.</margin>
And Diodorus himself openly asserted that they received this from the earliest Kings through a certain successive tradition, in these words:
> *The discovery of these metals is ancient, found by the old Kings. Truly, how much gold could be extracted in a short time from those inexhaustible gold mines by that innumerable multitude of men laboring for free? For the rocks were swollen with gold, and most full of gold-bearing veins, which were formed there partly by nature and partly by the accumulation of golden nuggets together with the stone...*

# CLASS X. HIEROGLYPHIC ALCHEMY. 433 CHAPTER VII

...the overflowing Nile had produced from coagulated [minerals]. Then, the Hebrews and other Eastern peoples, having received this art from the Egyptians, cultivated it with the greatest amount of time, labor, and diligence. Although, as I indicated a little earlier, I would not deny that a great abundance of gold and silver was also obtained through the singular industry of the art—specifically by performing the <term>fixation</term><note>Fixation: An alchemical process intended to make a volatile substance, like mercury, stable and resistant to fire.</note> of <term>mercury</term><note>original: "hydrargyri"</note> mixed with the remaining metals. For it is clear that they were skilled in this art from what we taught in the preceding sections regarding the nature of metals and their proximity to the Sun and Moon—that is, to gold and silver—based on the wondrous construction of the <term>Planetary characters</term><note>The symbolic link between the seven planets and the seven metals (e.g., Sun/Gold, Moon/Silver).</note>. For as Strabo rightly teaches, there are several mountains full of caverns on the shore of the Red Sea, in which a great abundance of mercury is collected for the use of the metallic art. Indeed, only he who is ignorant of the transmutative power of one metal into another can fail to know that there is a certain art of fixing mercury into true gold and silver. 

However, since we shall deal with this subject professionally, amply, and copiously in our book on the gold-making art in *The Subterranean World* <note>original: "Mundo Subterraneo," Kircher’s massive work on geology and chemistry</note>, we refer the curious reader there. In that work, he will find demonstrated whatever can be desired concerning this matter, through a diverse apparatus of experiments and practical rules established according to the model of nature. From what has been said thus far, it is clear enough 

<margin>The acquisition of gold is laborious</margin>

how much the thirst for this gold has filled human minds at all times; with what great care and anxiety they have sought its possession, and to how many labors they have exposed themselves to acquire it. Nature herself shows that gold is laborious to find, difficult to guard, anxious to gain, and situated in use between pleasure and pain; so that, accordingly, no one truly devoted to wisdom ought to seek or desire it greatly. Blessed, therefore, is he who, having despised and repudiated the allurements of such cheap earth, and being content with only the necessities, composes a tranquil life, purged of all the <term>passions of the soul</term><note>original: "pathematis," referring to emotional disturbances or suffering.</note>, so that he can say truly and from the heart that word of the Wise Man: 

> Lord, give me neither poverty nor riches, but grant me only the necessities for my sustenance. <note>A reference to Proverbs 30:8.</note>

Let us, therefore, cease to seek stability in this perpetual tide of fleeting things; let us leave the acorns to the pigs, the hay to the oxen, and the sensory foreboding of the storm to the frogs and crows; let us leave the filthy abyss of gold to the greedy. Relying on higher principles, let us seek with an eternal mind—and with all the zeal and exertion of the soul—not those things which are fluid in this economy of the sublunary world, but those which are contained in the everlasting treasures above the heavens. And these are the things which I have seen fit to communicate to the reader concerning the

<margin>Man desires to know the future.</margin>

# CHAPTER I. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

<margin>The Egyptians attributed a good and evil Spirit to every single thing.</margin>
...they believed that all things depended upon evil powers. For as we have declared at length elsewhere, it was a specific doctrine of the Egyptians that not only do individual human beings have two Spirits <note>Latin: *Genios*. In Roman and Egyptian thought, a 'Genius' was a guardian spirit or driving force inherent in a person or place.</note>, one good and one evil, assigned to them from birth by the supreme deity *Emeth* <note>A name used by Kircher for the supreme Egyptian God, likely derived from the Hebrew word for 'Truth'.</note>; but also that every single species of natural thing has the same assigned to it. The former of these, by its very nature, would assist the things committed to its protection by bestowing spiritual gifts of every kind; the latter, however, would always exist ready and prepared to inflict every kind of evil. Hence Servius, commenting on that passage in the sixth book of the *Aeneid*:
<margin>Servius.</margin>
*Each of us suffers his own spirit-destiny* <note>Latin: *Quisque suos patimur manes*. A famous line from Virgil regarding the afterlife.</note>, says that Virgil *understands a good and an evil Spirit*. And Orpheus in his *Prayer* says:
<margin>Orpheus.</margin>
*The noble spirit, and the spirit that brings pain to mortals.* <note>Kircher provides the Greek: Δαίμονα τ' ηγάθεον, καὶ δαίμονα πήμονα θνητῷ. Here 'Daimon' refers to a spirit, not necessarily a 'demon' in the modern sense.</note>
For they believed that a malignant Spirit was assigned to a person by a certain fate—as we have discussed in the section on Astrology—at that first moment when they are separated from the mother's womb. They believed this spirit to be of the same nature as the stars produced; if the star was good, the Spirit was good; if the star was evil, the Spirit was believed to be of an equally malignant nature. Hence,
<margin>In what the Magic of the Egyptians consisted.</margin>
their entire Magic seemed to rest upon this hinge: that each person should recognize which Spirit he had obtained at his first birth. Their entire study was occupied with this: that they might understand the inclinations, properties, and gifts in which that spirit excelled. If they could learn this, they thought the nature of these Spirits was such that they desired human honors and worship above all other things, and uniquely sought them out; and that each spirit would be more ready to help the more intensely it had been summoned by worship and great care. Hence
<margin>Iamblichus.</margin>
the Egyptians, according to the testimony of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note>, invented an art by which, through a mixture of worldly things appropriate to each Spirit, they could compel Spirits into statues, and by the utterance of specific words—or rather, portentous names—
<margin>Magic and Idolatry arose from Astrology and Oracles.</margin>
force them to reveal secrets. And from here, as if from a certain Trojan Horse, the origin of all Idolatry and Magic descended—namely from Astrology and the art of Oracles. All the dogmas of superstitious arts and divinations rest upon these two as if upon twin columns, as will become clear in the course of this treatise. Proclus describes all these things with copious reasoning in his book *On Sacrifice and Magic*, saying:
<margin>Proclus.</margin>

> *The ancient priests discovered the worship of superior powers from visible things, while they mixed some things and purified others; moreover, they mixed many things together. For this reason, by the very mixing of many things, they attracted heavenly influences; and that which they made as one out of many by composing it, they made similar to that One which is above the many. They established statues mixed from many and diverse materials. They also made composite scents, in which they gathered divine symbols into one by their accustomed art; they rendered it as a single thing, just as the divine exists—namely, according to an essence that encompasses many, or rather all, powers. The priests, therefore, through the mutual kinship and sympathy of things, brought them together into one; through opposition they expelled them, purifying, when necessary, with sulfur and asphalt—that is, sprinkling bitumen with sea water. For sulfur purifies because of the sharpness of its odor, while sea water purifies because of its fiery portion. <margin>The origin of the mystic chains.</margin>
Thus says Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Neoplatonist philosopher whose theories on "sympathy" between earthly and divine things heavily influenced Renaissance magic.</note>. They would impose a name upon the entity based on its effect, and from the individual things contained under that chain and joined into one, they fashioned an image from material analogous to said things. Then, having applied the conceived formulas of appropriate words, they compelled the Deity—or more truly the Demon—as if struck by a dreadful adjuration. Once compelled in the stated manner, the Demon gave responses concerning the outcomes of future events. And this was properly the Magic of the Egyptians. # CHAPTER II.
## Concerning the herbs and stones which the Egyptians used in their Magical operations.

<margin>The Egyptians used herbs in their sacred rites.</margin>
That the Egyptians for the most part used herbs in their sacred rites is shown by the frequent multitude of hieroglyphic herbs occurring everywhere on Obelisks and the Isiac Table <note>The Bembine Tablet of Isis, an elaborate bronze tablet depicting Egyptian mysteries, much studied by Kircher.</note>. For the Egyptians thought that individual herbs had their own appropriated presiding Genii, who, since they were believed to be moved with the greatest care and love toward the things committed to their faith, could consequently be drawn by such things and made to stand present for the revealing of secrets through preliminary sacrifices. They thought this was effected by a certain power implanted in the herbs themselves, since in their opinion, herbs were nothing other than certain particles of divinity. But this doctrine, as it is diametrically opposed to orthodox doctrine, has deservedly been outlawed and exiled for a long time as the root of all superstition; for herbs in magical use do not operate as natural virtues, but are only certain signs ordained by an implicit or explicit pact, which, when set in place, the Demon presents himself.

<margin>There is no physical power in herbs and plants to put spirits to flight or to attract them.</margin>
For if they attracted Genii through natural efficiency, they would necessarily impress some force upon them; but since no proportion mediates between corporeal things and spiritual substances, nor...

<margin>Theophrastus</margin>
Hence, Theophrastus not undeservedly calls these things "senseless and rather incredible" <note>original: "ἀνόητα καὶ ἀπιθανώτερα"</note>, foolish and unbelievable.

<margin>Magical stones among the Egyptians.</margin>
But let us proceed to stones, in which the same considerations occur as in plants. Among the Egyptians, these stones were especially memorable: the *Ananchites* and the *Atizoci*. Through the former,
<margin>Pliny</margin>
according to Pliny's testimony, the images of the Gods were summoned; through the latter, those carrying it were rendered invisible. Truly, he who has properly understood our arguments brought forth a little earlier will see that these things can stand by no reason, nor can they perform these things by natural force, but by the help of a Demon, who used the stones only as certain signs established by a pact. However, since stones, as well as animals, have been treated most amply in the *Pamphilian Obelisk* <note>A reference to Kircher's own earlier work on the Roman obelisk brought from Egypt</note>, we refer the reader there. Thus, no sacrifice was offered without a herb, no libation without stones or aromatics; for they thought that these alone could provide the effect of drawing down some Deity. But these things will be explained more clearly below.

# CHAPTER III.
## *Concerning the Divinations and Oracles of the Egyptians.*

<margin>The human mind always seeks the highest good.</margin>
Just as the human mind is perpetually driven by a tide of desires, so it lives in perpetual hope of the goods it desires; and while it breathes, it hopes without intermission for some highest and most excellent good. Since this cannot be granted outside of God, the Best and Greatest, the mind is consequently involved in perpetual anxiety, care, grief, and labor, and like a great tenth wave <note>A classical metaphor for an exceptionally large or "decuman" wave</note> driven by the ocean, it exists in perpetual restlessness. There is, moreover, a twofold nature of "the good" around which all human machinations and all industry turn as if on a hinge: namely, the goods of the body and the goods of the soul.
<margin>Goods of the body and goods of the soul.</margin>
The goods of the body are beauty, perfect bodily health, and pleasure. Since these can neither be preserved without the possession of things necessary for conducting life honorably, nor can these be had without riches, it is no wonder that there is such a great hunger for gold among all mortals, and such great zeal in acquiring riches. For by the possession of these, they trust they will soon be filled with an abundance of all goods and be free from all hardships. Yet because even these things do not fully satisfy a human, they desire the goods of the soul joined to the bodily ones; such as knowledge, honors, dignities, and power. All of these things, since they are uncertain in such an unstable...

# CHAPTER III. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’ HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

->**Man craves knowledge of the future.**<-
<margin>Man craves knowledge of the future.</margin>
...the wheel of fortune determines the outcomes, and for the most part, being uncertain in the impenetrable state of their future affairs and fluctuating between hope and fear, men crave the knowledge of future things with such zeal that they might learn from it what is to become of them, and whether they can promise themselves anything solid from those aforementioned goods. The Devil, the enemy of the human race and the cunning architect of deceits, knows this; hence he spreads as many diverse snares as there are appetites for human machinations, so that finally, under the hope of knowing the future, he may attack men, ensnare those he has attacked, and bring them entirely under his own power.

<margin>The Demon deceives men through Astrology and Polyomancy.</margin>
There are, moreover, two principal nets: Astrology and Polyomancy <note>Polyomancy: A general term for many forms of divination or "many-fold" fortune-telling.</note>. By the former, he teaches the lot which each person has obtained from the first moment of their birth, whether toward good or ill fortune; by the latter, as if under a certain veil of natural causes, he exhibits various kinds of divinations. By these, the unwary—while they too recklessly crave to pursue the good and avoid the evil—are deservedly deprived of the possession of the eternal good.

<margin>Ham first introduced Astrology and Polyomancy.</margin>
Therefore, Ham, the son of Noah, was the first to introduce these arts into the world under the mastery of the Devil; the Egyptians, instructed by Ham, poured these out into the entire world as if they were a handed-down inheritance. And concerning their Astrology, much has been said in its proper place; it remains for us to speak further of Divinations, their origin, and the methods of the Oracles.

<margin>The Egyptians worshipped Genii.</margin>
The Egyptians, therefore, with Mercury <note>The author refers to Hermes Trismegistus, often identified with the Egyptian god Thoth.</note> as their teacher, thought that besides the celestial Gods, certain natures were found midway between men and those Gods, which they called Angels, Demons, or Genii <note>Genii: Guardian spirits or tutelary deities believed to inhabit specific places or objects.</note>, or earthly Gods. To these they attributed the cause of the rise and fall of all Oracles, and thus held that Oracles lasted as long as the said Genii remained in the statues that poured forth the Oracles; and that the same perished when the images were abandoned by the Genii or Demons.

<margin>The dwelling place of the Genii.</margin>
They asserted that these Genii inhabit the region cast between heaven and earth, and that they consist of herbs, stones, aromatics, and other earthly materials containing a natural power of divinity within themselves. And just as they dwell near us, joined to us as if by a friendly kinship, so they are moved by a singular love toward the human race, and they think to help men in various and diverse ways, according to what their nature brings—by predicting the future through lots and by caring for other things pertaining to us.

<margin>The Genii entered into statues.</margin>
Wherefore, they also entered into statues duly prepared by them, and from those they gave responses to those consulting them; they remained in them for many years, all the more willingly as the statues were made of material more congruent to them, and as they knew how to more skillfully detain them with sacrifices, hymns, praises, and harmonies, by which they are delighted as if by the unique allurements of the Genii.

<margin>Trismegistus</margin>
Hermes teaches copiously that these things are so in the *Pimander* <note>The *Poimandres*, a foundational text of the Hermetic corpus.</note>, and assigns the cause why man prevails with such great power over Demons and Genii, and why they so easily submit themselves to his dominion:

<margin>The Genii were affected by men.</margin>
> *For since, he says, man is a venerable animal and a great miracle of the World, constituted from every mixture of nature—celestial, earthly, mortal, immortal—he is joined to both the lower and the higher things; by that part, indeed, which consists of soul, sense, spirit, and reason, he is joined to the divine; by that part which is made of fire, air, water, and earth, he is joined to the sublunary things. It happens that when he [withdraws] his mind from the body on account of the desires for those things which the mortal portion craves...*

...separates [the soul] as if abstracted from the body, transformed as if into a certain divine essence, so that it emerges either superior to the heavenly beings or equal in dignity. Thus, it acquires such fullness of power that, just as God is the creator of the heavenly Gods, so man is able to create those Gods who are attached to earthly dwellings—namely, statues animated with sense, full of spirit, and possessing foreknowledge of the future. Indeed, Hermes Trismegistus <note>original: "Mercurius"; the author refers to the legendary Hellenistic figure Hermes Trismegistus, supposed author of the Hermetic corpus</note> pursues this at greater length in the *Poimandres* <note>original: "Pimandro"; the first treatise of the Corpus Hermeticum</note>. To this he also adds that his ancestors did not have perfect knowledge of the celestial God; for had they known God, they would not have cared for earthly Gods. But being uncertain about Him, and thus wandering far from divine religion, they devised an art by which they might create Gods. They constructed statues, and since they themselves could not create souls, they summoned the souls of Demons or Angels into them. Once called, these spirits arrived, both because of the great power of these men and because Angels and Demons share such a connection with humans that they are drawn to obey them by their very nature.

<margin>The impious doctrine of Trismegistus concerning the cessation of Oracles.</margin>
And this is the opinion of Hermes regarding Oracles, which we thought should be explained briefly as an excerpt from the *Poimandres*. As for the rest which he pursues further, let the reader see the cited passage; there, shrouded in great darkness, he impiously explains the causes for the cessation of the Oracles. For he pronounces that the Oracles will fail when men become devoid of religion and impious; for then they will neither worship idols, nor manufacture them, nor be able to introduce the souls of Demons into them. The Demons, seeing themselves neglected, will depart even from the ancient statues. Thus, he ascribes the failure of the Oracles to the vices of men and the indignation of Demons, rather than to divine power.

<margin>Porphyry. Plutarch.</margin>
More correctly indeed, though they were impious, spoke Porphyry and Plutarch <note>Porphyry (c. 234–305 AD) and Plutarch (c. 46–120 AD) were Neoplatonist philosophers who wrote extensively on the decline of oracles</note>, both of whom cast the cause of the Oracles' cessation upon the Christian religion. The former also confesses in open words: "Mortals, from the time that JESUS has been worshiped, have perceived no utility from the Gods."

<margin>Why the Oracles ceased.</margin>
Therefore, the Oracles did not cease through a defect of human industry or negligence, but the arrival of the only-begotten Son of God upon the earth was the sole cause. By this, the power of darkness was dispelled, and the strengths with which the Demons were accustomed to deceive the human race were taken away, and Eternal Truth shone upon the world.

<margin>Nicephorus Callistus.</margin>
Even the Pythian Apollo <note>The deity of the Oracle at Delphi</note> was forced to confess this, even against his will. For according to the testimony of Nicephorus Callistus <note>A 14th-century Byzantine church historian</note>, when Apollo was asked by Caesar Augustus who would succeed him in the Empire, he remained silent for a long time. Though he was asked again and again to respond and reveal the cause of his silence,

<margin>The response of Apollo concerning the cessation of Oracles.</margin>
he finally broke out into these words:

> A Hebrew child, a God himself ruling the blessed Gods,
> Bids me leave this seat and return to gloomy Tartarus.
> Therefore, depart in silence from our altars hereafter.

<margin>Lactantius. The power of the Holy Cross against Oracles.</margin>
Lactantius Firmianus <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) and advisor to Constantine I</note> adds that in his times, the power of the cross was so great that when idolaters wished to sacrifice to the Gods, if anyone were present with the sign of the cross marked on their forehead, they could neither perform the sacred rites successfully nor obtain any response from the Seers.

For the Demon did not always give answers with a perceptible voice, but revealed what he wished through certain signs. From this first emerged various kinds of rites and ceremonies by which they were accustomed to purify the mind—as if by preparatory arrangements—so that they might become aware of future events. Later, having turned to vain observations, they held all the trifles of things encountered in their path as omens. But let us explain each point.

<margin>
Oracles in almost all the districts of the Egyptians.
</margin>
I find that there was an Oracle in almost all the Nomes <note>original: "Nomis"; the administrative districts of ancient Egypt</note> of Egypt, in which those consulting them received answers concerning various events. However, individual Oracles did not respond to every matter proposed to them, but only concerning those things consistent with their specific nature.

<margin>
The more famous Oracles of the Egyptians.
</margin>
In this manner, the Oracle of Serapis was consulted regarding those things which concerned the cultivation of the earth; that of Anubis regarding the sciences; that of Horus regarding the goods of the body and soul; and that of Isis regarding those things which concerned the Nile or fertility. But the Oracle of Ammon, established in the Libyan sands, as it was the most famous of all, so it gave answers concerning any matters proposed to it.

<margin>
The more famous Oracles of the Greeks.
</margin>
From these Oracles, four other Oracles of great name came forth in Greece—or rather, cursed shrines were raised to fascinate the minds of men: the Delphic in Ionia; the Trophonian <note>original: "Triphonium"</note> in Lebadea; the Branchidic in Milesia; the Sabaean in Phocis; that of Amphiaraus in Attica; the Sebennytic of Latona in Buto, Egypt; and those established in innumerable other places. All of these gave answers in obscure places possessed by malignant spirits, by voice, dreams, gesture, the nodding of statues, by sound, tinkling, or other signs. These were issued either by the Demon himself or by Pythons <note>prophetic spirits or those possessed by them</note> and Priests inspired by a soothsaying spirit, who rushed from caves and obscure, deep pits with a horrible sound and noise upon the Enthusiasts <note>those "filled with the god"</note> in the appearance of fire, by which they were enveloped on all sides. Driven into a frenzy, with a palpitation of all their limbs, upturned eyes, and distorted mouths, they spoke those things which the Demon suggested to them.

<margin>
The Devil through blind superstitions and impious ceremonies.
</margin>
In this way, Satan, the architect of superstitions, stealthily creeping into the minds of men through Idolatry, busied himself with instilling the devotions of various rites and ceremonies. By these, they might worship their fictitious Gods under the pretext of piety and virtue, so that under these titles he might involve and pollute them through every kind of impiety and wickedness, and thus divert the honor due to God to himself.

<margin>
Various kinds of Lot-casting and Auguries.
</margin>
Since, indeed, there was nothing so obvious to the senses that the Demon did not assume as certain signs to show his will to those consulting him, from this arose multiple kinds of divinatory Magic; from here sprouted the portentous offspring of every kind of lot-casting and augury. These took the etymology of their name only from the things through which the divination was instituted. Hence, they first undertook their divinations according to the series of the four elements, and called them by their own names: namely, <term>Pyromancy</term> (from fire), <term>Aeromancy</term> (from air), <term>Hydromancy</term> (from water), and finally <term>Geomancy</term> (from earth). For they thought that the Spirits exhibited their will through certain signs shining forth in the said four Elements; concerning which more will be said in the following pages. Nor did they stop here, but at the instigation of the Demon, they assumed everything for the sake of rightly performing the fanatical operations of impious divination. # CHAPTER IV. 446 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Hieroglyphics were thought to be effective in producing wonderful things.</margin>
...they were carried about, burning with zeal for the averting of evils. So that these things may be understood, it must be known that hieroglyphic symbols were not only significant of the highest things and the sublime mysteries of divinity, but were also effective in producing the wonderful operations which were thought to happen through them. Therefore, the hieroglyphics carved upon Obelisks did not only—as has been said—display the hidden theology concerning God and the Divinities, and their offices and ministries in this worldly Monarchy; but furthermore, they were believed to ward off the machinations and <term>counter-arts</term> <note>original: ἀντιτεχνίας (antitechnias); refers to the opposing "crafts" or tricks of hostile spirits</note> of evil Spirits, by the power of the potent Angels and the supreme authority of the highest Divinity, which was expressed beneath them. Hence, so that they might obtain their effect, they were first consecrated by the Priests with a great apparatus of rites and ceremonies. Once this was performed, they promised themselves that no malignant power or force hostile to the Egyptian land could remain. Indeed, the symbols—as will be demonstrated in the third Volume—were so aptly applied to the favorable assemblies of Spirits that, attracted by a likeness of nature and a certain friendly kinship which they held toward the things expressed through the symbols, they would take up the protection of the Egyptian land against contrary powers, even if unwillingly. To which Spirit any particular thing was subject, or with which presiding power the beings of the lower World and the Starry world agreed by a sympathetic (that is, friendly) kinship, they learned from the mystical chains of worldly things, which they called <term>cords</term> <note>original: σείρας (seiras); a Neoplatonic concept of "chains" or "links" connecting the divine realm to the physical world</note>, and from the ideal doctrine of the Obelisks, about which we have discussed copiously in the preceding classes of Astrology and Medicine.

<margin>Most Hieroglyphics were Amulets among the Egyptians.</margin>
I say, therefore, that almost all symbols and sacred inscriptions <note>original: hierogrammatismos</note> found on Obelisks and other Egyptian hieroglyphic monuments, as well as on the Bembine Tablet <note>original: Isiaca tabula; a famous bronze tablet depicting Egyptian mysteries, once owned by Cardinal Bembo</note>, besides signifying any most secret matters, were also used separately as amulets. They were plucked here and there by the Egyptians from the Obelisks as if from master-books <note>original: archetypis codicibus</note> and carried as certain sacred phylacteries <note>protective charms</note> on the neck, chest, hands, and other more private parts of the body, both against the violence of various diseases and enchantments, and for the acquisition of goods for the soul; indeed, for the same reason, they were even tied to animals as symbols to avert sterility. Long and lasting experience has taught this more than enough. For while I explore almost countless storehouses of antiquities, I find almost all the principal hieroglyphic symbols carved from various precious stones with a small loop attached to the back; which is an open sign that they served the private uses of men, suspended by a thread. All of these, engraved in copper, will be exhibited in Volume III.

<margin>Hieroglyphic Amulets carved on household items.</margin>
Nor were they displayed only on stones, but were engraved on ribbons, threads, papers, and metal tablets dedicated to the Gods, as will be said in its proper place; with such an increase of superstition that there was scarcely a child, a man, or a beast who did not have such fanatical delusions hanging upon them.

<margin>The superstition of the Egyptians passed to other Nations.</margin>
These things gradually spread to the nations neighboring Egypt—Arabia, Greece, Babylonia—and then infected all of Latium <note>The region of Rome</note>. Hence Festus <note>A Roman grammarian</note> says: *Ipsullices* <note>Small metal plates or figurines used in magic</note> were necessary plates for magic rites, engraved with certain characters in the likeness of men and women; whence the Magi who engraved and carved them were called by the Greeks *Stæchiomathici* <note>Those who learn the elements/signs</note> and by the Egyptians *Hieromanthæ* <note>Sacred diviners</note>. <margin>

Apollonius of Tyana.
</margin>
Cedrenus, in his account of Claudius, says that Apollonius of Tyana was especially skilled in the secrets of Egypt, *and that he consecrated symbols against snakes and scorpions so they would not strike.* <note>original Greek: Στοιχειῶσαι ὄφεις, καὶ σκορπίους μὴ πλήσσειν</note> He bound the serpents and scorpions with characters and seals so that they would not bite. 
<margin>Eusebius.</margin>
Eusebius also mentions these in Book 5 of the *Preparation for the Gospel*. He commands that certain lines be erased so that the spirit might depart; for he says these lines retain the spirit, as does a different style of clothing worn by those who carry the images of the Gods. A certain philosopher, according to Tzetzes, used *an image of the face of Charon carved on the base* <note>original Greek: Εἰκὼν ἐν πέζα προσώπου τοῦ Χάροντος</note> of a stone; while a plague was spreading in Antioch, he set up this image in the city and calmed the pestilence. Apollonius, following the Egyptian custom, carved a stork in marble and expelled the storks from Byzantium which were tainting the springs and wells by dropping snakes into them, as Herostratus testifies. The same man quelled a plague by burying a Demon under stones, which had been wandering about in the likeness of a beggar. Regarding him, 
<margin>Amulets of the earth among the Egyptians, and of the air, and of the Nile, etc.</margin>
Cedrenus says: *Even today the works of Apollonius remain active in certain places. The protective works endure and are effective, some for turning away harmful quadrupeds and birds, others for the restraint of river currents flowing out of order.* <note>original Greek: ἐνεργοῦσι τὰ ἀποτέλεσμα. Τὰ ἰσαμάρια... ὡς ἐποχὴν ῥευμάτων ποταμοῦ ἀτάκτως φερομένων</note> Among the Egyptians, there was no corner of the cities that did not swarm with things of this kind. There were amulets of the earth, designed for the fertility of the land, such as Serapis, cast from all the materials of the world; there were also Nilotic amulets, such as Canopus, for procuring the fertility of the Nile; there were amulets of the air, such as the *hawk-shaped* <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος</note> Hawk for warding off the contagion of plague; there were also amulets of fire, such as the *Good Spirit* <note>original Greek: ἀγαθοδαίμον</note> Asp for turning away the dryness of fire and heat; there were the Lares and Penates <note>Household gods</note> of cities and private homes, depicted as infants wrapped in swaddling clothes, by which it was believed malignant powers were dispelled; everyone had certain private amulets which were worn on the neck, chest, or hands against the harmful Typhonian <note>Referring to Typhon/Set, the god of chaos</note> force; and there were amulets for animals against the plague sent upon them by opposing powers, which were used everywhere. But since I discuss these throughout this work, I did not wish to be longer here. The Holy Fathers rightly rail against these things everywhere with the greatest rigor. 
<margin>
The Holy Fathers rail against Amulets.
Lactantius.
</margin>
Lactantius says in Book 1, Chapter 14: *Demons insinuate themselves into the bodies of men, and hidden secretly in the viscera, they impair health, cause diseases, terrify minds with dreams, and shake them with madness, so that they may force men by these evils to run to their aid.* 
<margin>Tertullian.</margin>
Tertullian in his *Apology*, Chapter 22: *Demons harm first, then prescribe remedies—new or contrary to the miracle—which afterwards cease to harm, and are believed to have cured.* 
<margin>Origen.</margin>
Origen against Celsus: *Why should I recount,* says Celsus, *those who taught purifications, and incantations for driving away diseases and warding them off, or the various images and forms of Demons, and besides these, amulets of different kinds in clothes, sleeves, stones, plants, and roots?* But let these remarks on amulets in general suffice.

<margin>Various amulets explained.</margin>
But so that the reader might recognize these more clearly *in a figure* <note>original Greek: ἐν τῷ τύπῳ</note>, I have decided to place several amulets here, from which the reasoning behind the rest may be more easily understood. Among Egyptian amulets, nothing was more common than Harpocrates, Horus, Apis, Osiris and Isis, and Canopus; the first of these was seen equipped with a Cornucopia in the form of a naked boy urging silence with his finger; the second likewise in the form of a boy, but wrapped in swaddling bands or a lattice-patterned garment; the third in the form of a bull's head; the fourth under various forms, now *hawk-shaped* <note>original Greek: ἱερακόμορφος</note>, now *dog-shaped* <note>original Greek: κυνόμορφος</note>, and sometimes lion-shaped; the fifth in the habit of a woman, equipped with a whip and a net, and other instruments, as appears in the following figure. ->[Image: A circular amulet featuring Horus standing on a pedestal. Above him is a winged sun disk. To his left is the name "HORUS" and to his right "THE WORLD" <note>original Latin: MVNDVS</note>. The pedestal contains small hieroglyphic symbols.]<-

By wearing the amulet of Harpocrates <note>The Greek name for the child-god Horus, often associated with silence and secrets</note>, they hoped they would become privy to secrets through various types of divination; that it was religiously worn is sufficiently demonstrated by the small loops <note>for a cord or chain</note>. Through the amulet of Horus, they believed they would gain knowledge of the nature of the world; through the amulet of Apis <note>The sacred bull of Memphis</note>, fertility; through that of Osiris, an abundance of celestial influence; through that of Isis, they hoped to obtain a wealth of all temporal goods pertaining to the Earth and the Nile.

Furthermore, nothing was more common than amulets depicting the Ibis, the Hawk, the Ox, the Dog, the Baboon <note>term: Cynocephalus (dog-headed baboon), sacred to Thoth</note>, the Cat <note>term: Aelurus (from the Greek for cat)</note>, and similar creatures; through all of these, they hoped to obtain private benefits. For example, through the Hawk, clarity of light both for the eyes and the intellect; through the Ox, the enlargement of domestic property; through the Dog, knowledge of sciences and arts; through the Baboon and the Cat, the attraction of the Lunar Divinity.

Among insects, there was also the Scarab, carved into specific and appropriate stones; it was a most powerful amulet, used everywhere to attract the Solar Divinity and established against all diseases of both body and mind. I have been sent a vast quantity of these from every storehouse of antiquity; you may see them, along with other diagrams of various forms and characters, in the *Hieroglyphic Theater* or Volume III, where I have provided the interpretation for each one.

# CLASS XI. HIEROGLYPHIC MAGIC. 449 CHAPTER IV.

Likewise, an image appears, marked **BC**, which is tripartite <note>divided into three parts</note>. On the front face, it represents the figure of a boy sitting with a swollen belly and feet, carrying a whip in each hand and trampling a Crocodile under each foot. On his shoulders sit two Hawks, one on each side. On his head, he wears a headdress marked with the image of a Beetle <note>original: *Scarabaeus*</note>, from the sides of which two idols hang with dangling arms and clenched hands, as appears in figure **A** (which is the scenographic side-view of the figure). On the back part, however, figure **D** is seen, notable for the veil, horns, and globe she carries on her head, with hands outstretched, dispersing rays as if from her entire body. 

But let us see what all these things signify. First, the entire image is of the size shown here, carved from green stone. That it was a portable amulet is sufficiently shown by the small loop or hole **T** in figure **A**, through which a thread was passed. It signifies Horus, the son of Osiris. For Horus—as has been proven by countless authorities in Volume I, Treatise III—was always represented under a boyish form. According to the testimony of Plutarch, he is mystically nothing other than the "machine of the sensible world" <note>the physical universe we can perceive</note>, which the Sun (or Osiris, indicated by the Beetle) governs and moderates with the highest wisdom through the ministry of the Solar Deities (indicated by the two Hawks) and the terrestrial Spirits (indicated by the household gods assisting at the sides).

<margin>
Images **A** and others shown elsewhere above.
</margin>

He is depicted in the form of a boy because the world of created things is continually "rejuvenated," as it were, by innovation. He is painted with a swollen body because he perpetually teems with the offspring and proportion <note>original Greek: *ἀναλογίᾳ* (analogia)</note> of generative things. He tramples a Crocodile under each foot—that is, he restrains the Bebonian or Typhonian malice <note>referring to Set/Typhon, the spirit of chaos</note> so destructive to the world, lest it grow strong. He keeps it in its place with a whip—that is, by the efficacy of his power. They believed that unless he restrained it, the entire world would necessarily perish. All these things are beautifully indicated symbolically through the battles and struggles of Horus and Typhon, about which you may read in Treatise III of Volume I. 

On the back part, however, through figure **D**, Isis (or the Moon) is expressed, as shown by the horns and veil with which she is always displayed. She teems with breasts because she is the mother of all inventions, and the avenger and reviver of Horus after he was extinguished by Typhon. While the world is oppressed by drought and a certain scorching force, she recalls it to balance and life by her moist influence, aptly indicated by the rays. 

<margin>
Other amulets of this kind.
</margin>

And this is the mystical and hieroglyphic significance of the said image; because of the great mysteries hidden beneath it, they judged it to possess the greatest power both for attracting Spirits <note>Genii</note> and for repelling evil ones. Hence, in the Isiac shrines, they would consecrate it with the greatest force of ceremony. For they believed it impossible that the said Deities would not be attracted—as if to a sign fitting for them—by this mysterious image which secretly indicated all their virtues and properties, and that through it, they promised an abundance of all good things and the turning away of evils to those wearing it. And this is the true and sincere interpretation of the chosen amulet.

By this it is indicated that whoever aspires to wisdom must, through frequent contemplation, commit that which he has learned through the tongue of a wise Master deep into the inner chambers of the heart. Truly, you will find these matters treated throughout this Work and in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. These were worn to participate in the influence of both the Solar Spirit and of Ammonian fertility.

<margin>The hieroglyphic Hand is explained.</margin>
There remains to be explained the hieroglyphic Hand marked N & O, the front face of which contains in the middle the face of Jupiter, from whose neck hangs the sacred amulet <term>periamma: a Greek term for a hung charm or pendant</term> of the Isiac Cross <note>the Ankh</note>, in that position of the fingers which you see; at the wrist, however, within a semicircular figure, the image of Isis is seen in a reclining posture, nursing her son Horus, with an attending Dove; by which it is indicated that oaths ought to be made to the Egyptian Jupiter through the sacred Cross of Isis, before the invocation and adjuration of Isis, the nourisher of worldly things, is performed. On the back part of the hand, marked with the letter O, reptiles of every kind are expressed, such as the Frog, Serpent, Lizard, and Tortoise, along with a Lituus <note>a curved ritual staff</note>, a Balance, and a Nilotic vessel. By the Frog, the moist Element is denoted; by the Tortoise, the earthly; by the Lizard, the aerial (because it seems to live on air like the Chameleon); and by the Serpent, the Element of fire is denoted. All these things draw life and nourishment from the great mother of the Gods, Isis, through the harmonic tempering of the Elements, which the Balance and the Lituus express. The adjuration was instituted thus:

> I adjure thee, O Jupiter
> Osiris, by the sacred Cross of Isis, by the archetypal Egg, by the knife
> of Arueris <note>Horus the Elder</note>, by the nourishment which Isis provides to Horus, by the Dove into
> which she was transformed while fleeing the wrath of Typhon, by the Balance of Omphta, by
> the Ophionian Serpent, by the Frog and Lizard of Momphta, by the
> Tortoise of Vulcan, by the Nilotic vessels, and finally by thy beneficent hand
> containing all things, that thou mayest grant what I command.

# CHAPTER V.

->*Concerning the horrific ceremonies with which the Egyptians used to consecrate their Idols in the inner sanctuaries.*<-

<margin>
The inner sanctuaries of the Egyptians in many Districts.
</margin>
<margin>
Clement.
