# CLASS XI. HIEROGLYPHIC MAGIC. CHAPTER X.

...the phases of the Moon, and others finally (lest any piece of astrological superstition be missing) are distributed into the twelve houses of the Heaven. They arrange and dispose these houses with their meanings in exactly the same manner as the astrologers. But I would be wasting time if I were to linger any longer in reviewing such trifles.

<margin>Geomancy of the Arabs is a terrestrial Astrology.</margin>
He who has rightly understood the Astrology of the Egyptians, as handed down in the Sixth Class, will easily gather what should be thought of <term>Geomancy</term><note>A method of divination that interprets markings on the ground or patterns formed by tossed handfuls of soil, rocks, or sand.</note>; and he will clearly see that it is nothing other than a kind of terrestrial Astrology, in which points denote the stars; the arrangements of points denote the constellations; and various classes mark the spaces both of the seven Planets and of the twelve signs of the zodiac and the lunar mansions. But since this Geomancy is an invention of the Arabs, and not particularly closely related to the Egyptian mysteries, I have decided to explain it only briefly.

From Geomancy was born another daughter—as they say, "from a bad egg comes a bad crow"—which the Turks nevertheless value highly. They possess a quite famous book concerning it, which they commonly call <note>original Arabic: قرعة جعفر الصادق</note> *The Lot of Jafar al-Sadiq*, that is, "of the Truthful One." A copy of this sort in my possession begins thus:

<margin>A Turkish divining book.</margin>
> <note>original Arabic: قرعة جعفر الصادق يوخذ عود مربع ويكتب هو الى الاربعة احرف ا ب ج د وارميه ثلثة مرات واطلب الاحرف التي تخرج في مواضعها تجد تحتها ما تطلب</note>
> *The Lot of Jafar al-Sadiq: Let a square piece of wood be taken, and let these four letters A, B, G, D <note>Alif, Ba, Jim, Dal</note> be written upon it; cast it three times, and seek the letters that come up in their places, and you will find beneath them what you seek.* ❀

That is to say: *The Lot of Jafar al-Sadiq: let a square piece of wood be taken, and let these four letters* ا ب ج د *be written; cast it three times, and seek the letters which come out, in their places, and you will find under them what you seek.* By this diabolical art, therefore, divination is established through four characters, ا ب ج د, in this manner: They inscribe these four Arabic characters on cubic dice, one on each side. After a preliminary prayer, they cast this die three times, and record the three letters collected from each throw. Suppose, for example, the first throw is the letter ب <note>B</note>, the second ج <note>G</note>, and the third د <note>D</note>; they then look for these three found letters ب ج د in the said book, and having read the Arabic text, they come to a knowledge of their fated lot. For they simply believe that what is related there will happen to you. But let us leave these formulas and arts, which contain absolutely no learning in themselves, as they are not at all consistent with our purpose. Nevertheless, at this point, something ought to have been said about the remaining arts, such as <term>Chiromancy</term><note>Palm reading.</note>, <term>Metoposcopy</term><note>Divination via the lines of the forehead.</note>, <term>Necromancy</term><note>Communication with the dead.</note>, and other monsters of superstition; but since we have chosen to propose in this place only those things which drew their origin immediately from the Egyptians, and have been touched upon by no one else that I know of, we have deliberately decided to omit the others.

<margin>The cunning of the Demon.</margin>
There are no truces, no peace, just as there is no limit to his hatred or envy. The pride of the enemy of God <note>Referring to Lucifer or Satan</note> always ascends, his malice grows, and his cruelty gains strength. The ancient architect of crimes always strives for the same ends; he leaves nothing inaccessible and nothing untried. In every age, he draws from the same quiver a primary lure: those arts that are as inquisitive as they are superstitious, and those many foolish inventions of Demons that drive the minds of mortals to madness—all of which are gathered under the name of Magic. We know of nothing worshipped with divine honor by the Egyptians and their heirs in past times that does not also seem to be worshipped in the present day, as was shown at length in the final treatise of the First Volume. Egypt never devised anything regarding the magic of symbols <note>original: "characteristicam Magiam," referring to the use of occult signs or sigils</note> that we do not see fully realized in this time, especially through the daring of wicked men. Therefore, whoever glories in the dignity of the Christian name ought to take primary care here: that in philosophizing, he does not seek to know beyond the boundaries of the most holy Canons prescribed for us. Rather, in doubtful matters exposed to the danger of Satanic illusion, he should discern cautiously and circumspectly what is to be

# FABIO CHIGI, CARDINAL OF THE HOLY ROMAN CHURCH,

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial E featuring scrolling floral and vine motifs within a rectangular frame.</image-desc>
<margin>The subject of metaphysical theology.</margin>
As I ponder more deeply the most eminent virtues of your soul—which I have known well for many years to be destined by divine providence for nothing but the most sublime heights—three things in particular occur to me which might contend among themselves for the leadership of your praises. On one hand, your learning in the <term>liberal arts</term><note>The "bonae artes" or "good arts," referring to the classical curriculum of grammar, rhetoric, philosophy, etc.</note> claims the first place for itself; <margin>Sweetness of character and humanity.</margin> on the other hand, that sweetness of character, tempered by both the highest kindness and a singular humanity, commands that learning follow it; <margin>Admirable piety.</margin> there also urges your proven piety, conspicuous in the moderation of your life and boiling over with a zeal for divine matters, which, being as far removed as possible from every shadow of ambition, and thus wrapping itself in its own virtue, happens to be all the more admirable. <margin>Created Cardinal of the Holy Roman Church by Pope Innocent X.</margin> This consensus of virtues has now appeared all the more illustrious since the Supreme Pontiff himself, Innocent X, delighted by their splendor, conferred upon you—who were thinking of no such thing—an eminent place by admitting you into the College of the Most Holy Senate <note>The College of Cardinals</note>, not only to adorn your virtue, but so that you also might be no small ornament to the Senate of the <term>Purple-clad Fathers</term><note>A traditional title for Cardinals, referring to the color of their robes.</note>. Since, therefore, it is your duty as a Prince of the Church to weigh sacred dogmas, to distinguish the heterodox from the orthodox, and to conform the minds of mortals to all holiness through the study of sacred institutions; <margin>A most wise judge of divine matters.</margin> certainly I have found no one to whom I might dedicate this argument of mine concerning the Theology of the Egyptians by better right than to you, the most wise judge of divine matters: being especially persuaded of this, that I shall gain much and be greatly indebted to you, if you deign to accept this discourse of mine, such as it is. <margin>Metaphysical theology etc. is not contained within narrow limits.</margin> For you are not one who contains yourself within the limits of philosophy and theology alone, but having wandered far wider through the poets, historians, and polymaths, you have finally achieved this: that you both think rightly and speak eruditely concerning whatever is brought forward. Therefore, you will gain nothing, or very little, by reading my works, except insofar as you, loving the trifles of a client most devoted to your virtues, allow them to be something in your sight, and thus feel the same about my writings as that man felt about similar things:

> A mole upon the face was the cause of its beauty. <note>original: "In facie naevus caussa decoris erat." A poetic sentiment suggesting that small flaws can enhance overall beauty.</note>

# CLASS XII.

## Metaphysical Theosophy, or Hieroglyphic Theology. <note>Theosophy here refers to "divine wisdom" (theos-sophia), the study of God through symbolic means.</note>

### PREFACE.

<margin>Egyptian Theology.</margin>
<image-desc>A large decorative drop cap 'A' at the start of the first paragraph, featuring ornate leafy and vine-like scrolls within a square frame.</image-desc>
WE APPROACH at last that secret Ark of Egyptian Theology, the end and goal of the entire hieroglyphic doctrine. Whoever penetrates this rightly will not only look up to, but also greatly marvel at, that wonderful sublimity and excellence of mind in those first initiators <note>original: "mystagogis," those who lead others into sacred mysteries</note>. One wonders how they were able to reach such a height of divine mysteries supported only by the aid of the light of nature. Thus, one is compelled to confess that in those deep shadows of Paganism, the Greatest and Best God—lest the entire knowledge of God handed down by the earliest Fathers utterly perish—imbued the lofty efforts of certain men devoted to the study of wisdom with a certain extraordinary and supernatural illumination. By this, in the manner of the Sibyls <note>Ancient prophetesses believed to have spoken divine truths without fully understanding them</note>, they spoke of things which they themselves did not know. <margin>Trismegistus, the Prince of Egyptian Theologians.</margin> Among the other priests of ancient wisdom, however, that Mercury Trismegistus holds the most important place. He was called "Theut" by the Egyptians and "Trismegistus" by the Greeks, <margin>Suidas.</margin> either because of the three powers in the divine nature first observed by him (as Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedist</note> maintains), <margin>Why he is called Trismegistus.</margin> or because of his triple status in life. For, by the tradition of all writers, he was the greatest Philosopher, the greatest Priest, and the greatest King, as we have demonstrated at length in Book 1 of the *Pamphilian Obelisk*. Just as he surpassed all previous philosophers in sharpness of intellect and excellence of learning, so he excelled all priests in dignity, greatness, and the worship of divine things; and having attained royal dignity, he obscured all the glory of previous Egyptian Kings through his administration of laws, his constant course of justice and equity, and the glory of his achievements. Among the philosophers, he was the first to turn from physics and mathematics to the contemplation of divine things; he was the first to dispute most wisely concerning the majesty of God, the order of spirits <note>original: "Daemonum," referring to intermediary spirits or celestial beings, not necessarily evil</note>, and the migrations of souls; he is deservedly the first Author of Theology. <margin>Orpheus, and other ancient theologians.</margin> Following him, Orpheus held the second rank of ancient Theology; Aglaophemus was initiated into the sacred rites of Orpheus; Pythagoras succeeded Aglaophemus in Theology; and Philolaus, the teacher of Plato, followed him. Thus, a sect of true ancient Theology, consistent with itself in all respects and composed of six theologians in a wonderful order, took its beginning from Mercury and was fully perfected by Plato. <margin>Iamblichus. The Theological books of Trismegistus.</margin> Moreover, according to the testimony of Iamblichus, Mercury first wrote many books pertaining to the contemplation of divine matters, which he also expressed in hieroglyphic letters. These were so filled with secret mysteries and oracles that he obtained the name not only of Philosopher, but also of Prophet. He seemed to have shown in clear words the ruin of the ancient religion, the rise of a new faith, the coming of Christ, the future judgment, the resurrection of the age, the glory of the blessed, <margin>St. Augustine.</margin> and the punishments of sinners; so much so that St. Augustine doubted whether he performed many of these things through skill in the stars or through the revelation of spirits; but Lactantius [placed] him among the Sibyls and Prophets...

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER I.

<margin>The author’s protestation in explaining the Theology of the Egyptians.</margin>
...he does not hesitate to enumerate. Therefore, I have undertaken to treat this Hieroglyphic Theology of Hermes <note>original: "Mercurij"; referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Egypt</note> in this place, as far as the weakness of my talent permits. While I do this, I wish nothing to be said, done, or explained here except according to the mind and opinion of the ancient authors; I intend to fulfill all the parts of a faithful Oedipus <note>A metaphor for a riddle-solver, referring to the hero who solved the Sphinx's riddle</note>. For whatever we are about to bring forward concerning the Holy Trinity, the soul and spirit of the World, the origin of Gods, Demons, and souls, the influences of divine Ideas into the lower World, the transmigration of souls, sacrifices and their reasoning, and similar matters—let the reader know that all these things must be read cautiously. For most are entirely contrary to the Orthodox faith and provided the first arch-heretics with the material and occasion for founding most foul dogmas, as <margin>Livius.</margin> *Livio Galante* proves at length in his *Platonic* Harmony and Orthodox Doctrine. Therefore, if any light of truth shines out in them, we shall consider it not so much a true exposition as a certain foreshadowing of Orthodox doctrine, brought forth by the sublimity of the natural light they possessed and the excellence of their talent; or, if they occasionally reason nobly about the nature of God, we shall judge that they snatched it by a supernatural concurrence of the Divine Will rather than comprehended it, as we said of the *Sibyls* <note>Ancient prophetesses believed by some Christians to have foreseen Christ</note>. Therefore, I wish all things to be said and explained only insofar as they serve the hieroglyphic doctrine, while we show not so much what they taught, but what they ought to have taught.

## CHAPTER I.

### On the origin and propagation of Ethnic <note>Gentile or Pagan</note> Theology.

<margin>Statius. Fear is the origin of Ethnic Theology.</margin>
*Statius* <note>A Roman poet</note> spoke rightly and wisely: *Fear first created Gods in the world*; for those primeval mortals, living by the judgment of the law of nature, heard many things from the first Patriarchs of the world concerning the supreme majesty of God, the supreme rigor of justice demonstrated in *Adam* and his descendants, the punishments for sins, and His other chastisements and vengeances. Struck by a certain panic fear, while they held all things suspect due to the hidden presence of the Divine Power, they gradually instituted sacrifices and various rites to appease the Deity. But when, by a certain indiscriminate knowledge, they perceived that God was in all things; and as the divine union was gradually torn and divided according to the nature and number of natural subjects, they fashioned as many Deities in the world as they recognized grades of being. <margin>The origin of Idolatry.</margin> From this it happened that they first pursued the Sun, then the Moon, and the other stars—both fixed and wandering—with singular worship as the habitations of the Divine Power. Afterward, turning to the elementary sphere, some placed fire, others air, some water, and many the earth among the Deities. Thus, with superstition pushing upon superstition, it shortly happened that they established as many Deities as there were creatures to be seen, and finally filled the whole world with this futile *Idol-mania*. Since these things have been declared at length throughout this work, I do not wish to dwell on them longer. <margin>The origin of Auguries.</margin> From here, with the Devil secretly insinuating himself into their operations, they gradually observed the movements of animals and the flights of birds—direct, oblique, above, and below—aroused by the demonstration of good or evil outcomes, as from those...

<margin>The origin of Astrology.</margin>
<margin>Trismegistus delivers a new Theology to the Egyptians.</margin>

Furthermore, when they more curiously scrutinized the rising and setting of the stars as if they were the movements of Deities, from that source Astrology emanated as the basis and foundation of all Idolatry, superstition, and divinations; and thus they adopted everything encountered by the senses as instruments for their divinations, as was related in the preceding Class <note>Kircher uses "Class" to refer to major thematic divisions of his book</note>. Therefore, when the World was imbued with this almost total blindness and ignorance, Hermes Trismegistus—having been instructed in the more divine dogmas of the first Patriarchs—began a new Theology concerning the one, true, and good God, and the arrangement and order of Angels and Demons. He did this so that the World would not be plunged into the ultimate abyss of darkness by so many fictions of empty Gods. He veiled this theology in certain clever symbols devised for that purpose, making it known only to Priests distinguished by wisdom and long experience, but entirely impassable to the uneducated and the superstitious common folk, carving it into stone against all the injuries of time. And these are those famous Theological books written by Hermes on Obelisks, according to the testimony of Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on Egyptian mysteries</note>; from these, Pythagoras and Plato drew the first foundations of their own doctrine. These obelisks, surviving in Rome to this very day, are admired as a document of ancient wisdom; I shall review their secret meanings in this Class only summarily, reserving a more detailed interpretation for Volume III.

## C H A P T E R II.

### Concerning the nature of God as He can be considered abstractly and inwardly, and concerning the definition of God and His various attributes exhibited hieroglyphically, according to the mind of the Egyptians.

<margin>The Platonic saying concerning the knowledge of God.</margin>
**I**t is a Platonic, and indeed most celebrated exclamation, that God is difficult to find and to know; for he asserts thus in the *Timaeus*: *To find the Maker and Father of the World is difficult, and when you have found Him, it is impossible to declare or speak of Him to the common people.* Since this is most true, the Egyptians therefore believed God should be worshipped by silence alone and intrinsic devotion.

<margin>Why the Egyptians painted and sculpted Harpocrates.</margin>

Wherefore, for the same reason, the Egyptians introduce God with a truly most appropriate symbol: sitting upon the aquatic lotus—which is a tree, according to the testimony of Iamblichus in his *Book on the Mysteries*. By this they signify that God, in his sovereignty, transcends the worldly mud <note>A play on words in Latin between "lotus" and "lutus" (mud)</note>, and does not touch it while governing, but holds a sovereignty that is entirely intellectual and empyrean <note>the highest heaven of pure fire or light</note>. For all things in the Lotus are round, both the fruit and the leaves; by which is signified the circular action of the divine mind, which always maintains itself in the same manner. God himself, therefore, exists within himself above this action, surpassing such sovereignty—holy, venerable, and resting entirely within himself; which is indeed signified by the act of sitting. But so that all these things may be explained more at length,

<margin>God can be considered according to those things which belong to him from within, and from without.</margin>

It must be noted that God can be considered in a twofold manner: either from within, and insofar as he is far removed from all fellowship of created things, covered by the inaccessible hiding place of his infinite essence alone; or insofar as he relates to creatures—or what is the same thing—insofar as he has unfolded from the inner chambers of his darkness and offers himself to be considered in created things. What the Egyptians felt regarding both modes of consideration must now be explained.

## **The Definition of GOD.**

<margin>What God is according to the Egyptians.</margin>

<margin>God is a Circle according to Trismegistus.</margin>

God is a circle, exceeding every mathematical periphery of a circle by an infinite interval. God is a circle, whose center of the periphery—that is, his internal essence—is equal to immensity, whose diameter coincides as one with the center and the circumference. # CHAPTER II. 502 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Aristotle.</margin>
...has the boundaries of its own being; but the circumference truly exceeds the limits of even infinite Worlds. In this circle, whatever is contained is entirely equal to the container; and as the Egyptian Theology of Aristotle <note>original: "Aristotelis Theologia" — Kircher refers to a Neoplatonic work falsely attributed to Aristotle in the Renaissance, which heavily influenced mystical geometry.</note> holds, whatever angles, sides, lines, and surfaces, or other imaginable things exist in other circles and figures, are present in this one; yet it is itself indivisible and immeasurable. From it, all lines—that is, the essences and forms of things—originate, and into the same they return, as if to the center of all nature. But let us explain these things a little more clearly.

<margin>The property of the Sphere and the Circle.</margin>
<margin>God is compared to the sphere and the circle.</margin>
It must be understood that in an infinite sphere, the three greatest lines—of length, breadth, and depth—concur in the center. However, the center of the greatest sphere of all (as we have taught in *Hieroglyphic Geometry*) is equal to both the diameter and the circumference. Therefore, the center must necessarily be equal to the three lines (since those three greatest lines of length, breadth, and depth are nothing other than diameters in the sphere). Indeed, in our way of conceiving it, the center is all three of these dimensions: length, breadth, and depth. Thus, it is necessary that the Greatest, the Simplest, and the Infinite coexist. For the length, breadth, and depth that are in God are one: the simplest and the greatest. Just as the center is indivisible and precedes all length, breadth, and depth, it is the end of all those things, as well as the middle; for in an infinite sphere, the solidity and the circumference are exactly the same. Furthermore, just as the infinite sphere is entirely in act <note>term: "in act" (in actu) — a philosophical term meaning fully realized or operational, as opposed to "in potential."</note> and most simple, so the Greatest is entirely in act in the simplest manner. And just as the sphere (as said in the *Geometry*) is the "act" of the line, the triangle, and the circle, so the Greatest is the act of all things. Therefore, every actual existence derives whatever actuality it has from Him, and every actual existence exists in act only insofar as it is within that infinite act. Hence, He is the Greatest, the "form of forms," and the "form of being," or the most actual entity. Whence Parmenides, considering these things, rightly <margin>What God is according to Parmenides.</margin> and subtly inferred: *God is He, for whom to be anything that is, is to be everything that is.* Therefore, just as the sphere is the ultimate perfection of figures, than which none is greater, so the Greatest is the most perfect perfection of all. Thus, everything imperfect is most perfect within Him; just as an infinite line is a sphere, and within it, curvature is straightness, composition is simplicity, diversity is identity, and "otherness" is unity. For it cannot be grasped how any imperfection could exist in God, since in Him imperfection exists as nothing other than infinite perfection, and possibility exists as infinite act. <margin>The sphere of the divine essence is the measure of all things.</margin> It is therefore clear how this sphere of the divine essence is the single most simple and most adequate measure of the entire Universe and of all things existing in the Universe; because in Him, the whole is not greater than its part, just as an infinite sphere is not greater than an infinite line. God, therefore, is the one most simple "reason" <note>original: "ratio" — can mean proportion, logic, or fundamental principle.</note> of the entire Universe. And just as after infinite circulations a spherical solidity finally emerges, so God is the greatest and simplest measure of all circulations; for all life-giving power, motion, and intelligence are from Him, in Him, and through Him. With Him, a single eighth sphere <note>note: In the old geocentric model, the "eighth sphere" was the realm of the fixed stars.</note> is no smaller than infinite ones, because He is the end of all motions, in whom every motion, as if in...

<margin>The Circle held in honor among the Egyptians.</margin>
Hence, not without reason, they held the circular figure in such honor that there is scarcely any hieroglyphic representing something divine that is not prefigured by this circular shape. Thus, you may see it inserted everywhere upon the heads of Gods and Deities; for they freely used mathematical figures of this kind to express the divine nature, endowed with a certain wonderful property, and the simplest diagrams removed from all mixture of mortal things, suitable for representing the simplest and most abstract thing of all, such as God is. But these things having been duly proposed, let us now see and examine the attributes by which they described God.

## § II.
### The Attributes of GOD.

<margin>God is called Mind by Trismegistus.</margin>
**GOD** is first called Mind by Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the wisdom of Thoth.</note>: 
> *Mind (I say, to use his words) and reason embracing itself, free from all bodily mass, foreign to error, impassible, intangible, self-assisting, purifying, and preserving all things, whose rays are goodness, Truth, the principal light, and the first form of souls.*

Hence, to Asclepius, asking what God might be, he responds:
> *That which is none of these things, yet is the cause of them all, present indeed to the whole, present also to each individual, nor does He permit anything not to be; all things from these which are, have been produced; but from nothing, nothing comes forth: for those things which least exist have no nature by which they might be made; on the contrary, those things which are, have no nature through which they might at some time not exist.*

But let us see by what hieroglyphics Trismegistus displayed the divine nature and its attributes.

# CHAPTER II. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

We shall explain the interpretation of the hieroglyphics in the third volume.
<margin>Trismegistus <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary "Thrice-Great" sage believed by Kircher to be a contemporary of Moses and the source of ancient Egyptian wisdom.</note></margin>
For whatever Trismegistus relates concerning God in the *Pimander* and *Asclepius* <note>Two of the most famous texts in the Corpus Hermeticum, a collection of Greek philosophical writings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus.</note> is nothing other than what is contained at the beginning of the Obelisks and in the aforementioned Bembine Tablet or Isiac Table, depicted through a wondrous metamorphosis of images.
<margin>Trismegistus describes God in five ways.</margin>
For in Trismegistus, we find God described in five ways: first, through certain absolutely fitting attributes; second, through negation; third, through analogy and metaphor; fourth, through contradictions; and fifth, through relation. All those among the Pythagoreans and Platonists who followed him have solemnly confirmed the same. For first, in the *Pimander*, he says that God is before all things, God is all beings and non-beings, God has all things within Himself, God was able to make all things, He holds all things in Himself, preserves all things, and turns all things back to Himself. God is therefore the first of all; for thus he says in the booklet *That Nothing Perishes*:

> *God is truly the first of all, is unbegotten, and the craftsman of the universe.*

He provides the reason for this statement: that something is called "absolutely first" if nothing exists before it; since nothing is before God, He is therefore the first of all.
<margin>God is compared to the Phoenix.</margin>
Hence, according to the testimony of Horus <note>Likely referring to Horapollo, the author of a 5th-century treatise on hieroglyphics.</note>, they expressed this not poorly through the Phoenix, as no one knows its origin, and it alone is the author of its own life and its own generator. Moreover, he proves that nothing existed before God as follows: If something existed before God, it is either more powerful than God Himself, or equal, or weaker. But it is none of these; therefore [nothing is before Him]. The minor premise is proven: Not more powerful, for if anything were more powerful before God, then the nature of God would necessarily cease to be, since He would lack something by which He is not the most powerful. Not equal, because if they are equal, both will be first beings; but this is impossible, since
<margin>Trismegistus held the highest conception of God.</margin>
in every genus there is only one that is greatest. Not weaker, since it could not be called "first"; for whoever says "first" also places it before a second and a third. All these things are beautifully demonstrated in the *Theology of Aristotle* <note>A Neoplatonic text falsely attributed to Aristotle in the Middle Ages and Renaissance.</note> according to the mind of the Egyptians, and they are in accordance with the mind of Plato. By similar reasoning, he proves that God is the first cause—indeed, the cause of causes—and the first mover; which Plato, Aristotle, and the rest of the Platonic theologians asserted, following Mercury <note>Mercury is the Roman equivalent of the Greek Hermes.</note>. But let us hear the very words of Mercury, who describes God through negation in the *Pimander*:

> *The Craftsman fabricated the entire World by the word, not by hands; but you, think of Him as always present, acting upon all things, the one God establishing all things by His will; for that is His body, not tangible, not visible, nor like any other; for it is neither fire, nor water, nor air, nor even spirit, but all things hang from Him; the Good is such that it belongs only to Himself.*

And a little later, he depicts His invisible presence in all things thus:

> *Lest the principal name of God be lacking to you, do not be ignorant that what seems hidden to most is actually clear; for if it were nowhere manifest, it would be nothing at all. Whatever offers itself to the sight is created; but what is hidden is eternal; nor is there a need for it to appear, since it never ceases to be; He places other things before the eyes, but He Himself remains secret, as one who enjoys eternal life; He brings all things plainly into the light, yet hides in the inner sanctums, for He is the only unbegotten one, incomprehensible to the imagination; but since all things become clear through Him, He shines through all and in all, and appears especially to those to whom He wished to communicate His name.*

And a little later:

> *For there is nothing in all of nature, which He Himself...*

<summary>Kircher discusses the Hermetic philosophy of God as the "First Cause" and "Craftsman," arguing that Egyptian hieroglyphics on obelisks and the Isiac Table encode these complex theological concepts. He cites the Pimander to show how God is understood through both His absolute power and His invisible, eternal nature.</summary>

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER II.

<margin><unclear>The wisdom of Trismegistus</unclear></margin>
...though he himself is not those things; he is indeed all things that are; he is also those things that least exist; those things which are, he has brought forth into the light; those things which are not, he has hidden within himself. Just as nothing can be made without a maker, so you must judge of God: unless he is always acting in all things, it is impossible for anything to exist, whether in heaven, the air, the earth, the sea, in the whole World, or in any tiny particle of the World, both in that which is and in that which does not exist. This God is better than any name; he is again the most powerful of all; he is visible to the mind, yet present to the eyes; he is incorporeal, yet, if I may say so, multi-corporeal; for there is nothing in bodies that he himself is not; for he alone exists as all things. Furthermore, he has all names, because he is the one Father; yet he has no name, because he is the Father of all. Who then shall praise you? One placed above you, or below you? Where shall I turn my eyes to praise you? Upward or downward? Inward or outward? There is no motion, no place around you, nor any other thing among all that exists; but in you are all things, from you are all things; you provide all things, and finally, you receive nothing, for you possess all things; and that which you do not have is itself nothing. When, O Father, shall I praise you? We are not able to grasp your time or your moment. In what matter especially shall I sing your praises? In those things which you have created? Or rather in those which you have not created? Perhaps in those which you have brought out of darkness into the light? Or in those which still lie hidden in secret places? Through what, finally, shall I sing hymns to your Divinity? In such a song of praise, shall I be my own master, or shall I become another? You are surely whatever I am; you are whatever I do; you are whatever I say; for you are all things, and there is nothing else besides you. That which is not, you are; you are everything that is born, and everything that is never born: the understanding Mind, the creating Father, the God who effects good and makes all things good. <note>original: "Hæc Mercur." — These are the words of Mercury/Hermes.</note>

<margin>A hieroglyph explaining the nature and property of God.</margin>
Who, I ask, can find for us a Christian who can bring forth higher and more correct thoughts concerning God? Who can find a Theologian who can feel more profoundly regarding the divinity? Certainly, all these things are found expressed most appropriately in the hieroglyphics through the image visible with the face of an Ibis, on a throne variously adorned, with a head-dress <note>original: "tutulo"</note> decorated with various symbols, and an Isimorphic scepter. For through the figure of the Ibis—a most lively, keen-sighted, and swift animal—what else do they signify but liveliness, or rather the very life of all things, and the swiftness of God, who is free from all motion because he sees all things as present? He searches and penetrates all things; nothing of the things hidden in the Universe escapes his eyes. What is meant by the seat, if not power over all things and eternal rest? What by the Isimorphic scepter <note>A scepter shaped like the goddess Isis, representing the receptive or "passive" principle of nature.</note>, if not the most absolute power and dominion over all things? For just as Osiris is the active principle of all things, so Isis is the passive principle. What is meant by the <term>flame-circle-wing-shaped</term> <note>original: "φλογο-κυκλο-πτερόμορφον" (phlogo-kyklo-pteromorphon). A composite Greek term describing a crown made of fire, circles, and wings.</note> head-dress, equipped with fire, a circle, serpents, and wings, if not eternity through the circle; the light of light through the fire; the life of lives through the serpents; and the swiftness of operations through the wings, he who caused all things by his will alone? But all these things will be treated more fully in the Obe—

<header>CHAPTER III. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.</header>

<margin>The Egyptian Priests, as suppliants to God, invoked the darkness.</margin>
...you will find explained in their proper place, both in the Pamphilian Obelisk <note>A reference to Kircher’s 1650 work on the Roman obelisk in the Piazza Navona</note> and in Volume III. Hence the Priests, in the mystic inner-sanctums of their rites, when about to pray to God, were accustomed to come forward into the midst of those same ornaments and hieroglyphic figures with which they had expressed the image of God, invoking darkness three times—that is, the impenetrable gloom of the divinity. By this very act, they were obscurely indicating that they were presenting, through hidden symbols and mystic wrappings of things, Him whom they could pronounce with no eloquence of speech. For they believed that symbols of this kind, known to God alone and acting as mirrors of His divine nature and essence, possessed more power than many long-winded words. They also believed they would adhere more intimately to God through this hidden display of symbols than by the utterance of voices and words that would soon perish. Anyone who aptly combines these details one by one will recognize that the Platonists received all these things word-for-word from Hermes <note>Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the origin of Egyptian wisdom</note>. But of these matters, we speak throughout this entire Work. Having premised these things, let us now see how the Egyptians displayed the relationship and the triple essence of God.

### CHAPTER III.

->Concerning the relative Attributes of GOD.<-

<margin>The relative attributes of God.</margin>
<margin>The Egyptians had an obscure knowledge of the Trinity.</margin>
That the Egyptians had some obscure knowledge of the Most Holy Trinity will become clear from those things which we shall bring forward shortly. Indeed, I do not believe this flowed from any other source than from the branch of successive tradition from the first Patriarchs. While Hermes, that most curious searcher of divine matters, enjoyed this tradition over a span of many years, it is no wonder that he fished out many lessons of divine science from them. He carved these for posterity as the highest and inaccessible sacraments, fortified against the rashness of the profane by hieroglyphics on stones intended to last forever—as has been copiously proved in the Pamphilian Obelisk and in Class II of this Volume. However, since the human intellect can by no means bear such a great and impenetrable light of the divine nature unless it is supported by the light of true faith, it is also no wonder that Hermes, lacking this light, did not correctly explain this mystery in some places. At times, he attributes three forms of existence to God, now calling them <note>original: "Τρεῖς δυνάμεις"</note> *three powers*, according to the testimony of Suidas <note>A 10th-century Byzantine encyclopedia</note> (for which reason he was also called Trismegistus, or "Thrice-Great"). Nevertheless, it cannot be denied that by adopting reasoning concerning this first and highest of all mysteries, he deservedly surpassed all subsequent Gentile Philosophers and Theologians by many leagues. For he describes the three <term>hypostases</term> <note>The distinct persons or underlying realities of the Trinity</note> in divine matters so clearly and distinctly that many doubt whether such things were uttered by some Christian Philosopher of the first century, or by a Gentile of the same century instructed by Christians. Certainly, Saint Augustine, marvelling at the writings of this Author, openly confesses that he, seized not only by human genius but by the inspiration of the Divine Spirit, brought forth so many and such great things unknown even to the Hebrews themselves, and known only to the Patriarchs. Thus, first is the Father through Himself, whom he elsewhere calls Mind; elsewhere, as above...

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. 307 CHAPTER III.

<margin>Trismegistus makes mention of the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit.</margin>
We have seen both Lord and Father, God, Source, Life, Power, Light, Mind, and Spirit; in which words mention is made not only of the Father himself, but also of the Son and of the Holy Spirit. "For of all things," he says, "he is Lord, and God, and source, and life, and power, and light, and mind, and spirit." <note>original Greek: Πάντων γάρ, inquit, κύριος, καὶ Θεός, καὶ πηγή, καὶ ζωή, καὶ δύναμις, καὶ φῶς, καὶ νοῦς, καὶ πνεῦμα.</note> But what is more admirable than this description? ***The Monad begat the Monad, and reflected love into itself.*** <note>The "Monad" refers to the "One" or the ultimate divine unity.</note> Where, by the "begetting Monad," he undoubtedly meant the Father; by the "begotten Monad," the Son; and by the "Love" proceeding from both, the Holy Spirit. He confirms this doctrine in the *Pimander* <note>The *Pimander* (or Poimandres) is the first and most famous text in the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom.</note> with these words: ***There was one sole intellectual light, namely the Father before the intellectual light; the union of this was nothing other than the Spirit containing all things.*** Who does not see in this that the first intellectual light is understood as the Father, the second as the Son, and the union as the Holy Spirit? The Greek words are: "In the One was intellectual light before intellectual light, and each was entirely luminous, and there was nothing else then but unity, and a spirit containing all things." <note>original Greek: Ἐν μόνῳ φῶς νοερὸν προφωτὸς νοεροῦ, καὶ ἑκάστη πᾶσα φωτεινός, καὶ οὐδὲν ἕτερον ἦν ἢ τότε ἑνότης, καὶ πνεῦμα πάντα περιέχον.</note> Regarding the second person, he also calls him the Son of God and the Luminous Word. "And the Mind, the luminous Word, is the Son of God." <note>original Greek: Ὁ δὲ νοῦς, φωτεινὸς λόγος, υἱὸς Θεοῦ.</note> ***For the Mind is the luminous Word, the Son of God.*** "For they are not divided from one another, for the union of these is life." <note>original Greek: Μὴ γὰρ δίστασαν ἀπ' ἀλλήλων, ἕνωσις γὰρ τούτων ἡ ζωή.</note> <margin>Trismegistus's doctrine on the Trinity.</margin> ***For these do not stand apart from one another, but the union of all is life.*** And from these things it is clear that Mercury <note>The author uses "Mercury" (Hermes) and "Trismegistus" interchangeably.</note> in this place did not only foreshadow the divine hypostases <note><term>hypostases</term>: A theological term for the distinct persons of the Trinity who share one essence.</note>, but also showed in the following words how these three persons produced all external works out of nothing into the light: "The Word of God leaped forth from the downward-tending elements into the pure creation of nature, and was united with the Creator, for he was of one substance." <note>original Greek: Ἐπήδησε ὁ θεὸς ἐκ τῶν κατωφερῶν στοιχείων, ὁ τοῦ Θεοῦ λόγος, εἰς τὸ καθαρὸν τῆς φύσεως δημιούργημα, καὶ ἑνώθη τῷ δημιουργῷ, ὁμοούσιος γὰρ ἦν.</note> ***The Word of God leaped forth immediately from the elements borne below, into the pure handiwork of God, and unites itself to the Creator Mind, for it was consubstantial.*** <note><term>consubstantial</term>: Meaning "of the same substance" (Greek: *homoousios*), the key term from the Council of Nicaea to describe the relationship between Father and Son.</note>

Here he exhibits in open words the Father through the "Creator Mind," the Son through the "Word of God," and the Spirit through the "union" by which the Word of God is united to the Creator Mind; and lest anyone believe this happens by some accidental union, he adds the words *homoousios gar en*: for the Word of God is consubstantial with the Creator Mind, of the same nature, essence, and substance. Since, indeed, the Word does not differ from the Creator Mind, as he asserts above, but is united to it, certainly this union of union, which is the Holy Spirit, must also be the same as the Father and the Son regarding nature and substance. Furthermore, he openly teaches that this first Mind is the generator and founder, not by hand, but by the word, in these words: "The intellectual nature of the word is a generative and creative nature; the Creator Father made the whole world, not with hands, but by the word." <note>original Greek: Φύσις δὲ νοερὰ αὐτῷ λόγῳ, φύσις ἐστὶ γεννητικὴ καὶ δημιουργική· Ἐν πάντα κόσμον ἐποίησεν ὁ δημιουργὸς Πατήρ, οὐ χερσίν, ἀλλὰ λόγῳ.</note> ***The intellectual nature of the Word is a generative and founding nature, and the Creator Father made the whole World, not with hands, but by the Word.***

<margin>The Theologians of the Heathens learned their Theology from Trismegistus.</margin>
And these are the pronouncements of Mercury concerning the Holy Trinity, from whom all posterity—Orpheus, Pythagoras, Plato, Zoroaster—derived most of their own ideas, as we have demonstrated in the *Sphinx Mystagoga*. <note>A reference to another of the author's works, likely Athanasius Kircher's *Oedipus Aegyptiacus* or related volumes.</note> For Zoroaster also calls God the "paternal Monad," and the Monad begetting two; "For the Monad is extended, which begets two;" <note>original Greek: Ταναὴ γάρ ἐστι μόνας, ἢ δύο γεννᾷ</note> <margin>Zoroaster's opinion on the Trinity.</margin> "For a Dyad sits beside him;" <note>original Greek: Δύας γὰρ παρὰ τῷ κάθηται</note> For the Dyad sits with this one. Thus the first generation of the extended Monad is the Dyad, which Dyad with the Monad makes a Triad, as he indicates in these words: "For in every world a triad shines, over which a monad rules." <note>original Greek: Παντὶ γὰρ ἐν κόσμῳ λάμπει τριάς, ἧς μόνας ἄρχει.</note> ***For in the whole World a triad shines, whose Prince is the Monad.*** For all things serve these three principles. "For they come and all things serve." <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἔρχονται εἶσι δ' οὐλεύουσι ἅπαντα.</note> For "The Father perfected all things, and delivered them to the second Mind:" <note>original Greek: Πάντα γὰρ ἐξετέλεσε πατήρ, καὶ νῷ παρέδωκε δευτέρῳ</note> ***The Father perfected all things, and delivered them to the second Mind***: which is the Son. But the third principle he calls the boundary of the paternal depth, as [above...]

But let us see how the transmitted doctrine agrees with the hieroglyphics, by which symbols Hermes expressed the aforementioned Sacraments of divinity. First, since the three forms in God (as the Egyptians call them, which the Orthodox call "hypostases" <note>The distinct persons of the Trinity: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit.</note>) are known under a unity of nature;

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a winged disk or globe, with a serpent entwined around it and its head visible at the top.</image-desc>

he placed a winged circle produced with a serpent as a symbol of this so secret mystery, as is evident from the Pamphilian Obelisk and from the Isiac Tablet (or Table), where it is seen placed above every single idol, as will be seen in its proper place. By the **circle**, he signified the pure form of divinity, the Eternal Power, immense, and abstracted from all the filth of matter; by the **serpent**, he aptly noted the second form of divinity (for the serpent is a most lively animal, and according to Horus <note>Referring to Horapollo, an author of a treatise on hieroglyphs.</note>, consists of no member except the mouth) or the Word of God, and the second Creator-Mind; by the **wings** fixed to the globe, he fitly expressed the third form of divinity, the Spirit pervading all things; and in this way, through the whole joined from the three and considered in the manner of a single entity, he indicated the divine nature consisting of three distinct powers. Truly, I would wish the curious reader to weigh the more abundant exposition of all these things, established by innumerable authorities, in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, Book 3, folio 400. Again, Hermes expressed all these things by an equal ratio through the **equilateral triangle**, yet with this difference: that in the circle he indicated the triune divine nature without any respect to creatures, but in the triangle he indicated the triune nature of divinity insofar as it implies a certain relation to creatures, with a wonderful force of genius; although both the circle and the triangle are entirely the same and one in the consideration of the divine nature; which I have now decided to explain a little more at length, so that that admirable vigor of genius and intellect in Hermes may become more clearly known.

The equilateral triangle as a symbol of the Deity.
</margin>

The circle is a figure of union and perfect simplicity, as was shown above, and the triangle in God is a circle, as we have said in *Hieroglyphic Geometry*; and thus the Trinity is Unity. Moreover, just as the circle is infinite, so also must the unity likewise be infinite: whence it is more one and identical than any expressible unity, so that it even precedes all relative oppositions, because there, "other" and "different" are not opposed to identity,

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. 509 CHAPTER III.

<margin>The infinite circle is the primary symbol of God.</margin>
And thus all things that exist, and all that pertains to Him, are Himself without diversity or "otherness." His goodness is not one thing and His wisdom another, but they are the same. Indeed, His duration is so great that in Him the past is not distinct from the future, nor the future from the present; rather, they are one single duration and eternity, devoid of all beginning and end. For in Him, the beginning is such that the end is that very same beginning. All of this is clearly evident from the concept of the **infinite circle**. Since this circle is the greatest possible, its diameter must also be the greatest, and consequently, the circumference will be equal to the diameter. Truly, an infinite diameter has an infinite middle; this middle is the center. Therefore, the center, the diameter, and the circumference are the same. From this, the meaning of the Hermetic definition cited above becomes clear: *God is a circle whose center is everywhere, and whose circumference is nowhere.* <note>This famous paradoxical definition is often attributed to Hermes Trismegistus or the "Book of the Twenty-four Philosophers."</note> He is, therefore, that greatest of all things to which the "smallest" is not opposed, but rather the center in Him is the circumference. From these points, it is clear how the greatest of all is most perfectly inside every simple and indivisible thing (because He is the infinite center) and outside all things contained within the circuit of the World (because His circumference is infinite). Because He penetrates all things, He is called the infinite diameter; because He is the beginning of all, He is called the center. You see, then, how the "Greatest" is identical to nothing else, yet not diverse from anything, and how all things are in Him, from Him, and through Him. For not to be in Him would be to be the "Greatest" itself, just as the minimum is the maximum. This applies to the measure of every <term>enclosure or circular motion <note>original Greek: περικυκλώσεως (perikyklōseōs)</note></term>, which moves from potentiality into act, and by returning from act to potentiality, is the measure of composition (from principles to individuals) and of resolution (from individuals back to principles), and of the perfect forms of circular operations and motions—those which return upon themselves and to their beginning, and similar things whose unity consists in a certain circular perpetuity. Indeed, the entire Trinity in Him is a most perfect unity. Just as in an infinite center, the center, diameter, and circumference are a most consummate union, so too are the Three Persons <note>original: hypostases</note> appropriately expressed: the Father as the center (the beginning of the circle), the Son as the diameter, and the Holy Spirit as the circumference uniting all things.

<margin>The properties of the circle express the whole of Theology.</margin>
From what has been said, it is also clear how the whole of Theology is aptly expressed through the properties of the circle. All the attributes of the divine essence are verified in relation to one another by a certain circular motion of the intellect, such that supreme justice is supreme truth, and supreme truth is supreme justice, and so it goes for the other attributes.

But let us return to the matter at hand.

<margin>The properties of the triangle express the properties of God.</margin>
The Egyptians adopted the equilateral triangle to indicate the "triform nature of God," as they call it. Since this nature is infinite in God, it must necessarily have three equally infinite angles; thus, the equality of the divine persons is rightly inferred from the infinite. However, since there cannot be multiple "infinites," it follows necessarily that in that great triangle of divinity, these three infinite angles—as well as everything else—are entirely one. Indeed, this triangle is a circle, and the circle a triangle; the angle is the side, and the side is the angle, just as the circumference is the diameter, and the diameter the circumference, and these two are one and the same center in divine matters. Nevertheless, because in a triangle there is a certain "otherness" according to our way of conceiving things...

is considered in this way because of the resulting angles, which are not present in a circle at all; hence, they quite appropriately adopted the circle as the prototype of the triform divine nature—as they call it—removed from all fellowship with created things. The triangle, however, represents the triform divine nature insofar as it proceeds outward. It is a Sphere from which three chains of triangles are drawn down: and indeed, through the sphere, the prototype of the divine essence is indicated; through the triangle, the triform nature of God; and through the three chains of triangles, the three Worlds—the Intellectual, the Sidereal <note>The stars and heavens</note>, and the Elementary. All of these are marked with the seal of the triangular character in the likeness of the divine mind, and they display the Ideas of all things existing in God, as we have shown extensively elsewhere, and as will be declared openly in Volume III; therefore, it is enough to have merely indicated those things in this place.

# CLASS 12. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER 4.

...from this voice of light, the Word came forth in finished form. This Word, standing by the moist nature, nourished it; and from the bowels of the moist nature, a pure and light fire immediately flew out and sought the heights. The light air, obeying the spirit, took its place in the middle region between fire and water. Earth and water lay mixed together, so that the face of the earth, overwhelmed by the waters, appeared nowhere. These two were then set in motion by the spiritual Word that moved over them, sounding in their ears. Then Pimander <note>Also known as Poimandres, the "Shepherd of Men," a divine intellect in Hermetic writings</note> said: "Pay attention to what this vision means, and I shall know," I said. Pimander then said: "I am that Light, the Mind, your God, more ancient than the moist nature which flowed out of the shadow. But the bud of the Mind is the shining Word, the Son of God." "What then?" I asked. "Think of it this way," he said, "that which sees and hears within you is the Word of the Lord, but the Mind is God the Father; for they are not distant from one another: their union is life."

<margin>Trismegistus's opinion on the production of the World.</margin>
All these things are said so aptly that he seems to have extracted them from Genesis. He then continues: "From where did the elements of nature flow?" Pimander: "From the will of God, which, having embraced the Word and having seen the beautiful World, decorated the rest of itself with vital seeds and elements according to that model. But the Mind, God, being most full of the fertility of both sexes, being life and light, brought forth with his Word another Mind, the Maker, who—being the God of fire and the Spirit of Divinity—then fashioned seven governors <note>The seven planetary deities</note> who encompass the sensible World in circles; and their arrangement is called Fate. Then the Word of God connected the pure craftsmanship of nature from the elements tending downward, and it was united to the Maker Mind. For it was of the same substance <note>original: "consubstantiale"</note>. And the elements of nature falling downward were left without reason, so that they are like mere matter. The Maker Mind, together with the Word, containing the circles and turning them with swift speed, turned his machine back on itself, and willed it to go from the beginning without beginning to the end without end. For it always begins there where it ceases. The circuit of all these things, just as the Mind itself willed, produced from the lower elements animals void of reason; for he did not provide them with reason. The air brought forth winged creatures, and the water the swimming ones. Water and earth were also distinguished from each other in the manner that pleased the Mind. Afterward, the earth brought forth the living creatures which it had held within, namely quadrupeds, serpents, wild beasts, both wild and domestic. But the Father of all, the intellect, being life and brightness, procreated a Man similar to himself, and rejoiced in him as his own son: for he was beautiful, and bore the image of his Father. For God, truly delighted by his own form, granted all his works to human use. But when Man had considered the procreation of all things in the Father, he himself also wished to create. Wherefore he fell from the contemplation of the Father into the sphere of generation."

<margin>The World was made by the Word of God according to Hermes.</margin>
Thus, according to Hermes, the World was established by the Word of God, which also agrees with the Orthodox faith, according to that saying: *By the Word of the Lord the heavens were made firm, and by the Spirit of his mouth all their power.* <note>A reference to Psalm 33:6</note>

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
To this alludes that saying of Zoroaster, as was shown above in the sayings of Class 3: *The Father completed all things, and delivered them to the second Mind.* But so that these things may be made more clear, it seemed best to begin a little deeper.

<margin>What the Paternal Depth is.</margin>
The World, therefore, emanated from the Paternal Depth <note>original: "fundum paternum"</note> composed of three triads, according to the mind of the Chaldeans and Egyptians. In what way the Paternal Depth—as we taught above in Class 3 in the Sayings of Zoroaster—is nothing other than the Paternal Word; for the Father finished all things, and...

# CHAPTER IV 512 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>The Chaldeans claim a threefold multitude of things.</margin>
He <note>The Father/First Principle</note> delivered to the Second Mind, who is the Son: whatever, therefore, was in the Father, this very thing he poured into the Son, that is, into his own "depth." With these things established, the Chaldeans <note>Refers to the authors of the *Chaldean Oracles*, a mystical text from the 2nd century AD</note> assert a threefold multitude of things; the first is in the Father, which is unbegotten and unproduced, and is a certain virtual multitude that is supremely one, and never departed from him. Another is in the Fatherly depth, that is, the Son, which as it emanated from the Father, is thus entirely indistinct, undivided, and uncreated from the same; for it was produced not out of nothing, but out of the greatest of all things; for if it was previously in the Father, and from him was diffused into his whole depth, and the Father is all things, then all things are not "nothing"; therefore they are not from nothing; therefore they are not created. Consequently, all those things which are outside the depth are properly said to be created, namely the Angelic, Starry, and Elemental Worlds; and they are beings either corporeal, or incorporeal, or both corporeal and incorporeal at once: for those things which are said to exist in the depth, although they are incorporeal, nevertheless in an ineffable way—inasmuch as they are uncreated—they transcend the things mentioned. But how this entire machine of the World, comprised of three partial Worlds, flowed forth from the depth, is so difficult to investigate that all efforts of the human mind grow dull in inquiring into it: for if they came forth from there, how shall they be called created? For in him all things were founded, in the heavens and on the earth, visible and invisible, and all things were created through him and in him, and again from him, and through him, and in him are all things. If therefore they were in him, how did they come forth from nothing?

<margin>How the Triple World was created from nothing.</margin>
But let us explain this knot, so difficult, as far as the nothingness of my talent permits. To create from nothing is to make a thing from no preceding matter, for matter is necessarily either subjected to or required for every making, fabrication, generation, workmanship, and artifice: but in the creation of the World, God had no need of matter from which, or out of which, he might make them, or in which he might form them; therefore God is rightly said to have made all things from nothing. *All things therefore the Father perfected, and delivered to the Second Mind;* for the divine emanation was not made by a leap from the Father into his depth; but was made from the Father into the ultimate boundary of his depth by an eternal, immutable, undivided, and indistinct action. Whatever things, therefore, were created outside the depth, were created by the Triune principle. The Father willed, the Word spoke, and they were made; as soon as the Word brought them forth, they were made, but no longer such as those which remained in him; since, separated from the essential Unity, they are no longer simply one, but a multitude, and that a varied one, diffused into many degrees, breadths, series, and chains; of which multitude the Triune God himself, through his all-encompassing simplicity, was the principle, and cause, and effector, and founder, and maker; and while he brings them forth from himself and outside himself, those things suddenly, as if departing from the one, are diffused into a multitude—not indeed imperfect, <note>original Greek: πατρικῆς ἀρχῆς πηγή τὸ μονάδα — "The source of the Fatherly principle is the Monad."</note>.

<margin>Zoroaster.</margin>
For nothing imperfect is whirled from the Fatherly principle, as Zoroaster says; nor do they come forth confused, for confusion is a certain greatest imperfection, but each in its own order. Thus, first the Angelic World, as the immediate work of God and closest to him; then the Starry and Elemental World, with all things which are contained in them...

Furthermore, the cause of this production was none other than the infinite goodness of God; for because He is good, He is Father; because He is Father, He is the beginning; because He is the beginning, He is the cause; and because He is the cause of things, He is God; and because He is the cause of all things, He is almighty. For these two names, **The Good** and **God**, according to the testimony of Hermes <note>referring to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary Hellenistic figure associated with the Hermetic corpus</note>, belong to Him alone. We have seen the production of things; now let us examine each work distinctly according to the mind of the Ancients.

# §. I.
->Concerning the Angelic or Intellectual World.<-

<margin>The Angelic or Intellectual World</margin>
The ancients saw that among all those things which have been produced, some are *self-subsisting* <note>original: "αὐθ’ ὑπόστατα" (auth' hypostata)</note>, that is, those which, relying upon their own existence <note>original: "hyparxi," a term for essential presence or substance</note>, essence, and powers, require no support from any other thing in order to be, except for God as their producer and Creator; for just as He produced them, so He always preserves and contains them lest they vanish into nothingness, turning them toward Himself and calling them back to Himself according to their strength and dignity. And these are the incorporeal things which they believed to exist in the Archetypal World: ideas, unities, essences, lives, intellects, and souls.

But others are *dependent-subsisting* <note>original: "ἑτερόστατα" (heterostata)</note>, that is, subsisting and existing in and through another, such as bodies and all corporeal things. Corporeal things include quantities, qualities, and their operations and passions, which require a body as a support, without which they would neither exist nor subsist, according to the definition of accidents <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, an "accident" is a property that cannot exist on its own but must belong to a substance</note>. Indeed, bodies themselves require a place in which to be, and matter into which forms may be introduced. Since, therefore, they recognized the *self-subsisting* and the *dependent-subsisting* as two extremes, they inferred that certain intermediaries were necessary to be placed between these extremes. And they said such intermediaries were, first, the Intelligences <note>Angelic beings or celestial minds</note>, the preservers of the world's craftsmanship; second, the very nature of things; and third, the entire breadth of the soul. 

And since each of these listed things necessarily possesses its own essence, power, and operation: first, just as *dependent-subsisting* bodies subsist in nature itself, so also they will have their power and operation in another. Thus, whatever they are seen to be able to do or to perform, they do and perform through the nature infused into them. Consequently, they can act neither upon themselves nor upon another. But if they can act neither upon themselves nor upon another, they cannot even preserve themselves; and if they cannot preserve themselves, they do not even contain themselves by their own powers. Therefore, they are contained and preserved by another. Truly, this preserving force can by no means be a body; it must therefore be preserved by something incorporeal, and indeed by something coextensive with the whole, which they called "Nature." Virgil alludes to this quite beautifully:

<margin>Virgil</margin>
> *A spirit within sustains, and Mind, infused through the limbs,*
> *Stirs the whole mass, and mingles itself with the great body.* <note>A quote from Virgil's Aeneid, Book VI, describing the "world soul."</note>

<margin>Zoroaster</margin>
And Zoroaster <note>The ancient Persian prophet, often cited in Renaissance magic and philosophy</note> clearly indicates this with the following exceedingly mysterious words:

# CHAPTER IV. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

->Around the back of the Goddess, infinite Nature is suspended,<-
->And tireless Nature rules over both the worlds and their works.<-

> *Above the back of the Goddess, tireless nature is raised up,*
> *And tireless nature commands the Worlds and their works.*

<margin>The Soul of the World.</margin>
By "the Goddess" in this passage, they understand nothing other than the Soul of the World <note>Latin: *Anima Mundi*; the vital force thought by ancient philosophers to animate all nature</note>; by "Nature," however, they signify the material, ethereal, and empyrean <note>The highest, most fiery level of heaven</note> worlds, upon whose back the Goddess sits untiringly, urging them toward operations suitable to each, and as Zoroaster <note>Referring to the *Chaldean Oracles* attributed to Zoroaster</note> says, *abundantly animating the light, fire, ether, and worlds* <note>original Greek: ἄρδην ἐμψυχῶσα φάος, πῦρ, αἴθερα, κόσμους</note>. See all these matters treated more extensively above in Class VI. For it is the Soul, as Zoroaster says, which adorned the great heaven, *For it is the Soul which adorned the great heaven, and adorns it together with the Father* <note>original Greek: Ψυχὴ γὰρ, ἡ κοσμήσασα τὸν μέγαν οὐρανὸν, καὶ κοσμοῦσα μετὰ τοῦ πατρός</note>; and she adorns it simultaneously with the Father. *And the Soul, by the power of the Father, remains a shining light, and is immortal, and is the mistress of life, and possesses many fullnesses of the world's bosoms* <note>original Greek: Ψυχὴ δ' δυνάμει πατρὸς ἔξα φαεινὸς, ἀθάνατός τε μένει, καὶ ζωῆς δεσπότις ἐστὶ, καὶ ἔχει κόσμου πολλὰ πληρώματα κόλπων</note>. Since the Soul, says Zoroaster, is reflecting by the power of the Father's fire, and remains immortal, she is the mistress of life and possesses the many fullnesses of the world's depths. Indeed, since she is intellectual, she contains the intelligible things in her mind, and brings sensation to the worlds: *In her mind she holds the intelligible things, but she applies sensation to the worlds* <note>original Greek: Νῷ μὲν κατέχει τὰ νοητὰ αἴσθησιν δ' ἐπάγει κόσμοις</note>. For in her mind she is an imitator, but she holds a certain part of the body, and through mixed channels, she effects the works of incorruptible fire; that is, the soul, participating through her mind, contains the things of the intellect, but she imparts sensation to the worlds and makes them sensible. This is because, as Zoroaster believes, she imitates the Father through the intellect, producing bodies through her ray—which is the nature infused into bodies—by various paths which he calls "channels." This is just as the Cabalists <note>Followers of Jewish Mysticism/Kabbalah</note> call the <term>Sephirotic</term> <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Kabbalah through which the Infinite is revealed</note> paths of the world "channels," as was seen in its proper place; working and perfecting all things by the instrument of eternal heat. Furthermore, above the soul are the Intellects, which take care of the worlds: *For the world has intellectual, unbending sustainers, but they are also the guardians of the works of the Father* <note>original Greek: Κόσμῳ γὰρ ἔχει νοεροὺς ἀνοχῆας ἀκαμπτᾶς, ἀλλὰ καὶ φρουροὶ τῶν ἔργων εἰσὶ τοῦ πατρός</note>. For the world has intellectual, inflexible sustainers who guard it by supporting it; but they are also the guardians of the Father's works. Therefore, this <term>Chain</term> <note>A concept of a vertical hierarchy connecting the lowest matter to the highest God</note> or *Seira* <note>Greek: Σειρὰ, meaning "cord" or "chain"</note>, as the Egyptians call it, is truly golden: consisting of the Father, the mind, the intellects, the soul, and nature. It was necessary that those bodies, which cannot be sustained, preserved, or guarded by themselves, be continually sustained and preserved first by the Father their maker, and then by the intellects, souls, and natures. This is in the same manner that Aristotle taught that the heavens are moved by intellects, preserved in that motion, and that the entire economy of the lower world is governed by them; and finally, that both being and living flow to all things from those which are above the heavens. But now let us examine the secret of the Angelic World a little more extensively.

<margin>The opinion of Pagan Theologians regarding the fecundity of God.</margin>
Thus the Creator Mind, according to the dogmas of the Egyptians, Chaldeans, and Platonists, having been made pregnant by the supernal influxes of the Word and the Good, can by no means be sterile. Instead, they say it brings forth continually, and contains, guards, and preserves the things brought forth—both the first things which proceeded from itself, and those which flowed further away from it.
<margin>The Father is the first Mind.</margin>
Moreover, they say that first beings flowed from itself, second beings from the first, third from the second, fourth from the third, fifth from the fourth, sixth from the fifth, seventh from the sixth, eighth from the seventh, ninth from the eighth, and tenth from the ninth. If they understand this "outflow" as a certain creative power, they do so falsely and

Thus, through these three triads, the nine Angelic Choirs are aptly indicated, according to the opinion of orthodox theologians. And just as in the Ideal or Archetypal World there is a triad—Father, Power, and Mind, that is, Father, Word or Son, and Spirit—so in each of the remaining triads of the Worlds there is a certain Paternal order, a Potential order, and a Mental order, so that it is necessary for the "Ideated" <note>The physical manifestation of an idea.</note> to correspond in every way to its idea and exemplar and be inwardly assimilated to it; and thus the first order in each triad flows into the second, and this into the third, by a certain wonderful virtue, and not the other way around. <margin>The three orders of Intelligibles according to Zoroaster.</margin> And indeed, the first order of the intelligibles is said to be that which is only understood, and this is the highest; the second, which is also the middle, belongs to both the intelligibles and the intellectuals, that is, of those who are understood and who understand, as Zoroaster says and as we have amply explained above in Class III; the third order is of the intellectuals, which only understands. From this it is easily gathered that the supreme order of the triads is above the intellect and is only understood by the middle order; while the third is illuminated by the middle ones, and understands both itself and the things above and below it, as Psellus <note>Michael Psellus, a Byzantine monk and scholar of the 11th century.</note> says. <margin>Psellus. St. Dionysius. But since no one until now has rightly interpreted this depth of mysteries—

# CHAPTER IV. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

...interpreted it, I have judged it to be my duty to set forth in this place the tenor of this entire Egyptian-Chaldean Theology, as far as the powers of my mind permit. Before this is done, it seemed best first to bring forward the text itself from Pletho <note>George Gemistos Plethon, a 15th-century Byzantine scholar who revived Neoplatonism.</note>; for he speaks thus in his exposition of the *Chaldean Oracles*:

> The Chaldeans establish seven corporeal Worlds: one fiery and first; after this, three ethereal; then three material, of which the last is called terrestrial and the "hater of light," which is the place beneath the Moon, embracing matter within itself, which they name the "depth." They believe there is a single principle of all things, and they profess it to be the One and the Good. Next, they worship the *paternal depth* <note>original: "πατρικὸν βυθὸν"</note>, that is, a certain Paternal foundation composed of three trinities; moreover, each trinity has a Father, a Power, and a Mind. Afterward follows the Iynx <note>A "wheel" or "charm" representing a mediating power or divine thought.</note> comprehensible by the mind. Closest to this are the *Connectors* <note>original: "συνοχεῖς"</note>, that is, the Governors of the Worlds: the fiery, the ethereal, and the material. After the Governors come the *Teletarchs* <note>original: "Τελετάρχαι"</note>, that is, the Princes of Ceremonies. These are succeeded by the Fathers of the perennial fountains, who are also called the Leaders of the World, *fount-like fathers, those called world-guides* <note>original: "πηγαῖοι πατέρες, οἱ καλούμενοι κοσμαγωγοί"</note>, of whom the first is called the "Once Beyond," after whom is Hecate, then he whom we have named the "Twice Beyond"; from this one are the three "Implacables," and the last of all is the *Sub-girdler* <note>original: "ὑπεζωκός"</note>. They also venerate a fount-like triad of faith, truth, and love; they also speak of the *Archic* <note>Ruling or primordial.</note> Sun from the Solar fountain, and the Archangelic, and the fountain of sense, and the judgment of fountains, and the lightning-fountain, and the fountain of mirrors, and the fountain of characters seated upon unknown symbols, and the fount-like summits of Apollo, Osiris, and Mercury. Truly, the Martial fountains are said to be of the centers, and of the elements, and the zone of dreams, and the fount-like soul. After the fountains, they say there are principles, for fountains are more primary than principles. The summit of the life-generating principles is called Hecate; the Middle is the *archic* soul; the End is *archic* Virtue. Furthermore, among them, the *Azonai* <note>Unzoned or unlocalized deities.</note> are Hecate, such as the "Three-Expositor," the Companion, and the "Ecclistica." The *Azonic* gods among them are Serapis, Dionysus, and the chains of Osiris and Apollo. They are called *Azonic* who live in freedom, exercising power over the "zone," presiding over the manifest Gods. They are called *Zonai*, however, because they separately revolve around the celestial zones and administer those things which are here; for the divine race among them is "zoned," to whom are distributed the regions of the sensible World, which it encircles as they are distributed by lot around the material place. After the zones, however, is the fixed circle containing the seven spheres in which the stars are located.

<margin>A summary of Egyptian-Chaldean Theology.</margin>
And this is the summary of Egyptian-Chaldean Theology. Since no one, as far as I know, has hitherto applied their industry to explaining this—what so many triads of Gods and so many linked series of names mean, and how they are truly and properly to be understood—we have led ourselves to interpret it, God willing.

<margin>The Theologians of the ancients recognized some Trinity in God.</margin>
It must be known first, therefore, that not only the Egyptians and Chaldeans, but also all the followers of Orpheus, Pythagoras, and Plato, recognized some triad in the divine nature; as this has been amply demonstrated in the preceding pages, I have judged it superfluous to repeat it here again. And so, according to that ineffable and uncomprehended triune archetypal pattern, all the remaining systems of the Worlds, both sensible and insensible...
