Hence they assert that the "Paternal Profundity" is composed of three triads, each of which has a Father, a Power, and a Mind. They call this profundity "composed," not formally—in the way that soul and body grow together into one man—or to put it another way, not intrinsically, but extrinsically through creative power. And these are nothing other than the nine orders of Angels, distinct in three triads according to the idea of the Divine Triad. Hence, the 
<margin>The Paternal Profundity can be understood in two ways.</margin>
Paternal Profundity can be understood in two ways: first, intrinsically, insofar as the whole paternal knowledge and perfect comprehension of itself is terminated in the depth, that is, in the Word or His Son alone; for He is, as Zoroaster says, the end of the paternal depth and the source of mental things, nor is there progress, but He remained in the paternal depth, and in the sanctuary <note>original: "adyto"</note> nourishing a God-nurturing silence. Second, 
extrinsicially, insofar as it looks toward works on the outside; and thus this Angelic depth can rightly be said to be composed of three triads. Moreover, 
<margin>The Paternal Profundity consists of three.</margin>
the paternal depth consists of three, which are Father, Power, and Mind; and these correspond to the Father, the Word or Son, and the Holy Spirit among Catholics; among the Egyptians to Hemphta, Ammon, and Ichton; among the Cabalists to <term>Keter</term> <gloss>Crown</gloss>, <term>Chokhmah</term> <gloss>Wisdom</gloss>, and <term>Binah</term> <gloss>Understanding</gloss>; among Orpheus and the Greeks to Uranus <note>original: "Cœlo"</note>, Saturn, and Jupiter. And this is that Sacrosanct Triad, one God, indicated or rather foreshadowed under the mystical coverings of words: Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—a triad perfected under a unity of nature, which, permeating all things yet segregated from all things, has snatched itself away into the heights from our senses and our thoughts in the abyss of its own dignity and supereminence.

<margin>Three Orders of Creatures</margin>
Accordingly, the Ancients believed that all orders and grades of creatures were marked according to this triad. Indeed, the first Triad contains only the order of Intelligibles <note>beings understood by the intellect alone</note>; the second contains the order of both intelligibles and intellectuals; the third, finally, contains only the order of intellectuals, as we have said. 
<margin>The triad of Iynges and the three orders.</margin>
The first order is called the *Iyngæan* <note>from "Iynx," a mystical transmission or "wheel" in Chaldean oracles</note>, which are the primary creatures of God: sublime, arduous Minds, abstracted not only from all senses, but even from thoughts; these are not incongruously equated with the Seraphim, Cherubim, and Thrones. For as Zoroaster rightly teaches: <margin>Zoroaster.</margin> *The intelligible Iynges themselves also understand from the Father; and they are moved by ineffable counsels so that they may understand.* <note>original Greek: "Νοούμενοι ἴυγγες πατρόθεν νοέουσι καὶ αὐταὶ... βελαῖς ἀφθέντοισι κινεόμεναι ἃς νοήσας"</note> These climb the lucid Worlds, and understanding the works of the Father, they revealed them to sensible works and bodies. Hence they are not poorly depicted by the Egyptians with a human face, the rest of the body clothed in a manifold covering of feathers and wings, as appears in the following 3 figures. <margin>The triad of Synoches, and the three orders.</margin>

> *For from him all things leap forth: the Implacable lightnings, and the bosoms capable of the whirlwind, of the all-illuminating vigor of the father-generated Hecate; and the flower of the Girdling fire and the strong one, mixing its own strength of vigor into the Synoches <note>original: "Synochis"; the "Connectors" who hold the universe together</note>, by which the World has mental sustainers, inflexible.*

<margin>The nine orders of the Intelligible World.</margin>
And these are the nine orders of the Intelligible World, by which Zoroaster teaches that the Paternal depth is composed, as if by three triads. All these things are explained more fully in the *Sphinx Mystagoga* <note>One of Kircher's own works on interpreting ancient mysteries</note>, in the exposition of the utterances of Zoroaster. We have seen the triads of the Intelligible World; now let us contemplate for a moment the triads of the Sidereal <term>Sidereal: relating to the stars and planets</term> World.

<margin>The fountain triad of the Intelligences presiding over the World.</margin>
The Chaldeans worshiped, as the text teaches, among other things also a fountain triad of faith (that is, of faithful care for the things committed to them), of truth, and of love; which triad was of the Intelligences presiding over the Sidereal World; and it was called the triad of faith, that is, of faithful care; of truth, that is, of their constant virtue in their operations; of love, that is, of the highest inclination and a certain sympathy in procuring the safety and preservation of the things committed to them. <margin>The seven fountains of the Planets.</margin> Furthermore, they fashioned seven fountains, which in a truly wonderful and appropriate way corresponded in the Intelligible and Intellectual World to the seven corporeal or material fountains of the Planets. The first fountain is called *Archicus*, that is, Imperial, and from the material fountain, Archangelic, which they also otherwise call the Solar World, because this, like a Prince and Leader, conducted the choir of the rest. The second fountain was the fountain of sense or of the sensitive nature, from which, as if from a certain Ocean, all things agreeable to the sensitive nature flowed forth, and it corresponded to Saturn, the presider over sense. The third fountain was the fountain-judgment, and it belonged to Jupiter, as he supplied the abundance of all judgment and of things necessary for the Sidereal economy and the right administration of the political World. The fourth fountain was called the lightning-fountain, and it rightly belonged to Mars, whose property it is to send forth lightnings, the terrors of wars, slaughters, plague, and similar evils...

<margin>The Zonal and the Zoneless.</margin>
And some of these they asserted to be *Azonoi*, that is, without zones, while others were *Zonaioi* <note>Zonal</note>. The former, because of the supreme protection they maintained over the World, were tied to no fixed zone; the latter, by contrast, revolve freely around the zones of heaven and perform the immediate duty of governing.

<margin>Material fountains, and their triad.</margin>
These are followed by the triads of the material fountains, and this is the Elemental World, distinguished by a triple triad of symbols. The **first triad** of principles procreating living beings: the summit is called Hecate; the middle summit, the *archic* <note>ruling or primordial</note> or principal soul; the extreme summit is called the *archic* virtue. The first presided over the procreation of animals, the second over the introduction of souls, and the third over the distribution of the virtues necessary for each thing to operate. The **second triad**, the eternal triad of the Chaldeans and Egyptians known as the Hecatic triad, contained the *Ekdotis* <note>the Giver</note>, the *Komas* <note>the Reveler/Guardian of villages</note>, and the *Eklytike* <note>the Releaser</note>. The *Telekadotis* <note>The Perfect Giver; original: Τελεκάδοτις</note> bestows all things upon the triple World; the *Komas* <note>original: κωμὰς</note> dwells in all the streets and crossroads of the triple World; the *Eclystice* <note>original: ἐκλυτική</note> encloses all things with its spirit. All these things are explained more extensively in the *Pamphilian Obelisk*, page 518. After these Zones, the Zodiac circle finally occurs, embracing the seven spheres of the Planets, over which the aforementioned orders of Intelligences were believed to preside. The **third triad** was of the Zoneless Gods, that is, of Serapis, Dionysus (or Bacchus), and the Spirits of Osiris and Apollo, connected in the manner of a Syrian chain, by which all and singular members of the three Worlds are connected by a certain wonderful reason to the harmony of the whole.

<margin>The Theology of the Chaldeans and Egyptians is the same.</margin>
And this was the Philosophy, or rather the Theology, of the ancient Chaldeans of Zoroaster: which indeed, if it be rightly compared with that of the Egyptians, you will find to be exactly the same, with only the terms changed. For in the *Pimander* and *Asclepius* <note>Key texts of the Hermetic tradition attributed to Hermes Trismegistus</note>, Hermes assigns various orders of Gods, such as the *Usiarchs* <note>Rulers of substance</note>, Horoscopes, Decans, and *Pantomorphs* <note>Those of all shapes</note>; furthermore, various choirs of Demons, Heroes, and souls. He also mentions the seven Zones; all of which, since they have been set forth in the *Systematics of the Worlds*, in the *Astrology of the Egyptians*, and in the *Sphinx Mystagoga*, I refer the Reader there.

<margin>Orders of Gods, and triads of orders from Iamblichus.</margin>

<margin>First triad of Gods: the principle, Hemphra, Ichton.</margin>

...as an indivisible and ineffable fire, filling the entire depth of the World. The fire of the Archangels is also undivided, having around it—whether before or behind—a vast multitude. The fire of the Angels is divided, but exists in the most absolute forms <note>original: "ideis," referring to Platonic Ideas or archetypes</note>. The fire of Demons is even more divided, but more narrowly circumscribed and easily described; among those who have seen higher things, it is easily held in contempt. The Heroic fire <note>The "Heroes" here refer to semi-divine spirits or elevated souls, not merely brave humans</note> possesses qualities similar to these, but not equal. The fire of souls is greatly divided and multiform, mixed from many natures of the World. 

The fire of the Gods is entirely stable in appearance; that of the Archangels participates in that stability; that of the Angels moves with stability; that of the Demons is unstable; that of the Heroes is more rapid; that of the Principalities arrives quietly; that of the Princes is indeed tumultuous; the fire of Souls is transformed by many movements. 

The Gods purify souls most perfectly; the Archangels recall them upward; the Angels merely loosen them from the bonds of matter. Demons draw them toward nature; Heroes lead them to the care of sensible works <note>tasks involving the physical senses</note>. The Principalities exhibit a presidency over worldly affairs, while the Princes show a zeal for material things. When Souls appear, they struggle and draw one toward generation <note>the process of physical birth and rebirth</note>. 

Whatever is pure and firm in an image encountered by us, attribute to the higher classes. Now, attribute that which is pre-eminently bright and remains firmly within itself to the Gods; that which shines and remains indeed, but as if in another, to the Archangels; that which remains in another, to the Angels. Likewise, whatever is mobile, wandering, and full of foreign natures, attribute everywhere to the lower orders.

The Princes are full of material fluids. Souls are filled with superfluous stains and foreign spirits; whenever they appear, each of these classes reveals itself. 

The Gods consume matter suddenly; the Archangels do so gradually; the Angels loosen one from it and recall one to the sublime. The Demons diligently entreat matter; the Heroes adapt themselves to it, managing it strenuously and conveniently with appropriate measures everywhere. The Principalities stand over it as superiors and show themselves in this manner. The Princes show themselves to be thoroughly filled with matter. Pure souls indeed come apart from matter, but impure souls show themselves to us enveloped in matter.

Whatever is cold and death-bringing within us, they erase; they foster heat and make it more effective for life. They also make all things congruent with the soul and mind, measuring them by the same standards, and they pour out light through an intelligible harmony. That which is not a body, they show as a body to the very eyes of the soul, through the eyes of the body.

The Demons, by their presence, weigh down the body, afflict it with diseases, or punish it in other ways; they also draw souls toward nature and do not depart from bodies and their kindred senses. They detain those who strive toward the celestial and divine fire in a lower place, nor do they loosen them from the bonds of fate. The Heroes do other things similar to the Demons, but they have this as their own: that toward works...

# CHAPTER IV. THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS.

...certain noble and great works awaken us. *Principalities* <note>original: "Principatus," a high order of spiritual beings</note> when appearing bestow worldly goods and supply all the things of this life; *Princes* bestow material and earthly goods. When *Souls* appear, if they are pure souls established in the Angelic order, they call us upward, provide salvation to the mind, and offer sacred hope and the sacred gifts for which one hopes. *Impure souls* twist toward generation <note>the cycle of physical birth and decay</note>, frustrate hope by taking away its fruits, and fill the observers with passions, binding the soul to the body. The appearance also designates the order which each one holds. *Gods* show Gods, or Angels standing around them; *Archangels* present Angels either preceding, surrounding, or following them, or some other crowd of Angels like bodyguards surrounding them; *Angels* present works appropriate to their order. *Good Spirits* <note>original: "Boni Daemones"</note> bring into view their handiwork and the goods they grant; *Avenging Spirits* show types of punishments; *Other Spirits*, however depraved they may be, appear surrounded by lethal and voracious wild beasts. *Principalities* demonstrate certain Provinces of the World with them; *Princes* bring into view the condition of matter, which lacks order and wanders. *The whole Soul*, held by no particular species, shows a fire without a fixed shape around the whole World; by which the nature of the World-Soul is signified as undivided, one, and addicted to no specific form. A *purified soul* shows a fiery figure, a pure fire, and a gleaming light that is simultaneously stable; she follows her sublime leader with a joyful good will, thus revealing the order she holds in her works. But the *soul that falls downward* appears dragging with her the signs of chains and punishments, showing herself weighed down by a composition of material spirits; she is occupied by the diverse disturbances of matter and submits herself to the empire of the Spirits who favor physical generation. When they appear, each shows the provinces and lots which they have been allotted to inhabit: the aerial ones show aerial fire, the earthly show earthly and black fire; the celestial ones show a more splendid fire; and within these three boundaries, all their orders are distributed. Gods demonstrate the principles of all orders in themselves when they appear; Angels declare that they depend on Archangels; Spirits and Heroes reveal that they minister to their superiors, though the latter do so differently than the former. *Principalities and Princes* show their prefecture; the former over the World, the latter over matter. *Souls* declare that they hold the last place of the superiors, whence together with themselves they designate the first places for the first, second for the second, third for the third, and the rest in the same order. Thus says Iamblichus <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher</note>.

<margin>Proclus.</margin>

<margin>The Chain of Gods.</margin>
The Chains of Gods and Goddesses, which Orpheus wove under poetic fictions and veils, seem to allude to nothing else but these <gloss>ranks</gloss> <note>original Greek: "τάξεις" (taxeis)</note> of worldly Divinities.

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER V.

# CHAPTER V.

->**Concerning Ideas, and what the Ancient Theologians—Zoroaster, Hermes, Orpheus, Pythagoras, and finally the Platonic school—understood by them.**<-

<margin>The origin of the doctrine of Ideas is from the Egyptians and Chaldeans.</margin>
That most celebrated doctrine of Ideas first found its origin among the Egyptians and Chaldeans; from whom Orpheus and Aglaophemus <note>Aglaophemus was the teacher of Pythagoras in the Orphic mysteries.</note> drew it, and from them Pythagoras brought it into Greece. Finally, Plato, having cultivated it with the greatest zeal, transmitted it to posterity. Consequently, it is most false that 
<margin>The doctrine of Ideas is falsely ascribed to Socrates by Aristotle.</margin>
Aristotle ascribes this doctrine first to Socrates. For he says that Socrates, while hunting for definitions, came upon the knowledge of the universal species, and thus gathered and established a certain species and form in his mind, which Plato later raised higher, lifted into the abstract, called an "Idea," and was the first to worship and introduce into Philosophy. This is an Aristotelian fiction falsely attributed to Socrates and Plato, since almost all the monuments of the Ancient Egyptians and Chaldeans are full of the doctrine of Ideas. 
<margin>Hieroglyphics are a weaving together of Ideas.</margin>
Indeed, the entire doctrine of hieroglyphics is nothing other than a continuous weaving together of ideal mysteries, as will be seen in its proper place. Certainly, 
<margin>The monuments of Trismegistus speak of Ideas.</margin>
Hermes Trismegistus <note>The legendary Hellenistic figure "Thrice-Great Hermes," supposed author of the Hermetic Corpus.</note> makes frequent mention of Ideas in almost all the monuments he left to posterity, as is evident in the *Poimandres*, the *Asclepius*, the *Minerva of the World*, and others. Indeed, at the beginning of the *Poimandres*, he confesses that through the reflected Idea of God the Father, he perceived in his mind a light endowed with innumerable powers. And in the same dialogue, at the end of the first discourse, when he names the entire universe the image of God, he acknowledges (which we shall later attempt to show from Plato) that in the same Maker of things, or in His Son, there exists the pattern and Idea of all things that consist of nature. In the second discourse, he calls the one God "the Good itself" and the "Idea of the Good." In the eighth discourse, he says, "Full is God the Father, instilling qualities into all Ideas into the sphere, as if into a circuit circumscribed by every quality." And in the twelfth discourse, he not only acknowledges the Idea of all things in God, but openly maintains that, besides this Sensible World, there is another exemplary and Intelligible World, in which the Idea of this world consists. Zoroaster, truly, both in his Oracles and as found in Proclus’s third Commentary on the *Parmenides*, mentions them everywhere: namely, how a multitude emanated from this fountain of ideas, and how the World was made according to them; and that they are the movers of all Worldly Systems, and that all are intellectual by essence, the concepts of the Father, the type and pattern of the World. But 
<margin>Proclus introduces Zoroaster speaking about Ideas.</margin>
let us hear the mind of Zoroaster in Proclus, reasoning thus about Ideas: *“The Paternal mind, understanding with supreme counsel, produced the omniform Ideas, which, flying out from one fountain, went forth; for from the Father was the counsel and the end. But they are divided, partitioned by intellectual fire into other intellectual things: for the King set before the multiform World an intellectual type, an incorruptible type; for the adornment of which he impressed a vestige upon the forms, through which the World appeared graceful with Ideas of every kind.”*

<meta>catchword: qua-</meta>

The author asserts that Egyptian hieroglyphics are essentially a symbolic representation of these divine Ideas.</summary>

# 524 THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>CHAPTER V.</margin>

> *...of which there is one source, from which they go forth, divided into others without width, flowing through the bodies of the World; which are carried like swarms around the vast forms, changed here and there; intellectual concepts from the Paternal source, plucking much of the flower of fire in the dreams of time; the primordial summit of the Idea first gushes from the Father, the self-flourishing source of this very thing.*
<note>original Latin: "quarum unus fons..." This is a poetic, Neoplatonic description of how divine ideas flow from God into the physical world.</note>

Where it is clearly evident that the Ideas of the divine Mind are certain patterns which emerge and leap forth <note>original Greek: προκύπτειν (prokyptein) - to peep forth or emerge</note> from the super-existential unity through the creative act; these are indeed united in the divine intellect, but outside of it they acquire a divisible nature. And so forth, as is clear from the context of the cited passage. We must now discuss, therefore, by what reasoning the Ancients arrived at the contemplation of such sublime matters.

<margin>
How the Ancients came to the knowledge of Ideas.
</margin>

For first, they recognized that this World could by no means exist of itself, much less the remaining members and parts of the World-machine, but that all these things necessarily exist from another; not indeed from a particular nature, nor from a universal one, nor from universal corporeal life, nor from an irrational soul, nor from a participated intellect; therefore, necessarily from an unparticipated and independent intellect—an absolute and essential intellect, which is the Life of lives, the Being of beings <note>original Latin: "Ens entium"</note>, and the Unity of all unities. And from this unity, which Zoroaster <note>The legendary Persian prophet, often cited in the Renaissance as a source of "Ancient Theology."</note> aptly calls the **primordial Idea**, all other unities flowed forth as if from a perennial spring. 

Thus God, about to establish the World, knowing Himself and clearly comprehending Himself as the cause of all things, necessarily knew all those things likewise for which He was to be the cause—namely the lives of things, their essences, and their unities—as if they were contained in the eternal bosom of the divine essence. Since these are causes within that immovable "Cause of causes," it is necessary that they are also the causes of all things produced externally; for He who establishes order in all things does so by His very being, and His being is the act of understanding itself. Therefore, by understanding Himself, He becomes the maker and founder of all things. 

It follows that the things He produces outside Himself must be similar to those He contains within Himself; for every action in an essence is such that what proceeds from the essence depends upon it; and hence it is that every cause produces an effect similar to itself. Therefore, those interior causes are the **Ideas** of things, which are brought forth from the essence as similar forms to the outside. For since the founding intellect holds within itself all beings distinguished by their variety, and through that action which belongs to the essence, brings forth a fruitful action which is *from* the essence, certainly all things are made through this and depend upon them. The variety of things in the World arises from the variety of the unities which are within the founding intellect. 

God, therefore, is either the simplest Mind having His essence in a perpetual act of understanding, or a certain substance in which this act of understanding is said to reside. Whichever we attribute to God, He cannot exist without the perpetual office of understanding; but there is no office of understanding without an "intelligible" <note>An object capable of being understood by the mind.</note>, since this is its object. Therefore, with God understanding always and from eternity, there must be certain everlasting intelligibles, and these must be eternal and immovable according to the condition of the divine nature. And these, according to the Ancients, are the **Ideas** or **Iynges** <note>term: Iynges (Greek: Ἴυγγες). In the Chaldean Oracles, these are "wheels" or "messengers" that transmit divine thoughts into the material world.</note> existing in the divine mind: concepts and certain patterns of things to be made, according to which both the World and all things in the World were created.

<summary>This page explains the Neoplatonic and Hermetic theory of "Ideas," arguing that the variety of the physical world originates from eternal, unified patterns within the Divine Mind, which the author links to the teachings of Zoroaster.</summary>

# CLASS 12. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER 5.

<margin>The Platonists embrace the doctrine of Ideas</margin>
For it was not only the ancient Egyptians who cultivated this study with the greatest zeal, but all the Platonists also embraced it with "both arms," as the saying goes. Furthermore, the Holy Fathers held it in high esteem, as is evident from Saint Augustine in Book 5, Chapter 15 of *On the Literal Meaning of Genesis*, where, explaining that passage of Saint John: *What was made, in him was life* <note>John 1:3-4. Augustine interprets this to mean that all created things existed as living "Ideas" in the mind of God before their physical creation.</note>, he philosophizes on the Platonic Ideas as follows:

<margin>The Holy Fathers make mention of the Ideas. St. Augustine</margin>
*“That which was made through him should be understood as being life in him; in which life he saw all things when he made them; and just as he saw them, so he made them. He did not see them for his own sake, but within himself he thus enumerated all things that he made. Nor is his vision different from that of the Father; rather it is one, just as their substance is one. For also in the Book of Job, Wisdom herself, through whom all things were made, is preached in this way: 'Where is wisdom found, or what is the place of Knowledge? Mortal man knows not its way, nor shall it be found among men'; and a little later: 'We have heard of its glory, the Lord has commended its way. For he himself perfected everything that is under heaven, and knows the things that are on the earth, and made all things; when he made the weights and measures of the winds; just as he saw them, he enumerated them.'”* <note>A paraphrase of Job 28. Augustine uses this to argue that God works from a pre-existing internal design.</note> By all of which, Augustine says, it is proved that all these things, before they were made, existed in the knowledge of the Maker; and certainly they were better there, where they are truer, where they are eternal and unchangeable. Although it ought to be enough that everyone knows and believes unshakably that God made all these things, I do not suppose anyone is so senseless <note>original: "excordem" - literally "heartless" or "witless."</note> as to think that God made things he did not know. Furthermore, if he knew them before they were made, they were known to him in that way in which they eternally and immutably live and are life; but they were made in the way that each creature exists within its own kind. The same Augustine, while approving this opinion of the Platonists in many other places, also writes in Chapter 28, Book 7 of *The City of God* that Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro, an ancient Roman scholar.</note> wished for the "Idea" to be signified by the name of Minerva by the Poets (who involve Philosophy in their own fashion), because she is the Wisdom of Jove, born from his brain. And in *Eighty-three Different Questions*, question 46, after he has distinguished between the Ideas in God and those in a greatly purified human mind, he adds this: *“What religious person, or one endowed with true religion, would deny such Ideas? Certainly no one, unless he wishes to say that the things which are from God do not have the property of existing, or are not ruled and governed by him; or if he grants this, he would wish to affirm that it happens without knowledge and reason—which would be to claim that God does what he does rashly. Since all these things are most absurd, it is necessary that we posit the existence of Ideas.”*

<margin>Ideas as the patterns of things in the creation of the World.</margin>
All of these points pertain to our understanding that, for the procreation of things—lest it seem rash and accidental—Ideas must be posited as certain primary patterns <term>exemplaria: models or blueprints</term> of the Creator. Indeed, so that things are not disordered <note>original: "άτακτα" (atakta) - Greek for "without order" or "chaotic."</note>, and so that the changes of lower things are by no means indeterminate, it is necessary that a certain order pre-exist in the reasons of nature and of this Creator; concerning which, see Plato treating the matter at length,

<margin>Plato.</margin>
where he introduces Socrates disputing with Hippias: for since the effects of God are substances in themselves, in no way can or should they be conceived in him as certain accidents or as multiple substances; they are, therefore, one certain thing there—that is, the very substance of God himself. It is necessary, therefore, that all things be found in God in the most perfect manner, and be united to him and to each other most perfectly. They cannot be in God in a more sublime way than if they are united most sublimely both to God and to themselves, as if they are God himself while in God. Nevertheless, the divine Idea is not absolutely the substance, but only insofar as it is a certain pattern and model <note>original: "παράδειγμα" (paradeigma) - Greek for "paradigm" or "example."</note> of this or that species.

<margin>
St. Thomas Aquinas, Part 1, Question 15, Articles 1, 2, 3.
Question 22, Article 1.
Question 103, Article 5.

</margin>
Therefore, just as many reasons are understood to arise from a single essence, so many **Ideas** are said to exist; and the perspectives by which these Ideas are multiplied are not created by the things themselves, but by the Divine Intellect comparing its own essence with those things (if one may speak in such a way). These concepts constitute the very first Theology, which the Egyptians—having drawn it either from Zoroaster or Hermes—handed down to posterity, veiled in hieroglyphic symbols as the most secret of all secrets. They believed that a soul, when properly purified through the continuous contemplation of these symbols, could return to its own **Idea**, from which it first flowed forth. Indeed, contemplate all these hieroglyphic matters as they are displayed to the eyes of the curious reader in the interpretation of the *Bembine Tablet* <note>The Mensa Isiaca, a famous bronze tablet with Egyptianizing motifs once owned by Cardinal Bembo.</note>. For just as they believed that all beings existing in the world first emanated from the **Parental Mind**, so they holily venerated all things as if they were certain particles of the divine essence. In this alone were they deceived: by thinking that the divinity was, as it were, cut into said particles, they laid the first foundations of **polytheism** <note>original: πολυθεότητος</note> or Idolatry, as has been said in its proper place, and will be discussed at length in the cited passage and above in Class VI, Chapter II.

# CHAPTER VI.

### *Concerning the Soul or Form of the Universe, according to the mind of the Egyptians and the Platonists.*

<margin>The Soul of the World according to the Ancients.</margin>
The ancient **Hieromystics** <note>Priests or initiates of sacred mysteries.</note> seem to agree on this one point: that a "possible essence" <note>A thing that has the potential to exist.</note> can by no means be brought into "actual existence" except through an essence that already exists in act. Since nothing can produce itself, nor can anything be its own cause (for it would have to exist before it existed), it follows that whatever produces another thing into actual existence must act with the highest counsel and intention, as Zoroaster says. Thus, through a rational arrangement, it would not arrive at actual existence by chance or accident. This sublime nature has been called by some the **Mind**, by others **Intelligence**, by others the **Soul of the World**, by others **Fate in substance**, and by others, such as the Platonists, the **Necessity of the Complexion**. For they estimated that "possibility" 
<margin>Cusanus.</margin>
(these are the words of Cardinal Cusanus <note>Nicholas of Cusa, a 15th-century philosopher and theologian.</note>) is determined by "necessity" through the Mind itself, so that what previously *could* be, now *is* in act. Indeed, they said that the forms of things are actually intelligible in that Mind, just as they exist in matter through a certain potential aptitude. Thus, the very "necessity of the complexion," containing within itself the truth of the forms along with those things that accompany them, moves the heavens; so that by means of motion, as if by an instrument, it might lead the potential aptitude into act—and as conformably as possible, equal to the intelligible concept of truth—once the form is granted as it exists in matter. Therefore, the true forms exist by nature in the **Soul of the World** before they exist in physical things. It pleased the Platonists that such distinct "ideated" things <note>Physical things modeled after Ideas.</note> are indeed many, but that they proceed with a certain natural order from the **Infinite Unity** (in which all things are one). In this way, while asserting God, they simultaneously established the Soul of the World, suggesting it was a certain "unfolding" <note>explicatio</note> of the Divine Mind. Thus, all things which are conceived to exist in God by way of a single exemplar, exist in the Soul of the World...

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. 527 CHAPTER VI.

...as if by way of many and distinct things. They held that God naturally precedes this complex of necessity; the World Soul naturally precedes motion; and motion precedes the temporal unfolding of things. This temporal unfolding follows the natural order which exists in the World Soul, and is called by the Platonists "fate in substance," for they believed that fate descends from her.

<margin>The World Soul is the cause of all motion according to the Platonists.</margin>
Furthermore, they said that all motion descends from the World Soul, which they claimed exists as a whole in the whole world and in every part of it, even though it does not exercise the same powers in all parts. Just as the rational soul in a human, though whole in the whole body and whole in every part, does not exercise the same operation in the hair as it does in the heart; so they maintained that in the World Soul itself all souls—whether they be in bodies or outside them—are enfolded. They believed it to be diffused throughout the Universe as a whole, not by parts (because they posited it as simple and indivisible), but whole in the earth, where it binds the earth together; whole in stone, where it effects the tenacity of parts; whole in water, whole in air, fire, and trees.

<margin>The World Soul fills all things.</margin>
Hence, as was said elsewhere, the Egyptians represented this Soul as evolved in a circle from the center of the Divine Mind, and called it a "self-moving number" consisting of the "Same" and the "Different" <note>A reference to Plato's *Timaeus*, where the soul is composed of the Same, the Different, and Being.</note>. They believed it was distinguished from the rational soul only by number; so that just as a man relates to his soul, so the Universe relates to the World Soul, and they believed all souls proceed from it and are finally resolved back into it, provided that sins <note>original: "demerita"</note> do not stand in the way.

<margin>The doctrine of the Platonists regarding the World Soul is contrary to orthodox doctrine.</margin>
And this is the opinion of the Platonists regarding the World Soul, which the Orthodox <note>The author refers to established Christian theologians.</note> deny. For although they may conceive of a World Soul as a certain universal form enfolding within itself the multitude of all forms, they do not speak of it as a separate form, but as existing "contractedly" <note>A technical term meaning "limited" or "particularized" within physical matter.</note> in actual things. For in any given thing, the form of that thing is "contracted"; nor does any medium intervene between the contracted and the absolute, as was imagined by those who called the World Soul "Mind." For God alone is the Soul and Mind of the world in the sense that the Soul is considered as something absolute in which all forms of things actually exist, and is called the Word of the Father <note>The Logos.</note>. Because the Ancients did not understand this, they substituted the World Soul in its place; see the hieroglyphic representation of this in the explanation of the Bembine Tablet <note>A famous bronze tablet of Egyptian-style imagery, also known as the Mensa Isiaca.</note>.

<margin>The Spirit of the Universe according to the Ancients.</margin>
Furthermore, the Ancients were of the opinion that the motion through which the connection of form and matter occurs is a certain "Spirit" acting as a medium between form and matter. They felt that this resided chiefly in the *Aplane* <note>The sphere of the fixed stars.</note>, the Planets, and earthly things. The later Greek Platonists, under a veil of words, not inaptly designated this as Atropos, Clotho, and Lachesis <note>The three Fates of Greek mythology.</note>. For there lie hidden in things certain causes of events—like a harvest in a seed—which, being enfolded in the World Soul as if in a ball of thread, are unfolded and extended through the force and efficacy of motions. And they called this the Spirit of the Universe, and represented it with various hieroglyphic ornaments (as will be seen in Volume III), diffused and contracted through all the paths of the World and its individual parts, which they called "Nature." Hence they defined the nature of all things that come to be through motion as a kind of "unfolding." Indeed, some called this Spirit uncreated, while others, more correctly and in accordance with orthodox doctrine...

# CHAPTER VI. 548 OEDIPUS AEGYPTIACUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM
<note>The title refers to Athanasius Kircher’s massive work attempting to "solve" the riddle of Egyptian hieroglyphs, likening himself to Oedipus solving the riddle of the Sphinx.</note>

<margin>What the Universal Spirit is.</margin>
They held, most fittingly, that a Spirit was created without which nothing could be one, nor could anything subsist. Indeed, this entire World, and all things that shine forth in the majesty of nature, are what they are through this Spirit naturally by a certain necessary connection; namely, so that through its medium, **potentiality** <note>original: *potentia* — the capacity to become something</note> may be in **act** <note>original: *actu* — the state of actually being something</note>, and through its medium, act may be in potentiality. And this is the motion of a loving connection toward unity, so that the Universe may be one of all things. For while things are moved individually to be that which they are in a better way, and no one thing is exactly like another, nevertheless, any given thing contracts the motion of any other in its own way. It participates, whether mediately or immediately, insofar as they are a universe; and through this motion, things exist in the best way they can. They are moved toward this end: that they may be preserved in themselves, or in their species, through the natural connection of different sexes (which, as they are united by nature folding the motion inward, so they are contracted into individuals through division). Let no one think here, however, that nature or motion is explained by motion that is simply maximum and absolute; for since in this state motion coincides with rest, it can be nothing other than God Himself, the Founder and immovable Mover of all things. For just as all potentiality is in absolute potentiality, which is the eternal God and Creator of all; and all form and act is in absolute form, which is the **Word of the Father** <note>original: *Verbum Patris* — a reference to the second person of the Trinity</note>, and the Son in divine matters; so the harmonic ratio of every connection and of all proportions is in the absolute connection of the divine Spirit. Thus, God is the one principle of all; in whom all things are, and through whom all things exist in a certain unity of a **triad** <note>original: *trias* — the Trinity</note>, by a certain shadowy likeness according to more or less "contracted" <note>A term from Nicholas of Cusa meaning the limitation of infinite being into specific, finite forms</note> degrees. Thus, there is one degree of potentiality, act, and the motion of connections in the **Intelligences** <note>Angelic or celestial beings</note>, where to understand is properly to move; and another degree of matter, form, and bond in corporeal things, where to exist is to move. All these things the Egyptians, with an admirable daring of genius, consigned to posterity veiled under **hieromantic symbols** <note>Sacred or divinatory signs</note>, as will be shown fully in its proper place.

### *Corollary.*

<margin>How "anything is in anything" is to be understood.</margin>
And from what has been said, it is clear how that saying of the Ancients—*anything is in anything*—is to be understood. For since God is so in all things that all things are in Him, it is certainly evident from this very fact that all things are in all things, and anything is in anything. For in order that anything might be in anything, the order of nature, as the most perfect universe, preceded all things; and thus in any creature, the universe itself both exists and receives all things, so that in that creature, they are the creature itself in a contracted way. However, the universe exists only in a contracted way within things; and every thing existing in act contracts the universe so that it may be in act what it is. But everything existing in act in God is, in act, all things. Now, act is the perfection and end of potentiality; hence, since the universe exists in any given act, just as the universe is immediately in God, it follows that to say "anything is in anything" is nothing other than saying that God is through all things in all things, and all things are through all things in God. He is indeed in all things without diversity, because anything is in anything; and all things are in God, because all things are in all things; but...

<summary>This page explores the metaphysical concept of the Universal Spirit as a connecting force that allows the "potential" to become "actual." It argues that the entire universe is interconnected such that God is in all things and all things are in God, a concept the author claims was hidden in Egyptian hieroglyphs.</summary>

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER VII

Since the universe is so contained in each thing that each thing is in the universe itself, and in each thing that which it is exists in a contracted <note>original: "contractè" - a philosophical term meaning "limited" or "individualized" as opposed to universal</note> state; it follows that anything in the universe is the universe itself, although the universe exists in each thing in a different manner, just as each thing exists in the universe. In this way, all things in a line are the line; in a stone, the stone; in a plant, the soul; in life, life; in sense, sense; in sight, sight; in hearing, hearing; in imagination, imagination; in reason, reason; in intellect, intellect; and in God, God. You see, therefore, how the unity of things—or the universe—exists in plurality, and conversely, plurality exists in unity; and how every actually existing thing finds its rest in this: because all things in it are all things, and they themselves in God are God. Truly, the unity of things is marvelous, their equality ineffable, and their connection—whereby all are in all—is astounding. Thus, all things rest in each thing, since one degree cannot exist without the other, not unlike the members of a body: each contributes to every other, and every member is immediately in the man through every other member, and the man is in every member through every other member; just as the whole is in the parts through each part in every other. Again, just as absolute humanity, which is unmixable and cannot be contracted, is nothing other than God himself; so contracted humanity in a man is the whole man, and exists contractedly in each of his parts, as the eye in the eye, the heart in the heart, the brain in the brain, and so with the rest. From these points, unless I am mistaken, you will easily gather how that exclamation of the Ancients—*that everything is in everything*—is to be understood. But we shall say more of these things in their proper place, as promised.

# CHAPTER VII.

## Concerning the descent and ascent of souls, and metempsychosis <note>The migration of the soul into a new body after death</note>, according to the mind of the Egyptians.

<margin>The metempsychosis of the Egyptians.</margin>
<margin>Platonic dogmas concerning the Souls of the celestial spheres.</margin>
It is a Platonic decree, as witnessed by the *Timaeus*, that the Maker of the World sows souls into the stars or celestial spheres; this is to be explained such that they wish us to understand not individual souls, but legions of souls assigned to individual stars. He adds, moreover, that God placed the souls in their own vehicles and taught them the nature of the universe and the laws of fate; and so, according to the Platonists, all the spheres are filled with a wealth of souls; Proclus and Iamblichus <note>Neoplatonist philosophers who integrated Egyptian and Chaldean wisdom</note> clearly teach that the Egyptians also held this view. Indeed, souls descend, drawn by a certain desire into the sphere of generation. For as Hermes says in the *Pimander* <note>A foundational text of Hermeticism</note>, *Man, when he had considered the procreation of all things in his Father, wished himself also to create, and thus fell from the contemplation of the Father to the sphere of generation.*

<margin>The descent and ascent of souls according to the Platonists.</margin>
Therefore, the descent of souls into the sphere of corruption is nothing other than the turning of the intellect from the divine contemplation of the Father toward the sensible and elementary World, from which they believed the coupling of the soul with an earthly body soon followed; and as the Egyptians say, the soul loses its wings in the very descent; it experiences a lot that is worse the more it is driven by a more vehement desire for lower things; so much so that they enter not only the bodies of men, but also those of any animals whatsoever.

<margin>The origin of metempsychosis.</margin>
From this arose that most celebrated doctrine of metempsychosis <note>reincarnation</note> by Hermes and Zoroa—

### CHAPTER VII 530 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

First taught to the Egyptians, as is found in the *Pimander* <note>The *Pimander* or *Poimandres* is the first treatise in the *Corpus Hermeticum*, a collection of Greco-Egyptian wisdom texts.</note>, this perverse doctrine found its greatest supporter and advocate in Pythagoras. Thus says 
<margin>Trismegistus.</margin> Hermes:
> *In these things which we have spoken of generally, have you heard how from the one soul of the entire Universe all souls flow forth, distributed as if throughout the whole World? Of these souls, the changes are many; some indeed for the better and more fortunate, others truly to the contrary. For the souls of reptiles are transformed into aquatic creatures; those of the water migrate into land animals, those of the earth enter into birds; those of the air are turned into men; and finally, the immortal souls of men pass into Spirits <note>original: "Dæmones" – in the Greek sense of intermediary spirits or guardians, not necessarily evil beings.</note>; at last they fly back happily into the choirs of the Gods. But the soul that has fallen into a human body, if it persists in evil, does not retain any part of immortality, nor does it enjoy the good; having retraced its path, it is cast down into reptiles. This is the judgment and punishment of the evil soul; the wickedness of the soul is ignorance. A soul ignorant of the nature of things and of the good, deprived of eyes, entangles itself in the passions of the body.*

These are the words of Mercury <note>Mercury is the Roman equivalent of the Greek Hermes, often identified with the Egyptian Thoth.</note>. Although a little later he asserts that the human soul does not enter anything except a human body in these 
<margin>Trismegistus's opinion on the Transmigration of the human soul.</margin> words:
> *Indeed, not every human soul, but only the pious one, is blessed and divine; after such a soul is released from the prison of the body through death, when it has undergone every contest of virtue and piety, it becomes either Mind or God. The contest of religious piety is this: to recognize God and to do injury to no one. However, the impious soul remains in its own nature, tormented excessively by itself; it seeks an earthly and human body to enter, for no body other than a human one can hold a human soul, nor is it right for a rational soul to fall into the body of a soul lacking reason; for divine law prohibits such a wicked degeneration.*

Plato, however, in the *Phaedrus*, describes the entire 
<margin>Plato on the descent and ascent of Souls.</margin> fate of descending souls, and the wings of the soul, by which through many circuits and revolutions it finally flies back to heaven from whence it came, in these words:
> *The rule of the Goddess Adrastia <note>A Greek goddess of inescapable destiny or nemesis.</note>, that is, of the inevitable Divine Power, is this: that whatever soul, having accompanied God, has glimpsed any of the Truths, shall be unharmed until another circuit; and if it can always do this, it shall be forever unhurt. But if, being unable to follow, it has not seen, and by some chance is weighed down, filled with forgetfulness and wickedness, and being weighed down it breaks its wings and falls to the earth; then the law forbids it in its first generation to go into any beastly nature, but commands that the one which saw the most should go into the birth of a Philosopher, or a seeker of beauty, or a lover; that which is in the second place, into a legitimate King, or a man of war, or a commander; the third into a governor of a Republic, or a manager of a household, or a merchant; the fourth into a hardworking athlete or one concerned with the healing and care of the body; the fifth into those who will be Prophets and concerned with certain mysteries; the sixth into a Poet or some other who is aptly engaged in imitation; the seventh into a craftsman or farmer; the eighth into a Sophist and demagogue; the ninth into a tyrant. In all these, whoever has lived a just life will afterwards obtain a better lot; but he who lives unjustly, a worse one. For no soul returns to the same place from which it set out for ten thousand years; for it does not recover its wings before this span of time, except for the soul of one who has philosophized without guile, and together with the study of wisdom has loved beauty.*

From these things it is clear that the wing of the soul is nothing other than a certain innate [quality] in the mind...

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER VII

...a tiny spark, through which, partly by the contemplation of truth and partly by the love of truth itself, the soul may be snatched up toward heavenly things. All of these points Proclus <note>Proclus (c. 412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher who summarized much of the ancient mystical tradition.</note> confirms regarding the soul and the Guardian Spirit in these words: <margin>What the wings of the soul are. Proclus.</margin>
> *Our souls wander here among the images of those things which they had seen in their true homeland, and they are more strongly affected by those images whose archetypes they had more attentively contemplated there; for some souls are suited to different spectacles, and therefore some dwell upon certain images and others upon different ones; for they love the likenesses of those things which they had gazed upon from that place. Those souls which were followers of great Jupiter <note>original: "Iouis" (Jove/Zeus). In this context, it refers to the supreme celestial deity or the planetary spirit of Jupiter.</note> on high, and circled around together with him, holding a leading rank among the twelve Princes of the entire Universe—these souls, perfected according to the likeness of their God, even having set out for this place, long for a commanding kind of life. And if they are ignorant of what is truly imperial, they pursue a visible Sovereignty among mere images; yet if they have obtained Wise teachers, an effect of this kind leads them to salvation through a certain return to the heavens. But if they drag out their delays among images, they decline into tyranny.*

Hence Socrates says in the *Republic* that souls recently departed from Heaven for the most part choose their lives. For since a little while before they circled together with the celestial Gods and inspected their powers dominating all things, they themselves also affect a similar command over others; and while most abuse this affection, very few use it rightly. Furthermore, to each of the stars in the outermost sphere, <margin>Plato thinks souls are assigned to individual stars.</margin> Plato thought the souls of individual men in the lower World corresponded, and that these souls are in some way governed by the virtues of those stars. For Plato says in the *Timaeus* <note>A famous dialogue by Plato concerning the creation of the universe.</note> that when God had established the Universe, he distributed a number of souls equal to the stars, assigning one to each, and having placed them upon these as if upon vehicles, he showed them the nature of the universe and declared the laws of fate: That these souls, subsequently bound to human bodies in their appointed times, would be entangled and agitated by various desires and the passions of pleasure, pain, and mixed love, as well as fear and anger, and other contrary sufferings. Those who overcome these sufferings will live justly, while those who are overcome and subjugated by them will live unjustly. He who rightly completes the race-course given to him by nature shall return to that star to which he was suited and live a blessed life. But he who acts to the contrary shall be forced to become a woman in his second birth, with his sex changed; and he who does not even then make an end of sinning, being depraved by an unmoving habit, shall enter a beastly nature similar to his own impulses; nor shall he cease from these changes until, his beastly passions having been extinguished, he is restored to his original nature. And in the *Phaedo* <note>Plato's dialogue on the immortality of the soul.</note> he says thus: <margin>The souls of the wicked according to Plato.</margin>
> *Therefore, the souls of the wicked are forced to wander around phantoms for so long until, with the desire for a bodily nature accompanying them, they again put on a body; and they put on, as is fitting, such characters as they exercised in life. Those who, devoted to the belly, lived a life through laziness and wantonness, and held no regard for weight or shame, it is fitting that they enter into asses and similar creatures; but those who followed injustices, tyrannies, and robberies above all others, it is right that they pass into the races of Wolves, Hawks, and Kites; each migrating into those species of animals which they resembled in life.*

Since many saw that this opinion of Plato’s was repugnant to reason, they said it was nothing other than a certain allegory, by which Plato hinted at the diverse and vicious habits by which men, being imbued, became like animals. Plotinus <note>The founder of Neoplatonism (c. 204–270 AD).</note> however, held that these things should be understood without any allegory, ridi- <margin>Plotinus.</margin>

### CHAPTER VII. OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

<margin><note>original: "Synesius lib. de Somn."</note> Synesius, in his book *On Dreams*</margin>
...with a truly remarkable discourse, he asserts in his book concerning the *Personal Daemon* <note>A "daemon" in this context refers to a guiding spirit or inner divinity, not an evil entity.</note> of each individual, which you may consult. The soul, finally migrating from the body, he says, passes into that very state in which it most abounded. Therefore, one must flee toward higher things, lest we be stained by sensory appearances, having obeyed—it is clear—sensible phantoms; nor should we be cast headlong into the vegetative soul, enslaved to the lust for procreation and ensnared by the sweetness of flavors. Instead, we must rise with all our strength toward the intellectual, toward the intellect, and toward God. Whoever, therefore, preserved their human character, are born again as men; but whoever used only their senses, return as brute animals. Yet, it is so that those who lived chiefly by sense combined with anger arise as wild beasts, and among them they carry the distinctions of such traits. Those who used their senses through concupiscence and pleasure return as lecherous and gluttonous animals. But if they lived not so much by sense along with these traits, but by a degeneration of sense, they sprout again along with the plants themselves. For in them, the vegetative power alone, or most especially, flourished; and their only care was to be transformed into plants. Furthermore, those who lived too much soothed by musical melodies, but were not depraved in other matters, are reborn as musical animals <note>Likely referring to songbirds.</note>. And those who ruled without reason become eagles, unless they are infected by some other wickedness. Those who, without wisdom, confidently handle sublime matters, often looking up into the sky, are changed into birds, always seeking higher things in flight. He who has attained civil virtue returns as a man. But he who has not sufficiently pursued civil virtue transforms himself into a social animal, such as a bee or similar creatures.

<margin><note>original: "Idem de Pro. lib. 1."</note> The same author, *On Providence*, Book 1.</margin>
The same author in Chapter 13 of Book 1 of *On Divine Providence*, adhering in this part to the Platonic doctrine, wishes for the most just vicissitude <note>The natural change or succession of states.</note> of all things to be admired. Moreover, he says, one must not despise what is commonly said: that it is not fitting to always look only at present things, but also at past and future cycles. For from there, a just repayment is made according to merit, while a change occurs from masters in a previous life to servants in the following life, provided the masters were wicked. And indeed, it is expedient for these men to be so changed. Furthermore, if they abused riches, they are transferred into the poor—where indeed, for the good to be poor is not useless. Likewise, those who have unjustly killed someone will similarly be killed unjustly. Unjustly, indeed, as far as it concerns the one who kills; but justly as far as it pertains to the one who is killed. Truly, he who suffers will thus be brought into the same state along with the one who is ready to perpetrate those things which he said the other suffered. Let no one think that anyone becomes a slave by reckless chance, nor that one becomes a captive by some accident, nor that the body is violated without reason. But because that person perpetrated what he suffers in the present: and he who once extinguished his mother, will in the future be extinguished by his son, having at some point been born a woman. And he who violated a woman, having then been born a woman, will be violated. But let us hear concerning these delusions <note>Kircher uses "deliramentis" to signal that as a Christian, he views the literal transmigration of souls as a theological error, despite its philosophical interest.</note> from Gregory of Nyssa, who disputes them no less learnedly than elegantly in his book *On the Soul and the Resurrection*; for he speaks thus:

<margin>Gregory of Nyssa</margin>
"I have heard," he says, "from those who hand down such things, that they posit certain nations of souls living in a peculiar city before they come to bodily life; which, in their thin and agile nature, wander and roam along with the revolution and preservation of the universe. But by a certain propensity toward vice and wickedness, as if with failing wings, the souls are driven back into bodies—first indeed human ones, then in the same way, on account of a habituation to irrational passions and disturbances, after they have departed from life, they degenerate into cattle, and then glide down even to this vegetative life lacking in sense: so much so that a nature thin and agile, such as the soul is, first..."

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER VII.

<page-num>533</page-num>

...first indeed it is made heavy and tends downward, migrating into human bodies on account of vice and wickedness: then, once the power endowed with reason is extinguished, it leads a life in those lacking reason: the gift of the senses also being taken away, it takes up in turn this life of plants, which is devoid of sense, and afterwards ascends again through the same steps and is restored to its celestial place. And a doctrine of this kind is easily perceived by those of even moderately practiced judgment to have no stable foundation within itself. For if the soul is dragged down from a celestial life to a woody <note>original: "ligneam"; referring to the life of plants or trees</note> life because of vice and wickedness, but from that life it runs back again to the celestial because of virtue, their reasoning is found to waver as to what it considers more excellent and more to be preferred, whether the woody or the celestial life. For it is a circuit and, as it were, a kind of orb, which is completed and finished through similar stages, the soul always—wherever it may be—having no firm or certain place of standing. For if it falls from an incorporeal life to a corporeal one, and from this to those things which lack sense, and likewise from there runs back again to the incorporeal, nothing else but an indistinct and undiscriminated confusion of both evils and goods is imagined and thought of by those who hand down these teachings. For neither will the celestial life remain in blessedness, if indeed the depravity of the one living there invades it; nor will the logs and trunks be devoid of virtue, if indeed they think the soul runs back from here to the good, but from there takes up the beginning of a vicious life. For if the soul which dwells together with heaven is afflicted with vice and wickedness, and on account of depravity is thrust down to a material and sylvan life, and is again carried up from here to lead a life on high; surely an inverted thing is asserted and affirmed by them: namely, that the material life contains an expiatory power for depravity, while the conversion and revolution of the fixed stars and the heavens exists as the cause and principle of evils for souls; if indeed from here, having acquired wings through virtue, they go away on high and contemplate celestial things; but from there, through vice and wickedness, as if having lost their wings, they become humble and abject, and being pressed to the earth, are mixed with the thickness of material nature. <margin>Marsilio Ficino.</margin> Marsilio Ficino <note>A celebrated Italian humanist philosopher of the 15th century who translated Plato into Latin.</note> labors in every way to free both the Ancients and especially Plato from the infamy of this mark, and asserts that they intended nothing else than that the foulness of vices—by whose contagion men, with their reason darkened, degenerate as if into a certain beastly nature—is such as the vice itself has expressed. His words are: *It seemed to Plotinus alone,* he says, *that the soul of a man sometimes becomes the soul of a beast; this displeased the other Platonists. They agree, however, that it transmigrates in turn into other men. Which, even if Plato does not hold as certain, he nevertheless holds as very probable. But as for it migrating into beasts, he often recounts it, but he does so with such a ridiculous manner, so far from his usual gravity, that he clearly demonstrates the thing itself must be denied: and an allegory must be sought. That is to say, that you may understand the passing into a brute in two ways: first, into the affection, imagination, and habit suitable to a brute; then into a habitation and familiarity among wild beasts for a time, for the sake of punishment. In the ninth book of the Republic, he refers the variety of beasts into which the transition is said to be made to the variety of concupiscence <note>Strong desire or lust</note> itself within us. And the same follows in the Phaedo. Moreover, in the Commentary on Plotinus, chapter 2, in the book on one's own demon <note>original: "demone proprio"; referring to the personal guiding spirit or 'daimon'</note>: Although the soul of a man,* he says, *is in some way changed within itself, it is nevertheless never transmuted beyond the certain limits of the human species.* Which also seems to have pleased Iamblichus...

# CHAPTER VII OF THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote on the mysteries of the Egyptians.</note></margin>
...when he said that the soul preserves its own species in every transformation. For the beginning of its motion originates from itself, and it is acted upon within itself. When it is said to be "all things," it must be understood that it is all things not in just any manner, but in its own way—that is, by the specific property of its own life. Therefore, do not say that if the soul is all things through natural potential, it therefore eventually becomes all things. For the soul itself never becomes a bodily form or a body; because clearly the soul is not such a form or body in a general sense, but specifically according to the mode of its own life. Thus, it does not become a beast: since the soul is not simply an animal, but only in a human mode. And in the same place, **Proclus** <note>A Greek Neoplatonist philosopher (412–485 AD) who headed the Academy in Athens.</note> along with the entire school of Platonists, says that he denies the intellectual soul can be so adapted to a wild body—which is utterly foreign to it—that it might at some time communicate with it in life.

<margin>Johann Reuchlin <note>A German humanist and scholar of Hebrew (1455–1522) who introduced Greek and Hebrew studies to German universities.</note></margin>
However, they think that the soul communicates with brutes at times in a certain likeness of life, and that **Plato** felt this as well. Regarding this opinion, **Johann Reuchlin** wrote in Book 2 of *The Art of the Kabbalah* that Pythagorean Metempsychosis <term>Metempsychosis: the transmigration of a soul into a new body after death</term> signifies nothing else to truly learned men than a likeness of motions and pursuits (which previously existed in someone now dead) being reborn in another now living. Thus it was said of old that Euphorbus was reborn in Pythagoras: because the martial virtue which had shone in the Trojan Euphorbus appeared in a certain way in Pythagoras, on account of the love with which he followed athletes. Wherefore, when the athletes themselves wondered why there was such a great love of fighting in a Philosopher devoted to literary study, he is said to have replied that this should not seem at all strange, because the soul of Euphorbus flourished in him—that is, the character, the pursuit, the motion, and the will of Euphorbus resided within him. Even though he was a teacher of peace and an author of quiet contemplation, he nevertheless felt within himself a certain longing, as it were, for the Trojan War. Having heard this, either through ignorance of the Pythagorean mysteries or through the perversity of the envious—who always distort the best things and change the words of others when reciting them—the rumor spread that the soul of Euphorbus, slain in the Trojan War, had migrated into Pythagoras. This opinion was later increased by the fables of the Poets and the additions of other writers. Yet nothing of this sort is found in the works of Pythagoras, in which are commemorated the "return-trip" <note>original: παλινδρομίαν (palindromian)</note>, the "psychic," the "physical," and his *Golden Verses*.

<margin>Tertullian on Metempsychosis.</margin>
And yet **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author (c. 155–220 AD) from Carthage.</note> in his book *On the Soul*, writes that the "Samian Sophist" (for so he names Pythagoras) was the author of this opinion for Plato. He claims that in order to persuade people of this, Pythagoras faked his own death: he hid underground for seven years; he condemned himself to endurance there; then, as if raised from the dead, he told these stories to others about the dead and the underworld. He said that he had once been Euphorbus, and he wished to prove this by the fact that he recognized the shield which Euphorbus had once consecrated at Delphi.

<margin>The Hebrews believed in metempsychosis.</margin>
Certainly, the Hebrews cherished this opinion above others, as was said above in Class IV regarding the Kabbalah; they call this metamorphosis *Gilgul* <note>original: גלגול (Gilgul), meaning "rolling" or "cycle"</note>, that is, the revolutions of souls. And by a Kabbalistic resolution <note>A method of interpreting Hebrew words by the numerical value or hidden meaning of their letters.</note>, they foolishly believe they can demonstrate from the word *Adam* <note>original: אדם (ADm)</note> that the soul of Adam, signified by the letter *A* <note>Aleph</note>, passed into the body of David, which they think the *D* <note>Dalet</note> signifies; and that the soul of David would migrate into the body of the Messiah, indicated by the *M* <note>Mem</note>.

But let us return to the Egyptians, from whose storehouse <note>original: "penua-" (catchword for "penuarium")</note> of deadly doctrine...

This madness truly seems to have flowed from no other source than a poorly understood sense of the Hermetic doctrine <note>The teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, a legendary Hellenistic figure combining the Greek god Hermes and the Egyptian Thoth.</note>, as we have shown extensively elsewhere and in the exposition of the hieroglyphics. <margin>

the part of heaven where the descent of souls occurs, Plato (having been taught by the Egyptians) asserts that the beginning of descending souls occurs from the sublime habitation of the superior World and the star-bearing sphere in the house of Cancer, which the Egyptians called the house of Sothis or the Dog Star; but the beginning of souls ascending again is established in Capricorn. Hence, they call the former the gate of men, and the latter the gate of the Gods. Yet let no one think that this descent and ascent of souls is to be understood according to physical location; rather, it is to be understood thus: since the Moon is the mistress of Cancer (for Cancer is, to this day, the station and domicile of the Moon) and is the closest genetic sphere to all celestial bodies; while Saturn is the <term>oikodespotes</term> <note>original: οἰκοδεσπότης; the "master of the house" or planetary ruler of a zodiac sign.</note> or lord of this house of the zodiac, being the most remote from that same sphere of generation; therefore, souls descend through Cancer—that is, through the lunar and vegetative instinct—weighed down by the passions and desires for fleeting things by which they are disturbed. Through Capricorn, however—namely, through the Saturnine and intellectual instinct, that is, by a new resuscitation of the ideal little-sparks, made through the continuous diligence of contemplation and the study of virtues—they ascend to the same rank from which they had fallen. Moreover, Saturn is nothing else in the mystical Theology of the Ancients (as we demonstrated in the third Class) but the Mind, by whose help alone superior things are sought; for since Saturn and Capricorn are of a dry nature, they make men especially fit for the exercise of intellectual things, with the spirit contracting and gathering into the innermost parts, and they incite and provoke one to contemplate. The Moon and Cancer, however, as they are of a moist nature, so they prevail especially with a dispersive and dilative power, and thus by their own force they incite and propel souls into the whirlpool of sensible spectacles and the genetic sphere. In the descent itself, the soul receives from the Divinity of Saturn (as the Platonists say) through itself, and from the light of Saturn through the ethereal body, a certain cloak—which Zoroaster calls the vehicle of the soul, and the Hebrews (as we taught in the Kabbalah) call the celestial garment—as a kind of incentive to more aptly carry out contemplation. From the Divinity and light of Jupiter, it receives the governance of political life; from Mars, magnanimity for repelling injuries; from the Sun, clarity of imagination and the senses; from Venus, love; from Mercury, knowledge, the interpretation of things, and rhetorical eloquence; and finally, from the Moon, it receives its aids for generating; and although all good things are given, which to...

</margin>
Nevertheless, they can degenerate toward evil through the contagion of earthly mixing; they believe this kind of descent occurs much like a momentary spreading of solar rays. Other Platonists believe that souls live for a certain time in each sphere according to a logic appropriate to that sphere, having obtained their own vehicles from each one; and finally, after many ages, they descend to the elementary sphere. There, they lead a "daemonic" <note>In the classical sense: a spirit intermediate between gods and men, not necessarily evil.</note> life in fire and air, and a human or animal life on earth; and finally, by similar steps of revolution, they return to the celestial dances of the Gods. Thus far the Platonists. All of these things align perfectly with what we proposed regarding the revolution of souls through the ten Sephiroth <note>The ten attributes or emanations in Jewish Cabala.</note> in the fourth Class, where we treated Cabalistic Astrology.

<margin>
The descent of souls is contrary to orthodox doctrine.
</margin>
However, all these things are contrary to orthodox doctrine, as we showed in the cited passage; nor do we wish these things to be said except insofar as they contribute to the exposition of Egyptian Philosophy, for without them, every interpretation and the very effort of "Oedipus" <note>A reference to the author's persona as the solver of riddles, after the mythical Oedipus who solved the Sphinx's enigma.</note> would be superfluous and in vain.

# C H A P T E R VIII.

->*Concerning the sacrifices, rites, and ceremonies which the Ancients*<-
->*used to employ both for purifying the soul and for attracting*<-
->*Divine Powers; which was the goal of mystical Theology.*<-

<margin>
Theurgy of the Egyptians.
</margin>
<margin>
A great part of the Hieroglyphics rests upon the Theurgy of the Egyptians.
</margin>
We read that the Egyptians, above all nations of the world, practiced this part of <term>Theurgy</term> <note>Theurgy: "God-working," a system of white magic practiced by Neoplatonists to achieve union with the divine.</note> which consisted of sacrifices, rites, ceremonies, and the proper performance of invocations of the Gods, which they also called the Priestly Art. For they believed that if they performed this legitimately, they would be filled with all good things and blessed with the company of the Gods. Hence, a great part of the hieroglyphics rests upon this <term>Theurgy</term>, as will be shown in the third Volume; indeed, whatever Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote "On the Mysteries of the Egyptians."</note>—the true and most genuine interpreter of the Egyptians—relates in his entire wonderful work on the mysteries of the Egyptians, seems to allude to this.

<margin>
The care for purifying souls among the Egyptians.
</margin>
And although most of these things are contrary to orthodox doctrine, it should nevertheless seem marvelous that the Egyptians, though situated in the deepest shadows of infidelity, held such a high regard for the proper purification of souls, and aspired with such great desire to the company of the Gods and the blessedness of celestial life. And although the Devil, the enemy of the human race, acting as the "Ape of Divinity" <note>A common medieval/early modern trope: the devil mimics God's works to deceive.</note> under a masked disguise, frequently mixed himself into all their operations, the lives of those who devoted themselves to Philosophy and <term>Theurgy</term> nevertheless had something superhuman mixed in, as is abundantly clear from the Hermetic works. This is something the Holy Fathers—Justin Martyr, Clement of Alexandria, and Augustine—marveled at, and it will be clearly evident from what follows.

<margin>
What the sacraments were by which "God-possession" was accomplished among the Egyptians.
</margin>
It is asked, therefore, first: what are the sacraments, and what is their power, by which the Egyptians believed they performed such great miracles? Iamblichus thinks that the Deific union, which they call <term>Theolepsia</term> <note>original: "Θεοληψία" — God-possession or being seized by the divine.</note> or <term>Theomorphosis</term> <note>original: "Θεομόρφωσιν" — being formed into the likeness of God.</note>, only...

Kircher discusses how the Egyptians used rites and sacrifices to seek divine union, noting that while these practices are heterodox, they contain a "superhuman" quality admired even by Church Fathers.</summary>
