# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER VIII.

...is provided both by a fitting observance of the divine precepts and works which exceed all understanding, and by the wondrous power of the symbols and sacraments devoted to the Divinities alone. For the Priests believed that by the very fact that the sacraments were performed, even if they themselves did not understand them or were occupied with something else, they nevertheless achieved their effect; for the power of the Gods, to which these things are referred, recognizes its own ineffable images through itself, and is not stirred by our intellect. For universal causes, as they say, are not moved by particular effects; hence, the more divine essences are not principally moved to action by our intellect. Rather, it is necessary that the intellect, the affection of a good will, and purity precede as certain dispositions and co-causes, as Iamblichus says. 

<margin>Iamblichus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher (c. 245–325 AD) who wrote extensively on theurgy and Egyptian mysteries.</note></margin>

But they believe that the sacraments themselves are what most strongly provoke the divine will; and thus divine things are incited by themselves, and do not receive the beginning of their action from any subordinate source. For just as the Egyptians and Chaldeans say that in agriculture, medicine, the art of images, and human intercourse, man opportunely adapts and disposes the matter, but a higher and universal cause applies the form; so in sacrifice, when there are symbols and <term>synthemata</term> <note>Tokens or "passwords" used in theurgy to connect the human soul with the divine.</note>—that is, seals and sacraments—the Priest provides the material elements, but God impresses His efficacy upon the sacraments. Is there not indicated here in some way, though under an obscure veil of words, the same thing that orthodox Theologians teach when they assert that the sacraments confer grace **by the work performed** <note>original: "ex opere operato" — a Catholic theological doctrine meaning the sacrament is effective by the rite itself, regardless of the priest's merit.</note>, and not by the work of the one performing it?

<margin>The care of the Egyptians in rightly performing their rites and ceremonies.</margin>

The Egyptians therefore believed that rites, ceremonies, and sacraments, when performed rightly and religiously, obtained great efficacy in their sacrifices. I said "rightly and religiously performed" because they believed that if they omitted even a single circumstance, the entire work would be void. Therefore, with the greatest zeal and intense care, they applied themselves to this one goal: to administer each and every thing as perfectly and sincerely as possible. For first, a place was required that was removed from all human company, which they called the <term>adytum</term> <note>The innermost sanctuary or "holy of holies" of a temple.</note>. 

<margin>With what preparation the Egyptian Priests entered the sanctuaries.</margin>

Hence, before they entered, they strove with the greatest zeal to dispose themselves to better receive the influences of the Gods through many days of abstinence, vigils, mortification of the body, and the subduing of earthly desires. Having entered the sanctuary, they wore a sacred garment, entirely analogous to the operations of the Gods; for they believed that mystical and symbolic bodily ornaments greatly pleased the Gods, and that the Gods were drawn to present themselves as if by a kind of bait, attracted to things most kindred and congruent to their nature. 

<margin>What the Egyptian Priests did in the sanctuaries.</margin>

Once these things were done, they added various transformations of the body into the name of the Divinity they were invoking, by which they believed the Divinities were wonderfully drawn. To these were added the recitation of hymns appropriated to each God, and the invocation of divine names under unknown words; finally, an exact selection of fumigations <note>Incense or ritual smoke.</note> suitable to each. When all these things had been mystically performed, they believed it was impossible for the Divinities not to present themselves voluntarily and carry out the requests of the Priests. For they believed that once these rites were properly performed, the purified soul was perfectly disposed to attain supreme illuminations, and the gift of Soothsaying and Prophecy was granted as a gift of the immortal Gods.

It details the rigorous physical and spiritual preparations Priests underwent to enter the sanctuary and invoke the divine.</summary>

# CHAPTER VIII. 538 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

Once this was obtained, they believed themselves to be free from fate, released from every bond of necessity, and blessed by the fellowship of the Gods—<note>original: "θεολήπτους καὶ θεομόρφους" (theoleptous kai theomorphous)</note> possessed by God and formed in the likeness of God—which was the sole end and goal of all <term>Theurgy</term> <note>Theurgy refers to "god-working," a ritual practice intended to invoke the presence of deities or achieve union with the divine.</note>. However, how one should proceed in rites and ceremonies of this kind has been discussed here and there throughout this and other works, and is explained specifically by Iamblichus in his book *On the Mysteries of the Egyptians*, to which I refer the reader. Orpheus certainly attributed the greatest power to fumigations and scents in sacrifices, which is why I have thought it appropriate to describe them in this place.

### Section One.

### *On the fumigations used in sacrifices from the Hymns of Orpheus.*

<margin>Fumigations used in sacrifices among the Ancients.</margin>
We have said throughout this work that the Egyptians placed great importance on <term>thyamiamata</term> <note>From the Greek 'thymiama,' meaning incense or aromatic substances burned during a rite.</note> or fumigations in their sacrifices and invocations of the Gods; for they thought nothing more pleasing could be offered to the Gods than presenting the specific types of spices, either simple or compound, appropriate to each. Hence Orpheus, a disciple of the Egyptians, intends this one thing in his mystical hymns to the Gods: to bring forth for each one the fumigation in the sacrifices that is fitting and congruent to them. But since all these things are seen everywhere displayed through hieroglyphic symbols, I have thought it appropriate to set down here the fumigations of the individual Gods, which were used either to appease the Gods or to attract them.

<margin>The fumigations of the individual Gods.</margin>
First, for the Goddess of those in labor, <term>Lithya</term> <note>Likely a variation of Eileithyia, the Greek goddess of childbirth.</note>, whom they call Prothyraea, he prescribes that a fumigation of storax <note>A fragrant resin.</note> should be used in sacrifices, by which they believed that <term>Empusas</term>, <term>Lamias</term>, and <term>Liliths</term> <note>Various classes of demons or night-monsters believed to threaten mothers and infants.</note> were driven away from inflicting evils upon those in labor. In this manner, he offers to the Goddess of Night, whom he also calls Cypris, lamps—that is, the splendors of fires—to dissipate the foul darkness. To the Sky, however, whom he calls the Father of the World and an outstanding Spirit, he offers frankincense; to the Ether, saffron; to Saturn, whom he also calls the first-born Phanes and Priapus, he offers myrrh, thinking he would be drawn by this. He concludes this hymn with this verse:

-> Come down rejoicing <-
-> To the holy rite, full of variety for those who reveal the mysteries. <-
> <note>original Greek: "Βαῖνε γεγηθὼς · Καὶ τελετὴν ἁγίαν πολυποίκιλον ὀργιοφάνταις."</note>

To Nature, the Stars, and the Moon, he offers spices; to the Sun, he offers <term>Libanomanna</term> <note>A high-quality incense consisting of the "manna" or fine dust of frankincense.</note> to obtain a blessed life; for he composed the hymn thus:

-> Hear my words, and reveal a pleasant life to the initiates. <-
> <note>original Greek: "Κλῦθι λόγων ἡδὺς δὲ βίον μύστησι πεφαίνε"</note>

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. 539
## CHAPTER VIII.

To Pan, he offers various <term>incenses<note>original: "suffimenta"</note></term> to obtain a good end to life, as is clear from the conclusion of the hymn. To Hercules, he offers frankincense to ward off evil harms. To Rhea, he applies spices to bring about peace along with wealthy possessions, and to banish the Fates to the ends of the earth. To Jupiter, storax <note>a fragrant resin</note> to attain blameless health, peace, and the glory of riches. To Juno, spices; to Neptune and Nereus, myrrh <note>original: "smyrnam"</note>, to obtain a prosperous journey by sea, and to entreat for peace and riches. To Proteus, storax, so that by holy providence he may send happiness of life to those learning the sacred mysteries, and grant a prosperous end to their labors. To the Earth, he grants every seed except beans and spices, intended both for increasing fruits and for entreating blessed times. To Cybele, the Mother of the Gods and wife of Saturn, he ordains incenses composed of various ingredients to receive the various gifts of the earth. To Mercury, the Messenger of the Gods, he bestows frankincense, that he may provide a good end to life, grace of speech in one's works, and for the perfecting of memory. To Dionysus or Bacchus, storax is offered, so that those things over which he rules may happen to be obtained with a joyful yield. To Minerva or Pallas, he consecrates and burns <term>Persian leaves<note>likely the Persea tree, often associated with Thoth/Hermes and Minerva in Egypto-Roman contexts</note></term> to obtain wisdom. To Apollo, he offers manna to entreat quiet and tranquil times. To Venus, any fragrant things of great efficacy, to win for himself the loves of mortals. To Adonis and Love <note>Cupid/Eros</note>, he exhibits spices to put to flight <term>ill-counsel<note>original Greek: "δισβουλίας" (disboulias), meaning harmful or foolish plans</note></term> or ruinous and absurd advice. To Nemesis, he ordains incenses composed of various things to obtain good thoughts and to calm unjust opinions. To Aesculapius, he provides manna for prosperous health and to obtain the happy effects of medicines.

<margin>The sacred rites of the Egyptians were not performed without fumigations.</margin>
From these things it is clearly established that the Egyptians did nothing in their sacrifices without fumigations; but rather offered their incenses according to the status of the Deity. Hence that famous *Kyphi* of the Egyptians, about which, according to the witness of Suidas, Julian the Philosopher wrote an entire book, being composed of sixteen species: which also Plutarch, in his book on Osiris and Isis, describes in these words:

<margin>Plutarch.</margin>
> This also offers some testimony for the sake of giving a reason: that the Egyptians call Myrrh *Bal*, a word which, if you interpret it, signifies the removal of madness. Furthermore, *Kyphi* is a mixture of sixteen things combined into one: honey, wine, raisins, galingale <note>original: "cyperi"</note>, resin, myrrh, asphalt, seselis <note>meadow saxifrage</note>, fragrant rush, bitumen, fig leaf, dock, both types of juniper (for they name two, the greater and the lesser), cardamom, and calamus. Moreover, they do not compose these species at random, but while the <term>perfumers<note>original: "seplasiarijs"</note></term> mix these things, sacred writings are recited. The number itself seems to hold something, because it is surely a square produced from a square <note>16 is 4x4</note>, the only one of such to be equally even, and having the same quantity of area as the number of its perimeter; but many of those things which are mixed contribute to this, being endowed with aromatic faculties. Therefore, *Kyphi* emits a sweet and useful exhalation, by which the air, having been changed by its Spirit, also affects the body, and acquires a mild temperament; it relaxes the distress and intensity of divine cares like certain chains of the soul without drunkenness: and it smooths the imaginative faculty of the soul and its capacity for dreams like a mirror, rendering it purer; no less effectively indeed than the sounds of the lyre, which the Pythagoreans used before sleep, charming away and calming the part of the soul subject to irrational and sudden movements.

# CHAPTER VIII. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM.

*...ing; for scents recall the failing senses, though often they conversely dull and lull them to sleep, as their exhalations spread through the body due to their lightness. Just as some physicians say sleep is brought on when the vapor of food, like a serpent, gently winds around the intestines and, by touching them, induces a certain tickling sensation. Furthermore, Kyphi is even mixed by the Egyptians for drinking, for it seems to cleanse the internal organs by its power of softening. Beyond these things, resin is the work of the Sun, and myrrh is a tear produced from stalks under the influence of the Moon. Moreover, of those things which are composed in Kyphi, there are some that delight more in the night, as they are nourished by cold spirits, Shadows, dew, and moisture; for the light of day is one and simple, and Pindar says the Sun is beheld through the empty ether; but the nocturnal air is mixed and tempered from various lights and powers, which flow together into one from all the stars like a seed. Therefore, it is not without reason that those simple things procreated by the Sun are burned during the day; while these mixed things, endowed with all kinds of qualities, are burned at the onset of night.*

<margin>How the Ancients attracted the Gods through fumigations, according to Iamblichus. <note>Iamblichus was a Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on Egyptian mysteries.</note></margin>

Since, however, the Ancients attributed so much power to fumigations for summoning Divine Beings, Iamblichus teaches the reason for this in these words: *For the Higher Beings are free from passion, since it pleases them that matter be dispersed and consumed by fire, and they render us foreign to passions, making whatever is within us similar to the Gods: just as fire renders all hard and opaque things similar to subtle and bright bodies, and lifts us upward through sacrifices. The consumption of these things by fire leads us to the fire of the Gods, just as fire lifts fire and brings back heavy and hard things together to the divine and celestial heights. Providing a bodily vehicle for spirits <note>original: "dæmonibus," referring to intermediary spirits, not necessarily evil demons</note>, it exists neither from matter, nor from elements, nor from any body known to us. Therefore, nourishment cannot be made for Spirits from elemental essence as if it were something entirely foreign; but just as the Gods divide matter with lightning-fire and separate from matter whatever things are indeed immaterial by essence but bound to matter, and render the impassible from the passible: so also our fire, imitating the action of divine fire, destroys whatever material thing it finds in the sacrifice, purifies it to known levels, and releases it from the chains of matter. Because of the purity of its nature, it makes things fit for communion with the Gods, and in the same way absolves us from the chains of generation, assimilates us to the Gods, makes us fit for the friendship of the Gods, and lifts our material nature to an immaterial nature.*

Yet because Iamblichus established a double order of Gods, partly material and partly immaterial; he therefore determined that they must be honored with different worship and sacrifices of a different nature. But since he there most aptly hints at the mind of the Egyptian Priests and the <term>Hermetic hieroglyphic dogmas</term> <note>Teachings attributed to Hermes Trismegistus, the legendary sage of Egypt</note>, I have thought it necessary to clarify his discourse, which is perhaps more obscure to them, in this <term>narrative</term> <note>original: "τὴν διήγησιν" (tēn diēgēsin)</note>.

<margin>The doctrine of Iamblichus concerning the double order of the Gods among the Ancients, and the manner of worshipping them.</margin>

*The best principle for all these things is that which declares the context of sacrifices, annexed consequently to the order of the Gods. We place some Gods as material, others as immaterial. The material ones are those who comprehend and entreat matter within themselves; the immaterial ones are those who are entirely segregated from matter. According to the Priestly art, therefore, it is fitting to begin sacrifices from the material Gods; for otherwise the ascent to the immaterial Gods is not open. These, therefore, have a certain communion with matter, insofar as they preside over and brood upon it; these same ones dominate in those things which happen around matter, such as division, percussion, and repercussion...*

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER VIII.

...to [change], mutation, generation, and corruption, as are all material bodies. If anyone, therefore, wishes to worship these beings rightly, he must certainly employ a form of worship according to their nature and sovereignty—that is, a material worship for material beings. For in this way, we shall be led in our entirety into a proper intimacy with them through all their parts, and we shall apply a kinship in worship that is suitable to them. Therefore, bodies deprived of life, the slaughter of animals, the destruction of bodies, multiform change and corruption, and the total casting away of preceding matter, is appropriate for the material Gods <note>The author is discussing the Neoplatonic concept of "Material Gods" who oversee the physical realm and thus require physical offerings.</note>: not indeed for themselves or for their own sake, but for the sake of the matter over which they preside. For even if they are greatly separated from this matter, they are nevertheless present to it at the same time; and even if they contain matter within an immaterial power, they nonetheless exist together with it. Now, governed things are not foreign to their governors, nor are adorned things foreign to those who adorn them. Furthermore, those things which are supplied as instruments are easily adapted by their proportions to those who use them. Wherefore, to employ matter in sacrifices is foreign to the immaterial Gods; but for all the material Gods, it is entirely consistent. It is worthwhile, moreover, to consider the twofold condition of our life. At times, we become entirely composed of soul, placed outside the body and elevated in mind; together with the whole company of immaterial Gods, we raise ourselves through sublime heights. At other times, however, we are bound by the earthly body and are corporeal, clearly encompassed by matter.

<margin>A twofold method of divine worship according to the doctrine of Iamblichus.</margin>
Similarly, there will be a twofold reasoning for divine worship: one will be simple, incorporeal, and pure from all generation <note>In this context, "generation" refers to the cycle of birth, change, and decay in the physical world.</note>, fitting for pure beings; the other, however, is full of bodies and entirely material action, suitable for beings not yet pure, and not yet purged from all generation. There are, therefore, two species of sacrifices: the purest sacrifices are those of men who are highly purified. This indeed rarely happens to one person, or to very few, as Heraclitus says. But material sacrifices, and those involved in change, are suitable for beings still occupied by the body. Therefore, for Cities not yet purged of their generative lot and corporeal companionship, unless you grant such sacrifices, you will wander away from both equally—from both immaterial and material goods. The former cannot receive them, and to the latter, you do not offer what is proper and consistent. Added to this is the fact that everyone ought to take care of their essence according to what they are, not according to what they are not. It is not right, therefore, to transgress this proper measure and nature of the worshiper. I judge that the properly adapted connection between the men who care and the powers who are cared for will choose a mode of worship convenient to itself; for a connection of that kind, tempered immaterially, chooses the immaterial, insofar as it is joined by purely incorporeal powers to the purely incorporeal themselves. A connection of that kind, adapted corporeally to bodies, chooses a similar worship for the essences presiding over bodies.

<margin>The method of expiation according to Iamblichus.</margin>
Often, for the necessary use of the body, we vow and perform something toward the Gods who govern the body and toward good Demons <note>original: "Dæmones." In the classical sense, these are intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not necessarily evil entities.</note>, namely while we strive to purge the body of certain stains and ancient filth, or to release it from diseases and provide health, or to remove heaviness and torpor, and to [effi-] <note>The text cuts off mid-word; the catchword "effi-" suggests "efficere" (to bring about/effect) lightness.</note>

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic distinction between material and immaterial worship, arguing that while pure souls may offer intellectual worship, physical sacrifices are necessary for those still bound to the material world and for the "Material Gods" who govern it.</summary>

# CHAPTER VIII. 542
## THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

...to apply efficacy, or to procure some other good for the body. In such a case, we shall not treat the body properly by some intellectual and incorporeal reasoning; for the body is not so constituted as to be capable of being cured in those ways. Rather, when it obtains things kindred to itself, then is the body cared for and purified by bodies. Therefore, the **ritual of sacrificing** for such a purpose will necessarily be corporeal; and thus it will purge the superfluities of the body, supply what is lacking according to necessity, and reduce whatever has been disordered back to proportion and order. 

We often sacrifice while asking the gods above for things suited to human life—namely, those things necessary for sustenance, or pertaining to those things we desire for the sake of the body. What, then, will come to us from the Gods themselves—who are entirely segregated from all human generation—that might contribute to putting to flight poverty or sterility, or bringing us abundance, or leading to other necessities of life? Truly nothing: for those who are absolved from all things do not handle gifts of that kind. 

If, however, someone should say that those **immaterial Gods** comprehend within themselves the **material Gods**, and embrace the gifts of these latter according to one primary cause, he would certainly be describing a certain abundance of divine bounty descending from that high place to the lower realms. But it must be granted to no one to say that those [higher gods], in handling these matters, perform actions closely related to human life; for the <term>dispensation</term> <note>Latin: *dispensatio*; the management or distribution of earthly affairs</note> of such things as are here is divided and particular, and is carried out with a certain turning toward these things. It is neither entirely segregated from bodies, nor can it admit a pure and sincere governance and prefecture. 

The mode of sacrificing appropriate for such matters, therefore, is one that has commerce with bodies and generation, not one that is entirely separated from matter and the body. For he who is altogether pure transcends such things and has no proportion to them; but he who uses bodies and their powers is most kindred to all such things, being able to supply certain prosperous things for life, to avoid the adversities threatening us, and to provide a moderate temperament for the human race. 

The vast multitude of men is subjected to **universal nature**, and is governed by natural forces, and inclines downward toward the works of nature, and completes the <term>dispensation of fate</term> <note>The unfolding of destiny within the physical world</note>, and undergoes the order of **fated works**, exercising practical reason only concerning natural things. 

A very few, relying on a **supernatural power of the mind**, depart from nature and betake themselves to a separate and unmixed intellect; whence they emerge superior to natural powers. Some, however, hold a middle ground between pure intellect and nature: of these, some follow each in turn, others lead a life mixed from both, and others are released from the lower things and transfer themselves to the better. 

Those, therefore, who are governed by universal nature, and who lead a life enslaved to their own nature and enjoy the powers of nature, will exercise a **worship** <note>Latin: *cultum*; religious service or devotion</note> suitable to nature and congruent with bodies moved by nature: choosing for this purpose locations, qualities, the matter of the air, the powers of matter, bodies, the qualities and habits of bodies, convenient movements, and the mutations of those things involved in generation and the like—both in the other parts of divine worship and in the ritual of sacri—

<meta>catchword: fican- (sacrificing)</meta>

<summary>This page argues that while the highest gods are immaterial, physical sacrifices are necessary for humans because our bodies and worldly needs require "kindred" material interventions. It categorizes humanity into three groups: those ruled by nature, those who transcend it through intellect, and those in between.</summary>

# CLASS XII. HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. 543 CHAPTER VIII.

Those who live by the mind alone, freed from the chains of nature, will meditate upon an intellectual and bodiless standard of worship in every part of their religion. Those who lead a middle life between the intellect and nature will likewise follow a middle religion, and according to the differences of that middle life, they will follow different modes of worship through middle means; for they will either deal with both by turns, or decline from one to the other, or touch upon lesser things so that through them they may attain the greater, believing they cannot otherwise reach the more sublime. In the genus of divine essences and powers, some indeed have the soul and nature subject to them—serving their works, as it were, insofar as they themselves wish; others, however, are entirely separate from soul and nature—I do not mean only from the mundane and generative soul <note>The "generative soul" refers to the aspect of the soul responsible for physical birth and biological life.</note>, but even from the divine soul and its nature.

<margin>Sacrifices must be established according to the nature of the Gods, following the mind of Iamblichus.</margin>
Finally, others hold the middle ground and reconcile the communion between the extremes, either according to one indissoluble bond, or according to an exuberant tradition of greater things, or according to an unimpeded reception of lesser things, or according to a bound agreement of both. When we worship the Gods who rule over soul and nature, it is not out of place to offer natural powers to them, and to consecrate to such Gods the bodies which are governed by nature. For all works of nature both obey them and contribute something to their administration. But when we desire to venerate Gods who are far removed and gathered in their own unity, we must worship them with honors entirely released from matter. For to these are owed intellectual gifts, incorporeal life, perfect virtue, consummate wisdom, and their respective duties. To the middle Gods, however, and the Leaders of middle goods, middle things are appropriate, as we have said.

Starting therefore from another principle—namely, from the World, the mundane Gods, and the distribution of the four Elements in the World made from a common lot according to the measures of the Elements, and from the circumference revolving in order around the centers—we have easy access to the truth of sacrifices. For if we are in the World, and are contained in it as parts, and are first generated by it, and are perfected by its total powers, and are composed of its four Elements, and hold a certain portion of life and nature obtained from it, we certainly ought not to omit the World and the mundane orders in divine worship.

Let us suppose, therefore, that around every part of the World there is indeed some body as we see, and that there are moreover incorporeal powers distributed in order within those bodies: the law of sacred rites thus rightly distributes like to like, and proceeds from the highest to the lowest through all the middle stages: applying bodies to the corporeal, and incorporeal things to the incorporeal, rendering to each its own. Nevertheless, if any religious person attains to a super-mundane Deity <note>original: "supermundanum Numen"; a divinity existing beyond the physical universe.</note> (which happens very rarely), he alone, placed apart from bodies and matter, surely pursues such a worship, united to the super-mundane Gods by a super-mundane power. But that which scarcely happens to one person at the very end of the Priesthood <term>Sacerdotium: the priestly office or the path of sacred rites</term> should not be established as a common law for everyone at the beginning or the middle of religion. For these people perform a corporeal worship in whatever way they can.

Every person skilled in the Priesthood will therefore confess that worship ought...

<meta>The catchword "tum" at the bottom right indicates the next page begins with the continuation of the word "cultum" (worship).</meta>

<summary>This page outlines a Neoplatonic hierarchy of religious worship based on the nature of the practitioner and the deity, arguing that while pure intellectual worship exists, most must use physical elements and "mundane" rites reflecting the structure of the universe.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion from the previous section of Athanasius Kircher's "Egyptian Oedipus," specifically within the "Gymnasium of Hieroglyphics." The text focuses on the Neoplatonic theology of Iamblichus regarding the necessity of complex ritual action.</meta>

# CHAPTER VIII. THE EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS’ GYMNASIUM OF HIEROGLYPHICS

...to offer to the gods above nothing partial or imperfect, but that which is fitting and whole. Since, therefore, before the Gods are present and descend to the earth, all the powers lying beneath them are moved and precede them like heralds and processions; surely he who does not distribute to all what is suitable to each, nor honors every single one with his own specific tribute, fails to attain the very presence of the Gods. But he who renders all the Divine Powers favorable to himself, offering pleasing things to each and similar gifts, is certainly not frustrated in the outcome, but receives the divine Choir with a complete and full presence. Since these things are so, it is not right for the rite of religion to be simple and composed of few elements, but multiform, consisting of every harmony, and constituted from all things everywhere in the world (so to speak).

<margin>The effects of the appearing Gods according to the mind of Iamblichus <note>Iamblichus (c. 245–325 AD) was a Syrian Neoplatonist philosopher who defended the use of theurgy, or "god-working" rituals, against purely intellectual philosophy.</note>.</margin>
For if that which is invoked in the Priesthood <term>Sacerdotio: the priestly office or theurgic rite</term> and is moved toward us were something simple and of only one order, then a simple mode of sacrificing would surely suffice. But in truth, no one knows how great a multitude of forces is usually stirred up when the Gods descend and are moved, except for those Priests who have already experienced it through the work itself. Therefore, only these men know what constitutes the most perfect fullness of worship, and how much the outcome frustrates us if even a few things are omitted. Just as in a harmony, if one string is broken, the whole suddenly becomes dissonant; so if one Divine Power is passed over without a rite, the common religion itself does not reach its desired end, for while this one is lacking, the sacred work lacks its structure and integrity. When the divine powers are about to descend openly to the senses, a manifest loss occurs to us if we pass over any of those above without honor. Similarly, when they come secretly in a sacred work, it is dangerous if you honor one indeed, but do not honor another according to his dignity and order. For those who defraud anyone of his proper honor confound the entire work of religion, while dissipating a single and total arrangement; nor, as someone might think, is the work of receiving then merely imperfect, but the whole structure perishes. What then? Does not the very summit of holiness return to the supreme principle and the One of the entire multitude of Divine Powers, and in that One worship all divine essences and dominions together? Without a doubt; but a summit of this kind arrives very late, and to very few; and we must think it goes best with us if such things happen at the end of life. But the present discussion does not lay down laws for such a God—for He is superior to law—but for those in need of some law, it enacts these laws of sacred rites for the present. The multitude of Divine Powers is like a certain World, having many orders breathing together into one order. Similarly, sacrifices ought to have the order of the Divine Powers, likewise breathing together into one order, so that individual rites correspond duly to individual Powers. Similarly, the things around us and within us are manifold, and they ought not to correspond to the divine causes of our affairs from only one part, but from all parts congruously, and thus ascend to the supreme leaders. Therefore, religious observance around us and within us performs various things. For it either perfects by propagating, or prunes, or cleanses, or orders those things lacking order, or separates them further from mortal error; finally, it makes all things familiar to the celestial powers...

<meta>The catchword "milia-" at the bottom indicates the next page begins with "miliaribus" or a similar continuation of "familiaria" (familiar/intimate).</meta>

<summary>This page explains the theurgic necessity of complex rituals, arguing that because the divine realm is a harmonious multitude, every specific power must be honored to ensure the success of a religious rite. It uses the metaphor of a musical string to show how omitting one element ruins the whole spiritual structure.</summary>
<keywords>Iamblichus, theurgy, ritual integrity, divine hierarchy, harmony, sacrifice, priesthood, Neoplatonism</keywords>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Hieroglyphic Theology, specifically focusing on the relationship between divine providence and material reality as understood by Neoplatonic philosophers.</meta>

### CLASS XII HIEROGLYPHIC THEOLOGY. CHAPTER VIII.

...establishes familiarity. But when both sides come together as one—on one hand the divine causes, and on the other, equal human preparations—then perfect religion accomplishes all things, and carries back great blessings from the sacrifices. Indeed, the exuberance of power in the highest causes of the universe is such that, just as it surpasses lower things in other respects, so it greatly surpasses them in this: namely, in the very magnitude of its presence. Thus, the greatest causes of all are most present to all things, so much so that the same power of each cause is always present everywhere in its entirety, free from any hindrance. By this reasoning, the very first principles shine down even upon the last; and immaterial principles are present to material things in an immaterial way. Let no one wonder if we say that some matter is pure and divine; for since matter itself was made by the Maker and Father of all, it has deservedly acquired a certain perfection of its own, making it fit to receive the Gods. These are the words of <term>Iamblichus</term> <note>A 4th-century Neoplatonist philosopher who defended the use of "theurgy" or ritual to reach the divine.</note>.

In these words, he primarily strives to show the supreme providence of the Gods, which he believed could be won over in no better way than through the sacred rites of religion; for providence certainly encompasses all things contained within the circuit of the World. But concerning these matters, let us hear <term>Proclus</term> <note>A later Neoplatonist (5th century) who systematized Greek philosophy.</note> on the soul and the demon <note>original: "dæmone" - here referring to a "daimon" or intermediary spirit, not an evil entity.</note>, where he indicates quite aptly and in summary the things we have reviewed so far, in the following words:

> *Those who are more diligent in assigning the reasons for things hand down these two most powerful elements of divine and Demonic providence. First, that providence proceeds from above through all things to the very last, and does not overlook any place, however small, leaving it devoid of itself. Second, that it receives absolutely nothing from the things it governs, nor is it filled by their nature, nor mixed with them anywhere. For it is not mixed with the governed simply because it preserves and arranges all things: for it possesses a divine and Demonic nature, not subject to the passions of particular souls. Nor, however, while it separately towers over the things that follow it, does it leave anything disordered or uncultivated among the lower things. On the contrary, for this very reason, it adorns all things becomingly, and remains detached from the things it dispenses. For it is equally beneficent and pure, the adorner of all things, and meanwhile free from the things it has cultivated. Running through all things, it is especially so because it is nowhere restrained. Even divine men provide for lower things most diligently and, at the same time, tranquilly. What then is to be said of the Gods themselves and the good Demons? Are they not present to all, yet free from all? Filling all things with themselves, they mix with nothing anywhere. Running through the universe, they have nowhere surrendered their own life.*

<margin>The Gods love their own affairs.</margin>
> *Shall we not confess that the Gods love their offspring? Just as the Poets feign that Jove loves a girl, and Venus herself. Surely because such love is a provider, a savior, a perfecter, and a sustainer of things divinely loved. Meanwhile, it is both beneficent and pure and unmixed, affected by no habit toward external things. Tell me, I pray, from where would such a privilege of love have fallen to the divine souls of men, unless it were first present in the Gods themselves? For whatever good and salutary quality belongs to souls has its defined cause from the Gods. For which reason <term>Plato</term> proves that the patterns of all virtues and bodily goods—such as health, strength, justice, and temperance—precede us in the possession of God. How much more, therefore, shall we confess that the principal cause of the gift of love is with the Gods? Especially since this affection of love, as <term>Socrates</term> says in the <term>Phaedrus</term>, by a divine...*

<summary>This page explores the Neoplatonic concept of Divine Providence, arguing that the highest divine causes are present in all material things without being corrupted by them. It cites Iamblichus and Proclus to explain how ritual and divine love connect the material world to the Creator.</summary>
<keywords>Providence, Neoplatonism, Iamblichus, Proclus, Matter, Divine Love, Theurgy, Plato, Socrates</keywords>

--- Page 554 ---
<meta>This page concludes the second part of Kircher's "Egyptian Oedipus," transitioning from the philosophical underpinnings of ancient theology to the practical interpretation of hieroglyphs found in the subsequent volume.</meta>

# CHAPTER VIII. 546 EGYPTIAN OEDIPUS: THE HIEROGLYPHIC GYMNASIUM

<margin>Love is inherent in all things.</margin>
...is granted by a certain gift. Therefore, the Gods love other Gods: the elder love the lesser by the gift of providence; the lesser, in turn, love the greater by a certain duty of conversion <note>The Neoplatonic concept of "epistrophe," where the created returns its gaze toward the creator</note>. Indeed, it is the role of souls—insofar as they are souls by virtue of reason—to perfect those things which are lesser and to provide for those below them. For it is for this very reason that they descend: for the sake of providing for generated things and for the care of mortals. Yet, to provide in such a way that the provider neither mixes with the governed, nor becomes bound by affection for them, nor receives anything from them, is the unique property of the Gods and of the good Daemons <note>In this context, "Daemons" refers to intermediary spirits or guiding geniuses, not evil entities</note>. Whenever this occurs in human souls, it happens through divine or Daemonic generosity.

<margin>Priesthoods and sacrifices.</margin>
In the most sacred sacrifices, Priests are accustomed to lead those present into admiration and stupor, either through words or through things shown to the eyes. For stupor <note>A state of awe or religious ecstasy</note> is accustomed to lay the soul open to God. Socrates would never have lived a life so devoted to love unless he had chosen it by the inspiration of a certain Daemon and held fast to that choice.

And these are the matters concerning the Theology of the Ancients which I have thought necessary to bring forward, insofar as they pertain to the business of hieroglyphs. Countless other things could certainly be said regarding Hermetic, Pythagorean, and Platonic dogmas. However, since mention of them is made everywhere throughout this entire Work, and I have conveniently reserved them for the exposition of the hieroglyphs in the third Volume, I have judged it superfluous to repeat them so many times.

---

## Conclusion of the Work.

Behold, kind Reader, having wandered far and wide through the hitherto unknown paths of the Egyptian Ocean, we have finally brought our Bark <note>A small sailing vessel; a common metaphor for a literary project</note> to the port from whence we departed. We have set out our wares; if we have brought anything worthy of praise among them, you should credit it to God, the Best and Greatest, the sole giver of all good things. If not, I would wish that you find merit in the attempt.

### END OF THE SECOND PART.
